Title: White paper internet the prudential consequences
text: 30 janvier 2001 Speech by Jean-Claude TRICHET Governor of the Banque de France Chairman of the Commission bancaire * White Paper Internet: the Prudential Consequences * INTRODUCTION THE OPPORTUNITIES AND RISKS ARISING FROM THE USE OF THE INTERNET FOR THE BANKING AND FINANCIAL INDUSTRY * 30 January 2001 * 1 On behalf of the Banque de France and the Commission bancaire, allow me to welcome you to this meeting held to present the White Paper on the prudential consequences of the Internet. It gives me great pleasure, today, to introduce a topic which as Governor of the Banque de France and Chairman of the Commission bancaire is of particular importance to me as it deals with the opportunities and risks arising from the banking and financial sector's use of the Internet. This morning's programme is rich. The various speakers shall no doubt help us attain a better understanding of the subject and grasp the issues at stake. The programme should lead us naturally to examine the nature and content of the answers that central banks and supervisory authorities can provide. In an unstable and volatile economic and financial environment, risk control must be a primary objective for all authorities, central banks and supervisors. In this respect, new technologies and notably online banking are considerably modifying the framework of the banking business and generating new risks. The Internet has developed very rapidly in the banking and financial spheres, the most notable example being online broking. The number of customers using electronic banking services has increased dramatically in recent years. Though in France the number of Internet users still stands at a mere 15% of the population, one must also take into account the widespread use of the Minitel and the Internet's strong prospects of expansion. At the same time, as most banks are now providing such services, the spectrum offered is continuously widening. Initially restricted to the checking of bank balances and online brokerage, services provided online have gradually come to encompass all banking and financial transactions. 2 * 1- Allow me to point out rapidly that the work carried out within the framework of the White Paper is part and parcel of global efforts to maintain the stability of the banking and financial system The issue of the emergence and impact of new technologies falls within the realm of overall considerations on financial stability. It is a subject to which central bank governors pay close attention. We must bear in mind, in this regard, that electronic banking transcends traditional borders, be they geographical or sectorial. It therefore calls for heightened co-operation between the various authorities. The work carried out by the electronic banking working groups within the Basle Committee, the Financial Stability Forum or the Contact Group of European banking supervisors illustrates the efforts made to enhance the functioning of the international financial system. While a raft of studies and analyses on the Internet have been carried out, one seldom comes across a report encompassing the whole of the prudential field. The Commission bancaire and the Banque de France, in close collaboration with the banking profession, carried out an extensive analysis of the risks arising on the use of the Internet and reviewed best practices in this field. However, as I shall endeavour to show, the White Paper goes beyond a simple diagnosis. 3 What are the exact objectives of the White Paper? It has a threefold aim: y First, to recapitulate and analyse the risks the Internet creates for credit institutions and to review laws and regulations in force with regard to this new medium. y Second, the White Paper is a compendium of best practices for the use of the Marketplace. It takes three aspects into special consideration: - conditions governing access to the profession, - security, - and lastly, internal control and the fight against money laundering. y On this basis, the White Paper draws up a number of recommendations for managers of credit institutions and investment firms. It moreover proposes several prudential rules relating to information systems and transaction security. More generally, these proposals come within an international perspective, in step with ongoing work within the Basle Committee. * 2- The Internet has profoundly changed banks' relations with their customers and created new strategic and commercial opportunities. One obvious advantage of the Internet is that it enables the substantial cutting of costs, be they infrastructure or transaction costs, given that data entry is shifted to the customer. 4 Similarly, banking services provided on the Internet can be better adapted to customer profile and expectations. This makes it possible to set prices more accurately and examine the related costs and incomes in closer detail. E-banking therefore helps to reach new customer groups, especially in the broking business. With the amortisation of initial investments, the Internet should eventually help to boost productivity and enable an increase in fees in relation to the provision of ampler online services. The Internet contributes to structuring the banking sector in several respects. The quest for economies of scale leads to partnerships not only between banks but also with non-banking participants. The Internet should therefore speed up the restructuring of the industry and the rationalisation of services. The issues at stake with regard to the organisation of the banking sector and the banking business as a whole are quite clear. Uncertainty also prevails regarding the profitability of operations as demonstrated by the disappointing performances recorded by a number of electronic banks in various countries. In any case, competition is now keener. With the Internet, notwithstanding substantial marketing outlays, which tend to increase the cost of acquiring new customers, subsequent costs are lower because a branch network is no longer necessary. Furthermore, the Internet allows the direct and immediate comparison of the various services available, which could lead to greater customer volatility. The banking community has nevertheless displayed a real ability to react and adjust to a new environment. Of course, the answers vary from country to country. Transformations are already underway in Anglo-Saxon and 5 Scandinavian banking systems. Nevertheless, electronic banks do not always enjoy the expected success and are often seeking to create networks. The organisation and structure of the French market are characterised by certain unique features. Though exclusively online banks have indeed increased their relative share, traditional institutions continue to hold most of the market share and appear to favour a multi-channelapproach centred on the customer. The Internet is, in this context, one of many means of access and distribution, in addition to the branch network. It is seen more as a vector for improving the service rendered. In this domain, traditional banks may profit from their current structures. * 3- But the Internet exposes the banking community to new risks, which require supervisors to be more vigilant and to adapt their monitoring tools I shall not, in this paper, take a detailed look at all the risks but rather simply review their main features. I shall not go back over financial risk, which was touched upon earlier. Firstly, the risk linked to net banking and finance can be strategic. The scope and pace of investments aimed at guaranteeing a successful adaptation to the new deal are uncertain in a context of technological transformation and rapidly changing customer behaviour. Bank managers should therefore be fully aware of the impact which the chosen strategies may have on their bank's organisation and performance. This requires defining a comprehensive policy for controlling the development of this new medium.  Secondly, the Internet exposes the banking community to operational risks whose impact could be significantly stronger than previously. It is important to both identify and analyse these risks. They relate 6 primarily to the organisation and implementation of internal control procedures, operational security and the supervision of money laundering. The use of the Internet can generate the risk of managers failing to sufficiently master new and increasingly complex situations. Frequently outsourcing certain functions can weaken supervision and lead to a relative loss of control over operations. Supervisors must be particularly attentive to this aspect by making sure that the bank is capable of choosing its partners and setting up the adequate procedures for controlling them and identifying responsibilities. The opening up of exchange channels and data processing activities has made the task of ensuring the security of information systems which is a key element even more delicate. In this respect, the White Paper formulates a number of proposals. I would like to mention two of them in passing: the drafting of a protection profile by the French Banking Organisation and Standardisation Committee and the definition of an Internet security policy, a guide to which was proposed by the Forum de competences (professional body grouping French credit institutions). Another important issue in the field of new technologies is legal security. The risks are manifold and stem, inter alia, from the problems of ascertaining the legal quality and capacity of customers and online service providers or of authenticating operations. The risk arising from cross-border activities should be studied in-depth in this regard. The conditions of access to the profession for new entrants to the market are among the most sensitive issues. Lastly, malfunctions which could occur in online operations may undermine customers' confidence in their bank. This reputational risk could be very damaging and spread to the entire banking community. Consequently, 7 it is of the utmost importance to have reliable and secure procedures and systems as soon as online services are accessible. Supervisors' answers cannot be based on an exclusively individual risk analysis, but also on a macro-prudential approach in order to take account of systemic risk. * To conclude, I would like to emphasise that nothing is ever final in the field of prudential supervision. The risks evolve in step with technological innovations and thus call for constant adjustment. The White Paper demonstrates if there was a need to do so the banking and financial industry's ability to comprehend and deal with these new issues. This, you will agree, is very encouraging. I thank you for your attention and wish you an excellent meeting. 8

Title: General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies
text: SPEECH BY JEAN-CLAUDE TRICHET GOVERNOR OF THE BANQUE DE FRANCE PRESIDENT OF THE BANKING COMMISSION ----- GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE FRENCH ASSOCIATION OF FINANCIAL COMPANIES 24 June 2003 ----- Mr President Thank you for giving me the floor again in this Chamber. The meeting of the General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies is always an excellent opportunity for me to exchange with the profession some reflections on the major themes of banking news and on the evolutions of our financial and regulatory environment. As you know, I remain very attentive to the place and role that the institutions you represent occupy within our banking landscape. Your Houses, which, it is true, have undergone significant changes both in their number and in their shareholding, as you noted, Mr President, retain an important place within the French banking system, in particular because of the specific skills they have been able to develop over time. 95 Allow me, Mr President, first of all to shed some brief light on the recent developments in the activity and results of the banking sector in 2002 The French banking system is exposed to the deterioration of its banking sector. economic and financial environment. However, overall, the results of French credit institutions remain satisfactory, thanks to a relatively buoyant domestic activity, particularly in retail banking. On the other hand, it is true that institutions that are particularly internationalised and exposed to investment banking activities have had to suffer from the decline in equity markets and the lower credit quality of certain counterparties. All in all, however, French banks continue to occupy a decent place in Europe in terms of profitability. I will have the opportunity to analyse more fully the activity and results of the entire French banking system when the Banking Commission presents its annual report for 2002 on 2 July. Concerning more specifically, the activity of specialized institutions, the year 2002 is satisfactory since, in this period of weak economic growth, their outstanding credit was up overall by 2.7% as indicated by the figures established by your association. The financing of equipment for both companies and individuals1 still constitutes the majority of outstanding credit. Private customers are the most dynamic in both the consumer credit segment (4.1%) and the mortgage segment (2.5%). These good performances are reflected in the 2002 results since, on the basis of a sample of 444 financial companies, the Banking Commission found that net banking income increased by 6%. I note with satisfaction that structural costs remain relatively contained (3.7%). The provisioning effort has certainly increased significantly, but 1 In the ASF's statistics, the concept of equipment for individuals includes earmarked financing (e.g. automobile), revolving credits, personal loans and leasing. This notion largely corresponds to that of consumer credit. 2 this is, in part, due to a relatively low 2001 base. In total, the net income of the sampled financial corporations increased by 6.5%. Beyond economic developments, I would like to stress once again the need for the banking system as a whole to adopt fair pricing of the supply of financing and efficient management of credit risk. Thus, your Houses have been able to develop risk selection and pricing techniques that are based on essential principles from a prudential point of view and that are also very well in line with the reform of the international solvency ratio. 95 In this regard, the reform of the international solvency ratio makes it possible to approach risks in a more discriminatory way while avoiding distortions of competition. As credit institutions operate in a largely open and internationalized environment, the authorities had to adapt the regulatory and prudential framework to support this movement. The new solvency ratio will allow for better microprudential stability with a better risk-proportionate ratio (Pillar 1), better consideration of risk profiles (Pillar 2) and greater market discipline (Pillar 3). At the same time, it will contribute to better overall stability through a more efficient allocation of funding through a better managed "risk-reward" couple. The greater sensitivity to risks of the new system does not imply pro-cyclicality but avoids brutal "stop and go" phenomena when the risk is perceived too late. Similarly, banking strategies, defined in the long term, must be compatible with this logic of capital allocation and adequate pricing of credit risk. However, the sensitivity of strategies to the cost factor in regulatory capital should not be exaggerated, as many other elements are involved in determining them. 3 The reform process is now nearing completion and the new rules are expected to enter into force in 2006. In parallel with the Basel reforms, work is continuing in Brussels to draw up a draft Directive that will impose compliance with these rules on the entire banking sector. The 3rd Basel Consultative Document and the results of the Impact Assessment were published at the beginning of May. The main conclusions are that if the overall capital requirements remain unchanged, institutions that opt for internal rating systems will benefit from a slight comparative advantage resulting from a better perception of risk. 95 The redesign of accounting standards is also a key topic importance for credit institutions. This reform aims at the harmonisation of European accounting standards is provided by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), an international accounting body of private status. The European Accounting Regulation of 19 July 2002 will oblige, from 1 January 2005, listed companies to prepare their consolidated accounts in accordance with international standards (IAS) endorsed by the European Commission. While these developments primarily concern large listed groups and their subsidiaries, French accounting rules have also tended, since 1999, to converge towards this international system. This development will require a profound adaptation of information systems. This new framework should allow for greater comparability of accounting statements. However, some of these new standards deviate from traditional banking management rules and could result in greater volatility in earnings and equity. That is why, in public discussions organised by the IASB in early March 2003, we stressed the need to adapt certain provisions, for example with regard to hedging techniques. Discussions are currently taking place between the European Banking Federation and the IASB. We follow them closely. 4 95 With regard to the process of European harmonisation and, more specifically, the draft directive on consumer credit, I would like to point out that the internal market for retail financial services remains insufficiently developed, despite the advent of the euro and the development of new distribution channels such as the Internet. Thus, only consumer confidence will allow the development of such activities and this confidence requires in particular a high degree of harmonization. For the time being, this proposal for a directive is still being discussed in Brussels. 95 I would now like to conclude on more domestic considerations. The Banque de France has been entrusted by the State with the task of ensuring the processing of over-indebtedness files, which represents a significant burden on its services. In France, over-indebtedness affects nearly half a million families. As part of the City Bill, the question of the establishment of a civil bankruptcy regime is addressed. This regime is based on the cancellation of the debts of over-indebted households after the sale of their seizable assets. Such measures would apply to persons who are manifestly insolvent and in good faith. In this regard, I can assure you that the Bank of France will continue to fully carry out its missions and will therefore ensure that over-indebted persons who present a real situation of financial distress are referred to this regime compared to those who would try to evade their obligations abusively. * 5 Thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you again. I would also like to pay tribute, Mr President, to the quality of the work you have done throughout your term at the head of the ASF and the excellent relations it has maintained, under your presidency, with the services of the Banque de France and the Banking Commission. 6

Title: Annual report of the French banking commission for 2002
text: PRESENTATION OF THE 2002 ANNUAL REPORT OF THE FRENCH BANKING COMMISSION (COMMISSION BANCAIRE) Jean-Claude Trichet, Governor, Banque de France, Chairman, Commission Bancaire 1. 2002 SHOWED THAT FRENCH CREDIT INSTITUTIONS WERE CAPABLE OF WITHSTANDING A LESS FAVOURABLE ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL ENVIRONMENT Measured on a parent-company basis, the aggregate net income of French credit institutions in 2002 was similar to 2001's figure of nearly 18 billion euro. This result is all the more remarkable because it was achieved despite negative cyclical developments. Once again, domestic retail banking was the mainstay of profitability. 1.1. Slower economic growth and high equity market volatility formed the backdrop for 2002 Although the world economy picked up slightly in 2002, expanding by 3.0 per cent compared with 2.3 per cent in 2001, it was much more sluggish than in 2000, when growth came in at 4.7 per cent. Furthermore, in the euro area, GDP growth continued to slow, decelerating from 3.4 per cent in 2000 to 1.4 per cent in 2001 and 0.8 per cent in 2002. As in 2001, France's economy grew slightly faster than average, with 1.2 per cent. Sector-related problems fostered a climate of uncertainty that affected growth. They resulted chiefly from the bursting of the Internet bubble, developments in telecommunications, transport and energy, and entrenched geopolitical tensions in Latin America and the Middle East. This naturally impacted the financial health of the corporate sector, and business failure rates rose to levels comparable to those of the early 1990s. These economic trends, combined with the discovery of egregious shortcomings in corporate governance, fuelled misgivings about stockmarkets. And amid a global bear market, equity volatility soared. Consequently, as in 2001, capital market business in the broad sense of the term  securities, mergers and acquisitions, and the fees and commissions charged for these activities  were adversely affected. 1.2. Despite an unfavourable climate in 2002, French credit institutions reported net income on a par with 2001. French credit institutions reported net income of 17.7 billion euro in 2002, the same as in 2001. This works out to a return on equity of 9.4 per cent for the industry as a whole. As in previous years, these results were largely attributable to retail banking business in France. Consumer credit and home loans continued to grow, along with specialised financial services. In addition, falling interest rates had a positive effect on interbank business  which in France has always been significant  and drove down the net expense on these transactions. By contrast, capital market activities and asset management were hit by financial market turbulence, giving rise to substantial provisions in some cases. Furthermore, for the second year running, fees and commissions contracted as a percentage of net banking income, falling to 26 per cent compared with nearly 30 per cent in 2000. 2 1.3. Diversification has helped French credit institutions to offset negative cyclical trends As in previous years, conventional retail banking activities cushioned the negative impact of trends in investment banking and asset management in 2002. On the international front, too, retail banking was a major avenue of development for leading French banks. It must be stressed, however, that the consolidated accounts of France's largest banks were slightly less positive in 2002, even though the overall situation was satisfactory. In this regard, the dollar-euro exchange rate had an impact on the foreign activities of these banks, denominated in euros, which were also exposed to the negative earnings momentum of subsidiaries specialising in equity-related businesses. 2. FRENCH BANKS MUST BUTTRESS THE ELEMENTS THAT HAVE ALLOWED THEM TO WITHSTAND CYCLICAL CONTINGENCIES FOR THE PAST FEW YEARS In addition to diversifying their business lines  and I am pleased to note that securities analysts are now taking this factor into account when assessing different banking industries  French banks have improved their capacity to withstand cyclical contingencies. That ability must naturally be maintained and strengthened. 2.1. French banks used the healthy profits of the late 1990s to strengthen their capital base French credit institutions have entered the cyclical downswing on a sounder financial footing. To illustrate that point, a review of the French banking system since the late 1960s is included in the appendixes to this Annual Report. Book capital is now equivalent to 5.2 per cent of total assets, compared 3 with 4.2 per cent in the mid-1990s. The Commission Bancaire is at pains to ensure that all French banks  small and large  build up their capital gradually but steadily until it well exceeds the regulatory minimum. Furthermore, provision cover for doubtful loans now stands at 60.4 per cent. The industry must pursue this prudential policy. In particular, as we have been urging for several years, it must capitalise on the progress made in future risk analysis, based on statistical databases and stress testing, to adopt a more forwardlooking provisioning policy. This has already been accomplished in several areas of sectoral or geographical risk. That being said, we firmly believe that international accounting standards should move in this direction, fostering the widespread use of forward-looking provisions and thereby contributing immensely to financial stability. In a context of economic crisis, the constant strengthening of French credit institutions' financial structure gives them an appreciable safety margin, which could also allow them to play a part in the consolidation of Europes financial industry. 2.2. Priority has rightly been placed on controlling risks and ordinary profitability The other fundamental elements that contribute to the resilience of French banks' earnings are risk management and control over operating conditions. As you know, the Commission Bancaire places a premium on ensuring that French banks, and credit institutions in general, generate satisfactory profits at operating level. Gross operating income is the first fall-back  before regulatory capital  for satisfying provisioning requirements, which naturally become more acute when economic conditions turn down. Accordingly, final operating margins must be sufficiently wide. This is also essential so that banks can tap the markets, at optimal cost and with sufficient independence, for the 4 financing they need to develop and to secure their future. To that end, the Commission Bancaire makes sure that cost-to-income ratios, which measure operating expenses as a percentage of overall operating profit, are not excessive. Spontaneous action by banks themselves has naturally been crucial in this respect. This trend must continue. The same applies to efforts to improve the selection, monitoring and control of risk. Thanks partly to those efforts, it has been possible to confine loss-risk and provisioning requirements to securities portfolios and capital market business in general, as well as to some large corporate loans, particularly in the USA. Further improvements in internal controls, at the instigation of the Commission Bancaire, are naturally of major importance. When the economic and financial environment is dominated by uncertainty, the only cogent strategy is to reduce the factors that produce risk. Apparently there is room for further improvement in areas such as the spreading of credit risk. Furthermore, stricter internal controls could be applied to capital market intermediation and to the management of specific factors such as operating risk. 3. WITH TIGHTER CONTROL OVER PROCESSES, INFORMATION SYSTEMS, OPERATIONS AND RISK, FRENCH CREDIT INSTITUTIONS SHOULD BE ABLE TO COPE WITH FUTURE DEVELOPMENTS Aside from the cyclical aspects I have just mentioned, the short-term outlook is characterised by both the increasing interplay between the financial and non-financial spheres, owing to the development of new risk-transfer instruments, and by closer harmonisation of the rules applicable to different economic agents. 5 3.1. Careful attention must be paid to the characteristics and consequences of risk transfer transactions Credit derivatives, and products and techniques like securitisation that produce similar results, are a means of reducing the loan-loss exposure of credit institutions, which are net risk-sellers. These instruments can be useful for mitigating risk exposure, provided naturally that banks act as protection buyers. However, the characteristics and consequences of the development of these products must be closely scrutinised, both by credit institutions operating in these markets and by the authorities responsible for maintaining financial stability. Institutions must pay particular attention to the real impact of risk transfer. They must also keep close watch on the resulting counterparty risk that attaches to the protection seller. The question of risk transfer is also under scrutiny because of the treatment of the special purpose vehicles to which assets are sold. On this point, the accounting rules currently under review at the international level seem to focus quite rightly on the reality of risk transfer. Credit institutions must therefore analyse this criterion in greater detail. The issue is also of interest to the authorities responsible for financial stability. As standardised risk-transfer instruments develop, they are likely to come into wider use. So far, market participants have not properly identified or analysed the likely knock-on effects, whether direct or indirect. For this reason, there is a vital need for improvements in the prudential reporting and market transparency of these transactions; there is also a need for greater harmonisation of the rules and regulations applicable to institutions in different countries and to different types of company. The aim should be to record the risk where it is actually borne, both economically and financially. In addition, the authorities responsible for different financial sectors must coordinate their efforts to jointly identify where risks lie and to measure their extent. The Banque de France and the 6 Commission Bancaire are working to that end with their counterparts in the insurance industry and the securities markets. 3.2. The future solvency ratio will better reflect the economic realities of banking risk The finishing touches are being put to the solvency ratio, due to come into force in 2006. The new ratio will cover a broad spectrum of activities and risks, based on an approach tailored to the degree of sophistication of financial market participants, both in the G10 and beyond. From a prudential standpoint, the ratio will capitalise on the progress already made in improving risk supervision and control, while making it easier to compare methods at the international level. Accordingly, it is clearly important that credit institutions should actively pursue the work they have done so far. In this respect, I think it is safe to say that French banks operating in the international arena are making every effort to ready themselves for 2006. 3.3. New accounting standards should foster international harmonisation and promote greater financial transparency The introduction of new accounting standards is a major undertaking for companies in general and for credit institutions in particular. The aim of this project is highly ambitious, namely to arrive at worldwide standards that can improve financial security and accounting transparency. This is necessary to restore confidence in financial markets. At the internal level, credit institutions must quickly adapt their information systems to these new requirements. However, there are in-depth discussions at present about the draft standards applicable to financial instruments. We have taken part in these discussions and advocated caution, in particular, in view of the strong temptation to give precedence to the mark-to-market and mark-to-model approaches, which are more sensitive to calculation parameters than to the actual situation of the 7 reporting entity, with the result that earnings and equity likely to become abnormally volatile. I hope that the outcome of these discussions will lead to accounting procedures that take into consideration the realities of credit institutions operations and business practices. As you are aware, the quality of the accounting rules applicable by banks is of fundamental importance for supervisors. Moreover, the appendixes to this Annual Report include a study of the prudential consequences of the international accounting standards that will apply in Europe from 2005 onwards. * In sum, French credit institutions in 2002 amply displayed their ability to withstand cyclical contingencies. Improvements can still be made in terms of risk spreading and surveillance. This is one of the factors to which the Commission Bancaire will play close attention as banks prepare and phase in information systems ahead of the introduction of Basel 2 and new accounting standards. In addition to the two studies I have already mentioned, the appendices of the Annual Report include a review of risk management in financial conglomerates. Let me also mention that a summary of the Commission Bancaires judicial decisions is being published at the same time as the Annual Report. This first edition will be updated yearly. 8

Title: Declaration after appointment to the ECB
text: Brussels, 16 October 2003 Statement made by Mr Jean-Claude Trichet to the Council meeting at the level of Heads of State and Government: "Mr President, I am very honoured by the confidence that the European Council has just shown in me. The responsibility that the Council entrusts to me is heavy. I will do everything I can to prove myself worthy of your trust and to carry out these very important functions in accordance with the Treaty. Together with my colleagues on the Executive Board of the European Central Bank, with the Governing Council, with the Eurosystem as a whole, I will endeavour to keep intact the remarkable legacy bequeathed by my predecessor Wim Duisenberg: confidence in the euro, our currency, which he was able to preserve and strengthen, and the smooth functioning of Europe's entire monetary team - the ECB, the Eurosystem and the European System of Central Banks - which the successful introduction of banknotes and coins has demonstrated in the eyes of all. "

Title: Accession to the euro
text: Seminar of 5 March 2004: Introductory statement by Mr. Noyer Distinguished Presidents and Governors, Ladies and gentlemen It is a great honour for me to welcome you here in Paris for the latest seminar on the accession process, co-organised by the European Central Bank and the Bank of France. This seminar follows those in Helsinki, Vienna, Berlin, and Genval. Thank you all very much for accepting the invitation to participate. As Jean-Claude Trichet said yesterday, the European System of Central Banks, the Eurosystem and the central banks of the acceding countries have now been preparing for enlargement for a long time: this seminar is one of the many manifestations of the close collaboration that already exists within the wider community of central banks. At this final stage of preparation for entry into the European Union, it seemed essential to us to discuss, during the sessions of this seminar, the three crucial themes of exchange rate policy in the framework of the European Exchange Mechanism (ERM2), budgetary discipline in the framework of the Stability and Growth Pact, and issues related to financial and accounting standards and corporate governance. * 1. With regard to MCE2, it would seem to me useful if this seminar made it possible to deepen the exchange of experience between us. Last December, the Governing Council published its position, which takes into account, on the one hand, the experiences of the countries that have already participated in the EMS, and on the other hand, the exchanges of views that the Eurosystem and the acceding countries have already had in the context of previous seminars, or at meetings of the General Council, the International Relations Committee and the Market Operations Committee, especially. I will briefly recall some essential elements of this position paper of 18 December. From 1St May next, the new Member States will have to treat their exchange rate policy as a matter of common interest: they will indeed be members of the same single market, economic and financial. In view of the significant disparity between the acceding countries in terms of economic structures, monetary policies and exchange rate regimes, as well as the degree of nominal and real convergence already achieved, it is not possible to define or recommend a single scheme for participation in the ERM2, and subsequently for the adoption of the euro. But ERM2 will play a dual role, in the same way, for the acceding countries: on the one hand, it will make it possible to manage the exchange rates of the currencies of the Member States and will promote the process of convergence; on the other hand, participation without serious tension for at least two years in the ERM2 is itself part of the convergence criteria for the adoption of the euro. Accession to the MCE2 can in principle take place at any time upon entry into the European Union. However, it appears necessary that a significant adjustment of economic policies takes place prior to participation in the mechanism, and in particular that credible fiscal consolidation has been implemented. This will facilitate the determination for each country of the conditions for its participation in ermE2, in particular the determination, through a multilateral procedure, of the central rate. The choices concerning the date of accession and the duration of participation in the ERM2 will have to be decided in the light of the prospects for achieving sustainable economic convergence. The main objective is to promote the macroeconomic stability of the acceding countries, to make the best contribution to sustainable growth and to prepare economic agents for the next step: the irrevocable fixing of exchange rates with the main economic and financial partners. 2. The second session of our seminar will be devoted to budgetary discipline, within the framework of the Stability and Growth Pact. The key function of the Pact is to ensure the credibility of the institutional framework and confidence in the public finances of the euro area. It is the instrument for ensuring overall policy mix coherence in the euro area and strengthening the conditions for price stability. It must therefore be respected in every respect by all the countries of the euro area. As regards the situation of the current area countries, the position of the Eurosystem is already well known. We have publicly expressed our concerns about the conclusions of the ECOFIN Council of 25 November 2003. We share these concerns with the European Commission and respect its decision to seek legal clarification. We consider that, in any event, it is imperative that the Governments concerned live up to their responsibilities and commitments. With regard to the acceding countries, the Pact also provides an essential guiding framework for sound fiscal policies, consistent with the prospect of participation in the ERM2 and the ultimate objective of entry into the euro area. The Pact will apply upon accession since the "convergence programmes" will reflect the commitment of the new Member States to avoid excessive public deficits. By design, this framework will, of course, promote nominal convergence. But by encouraging public sector reform, it will also be a powerful instrument of real convergence. The acceding countries are currently facing significant challenges in terms of public finances: their public deficits have recently tended to widen as a result of both cyclical and structural factors, for example due to expenditure related to reforms of social security systems, or industrial and banking restructuring. Moreover, they are already, and will be even more confronted, like all the countries of the European Union, with the phenomenon of the ageing of their population. In this context, I have no doubt that the acceding countries will actively contribute to the joint reflection on ways of strengthening the effective application of the common sense rules contained in the Pact. 3- The third and final session of the seminar will be devoted to issues relating to financial standards, accounting standards and corporate governance, topics closely related to the issue of financial stability. Maintaining financial stability is a permanent challenge for all the countries of the European Union and this issue must of course also be treated as a subject of common interest: the free movement of capital and the single financial passport contribute, in fact, to the emergence of a vast single financial market and the latter has led us to adapt our methods of financial regulation and banking supervision, according to the orientations recommended by Alexandre Lamfalussy. The adoption of the 'acquis communautaire' by the acceding countries in terms of financial standards, accounting standards and corporate governance is an important step in the process of convergence of financial structures, and we welcome the fact that it has so far been almost achieved or on track to be achieved. Convergence in this area has already reached a high level and on this point I will only stress, at this stage, the need for effective and independent financial supervisory authorities. But the challenge of financial stability also implies going beyond the adoption of the "acquis communautaire": this acquis must be effectively implemented and its evolution must constantly adapt, which must itself correspond to the evolution of financial systems. I would simply like to emphasise right now, on this point, the responsibility that we all have to strengthen the confidence of economic actors in the financial system of the enlarged Europe.
