Title: The euro five years after achievements and new challenges
text: THREE / DEER 04216 Speech by Mr Christian Noyer Governor of the Banque de France THE EURO FIVE YEARS LATER: ACHIEVEMENTS AND NEW CHALLENGES 25 MAY 2004 LAUSANNE 1 Ladies and gentlemen, it is a great pleasure for me to be here to talk to you about the single European currency, which is one of the european Union's most remarkable achievements. European countries have long been divided, and the European continent has just reunited with the entry of ten Central and Eastern European countries into the European Union. A few days ago, we celebrated the 54th anniversary of Robert Schumann's famous declaration, which contains these famous phrases: "Europe will not be made in a day [...] it will be based on concrete achievements [...] creating de facto solidarities between peoples. In fact, there is hardly a fact that creates more solidarity than money, and that is why it is a fundamental stone of the European edifice, even if it still concerns only 12 out of 25 countries. I would like to present to you, first of all, the achievements of the single monetary policy, and in particular to analyse the success of the euro, achieved thanks to the solid foundations on which it is based (Part 1). I would then like to touch briefly on economic integration: the euro has indeed been a powerful factor in economic and financial integration, accentuated today by its growing international role (Part 2). Secondly, I would like to stress that EMU, in order to be a full success, will have to face challenges such as budgetary cohesion and structural reforms (Part 3). PART 1: THE SUCCESS OF THE EURO RESTS ON SOLID FOUNDATIONS The euro is based first of all on two solid foundations: the single monetary policy (A), on the one hand, and the proper functioning of macroeconomic cooperation in EMU (B), on the other. Has. The achievements of the single monetary policy After five years, the single monetary policy conducted by the Eurosystem, i.e. the whole of the European Central Bank and the 12 central banks of the euro area member countries, has been crowned with many successes. The changeover to the euro, in scriptural and then fiduciary form, is certainly the most emblematic event. The single currency has long met with the scepticism of many observers who considered it unrealistic, in the first place, to launch a new currency, the name of which itself was not fixed until the Madrid European Council of December 1995, and secondly 2 It is necessary to envisage a single monetary policy for a set of countries which, despite the speed of their convergence, nevertheless had significant disparities. The prospect of the creation of new institutions, in particular the European Central Bank, has also given rise to many debates. The issues focused mainly on the institutional and operational framework (Al) and on the strategies (A2) of a single monetary policy. Today we can evaluate its achievements (A3). A.1. A modern institutional and operational framework A wealth of literature has been devoted over the past decade to issues relating to the independence of central banks, the concepts of transparency and monetary strategy, and the communication of monetary policy decisions. Having benefited from this analytical expertise and the experience of the national central banks of the member countries, the Eurosystem is based first of all on a modern institutional framework, based on the principles of independence, transparency and accountability and, finally, on operational decentralisation. A.1.1. The independence of the Eurosystem promotes price stability The Eurosystem's priority task, according to the Maastricht Treaty, is to ensure and maintain price stability. As many empirical studies have shown, a nation's anti-inflationary performance seems to be highly correlated with the degree of independence of its central bank. The independence of the European Central Bank and the 12 central banks of the euro area member countries is therefore enshrined in the Treaty. Functionally, this means that, in the exercise of their tasks, neither the European Central Bank nor the national central banks of the Eurosystem seek or take instructions from the Community institutions, national governments or any other body. This is full independence in the institutional, operational and financial sense. A.1.2. Transparency and accountability are also essential to gain credibility Naturally, the independence of these institutions is matched by transparency of their decisions and accountability to the public and its representatives. In the case of new institutions, such as the ECB, transparency is even more essential to establish their credibility and to establish the confidence of economic agents in a currency. For 3 to establish this credibility, to gain this trust of the agents, it is absolutely imperative to be understood and for this it is necessary to be transparent. In this area too, the imperatives of accountability and transparency are enshrined in the Treaty in very general terms, but the Eurosyte8me has gone beyond its institutional obligations in several areas. First, the Governing Council clarified its definition of price stability (lower, but close to, increase of 2% in the medium term). Secondly, the ECB has gone beyond the accountability requirements established by the Treaty by establishing regular hearings of the President before the European Parliament and regular informal meetings with the Eurogroup of Finance Ministers. Another sign of transparency is the regular publication of reports on economic developments and central bank analyses, of which the ECB's Monthly Bulletin is the best-known vehicle. Finally, most importantly, at the end of each of the meetings devoted to monetary policy decisions, the President and Vice-President of the ECB hold a press conference followed by an open exchange with journalists, the details of which are published on the ECB's website. It is perhaps important to recall that the ECB was the first of the central banks to undergo this type of exercise, which provides a unique opportunity to explain and comment on monetary policy decisions, immediately and in detail. On the other hand, the Governing Council of the ECB chose not to publish the minutes of its meetings. Indeed, the publication of the minutes has certain disadvantages. First, when they are very detailed, participants risk "speaking for the minutes", whereas, when they are not detailed, they are of little more interest than a simple communique9. Secondly, they can complicate the evolution of the positions taken by its members in the light of the arguments developed. Finally, most importantly, in the case of the euro area, the analysis of votes could be read and interpreted in the light of national concerns or interests, which would be misleading and could threaten both the independence of governing council members and the credibility of our decision-making processes. A.1.3. The Eurosystem is based on operational decentralisation The third element, operational decentralisation, is a key feature of the Eurosystem. The division of roles between the ECB and the national central banks is one of the elements of its cohesion and its main driving force. According to this principle, monetary policy decisions are taken centrally, by the Governing Council of the ECB, but implemented by the national central banks. 4 Unlike the United States, the use of technologies and means of communication modern has made it possible to carry out market operations simultaneously in all national central banks, not to concentrate them in a given geographical point. The the same system applies to other monetary areas (cash management, payment, etc.). A.1.4. The Eurosystem benefits from an efficient operating framework In addition to this modern institutional framework, the Eurosystem also benefits from a framework particularly efficient operational. The success of the changeover to the euro is one of them. technical, a particularly edifying illustration. This operational framework is based on two main orientations: - a coherent range of monetary policy instruments, developed in accordance with the principles of free competition, equal treatment, simplicity and transparency: these instruments enable the adjustment of bank liquidity and the efficient management of interest rates; - procedures ensuring a high level of security for all transactions interbank and high-value payments within the euro area and with other Economic Union, in particular the Target system, whose role has been decisive in the euro money market integration process. A.2. The strategic framework The successes of the single monetary policy are also based on its policy framework, which can be characterised by two main elements: a quantitative definition of price stability and a medium-term stance of monetary policy. A.2.1. A quantitative definition of price stability The definition adopted by the Governing Council of the ECB in October 1998 was confirmed and clarified in May 2003, following an in-depth review of its strategic framework by the Eurosystem. At the end of this evaluation exercise, the Governing Council clarified that price stability was defined by annual HICP growth close to, but less than 2% in the medium term. This definition calls for several comments: - by specifying that inflation should be close to 2%, the Governing Council has everything first of all, it was necessary to confirm the symmetrical nature of its strategy by excluding deflation. This precision also allows the consideration of possible measurement biases on the price index, as well as inflation differentials within the euro area; - the quantitative definition of monetary stability brings the policy framework closer to 5 the Eurosystem of central banks based on inflation targeting, especially when considering a broad meaning of inflation, such as that presented under the term "flexible inflation target". The big difference lies in the role of forecasts from an econometric model, which play a leading role in "pure" inflation-targeting strategies, while they are only one element, albeit an important one, in the decision-making process of the Governing Council of the Eurosystem. A.2.2. A "medium-term" orientation What exactly are the implications of this medium-term approach to the ECB monetary policy? - The first is that the single monetary policy strategy does not have a fixed horizon, determined once and for all ex ante, but aims, as far as possible, to take account the "long and variable delays in monetary policy" dear to Milton Friedman. The plug in view of this uncertainty is particularly important in the case of the euro area, of which the "deep structural parameters" are partly ignored. More prosaically, this The medium-term stance of the single monetary policy recognises that it is impossible for a central bank, to accurately control the trajectory of prices in the very short term. - The second implication is that indicators relevant to monetary policy must reflect, almost exhaustively, the main factors causing inflation in the short and long term. From this point of view, the monetary policy strategy seeks, as far as possible, to mobilize "complete information". This is reflected in the notions of economic approach and monetary approach (which are also referred to as two-pillar approach) which are taken up in particular at the press conferences of the President of the ECB following monetary policy decisions. The economic approach reviews short-term, economic and financial indicators related to the main determinants of inflation in the short term; the monetary approach is based on the monetary explanation of long-term inflation. The medium-term orientation of the Single monetary policy makes it necessary to link these two approaches complementary to the inflationary phenomenon. In this respect, the monetary policy strategy of the BCE is more comprehensive than pure inflation-targeting or pure monetary targeting strategies. A.3. The achievements of the ECB's monetary policy What first assessment can be made after these first five years of implementation of the single monetary policy? 6 I would like to highlight three essential points. - First, the achievement of monetary policy objectives: While it has faced a series of unfavourable exogenous supply shocks (on oil prices, food, services prices), leading to a HICP evolution of more than 2% year-on-year from 2000 to 2002, and fluctuating around this level since, the single monetary policy has managed to stabilise and anchor, over the entire financial period, medium- and long-term inflation expectations around 1.8 to 1.9%. This represents a level close to, but below, 2% in line with its definition of price stability. And this, whether we consider inflation expectations from surveys (for example, Consensus Forecast, or the ECB's survey of professional forecasters) or those derived from market data, including inflation-linked government securities. Despite these price pressures, financing conditions, which reflect in particular the low level of short- and long-term interest rates in the euro area, remained particularly favourable. These good results illustrate the credibility of the single monetary policy. - Second, the understanding and predictability of monetary policy actions: Contrary to some misconceptions, most monetary policy decisions have been perfectly anticipated by the markets. This diagnosis comes from the studies conducted by the Eurosystem but also from the reports published by the "ECB Watchers", with whom, moreover, the ECB maintains regular links, in particular in the form of annual conferences. A comparison with the Fed does not show any real difference between the two institutions in terms of the ability of the markets to anticipate the monetary policy decisions of the two institutions. This is a sign of the transparency of the single monetary policy. The fact, in particular, that the ECB chose means of communication other than the publication of the minutes of the meetings of the Governing Council did not prevent it from achieving a high level of understanding and predictability. - Thirdly, the confidence and approval of European citizens: Indeed, the euro has easily imposed itself on economic agents and is now part of the daily lives of European consumers. And surveys confirm that the public has confidence in the euro, which they consider a sound currency, and in the Eurosystem as a central bank. However, two factors of concern remain. The first is the natural difficulty of moving towards an entirely new price benchmark - and it can take many years before all economic agents have fully integrated it. The second factor is the perception of excessive price increases by 7 consumers, linked to the changeover to the euro in cash. Indeed, public attention focused on a small number of goods and services that experienced abnormal price increases during this event, leading to a misperception of the real rate of inflation. Fortunately, this gap between perceived and actual inflation is likely to disappear in the near future. B. Multilateral surveillance procedures within EMU EMU, which combines a single monetary policy with twelve governments responsible for budgetary and structural policies, requires an institutional framework to ensure coherence. For this framework to be fully operational, it must be simple, easy to implement and capable of ensuring sound and sustainable fiscal policies. Indeed, multilateral surveillance processes have been designed from the outset in order to achieve a satisfactory level of cohesion in the policies followed by all Member States. B.1. A framework of multilateral surveillance procedures The implementation of surveillance is entrusted to the Eurogroup (euro area countries) and the Ecofin Council (all EU countries), together with the European Commission. Mutual surveillance combines multilateral surveillance and dialogue procedures, compliance with common rules and provisions, and member States' commitment to good practices and common objectives. The construction of Europe is a project in constant evolution and each meeting of the European Council has given rise, in the recent past, to processes that have taken the name of the places where summits were held. This applies to processes in areas such as labour markets (Luxembourg process), economic reform of goods and capital markets (Cardiff process) and macroeconomic dialogue to promote responsible wage developments (Cologne process). The Stability and Growth Pact (SGP) is another coordination and surveillance process, and the most widely debated of all: it consists of examining national budgetary policies at Community level from a medium-term perspective. At the centre of the coordination process are the Broad Economic Policy Guidelines (BEPGs), which contain a medium-term assessment of the state of convergence of national economic policies. EPGs play a crucial role as all the coordination processes mentioned above must be consistent with their recommendations. Updates to the Stability and Growth Pact and BEPGs are presented on a multiannual basis and their implementation is reviewed 8 every year. B.2. The acceding countries will respect the same rules Let me emphasise that the ten new Member States are already accustomed to mutual review processes. Since their accession on 1 May 2004, the budgetary policy of the ten new Member States has been subject to the same review measures as that of the other Member States. Budget deficits are a key concern for the new EU countries. As the adoption of the euro is subject to compliance with the budget deficit criterion within the meaning of Maastricht, these countries are now forced to undertake substantial budgetary reforms, especially since their deficits stem from structural inadequacies. PART 2: THE EURO: A POWERFUL ENGINE FOR GREATER ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL INTEGRATION AND INTERNATIONAL RECOGNITION The strengthening of the operational and institutional framework goes hand in hand with the increasing convergence of the monetary area (A) and with the strengthening of the role of the euro at international level (B). Has. The pillars of an optimal monetary area Increasing convergence is the result of sound macroeconomic fundamentals (Al) and economic homogeneity (A2), reinforced by the integration of the financial sector (A3). The adoption of the same currency by eleven and then twelve European countries is an unprecedented fact. This adoption is justified by an increasing convergence of the economies in question during the nineties. While it seems abusive to regard the euro area as an optimal monetary area, as Robert Mundell understood it, several recent studies have shown that the process of convergence, economic homogeneity, the degree of synchronization of business cycles and the propensity of the economies of the zone to trade with each other have increased since the implementation of the single monetary policy. The latter, by also succeeding in anchoring inflation expectations in all Member States at a low level, has shown itself capable of imposing a high degree of nominal convergence. Finally, economic and monetary union has protected its members from the exchange rate crises and macroeconomic imbalances that characterized the European situation a little over a decade ago. 9 Ly. The euro area is characterised by solid economic fundamentals The euro area economies are characterised by a high degree of structural convergence, a low level of inflation currently close to 2%, and favourable monetary and financial conditions for economic activity. These favourable financing conditions are also explained by the resilience of the euro area's financial and banking systems to the various shocks that have affected the global economy: sound infrastructure, good performance of banks and financial institutions, progress in complying with international standards. Private savings are also abundant. In addition, the euro area is an attractive economy because of the quality of its workforce (almost 5% of GDP is, for example, spent on education) and its infrastructure. These various assets enabled it to attract nearly 80112 billion in direct investment in 2003 (compared to 8082 billion in the United States). A.2. Increasing economic homogeneity favours the transmission of monetary policy While monetary union does not necessarily imply that all Member States have the same rate of growth or inflation at all times, a number of recent empirical studies illustrate an increasing economic homogeneity within the euro area. In terms of activity first of all, several studies presented under the aegis of a joint working group between the CEPR (Centre for Economic Policy Research) and the Eurosystem show that the correlation between cyclical fluctuations in economic activity as a whole, but also in consumption and investment in most euro area countries, already strong before the implementation of the single monetary policy, has increased since 1999. According to some measures, a common 'European' component would play a more important role than the national components in cyclical fluctuations in activity in most of these economies. The degree of correlation between national and aggregate cycles at euro area level would thus vary in the range between 0.70 and 0.92. In terms of inflation, the degree of dispersion of inflation rates within the euro area would not be much higher than that observed in the United States, where there are recall forces such as the presence of a single federal budget balancing cyclical differences between regions, more unified markets for goods and services and labour, a single monetary policy since 1913 - much stronger than in the eurozone. Thus, in these first years of EMU's existence, the standard deviation of the annual price change in the twelve countries of the euro area is estimated to be close to 1.1 against 0.8 for the fourteen regions of the Member States. 10 United. Finally, recent updates of the Eurosystem's important research on the transmission mechanisms of the single monetary policy suggest an increasing homogeneity in the responses of member countries' economies to monetary policy impulses. A.3. Financial sector integration is almost complete The introduction of the euro has acted as a catalyst for financial integration. The latter is almost complete as far as the euro money market is concerned. In the first weeks of the implementation of the single monetary policy, price differences in national interbank markets faded rapidly to less than 5 basis points, which corresponds to the bid-ask spread usually found in this market. A similar integration movement has also occurred in European bond markets, where there has been a tightening of government bond yields, as well as in derivatives markets with the impressive development of Eurex and, to a lesser extent, in stock markets and the corporate debt market. The euro area and, more broadly, the European Union now have a coherent financial architecture. First of all, the implementation of the Financial Services Action Plan, defined at the Lisbon European Council in March 2000, is being completed. Secondly, the "Lamfalussy process" should promote the establishment of a new institutional architecture in the field of supervision and regulation of the financial sector - that is to say, securities markets but also banks and insurance - in particular by developing more flexible and uniform technical rules. B. The euro now plays the role of international currency and nominal anchor. The available data confirm the growing role of the euro at international level. At the regional level, it plays a leading anchor role, making it the valuable vector of a culture of stability. The growing role of the euro at international level is the result of the development of both its use at private level (B1) and its official role (B2). B.1. The evolution of the private use of the euro The euro has the key functions attributed to any international currency: it is already a leading investment and financing currency and an important intermediary for international trade. Although it is still limited, its role as a currency of 11 billing is expected to grow in the coming years. B.1.1. A key financial instrument at global level The use of the euro as an investment and financing currency on international capital markets has developed immediately. In 2003, it accounted for almost 60 per cent of net issuances of international debt securities, up from 33 per cent in 1998. Today, nearly 41% of outstanding debt securities is denominated in euros compared to 28% in 1998, a proportion comparable to that of the dollar, whose share has remained remarkably stable during this period. Another very remarkable development is the emergence of a market for "corporate" securities, i.e. securities issued by companies, the volume of which grew significantly during the first years of the euro. The best allocation of savings in Europe requires capital markets to be more efficient and integrated. However, this integration has not yet been fully completed, particularly as regards the repo, deposit and securities markets. Finally, the euro area is lagging behind in terms of the equity market. According to BIS data, while 32% of international bank claims were concentrated in the euro area in 2002, compared with slightly less than 15% in the United States, the euro area market capitalisation represented only 16.1% of the global market capitalisation compared to 48.5% for the United States. B.1.2. An important intermediary of trade As an intermediary of trade, the euro accounts for 25% of foreign exchange transactions, i.e. half as much as the dollar. However, the share of the euro is greater than the sum of the shares of the former European national currencies. This result was not obvious at the time of the introduction of the euro. 95 An increasing role as invoicing/settlement currency With regard to the use of the European currency in international trade, between 50% and 60% of trade between almost all euro area countries and the rest of the world was denominated in euro in 2002. This applies to both exports and imports. With regard to EU trade with third countries, 54% of Japanese exports to the European Union were invoiced or settled in euro in 2002 (44% in 2000) and 31% of Japanese imports from the European Union were denominated in euro (compared to 17% in 2000). 12 In countries where integration with the euro area is very high, such as the countries of Central and Eastern Europe, the use of the euro in trade is also very high, with 60% to 80% of exports/imports being invoiced or paid in euros. 95 A more limited role on commodity markets On the other hand, the use of the single currency is more limited on commodity markets, especially oil. The dollar still plays a preponderant role, which should continue, given the phenomena of inertia related to the effects of "network". This is not surprising, since the acquisition of international status is, in all respects, a long process. All in all, these developments underline the fact that the euro has been able to inspire confidence among private investors and promote greater liquidity in capital markets. B.2. The growing official role of the euro The growing demand for the euro as a reserve and reference currency has also strengthened its official role. B.2.1. A factor in the diversification of foreign exchange reserves The euro has become a stabilising factor in the international monetary system, particularly thanks to its function of diversifying international reserves. According to the latest available IMF data, the euro is the second reserve currency after the dollar. Its share was 18.7 per cent in 2002 compared to 12.6 per cent in 1999. This trend offers many countries a valuable buffer against large exchange rate fluctuations, as public investors can diversify their reserve assets. The growing share of the euro in international foreign exchange reserves is expected to increase further in the coming years. Asia's major central banks have expressed their intention to better balance the share of the euro and the dollar in their assets, a phenomenon that is all the more important given the region's relative weight in international foreign exchange reserves. When fully implemented, these decisions could therefore lead to a rebalancing of international foreign exchange reserves in favour of the euro: the dollar currently represents 64.5% against 18.7% for the euro. B.2.2. A factor of stability for many exchange rate regimes Far from being the mere addition of previous European currencies, the euro has inherited the 13 the most interesting features of the old national currencies. The positive effects have been noticeable. The euro put an end to currency crises and created a historically low interest rate environment. Even if these two elements are sometimes forgotten, it is interesting to note that Europe has not experienced tumult as a result, for example, of the uncertainties created by the recent geopolitical tensions at the global level, which would have caused, in the past, strong turbulence. These benefits are perhaps even more valuable for neighbouring countries, as 51 of them have already adopted the euro as the reference currency for their exchange rate regimes, either as a single anchor (in about 30 cases) or as part of a basket of currencies. The use of the euro in the exchange rate regimes of third countries mainly concerns regions which have established close links with the euro area or which have set up special institutional arrangements with the EU (acceding and candidate countries, Balkans, North Africa and CFA franc zone). In any case, these exchange rate regimes are the result of a unilateral decision, which does not involve any commitment on the part of the Eurosystem. However, close links with the euro can have the effect of "importing" credibility, provided that appropriate policies are pursued simultaneously. More fundamentally, the euro contributes to developing a culture of stability in a large number of countries, as it also helps to influence the expectations of economic agents. Admittedly, it is not possible, in the space of a few years, to fully assess the achievements made possible by the euro, but it is clear that the single currency provides a good example of the economic prosperity that discipline and determination can bring. With regard to the ten new EU countries, let me stress that the criterion of exchange rate stability within ERM II requires that this stability be achieved before the adoption of the single currency. The advantage is that the adoption of the euro will be the culmination of a structured convergence process within a multilateral framework. This is certainly one of the most important challenges facing the euro area in the coming years, challenges that I will now tell you about. PART 3: THE CHALLENGES OF THE SINGLE CURRENCY As the euro's environment continues to change, public authorities face new challenges when formulating and implementing their economic policy decisions. I would like to draw attention to three of these challenges which, in my opinion, 14 will have a strong impact on the future of the euro and european integration. Firstly, it is necessary to strengthen the EU's budgetary coordination in order to consolidate the foundations on which the euro is based, at a time when fiscal policies in Europe are facing specific challenges such as an ageing population. Second, there is a need to implement structural reforms (B) to better prepare countries for the challenges ahead. Finally, the enlargement process (C), which is certainly already a reality, will require further efforts to ensure that the new Member States make further progress and eventually catch up. Has. The need for greater budgetary cohesion and coordination within of the Union Compliance with the rules and procedures set out in the Treaty and the provisions of the stability and growth impose the same budgetary discipline on all Member States : the budget deficit must not exceed the ceiling of 3% of GDP and the total debt ratio should not exceed 60% of GDP. These limits help to ensure an optimal policy mix in the euro area level, as a lax fiscal policy may, in the long term, jeopardize the achievement of price stability. Finally, they maintain growth and sustainable employment and are conducive to economic stability. Budgetary discipline is indeed of paramount importance for EMU, as it is a a necessary corollary of the single monetary policy. Member States are expected to consider their economic policies as matters of "common interest", being given the impact that their budgetary decisions may have on the euro area in its together. In a monetary union, it is of the utmost importance to deal with " free-riding behaviour, hence the "no" clause bailout" enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty. The institutional framework for the coordination of national economic policies has been well established worked in the past. However, the economic difficulties faced by many European countries have drawn strong criticism of the provisions of the Treaty and the Stability and Growth Pact. However, it is not a question of improving the formulation of the Stability and Growth Pact but rather the modalities of its implementation. - The rules themselves leave sufficient leeway to deal with a slower growth. In line with the concept of balancing budget balances 15 EU Member States have committed themselves to achieving and maintaining, during the economic cycle, a budgetary situation "close to balance or in surplus". This requirement must be able to cope with asymmetric shocks and fluctuations cyclical, while allowing the automatic stabilisers to fully exercise their Belongings. This flexibility is essential to overcome asymmetric shocks while preserving the long-term sustainability of public finances and the autonomy of monetary policy. All improvement that can be made to the implementation of these rules is in the very interest of the Member States. - The real problem is the implementation of the Covenant: in particular, incentives. should be created with a view to strengthening the implementation of sound fiscal policy in times of high economic conditions. When growth is strong, countries need to mobilize even more to reduce their deficits or generate surpluses and thus reduce the stock public debt that can remain at high levels. This means that in times of In a favourable economic environment, less lax fiscal policies are needed to ensure the long-term sustainability of public finances. Respect for the central objective of a balanced budget is all the more essential as the European Union will have to tackle the problem of the rapid ageing of the population, of which the implications for public finances are considerable, both from the point of view of health than pension plans. Given that, in these areas, reforms risk to be perceptible only in the medium and long term, it is essential that European countries take all necessary measures to prevent the consequences of such developments demographics, particularly in budgetary terms. Implementation of fiscal policies It also means improving the quality of public spending. A first step in this direction would be to focus the adjustment process on expenditures. current rather than on investment, unlike what has been done in most country in the late nineties. More generally, EU countries must undertake structural reforms to strengthen growth potential and promote job creation. On these points, the Eurosystem has repeatedly called on these countries without possible ambiguity in carrying out these reforms. B. Structural reforms need to be carried out in several areas, however, in Europe, particularly in the euro area, there are still significant structural rigidities that need to be addressed if the highest possible non-inflationary growth is to be promoted. I would like to mention here several avenues which are also the subject of a 16 consensus in the Governing Council of the euro area. They relate in particular to the efforts to be pursued with regard to the role and importance of research (B1) in increasing the growth potential of the euro area, the development of "agglomeration forces" to facilitate the location of enterprises (B2), the efforts to be made finally to increase flexibility on the labour market and the integration of the markets for goods and services (B4). B.1. A knowledge-based economy With regard to the first point, the strategy adopted unanimously at the Lisbon European Council in March 2000, which aims to make the European Union "the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustainable economic growth accompanied by qualitative and quantitative improvements in employment and greater social cohesion", provides a frame of reference to guide public action. In particular, it stresses the importance of research, innovation and the dissemination of new technologies in raising the level of productivity of the economy. It also aims to give the European economy and all EU member countries more flexibility, more activity, and more jobs. This is an ambitious strategy but crucial for the future of Europe and the euro area. B.2. The competitiveness of enterprises In this context, in particular because of international competition, it is also crucial to develop the "agglomeration forces", i.e. the incentives that force companies to concentrate geographically in order to benefit from economies of scale and external. In particular, the existence of an area with high purchasing power is one of the important factors in the location of European companies. I have already mentioned the attractiveness of the euro area, but we need to go even further, particularly as regards controlling costs, particularly wage costs, and the need to ensure an environment favourable to the competitiveness of European companies. Indeed, jobs are preferably created in economies that know how to moderate their unit production costs and offer an environment as favourable as possible to the competitiveness of enterprises. This presupposes the continuation, if not the intensification, of structural reforms in the labour market and in the goods and services markets. B.3. Flexibility in the labour market 17 As far as the labour market is concerned, the euro area is characterised by a low employment rate, close to 62% in 2002 compared to 75% in the United States, which translates into a significant loss in terms of GDP per capita (almost 25% lower than in the United States). This low employment rate is the result of the high level of unemployment in the euro area, currently close to 9%, and the low participation rate. As unemployment in Europe is essentially of structural origin, it is therefore important to make the labour market more fluid and to preserve an incentive structure to raise the participation rate. This presupposes, in particular, the implementation of measures to reduce labour costs and business burdens, but also the promotion of incentive structures for the working population among the youngest age groups but also the oldest and the least qualified. Contrary to what is observed in the United States, where there is a long tradition of professional and geographical mobility, cultural and linguistic differences are still an obstacle to the mobility of the labour factor in Europe. The low level of occupational and geographical mobility also depends on an probably insufficient differentiation of wages in the euro area countries, which would make it possible to better reflect differences in terms of productivity gains or development between regions or sectors of activity. B.4. The integration of the markets for goods and services The increase in the level of productivity in the euro area is also based on the deepening of reforms in the market for goods and services, since the European backwardness, particularly vis-e0-vis the United States, is also due to the presence of structural rigidities linked to the existence of barriers to entry into this market. However, in the absence of competitive pressures, there is little incentive for firms to increase their efficiency. Regulatory reforms must therefore be undertaken both at member country level and at the level of the Economic Union as a whole. According to research carried out under the aegis of the CEPR and the Eurosystem, the creation of the single market has already been a major step, but the objective remains that of a full integration of the market for goods and services at European level. This applies in particular to the services sector, where, it must be admitted, progress has been less marked than in other sectors of activity. Admittedly, this is still partly explained by cultural differences. The fact remains that the public authorities, at both national and Community level, must continue their efforts and promote the degree of competition and integration in all sectors of activity. I mentioned the services sector, but this is also the case for the 18 energy, in particular electricity, transport, in particular rail, or postal services. C. The challenge of enlargement Ten new countries joined the EU on 1 May 2004. They are intended to adopt the euro after having met the nominal convergence criteria. Beyond the institutional challenges that remain (independence of central banks, adaptation of banking systems, fight against money laundering, etc.), the major challenge facing us is to meet the challenge of real convergence between Eastern and Western Europe. This will require years of major structural reforms to accelerate growth and close the East-West divide; it presupposes, in particular, respect for the macroeconomic framework to which all the Member States party to the euro today have consented, in particular the successful participation in the ERM2. It is indeed necessary to avoid any precipitation damaging to competitiveness and to carry out fundamental reforms, particularly in terms of the sustainability of public finances, prior to the entry into this exchange rate mechanism, a guarantee of a real sustainable convergence beneficial to the whole area. Conclusion I would like to conclude by saying that the euro has met all our expectations. After the unprecedented challenge of the continent-wide cash changeover, the euro was successful, the euro virtually instantly replaced the old national currencies, with no logistical disruption. It has promoted stability through its credibility and has protected many countries in the zone from excessive exchange rate volatility and financial market turbulence. These results must be highlighted all the more acutely since for several years it had been said that the euro would remain a "sea snake" or that it would create significant macroeconomic difficulties. These scenarios did not materialize. The euro therefore represents a major cornerstone of European integration. That said, and regardless of its own merits, a currency is not an end in itself even if the new Member States are ardently determined to adopt it as soon as possible. Participation in monetary union must be based on a process of sustainable convergence. The enlargement of the euro area will give new impetus to meeting the challenges in this respect, as policymakers are now under much greater pressure to deal with difficulties when they were previously unaware of them. This is an essential contribution to the construction of a stronger European Union, to which I adhere. 19 vigorously. In conclusion, let me express my confidence in the future of the euro, which, five years after its creation, is the clear symbol of European identity and its strength. 20

Je voudrais attirer l'attention sur trois de ces dfis qui,  mon avis, 14 pseront fortement sur l'avenir de l'euro et de la construction europenne. En premier lieu, il est ncessaire de renforcer la coordination budgtaire de l'UE afin de consolider les fondements sur lesquels repose l'euro, dans une priode o les politiques budgtaires en Europe doivent faire face  des dfis spcifiques tels que le vieillissement de la population. A. La ncessit d'un renforcement de la cohsion et de la coordination budgtaires au sein de l'Union Le respect des rgles et des procdures formules dans le Trait et des dispositions du Pacte de stabilit et de croissance imposent la mme discipline budgtaire  tous les tats membres : le dficit budgtaire ne doit pas excder le plafond de 3 % du PIB et le ratio d'endettement total ne devrait pas dpasser 60 % du PIB. Or, il ne s'agit pas d'amliorer la formulation du Pacte de stabilit et de croissance mais plutt les modalits de sa mise en uvre. - Les rgles elles-mmes laissent une marge de manuvre suffisante pour faire face  un ralentissement de la croissance. Des rformes structurelles doivent tre accomplies dans plusieurs domaines Il subsiste nanmoins en Europe, en particulier dans la zone euro, d'importantes rigidits structurelles qu'il s'agit de rsoudre si l'on souhaite promouvoir la plus forte croissance non inflationniste possible. B.1. Une conomie fonde sur la connaissance S'agissant du premier point, la stratgie adopte  l'unanimit lors du Conseil europen de Lisbonne en mars 2000, qui a pour objectif de faire de l'Union europenne  l'conomie de la connaissance la plus comptitive et la plus dynamique du monde, capable d'une croissance conomique durable accompagne d'une amlioration qualitative et quantitative de l'emploi et d'une plus grande cohsion sociale , fournit un cadre de rfrence pour guider l'action publique. La flexibilit sur le march du travail 17 En ce qui concerne le march du travail, la zone euro est caractrise par un faible taux d'emploi, proche de 62 % en 2002 contre 75 % aux tats-Unis, ce qui se traduit par une perte non ngligeable en termes de PIB par habitant (prs de 25 % infrieur  celui des tats-Unis). B.4. L'intgration des marchs des biens et services L'accroissement du niveau de productivit dans la zone euro repose galement sur l'approfondissement des rformes sur le march des biens et services car le retard europen, vis-vis notamment des tats-Unis, trouve galement son origine dans la prsence de rigidits structurelles lies  l'existence de barrires  l'entre sur ce march. Or, en l'absence de pressions concurrentielles, les entreprises ne sont gure incites  accrotre leur efficacit. Des rformes rglementaires doivent donc tre entreprises tant au niveau des pays membres qu'au niveau de l'Union conomique dans son ensemble. D'aprs les travaux de recherche conduits sous l'gide du CEPR et de l'Eurosystme, la cration du march unique a dj constitu une tape majeure mais l'objectif reste bien celui d'une intgration complte du march des biens et services au niveau europen. Cela concerne notamment le secteur des services o, il faut bien le reconnatre, les progrs ont t moins nets que dans les autres secteurs d'activit. Je mentionnais celui des services, mais c'est galement le cas des secteurs de 18 l'nergie, notamment lectrique, des transports, notamment ferroviaires, ou encore des services postaux. C. Le dfi de l'largissement Dix nouveaux pays ont rejoint l'UE le 1er mai 2004. Ils ont vocation  adopter l'euro aprs avoir satisfait aux critres de convergence nominale. Cet objectif ncessitera des annes d'importantes rformes structurelles favorables  une acclration de la croissance et au comblement du foss Est-Ouest ; il suppose notamment le respect du cadre macroconomique auquel tous les Etats membres partie  l'euro aujourd'hui ont consenti, notamment la participation russie au MCE2. Il faut en effet viter toute prcipitation dommageable  la comptitivit et procder aux rformes de fond, notamment en matire de soutenabilit des finances publiques, pralablement  l'entre dans ce mcanisme de change, gage d'une convergence relle durable profitable  l'ensemble de la zone. Title: Basel II genesis and challenges Conclusion
text: EUROSYSTEM BANKING COMMISSION CONFERENCE-DEBATE ASSOCIATION OF FINANCIAL ECONOMICS BASEL II: GENESIS AND CHALLENGES THURSDAY, 27 MAY 2004 CONCLUSION BY CHRISTIAN NOYER INTRODUCTION Ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, As a conclusion to this conference-debate that brought us together today, let me begin by saying how delighted I was to welcome so many eminent speakers and participants to the Golden Gallery. This conference-debate provided an opportunity for an extremely fruitful exchange of views on the new capital adequacy framework proposed by the Basel Committee. It was a very rich and useful extension of the publication of the special issue of the Revue d'e9conomie financie8re devoted to Basel II. I would then like to tell you how much, on the occasion of this conference, I felt, like all the participants, the extent of the efforts dedicated to the success of this reform and the importance of the stakes of the latter. Among the conclusions I would be tempted to draw, I would mention the following points. 1 1. First of all, after five years of work and on the eve of the publication by the Basel Committee of the new mechanism, scheduled for the end of next month, it is both remarkable and reassuring to note that a very broad consensus has emerged around this reform. The idea of having a more risk-sensitive solvency standard, i.e. better able to measure the reality and overall risks to which banks are exposed, was unanimously approved. This consensus is no coincidence. In the first place, the genesis of Basel II, as recalled by the various contributions of the Financial Economics Review and today's debate, is mainly explained by the meeting of common interests between banking supervisory authorities and banks. For banking supervisors, the primary objective of this reform is to encourage institutions to improve their ability to measure, manage and cover their risks in order to preserve their solvency and thus strengthen financial stability. For banks, who have also strongly hoped for this, this reform is an opportunity to equip themselves with the best risk management systems in order to increase their competitiveness and improve their results. By aligning the new capital requirements with best management practices for credit institutions, the Basel Committee could only make the New Arrangement more risk-sensitive and converge the economic vision and regulatory perception of these risks. Moreover, and beyond the objectives of the reform, this consensus is the result of the methodology adopted by the Basel Committee. Indeed, the process of drawing up the new system was designed with very close involvement of the banking profession and regularly assessing the effects of the proposals made by the Committee. In this regard, I will mention only the three consultation periods launched in June 1999, January 2001 and April 2003 respectively and the various impact studies following those consultations. This intense and ongoing dialogue between institutions and banking supervisors also explains why the preparation of the reform alone has already made it possible to make a lot of progress, both in understanding risks and in strengthening the tools for measuring and managing these risks. The high quality of this dialogue is an asset to be preserved because Basel II, like any prudential standard, is called upon, both in its content and in its implementation, to evolve to adapt to the permanent movement of innovation that drives banking and financial activities and their management methods. 2 2. My second point concerns the attention rightly paid by all stakeholders to the new conditions for the exercise of banking activity posed by the new prudential framework and, in particular, to the issue of a level playing field. Although the regulatory capital cost of a credit is only a minority part of the overall cost of the credit, the scope and application of a solvency standard may constitute, if one is not careful, a factor of distortion of competition. In this regard, I would stress the importance of the parallelism of the reform initiated by the Basel Committee and that undertaken by the European Commission in the context of the reform of the Capital Requirements Directive. This directive, while taking into account some European specificities, will be very close to the Basel II system. Like the latter, it will be based on three mutually reinforcing pillars: a calculation of minimum capital requirements (first pillar), a strengthened supervisory process (second pillar) and an effective use of market discipline (third pillar). This maximum possible coherence between Basel II and the European Directive, in terms of content and timing of development and implementation, was a necessity to ensure a level playing field between European institutions and other international banks in the G-10 countries. The European choice to apply the Directive, unlike Basel II, not only to all credit institutions but also to all investment firms should not call this principle into question. In the first place, this choice makes it possible to avoid any distortion of competition in Europe between financial institutions of different categories but likely to provide identical services. In addition to the intellectual coherence that exists in applying the same rule to a given risk regardless of the bearer of that risk, I would point out that the European market for financial services cannot function without strict equality of competition between institutions. Secondly, possible distortions between European investment firms and those from third countries, in particular the United States, should be very limited. Indeed, on the one hand the subsidiaries of the latter in Europe will be subject to the directive, on the other hand the major American investment banks will be able to opt for the rules laid down in Basel II. 3 This constant concern for respect for a level playing field is reflected not only in the very design of the new capital adequacy rules but also in efforts to harmonise the practices of banking supervisors. Consistent implementation of the new system presupposes, even before its entry into force, a convergence of supervisors' practices both at international level, between the European Union and third countries, and within the European Union itself. This is all the more necessary since, as has been pointed out during this debate, the new arrangement will on the one hand give supervisory authorities the possibility of exercising certain so-called 'national discretion' options under Pillar 1 (i.e. in the way in which capital requirements are calculated), and on the other hand will strengthen their role, in particular through Pillar 2. While such national room for manoeuvre is essential to take better account of the specificities of a market or situation, their use must not undermine the level playing field. This is why the Basel Committee set up a working group in December 2001 to define the practical modalities for the application of Basel II (Accord Implementation Group), particularly in its transboundary aspects, and to reflect on the conditions for the implementation of Pillar II. Similarly, at European level, the Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS), set up as part of the extension of the Lamfalussy process to the banking sector as requested by the Ecofin Council of 3 December 2002, is responsible for harmonising banking supervision practices by ensuring very close cooperation between the supervisory authorities. Extensive convergence work is already underway in this House, which has the power to enact measures of sound practice complementary to the directive. The strengthening of this cooperation is, moreover, all the more essential given that the European Union has just enlarged to include ten countries whose banking sectors have important specificities. In addition, the submission of common reporting documents for Basel II in Europe could be a concrete case of this harmonisation that I am calling for. 4 3. The third lesson I would draw from this conference is the unanimous recognition of the profoundly innovative nature of Basel II. Innovative, because the future prudential framework is at the same time more complete in the understanding of banking risks, more flexible and finer in the measurement of these risks and more prospective in the prevention of the latter. Basel II is first of all a more complete system insofar as all the risks to which a bank is exposed will have to be taken into account in the apprehension of the risk profile of the latter. The introduction of a requirement to cover operational risk with own funds under Pillar 1 is not the only example of this. I would also mention the requirement, under Pillar 2, for an assessment of risks that are more difficult to measure but nevertheless essential to monitor and control, such as interest rate risk in the bank portfolio, credit concentration risk or legal risk. The new system is then more flexible and risk-sensitive than the current standard. The approach proposed by the Basel Committee could only be evolutionary since the ambition of the reform was to promote the adoption of best practices in the profession. This is why the Committee has developed a menu of options for each type of risk, in all proportions, in line with the existing market risk regime, taking into account the state of the art within the institutions. Pillar 1 of the new framework thus offers several options for banks to calculate capital requirements for their credit and operational risk, with each bank choosing to choose the option best suited to its level of sophistication and risk profile. The most innovative part of Basel II in this respect is the possibility for banks to use, within the limits set by the new framework and under the supervision of their supervisory authority, their own internal risk assessment systems. By making internal analysis an essential part of the new framework and by prudentially recognising the latest risk-reduction techniques, such as credit derivatives, the Basel Committee has thus developed a standard that is much more sensitive to these risks. In addition, this standard will be better able to incorporate technical innovations as well as advances made by the banking industry. 5 Finally, the prospective dimension of the new system deserves to be highlighted. The latter's ambition is to encourage banks to measure and manage their risks not only more finely but also more dynamically, i.e. more prospectively throughout the economic cycle. Thus, in terms of credit risk, the calculation of capital requirements under Pillar 1 will be carried out by the main banking groups on the basis of their internal ratings as assessed in principle over a one-year horizon but in practice over a more distant horizon. The use of 'forward-looking' internal credit risk ratings and the ex-post control of these ratings should make it possible to contain very largely the risk of pro-cyclicality, i.e. the risk of amplification of economic cycles, of the new system. In addition, this capital calculation will have to be carried out on the basis of particularly deep data histories, covering a complete economic cycle. I would mention in this respect only the requirements laid down in the advanced approach to internal ratings, namely data histories of five years for the probabilities of failure and seven years for the loss rates used. In addition, under Pillar II, banks using the internal ratings approach will have to carry out stress tests and, depending on the analysis of the results of the latter, hold additional capital to cope with a less favourable economic environment. By asking banks to understand their risks more dynamically and to anticipate more the deterioration of these risks, the Basel Committee intends to make the new system play a more stabilizing role with regard to fluctuations in the credit cycle. I would not surprise you by indicating that, in my opinion, this role would be all the more important if a dynamic provisioning system, or ex ante, consisting in provisioning the expected losses statistically on a loan as soon as that loan was granted, were put in place. This presupposes both the adaptation and harmonization of national accounting regimes but also a better articulation between the new capital adequacy system and the reform of accounting rules initiated by the IASB (International Accounting Standards Board). I will come back to this last point a little later. 6 Let me at this point recall the importance, in terms of provisioning, of the decision taken by the Basel Committee on 10 and 11 October 2003 in Madrid to calibrate capital requirements only on unexpected losses (UL). The mechanism on which the calibration of the new system is now based should encourage banks to provision more and more dynamically for their expected losses. Indeed, this mechanism provides that any shortfall in covering, by provisions, the expected losses will have to be deducted from the banks' own funds, up to 50% on their core own funds and 50% on their additional own funds. Any excess cover for these losses may be included, within a certain limit, in the calculation of additional own funds only. The concern for a more forward-looking solvency standard is also reflected in the advanced approach to measuring operational risk as proposed by the Committee. Internal models for calculating capital requirements for this risk will need to be fed both by historical data, i.e. internal and external loss data, and by forward-looking data, including scenario analyses and risk indicators. Complementing historical observation, the use of forward-looking elements will also allow for better consideration of future changes in operational risk management. Thus, the reform initiated by the Basel Committee and the European Commission, by encouraging a more dynamic understanding of banking risks and a more forward-looking management of the capital needed to cover them, will help to prevent both systemic banking crises and individual bank failures more quickly and effectively. 4. In addition to the innovative nature of Basel II, and this will be my fourth observation, I would like to return to the structuring aspects of this reform, both in terms of the organisation and conduct of banking activities and in terms of behaviour. Indeed, this new system concerns all levels of the bank's organizational system and all its businesses. The plurality of options offered by the reform, both for the measurement of credit and operational risk, encourages better risk management as the more sophisticated the option chosen, the less capital requirements the capital requirements 7 should be high. The use of the most advanced approaches to measuring these risks requires the establishment of reliable and comprehensive information systems. Thus, under credit risk, the systems used in the process of assigning and supervising internal ratings will have to be strengthened in order to ensure, inter alia, the completeness and integrity of the latter. Similarly, for the measurement and management of operational risk, an effective process for collecting information on losses, firmly established in the business lines, will have to be implemented to feed into the internal models developed by the institutions. This excellence of information systems cannot be conceived without an appropriation of the reform at all levels and by all professions and therefore without a dissemination of a real "risk culture" within institutions. This presupposes, as has been emphatically emphasized, not only the full involvement of legislative organs and Directorates-General in the implementation of this reform, but also a continuous review of internal control functions. By favouring approaches based on banks' internal measurement systems, Basel II is more sensitive to the risks incurred by banks but also more demanding on the quality and robustness of their internal control. This requirement builds on the principles laid down in this area by the Basel Committee shortly before the start of the reform, including the Basic Principles for Effective Banking Supervision in September 1997 and the Principles for the Evaluation of Internal Control Systems in September 1998. The latter recall, and I quote, that 'an effective internal control system is an essential component of the management of an institution and constitutes the basis for the safe functioning of a banking organisation'. In general, the internal control of institutions should be strengthened under the effect of Basel II, the requirements set by the Committee, in particular in the context of advanced risk measurement approaches, placing audit and risk control functions at the heart of the new framework. Basel II requires the establishment of an independent, robust and transparent internal control system. Under Pillar 1, i.e. the calculation of minimum capital requirements, banks wishing to use internal rating approaches for credit risk and a 8 This will require an advanced approach to operational risk to meet qualitative requirements in terms of corporate governance, audit and internal control. In particular, the credit and operational risk control functions are to be clearly separated, and therefore independent, from the business functions. The internal auditors will, for their part, have to ensure the quality of this independent control, in charge of evaluating and monitoring the performance of internal risk measurement systems, and its compliance with all the regulatory requirements set. The robustness of the internal control system will also have to be assessed in the light of Pillar 2. Among the elements ensuring the existence and proper functioning within banks of a process for assessing the overall adequacy of their own funds is a review by internal control of that process in the light of the nature, scope and complexity of their activities. Finally, the third pillar of the new framework requires institutions to publish information on their internal control framework for both credit and operational risk. Those requirements should significantly reinforce the importance attached to the quality of internal control in assessing the soundness of an institution. It is also interesting in this regard to note that at the level of credit rating agencies the effectiveness of internal control functions is gradually becoming one of the criteria for assessing the economic prospects of listed companies. In the same vein, it can be seen that these agencies are also attaching increasing importance in their rating policy to the operational risk management framework implemented by banks. This leads me to stress the equally structuring nature of the reform on the behaviour of banks and their managers. The third pillar of Basel II aims to improve the information provided to the market by banks and thus to exert greater pressure on them to promote better risk management and more responsible behaviour. It therefore requires institutions to publish quantitative and qualitative information, more reliably and frequently, on the level of their own funds and risks and on the methods of assessing them. By getting market participants to better monitor banks' risk profile and behaviour, the new framework will strengthen 9 the complementary role of prudential supervision, played by market discipline, which will in turn contribute to strengthening the action of the supervisory authorities. 5. This desire of the Basel Committee to promote market discipline through more reliable and frequent information leads me to a fifth and final remark on the relationship between the future accounting rules developed by the IASB and the new capital adequacy framework. Overall, most of the standards issued by the IASB are quality standards and were adopted by the European Commission in 2003. The standards still under review and particularly important in the banking field are IAS 32 and IAS 39 on financial instruments. These standards, which are scheduled to apply in 2005 for listed companies, include very relevant provisions on the consolidation of special purpose entities, as recent financial scandals have shown the dangers of misuse of accounting standards in this area. However, it is desirable to make certain provisions of the standards issued by the IASB more compatible with the prudential objectives sought by the Basel Committee. This is particularly the case with IAS 39. A first concern concerns the method of accounting at 'fair value' of financial instruments - which correspond, according to the IASB's definition, to almost all of the balance sheet and off-balance-sheet of credit institutions - and in particular when this method of valuation is offered, on option, to a very large number of items. The use of this option has recently been framed by certain provisions of the IASB but may still seem too general. In fact, there is a risk that a large part of the balance sheet items will be valued on the basis of data and models that are difficult to verify. Another concern arises from the current proposals for the accounting treatment of so-called macro-hedging operations, which are frequently used by banks to hedge their overall interest rate risk. As it stands, these proposals, which are still under discussion with European banks, are ill-adapted to their management methods and in particular to the coverage of their demand deposits, which constitute for them an important factor of stability. Finally, the provisioning rules, in particular the provisioning of expected losses at the level of a credit portfolio, appear to be perfectible to better articulate prudential and accounting. 10 Faced with these concerns and that of increased volatility in banks' capital, the banking supervisory authorities have alerted the European authorities to the potentially negative effects of these IASB proposals on financial stability. In addition, the Basel Committee is currently conducting an in-depth reflection on the possible restatements that should be carried out on future accounting data for the calculation of prudential requirements - and in particular the definition of own funds - if, ultimately, the standards developed by the IASB do not allow a sufficiently prudent assessment of the financial situation of institutions. CONCLUSION To conclude, as I also indicated at the very beginning of my speech and as the Basel Committee announced in its press release of 11 May, I would like to recall that the new Agreement - that is, the version of the text that is to serve as a common basis for national legislative processes - is to be published at the end of June. At its meeting on 11 May, the Committee reached consensus on a number of important issues relating to: - the start date of implementation of the reform; - how to calculate the average loss rates used for the calculation of own funds. regulatory; - and the modalities of implementation of the new system, in particular for the validation of the internal models for measuring operational risk developed by banking groups with a strong international presence. The consensus reached by the Basel Committee, which I am the first to welcome, both Governor of the Bank of France and Chairman of the Banking Commission. However, it is important to remember that this consensus is only one step, albeit a decisive one, in the reform that will soon be submitted to the Council and the European Parliament. In addition to a general appropriation of the reform, institutions will in particular have to complete their efforts to improve their information system and to effectively articulate the entire new system with the management of the profitability of their risk-adjusted capital. In the same way, the supervisory authorities 11 will have to use the time available to them between now and the implementation of the reform to further increase their coordination efforts and analyse the possibility of final technical adjustments, in particular in the light of the results of the parallel conduct of the Basel I and Basel II arrangements planned for the financial years 2006 and 2007. In this regard, the Basel Committee has already begun an in-depth reflection on several areas for improving the risk sensitivity of the new system. This is particularly the case for items included in trading portfolios. The Committee has thus set up a joint working group with the International Organisation of Securities Commissions to analyse how counterparty risk is measured on derivatives and temporary disposals of securities. At a more global level, the issue of the definition of regulatory capital and its relationship to future accounting standards is also on the Committee's mind. In the same way, the Committee will have to integrate, in due course, into the regulatory framework, the progress made by the profession in the internal modelling of credit risk and move towards the prudential recognition of internal models. Such recognition, considered premature by the Committee in the context of the current reform, will thus lead to a new rapprochement between the economic capital calculated by the banks and the regulatory capital. While the history of prudential regulation has accelerated significantly with Basel II, it is by no means complete and it will have to continue to adapt to the constant movement of innovation within financial institutions. By a third agreement, or Basel III, there is no doubt that the risk sensitivity of the new framework, its flexibility and its incentive for as many banks as possible to adopt best risk management practices by as many banks as possible will have greatly contributed to strengthening the robustness of institutions, the soundness of banking systems and thus financial stability. In the meantime, and this will be my closing remarks, I would like once again to thank today's speakers and all the contributors to this special issue of the Revue d'e9conomie financie8re for reminding us of the importance of this reform and for providing us with their vision of the main issues related to it. Thank you for your attention. 12
