Title: General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies
text: SPEECH BY CHRISTIAN NOYER GOVERNOR OF THE BANQUE DE FRANCE PRESIDENT OF THE BANKING COMMISSION ----- GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE FRENCH ASSOCIATION OF FINANCIAL COMPANIES 22 June 2004 ----- Mr President Thank you for giving me the floor in this Chamber where I am delighted to speak for the first time. Like my predecessor, I attach particular importance to this assembly, which is for me an excellent opportunity to exchange with the profession some reflections on the major themes of banking news and on the evolutions of our financial and regulatory environment. As a preamble, let me first of all take up before you a theme developed a few moments ago by Mr Lemasson, that of the continuity of the excellent relations between the ASF and the banking authorities. In a context marked by rapid regulatory change, I would like to stress the importance of the constructive nature of our exchanges. Under the direction of Ms. Nouy, the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission will remain the attentive interlocutor of your Houses, ensuring tangible results to the fruitful dialogue that we conduct, together, in terms of monitoring activity, risk monitoring, and french and international regulatory developments. You also mentioned, Mr President, the banking law of 1984: with a retrospective of 20 years, I would like to stress in a word the extent of the transformation of the French financial sector that the banking law has entailed. Over the last twenty years, the banking system has undergone a profound restructuring and concentration, as evidenced in particular by the reduction of more than half of the number of credit institutions, from 1 935 when the Committee of Credit Institutions was set up to 925 on 31 December 2003 after having reached a maximum of 2 152 in 1987, and the fact that the six main banking groups now account for more than 80 per cent of loans and nearly 90 per cent of deposits in the entire banking system. The evolution of the category of financial corporations has been very significant in this movement of rationalization and renewal, since their number, which was 940 in 1984 and which had reached a maximum of 1,209 in 1990, stood at 458 as at 31 December 2003. This restructuring of the population of financial companies, although important but identical in percentage to that of all credit institutions, hides a real dynamism: indeed, their market share increased significantly overall (11.7% of loans in 2003, against 7.4% in 1990), and sectorally it increased in equipment loans where it reached 12.3% at the end of 2003 while it fell a little in housing loans (10.6%) and in consumer credit (25.5%). As far as regulation is concerned, it is not for me, as you will understand, to prejudge the intentions of the legislator with regard to consumer protection. In this area, you know that there have been many initiatives over the past year and that a project designed at European level, centrally, has been able to elicit, particularly from you, quite strong reactions. In the area of competence of the Banking Commission, I would like to assure you that we pay particular attention to ensuring that the legislative framework around consumer credit is well adapted to what is possible, reasonable to do, without excessive requirements for the profession and responding to the real needs of consumers. 2 95 Allow me, Mr President, first of all to say a few words about the recent developments in the activity and results of the banking sector in 2003, and to clarify the specific situation of specialised financial companies. With regard to the 2003 financial year, I note that the results published by the main French banking groups showed a significant increase; the same is true of the first quarterly results of the current financial year, which bodes well for 2004. While the economic recovery is gradually taking place in Europe, the evolution of risks still needs to be closely monitored. The year 2003 saw a gradual improvement in the economic and financial environment. French credit institutions benefited from sustained domestic activity, particularly in the area of housing credit. The gradual recovery in equity markets has benefited investment banking as well as asset management. In this context, French credit institutions recorded significantly higher results. These results are the result of the diversification of the activity of French establishments, better controlled operating costs and risks generally kept under control. As I mentioned a moment ago, it is essential that credit institutions maintain their efforts to select and rigorously manage risks. Preparing for the new international solvency ratio is also a major challenge by making it possible to further improve management methods. Like other major projects, this reform requires significant human and financial investments, but it will allow institutions to manage their risks more effectively, in particular by adapting their pricing more finely to the risks incurred. 3 Concerning more specifically the activity of specialized institutions, 2003 can be considered a positive year since, during a period of slow economic recovery, their outstanding credit recorded an overall increase of 3.1% as indicated by the figures established by your association. While the financing of equipment for companies and professionals recorded only an increase of 0.8%, private customers remained more dynamic in the consumer credit segment (3.0%) and in the mortgage segment (5.0%), marking, in the latter case, a clear increase compared to the previous year. I therefore note that the increase in the new appropriations allocated in 2003 was at a much faster pace than the increase in GDP. These good performances are reflected in the 2003 results since, on the basis of a sample of 432 financial companies, the Banking Commission found that net banking income recorded an increase of 6% in metropolitan activity. I also note with satisfaction that overheads were remarkably under control during this financial year, remaining contained at 0.3%. In total, the net income of the sampled financial corporations increased by 8%. If we now include international activity, this increase reaches 9.5%, which reflects the growing contribution of the locations of your establishments abroad. In particular, the development of partnerships with local institutions that wish to benefit from the level of expertise of French institutions in the consumer credit sector seems particularly promising. 95 Turning now to the evolution of the legislative and regulatory framework governing your activity, it seems to me necessary to draw up an initial assessment of international developments, numerous in 2003, and for some of them still in progress As I have just pointed out, credit institutions operate in a largely open and internationalized environment, with the authorities having to adapt not only the regulatory and prudential framework to support this movement, but also to take into account some of the specificities of your institutions' activities. 4 I will not go back over the general provisions of the reform of the cross-border solvency ratio, which are now known to all. I would, however, like to highlight the important progress made in recognising the specific features of consumer credit on the one hand and leasing, factoring and guarantee techniques on the other. As regards consumer credit, the introduction of new rules on the calculation of capital requirements as from 31 December 2006, via the "Basel 2" ratio and its European version, has important consequences likely to modify the offer and increase the use of this type of financing by individuals. Indeed, regardless of the approach chosen, standard or based on internal ratings, the capital requirements on consumer credit should be lower than at present. In general, moreover, the technical work that has been carried out on this subject shows that, overall, the implementation of Basel 2 should lead to a reduction, sometimes significant, of the regulatory capital requirements for your members, especially when the method of internal models is used. Since consumer credit institutions generally have comprehensive and historically deep databases, it should be relatively easy for them to comply with the criteria for moving from the standard method to the advanced method based on internal ratings. This will also enable them to strengthen their risk monitoring systems. A few words also about leasing, factoring and suretyship: As you know, the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission has worked throughout recent years and in all its components to ensure that the specificities of your businesses are taken into account as widely as possible, particularly in the areas of leasing and factoring. This has resulted in very positive results for your profession. The internal models method is also the means of dealing with technical subjects that could not all be solved in the standard method. 5 All in all, the new solvency ratio should therefore give more appropriate treatment to the activities of financial companies than the one currently in force. I welcome this result of the fruitful dialogue between your Association and the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission. 95 With regard to the European harmonisation process and, more specifically, the Consumer Credit Directive, The initial draft was adopted in principle by the plenary assembly of the European Parliament on 5 November 2003. On 16 March, however, this version was amended by more than 150 amendments aimed at reducing the scope of transactions covered by the Directive, even if the aim of the European legislator remains that of optimal harmonisation of the rights of borrowers. These efforts, aimed at increasing the transparency and rigour of procedures and developing the internal market in financial services, have resulted in a text that is undoubtedly more balanced and more in line with the expectations of the various players in the file. 95 In addition, the accounting treatment of consumer credit will also evolve at a rapid pace This reform, which aims to harmonise European accounting standards, is based, as you know, on the standards developed by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). The European Accounting Regulation of 19 July 2002 will oblige, from 1 January 2005, European listed companies to prepare their consolidated accounts in accordance with these international standards (IAS, IFRS), once they have been endorsed by the European Commission. 6 While these developments primarily concern large listed groups and their subsidiaries, French accounting rules have also tended, since 1999, to converge towards this international system. This development will require an often significant adaptation of information systems. This new framework should allow for greater comparability of accounting information at European level. As you know, some points of IAS 39 on the recognition and measurement of financial instruments, which is the most important standard for credit institutions within this new accounting framework, are still under discussion. The ongoing negotiations could be concluded fairly quickly now. In practice, the impact of IAS 39 on the provisioning of consumer credit risk, even if its provisions appear more restrictive than the current French rules, should be limited since IAS 39 allows the provisioning of these credits on a collective basis, using historical data as well as the judgment of credit risk experts. The impact of IFRS on factoring and leasing activities could potentially be more significant as a result of, respectively, more complex conditions for the disposal of financial assets from the balance sheet subject to a series of fairly restrictive conditions, and rules for distinguishing between operating and financial leasing that may not overlap with the boundary currently defined in France between leasing and leasing. The institutions concerned should study precisely the impacts of these new accounting rules, which should allow them to adapt quickly and at the cost of some adjustments to the new framework. 7 95 On a more domestic level now, and echoing the concerns you expressed in your introduction, Mr President, I would like to stress that Your members must continue to ensure the prevention of over-indebtedness, in a context where the number of cases handled by the Over-indebtedness Commissions increased again in 2003. I am confident that this vigilance will continue, as well as that we will continue to exercise a cautious stance on risk monitoring. As part of a healthy development of consumer credit, which is also encouraged by the public authorities, your institutions naturally have a central role to play. As you pointed out, Mr President, the Financial Security Act now requires all public limited companies to draw up a report on internal control procedures in the interests of greater transparency. In this respect, credit institutions already have extensive experience in this area under banking regulations and more specifically, under Regulation CRBF No 97-02. Therefore, although the financial years are separate, your institutions, in liaison with their auditors, should not encounter significant difficulties in this case. A few more words on internal control to indicate that it must also cover subcontracting. A reflection was carried out within the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission on this subject, in parallel with European work. This could lead to clarification of the expectations of the banking authorities in this area. The same is true in the area of compliance, which is an increasingly important obligation for financial institutions and for which the Basel Committee has prepared a draft that has been the subject of consultation with the profession. 8 The Financial Security Act, containing provisions whose primary objective is precisely to prevent over-indebtedness, has also profoundly reformed banking and financial canvassing in France. This reform, which is essential in view of the old system, which is scattered and stems from often old texts, now offers a harmonised framework which should eliminate the difficulties of application raised previously. The publication by the summer of two decrees, on which the CNIL has been seized, will allow us to fully appreciate the effects of this reform, in particular through the file of canvassers. This roster, which the Bank of France should take over the operational management, will allow better information for the public, harmonize practices and reassure investors. With regard to over-indebtedness, as you rightly pointed out, the regulatory texts conditioning the entry into force of the reform of the treatment provided for by the law of 1 August 2003 - known as the "Borloo" law - were published in February and, with regard to the ministerial circular of application, in March 2004. We therefore do not currently have sufficient hindsight to draw up an assessment, especially since, because of its innovative nature, the application of this reform implies significant changes in the practices of the various actors, notably over-indebtedness commissions and judges. Indeed, while maintaining the fundamental role of over-indebtedness commissions, which remain the entry points for all cases and which will continue to deal with the greatest number of them, this law allows debtors whose situations are the most critical and for whom the commission considers that no improvement is possible, to benefit from a "second chance" consisting in the total cancellation of their debts by the judicial authority in return for the liquidation of their property. 9 The Bank of France, in its role of managing the secretariats of the over-indebtedness commissions, will refer all debtors under the new procedure to justice while remaining vigilant towards those who would try to use it to unduly evade their financial commitments, thus ensuring that it applies only to people in real financial distress. * Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you. The Bank of France, the Banking Commission, as well as the Committee of Credit Institutions and Investment Firms will ensure, Mr President, that the quality and richness of the relations between your association and all the representatives of the banking authorities continue and are further strengthened, if possible, in this period of economic and regulatory developments. 10

Title: Annual report
text: PRESENTATION OF THE ANNUAL REPORT OF THE BANKING COMMISSION FOR 2003 Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France, President of the Banking Commission 1. IN 2003, IN A CONTRASTING ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL ENVIRONMENT, FRENCH CREDIT INSTITUTIONS GENERATED SOLID RESULTS On the basis of their social accounts, the net result of all in 2003, credit institutions remained close to that obtained in 2002, i.e. nearly EUR 18 billion. This stability can be explained, in large part, by an economic situation that has remained difficult in the euro area. However, if we take into account the entire global activity through the consolidated accounts of the main groups, the increase was strong, with net income group share increasing by 27%. In fact, the improvement in the global economic and financial environment has generated results that have complemented the continued solid profitability of retail banking. This growth in results was confirmed in the first quarter of 2004. 1.1. The financial year 2003 was marked by an improvement in world economic and financial conditions, but also by a difficult economic situation in the euro area As you know, the recovery in economic growth has taken place. confirmed during 2003. Global growth reached 3.9 per cent, up from 3 per cent in 2002. However, these overall rates mask contrasting trends depending on the geographical area. The growth rate improved markedly in the United States, Japan, as well as in the major emerging countries. The economic recovery has accelerated in the United States. At the same time, the situation has eased in emerging countries. In addition, some sectors that had experienced difficulties (telecommunications, energy, aeronautics) have seen their situation stabilize or even improve, even if some major players remain convalescent. With the exception of the United Kingdom and Spain, however, growth remained weak in Europe, where the number of business insolvencies continued to rise. In this environment, French growth slowed down (0.5%, compared with 1.1% in 2002), in line with that of the euro area, but more obvious signs of recovery appeared at the end of the year and were confirmed at the beginning of 2004. From the second quarter of 2003 onwards, the financial markets showed a strong recovery which contrasted with the developments of previous years, marked by the bursting of the Internet bubble and by the setbacks in the telecommunications, transport and energy sectors. The CAC 40 thus gained 16% in 2003. Risk premia on corporate and emerging market debt have fallen sharply, to a degree that has also attracted the attention of central banks and banking supervisors, who are always concerned about fair risk pricing. 2 1.2. The results of the main French banking groups increased in 2003, mainly due to the diversity of their activities The aggregated 2003 net result of French credit institutions calculated on a social basis amounted to EUR 17.4 billion, slightly down on 2002, when the level was particularly high. However, on the basis of the consolidated financial statements published by the seven main banking groups, which give a more complete view of performance by including the contribution of subsidiaries abroad, net income increased by 27%. In fact, international activities, whether in local banking or investment banking, contributed significantly to the positive evolution of performance, thanks to the improvement in the global economy. For the first time in two years, the recovery in financial markets had a very positive impact on investment banking and asset management. The analysis of developments should not make us forget that retail banking remains, in France, a key driver of results. This phenomenon is mainly fuelled by the increase in housing financing, whose outstanding amounts have continued to increase sharply, and by the development of so-called specialized services. The maintenance of historically low interest rates has been an important factor in supporting demand and has eased the financing costs of institutions. 1.3. The overall risk burden has increased little, but its nature has changed. resulted in a reduction in provisioning expenses. At the same time, business insolvencies, especially medium- and small ones, have increased in Europe, leading to needs 3 additional but limited provisioning. In addition, the difficulties of a few large European companies have created additional coverage needs. Given the uncertainties of the economic situation, French banks have generally maintained their level of provisioning (bad loans are covered by provisions of up to 60% on average). This cautious attitude must, of course, be maintained. 1.4. The control of operating conditions must remain a priority The operating coefficient of French banks, the ratio which relates to the overheads to net banking income have improved while still at a level slightly higher than the European average. Efforts in this area must therefore not be relaxed and the Banking Commission will continue to endeavour to ensure that credit institutions achieve sufficient operating profitability, paying particular attention to the reduction of the operating ratio. It is also essential that operating margins cover all costs, including risk. 2. THE OVERALL STRENGTH OF FRENCH BANKS HAS BEEN FURTHER STRENGTHENED. In addition to profitability, the regular strengthening of the financial base and improving the quality of management are essential assets, recognized by the international community, of French banks in the face of structural and cyclical developments. These guidelines, which are encouraged by the action of the supervisory authorities, should be continued. 4 2.1. French banks regularly consolidate their financial base... French banks continued to strengthen their capital and have increasing market capitalizations. Accounting own funds now account for 5.4% of the total their balance sheet (compared to 5.2% in 2002), which has been steadily increasing for several years. The Banking Commission has ensured that the major French banking groups maintain capital levels, in particular "core" (Tier 1), above the regulatory minimums and adapted to their activity and risk profiles. The progress made in forward-looking risk analysis in the context of solvency ratio reform, through the use of statistical databases and the implementation of stress scenarios, contributes to this much-needed development. The solvency ratios of French banks therefore continue to rise and place them in a good position compared to their European counterparts, especially since the composition of these capital capitals monitored by the Banking Commission is particularly satisfactory in the light of international standards. 2.2. ... which gives them the means to be present in diversified and dynamic markets This financial situation has given in particular to French banks the necessary room for manoeuvre to finance their external growth operations. Such transactions, which may involve significant price and execution risks, must of course be selected with caution and rigour. French banks have a dense domestic network, which offers a very wide range of services and ensures a recurrence of results. This 5 diversity of their activity seems to be an asset, illustrated, for example, by the dynamism of consumer credit, to which a study is devoted in the annex to the Annual Report. The know-how developed in various businesses and a strong presence on the main capital markets are also a guarantee of dynamism and responsiveness to the main financial developments. Finally, French banks have invested in expanding markets (Eastern Europe, United States). 3. RISK MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL MUST CONTINUE TO PROGRESS Credit institutions and investment firms that are placed under the prudential supervision of the Banking Commission are encouraged by it to adopt or pursue long-term strategies based on prudent management methods, sustainable in their principles, but evolving in their modalities. 3.1. The reform of the solvency ratio is a structuring model for risk management The reform of the international solvency ratio is to a large extent finalised, with the text of the agreement to be published in the coming days, for application at the end of 2006 or, for the most advanced methods of measuring credit and operational risk, at the end of 2007. The main French banks have integrated the developments linked to this reform, adapting their information systems and operating methods. They must ensure that the conditions are in place that can allow the validation of their internal rating systems by the Banking Commission. The latter is reasonably confident in the good level of progress of the major French banks. The application of this reform at European level to 6 all credit institutions and investment firms will, however, require the involvement of all taxable firms. The reform of the international solvency ratio encourages credit institutions to anticipate the occurrence of risks by setting up comprehensive information systems and statistical forecasting tools. It is therefore desirable that these arrangements be operational as soon as possible, taking into account the delays associated with the establishment of historical databases and the development of the most advanced methods, as recently expressed by the Basel Committee. Finally, it is important that credit institutions and investment firms measure all their risks, including in their most day-to-day activities, and allocate the necessary own funds to them, as required by the reform of the solvency ratio by including in Pillar 1 the coverage of operational risks. The complexity and scope of these risks justified the inclusion of a study on this topic in this annual report. 3.2. The quality of internal control is an essential foundation of banking management In an economic and financial environment characterised by uncertainty, and sometimes through volatility, reducing risk factors is the only appropriate strategy. The effectiveness of internal control is an essential axis of this strategy and its necessity is recalled by the evolution of the legal framework and by current events. At European and international level, the Banking Commission has played a very active, even pioneering, role in promoting as early as 1997 a precise, detailed regulation on internal control and inspiring, to a large extent, the 7 work of the Basel Committee on this subject. More recently, the obligations created by the Financial Security Act have completed this system. In fact, French credit institutions must ensure that their corporate governance and internal control systems are strengthened. Even if banks do not seem to be among the actors most involved in the dysfunctions that have occurred, recent financial events on the other side of the Atlantic and in Europe have been a reminder, if need be, of the responsibility that all financial market participants bear for its proper functioning. It is therefore essential that the so-called "compliance" structures and procedures be further strengthened within French credit institutions and investment firms, which aim to avoid the risks of non-compliance with the laws, regulations and ethical standards governing banking and financial activity. Such discipline also reduces the risks of reputation or liability. I invite you, for further developments on this subject, to refer to the study of this year's report devoted to it. 3.3. A major effort to adapt is required in order to apply the new European accounting rules The application, scheduled for 1 January 2005, of IAS/IFRS to Consolidated accounts of listed companies in Europe will have very important effects for banks, due to the novelties introduced by IAS 32 and 39 on financial instruments. Certain provisions, such as those relating to macro-hedging and the fair value option, are significant technical issues for European banks. 8 These new standards promote the valuation of balance sheets at market prices or at supposedly equivalent prices, which is likely to increase the volatility of results and equity and to reduce, due to the fact that the amounts displayed have become largely ephemeral, their understanding by third parties. Certainly, French banks have developed asset-liability management tools that desensitize them, at least partially, to the impact of changes in the main financial parameters. Particular attention will have to be paid to these developments, in particular in the context of Pillar 2 of the new solvency ratio. The supervisory authorities will request in France and in the world prudential restatements resulting from the cooperation between supervisors, in which the Banking Commission has taken an active part. They will also invite all relevant stakeholders to apply the new accounting standards in the interests of prudence, in particular in the area of the establishment of provisions for signature risks. * ** French credit institutions showed in 2003 that they could take advantage of a very changing economic and financial context to further improve their performance. This ability is the result of generally prudent development strategies, and the action of institutions and the Banking Commission to improve risk management. The general economic improvement, which has yet to be confirmed, must in no way call into question the guidelines implemented for several years. It is essential that institutions maintain rigorous risk selection, appropriate pricing and further strengthen their internal control requirements. 9
