Title: A specialised decentralise and cooperative approach for financial sector supervision in Europe
text: FINANCE FORUM AMBROSETTI, 11 ET 12 MARS 2005 INTERVENTION DE M. NOYER AU COURS DE LA SESSION GOVERNING THE GLOBAL ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL SYSTEM A SPECIALISED, DECENTRALISED AND COOPERATIVE APPROACH FOR FINANCIAL SECTOR SUPERVISION IN EUROPE Introduction Ladies and gentlemen, Let me start by expressing my gratitude for having been invited to participate in this forum. I am greatly honoured to have been asked to address a number of critical economic and financial issues, which are of particular importance nowadays given the key role supervisory authorities play in promoting financial stability.. This session, entitled Governing the global economic and financial system, raises a fundamental question: What is the most effective supervisory framework for financial stability?. As Governor of the Banque de France and Chairman of the Commission bancaire, I would like to start by addressing the three issues that are of particular interest to supervisors and that underpin our attempts to achieve a coherent approach to financial stability: How to capture all material risks arising from the financial sector, which is characterised by its capacity for innovation? What are the conditions for ensuring prompt and appropriate reactions from the supervisory authorities in the event of financial turbulence? How to deal with the increasing globalisation of financial groups? 1 Let me say right away that there is no single answer to these questions, and therefore no single theoretical supervisory framework for addressing them. However, one important lesson I have drawn from my experience and knowledge of financial sectors is that financial sector supervision should be underpinned by three mutually reinforcing pillars in order to be efficient: Specialisation (I) Proximity (II) Co-operation (III) I would now like to outline these three pillars: I. SPECIALISATION SUPERVISORY AUTHORITIES MUST FOCUS ON THE RISKS TAKEN BY EACH CATEGORY OF FINANCIAL INSTITUTION As you know, banking, insurance and securities activities - which lie at the heart of the financial sector - are in the hands of three different types of undertakings: credit institutions, insurance companies and investment firms. I will leave aside the issue of market supervision although this is not a trivial one, as illustrated by the recent spate of large corporate failures. However, the rationale behind market regulation clearly differs from the prudential supervision applied to financial corporations. Whereas market authorities chiefly seek to ensure market transparency and integrity, the prudential supervision of financial institutions is aimed at ensuring their solvency and liquidity. I would like to point out that the objectives of insurance company supervision differ from those of credit institution supervision; this difference is too often underestimated. Although these two sectors share common concerns, such as the need for financial stability, insurance and banking supervisors will not always choose the same course of action given that their objectives and tasks are different. 2  One major reason for adopting different approaches with regard to credit institutions and insurance companies is the location of their risks. For banks and investment firms, risks tend to appear on the assets side of the balance sheet, whereas for insurance companies, the main financial risks appear on the liabilities side of the balance sheet (i.e. the main risk is unanticipated claims by policyholders).  This difference is also reflected in the European regulatory framework. Each sector is governed by specific sectoral directives. We could sum up the difference as follows: Banks are free to determine the nature, horizon and composition of assets. However, the level of their capital must reflect the risks attached to these assets. Insurance companies have to comply with directives on the composition and horizon of assets. They must also respect a solvency margin to ensure that their liabilities are properly valued. Given these differences between insurance and banking regulations, it is not obvious that a global supervisory approach could be adopted. It can be argued that a variety of factors, including regulatory liberalisation, disintermediation, financial innovation, technological progress and even cross-sector risk transfers, have blurred the traditional distinctions between different markets, products and intermediaries within the financial sector. I do not deny this. But in reality, the magnitude of this trend towards the emergence of financial conglomerates and the blurring of distinctions between banks, investment firms and insurance companies should not be overestimated, since it is still fairly limited. Groups remain concentrated on their principal activity: they are either largely bank-oriented or insurance-oriented. The specificity of each financial sector should lead to a tailored supervisory approach, which is easier to implement for specialised supervisory structures than for integrated ones. 3  Banking and insurance are distinct financial sectors with specific risks. Each sector is subject to specific rules - i.e. accounting standards, taxation, and safety nets - that are organised at a sectoral and national level. Given these differences, it is quite difficult to achieve a full consolidation of banking and insurance activities, even at a national level for supervisory purposes. Co-operation between all sectoral supervisors is more effective for assessing the potential weaknesses of financial groups or conglomerates. For instance, the different French financial authorities work in close co-operation, and this co-operation is, in practice, facilitated by organic links.  A specialised co-operative supervisory approach enables the supervisory authorities to cover the whole range of financial groups activities, while the different types of activity can be clearly identified, by means of dedicated legal entities for instance. There is thus an incentive for the groups risk management to clearly separate its different financial activities. This separation helps strengthen the fire walls between the different activities in order to limit intra-group exposures and thus reduce the risk of contagion.  Moreover a specialised organisation answers the increasing need for enhancing financial authorities expertise. To put it simply, in a context of increasingly complex financial markets, specialisation fosters the development of human skills within the authorities. Let me now turn to my second pillar: proximity or decentralisation. 4 II. DECENTRALISATION THE GEOGRAPHICAL PROXIMITY BETWEEN SUPERVISORY AUTHORITIES AND THE INSTITUTIONS THEY SUPERVISE IS A KEY FACTOR OF EFFICIENCY The issue of an integrated European financial supervisory authority is being increasingly debated. Let me say right away that I am strongly in favour of a European and international convergence of supervisory practices and I will outline this in the third part of my presentation. Yet I believe that the creation of a single authority may raise more practical issues than it will solve real problems. The point is not to think about new institutional arrangements but rather to look for an effective supervisory approach for financial sector supervision. From this point of view, the proximity between supervisory authorities and the institutions they supervise is a key factor. .  First, geographical proximity between banks and their supervisors makes it possible to acquire an in-depth knowledge of the financial institutions and of the markets on which they operate. Would a supervisory authority be able to monitor institutions effectively if it were located thousands of kilometres away? If the supervisory team did not speak the same language as the bank staff? If the supervisors did not know the specificities of the domestic market? Frankly speaking, I have strong doubts about the ability of a remote supervisor to perform effective and in-depth supervision.  Second, proximity between banks and supervisors provides a privileged access to information and constitutes a good framework for on-site inspections. Problems within financial institutions are rapidly detected and supervisors are able to take prompt corrective action  Finally, the European level is not the most appropriate level for banking supervision. Indeed, apart from a few exceptions - Banco Santander-Abbey National or Dexia for instance - most of the European banks have a strong domestic feature. Furthermore, a large number of banks are not confined to the European market, but are of international dimensions. 5 It is not surprising that strengthening the co-operation between supervisors both on a crossborder and a cross-sector basis appears to be the best way to respond to the challenge of financial sector globalisation. Let me now outline the third pillar, enhanced co-operation. III. CO-OPERATION GREATER CO-OPERATION BETWEEN AUTHORITIES ENSURES AN EFFECTIVE SUPERVISION OF LARGE FINANCIAL GROUPS AND CONGLOMERATES The reality of the international dimension of financial groups and of the expansion of financial groups with cross-border activities is not called into question. First of all, I would like to stress that supervisors are not lagging behind financial groups. For decades they have dealt with the process of globalisation by establishing a dynamic co-operation both at the European and the international level. This fruitful co-operation has not been confined to the banking sector but has also covered cross-sectoral issues. In my opinion, strengthening concrete co-operation is most promising than banking on a hypothetical integration. I do not need not emphasise how the work of international fora, such as the Joint Forum, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision or the IOSCO, has contributed to promoting a comprehensive oversight of financial sectors. These bodies have published many studies, guidelines or core principles which provide an answer to some of the major cross-sectoral questions raised by financial sectors (solvency rules, corporate governance, anti-money laundering, etc.).  I will not list all of the documents published by these institutions. Instead, I would like to highlight the new impetus given to European supervision by the Lamfalussy process. Indeed, with 25 States, it had become essential to set up a new platform for co-operation. The establishment of three sectoral Level 3 Committees (CEIOPS for insurance, CESR for securities and CEBS for banking) has created strong incentives for enhanced co-operation in the area of supervision. Common European regulations have existed for decades (1st banking directive in 1977 and 1st insurance directive in 1979) but the value added of this approach is to promote a common and effective implementation of these regulations. 6 For instance, the CEBS is currently working on the concrete implementation of the revised Capital Adequacy Directive (CAD 3). Crucial issues, such as co-operation between the home country supervisor and the host country supervisors are being discussed. Clear and balanced rules are needed to allocate tasks between the different national authorities. The revised directive solves this problem by setting clear principles for the supervisor on a consolidated basis. However, the directive does not offer any solutions as regards the practical implementation of the directives provisions. In this context, the CEBS has drawn up some guidelines on this issue and is about to publish a paper which clarifies a number of points in the directive, such as the planning and coordination of supervisory activities in going concern, as well as in emergency situations.  It can be argued that these Lamfalussy Level 3 Committees are sector-specific and are therefore not suited to deal with cross-sectoral groups such as financial conglomerates. In order to tackle cross-sectoral issues, one must not ignore the various interactions between them. The joint meetings of the three secretariats in the framework of the three Level 3 Committees ensure an active and consistent approach to financial issues. They are in charge of issues of common concern, such as the supervision of financial conglomerates or guidelines on outsourcing. Moreover, the presence of observers from other committees in certain CEBS, CESR and CEIOPS working groups also contributes to strengthening the consistency of financial supervision. For instance, CEBS observers were present in CESR working groups on credit rating agencies. In return, the CEBS invited a CESR member to participate in its working groups on external credit assessment institutions. This cross-fertilisation is a crucial factor for furthering European convergence.  Last but not least, this active and daily co-operation should not be restricted to the European level. As the experts in charge of assessing the European Financial Services Action Plan have pointed out, international co-operation between supervisors must be further developed. That is why I am in favour of reinforcing the transatlantic dialogue. I was in the United States last week to meet monetary and financial authorities as well as representatives from the private sector. In return, the Commission bancaire welcomed a delegation of US Congressmen in midFebruary. 7 We could illustrate this transatlantic co-operation by referring to the issue of financial conglomerate supervision. Indeed, for the past few weeks, we have been having active discussions with the US authorities on the issue of financial conglomerates. European Member States have made assessments and established parallels between US regulations and the recent Financial Conglomerate Directive. This dialogue has enabled us to sign information-sharing agreements with a number of US authorities and to define a comprehensive supervisory monitoring process of international groups. It should not only lead to the removal of all divergences in terms of supervision - either between sectors or between countries - but also to the creation of a competitive level playing field and to the promotion of financial stability.  Let me also remind you that when there is a will, there is a way. I would like to mention, for example, the work carried out by the CEBS, notably on the definition of a Common European Reporting (COREP) framework for the new solvency ratio. Within this framework, all EU Member States will use the same templates and the same method for computing the ratio, including the use of common prudential filters for calculating the level of regulatory capital. This common reporting framework is a great achievement as it will considerably speed up the convergence of supervisory practices and significantly reduce the regulatory burden for financial institutions. It is a clear illustration of an effective and efficient co-operation between supervisors. Finally, I would like to stress that co-operation has not only been strengthened with banks but also across a whole range of sectors. It has enabled supervisory authorities to cover the whole spectrum of a groups activities, while retaining an in-depth knowledge of each of its activities. Conclusion Let me conclude my presentation by reminding you of my introductory question: What is the most effective supervisory framework for financial stability?. What I have tried to do in my short presentation today is to show that the institutional framework is not in itself a guarantee of effective supervision and that, at the end of the day, different ways of addressing institutional issues may lead to the same satisfactory results. 8 However, I am convinced that the specialisation of supervisory authorities and their proximity with financial institutions, together with strengthened co-operation between supervisors on a cross-border and cross-sector basis, are key factors for ensuring effective financial sector supervision and therefore contributing to financial stability. Thank you very much for your attention. 9

Title: The euro as a stable currency at the service of a dynamic economy
text: Speech by Mr Christian Noyer Governor of the Bank of France THE EURO: A STABLE CURRENCY AT THE SERVICE OF A DYNAMIC ECONOMY 31 MARCH 2005 UNIVERSITY OF SOCIAL SCIENCES TOULOUSE 1 Update of the Lausanne and Rennes speeches delivered in 2004, which benefited from the contribution of the European Relations Service. 1 PART 1: THE SUCCESS OF THE EURO RESTS ON SOLID FOUNDATIONS A. The achievements of the single monetary policy A.1. A modern institutional and operational framework A.1.1. The independence of the Eurosystem promotes price stability A.1.2. Transparency and accountability are essential to ensure A.1.3 credibility. The Eurosystem is based on operational decentralisation A.1.4. The Eurosystem benefits from an efficient operating framework A.2. Strategic framework A.2.1. A quantitative definition of price stability A.2.2. A "medium-term" orientation A.3. The achievements of the ECB's monetary policy B. Multilateral surveillance procedures within EMU B.1. A framework of multilateral surveillance procedures B.2. The new Member States respect the same rules PART 2: THE EURO: A POWERFUL ENGINE FOR GREATER ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL INTEGRATION AND INTERNATIONAL RECOGNITION A. The pillars of an optimal monetary zone Ly. The euro area is characterised by strong economic fundamentals A.2. Increasing economic homogeneity favours the transmission of monetary policy A.3. The integration of the financial sector is almost complete B. The euro now plays the role of international currency and nominal anchor B.1. The evolution of the private use of the euro B.1.1. A key global financial instrument B.1.2. An important intermediary of exchanges B.2. The growing official role of the euro B.2.1. A factor in the diversification of foreign exchange reserves B.2.2. A factor of stability for many exchange rate regimes B.3. The Eurosystem's position on the development of the international role of the euro PART 3: THE CHALLENGES OF THE SINGLE CURRENCY A. The need to strengthen budgetary cohesion and coordination within the Union B. Structural reforms need to be carried out in several areas B.1. A knowledge-based economy B.2. The competitiveness of enterprises B.3. Flexibility in the labour market B.4. The integration of markets for goods and services C. The challenge of enlargement CONCLUSION 2 Ladies and gentlemen 95 It is a great pleasure for me to speak at the University of Social Sciences of Toulouse, a world centre of excellence for research in economics, to talk to you about the euro, which is one of the most remarkable achievements of the European Union. 95 The legal basis for the single currency is the Treaty establishing the European Community, Article 105 of which states: "The main objective of the ESCB is to maintain price stability". Price stability and the convergence of the economies of the euro area are essential prerequisites for the single currency to be able to give its full support to the general economic policies in the Community, with a view to contributing to the achievement of the Objectives of the Community, as defined in Article 2" of the Treaty. 95 First of all, I would like to mention the foundations on which the success of the euro rests, namely, in particular, the single monetary policy and macroeconomic cooperation within the Economic and Monetary Union (Part 1). I would then like to touch briefly on economic integration within the euro area: the euro has indeed been a powerful factor in economic and financial integration, accentuated today by its growing international role (Part 2). Finally, I would like to recall the challenges that EMU, in order to be a full success, must face, namely, in particular, budgetary cohesion, structural reforms and the enlargement of the Union (Part 3). PART 1: THE SUCCESS OF THE EURO RESTS ON SOLID FOUNDATIONS These are the single monetary policy (A), on the one hand, which has made it possible, thanks to an effective and well-adapted policy framework, to achieve significant progress, and the proper functioning of macroeconomic cooperation in EMU (B), on the other. 3 Has. The achievements of the single monetary policy Over the past six years, the single monetary policy conducted by the Eurosystem, i.e. the whole of the European Central Bank and the twelve central banks of the euro area member countries, has been crowned with many successes. The successful changeover to the euro, in scriptural and then fiduciary form, is the first of these, probably the most emblematic. Before being in place, the single currency was long met with scepticism from many observers who considered it unrealistic to launch a new currency, the name of which itself was not fixed until the Madrid European Council of December 1995. Others questioned the possibility of considering a single monetary policy for a set of countries which, despite the speed of their convergence, still had significant disparities. The prospect of the creation of new institutions, in particular the European Central Bank, was also at the origin of many debates, the themes of which were mainly focused on the institutional and operational framework (Al) and on the strategies (A2) of a single monetary policy. Today, we can evaluate these achievements (A3). A.1. A modern institutional and operational framework The Eurosystem's institutional framework is based on the principles of independence, transparency and accountability and, finally, operational decentralisation. In this respect, the Eurosystem benefits from all the experience gained by the national central banks of the member countries. A.1.1. The independence of the Eurosystem promotes price stability 95 As many empirical studies have shown, there is no correlation between central bank independence and employment growth or volatility. In contrast, a nation's anti-inflationary performance seems to be highly correlated with the degree of independence of its central bank. 95 According to the Maastricht Treaty, the Eurosystem's main task is to ensure and maintain price stability. The independence of the European Central Bank and 4 of the twelve central banks of the member countries of the euro area is therefore enshrined in the Treaty. 95 Functionally, this means that, in the exercise of their tasks, neither the European Central Bank nor the national central banks of the Eurosystem seek or take instructions from the Community institutions, national governments or any other body. This is full independence in the institutional and operational sense. A.1.2. Transparency and accountability are essential to ensure credibility 95 Naturally, the independence of these institutions is matched by the transparency of their decisions and accountability to the public and its representatives. In the case of young institutions, such as the ECB, transparency is even more essential to establish their credibility and establish the confidence of economic agents in a currency. To establish this credibility, to gain this trust of agents, it is absolutely imperative to be understood and for this it is necessary to be transparent. 95 The imperatives of accountability and transparency are enshrined in the Treaty in very general terms. The Eurosystem has gone beyond its strict institutional obligations in these areas: - firstly, the Governing Council clarified its definition of price stability (increase of less than, but close to, 2% in the medium term); - secondly, the ECB has gone beyond the accountability requirements established by the Treaty by establishing regular hearings of its President before the European Parliament and regular informal meetings with the Eurogroup of Finance Ministers; - another sign of transparency is the regular publication of reports on economic developments and central bank analyses, of which the ECB's Monthly Bulletin is the best-known vehicle; 5 - Finally, most importantly, at the end of each of the meetings devoted to monetary policy decisions, the President and Vice-President of the ECB hold a press conference followed by an open exchange with journalists, details of which are published on the ECB's website. It is important to recall that the ECB was the first of the central banks to undergo this type of exercise, which provides a unique opportunity to explain and comment on monetary policy decisions, immediately and in detail. 95 On the other hand, the Governing Council of the ECB has chosen not to publish the minutes of its meetings. Indeed, the publication of the minutes has certain disadvantages: - first of all, when they are very detailed, the participants risk "speaking for the minutes", whereas, when they are not detailed, they are of little more interest than a simple press release; - secondly, they may complicate the evolution of the positions taken by its members in the light of the arguments developed; - finally, what is most important, in the case of the euro area, the analysis of votes could be read and interpreted in the light of national concerns or interests, which would be misleading and could threaten both the independence of the members of the Governing Council and the credibility of our decision-making processes. A.1.3. The Eurosystem is based on operational decentralisation 95 The third element, operational decentralisation, is a key feature of the Eurosystem. The division of roles between the ECB and the national central banks is one of the elements of its cohesion and its main driving force. According to this principle, monetary policy decisions are taken centrally, by the Governing Council of the ECB, but implemented by the national central banks. 6 95 A key point is that it is the national central banks - excluding the ECB - that keep the accounts of commercial banks, and are therefore able to ensure their refinancing and the cohesion of national settlement systems. The use of modern technologies and means of communication has made it possible to carry out market operations simultaneously in all the national central banks, instead of concentrating them at a given geographical point and thus perfectly reconciling the decentralisation of operations and the unity of the euro area money market. The same system applies to other monetary areas (cash management, payment systems, etc.). A.1.4. The Eurosystem benefits from an efficient operating framework In addition to this modern institutional framework, the Eurosystem also benefits from a particularly efficient operational framework, which is based on two components: - a coherent range of monetary policy instruments, developed in accordance with the principles of free competition, equal treatment, simplicity and transparency: these instruments must allow the adjustment of bank liquidity and the effective management of interest rates in all circumstances; - procedures ensuring a high level of security for all interbank transactions and high-value payments within the euro area and with other countries of the Economic Union, in particular the Target system, whose role has been decisive in the process of integration of the euro money market. A.2. The strategic framework The effectiveness of the single monetary policy also depends on its policy framework, which can be characterised by two main elements: a quantitative definition of price stability and a medium-term stance of monetary policy. 7 A.2.1. A quantitative definition of price stability 95 The definition adopted by the Governing Council of the ECB in October 1998 was confirmed and clarified in May 2003, following an in-depth review of its policy framework. At the end of this assessment exercise, the Governing Council clarified that price stability is defined by annual HICP growth close to, but below, 2% over the medium term. 95 This definition calls for several comments: - by stating that inflation should be close to 2%, the Governing Council first wanted to confirm the symmetrical nature of its strategy by excluding deflation situations. This precision also makes it possible to take into account possible measurement biases on the price index, as well as inflation differences within the euro area; - the quantitative definition of monetary stability brings the Eurosystem's policy framework closer to that of central banks based on inflation targeting, in particular when considering a broad meaning of inflation, such as that presented under the term 'flexible inflation target'. The big difference lies in the role of forecasts from an econometric model, which play a leading role in "pure" inflation-targeting strategies, whereas they are only one element in the decision-making process of the Governing Council of the ECB. A.2.2. A "medium-term" orientation What exactly are the implications of this medium-term stance of the ECB's monetary policy strategy? 95 The first is that the single monetary policy strategy does not have a fixed horizon, determined once and for all ex ante, but aims, as far as possible, to take into account the "long and variable delays in monetary policy" dear to Milton Friedman. Taking this uncertainty into account is particularly important in the case of the euro area, whose "deep structural parameters" are partly unknown. 8 More prosaically, this medium-term stance of the single monetary policy recognises that it is impossible for a central bank to accurately control the price path in the very short term. 95 The second implication is that indicators relevant to monetary policy must reflect, almost exhaustively, the main factors driving inflation in the short and long term. From this point of view, the monetary policy strategy seeks, as far as possible, to mobilize "complete information". This is reflected in the concepts of economic approach and monetary approach (also known as a two-pillar approach) which are taken up in particular at the press conferences of the President of the ECB following monetary policy decisions. The economic approach reviews short-term, economic and financial indicators in relation to the main determinants of short-term inflation; the monetary approach is based on the monetary explanation of long-term inflation. The medium-term stance of the single monetary policy makes it necessary to link these two complementary approaches to inflationary. In this respect, the ECB's monetary policy strategy is more encompassing than pure inflation-targeting or pure monetary targeting strategies. A.3. The achievements of the ECB's monetary policy What first assessment can be made after these first six years of implementation of the single monetary policy? 95 I would like to highlight three key points: - First, the achievement of monetary policy objectives. While faced with a series of adverse shocks (on oil prices, food, services prices, administered prices and indirect taxation), leading to HICP developments exceeding 2% year-on-year from 2000 to 2002 and in 2004, the single monetary policy managed to stabilise and anchor, over the entire year period, medium-term inflation expectations around 1.8 to 1.9%. This represents a level close to, but less than, 2% in line with its definition of price stability as shown, for example, by inflation expectations from surveys (e.g. Consensus Forecast, or the 9 BCE with professional forecasters). Financing conditions, which reflect in particular the low level of short- and long-term interest rates in the euro area, remained particularly favourable. These good results illustrate the credibility of the single monetary policy. - Second, the understanding and predictability of monetary policy actions. Contrary to popular belief, most monetary policy decisions have been perfectly anticipated by the markets. This diagnosis comes from the studies conducted by the Eurosystem but also from the reports published by the "ECB Watchers", with whom, moreover, the ECB maintains regular links, in particular in the form of annual conferences. A comparison with the Fed does not show any real difference between the two institutions in terms of the ability of markets to anticipate monetary policy decisions. This is a sign of the transparency of the single monetary policy. The fact, in particular, that the ECB chose means of communication other than the publication of the minutes of the meetings of the Governing Council did not prevent it from achieving a high level of understanding and predictability. Thirdly, the trust and approval of European citizens. Indeed, the euro has easily established itself among economic agents and is now part of the daily lives of European consumers. And surveys confirm that the public has confidence in the euro, which they consider a sound currency, and in the Eurosystem as a central bank. 95 However, two factors of concern remain: - the first lies in the natural difficulty of moving towards an entirely new price reference system - and it may take many years before all economic agents have fully integrated it; - the second factor is the perception of excessive price increases by consumers, linked to the changeover to the euro cash. Indeed, public attention focused on a small number of goods and services that experienced abnormal price increases during this event, leading to a misperception of the real rate of inflation. This mismatch between perceived and actual inflation is fortunately gradually being reduced. 10 B. Multilateral surveillance procedures within EMU In EMU, where a single monetary policy coexists with twelve governments responsible for fiscal and structural policies, an appropriate institutional framework is essential to ensure overall coherence. This is in particular the purpose of the Stability and Growth Pact, which specifies and supplements the relevant provisions of the Treaty. For this framework to be fully operational, it must be simple, easy to implement and capable of ensuring sound and sustainable fiscal policies. Thus, multilateral surveillance processes have been designed from the outset, in order to achieve a satisfactory level of cohesion in the policies followed by all Member States. B.1. A framework of multilateral surveillance procedures 95 The implementation of surveillance is entrusted to the Eurogroup (informal meeting of finance ministers of euro area countries) and the Ecofin Council (meeting of finance ministers of all EU countries, with decision-making power), together with the European Commission. Mutual surveillance combines multilateral surveillance and dialogue procedures, compliance with common rules and provisions, and member States' commitment to good practices and common objectives. The construction of Europe is a project in constant evolution and each meeting of the European Council has given rise, in the recent past, to processes that have taken the name of the places where summits were held. This applies to processes in areas such as labour markets (Luxembourg process), economic reform of goods and capital markets (Cardiff process) and macroeconomic dialogue to promote responsible wage developments (Cologne process). 95 The stability programmes (for euro area Member States) and convergence programmes (for non-euro area Member States) make it possible to examine national budgetary policies at Community level from a medium-term perspective and to assess their conformity with the provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact. At the centre of the coordination process are the Broad Economic Policy Guidelines (BEPGs), which contain a medium-term assessment of the state of convergence of national economic policies. BEPGs play a role 11 crucial because all the coordination processes mentioned above must be compatible with their recommendations. Program and BEPG updates are presented on a multi-year basis and their implementation is reviewed annually. B.2. The new Member States shall comply with the same rules Let me point out that the ten new Member States are already accustomed to mutual review processes. Since their accession on 1 May 2004, the budgetary policy of the ten new Member States has been subject to the same review measures as that of the other Member States. Budget deficits are a key concern for the new EU countries. As the eventual adoption of the euro is subject to compliance with the budget deficit criterion in the sense of Maastricht, these countries are now forced to undertake substantial budgetary reforms, especially since their deficits are largely due to structural inadequacies. PART 2: THE EURO: A POWERFUL ENGINE FOR GREATER ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL INTEGRATION AND INTERNATIONAL RECOGNITION The strengthening of the operational and institutional framework goes hand in hand with increasing convergence within the monetary area (A) and with the strengthening of the role of the euro at international level (B). Has. The pillars of an optimal monetary zone Increasing convergence is the result of sound macroeconomic fundamentals (Al) and economic homogeneity (A2), reinforced by the integration of the financial sector (A3). The adoption of the same currency by eleven and then twelve European countries is an unprecedented fact. This adoption was only possible thanks to the increasing convergence of the economies in question during the nineties. If it seems abusive to consider the euro area as an optimal monetary zone, as Robert Mundell understood it, 12 however, several recent studies have shown that the convergence process, economic homogeneity, the degree of synchronization of business cycles and the propensity of the economies of the zone to trade with each other have increased since the implementation of the single monetary policy. The latter, by also succeeding in anchoring inflation expectations in all Member States at a low level, has shown itself capable of imposing a high degree of nominal convergence. Finally, economic and monetary union protected its members from exchange rate crises and macroeconomic imbalances that affected them quite frequently, just over a decade ago. Ly. The euro area is characterised by solid economic fundamentals 95 The euro area economies are currently characterised by a high degree of structural convergence, a low level of inflation, close to 2%, and favourable monetary and financial conditions for economic activity. These favourable financing conditions are also explained by the resilience of the euro area's financial and banking systems to the various shocks that have affected the global economy: sound infrastructure, good performance of banks and financial institutions, progress in complying with international standards. Private savings are also abundant. 95 In addition, the euro area is an attractive economy because of the quality of its workforce (e.g. almost 5% of GDP is spent on education) and infrastructure. 95 These various assets enabled it to attract 8067 billion in direct investment in 2004. A.2. Increasing economic homogeneity favours the transmission of monetary policy While monetary union does not necessarily imply that all Member States have the same rate of growth or inflation at all times, a number of recent empirical studies illustrate an increasing economic homogeneity within the euro area. 13 95 In terms of activity first of all, several studies presented under the aegis of a joint working group between the CEPR (Centre for Economic Policy Research) and the Eurosystem show that the correlation between cyclical fluctuations in economic activity as a whole in most euro area countries, already strong before the implementation of the single monetary policy, has increased since 1999. The same applies to consumption and investment. According to some measures, a common 'European' component would play a more important role than the national components in cyclical fluctuations in activity in most of these economies. The degree of correlation between national and aggregate cycles at euro area level would thus vary in the range between 0.70 and 0.92. 95 In terms of inflation, according to the work carried out by the Eurosystem, the degree of dispersion of inflation rates within the euro area would not be much higher than that observed in the United States, where there are much stronger recall forces than in the euro area - such as the presence of a single federal budget balancing cyclical differences between regions, more unified markets for goods and services and labour, a single monetary policy since 1913. Thus, in these first years of EMU's existence, the standard deviation of the annual price shift in the twelve countries of the euro area is estimated to be close to 1 point against 0.8 points for the fourteen metropolitan areas of the United States. 95 Finally, recent updates of the Eurosystem's important research on the transmission mechanisms of the single monetary policy suggest that the responses of member countries' economies to monetary policy impulses are increasingly homogeneous. In particular, the standard deviation of the time taken to adjust lending rates to changes in the policy rate would, on average, have halved since the implementation of the single monetary policy. A.3. Financial sector integration nearing completion The introduction of the euro acted as a catalyst for financial integration: 14 - the latter is almost complete as regards the euro money market. From the first weeks of the implementation of the single monetary policy, the price differences observed on the national interbank markets faded very quickly to less than 5 basis points, which corresponds to the bid-ask spread usually observed in this market; - a similar integration movement has also occurred in the European bond markets, where there has been a tightening of government securities yields, as well as in derivatives markets with the impressive development of Eurex and Liffe and, to a lesser extent, in the stock markets and the market for corporate debt issues; - the euro area and, more broadly, the European Union now have a coherent financial architecture. First of all, the implementation of the Financial Services Action Plan, defined at the Lisbon European Council in March 2000, is being completed. Secondly, the "Lamfalussy process" should promote the establishment of a new institutional architecture in the field of supervision and regulation of the financial sector - i.e. securities markets but also banks and insurance - by developing more flexible and uniform technical rules. B. The euro now plays the role of international currency and nominal anchor The available data confirm the growing role of the euro at international level. At the regional level, it plays a leading anchor role, making it the valuable vector of a culture of stability. The growing role of the euro at international level is the result of the development of both its use at private level (B1) and its official role (B2). However, the Eurosystem observes a position of neutrality vis-e0-vis the external development of its currency (B3). B.1. The evolution of private use of the euro 15 The euro has the key functions attributed to any international currency: it is already a leading investment and financing currency and an important intermediary for international trade. Although it is still limited, its role as a billing currency is expected to grow in the coming years. B.1.1. A key global financial instrument 95 The use of the euro as an investment and financing currency on international capital markets has developed immediately. Between mid-2003 and mid-2004, it accounted for 33 per cent of net issuance of international debt securities2, up from 20 per cent in 1998. In mid-2004, almost 31% of the stock of international debt securities3 was denominated in euro, compared with less than 20% in 1998. 95 Another very remarkable development is the emergence of a market for "corporate" securities, i.e. securities issued by companies, whose volume grew significantly during the first years of the euro. 95 The best allocation of savings in Europe requires capital markets to be more efficient and integrated. However, this integration has not yet been fully completed, particularly as regards the repo, deposit and securities markets. 95 However, the euro area is lagging behind in terms of equity markets. According to BIS data, the eurozone's market capitalization represented only 16.1% of the global market capitalization compared to 48.5% for the United States. But the euro has fostered a tendency to regroup the European financial centres already in place. B.1.2. An important intermediary in trade 2 According to a narrow definition, i.e. not including international issues in euro by euro area residents. 3 According to the same definition. 16 As a trading intermediary, the euro was involved in 37% of foreign exchange transactions in 2004, compared with 88% for the dollar. However, the share of the euro is greater than the sum of the shares of the former European national currencies. This result was not obvious at the time of the introduction of the euro. 95 A growing role as a billing/settlement currency: - with regard to the use of the European currency in international trade, between 50% and 60% of the trade of almost all euro area countries with the rest of the world was denominated in euro in 2003. This applies to both exports and imports. With regard to EU trade with third countries, 54% of Japanese exports to the European Union were invoiced or settled in euros in 2002 (44% in 2000) and 31% of Japanese imports from the European Union were denominated in euros (compared to 17% in 2000); - in countries which are not members of the zone but where integration with the euro area is very high, such as the new Member States of Central and Eastern Europe, the use of the euro in trade is also very marked, with 40% to 80% of exports/imports being invoiced or paid in euro. 95 On the other hand, the use of the single currency is more limited on commodity markets, particularly oil. The dollar still plays a preponderant role, which should continue, given the phenomena of inertia related to the effects of "network". This is not surprising, since the acquisition of international status is, in all respects, a long process. All in all, these developments underline the fact that the euro has been able to inspire confidence among private investors and promote greater liquidity in capital markets. B.2. The growing official role of the euro The growing demand for the euro as a reserve and reference currency has also strengthened its official role. 4 Since foreign exchange transactions always involve two currencies, the sum of the shares of the currencies is equal to 200%. 17 B.2.1. A factor in the diversification of foreign exchange reserves The euro has become a stabilizing factor in the international monetary system, particularly thanks to its function of diversifying international reserves. 95 According to the latest available IMF data, the euro was the second reserve currency after the dollar in 2003. The euro currently represents 19.7% against 63.8% for the dollar. The share of the euro has increased: it was only 12.6% in 1999. This trend offers many countries a valuable buffer against large exchange rate fluctuations, as public investors can diversify their reserve assets. 95 Several central banks in emerging countries (European, Middle East and especially Asia)5 have recently announced their willingness to increase the share of the euro in their reserves. This phenomenon is all the more important given that Asia's relative weight in international foreign exchange reserves is high (66% including India). B.2.2. A factor of stability for many exchange rate regimes 95 Far from being the mere addition of previous European currencies, the euro has inherited the most remarkable characteristics of the old national currencies. The positive effects have been noticeable. The euro has created an environment of historically low interest rates. In addition, it put an end to intra-European exchange rate crises. Even if these two elements are sometimes forgotten, it is interesting to note that Europe has not experienced tumult as a result, for example, of the uncertainties created by the recent geopolitical tensions at the global level, which would have caused, in the past, strong turbulence. 95 These benefits are perhaps even more valuable for neighbouring countries, since 50 of them (including those in the franc zone) have already adopted the euro as their currency. 5 Ex: Russia, Ukraine, Korea, Japan, China, OPEC countries. 6 Ex: Russia, Ukraine, Korea, Japan, China, OPEC countries. 18 reference for their exchange rate regimes, either as a single anchor (in about 30 cases) or as a component of a basket of currencies. 95 The use of the euro in the exchange rate regimes of third countries mainly concerns regions which have established close links with the euro area or which have set up special institutional arrangements with the EU (acceding and candidate countries, Balkans, North Africa and the franc zone). In any case, these exchange rate regimes are the result of a unilateral decision, which does not involve any commitment on the part of the Eurosystem. However, close links with the euro may have the advantage for these countries of "importing" credibility, provided that appropriate policies are pursued simultaneously. 95 With regard to the ten new EU countries, let me stress that the criterion of exchange rate stability within ERM II requires that this stability be achieved before the adoption of the single currency. The advantage is that the adoption of the euro will be the culmination of a structured convergence process within a multilateral framework. This is certainly one of the most important challenges facing the euro area in the coming years. B.3. The Eurosystem's position on the development of the international role of the euro 95 The Eurosystem observes an official position of neutrality vis-e0-vis the external development of its currency, which means that it does not promote or prevent the development of the international role of the euro, as it considers that it is a process essentially driven by the markets. 95 In addition, the Eurosystem is aware of the need to avoid too abrupt developments, which could lead to excessive volatility or misalignment of exchange rates. 95 In fact, conducting a monetary policy oriented towards maintaining price stability is the best contribution that the Eurosystem can make to development 19 international currency, because it promotes confidence in the value of the euro and strengthens the credibility of the zone. PART 3: THE CHALLENGES OF THE SINGLE CURRENCY As the euro's environment continues to change, public authorities face new challenges when formulating and implementing their economic policy decisions. I would like to draw attention to three of these challenges which, in my opinion, will weigh heavily on the future of the euro and european integration. Firstly, it is necessary to strengthen EU budgetary coordination in order to consolidate the foundations on which the euro (A) is based, at a time when fiscal policies in Europe are facing specific challenges such as an ageing population. Second, there is a need to implement structural reforms (B) to better prepare countries for the challenges ahead. Finally, the enlargement process (C), which is certainly already a reality, will require further efforts to ensure that the new Member States make further progress and eventually catch up. Has. The need to strengthen budgetary cohesion and coordination within the Union 95 Compliance with the rules and procedures set out in the Treaty and the provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact impose the same budgetary discipline on all Member States: the budget deficit must not exceed the ceiling of 3% of GDP and the total debt ratio should not exceed 60% of GDP. These limits help to ensure an optimal policy mix at euro area level, as a lax fiscal policy may ultimately jeopardise the achievement of price stability. Finally, they maintain sustainable growth and employment and are conducive to economic stability. 20 95 Budgetary discipline is indeed of paramount importance for EMU, as it is a necessary corollary of the single monetary policy. Member States are expected to regard their economic policies as matters of "common interest", given the impact that their budgetary decisions may have on the euro area as a whole. In a monetary union, it is of the utmost importance to avoid "free rider behaviour", hence the 'no bailout' clause in the Maastricht Treaty. 95 The institutional framework for coordinating national economic policies has worked well in the past, leaving sufficient room for manoeuvre to cope with a slowdown in growth. In line with the concept of balancing structural budget balances, EU Member States have committed themselves to achieving and maintaining a "close to balance or surplus" budgetary position over the business cycle. This requirement should make it possible to cope with asymmetric shocks and cyclical fluctuations, while allowing automatic stabilisers to have their full effect. This flexibility is essential to overcome asymmetric shocks while preserving the long-term sustainability of public finances and the autonomy of monetary policy. 95 However, the difficulties faced by many European countries have given rise to strong criticism of the budgetary provisions of the Treaty and the Stability and Growth Pact. In this context, the European Commission presented reform proposals last September; discussions in the Council of Ministers were finally concluded in March and the agreement on this reform, which aims to modify the modalities of the implementation of the Pact, was endorsed at the European Council on 22-23 March. These amendments focus on two aspects: the preventive arm and the corrective arm of the Compact: - (FR) On the preventive arm, the most interesting change has been to seek a more symmetrical application of the Pact, in periods of low and high economic conditions, by encouraging Member States to strengthen the implementation of a sound budgetary policy in periods of high economic conditions. When growth is strong, countries need to mobilize even more to reduce deficits or generate surpluses and thus reduce the stock of public debt, often to high levels. This means 21 that in times of favourable economic conditions, less lax fiscal policies are needed to ensure the long-term sustainability of public finances. On the other hand, other changes, such as the differentiation by country of the medium-term objective, or the taking into account of the impact of structural reforms - for example of pension systems - are questionable, in particular because they are likely to increase the complexity of the Pact and reduce the effectiveness of the preventive arm. - (FR) On the corrective arm (i.e. concerning the implementation of the excessive deficit procedure in respect of a Member State that does not comply with the 3% and 60% reference values), the amendments introduced clearly lead to a relaxation of the Pact. One example is the new definition of "exceptional and temporary circumstances", which avoids triggering the excessive deficit procedure when the growth rate is negative or very low relative to potential. It should also be noted that a list of "relevant factors" - which are taken into account when assessing whether the government deficit is exceeded above the 3% of GDP reference value - which includes, in particular, expenditure on research and development, official development assistance and expenditure related to the reform of pension systems or the unification of Europe. Finally, it is necessary to highlight a general extension of the deadlines granted to the States for the correction of the excessive deficit. 95 Following this agreement by the Council of Ministers on improving the implementation of the Pact, the Governing Council of the ECB has spoken publicly to express its concerns. He recalled that sound fiscal policies and a monetary policy focused on price stability are essential for the success of Economic and Monetary Union. They are indispensable conditions for macroeconomic stability, growth and cohesion in the euro area. The Governing Council of the ECB stressed the imperative that Member States, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union implement the revised framework in a rigorous and coherent manner, conducive to the conduct of prudent fiscal policies. Compliance with the central objective of a balanced budget remains all the more essential as the European Union will have to tackle the problem of ageing. 22 rapid population, whose implications for public finances are considerable, both in terms of health spending and pension systems. Given that reforms in these areas are likely to be noticeable only in the medium and long term, it is essential that European countries take all necessary measures to prevent the consequences of these demographic developments, particularly in budgetary terms. 95 The implementation of sound fiscal policies also requires improving the quality of public spending. A first step in this direction would be to focus the adjustment process on current expenditure rather than investment, unlike what was done in most countries in the late nineties. More generally, EU countries need to undertake structural reforms aimed at strengthening growth potential and promoting job creation. On these points, the Eurosystem has repeatedly and unambiguously called on these countries to carry out these reforms. B. Structural reforms need to be carried out in several areas Nevertheless, in Europe, particularly in the euro area, there are still significant structural rigidities that need to be addressed if the highest possible non-inflationary growth is to be promoted. I would like to mention here several avenues which are also the subject of a consensus within the Governing Council of the euro area. They relate in particular to the efforts to be pursued with regard to the role and importance of research (B1) to increase the growth potential of the euro area, the development of "agglomeration forces" to facilitate the location of enterprises (B2), the efforts to be made finally to increase flexibility on the labour market (B3) and the integration of the markets for goods and services (B4). B.1. A knowledge-based economy With regard to the first point, the strategy adopted unanimously at the Lisbon European Council in March 2000, which aims to make the European Union "the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustainable economic growth accompanied by a qualitative and quantitative improvement in employment". 23 and greater social cohesion", provides a frame of reference to guide public action. In particular, it stresses the importance of research, innovation and the dissemination of new technologies in raising the level of productivity of the economy. It also aims to give the European economy and all EU member countries more flexibility, more activity, and more jobs. This is an ambitious strategy but crucial for the future of Europe and the euro area. B.2. The competitiveness of enterprises In this context, due in particular to international competition, it is also crucial to develop "agglomeration forces", i.e. incentives that force companies to concentrate geographically to benefit from economies of scale and external. In particular, the existence of an area with high purchasing power is one of the important factors in the location of European companies. I have already mentioned the attractiveness of the euro area, but we need to go even further, particularly as regards controlling costs, particularly wage costs, and the need to ensure an environment favourable to the competitiveness of European companies. Indeed, jobs are preferably created in economies that know how to moderate their unit production costs and offer an environment as favourable as possible to the competitiveness of enterprises. This presupposes the continuation of structural reforms in the labour market and in the goods and services markets. B.3. Flexibility in the labour market 95 As far as the labour market is concerned, the euro area is characterised by a low employment rate, above 63% in 2004 compared to 75% in the United States, which translates into a significant loss in terms of GDP per capita (almost 25% lower than in the United States). This low employment rate is the result of the high level of unemployment in the euro area, currently close to 9%, and above all the low participation rate. 95 As unemployment in Europe is essentially structural in origin, it is therefore important to make the labour market more fluid and to preserve an incentive structure to raise the participation rate. This presupposes, in particular, that 24 implements measures to reduce labour costs and business burdens, but also to promote incentive structures for workers among the youngest age groups but also the oldest and the least qualified. Contrary to what is observed in the United States, where there is a long tradition of professional and geographical mobility, cultural and linguistic differences are still an obstacle to the mobility of the labour factor in Europe. The low level of occupational and geographical mobility also depends on an probably insufficient differentiation of wages in the euro area countries, which would make it possible to better reflect differences in terms of productivity gains or development between regions or sectors of activity. B.4. Integration of markets for goods and services 95 The increase in the level of productivity in the euro area is also based on the deepening of reforms in the market for goods and services, since Europe's backwardness, particularly vis-e0-vis the United States, also stems from the presence of structural rigidities linked to the existence of barriers to entry into this market. However, in the absence of competitive pressures, there is little incentive for firms to increase their efficiency. 95 Regulatory reforms must therefore be undertaken both at member country level and at the level of the Economic Union as a whole. According to research carried out under the aegis of the CEPR and the Eurosystem, the creation of the single market has already been a major step, but the objective remains that of a full integration of the market for goods and services at European level. This applies in particular to the services sector, where, it must be admitted, progress has been less marked than in other sectors of activity. Admittedly, this is still partly explained by cultural differences. The fact remains that the public authorities, at both national and Community level, must continue their efforts and promote the degree of competition and integration in all sectors of activity. I mentioned services, but this is also the case in the energy sectors, particularly electricity, transport, particularly rail, and postal services. 7 This figure will be updated when Eurostat publishes the 2004 statistics (officially before the end of March). 25 C. The challenge of enlargement Ten new countries joined the EU on 1 May 2004. They are intended to adopt the euro after having met the nominal convergence criteria. Beyond the institutional challenges that remain (independence of central banks, adaptation of banking systems, fight against money laundering, etc.), the major challenge facing us is to meet the challenge of real convergence between East and West Europe. This will require years of major structural reforms to accelerate growth and close the East-West divide; it presupposes, in particular, respect for the macroeconomic framework to which all the Member States party to the euro today have agreed, in particular the successful participation in ERM II. It is indeed necessary to avoid any precipitation damaging to competitiveness and to carry out fundamental reforms, particularly in terms of the sustainability of public finances, prior to the entry into this exchange rate mechanism, a guarantee of a real sustainable convergence beneficial to the whole area. Conclusion 95 I would like to conclude by saying that the euro has met our expectations. After the unprecedented challenge of the continent-wide cash changeover, the euro was successful, the euro replaced the old national currencies almost instantly, without logistical disruption. It has promoted stability through its credibility and has protected many countries in the zone from excessive exchange rate volatility and financial market turbulence. These results must be emphasised all the more insistently since for several years it had been said that the euro would remain a "sea snake" or that it would create significant macroeconomic difficulties. These scenarios did not materialize. 95 The euro therefore represents a major cornerstone of European integration. That said, and regardless of its own merits, a currency is not an end in itself even if the new Member States are ardently determined to adopt it as soon as possible. Participation in monetary union must be based on a process of sustainable convergence. The enlargement of the euro area will give new impetus in this respect to the meeting of challenges, as economic policy-makers suffer 26 now a much stronger pressure in dealing with difficulties when they could ignore them before. This is an essential contribution to the construction of a stronger European Union, to which I strongly adhere. In conclusion, let me express my confidence in the future of the euro, which, six years after its creation, is the clear symbol of European identity and its strength. 27
