Il est important que les tablissements de crdit franais intgrent dans les meilleurs dlais ce nouveau dispositif, en troite coordination avec la Commission bancaire. Pour sa part, celle-ci mobilisera tous les moyens  sa disposition pour que ces nouvelles modalits dinformation soient mises en place  bonne date. En matire de stabilit financire, le Comit de supervision bancaire, qui runit, au sein de la BCE, les superviseurs bancaires et les banques centrales nationales du SEBC, a poursuivi ses travaux relatifs au suivi des volutions conjoncturelles et structurelles du systme financier europen, en les largissant aux autres domaines du secteur financier, telles que les assurances ou les marchs financiers. Tous ces travaux, nombreux et intenses, qui se dveloppent au niveau europen visent  promouvoir toujours davantage le dialogue, la coopration et lharmonisation concrte des pratiques de supervision entre les 25 pays de lUnion. Le schma institutionnel actuel, qui repose sur deux jambes, lune nationale, lautre europenne, a fait preuve en 2005 de sa capacit  mettre en uvre des normes communes 10 dapplication et de supervision de la rforme  Ble II  et des IAS/IFRS. Il a ainsi confirm sa solidit et son adaptabilit. * * * * * Pour rsumer et conclure, je dirai que les tablissements de crdit et les entreprises dinvestissement franais ont prsent de bonnes performances  lissue de lexercice 2004, mais doivent privilgier davantage des modes de gestion prudents et axs sur une vision de long terme. La mise en place de dispositifs prudentiels nouveaux, y compris de nature qualitative, doit constituer un facteur puissant et rapide de progrs  cet gard. Mais il importe aussi que les banques renforcent leurs propres vigilance et prudence dans les diffrents domaines que jai voqus. Cest dans ces conditions que la place bancaire franaise, aujourdhui incontestablement solide et performante, maintiendra son rang international et poursuivra son dveloppement domestique et mondial. 11

Title: Corporate governance and banking do banks govern themselves like other companies
text: "Corporate governance and banking: do banks govern themselves like other companies" Presentation by Christian NOYER, Governor of the Banque de France delivered as part of the seminar series "Law, Economics and Justice in the Banking Sector" Court of Cassation Monday, 10 October 2005 --------- Corporate governance is a good concept that we unfortunately tend to rediscover only in bad times. In fact, it is the periods of slowing growth or the difficulties encountered by certain groups that lead to questions about the way decisions are made in the company, and its organizational structures. Do they make it possible to take into account all the interests at stake, not only those of the owners of the company but also those of other stakeholders (investors, markets, general interest)? Sometimes, failures highlight strategies, or even individual behaviors of leaders, of flight forward, tending to mask difficulties. Similarly, when sluggish demand weighs on the cash position of companies, when the valuation of their assets is contested, the natural tendency is to denounce the errors of management systems to explain the fall in performance. Conversely, in a phase of strong growth, markets more easily "forgive" negligence or mistakes and good governance is no longer necessarily a priority. But it is before the difficulties that the necessary precautionary measures must be taken, especially when they concern the structures. From this point of view, it is indisputable that the banking sector has a specificity. Banks receive deposits from the public, and the proper functioning of their deposit accounts is essential for the 99% of French people who hold them. In addition, they are very closely linked to each other by their participation in payment systems: national interbank systems thus exchange in France in four days sums greater than the amount of the annual Gross Domestic Product of the France. The importance of the consequences that the failure of a banking company can have for the financial system and for the economy as a whole led to the generalisation - well before the current debates on governance - of a system of regulation of banks which obviously also incorporates standards of good governance. The current debates on companies also take up some of the issues already dealt with by banking regulation, such as the importance of internal control systems. The analysis of the particularities of banking activity makes it possible to understand how the specificity of this sector is reflected in the field of governance. I - Banking activity has specificities with regard to governance A) Banking activity can be carried out in a wide variety of legal forms Under French law there is no particular legal form of credit institutions, even if, following the Community harmonization of 1977, only legal persons can carry out banking activities, putting an end to the long history of private banking personal enterprise. Outside the mutual sector, the form of public limited company is the most widespread but we can also find examples of other types of companies (limited partnerships, in particular). I note that the Committee of Credit Institutions and Investment Firms, which is responsible for 'verifying the adequacy of the undertaking's legal form for the exercise of the activity of a credit institution', has so far never authorised limited liability companies as banks. It also considered it necessary to pay particular attention to ensuring that the operational flexibility allowed by the simplified joint-stock company did not impede the requirements of prudential security. As such, he expressly stated that institutions wishing to adopt this form must provide in their statutes for the existence of a collegiate body, in charge in particular of designating and dismissing responsible managers other than the president. It is clear that it is precisely a specific concern for governance that guides its action. The aim is to strengthen the balance in the exercise of management and control functions, regardless of the legal form adopted. The corporate bodies of banks must therefore comply with both the same rules, including criminal rules, as those governing other industrial and commercial enterprises and the constraints specific to their sector. Added to this can be the impact of regulations enacted to protect the integrity of capital markets, which affect banks in the same way as other participants in these markets. As soon as a bank goes public, the whole scheme to guarantee the rights of minority shareholders, for example, will apply in full. I also note that there is no mitigation of the banker's liability on the ground that it would be more difficult to evaluate a complex financial product than an industrial product. On the contrary, the banker is considered a risk professional; he is expected to master them better than any other company. B) Banking activity has specificities with regard to governance Summarized simply, and according to the terms of French law, banking activity essentially consists of receiving deposits, granting credits and making available or managing means of payment. All these activities have a common denominator: risk-taking over time. The job of a banker is to know how to combine these different risks in a complex assembly of prudence and profitability. The essential tool for its activity is the trust that customers give (or do not grant) to the establishment. This simple puts the bank in a very special situation, since it must ensure the permanence of this trust, even though the nature of its activity can make the risks more difficult to control by the usual governance mechanisms. Trust must be exercised on an ongoing basis The breakdown of public confidence in a bank has an immediate consequence: it usually signs the death warrant of the institution. I think it can be said that a non-financial company does not suffer from this constraint in such a strong way. If, for example, a car manufacturer markets a dangerous model, it is likely that a sharp drop in sales will follow public awareness; it is not certain, however, that it will prove insurmountable. The mistrust will probably be targeted at one model and not at the whole production. Similarly, when a supplier has doubts about the business practices of one of its customers, it will not seek to stop all business flows. Most of the time it will be content to impose stricter operating conditions (orders confirmed in writing, cash payment etc.). On the other hand, if doubt arises about the financial health or reputation of a bank, it is all its customers and suppliers (other banks) who will suddenly seek to withdraw their funds and stop lending, thereby causing the cessation of payments in a very short time. However, the nature of the activity can sometimes make it difficult to detect errors or embezzlement early in a bank. The banking activity, by its volume and complexity, makes it necessary to follow up very closely. A large bank manages millions of accounts and dematerialized transactions, sometimes very complex. This makes it difficult, in the absence of sufficiently rigorous internal control systems, to detect problems that may arise on the part of legal entities or customers whose beneficial owner is not the apparent owner. In addition, experts in the financial circuits have been able, in some cases, to use their expertise to conceal the real situation of the bank or its customers (Enron, Parmalat). In this highly technical financial environment, it is not always easy for those in governance roles to have a complete and accurate understanding of the operations and activities carried out. It is difficult for the shareholders present once a year at the board approval meeting, but also for the members of the board of directors, or even the managers themselves, to accurately assess very complex risks. Yet these risks, even located in one place, can lead to a very serious crisis. And the impact of such a crisis can be damaging to others than the managers or shareholders who bear legal responsibility for it. This is why there is a consensus that banking activity must be structured by strict rules aimed at reducing the likelihood of these risks occurring. To this end, the quantitative management rules - the ratios - would be ineffective if they were not accompanied by good rules of governance of the banking company. * * * II - Special rules help reduce the risk of poor banking governance In all major countries, legal and regulatory provisions govern the way banks are managed. And, as in the prudential field as a whole, there is a trend towards a strengthening of requirements, agreed at international level, to take account of the increasing sophistication of risk management. A) Legal and regulatory provisions specifically regulate the management of banks The control of banking risks requires not only individual skills, but also a balanced exercise of management functions, accompanied by control instruments adapted to the activity. Leaders must be honorable and competent No public authority verifies the morality of the persons called upon to lead an industrial group. To run a bank, you must meet certain conditions of good repute. In France, the case-law of the Council of State and now Law 1 expressly provide that this assessment is not limited to verifying the absence of certain criminal convictions. The Committee on Credit Institutions and Investment Firms shall make this assessment when entering the profession. These conditions are also subject to the permanent supervision of the Banking Commission, which has the power to pronounce as a disciplinary sanction the compulsory resignation of the directors. A bank executive cannot be alone The European legislator wisely considered that "four eyes see better than two". Since the solitary exercise of power has eminent defects, the Monetary and Financial Code (Art. L. 511-13) provides that "the effective determination of the direction of the activity" must be ensured by at least two persons. The term "effective" in the law makes it clear that it must be a real sharing of power and not an appointment to office. 1 See Article 500-1 of the Monetary and Financial Code as amended by Ordinance No. 2005-429 of 6 May 2005. honorary, which would only apparently satisfy the rule. Banking supervisors exercise close supervision on this point. Particular attention is paid to shareholding Not only the managers, but also the main shareholders of a bank, are subject to control aimed at strengthening the security of the activity. Thus, changes in shareholding are subject, in France, to the authorisation of the Committee of Credit Institutions and Investment Firms as soon as they exceed 10 % of the voting rights. In all these decisions, the Committee of Credit Institutions and Investment Firms shall be attentive to ensuring that the distribution of capital allows for efficient management, under conditions of clear holding of responsibilities. It is important that, as soon as an institution is set up, the conditions for effective governance can be put in place. This requires a good involvement of shareholders in the supervision of management. Legislative and oversight bodies are entrusted with specific functions The law or regulations require the management or administrative bodies of banks to comply with certain due diligence, beyond the general obligations of holding shareholders' meetings, drawing up accounts, etc. For example, managers are required to report annually to the Council on the activities and results of the internal control system, the main lines of which are to be set by the Council (see, for example, in the area of delegations). I note that the Law of 1 August 2003 on financial security now requires publicly traded companies to submit a report on internal control to shareholders' meetings. As regards credit institutions, they must also submit to the Council an annual report on the measurement and supervision of risks. Similarly, the law provides for the communication of the results of the on-the-spot inspection of the banking supervisory authority to the collegiate administrative or management supervisory bodies. It can thus be seen that the regulations provide the college bodies with the means to exercise their powers and in particular to be kept regularly informed of the evolution of the activity and the monitoring of risks. In this regard, mention should be made of the development of audit committees, which are emanations of the Boards and in which the auditors are associated. These whose appointment requires an opinion from the Banking Commission, are required to report to it as soon as possible any fact likely to have significant effects on the financial situation, the result or the assets of a bank, before a danger arises on the continuity of the operation. This last example highlights a characteristic common to the provisions specific to the banking and financial world: what matters is the early detection of difficulties, before they have become too serious. Adequate treatment must prevent the crisis rather than having to treat it a posteriori. This is perhaps why, compared to the measures applicable in the area related to public offerings, these banking arrangements have developed mainly upstream, by strengthening internal control systems, rather than downstream, by the information given at the time of shareholders' meetings. It is for this reason that, in France, we attach great importance to the internal control function and that we are constantly adapting the provisions concerning it. Until recently, internal control rules have been strengthened, in particular as regards the system for monitoring the compliance of banking activity with laws and regulations and the use of outsourcing2. But we are also active participants in the international movement that accompanies in a concerted way the increasing internationalization and sophistication of banking activities. B) The French vision of governance is shared at the international level The idea that this atypical profession calls for specific governance rules is widely shared by all our partners. The fundamental principles are almost universally applicable The need to entrust legislative bodies (board of directors or equivalent) with broad missions and, if possible, specified in texts is widely recognized. Only a strong involvement of the latter can limit the risks of bad governance. The obligation to subject managers to an assessment by the banking authorities is also universally accepted. Some countries extend it to directors. The same applies to the authorization to be given to shareholders. The 2 Reference: Order of 31 March 2005 amending Regulation No 97-02. This amendment shall enter into force on 1 January 2006. the constraint of good repute is a concern consistently expressed by banking supervisors in developing countries. The duality of leaders is also practiced everywhere, sometimes with increased formalization in management acts. Some countries thus require a duality of signature for any act binding the bank vis-e0-vis third parties. International cooperation is absolutely essential for the proper cross-border implementation of these principles Given the importance of cross-border transactions in banking, good international cooperation is essential for the effective implementation of the principles of good governance. Borders should not prevent the governing bodies of a group from exercising their oversight over all the activities it carries out and the entities that compose it. The Basel Committee of Banking Supervisors has recently produced new recommendations to this effect. Considering that the general rules of companies were not sufficient to frame the governance of banks, the Basel Committee, which brings together the supervisors of the major countries (G10), produced a first set of recommendations in 1999 and put for consultation, in July 2005, a revised, more demanding version of the banking governance standards. In addition to recalling the need for a clear expression of the company's strategy and values, the Basel document emphasizes the importance of having an organization with clear lines of responsibility, qualified directors capable of independent judgment, managers who are not only involved in day-to-day business, auditors whose work is actually used, an environmentally compatible remuneration policy, a sufficient degree of transparency, and finally an environment conducive to good corporate governance. In addition, there is a fundamental point, but one that is relatively recently expressed: the quality and good understanding of the operational structure of banking groups. What the Basel Committee calls "Know your structure". Experience has taught us that an uncontrolled development of legal structures that are not very transparent, or located in countries that impede the exercise of good governance, can lead to serious setbacks. The Parmalat case is an illustration of this. More than anywhere else, in view of the ease of setting up non-transparent entities, where appropriate in jurisdictions that are themselves adept at non-transparency - for example, some offshore centres - it is important that banks' boards of directors ensure strict operating rules, ensuring a good level of transparency. The consultation, which is currently taking place on the document published by the Basel Committee, tends to show that banks are aware of the need to respond to the challenges of financial innovation by strengthening governance structures. The more complex the risks taken, the more important it is to strengthen the quality of the operating procedures, with the necessary checks and balances. Thank you

Title: The euro as a stable currency at the service of a dynamic economy
text: Speech by Mr Christian Noyer Governor of the Banque de France THE EURO: A STABLE CURRENCY AT THE SERVICE OF A DYNAMIC ECONOMY BESANc7ON, DECEMBER 8, 2005 Ladies and gentlemen 95 It is a great pleasure for me to speak at the University of Besane7on, to talk to you about the euro, which is one of the most remarkable achievements of the European Union. 95 In recent months, in the wake of the psychological shock created by the negative result of the referendums on the European constitution in France and the Netherlands, several public accusations have been made of the single currency, and many commentators question the link between the adoption of the euro and the languor of the euro zone economy. Some have even gone so far as to question its sustainability. 95 I will not surprise you by telling you that these criticisms and questions seem absurd and unfounded to me. Above all, I would like to highlight two crucial things: - the first is that the euro zone is characterised by a very great divergence in the degree of flexibility of economies: on the one hand, countries whose economies are only slightly hampered by the classic structural rigidities of old Europe: Spain, Ireland, etc. On the other, heavyweights who are moving very slowly in the path of economic reforms: Germany, France, Italy. However, there is a fairly large correlation between the performance in terms of potential growth and the degree of adaptability of the economies of the different countries of the zone. To point the finger at money as the source of the economic difficulties of the zone as a whole is to deny this reality; - the second is that the introduction of the euro has been and remains an extraordinary success. However, this success is not the result of a wave of a magic wand, but of the fact that this introduction has been carefully thought out, and that the foundations of economic and monetary union that have been put in place are extremely solid and effective. First of all, I would like to mention the achievements of the single monetary policy and then macroeconomic cooperation within economic and monetary union. Finally, I would like to touch briefly on economic integration within the euro area. 2 PART 1: ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE SINGLE MONETARY POLICY The legal basis for the single currency is the Treaty establishing the European Community, Article 105 of which states: 'The main objective of the ESCB shall be to maintain price stability'. Price stability and the convergence of the economies of the euro area are essential prerequisites for the single currency to be able to give its full support to the general economic policies in the Community, with a view to contributing to the achievement of the Objectives of the Community, as defined in Article 2" of the Treaty. For almost seven years, the single monetary policy conducted by the Eurosystem, i.e. the whole of the European Central Bank and the twelve central banks of the euro area member countries, has been crowned with many successes. The successful changeover to the euro, in scriptural and then fiduciary form, is the first of these, probably the most emblematic. I will first recall the institutional and operational framework (A) and the strategy (B) of the single monetary policy before discussing these achievements (C). Has. A modern institutional and operational framework The Eurosystem's institutional framework is based on the principles of independence, transparency and accountability and, finally, operational decentralisation. A.1 The independence of the Eurosystem promotes price stability 95 As many empirical studies have shown, a nation's anti-inflationary performance seems to be highly correlated with the degree of independence of its central bank. 95 According to the Maastricht Treaty, the Eurosystem's main task is to ensure and maintain price stability. The independence of the European Central Bank and the twelve central banks of the member countries of the euro area is therefore enshrined in the Treaty. 3 95 Functionally, this means that, in the exercise of their tasks, neither the European Central Bank nor the national central banks of the Eurosystem seek or take instructions from the Community institutions, national governments or any other body. A.2. Transparency and accountability are key to credibility 95 Naturally, the independence of these institutions is matched by the transparency of their decisions and accountability to the public and its representatives. To establish the credibility of the central bank, to gain the trust of agents, it is absolutely imperative to be understood and for this it is necessary to be transparent. 95 The imperatives of accountability and transparency are enshrined in the Treaty in very general terms. The Eurosystem has gone beyond its strict institutional obligations in these areas: - firstly, the Governing Council clarified its definition of price stability (increase of less than, but close to, 2% in the medium term); - secondly, the ECB has gone beyond the accountability requirements established by the Treaty by establishing regular hearings of its President before the European Parliament and regular informal meetings with the Eurogroup of Finance Ministers; - another sign of transparency is the regular publication of reports on economic developments and central bank analyses, of which the ECB's Monthly Bulletin is the best-known vehicle; - Finally, most importantly, at the end of each of the meetings devoted to monetary policy decisions, the President and Vice-President of the ECB hold a press conference followed by an open exchange with journalists, details of which are published on the ECB's website. It is important to remember that the ECB was the first of the central banks to undergo this type of exercise, which provides a 4 a unique opportunity to explain and comment on monetary policy decisions, immediately and in detail; - on the other hand, the Governing Council of the ECB has chosen not to publish the minutes of its meetings. Indeed, the publication of the minutes has certain disadvantages. Notably, in the case of the euro area, the analysis of votes could be read and interpreted in the light of national concerns or interests, which would be misleading and could threaten both the independence of governing council members and the credibility of our decision-making processes. An exhaustive report would also be liable to complicate the development of decision-making. Succinctly, it would not add anything to the Chairman's record. A.3. The Eurosystem is based on operational decentralisation 95 Operational decentralisation is a key feature of the Eurosystem. 95 The use of modern technologies and means of communication has made it possible to perfectly reconcile the decentralisation of operations with the unity of the euro area money market. B. The Strategic Framework The effectiveness of the single monetary policy is also based on its policy framework, which can be characterised by a quantitative definition of price stability and a medium-term orientation. B.1. A quantitative definition of price stability 95 The definition adopted by the Governing Council of the ECB in October 1998 was confirmed and clarified in May 2003. Price stability is defined by annual HICP growth close to, but below, 2% over the medium term. 5 95 The Governing Council thus confirmed the symmetrical nature of its strategy by excluding deflation situations. This clarification also makes it possible to take into account the differences in inflation within the euro area. B.2. Medium-term guidance 95 This medium-term stance of the single monetary policy recognises that it is impossible for a central bank to accurately control the price path in the very short term. As a result, indicators relevant to monetary policy must reflect, almost exhaustively, the main drivers of inflation in both the short and long term. This is reflected in the concepts of economic approach and monetary approach (also known as a two-pillar approach). The economic approach reviews short-term, economic and financial indicators in relation to the main determinants of short-term inflation. The monetary approach is based on the monetary explanation of long-term inflation. C. Achievements of the single monetary policy I would like to highlight three key points: 95 First, while it has been confronted with a series of adverse shocks (on oil prices, administered prices, etc.), the single monetary policy has managed to stabilise and anchor, over the entire exercise period, medium-long-term inflation expectations of around 1.8 to 1.9%. However, in the context of the recent rise in oil prices, some expected inflation indicators, including those from financial markets, have tended to rise slightly above 2 per cent. The recent rise in interest rates has helped to bring these medium- and long-term inflation expectations back to levels consistent with price stability in the euro area. 95 Second, most of the Eurosystem's monetary policy decisions have been fully anticipated by the markets. Contrary to popular belief, the comparison with the Fed does not show any real difference in predictability vis-e0-vis 6 markets. The fact that the ECB chose means of communication other than minutes did not affect the understanding and predictability of its monetary policy (the ECB watchers' reports are clear in this respect). 95 Thirdly, the euro has become established among economic agents and is now part of the daily lives of European consumers. PART 2: MULTILATERAL SURVEILLANCE PROCEDURES IN EMU In EMU, where a single monetary policy coexists with twelve governments responsible for fiscal and structural policies, an appropriate institutional framework is essential to ensure overall coherence. This is particularly the purpose of the Stability and Growth Pact. For this framework to be fully operational, it must be simple, easy to implement and capable of ensuring sound and sustainable fiscal policies. Thus, multilateral surveillance processes have been designed from the outset, in order to achieve a satisfactory level of cohesion in the policies followed by all Member States. Has. A framework of multilateral surveillance procedures 95 The implementation of surveillance is entrusted to the Eurogroup (informal meeting of finance ministers of euro area countries) and the Ecofin Council (meeting of finance ministers of all EU countries, with decision-making power), together with the European Commission. Mutual surveillance combines multilateral surveillance and dialogue procedures, compliance with common rules and provisions, and member States' commitment to good practices and common objectives. 95 Compliance with the rules and procedures set out in the Treaty and the provisions of the Stability and Growth Pact impose the same budgetary discipline on all Member States: the budget deficit must not exceed the ceiling of 3% of GDP and the total debt ratio should not exceed 60% of GDP. These limits help to ensure an optimal policy mix at euro area level, as long as 7 a loose fiscal policy may ultimately jeopardize the achievement of price stability. Finally, they maintain sustainable growth and employment and are conducive to economic stability. 95 Budgetary discipline is indeed of paramount importance for EMU, as it is a necessary corollary of the single monetary policy. Member States are expected to regard their economic policies as matters of "common interest", given the impact that their budgetary decisions may have on the euro area as a whole. In a monetary union, it is of the utmost importance to avoid "free rider behaviour", hence the 'no bailout' clause in the Maastricht Treaty. 95 A reform of the Stability and Growth Pact (SGP) was adopted by the European Council on 22 March 2005, following the Commission's reform proposals of September 2004. This reform confirms the important role of the Pact in terms of budgetary discipline, clarifies the conditions for triggering the Excessive Deficit Procedure and introduces a slight extension of the deadlines for correcting excessive deficits. 95 Following this agreement by the European Council, the Governing Council of the ECB has spoken publicly to stress the imperative that Member States, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union implement the revised framework in a rigorous and coherent manner conducive to the conduct of prudent fiscal policies. B. The new Member States comply with the same rules Let me point out that the ten new Member States are already accustomed to mutual review processes. Since their accession on 1 May 2004, the budgetary policy of the ten new Member States has been subject to the same review measures as that of the other Member States. These countries are now forced to undertake substantial fiscal reforms, especially since their deficits are largely due to structural shortfalls. 8 PART 3: THE EURO: A POWERFUL ENGINE FOR ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL INTEGRATION AND EUROPE'S INTERNATIONAL INFLUENCE The euro is based on solid fundamentals and has favoured as much as benefited from near-complete financial integration. It now plays the role of an international currency. Has. Strong fundamentals and strong economic homogeneity The euro area economies are currently characterised by a high degree of structural convergence, a low level of inflation, close to 2%, and favourable monetary and financial conditions for economic activity. While monetary union does not necessarily imply that all Member States have the same rate of growth or inflation at all times, a number of recent empirical studies illustrate an increasing economic homogeneity within the euro area. 95 In terms of activity first of all, several studies presented under the aegis of a joint working group between the CEPR (Centre for Economic Policy Research) and the Eurosystem show that the correlation between cyclical fluctuations in economic activity as a whole in most euro area countries, already strong before the implementation of the single monetary policy, has increased since 1999. The degree of correlation does not appear to be significantly different from that of the United States: the order of magnitude of the standard deviation is the same between the 4 major countries of the Euro Zone and the 12 American economic zones (1 point) as well as between the 50 American States and the 12 States of the Euro Zone (2 points). 95 In terms of inflation, according to the work carried out by the Eurosystem, the degree of dispersion of inflation rates within the euro area would not be much higher than that observed in the United States, where there are much stronger recall forces than in the euro area - such as the presence of a single federal budget balancing cyclical differences between regions, more unified markets for goods and services and labour, a single monetary policy since 1913. Thus, over these first years of EMU's existence, the standard deviation of the annual price shift in the twelve 9 Eurozone countries are estimated to be close to 1 point compared to 0.8 points for the fourteen metropolitan areas of the United States. 95 Finally, recent updates of the Eurosystem's important research on the transmission mechanisms of the single monetary policy suggest that the responses of member countries' economies to monetary policy impulses are increasingly homogeneous. In particular, the standard deviation of the time taken to adjust bank credit rates to changes in the policy rate would, on average, have halved since the implementation of the single monetary policy. B. Almost complete integration of the financial sector 95 The latter is almost complete as regards the euro money market. 95 A similar integration movement has also occurred in the markets European bonds, where there has been a tightening of government bond yields, as well as in derivatives markets and, to a lesser extent, in stock markets and the corporate debt market. 95 The euro area and, more broadly, the European Union now have a coherent financial architecture. The implementation of the Financial Services Action Plan, defined at the Lisbon European Council in March 2000, is being completed. The "Lamfalussy process" is expected to foster a new institutional architecture in the area of financial sector supervision and regulation. C. The euro now plays the role of international currency The growing role of the euro at international level is the result of the development of both its use at private level and its official role. 95 The euro has the key functions attributed to any international currency: it is already a leading investment and financing currency (31% of outstanding international debt securities) and an important intermediary in international trade (involved in 43% of foreign exchange transactions). Even if it is 10 still limited, its role as a billing currency is expected to develop in the coming years. 95 According to the latest available IMF data, the euro was the second reserve currency after the dollar in 2004; and its share seems to have increased sharply since 1999 despite a slight decline between 2003 and 2004. 95 The use of the euro in the exchange rate regimes of third countries mainly concerns regions which have established close links with the euro area or which have set up special institutional arrangements with the EU (acceding and candidate countries, Balkans, North Africa and the franc zone). 95 With regard to the ten new EU countries, let me stress that the criterion of exchange rate stability within ERM II requires that this stability be achieved before the adoption of the single currency. The advantage is that the adoption of the euro will be the culmination of a structured convergence process within a multilateral framework. This is certainly one of the most important challenges facing the euro area in the coming years. Conclusion 95 I would like to conclude by saying that the euro has met our expectations. It has promoted stability through its credibility and has protected many countries in the zone from excessive exchange rate volatility and financial market turbulence. 95 The euro therefore represents a major cornerstone of European integration. That said, and regardless of its own merits, a currency is not an end in itself even if the new Member States are ardently determined to adopt it as soon as possible. Participation in monetary union must be based on a process of sustainable convergence. Indeed, beyond the institutional challenges that remain (independence of central banks, adaptation of banking systems, fight against money laundering, etc.), the major challenge that opens up to us is to take up the challenge of real convergence between East and West Europe. This objective 11 will require years of major structural reforms to accelerate growth and close the East-West divide; it presupposes, in particular, respect for the macroeconomic framework to which all the Member States party to the euro today have agreed, in particular the successful participation in ERM II. It is indeed necessary to avoid any precipitation damaging to competitiveness and to carry out fundamental reforms, particularly in terms of the sustainability of public finances, prior to the entry into this exchange rate mechanism, a guarantee of a real sustainable convergence beneficial to the whole area. 12

Une rforme du Pacte de stabilit et de croissance (PSC) a t adopte par le Conseil Europen du 22 mars 2005, faisant suite aux propositions de rforme de la Commission de septembre 2004. Cette rforme confirme le rle important du Pacte en matire de discipline budgtaire, prcise les conditions de dclenchement de la Procdure pour dficit excessif et introduit un lger allongement des dlais de correction des dficits excessifs.  A la suite de cet accord du Conseil Europen, le Conseil des Gouverneurs de la BCE sest exprim publiquement pour insister sur le fait quil est impratif que les tats membres, la Commission europenne et le Conseil de lUnion europenne mettent en uvre le cadre rvis dune manire rigoureuse et cohrente, propice  la conduite de politiques budgtaires prudentes. Ces pays sont maintenant contraints d'entreprendre des rformes budgtaires substantielles, d'autant plus que leurs dficits proviennent en grande partie d'insuffisances structurelles. 8 PARTIE 3 : L'EURO : UN MOTEUR PUISSANT DINTGRATION CONOMIQUE ET FINANCIRE ET DE RAYONNEMENT INTERNATIONAL DE LEUROPE Leuro repose sur des fondamentaux solides et a favoris autant que bnfici dune intgration financire presque acheve. Des fondamentaux solides et une grande homognit conomique Les conomies de la zone euro se caractrisent, actuellement, par un important degr de convergence structurelle, un faible niveau d'inflation, proche de 2 %, et des conditions montaires et financires favorables  l'activit conomique. Si l'Union montaire n'implique pas ncessairement que tous les tats membres affichent,  tout moment, le mme taux de croissance ou d'inflation, un certain nombre de travaux empiriques rcents illustrent une homognit conomique croissante au sein de la zone euro.  En termes d'activit tout d'abord, plusieurs travaux prsents sous l'gide d'un groupe de travail commun entre le CEPR (Centre for Economic Policy Research) et l'Eurosystme montrent que la corrlation entre les fluctuations cycliques de l'activit conomique dans son ensemble dans la plupart des pays de la zone euro, dj forte avant la mise en uvre de la politique montaire unique, s'est accrue depuis 1999. Le degr de corrlation napparat pas sensiblement diffrent de celui des Etats-unis : lordre de grandeur de lcart type est le mme entre les 4 grands de la Zone euro et les 12 zones conomique amricaines (1 point) ainsi quentre les 50 Etats amricains et les 12 Etats de la Zone Euro (2 points).  En termes d'inflation, selon les travaux mens par lEurosystme, le degr de dispersion des rythmes d'inflation au sein de la zone euro ne serait pas nettement suprieur  celui que l'on observe aux tats-Unis o existent des forces de rappel bien plus fortes que dans la zone euro - telles que la prsence d'un budget fdral unique quilibrant les diffrences cycliques entre rgions, des marchs des biens et services et du travail plus unifis, une politique montaire unique depuis 1913. Ainsi, sur ces premires annes d'existence de l'UEM, l'cart-type du glissement annuel des prix dans les douze 9 pays de la zone euro serait, selon les estimations, proche de 1 point contre 0,8 point pour les quatorze zones mtropolitaines des tats-Unis.  Enfin, les mises  jour rcentes de l'important travail de recherche effectu par l'Eurosystme sur les mcanismes de transmission de la politique montaire unique tendent  indiquer une homognit croissante des rponses des conomies des pays membres aux impulsions de la politique montaire. Notamment, lcart-type des dlais dajustement des taux des crdits bancaires aux variations du taux directeur aurait, en moyenne, diminu de moiti depuis la mise en uvre de la politique montaire unique. B. Une intgration presque acheve du secteur financier  Cette dernire est quasiment acheve en ce qui concerne le march montaire de l'euro.  Un mouvement d'intgration comparable s'est galement produit sur les marchs obligataires europens, o l'on a pu constater un resserrement des rendements des titres d'tat, ainsi que sur les marchs drivs et, dans une moindre mesure, sur les marchs boursiers et le march des missions de titres de dette pour les entreprises. Le  processus Lamfalussy  devrait favoriser la mise en place d'une nouvelle architecture institutionnelle dans le domaine de la supervision et de la rglementation du secteur financier. C. L'euro joue dsormais le rle de monnaie internationale Le rle croissant de l'euro  l'chelle internationale rsulte du dveloppement  la fois de son utilisation au niveau priv et de son rle officiel.  L'euro possde les fonctions-cls que l'on attribue  toute monnaie internationale : il s'agit dj d'une monnaie de placement et de financement de premier plan (31 % de lencours de titres de crances internationales) et d'un intermdiaire important des changes internationaux (impliqu dans 43 % des oprations de change). En effet, au-del des dfis institutionnels qui subsistent (indpendance des banques centrales, adaptation de systmes bancaires, lutte contre le blanchiment, etc.), le dfi majeur qui s'ouvre  nous est de relever le pari de la convergence relle entre l'Est et l'Ouest de l'Europe. Title: Personal services and universal service employment cheque
text: Speech by Christian NOYER, Governor of the Banque de France delivered at the conference "Personal Services and Che8que Emploi Service Universel" Tuesday, 14 February 2006 Minister, Ministers, Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, It is not every day that we see the birth of a new means of payment and this type of opportunity is important, especially for the Bank of France which has a long tradition of helping to design safe and efficient means of payment. Human services are bound to develop undeniably. In our society, marked in particular by the ageing of the population and the high rate of activity of women, they make it possible to improve the living conditions of many fellow citizens and therefore constitute an important source of employment. The government wanted to support the development of this sector of activity by taking a series of measures, including the creation of the Universal Service Employment Cheque. The CESU, since it should be called that, is a means of payment intended for individuals, who will thus be able to pay in all simplicity and security the services they have been able to benefit from. The Bank of France naturally provided all its support and expertise to the implementation of the CESU. In close collaboration with the National Agency for Personal Services and the banking profession, it has endeavoured to ensure that this means of payment can be used in optimal conditions of efficiency and security. These conditions are indeed essential to ensure the adherence and trust of users. Now that the CESU is a reality, I have no doubt that it will meet with rapid success, given the broadening of the range of services that can be paid for by this means of payment and potential acceptors. In addition, new features will soon complete the system and make it even more attractive and better adapted to the characteristics of the personal services market. On the one hand, banks will offer a CESU collection service at their counters, thus providing employees with a local service. On the other hand, issuers are thinking about new processing methods, which will make it possible to move away from paper and to evolve towards dematerialized solutions. I therefore hope that the CESU will make a decisive contribution to the development of personal services.

Title: Presentation of the Annual report
text: COMMISSION BANCAIRE 2005 ANNUAL REPORT PRESENTATION BY Christian Noyer, Governor, Banque de France, Chairman, Commission Bancaire The Commission Bancaire is pleased to publish its 2005 Annual Report today. Allow me to draw your attention to some salient aspects of the French banking system and its supervisory framework. The situation is characterised by:  a sharp rise in revenue and income;  a change in business activities that underscores the vital need for rigorous risk management;  major operational challenges. 1. SHARP RISE IN REVENUE AND INCOME France's main banking groups reported a 29.5% rise in consolidated net income in 2005, continuing the uptrend of 2003 and 2004. On a parent company basis, the aggregate net income of all credit institutions grew 17.5% year on year to 26.9 billion. Similar increases were observed in France's neighbours. 1.1. All business lines contributed to the increase The seven main banks that prepared their accounts under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) recorded a larger rise in net banking income (NBI) than they did in 2004, with a gain of 11.1% compared with 4.6%. For French credit institutions as a whole, NBI growth was lower, at 7.2% compared with 4.8% in 2004. This reflects the substantial contribution made by non-banking subsidiaries, especially insurance companies, to income expansion. The difference between parent-company and consolidated results is partly attributable to the first-time adoption of IFRS for consolidated financial statements. Domestic and international retail banking (including specialised financial services) is still the main profit driver for French banks  it accounted for 60.5% of NBI in 2005  despite a slight decline caused mainly by the comparatively small increase in NBI from domestic retail business. Margins once again contracted, even though outstanding loans rose steeply. The uptrend in equity markets since 2004 combined with persistently low interest rates contributed significantly to performance in asset management and also supported activity in corporate and investment banking, which accounted for one-quarter of NBI. Overheads jumped by some 8%. This mainly concerns personnel expenses, which increased in order to reward strong performances in numerous business lines. The mean cost-to-income ratio, which measures overheads as a percentage of NBI, improved on average for the main French groups, from 64.5% to 62.3%. Nevertheless, it is still slightly less satisfactory than the mean ratio for the main European banking groups. Consequently, further improvements in cost-to-income ratios are necessary. Provisions for the immediate cost of credit risk fell to an all-time low in 2005. The largest banking groups reported a 9.8% decline in immediate credit-risk costs, composed essentially of net allocations to doubtful-loan provisions. This decline once again contributed to the higher net profitability of French banks. 2 1.2. French credit institutions were dynamic as economic and financial conditions remained positive Global growth slowed slightly in 2005 from the historically high level reached in 2004. The slowdown was particularly noticeable in the euro area, where growth contracted from 2.1% in 2004 to 1.4% in 2005. Growth in France followed a similar pattern: it eased to 1.2% owing to a deterioration in external trade but was still buoyed by household consumption. Like their foreign counterparts, French banks took advantage of exceptionally positive conditions in the corporate sector, reflected in a continued decline in the bankruptcy rate. The banks were extremely active in the market for debt securities and credit derivatives for private and public issuers (i.e. corporates and sovereigns). Risk premia in these markets continued to shrink, revealing a growing disconnection between risk estimates and economic and financial fundamentals. The financial markets to which banks are committed are highly sensitive to pressures that could surface following sharp swings in economic and financial variables at international level. Once again, credit institutions were highly active in financing the French economy, starting with personal lending for home ownership, among other things. Loans outstanding to customers in metropolitan France rose 10.6% in 2005, mainly because of an increase in outstanding home loans, which grew at an annual rate of 15.5%, compared with 12.8% in 2004 and 8.3% in 2003. Loans to businesses, i.e. non-financial companies and sole proprietors, were also up sharply, increasing 8.3% and amplifying the trend that began in 2004 with a 6.9% rise (compared with a 2.8% decline one year earlier). 3 2. CHANGE IN BUSINESS ACTIVITIES UNDERSCORES THE VITAL NEED FOR RIGOROUS RISK MANAGEMENT 2.1. Business growth must remain under control French banks make an active contribution to financing the country's economy and they operate in the main international financial markets. They should therefore place a priority on maintaining overall asset quality and seeking recurring income streams. It would appear, however, that they have partially overlooked these priorities amid brisk growth in some of their business lines. This is the case for home lending, to which I once again draw your attention, because the messages of caution from the Banque de France and the Commission Bancaire have still not been properly heeded by the institutions to whom they are addressed. Lending terms are constantly being relaxed, especially as regards downpayments; and margins are wafer-thin, even if the resulting customer relationship may ultimately generate some additional revenue. Taken together, these factors could have a detrimental effect on the solvency of households, and on the financial situation of the banks that lend to them, if housing market conditions or interest rates become less benign than at present. The same observation is becoming increasingly germane to the market for corporate financing, where narrowing margins and relaxed lending terms have also been observed. Lower compensation for risk has spurred a sharp increase in volumes, especially with the riskiest counterparties. Moreover, some types of financing vehicle have inherently high risks for lenders because of the leverage they generate. Some credit institutions are heavily committed to leveraged buy-outs, which multiplied in 2005 and for ever increasing amounts. They are therefore acutely exposed to an increase in companies' difficulties or to a rise in the bankruptcy rate. For this reason, a close watch must be kept at all times on the type of commitments and the quality of counterparties. 4 I cannot help but mention the recent increase in volatility in some emerging financial markets, which has caused commodity prices to fluctuate significantly. Many large French banks are committed to these markets, which are highly sensitive to cyclical movements, whereas risk premia were extremely low in 2005. I urge the banks concerned to closely monitor their current exposures and to be especially careful when choosing their future commitments. Furthermore, some banks have built up their positions either in high-yielding but illiquid market segments such as credit derivatives or in relation to counterparties that are lacking in transparency, especially hedge funds. These positions have resulted in a sharp rise in risk relative to the underlying assets and to counterparties. These developments justify the concerns expressed by supervisory authorities, and by market participants themselves, regarding the need to promote and enhance risk management techniques, particularly for complex transactions. 2.2. Financial safeguards must enable institutions to cope with a possible cycle downturn Because provisions and reserves are very low  the level fell even further in 2005  they are less and less effective as a safeguard in the event of a credit cycle downturn, which many analysts are now expecting. The aim of provisioning is to be able to cope with a possible decline in counterparty quality. This can happen extremely quickly, as past experience has demonstrated. Credit institutions must therefore remain on their guard and take into account their long-term risk patterns, having regard to prevailing accounting standards, in order to allow for cyclical fluctuations in the business concerned. Moreover, the Tier 1 solvency ratios of France's largest banks have hardly changed year on year despite a sharp rise in net income. This is significant because ample, highquality capital is needed to cover risk and ensure successful organic and external growth. Banking executives must announce and implement clear policies to strengthen their financial structures and preserve their medium-term and long-term profitability rather than systematically seeking immediate returns for shareholders. 5 3. OPERATIONAL CHALLENGES 3.1. Internal control organisation and procedures can be improved in several areas Let me mention three areas where, in my opinion, credit institutions and investment firms need to make progress. The first of these, which I mentioned earlier, concerns the management of risk on complex transactions and transactions with hedge funds. Although French banks should not be the recipient of the harshest critics on these topics, they must ask themselves whether their operational mechanisms are effective. In terms of priorities, they must spread their risks, take sufficient collateral on routine transactions, develop stress tests and take a proactive approach to settling failed trades in back offices. The second area is customer relations. Credit institutions and investment firms are now working with user representatives and public authorities to improve commercial practices and make them more transparent. However, further progress can be made, especially by adopting the recommendations set out in the Delmas-Marsalet report on financial product marketing. In this respect, the new regulation on internal control that came into force on the 1st of January 2006, which the Commission Bancaire naturally played an active role in drafting, includes innovative provisions governing the way in which banks ensure the regulatory compliance of their operations. This will contribute significantly to the quality of the relationship between banks and their customers. The third area is business continuity plans. In accordance with international principles and in harmony with ongoing work on the robustness of market infrastructures, these plans must be reinforced and tailored to the new, extreme risks that could affect the financial sector. 6 3.2. Management procedures must be adapted to new accounting and prudential standards France's largest banking groups have completed their first financial year under IFRS. To that end, they rapidly upgraded their information systems to meet the new regulatory requirements and incorporate them into their routine management operations. In particular, the broader reference to market values, or to model values that replicate them, has made it necessary to demonstrate that the parameters used in the calculations are relevant and to anticipate how these measurement methods will affect the presentation of activities and results. In practice, while substantive changes have occurred in the structure of banks' balance sheets, the impacts have been comparatively modest, notably as regards regulatory capital. That said, the long-term consequences of the new standards must not be underestimated, especially as regards credit risk provisioning. A special study in the annexes to this annual report provides further details about the impact of IFRS on the financial statements of French banks. The directive on the capital adequacy of credit institutions and investment firms was approved in October 2005. It is now being transposed in the Member States of the European Union (EU) and will come into force on the 1st of January 2007 (1st of January 2008 for the more advanced measurement approaches). Pertinent information about the situation of French banks was provided by the Basel Committee's fifth quantitative impact study of leading banks (QIS 5) and by the audits carried out to ensure that internal risk-measurement systems were compliant with the supervisory criteria for advanced measurement approaches. French institutions have made rapid progress with their methodologies and computation tools, but they need to make further efforts, especially as regards the accurate measurement of credit risk and operational risk. 7 4. THIS IS THE SETTING FOR THE COMMISSION BANCAIRE'S ACTION 4.1. in France As you know, supervisory action is enshrined in the Basel II reforms as one of the three pillars of the future prudential framework. But that action was already contributing to stronger banking structures and improved management practices in France, even before the Basel Committee's advances. Extensive regulatory developments have taken place in our banking industry in recent years, leading to an overall improvement in the standards used to manage banking risk. For brevity's sake, let me cite just two examples. First, the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing has prompted financial institutions to introduce practical procedures for identifying and preventing suspicious transactions. Second, the development of the internal control and compliance functions is vitally important given that institutions are nowadays exposed to a variety of risks and the attendant consequences in terms of reputation. These mechanisms need to be buttressed by proper corporate governance, a point made in a special study of this issue, which you can find in the annexes to the annual report. The Commission Bancaire also acts in close cooperation with the other financial authorities, since industry players sometimes share the same structures and are exposed to the same risks. This cooperation makes for comprehensive and effective supervision of the entire financial industry, while allowing each authority to fulfil its own statutory missions. 4.2.  and in the European framework of decentralised banking supervision The Commission Bancaire devotes much of its efforts to harmonising banking supervisory practices through the Basel Committee, the Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS)  chaired by the Commission Bancaire's General Secretary since January 2006  and the Banking Supervision Committee of the European Central Bank. 8 In 2005, for the implementation of the new capital adequacy framework, CEBS laid down guidelines for cooperation among European supervisors on the supervision of cross-border groups. It outlined practical procedures for cooperation between consolidating and host supervisors, particularly as regards exchanging information and assessing groups' internal rating systems. The Commission Bancaire intends to continue collaborating with fellow supervisors by setting up cross-border operational networks. The Commission Bancaire also played a prominent role in defining COREP and FINREP1, the common reporting formats that will come into effect in 2007 in the Member States represented on CEBS. These new formats are designed to allow institutions, particularly those with cross-border facilities, to reduce the operational cost of supervisory reporting. This aim should be furthered by the use of XBRL, the new data transmission standard recommended by CEBS. The aim of all the work done at the European level is to promote continually enhanced dialogue and cooperation on supervisory practices among the 25 EU countries. The current institutional structure  in both its national and European dimensions  has shown that it can easily accommodate sweeping reforms such as Basel II and IFRS. It has also shown that it is able to discharge its duties of ongoing banking supervision in the best possible conditions. * * * * * Let me finish by saying that, on the whole, the French banking system seems efficient and robust. This is a key advantage for a healthy economy that needs to be able to count on high-quality and needs-responsive financing mechanisms, investments and financial services at all times. 1 COREP: COmmon REPorting. FINREP: FINancial REPorting. 9 Banks have performed strongly for several years, but this does not immunise them against a downturn in current conditions. Risks must be anticipated at the earliest possible moment, that is to say, when they are taken. This should be reflected not only in pricing but also in proper provisioning and appropriate levels of capital. Under these conditions, the French banking system will remain both resilient and competitive. 10

Title: General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies
text: SPEECH BY CHRISTIAN NOYER GOVERNOR OF THE BANQUE DE FRANCE PRESIDENT OF THE BANKING COMMISSION ----- GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE FRENCH ASSOCIATION OF FINANCIAL COMPANIES 28 June 2006 ----- Mr President Thank you for giving me the floor again in this Chamber. The meeting of the General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies is always an excellent opportunity to present some reflections on the major themes of banking news and on the evolutions of our financial and regulatory environment. I - First of all, Mr President, I would like to give a brief overview of the results of the banking sector as a whole, with particular light on those of financial companies. While last year was marked by a slowdown in economic growth in France and Europe, French credit institutions nevertheless benefited from sustained domestic activity in all sectors. With regard to the financing of the economy, outstanding housing credit and cash flow recorded strong increases of 15.5 per cent and 9.9 per cent, respectively. Credit to businesses (including individual entrepreneurs) confirms its recovery with an increase of 8.3% in outstandings. Thus, in a favorable stock market context, all businesses, from investment banking to specialized financial services, recorded improved results. The improvement in the profitability of credit institutions is due to the strong growth in net banking income. Thus, the seven main groups recorded a cumulative increase in their GNP of 11.1% while that of the banking system as a whole recorded an increase of 7.2%, the difference being explained by the performance of foreign or non-bank subsidiaries. However, this good performance should not mask the persistent decline in margins. For their part, the general expenses of the main banking groups recorded a sustained increase of 8% due to the dynamism of remuneration, particularly variable. In total, the average operating ratio improved by more than two points to 62.3%, but French banking groups remain slightly above the average of the major European banking groups. This illustrates the necessary vigilance of institutions regarding the evolution of their structural costs. The provisioning effort of the main banking groups continued to decline in 2005. While this 9.8 per cent decrease is more limited than in 2004, it remains a concern because it reflects less protection against a possible reversal in the credit cycle. In total, the main banking groups and the banking system as a whole recorded an increase in their net income in 2005 of 29.5% and 17.5% respectively. These increases, which can also be observed in other European countries, should not obscure the fact that margins remain narrow and that the level of solvency of credit institutions is no longer increasing. I therefore call on banking leaders to ensure that financial structures are strengthened and that profitability is maintained in the medium and long term, in particular through adequate credit pricing. 2 For their part, the specialized credit institutions recorded, as you indicated, Mr President, a good year in 2005. Indeed, your association publishes increases in outstanding amounts of 11.9% for housing financing and 7.2% for consumer credit for individuals. With regard to the financing of business equipment, outstanding amounts increased by 5.7%. The statistics of the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission on a constant and representative sample of financial companies show an increase of 14.5% in the net banking income of this legal category of institutions. For their part, structural costs increased by almost 9.3% as a result of staff costs. As a result, the net operating ratio improved by more than 2 percentage points to less than 50%. The provisioning effort has increased significantly but represents less than 4% of the net banking income of the sample. The net income of the sampled financial corporations increased by 18.6%. All in all, and this recommendation is all the easier to state when the situation is so favourable, I would remind you that it is essential that credit institutions maintain the necessary discipline in terms of pricing, cost control and strengthening of their financial structure. II - I would now like to discuss with you the evolution of the legislative and regulatory framework The Bank of France and the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission are paying particular attention to the negotiations on the proposal for a European directive on consumer credit agreements. At the level of the bodies of the Place de Paris, this draft directive was examined by the Advisory Committee on Financial Legislation and Regulation (CCLRF) during its meeting last January. The CCLRF, which I would remind you 3 includes representatives of sectoral professional associations and also consumer associations, issued a generally favourable opinion. It considered that support should be given to the new method, known as "full targeted harmonisation", which consists in reserving full harmonisation to those aspects which are really important for freedom of provision and competition. It will be implemented for the first time by the European Commission on the occasion of this text, which will therefore have the value of a "test" of a method that in principle meets the wishes of French professional associations. This single market for consumer credit requires a high level of protection of consumers' interests, based on a uniform legal framework within the European Union, which also guarantees equal competition between economic operators. The France is therefore in favour of maximum harmonisation and opposes the introduction of the principle of mutual recognition, particularly as regards the application of such a principle to the provisions laying down the conditions for the conclusion and performance of a credit agreement concluded by a consumer. This position consistently taken by the French delegation during the European negotiations was solemnly reaffirmed by the National Assembly on 25 May 2006. The Commission adopted a resolution on the draft Directive on consumer credit agreements recalling its commitment to the unity of the law applicable to the contract and therefore calling for the principle of mutual recognition not to apply to the provisions governing the relationship between an individual and a creditor. The latest developments in the European negotiations have shown that the French position is shared by a majority of the Union's Member States. The debate of principle, which you quite rightly mentioned, Mr President, between mutual recognition and maximum harmonisation, seems to lead to maximum harmonisation, satisfactory for national authorities, economic operators and consumers. I would add, however, that if the new draft directive is a significant improvement over the first draft presented by the Commission. 4 in September 2002, it raises at least two serious problems of scope. Thus, the France requests that under no circumstances does the Directive open up the possibility that professional lenders may be mere natural persons, as is the case in a neighbouring Member State (United Kingdom). In addition, we want mortgage credit to remain excluded from the scope of the directive. In any case, my services will remain particularly mobilised in order to avoid any risk of distortion of competition between lenders and to maintain a high level of consumer protection for consumer credit involving foreign lenders and credit intermediaries. With regard to international cases, the new regulatory framework of capital requirements is nearing completion and will be ready before the entry into force of the new ratio on 1 January 2007. Indeed, the directive transposing Basel II into European law (known as "CRD") was formally adopted by the Council and Parliament during this month. In the autumn of 2004, the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission, within the framework of a working group involving the profession, the Treasury and the Advisory Committee on Financial Legislation and Regulation, drew up a first draft regulatory text to transpose the CRD. This project will be the subject of a formal consultation of the profession during the autumn. In this regard, I am pleased with the quality of the relations between the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission and the ASF, which have led to the characteristics of your members' activities being taken into account in the drafting of texts. You are asking me about the possibility of setting up a European banking supervisor. While there are transnational banking players, I would remind you that the markets are still essentially national, with different characteristics from one country to another. However, it is fundamental, both for financial stability and for the competitiveness of European banks, that supervisory practices be 5 Converging. From this point of view, with the creation of the so-called Level 3 Committees of the Lamfalussy procedure, and in particular, in the banking sector, of the Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS), the situation has developed very positively. We can now say that European supervision is already a reality but it operates according to a decentralised model, which allows it to remain close to the supervised entities, but with coordination carried out by the Lamfalussy Committees. The achievements of the CEBS are already numerous, with, for example, the gradual establishment of a european harmonised framework for the production and reporting of prudential and accounting statements. I have also noted with satisfaction that to share these visions. With regard to the creation of a single payments area in Europe, the expected benefits lie in the economies of scale enabled by common instruments and standards, and the eventual consolidation of infrastructure. In order to carry out this project, European credit institutions have set up the European Payments Council, the EPC, which is responsible for leading and piloting this project at European level. With regard to the Paris market, as you know, the Banque de France and the French Banking Federation created a National Committee for SEPA, which they co-chair, and which held its first meeting on 7 April 2006. The SEPA project will have a significant impact not only on the organisation of credit institutions but also on retail payment infrastructures in Europe. In this context, I would like to welcome the decision taken by the local government to start work on a new system for mass payments, the STET, which, in addition to the necessary renewal of our technical infrastructures, will allow us to benefit from an important asset in the movement to consolidate retail infrastructures that is beginning. 6 With regard to over-indebtedness, I have noted the apparent paradox that you have mentioned between a certain official discourse on the distribution of credit and legitimate concerns about over-indebtedness. On this point, any confusion should be avoided. The controlled development of credit to households is a normal development in a society such as ours. It is therefore understandable that governments are focusing on establishing mechanisms for easier access to credit. On the other hand, the analysis of the phenomena of over-indebtedness, which we have observed in recent years, shows that these are the result of multiple factors and are, to a large extent, disconnected from the evolution of credit in general. The latest typological survey we carried out shows that the majority (more than 70%) of situations of over-indebtedness result, not from an excessive distribution of credits, but from an accident of life that occurred during the repayment period. These general considerations do not, of course, mean that credit institutions can reduce their vigilance in granting credit to individuals. In this regard, I strongly hope that they will use all the means at their disposal to stop over-indebtedness: examining the situation of borrowers, scoring systems and, consulting the File of Incidents of Repayment of Credits to Individuals managed by the Bank of France (which can now be consulted in real time). You also mention the embarrassment that can cause for the institutions you represent a possible conflict of regulations such as those to which the CNIL and the Banking Commission are required to ensure. In this respect, you want these authorities to coordinate their actions and provide consistent instructions for use. I must first recall that cooperation already exists between these two authorities, whose services regularly consult each other on subjects of common interest in order to reconcile the imperatives resulting from the regulations they are responsible for enforcing. Thus, the single authorizations granted by the CNIL in the areas of 7 the fight against money laundering and scoring methods for the purpose of granting credits are provided for by the law "Informatique et Liberte9s". They exempt institutions from taking binding steps. These authorisations are submitted in advance to the services of the Banking Commission so that they can ensure that they are compatible with the rules it is responsible for enforcing. An exchange of views ensues to arrive at a position that gathers consensus. I can thus say that this collaboration, in this area as in others, makes it possible to find, despite the different purpose of the applicable texts, solutions to the potential difficulties raised by the institutions concerned. Rest assured, Mr. President, that the teams of these authorities are determined to continue to work together to ensure coherence between their respective fields of action. Finally, I am fully aware of the burden of declarative obligations on the profession. The consultation launched in recent weeks should ultimately make it possible to improve the situation while ensuring a level of information compatible with the missions of the Bank of France, the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission and the European Central Bank. * Mr President, thank you for the opportunity to share these thoughts with you. The Banque de France and the Banking Commission will ensure that the quality and richness of the relations between your association and the representatives of the supervisory authorities are maintained and safeguarded. 8
