Title: Global savings allocation from a European perspective
text: Economic Meetings of Aix-en-Provence 8 July 2006 Session: "The allocation of savings" Global Savings Allocation - A European Perspective By Christian NOYER Governor of the Bank of France I have been asked to present a European point of view. I will come to that in a moment. Before I do, however, I would like to reflect before you for a moment on what would be the vision of a man from another world, for example a Martian, who would contemplate today the flows of global savings. This Martian, whom I suppose by hypothesis has a good general economic culture, but without excess of sophistication, could not fail to be surprised by the spectacle that would be offered to him: that of 1.2 billion "poor" Chinese, with an average income of 900 dollars per year who, individually, lend each year according to sources from 100 to 170 dollars - that is - to - say 12 to 20% of their income - to American residents, whose income is fifteen times higher than theirs. This is to finance, essentially, the private and public consumption of these 300 million Americans. This Martian could not fail to wonder: is there not a better use of their income for these Chinese savers, even though, for many of them, the basic needs of education, health and infrastructure are far from being met? In the absence of further analysis, this Martian would inevitably conclude that the allocation of global savings is not optimal today and that much remains to be done for the international capital market to effectively perform its basic functions. Based on this observation, what arguments could we put forward to reassure him? At least three of them can be found: First, note that if the United States attracts Chinese savings, (and, more generally, that of emerging countries) it is for good reasons. Admittedly, it is not clear, as some claim, that investment in the United States offers a private return (let alone a social return) higher than that of emerging countries. But the US capital market is still the most liquid, the deepest, and therefore the "safest" in the world, even if this comparative advantage is shrinking compared to the eurozone market. It is therefore rational for all global savers to allocate a fraction of their investments to it, even if they provide a lower return than other, naturally riskier jobs. Second, it may be advantageous for Chinese residents to finance U.S. consumption, if this financing helps to develop exports, and thus Chinese production and growth. This is the thesis of the "new Bretton Woods": by stabilizing its exchange rate against the dollar, China is equipping itself with a powerful instrument to support the industrialization of its economy. There is, of course, a price to pay: it is the accumulation of poorly remunerated foreign exchange reserves subject to the risk of capital loss, if the dollar depreciates. But this price is low compared to the benefits in terms of growth, employment and living standards of such an industrialization strategy. As a result, this policy is a winner for many years to come, which guarantees the stability of the current allocation of global savings. Finally, suppose that our Martian, on the occasion of his interstellar journey, became familiar with the notion of "dark matter", or "dark matter", well known to cosmologists, but also for a few months to economists. It could be that our perception of the magnitude of U.S. financing needs is biased. While the United States is accumulating a growing net foreign debt, now equivalent to a quarter of GDP, its income balance continues to run a surplus. This paradox would be explained by the presence of a "dark matter", which the usual statistics do not count, representative in particular of the American technological advance, which would explain the over-remuneration of their assets held in the rest of the world. Far from being an indebted country, the United States would still be net creditors to the rest of the world. At this point, our Martian is shaken, but not totally convinced. As we developed our argument, he had time to research and reflect. He wondered, in particular, whether China could obtain the same benefits by developing its domestic capital market and stimulating its domestic consumption. With a developed financial market, it would be possible to offer Chinese savers liquid and safe investments. Higher consumption would also allow them to enjoy a better life, while stimulating their industry and growth. Finally, our Martian might note that the US income balance was negative two quarters out of four in 2005, and that there will soon be no more paradox of the income balance to explain. Our interplanetary visitor, at the end of his reflections, could be tempted to conclude that it would be in the interest of Chinese residents to save less. Symmetrically, it could advise U.S. residents to save more. It could all the more easily convince them that the future income deficit could change the way public opinion perceives the current account deficit. For the first time, in fact, it will result in a real drain on American domestic resources. It is here, it seems to me, that the "Martian" point of view would join the European point of view. Europe, as such, occupies a "neutral" position in the allocation of global savings. Its current account balance is close to equilibrium. Its intermediation role is set to expand with the internationalisation of the euro and the development of European financial markets. But what matters to Europe today is not so much the allocation of global savings, but its formation and level. And we can probably consider that the Chinese savings rate (51% of GNP in 2005) is too high while that of the United States is too low. The real question, concerning financial markets and their functioning, is that of their possible role in the formation of these imbalances. First, as markets grow and improve, they are increasingly financing current account imbalances and thus contributing to their sustainability. After all, according to some analysts, this is not a bad thing. Whether we share this optimism or not, we cannot forget other less reassuring elements. The weakness of US savings is probably linked to the wealth effect caused by inflation in real estate and, to a lesser extent, financial assets. And this inflation is facilitated, even encouraged, by the recent development of certain financial innovations. Symmetrically, Chinese savings are probably excessively stimulated, or even "forced" by the absence of financial markets, allowing, for example, a normal development of housing credit. Europe is an open economic whole. For this reason, it cannot regard with indifference the accumulation of internal and external financial imbalances, even if it does not contribute directly to them. It therefore has a major interest in rebalancing saving behaviour around the world. But, as the Martian's fable shows, it is also in the interest of the international community as a whole. Over a long period of time, the financing of high-standard-of-living consumers by savers who have just emerged from poverty is both contrary to economic efficiency and, perhaps, to the fundamental ethical requirement.

J'y viendrai dans un instant. Ce Martien, que je suppose par hypothse dot d'une bonne culture conomique gnrale, mais sans excs de sophistication, ne pourrait manquer d'tre tonn devant le spectacle qui s'offrirait  lui : celui de 1,2 milliards de Chinois "pauvres", avec un revenu moyen de 900 dollars par an qui, individuellement, prtent chaque anne selon les sources de 100  170 dollars  c'est    dire 12  20% de leur revenu -  des rsidents amricains, dont le revenu est quinze fois suprieur au leur. En l'absence d'analyses plus pousses, ce Martien conclurait invitablement que l'allocation de l'pargne mondiale n'est pas, aujourd'hui, optimale et que beaucoup reste  faire pour que le march international des capitaux remplisse efficacement ses fonctions de base. Partant de ce constat, quels arguments pourrions nous avancer pour le rassurer ? On peut en trouver au moins trois :  D'abord noter que, si les Etats-Unis attirent l'pargne chinoise, (et, plus gnralement celle des pays mergents) c'est pour de bonnes raisons. Certes, il n'est pas clair, comme certains le prtendent, que l'investissement aux Etats-Unis offre un rendement priv (et encore moins un rendement social) suprieur  celui de pays mergents. Mais le march amricain des capitaux reste encore le plus liquide, le plus profond, et, donc, le plus "sr" du monde, mme si cet avantage comparatif se rduit par rapport au march de la zone euro. Il est donc rationnel, pour tous les pargnants mondiaux, d'y allouer une fraction de leurs placements, mme si ceux-ci procurent un rendement infrieur  celui d'autres emplois, naturellement plus risqus.  Ensuite, il peut tre avantageux, pour les rsidents chinois, de financer la consommation amricaine, si ce financement permet de dvelopper les exportations, et donc la production et la croissance chinoises. C'est la thse du "nouveau Bretton Woods" : en stabilisant son taux de change par rapport au dollar, la Chine se dote d'un instrument puissant de soutien  l'industrialisation de son conomie. Il y a, certes, un prix  payer : c'est l'accumulation de rserves de change mal rmunres et soumises au risque de perte en capital, si le dollar se dprcie. Mais ce prix est faible au regard des avantages que procure, en termes de croissance, d'emploi et de niveau de vie, une telle stratgie d'industrialisation. De sorte que cette politique est gagnante pour encore de longues annes, ce qui garantit la stabilit de l'allocation actuelle de l'pargne mondiale.  Enfin, supposons que notre Martien,  loccasion de son voyage interstellaire, se soit familiaris avec la notion de  matire noire , ou  dark matter , bien connue des cosmologistes, mais aussi depuis quelques mois des conomistes. Il se pourrait que limage que nous nous faisons de lampleur des besoins de financement amricains soit biaise. Alors que les Etats-Unis accumulent une dette extrieure nette croissante, quivalente aujourdhui  un quart du PIB, leur balance des revenus continue de dgager un excdent. Ce paradoxe sexpliquerait par la prsence dune  matire noire , que les statistiques usuelles ne comptabilisent pas, reprsentative notamment de lavance technologique amricaine, qui expliquerait la sur-rmunration de leurs actifs dtenus dans le reste du monde. Loin dtre un pays endett, les Etats-Unis seraient toujours crditeurs nets sur le reste du monde. A ce stade, notre Martien est branl, mais pas totalement convaincu. Pendant que nous dveloppions notre argumentation, il a eu le temps de se documenter et de rflchir. Il se demande, notamment, si la Chine ne pourrait obtenir les mmes avantages en dveloppant son march interne des capitaux et en stimulant sa consommation domestique. Avec un march financier dvelopp, il serait possible d'offrir aux pargnants chinois des placements liquides et srs. Une consommation plus leve leur permettrait, par ailleurs, de bnficier d'une vie meilleure, tout en stimulant leur industrie et leur croissance. Enfin, notre Martien pourrait noter que la balance des revenus amricaine a t ngative deux trimestres sur quatre en 2005, et quil ny aura bientt plus de paradoxe de la balance des revenus  expliquer. Notre visiteur interplantaire, au terme de ses rflexions, pourrait tre tenter de conclure quil serait de lintrt des rsidents chinois de moins pargner. Symtriquement, il pourrait conseiller aux rsidents amricains dpargner davantage. Il pourrait dautant plus facilement les convaincre que le dficit  venir de la balance des revenus pourrait venir modifier la manire dont lopinion publique peroit le dficit courant. Pour la premire fois, en effet, il se traduira par une vritable ponction sur les ressources domestiques amricaines. C'est ici, me semble-t-il que le point de vue "martien" rejoindrait le point de vue europen. L'Europe, en tant que telle, occupe une position " neutre" dans l'allocation de l'pargne mondiale. Son solde des paiements courants est proche de l'quilibre. Son rle d'intermdiation est appel  s'tendre avec l'internationalisation de l'euro et le dveloppement des marchs financiers europens. Mais ce qui compte aujourd'hui, pour l'Europe, ce n'est tant pas l'allocation de l'pargne mondiale, que sa formation et son niveau. Et l'on peut sans doute considrer que le taux d'pargne chinois (51% du PNB en 2005) est trop lev tandis que celui des Etats-Unis est trop faible. La vraie question, concernant les marchs financiers et leur fonctionnement, est celle de leur rle ventuel dans la formation de ces dsquilibres. D'abord,  mesure qu'ils se dveloppent et se perfectionnent, les marchs financent de mieux en mieux les dsquilibres des paiements courants et contribuent ainsi  leur soutenabilit. Aprs tout, selon certains analystes, ce n'est pas une mauvaise chose. Que l'on partage ou non cet optimisme, on ne peut oublier d'autres lments moins rassurants. La faiblesse de l'pargne amricaine est sans doute lie  l'effet de richesse que provoque l'inflation des actifs immobiliers et, dans une moindre mesure, financiers. Et cette inflation est facilite, voire encourage, par le dveloppement rcent de certaines innovations financires. Symtriquement, l'pargne chinoise est sans doute excessivement stimule, voire "force" par l'absence de marchs financiers, permettant, par exemple, un dveloppement normal du crdit  l'habitat. L'Europe est un ensemble conomique ouvert. Pour cette raison, elle ne peut considrer avec indiffrence l'accumulation de dsquilibres financiers internes et externes, mme si elle n'y contribue pas directement. Elle a donc un intrt majeur  ce que s'opre un rquilibrage des comportements d'pargne dans le monde. Mais, la fable du Martien le montre : c'est aussi l'intrt de la communaut internationale dans son ensemble. Sur longue priode, le financement des consommateurs  haut niveau de vie par des pargnants  peine sortis de la pauvret est  la fois contraire  l'efficacit conomique et, peut tre,  l'exigence thique fondamentale.

Title: Opening speech of the first Franco-Chinese financial forum
text: Speech by Mr Christian Noyer Governor of the Banque de France OPENING SPEECH OF THE FIRST FRANCO-CHINESE FINANCIAL FORUM 21 September 2006 Beijing Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to address you this morning and to lend my full support, alongside Governor ZHOU and the People's Bank of China, to this 1st Franco-Chinese Financial Forum organized today in Beijing. I am convinced that this day will allow for a broad dialogue between the financial communities of our two countries. We want to encourage cooperation between all Chinese and French financial players, central banks and regulators of course, but also between professional federations, financial companies, as well as between academics. These should not be one-day discussions. On the contrary, I encourage you to strengthen today the already existing links of nourished and long-term cooperation. I will articulate my remarks around three main axes: the first, the importance of a developed and efficient financial system to support economic growth; the second, the conditions for successful financial development; the third, the cooperation and the role that French and European actors can play in this process in China. * This first Sino-French Forum takes place at a decisive period in China's economic and financial history. The integration of the latter into world trade has progressed dramatically. China has also opened up to capital flows. It is now at the heart of many international economic and financial debates. The France and China share similar experiences. Indeed, French finance has experienced, in the recent past, the same transformations as 2 those that Chinese finance is now going through: financial deregulation, the opening and privatization of the banking system, disintermediation and the development of financial markets, the gradual opening up to international capital movements. China needs to develop its own capital market more broadly, both to select the best investment projects, spread the risk among the different agents, and offer Chinese savers safe and liquid investments. Better return on savings would help increase the consumption incomes of Chinese households, allowing them to improve their well-being, while boosting production and economic growth. This development must go hand in hand with the opening of the Chinese financial system to the outside world. I would even say that this openness is inseparable from the healthy development of the financial system. It alone is the guarantee of a rapid adoption of international standards in financial matters. More competition for the allocation of financial flows and risks improves the efficiency of the economy as a whole. This competition must take place not only between intermediaries and financial markets in the same country, but also between local and foreign actors, and more broadly between national financial systems. In practice, the presence of non-resident financial actors seems to me to be an essential spur to the proper functioning of the Chinese financial system. It helps to expand and improve the offer of investments and financing for Chinese investors. * However, the development and greater openness of the financial system must not be done in a disorderly or hasty manner. Has 3 In this regard, I particularly appreciate governor ZHOU's concept of "financial ecology". And, I consider fundamental the role played by central banks in protecting the financial "ecosystem". Central banks are inherently interested in the efficiency and stability of the financial system. Ensuring the health of this "ecosystem" requires continuous monitoring and improvement of both the financial machinery and the general business environment. This is the legal and accounting framework, of course, it being understood that it must be applied. It must guarantee the legal certainty of financial transactions, in particular as regards the regulation of bankruptcies. Information on counterparties must be truthful. It is also important that the intermediaries, financial or otherwise, are strong and the statistical apparatus efficient. More generally, strong market discipline is required. The internal improvements required go hand in hand with the adaptation of the Chinese financial system to international financial developments. We are currently witnessing significant structural changes within the Chinese banking sector. At the same time, the Strong Will of the Chinese authorities to build a robust supervisory system and a clear regulatory framework are essential to promote foreign participation. These efforts, both in regulatory matters (on banks' internal control, on taking into account operational and market risks), and in terms of supervision (strengthening on-site inspection procedures and desk-based supervision), can be seen as a desire and willingness on China's part to comply with international best practices and standards. In this perspective, and as the France did, a review of China according to the IMF-World Bank's Financial Stability Assessment Program would be an important new signal. This is all the more so since China has 4 actively participated in the revision of the fundamental principles for effective banking supervision, which will be officially presented at the International Conference of Banking Supervisors (ICBS) next October in Merida. Similarly, the promotion of a strong culture of risk management monitoring and control within financial institutions can be achieved quickly by benefiting from the practices of the most successful banks on the international scene, particularly in the key areas of corporate governance, internal control, risk measurement and management. In this regard, the effective implementation of the new capital adequacy framework, Basel II, is a key challenge for both resident and non-resident banks. In particular, it involves strengthened ties between Chinese and foreign supervisors, in the context of the home-host dialogue. This is particularly important for the France, as our major banks in China will adopt the most advanced approach enabled by Basel II, to assess and manage credit, market and operational risks. As you can see, the task is heavy, and building such an "ecosystem" can only be the result of a medium-term process. A lot has already been done by the Chinese authorities, in a short time; but much remains to be done to avoid any disappointment. Of course, brutal reform is not in the interest of either China or the rest of the world. We note with interest the gradual and sequenced approach taken by the Chinese authorities. A gradual approach does not mean immobility. Recent reforms underscore China's determination to move forward: gradual increase in the flexibility of the exchange rate regime; gradual opening of financial markets to foreigners within the framework of 5 QFII (Qualified Foreign Institutional Investors) licenses; recent launch of QDII (Qualified Domestic Institutional Investors), all very encouraging signs. Inflows and outflows generated by qualified investors (about USD 10 billion in both directions) are still limited in scale. I hope that the volumes concerned will increase rapidly. Similarly, in line with the World Trade Organization (WTO) timetable, China has increased the opening up of its financial system. Whether for banks or insurance companies, the Chinese territory is increasingly widely accessible to foreigners. In turn, recent initiatives by major international financial institutions show that foreign banks have responded very positively to these strategic changes. French banks must not stay away from these developments. The ongoing efforts to homogenize financial market regulations in China must also receive a great deal of attention from us, as they form the backbone of many of the activities developed by French banks. Finally, of course, in less than three months, personal banking services will be legally open to foreigners. We are following this movement with great attention. * In this process, foreign actors, and particularly French and European actors, can provide valuable help, for the benefit of all. Cooperation between Chinese and French financial authorities is already a reality. For example, we have signed a cooperation agreement (memorandum 6 of understanding) with the China Banking Regulatory Commission (CBRC) last year. Exchanges with our colleagues at the PBoC and the CBRC are nourished and continuous, whether in Beijing, Paris, or on the occasion of international meetings. Like this institutional cooperation, it is also important that the other players in our two financial industries cooperate actively. I therefore hope that this day of meetings will be an opportunity for the financial actors of our two countries, to better know the specificities and talents of each other. The Place de Paris has a lot to offer. Its members are a source for Chinese companies of technical knowledge transfers and good practices. It has performed very well in recent years, reflected in the significant increase in market capitalization, the growing presence of foreign investors and the very strong activity of the asset management activities. Let me highlight a few aspects of this: - in a context of increased international competition, the pan-European stock exchange Euronext (which includes Paris, Amsterdam, Brussels and Lisbon) has strengthened its infrastructure, while receiving several important proposals for mergers with other market companies. The launch in 2005 of Alternext, an unregulated market for listing small and medium-sized enterprises, is already a success. A Chinese company even plans to list before the end of the year. While already owning Liffe, the world's largest futures market, Euronext more recently acquired the MTS platform as part of a joint venture with Borsa Italiana. This is Europe's leading platform for wholesale exchanges of government securities. 7 - Paris also made a decisive contribution to the launch of the Common Label for European Short-Term Markets (STEP), a significant step towards fully integrated European markets. The France remains a dominant market for short-term securities. It ranks first for euro-denominated securities with a volume of 80350 billion. - Paris has, of course, leading banks, both at European and global level. These banks rely on good business models in their domestic market, which are both varied and stable. This solid foundation allows them a strong internationalization. They enjoy strong profitability and steady growth. In addition, the solvency ratio of the main banking groups is at a high level (more than 8% tier 1 on average), demonstrating the soundness of their financial structures. I also note that they are among the world leaders in asset management and derivative financial transactions. Above all, these companies have unanimously recognized expertise and capacity for innovation, which go hand in hand with the implementation of advanced approaches to risk measurement and control. Some areas of expertise of the French financial industry seem to me to be particularly relevant in the Chinese context: close historical links with the public sector, proven experience in the exercise of banking and insurance professions in rural areas, powerful cooperative networks in both the banking and insurance fields. So many useful examples for Chinese reformers, opportunities for cooperation between our two financial industries. Thank you for your attention. 8

Title: What future for microcredit in France and industrialized countries
text: Breakfast debate on 21 March 2007 at the Banque de France ---------- "What future for microcredit in France and industrialized countries?" ---------- Speech by Christian NOYER, Governor of the Banque de France It is a great privilege for me to welcome this morning Professor Muhammad YUNUS, Nobel Peace Prize 2006, known internationally as "the banker of the poor". Everyone remembers that he founded grameen Bank more than 30 years ago to lend small amounts to people who do not have access to the "normal" banking system, and allow them to create their micro-activity. Since then, 7 million people have benefited from these microcredits. It is also a great pleasure for me to welcome Mrs. Maria Nowak, who will discuss the fundamental role of the association she chairs, the Association for the Right to Economic Initiative (ADIE), which carries out nearly 8,000 solidarity loans per year. 2005 was declared by the United Nations the "International Year of Microcredit", with the objective of "strengthening financial sector advances in promoting sustainable pro-poor financial services in all countries". The French authorities and the Banque de France fully support this idea of a "financial sector open to all". Microcredit is primarily conceived as an instrument in the fight against poverty. Microfinance institutions are mainly present in Southeast Asia, South America and Africa. Even in these regions, however, microcredit affects only 103 million people, barely 2 per cent of the estimated total population excluded from the traditional banking system. But microcredit also has a key role to play in industrialized countries, particularly in Europe and France. I am convinced, and so are the public authorities of our country, that it is a useful instrument for financing the needs of those who are "neglected by the banking system". Thus, in France as in Europe, we can consider that microcredit is a response to two segments of needs, and therefore of customers: that of financing the creation or development of micro-enterprises, in particular when it comes to the creation of enterprises by a job seeker; it is "professional microcredit"; that of punctual assistance to people in difficulty, in support of a specific project: it is the "social microcredit". In France, microfinance is developed by specialized microcredit associations. Of course, although banks are their partners, these associations are prescribers, and often distributors of loans. I have already welcomed the exceptional results achieved by ADIE, under the leadership of Mrs Maria Nowak. I would mention the 10,000 loans of honour per year made by the network France initiative or the guarantees granted by France Active, as well as the major role of Secours Catholique. In recent years, France has considerably increased the resources devoted to the development of microcredit. The French public authorities have thus decided to set up the Social Cohesion Fund, endowed with 73 million euros, which guarantees small loans granted to people in difficulty. The France was also the first European country to adapt its financial legislation to the requirements of microcredit. - An amendment to the banking law passed in 2001, approved by the Banque de France, allows associations that finance and support unemployed entrepreneurs to borrow to lend. - The rate of attrition to sole proprietorships was abolished in 2005, to facilitate loans to the most modest people. - Finally, I understand that the public authorities are considering a further expansion of Article L.5116 of the Monetary and Financial Code to also allow associations to borrow to lend for "a professional, training or social project for people in a situation of exclusion or precariousness". The Bank of France fully supports this idea. With regard to our own actions in particular: In September 2006, the Banque de France created a "Microfinance Observatory", in liaison with the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the Caisse des De9pf4ts et Consignations. it is ready to support initiatives to promote, and disseminate, 'good practices' for donors in the microfinance sector." the Bank is ready, in liaison with the institutions already mentioned, to lead or participate in any think tank on an action plan aimed at the development of microcredit in France. Finally, many former directors and executives of the Banque de France are ready to structure themselves in order to provide their contribution and support to partner associations.

Title: How to assess risks and vulnerabilities
text: Economic Meetings of Aix-en-Provence 6 July 2007 Session 2 - Financial globalization, a force for convergence? How to assess risks and vulnerabilities? Christian Noyer Governor of the Bank of France Despite the recent upward correction in long-term rates, recent market developments should not add to the euphoric atmosphere of a beautiful Provene7al afternoon. The moderation of global inflation has helped stabilize interest rates at historically low levels; this factor and the abundant global liquidity largely explain the low volatility of risk premia observed on the major asset classes; credit spreads on emerging countries are close to historical lows; Asian surplus savings appear to be adjusting harmoniously to the current account deficit of the United States,.. These trends encourage a very favorable diagnosis of the international financial system, even if Dr. Knock's aphorism about health comes to mind: ".. a precarious state that does not bode well! " But I will not assume the role of Cassandra and will confine myself here to mentioning the potential risks that seem to me today to be relevant from the point of view of a supervising central banker. No one disputes in theory the efficiency gains linked to the development of the global capital market, in terms of savings allocation, diversification and risk allocation, technology transfers. In addition, empirical work (IMF) or simple observation indicates a positive relationship between the growth of emerging countries and their financial integration with the rest of the world, and more generally between the rise of financial markets and global economic growth. Financial globalization is no less bad press (including among some economists!), because it would carry several major defects, which must undoubtedly be put into perspective: 3/4 The macroeconomic cost of crises for emerging economies: we cite the case of Thailand, where the decline in GDP was 8% and that of investment by nearly 50% between 1996 and 1998, and that of Indonesia. But these countries lacked a mature risk assessment system and prudential frameworks to absorb significant capital flows towards the most productive investments. The main lesson to be drawn from this is that the opening of the capital account presupposes a sufficient degree of transparency and supervision of banking and financial transactions, in accordance with international codes and standards; 3/4 The "classic" dysfunctions of any capital market, amplified by the effects of size and contagion attached to globalization. A good illustration of this can be found in the Russian or Argentine crises: asymmetries in information on the economic and financial situation involving "moral hazard" behaviour on the part of borrowers; inconsistency of private investors assured of a bail-out. The IMF has been pulling out of it since the lessons learned by formalizing strict conditions for access to exceptional resources, such as debt sustainability and the quality of adjustment programmes; 3/4 The myopia of the markets, favoring an illusory macroeconomic stability. The "new Bretton Woods" system1 would be pernicious from this point of view, as the recycling of Chinese savings into the US current account deficit would delay inevitable macroeconomic adjustments. Effective in balancing the supply and demand for savings with fluidity, markets would misjudge the risks of unsustainability. Perhaps, but have they not always ended up sanctioning macroeconomic situations or commitments deemed by all unsustainable in the near future? During the EMS crisis in 1992/1993, for example, or the Asian crisis of 1997/1998, the so-called "self-fulfilling" expectations were verified whenever the "fundamentals" justified it, never when the diagnosis was more shared. This is why, apart from the fact that international dollar holders today have no more interest in it than issuers, a generalized crisis of confidence in the sustainability of US external debt seems very unlikely. 3/4 Finally, the idea that speculation, in the sense of continuous arbitrage by participants to take advantage of price differentials or actual or anticipated remuneration within each market or between the different markets, would constitute a fundamental factor of instability, particularly in the foreign exchange market, remains well established. However, expectations play rather as a reminder force and the diversification of risks leads to a de facto solidarity of international investors, itself stabilizing which can of course be weakened by the inconsistency of monetary policy signals. Don't cry wolf.. without concealing the vulnerabilities attached, in particular, to recent innovations in financial markets. I will mention four of them, which ultimately relate to two main concerns: Are risks properly assessed? By whom are they worn? 3/4 The rapid growth of leveraged transactions, derivatives, LBO/Mergers and Acquisitions (more than 300% growth since 2002) or carry-trade raises questions about the dopant effect of low interest rates on the growth of these markets and therefore their vulnerability to a default that is always possible in the debt chain, especially in the event of an increase in the cost of liquidity. One could then fear very destabilizing and potentially contagious correction movements due to the typically reinforced correlation of expectations in the event of a crisis. 3/4 The assessment of specific categories of risk may seem overly optimistic. So I do not underestimate the economic progress in most of the major emerging countries, but the memory of recent debt crises seems to have emerged too quickly from the memory of the markets. A possible perverse effect of this generalized flattening of risk premiums is to encourage investors to seek ultimate remunerative niches, by definition of poor quality. Banks must also learn as a preventive measure the lessons of the increase in the risk of borrower default observed in the United States for the subprime category. 3/4 The transparency of the operations of institutions specializing in so-called "alternative" management, such as Hedge Funds, which represent more than 40% of the volume of transactions on certain large equity markets, between 25% and 50% of transactions on derivative markets according to estimates, remains insufficient. However, hedge funds, via pension funds, manage, probably without the knowledge of a fraction of end investors, an increasing share of intermediated savings. In these circumstances, there is reason to fear a gap between the desired or perceived risk and the risk actually borne by these investors; 3/4 Finally, there is the question of the robustness of risk transfer mechanisms. How to accurately trace the risk in the case of an LBO arrangement, for example, financed to the tune of two-thirds by bank debt, to be then sold via a securitization vehicle to other investors (specialized funds or Hedge Funds) whose shares are 1 Dooley, Forlkerts-Landau et Garber ultimately find in a pension fund .. ? these transfer mechanisms have not yet been tested by a confrontation with large-scale shocks, such as a rapid rise in default rates. In this regard, we encourage banks to develop internal models to link all sophisticated risk components. Roger Ferguson, at a conference on globalization last summer in Jackson Hole, noted that the profession of policy makers had become "easier and harder". Easier perhaps, because the increased flexibility of markets explains the greater resilience of economies that have become more stable( or less unstable). Surely more difficult, because their interdependence increases the risks of externality and the need for coordination. The latter is already narrow in the area of supervision of banks and markets, because financial stability is undoubtedly a collective good. We can still improve it in areas such as the collection of data on derivatives markets, standards for the dissemination of information by financial institutions, including hedge funds, etc. Transparency, which is a prerequisite for effective supervision, seems to me to be an essential condition for the discipline and efficiency of globalised markets.

Title: Payment Card Security Observatory
text: Press conference of 10 July 2007 Introductory remarks by the President Ladies and Gentlemen, I am pleased to present to you today the fourth annual report of the Payment Card Security Observatory. The first observation that must be made is that the card has become in recent years the most frequently used means of payment by the French. In 2006, the number of card transactions exceeded 7 billion, while about 3.5 billion cheques were issued. The importance of users' trust in this means of payment is therefore crucial. The work carried out by the Observatory since 2003 has made it possible to measure the efforts made by issuers and traders to promote the security of this instrument and limit its fraud. The work of 2006, which I will comment on today, confirms the mastery of this security and the stability of the level of fraud in France. However, we wanted to complete our indicators by ordering, for the first time this year, a survey on the perception by holders of the security of their payment card. I propose to briefly present the results of the work carried out in 2006 by the Observatory on the various areas of intervention entrusted to it by the legislator: the monitoring of security policies, the development of fraud statistics and technology watch. I will also make a special point about this year's survey, the results of which are instructive. I will tell you Press conference of 10 July 2007 1/7 invites you to refer to the sheets attached to the press kit that has been distributed to you. The security of the personalization chain The observatory's first mission concerns the monitoring of security measures put in place by credit institutions and traders. To continue the work carried out in previous years, the Observatory focused in 2006 on the security measures taken during the "personalization" of cards. The personalization phase consists in introducing on the blank cards produced by manufacturers the information relating to the issuer and the holder in order to allow their use by the holders. The security of this process is crucial because it is all the sensitive card data that is used during it. To prevent the risk of theft, copying or misappropriation of this data, personalization operations must therefore be subject to high security measures. The Observatory found that card issuers and networks impose high-level requirements on providers in charge of personalisation, subjecting them to prior approval and regular checks. As a result, no incidents affecting the security of these operations were identified in France. Fraud statistics for 2006 The Second Task of the Centre is to compile fraud statistics. The figures collected cover almost all payment cards issued in France, i.e. 78.6 million cards. To compile its statistics, the Observatory was able to rely this year not only on its usual contributors (in particular the 150 members of the CB system and the main issuers of private cards) but also on a specific survey conducted by the Federation of e-commerce and distance selling (FEVAD) among its members for fraud on remote payments. Press conference of 10 July 2007 2/7 The data collected make it possible to make 3 observations: - after the sharp declines observed between 2003 and 2005, fraud appears stable in 2006: the overall fraud rate remains almost at its level of last year, at 0.064%, although it should be noted an increase in the total amount of fraudulent payments due to the sustained growth in the volume and value of transactions (this amount stood at EUR 252.6 million in 2006 in 2006), compared with 80235.9 million in 2005). - the distribution of fraud by geographical area remains marked by an imbalance between national and international transactions: 60% of fraud concerns international transactions, while this type of transaction accounts for less than 10% of the value of card payments recorded in French systems. However, there is an encouraging shift in the decline in the fraud rate on international transactions, from 0.40% to 0.36%, due to the migration of French card systems to EMV standards, which is therefore beginning to bear fruit. - the fraud rate on remote payments increases slightly, and remains much higher than that of local and AUTOMATED payments: 0.199% against 0.024%. According to the analyses conducted in 2006, it appears that this rate varies according to the method of payment at a distance and is higher for payments on the Internet than for payments by mail and telephone. The persistence of a greater vulnerability to fraud of remote card payments leads the Observatory to insist on the importance of compliance with the security measures recommended by issuers, in particular the systematic use of the visual cryptogram (CVx2) in remote payment and the verification of the identity of buyers by merchants. Technology watch The third mission of the Observatory is to ensure a technological watch in the fight against fraud. In 2006, the Observatory conducted two studies: one Press conference of 10 July 2007 3/7 on the impact of the use of so-called "open" networks and technologies in the payment card environment, and the other on the security of payment and withdrawal machines. You will find these detailed studies in the report. I would like to indicate here the main recommendations they call for. ? With regard to the increasingly frequent use in the payment card environment of so-called "open" technologies and networks such as the Internet, the Observatory considers it necessary to implement appropriate measures, including the use of secure protocols and the protection of the logical integrity of the equipment used. To this end, the Observatory encourages all stakeholders to comply with requirements formulated on this subject by the Groupement des Cartes Bancaires "CB". ? Regarding the security of payment and withdrawal machines, the Observatory notes that the main vulnerability lies in the hacking of track readers. It therefore recommends that manufacturers of such equipment and their operators: o to remove, on the one hand, the track readers of the PLCs when functionality is not necessary; o to study, on the other hand, the feasibility and efficiency of separating track readers and chip readers, in particular on the most exposed PLCs; o and finally, to continue to improve the physical protection devices of PLCs. The Observatory also encourages issuers and merchants to develop communication campaigns vis-e0-vis holders to attract their attention during ATM transactions. Press conference of 10 July 2007 4/7 Cardholders' perception of card security As I mentioned in the introduction, this year the Observatory has carried out unprecedented work aimed at better understanding the perception that cardholders have of the security of their cards. This study thus complements the statistical indicators on fraud that the Observatory collects from issuers and traders. The Observatory commissioned the CSA Institute to carry out a survey, conducted on a representative sample of 1,005 people aged 18 to 74 living in metropolitan France. This survey confirms the importance of the card in the range of payment methods used by the French. Its use is now totally trivialized for a large majority of holders, even if a part of the population remains reluctant to use the card to pay remotely (by phone, mail or on the Internet) and abroad. The card also benefits from an excellent image: it is the means of payment perceived as the safest by the French: 80% of holders consider that it is quite safe or very secure. In addition, the security measures put in place and the recommendations of banking institutions are generally known and appreciated: a large majority of holders say they comply naturally. However, risky behaviours remain: 5% of carriers say they do not follow any of these recommendations. In addition, more than one in two card users report lending their card to their loved ones, which is behavior that goes against the most basic security measures. This is why the Observatory wanted to remind bearers of the precautionary reflexes to adopt in the use of their cards. To this end, he has drawn up precautionary statements which you will find in Sheet D of the press kit. Of course, these tips complement the messages that banks and consumer associations already broadcast for each means of payment. Press conference of 10 July 2007 5/7 I invite you to spread this message as widely as possible, especially given the summer period that is beginning, since it is often an opportunity for cardholders to use their card more intensively and far from their usual place of residence. Conclusion In conclusion, I would like to emphasise the high level of security of payment cards today in France, which the Work of the Observatory makes it possible to highlight. However, the stakes in this area are numerous. The first is to constantly maintain a level of security requirements adapted to technological developments which, in this field, appear regularly. It is also about effectively combating all forms of fraud and ensuring that fraudsters cannot take advantage of less controlled situations. From this point of view, fraud on distance payments and cross-border payments must continue to be the subject of special attention and determined action by all parties concerned. Finally, it is necessary to prepare for the major developments that will be represented by the opening up of the European market in the field of cards. Indeed, as you know, 1 January 2008 will mark the start of the European Payments Area project, "SEPA", which will offer tremendous opportunities for payment service providers. The cards issued in each of the European countries will thus be able to be used in the other countries as easily as in their country of issue. The forthcoming application of the Payment Services Directive will make it possible to standardise the rights of users in each country. However, the different card schemes operating in Europe will adopt the same high level of security to maintain effective protection against fraud. This is, I believe, a major challenge for the years to come. That is why, for 2007, the Observatory has decided to devote part of its work to this subject. Thank you for your attention. LObservatoire a confi  linstitut CSA la ralisation dun sondage, conduit sur un chantillon reprsentatif de 1 005 personnes ges de 18  74 ans rsidant en France mtropolitaine. Ce sondage confirme limportance de la carte dans la gamme des moyens de paiement utiliss par les Franais. Son usage est aujourdhui totalement banalis pour une grande majorit de porteurs, mme si une part de la population reste cependant rticente  lutilisation de la carte pour payer  distance (par tlphone, par courrier ou sur Internet) et  ltranger. La carte bnficie en outre dune excellente image : elle est le moyen de paiement peru comme le plus sr par les franais : 80 % des porteurs considrent quelle est assez sre ou trs sre. En outre, plus dun utilisateur de carte sur deux dclare prter sa carte  ses proches, ce qui est un comportement qui va  lencontre des mesures les plus lmentaires de scurit. Cest la raison pour laquelle lObservatoire a souhait rappeler aux porteurs les reflexes de prudence  adopter dans lutilisation de leurs cartes. Il a pour cela labor des conseils de prudence que vous trouverez en fiche D du dossier de presse. Bien videmment, ces conseils compltent les messages que les banques et les associations de consommateurs diffusent dj pour chaque moyen de paiement. Confrence de presse du 10 juillet 2007 5/7 Je vous invite  diffuser ce message le plus largement possible, notamment compte tenu de la priode estivale qui dbute, puisque cest souvent loccasion pour les porteurs dutiliser leur carte de faon plus intensive et loin de leur lieu de rsidence habituelle. Conclusion En conclusion, je voudrais insister sur le niveau lev de scurit des cartes de paiement aujourdhui en France, que les travaux de lObservatoire permettent de mettre en vidence Les enjeux en la matire sont toutefois nombreux. De ce point de vue, la fraude sur les paiements  distance et les paiements transfrontaliers doit continuer  faire lobjet dune attention particulire et dactions dtermines de la part de toutes les parties concernes. Enfin, il convient de se prparer aux volutions majeures que reprsentera louverture du march europen dans le domaine des cartes. Title: 25 years of FIBEN
text: "25 YEARS OF FIBEN" SPEECH BY MR. NOYER, GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF FRANCE Galerie Dore9e, September 12, 2007 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you today to the Golden Gallery to discuss with you the development of FIBEN. From 1982 to today, FIBEN has evolved from the concept of Business Banking File to that of an online service of information on corporate credit risk. This evolution has accompanied and often anticipated the modernization of the credit market for French companies. However, I do not wish to go back over these 25 years, which are rich in technical and methodological innovations, as was presented to you by Mr Gaudichet and Mr Barroux. If we had been given the free choice of the date of this anniversary, we would have had no better choice than this month of September. There is, of course, a coincidence with the implementation of Basel 2. There is also the news of recent weeks, that of the subprime credit crisis in the United States which shows us the usefulness for central banks to have tools allowing banks to mobilize a wide collateral. Many debates preceded the establishment of the single list of eligible assets for Eurosystem operations and the inclusion of bank loans in this list. Undeniably, the events of recent weeks have changed the terms of this debate and demonstrated the interest of a large pool of eligible assets to manage both the current and the exceptional. 1 This anniversary of FIBEN offers me the opportunity to share some reflections on the values that guide its development and condition its future. What is FIBEN today? I will focus on three of its characteristics that seem to me to be very structuring: - FIBEN is first and foremost a pool of shared information for the banking profession: mutualized, in the sense that banks, FIBEN's customers, provide information on risks and non-payments, whose interest is increased because the Banque de France aggregates them, combines them with other sources, and returns them with added value. This model is undeniably, tomorrow as today, the foundation of FIBEN as a "tool of Place"; - FIBEN is then an offer of value-added services: of course, the Banque de France listing; but also, a wide range of information accessible online to calibrate or contribute to the proper functioning of banks' internal rating systems. I am thinking, for example, of information on financial links, which is absolutely essential for measuring the interdependence of companies, and whose collection requires extreme rigour and a lot of responsiveness; - FIBEN is finally a productivity tool for the banking profession and more indirectly for companies. Indeed, more than on the mass of information as such, FIBEN focuses on the collection of relevant information, reducing information asymmetries between lenders and borrowers. The Bank's desire here is to provide the banking profession with services that make it possible, for example, to reduce the time required for banking decision-making, or to limit the amount of additional information that banks wish to request from companies - in a word, the Bank facilitates banks' access to "relevant" information both from the point of view of credit analysis and from the point of view of its ease of integration into the process of preparing credit decisions. From the point of view of a central banker, FIBEN is an excellent tool for understanding the structure of French SMEs. At a time when we are wondering about their ability to grow, about their financing, while we are wondering about the means to boost a fabric of SMEs that are 2 In terms of density, export competitiveness and the fabric of German SMEs, FIBEN's information provides answers that make it possible to formulate a precise diagnosis, as will be shown by the special SME issue of the Bank of France bulletin which should be published at the end of the month. I would also say that the permanent enrichment of the FIBEN offer is part of a process to strengthen financial stability. FIBEN is a database on companies that uses best practices in information management, which is based on a solid base of selected, verified, relevant information. This seems to me likely to provide effective assistance to banks in the implementation of "home"home" credit analysis models, in their decisions to grant financing, in monitoring their risks, in prospecting for new customers and therefore in total in controlling their credit risk. How does FIBEN fit into the current environment and what is its future? Three elements are undeniably becoming more important in the exercise of the business of credit to companies: - company rating: this is omnipresent for investors. With Basel 2 it becomes important for all companies, including those that today do not use the financial markets; - Secondly, the importance of financial innovation and the speed of changes in the industrial fabric. This assumes that the diagnostic tools are not fixed. To remain competitive, i.e. to remain centres for method design, decision-making centres and the confrontation of opinions in terms of risk assessment, financial centres must have a fundamental and operational research capacity in terms of credit risk analysis, in terms of business diagnosis; - Third element, the importance of which is shown by current events: transparency. In credit risk analysis, as in other areas of banking activity, transparency does not necessarily coincide with the abundance of information. Rather, it seems to me that transparency is part of a magic square whose four sides would be the relevance, intelligibility, freshness and accessibility of information. 3 Obviously, what will guide the Banque de France in its choices for the evolution of FIBEN will be the way to respond to these three environmental parameters, in consultation with the banking profession. - Corporate rating is already at the heart of fiben's service offering, so much so that banks, like companies, use almost as substitutable terms "FIBEN" and "Bank of France rating". Since 2004, the Banque de France listing has been compatible with the requirements of the Basel Agreement2, which has made it possible to acclimatise companies to this "synthetic image" of their financial situation; this was officially recognised this year, as you know, by the inclusion of the Bank of France on the list of external credit assessment bodies, in accordance with the procedures coordinated by the European Committee of Banking Supervisors and a great deal of attention paid to the existence of indisputable Chinese walls. Building on its branch network, the Bank of France will continue its effort to explain listing to companies. Raising business leaders' awareness of the financial factors that determine the sustainable growth of their business whenever possible is part of a constant effort at financial education. This effort is one of the foundations on which a good relationship between banks and companies is built. It seems to me that the Bank of France, certainly within the limits of its means, and also the banking profession must contribute to this educational approach. - With regard to the ability to constantly adapt credit risk diagnostic tools, our financial centre has solid assets. On the one hand, a fruitful academic tradition of conceptual thinking on accounting, financial analysis and management sciences; on the other hand, skills that have developed and sharpened thanks to the implementation of banks' internal notes. In this context, the Bank of France brings and will continue to contribute its expertise, sharing its research in areas such as scoring methodology, the application of expert systems to financial analysis, and methods for evaluating the performance of rating systems. - I come back to transparency, through the four dimensions, relevance, intelligibility, freshness, accessibility. FIBEN reflects our desire to promote transparency in all these dimensions: relevance, because the 4 pooling information naturally requires a detailed listening to the needs of the banking profession; intelligibility, through the action of "FIBEN correspondents" and Bank of France analysts who explain the FIBEN approach to banks and companies; freshness, by the significant investment made in the automation of power supplies, for the information of the commercial courts today, for the balance sheets tomorrow; "accessibility", through the structuring of a modular offer disseminated by the technical vectors POBI, the Internet access portal, and FIBORD, which offers a computer-to-computer link; To conclude, I would like to point out that FIBEN, a tool at the service of the banking profession, is fundamentally designed to promote high standards for the analysis of corporate credit risk; to speak of "high standards" should not be understood in the sense of excessive severity, but of high quality. FIBEN aims to foster an effective and relevant diagnosis of companies to promote what central bankers call a rational allocation of credit. A tool at the service of the banking profession, FIBEN also finds its raison d'eatre in the more global objective of preserving financial stability and the proper functioning of the credit market. In this sense, it is part of an approach at the service of companies and the French economy in general. 5

Title: Keynote address Prevention and management of credit card fraud
text: Symposium Prevention and management of credit card fraud - January 17, 2008 Opening speech by Mr. Noyer, Governor of the Bank of France Mr President, ladies and gentlemen I am very pleased to open this symposium on the prevention and management of credit card fraud. I will address you today, of course, as Governor of the Banque de France, responsible for ensuring the security of non-cash means of payment, but also in my capacity as President of the Payment Card Security Observatory, a consultation body created by the legislator and which has contributed, since 2002, to mobilizing all the parties concerned in France by security issues. As you have pointed out, Mr President, the use of cards is based, like money, on the confidence of users in this instrument, which means that we must not compromise with security and guarantee the mobilisation of all the players. I am thinking first of all of those who implement the payment system and who use it: banks, merchants, holders, but I do not forget, and today's assistance testifies to their involvement, those police, gendarmes, magistrates, who through their action of prevention, detection and repression contribute to the fight against fraud. What observations can we make at the beginning of 2008 on these subjects? 95 First, that the use of the card has become highly trivialized and that it has become the preferred payment instrument of the French. 95 Secondly, that by the effect of continuous efforts, we now have in France a strong control of card security. These efforts make it possible to contain the level of fraud, despite the constantly renewed imagination of fraudsters. 95 Finally, that these concerns now go far beyond French territory alone. With the project to create a European Payments Area - SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) - each national system should open up to cards from other countries, in order to facilitate the use of this instrument throughout Europe. But to succeed in this movement, it is essential that each of these systems ensures that a high level of security is implemented. I would like to elaborate, if you wish, on each of these three points. 1. The payment card, the preferred payment instrument of the French Introduced in France forty years ago, the card has gradually become commonplace. In 2006, there were nearly 80 million payment cards in circulation (including about 55 million "CB" cards), which made it possible to carry out nearly 7 billion transactions representing more than 350 billion euros. The card is now the most used non-cash means of payment in France with 37% of transactions, far ahead of the cheque (26%) which was still the most used in 2002. The France alone accounts for 36% of card payments in the euro area (2006 figures). This intensive use alone testifies to the capital of trust that the card now enjoys. Last year, the Payment Card Security Observatory focused on better estimating this trust by conducting a survey of cardholders. A majority of them cite the card as the safest means of payment, while only 2% of the population do not have one because they have security concerns. However, this excellent trust is not unreasonable: the French are more vigilant about their transactions remotely or abroad and this seems justified if we judge by the fraud rates that are higher for these types of transactions than for local payments. 2 2. Continuous efforts to control security have helped contain fraud The choices made for many years by "Cartes Bancaires" in terms of security have greatly contributed to the control of fraud. The generalization of the chip and the confidential code from 1992 paved the way worldwide for the EMV standard, which is now becoming widespread in different regions of the world and which is adopted in Europe for SEPA. More recently, the gradual transition from cards to DDA technology, supported by the Bank of France, is also a decisive step towards reducing counterfeit fraud in local payments. These efforts have a visible effect on the fraud rate, which is maintained from year to year, as shown by the statistics published by the Observatory, at a relatively low level compared to the few foreign data available. In 2006, the card payment fraud rate remained stable at 0.064%. The total amount of fraud amounts to 80252.6 million. In my opinion, this does not mean that we should relax our efforts. The fight against fraud requires the permanent adaptation of the means of protection to new attacks deployed by fraudsters. From this point of view, many of you know how rapid and sometimes surprising the changes are. Two sectors are currently particularly at risk. These are: 95 On the one hand, international transactions. However, the migration of European card systems to EMV standards makes it possible to gradually reduce the risk of using counterfeit cards abroad. Today you will benefit from presentations on police and judicial cooperation at European and international level, which I consider to be a particularly important subject. 95 On the other hand, remote payments (by telephone and Internet), for which the fraud rate appears to be significantly higher than for proximity and AUTOMATED payments. It is clear here that the security arrangements should be strengthened. To this end, I hope that institutions can quickly deploy solutions for strong authentication to their holders. 3 The Bank of France has worked extensively within the Eurosystem to develop a common supervisory framework for all central banks that is applicable to the different card payment systems. It has just been made public on 11 January and will soon be implemented throughout Europe. 3. Prospects for European openness At the beginning of 2008, a few days before the official start on 28 January of the first SEPA transfers, we must also mention the European opening of the various national card payment systems. Several main principles have been set by the European banking community to frame this opening. This can be done either by alliances between different systems or the expansion of a system, or by co-branding a national system with the Visa and Mastercard networks (which is the case today for "Bank Cards"), or, finally, by abandoning the national system and directly using an international network such as Visa or Mastercard. I would like to say that, from the point of view of the Eurosystem central banks, the choice between these scenarios, which is expected from the various national communities, must not lead to the opposite effect of the desired objective, which is to open up the market to greater competition between systems. However, it could be feared that this would be the case if, for example, none of the national systems managed by its critical mass to represent an economically viable alternative to the international Visa and Mastercard networks. That is why the Eurosystem is calling for the existence of a European card system. I am personally convinced that this can only be the result of systems that already account for a major share of payments in Europe. With its 36% of transactions within the euro zone, "Bank cards" seems to me to have to count naturally among them. However, as President Guitton has pointed out, this European construction cannot be envisaged without total legal certainty. I note that the announcement by the European Commissioner for Competition on 19 December concerning Mastercard's interchange fees raises many questions about 4 the legality of these commissions and therefore on the economic model of interbank card payment systems. I hope that the elements of clarification in this area will be made as soon as possible. Only then will the European electronic banking landscape be able to take shape clearly. It is also on this condition that European standardisation bodies will be able to make strong choices in terms of security standards for cards, terminals and transaction flows. It is on this condition, finally, that Europeans will be able to participate effectively in the security choices made by international networks. Conclusion To conclude, I would like to highlight three points that seem essential to me: 95 The level of fraud is well controlled in France, thanks to a constant watch of all the actors and to an internationally recognized level of expertise. This high level of requirement has directly contributed to the high use of the card by the French. It is important that the standardisation adopted at European level benefits from these advances and allows constant adaptation to the various developments in fraud. 95 Eurosystem central banks attach great importance to the security of card payments. They will ensure that common security principles are respected throughout Europe. 95 Finally, it is important that the SEPA project does not result in a drastic reduction in competition. It is therefore desirable that a European card system competing with Visa and MasterCard can be created, so that SEPA is a project that benefits everyone, banks, merchants, and cardholders. To this end, it is important for the Commission to clarify its position on interchange fees, part of which makes it possible to finance the various means used to combat fraud. Thank you for your attention. 5
