Title: General Assembly of the Office for Banking and Financial Coordination
text: General Assembly of the Banking and Financial Coordination Office Speech by Christian Noyer Governor of the Bank of France 25 June 2008 Mr President Thank you for giving me the floor again in this Chamber. The meeting of the General Assembly of the Office for Banking and Financial Coordination is always an excellent opportunity to exchange with the profession and more particularly, today, to reflect on the origins and lessons to be learned from the financial crisis in terms of prudential regulation and supervision. Before I even touch on these subjects, I would like to begin by saying that I am making this statement as Governor of the Bank of France, Chairman of the Banking Commission. Never before has the Banking Commission's backing of the Banking Commission to the Banque de France been so justified. The crisis I will come back to demonstrates how crucial the effectiveness of the relationship between the supervisor and the stability officer is in addressing the challenges that arise. * * * Let us first turn to the causes of the crisis. As you have pointed out, it is undeniable that innovation and risk-taking have been fostered by exceptional economic and financial conditions, characterised by strong economic growth, historically low interest rates, abundant market liquidity and particularly low signing premiums. This has led to a widespread perception that investment opportunities in apparently good quality assets are almost limitless and has altered the judgment of actors, be they lenders, arrangers, investors or rating agencies. In this context, the "originate-to-distribute" model, which consists in banks transferring as quickly as possible to the market a large part of the risks associated with the loans they grant or acquire and not, as in the past, to keep them for a long period of time, has not made it possible to provide adequate incentives. In particular, "originator" institutions have not been sufficiently encouraged to assess their risks satisfactorily. The complexity of transactions has also generated information asymmetries and an over-reliance on external risk ratings. Finally, insufficient transparency in financial reporting has increased risk aversion in times of crisis, leading to an unusual drying up of liquidity. In total, French banks (I am not thinking here particularly of the members of the OCBF, who have not been affected to date for the most part) have been affected through several main channels. First, through their direct exposures to US subprime households or through their indirect exposures via portfolios of structured instruments (RMBS or CDOs) themselves exposed to subprime risk. Secondly, through exposures to securitisation vehicles (conduits or structured investment vehicles - SIVs) in particular through liquidity lines, the management of which will have to be more rigorous in the future. Thirdly, through exposures to assets taken over from securitisation vehicles, or even UCITS, which were facing liquidity problems; it is the phenomenon of re-intermediation that will have to be better taken into account in forward-looking planning in terms of capital. Fourthly, by the exposures of French banks to so-called "monoline" credit enhancers, as shareholders or because they are direct counterparties of these insurers to whom they have purchased protection against the risk of default of securities issuers via Credit Default Swaps - CDS - the importance of which you stressed for financial stability. In this respect, the failures of "monolines" perfectly illustrate the example of "wrong way risk", that is to say the risk of an adverse correlation between the amount of exposure to a counterparty and the credit quality of the latter, which will have to be managed more finely in the future. Managing, in a forward-looking manner, the correlations between risks in times of crisis, and, more specifically, that between the risk on an underlying (the hedged element) and the counterparty risk on the protection provider (the hedging element), is indeed a key issue. All in all, the crisis resulted in fair value losses in the transaction portfolios of French credit institutions and a decline in income in corporate and investment banking. Nevertheless, the French banking sector has demonstrated its good capacity for resilience, in particular by maintaining an adequate level of solvency, thanks to the existence of effective growth drivers. Many business areas remain well oriented: the continued growth in retail banking (9.1% in 2007 compared to 2006) or the dynamism of specialized financing are examples. * * * Before turning to regulatory and prudential responses to the financial crisis, I would like to consider, in a second step of my presentation, a set of good practices that have enabled some groups to limit the effects of the financial crisis more than others. These practices, described in the report of the Senior Supervisors Group, published in March 2008, are mainly of four kinds. First, the importance of the role of corporate governance in risk management is reaffirmed. The involvement of managers, combined with an organization that is both conducive to the flow of information and concerned with preserving the independence of the risk management function, are in particular key elements of the robustness of any internal control system. Secondly, in the area of credit and market risk management, the need to complement external measures or ratings with internal risk analyses is also highlighted. The multiplicity of risk measurement instruments, with a view to compensating for individual shortcomings, and the use of relevant stress scenarios also appear crucial. General Assembly of the Office for Banking and Financial Coordination, by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France - 25 June 2008 - 2 Thirdly, with regard to liquidity risk management, its effectiveness is based in particular on robust continuity plans and a good adaptation of measurement and supervisory instruments to the risk profile of each institution. Finally, it appears from the first observations that the banks best equipped to meet the challenge posed by the valuation of certain structured products such as CDOs, in the absence of market prices, are those which, on the one hand, invested the earliest to develop rigorous valuation and valuation control procedures, on the other hand, have developed their knowledge of the risks inherent in complex products while diversifying their sources of information and valuation approaches. * * * With these initial lessons, I will finally come to the main regulatory and prudential projects that we must undertake or continue in response to recent financial turbulence. First of all, the origin of the crisis reinforces the primary objective as well as the overall economy of Basel II, which focuses on the management of banking risks by encouraging banks to constantly improve their ability to measure, manage and cover these risks and provides a more comprehensive prudential framework better adapted to the challenges related to the predominance of the "originate-to-distribute" model. Unlike Basel I, Basel II provides for specific treatment of securitisation under Pillar 1. The crisis has also led the Basel Committee to launch a project to deepen, not to say tighten, the Agreement on some of its aspects, including the treatment of liquidity lines and complex products, such as securitizations of assets already securitized. In addition to a broader scope of risks covered by Capital Under Pillar 1, Basel II gives banks and supervisors an essential tool, Pillar 2, to assess the specific risk profile of each institution and to take into account certain risks that are difficult to quantify but can have a strong impact on both solvency and liquidity profile. In particular, the crisis has highlighted the need for greater emphasis on reputation risk management as well as on the supervision of refinancing risk (funding liquidity). Basel II also promotes crisis scenarios as an essential tool for risk management and measurement. With regard to liquidity risk, I would like to inform you that the work carried out by the Committee of European Banking Supervisors and the Basel Committee has just led to the simultaneous publication of recommendations, which should contribute to strengthening the prudential framework in this area. In addition, the new prudential framework aims to substantially strengthen transparency and thus market discipline. Pillar 3 of the scheme lays down numerous requirements for the disclosure of qualitative and quantitative disclosures on own funds and risks, including with regard to securitisation operations. We have also undertaken a series of important actions, which are directly in line with the general framework of the recommendations made by the Financial Stability Forum, in response to the financial crisis, under the impetus of the G7. General Assembly of the Banking and Financial Coordination Office, by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France - 25 June 2008 - 3 There are many areas of action, but I shall retain, in particular, the following axes. In the first place, improving transparency and financial communication was very quickly identified as one of the essential conditions for ending the crisis. We have therefore encouraged French banks, together with the Compagnie nationale des Commissaires aux comptes, to communicate in detail about their exposures to the subprime crisis. A joint working group bringing together the services of the Banking Commission and the Autorite9 des marche9s financiers, as well as representatives of the profession, also made it possible to clarify best practices in this area. Initial progress has already been made in this area and further improvements can be expected for the accounts for the first half of 2008. More generally, the Basel Committee plans to publish in 2009 recommendations on information to be disseminated in response to the requirements of Pillar 3 of Basel II. In terms of asset valuation, exchanges with institutions have also made it possible to reaffirm the priority that must be given to prices and data directly observable on the markets. Where banks have been forced to use valuation models as a result of the disappearance of liquid prices in certain markets, recommendations have focused on taking into account all risk factors (including liquidity or counterparty risks) and the rigour of the process of determining these prices. As regards the role of credit rating agencies, areas for improvement of the quality of rating processes, the management of possible conflict of interest issues or the introduction of a differentiated rating for securitisation transactions. The full implementation of these recommendations is all the more necessary as external rating plays a significant role in the implementation of Basel II. However, I am not sure that we should rush into the adoption of a regulation of the rating activity. On the other hand, a track such as that of a European registration, proposed by the Minister of the Economy, Industry and Employment, seems to be among the possible measures in the short term. In addition, several elements of the draft revision of the directive that transposed Basel II into European law, known as the "CRD", provide a direct response to the financial crisis, complementing the panoply of actions already undertaken elsewhere, at European or international level. First of all, an important part of the project concerns arrangements for the supervision of cross-border groups and the strengthening of the crisis management mechanism. Colleges of supervisors will thus be formally recognised and, in a number of cases, whether in the case of prudential reporting or Pillar 2 of Basel II, supervisory decisions concerning subsidiaries will have to be subject to closer consultation between the supervisor of the parent company and that of the entity or entities concerned. Admittedly, the search for greater efficiency should have led from the outset to a further strengthening of the role of the supervisor of the parent company, but this is a first proposal, which is subject to change in the context of the discussions in the Council and the European Parliament. In addition, although work was initiated before the crisis in the summer of 2007, the clarification of the conditions for eligibility of hybrid capital instruments for classification as tier 1 capital will contribute to strengthening the quality of the latter and, consequently, the soundness of the European banking system. As you know, this strengthening of the European legislative framework in the prudential field is coupled with measures designed to increase the effectiveness of banking supervision in Europe. The Committee of European Banking Supervisors has focused its priorities on the effective convergence of supervisors' practices and the establishment of tools and mechanisms to meet this objective. As part of the review of the Lamfalussy process, which was completed at the end of 2007, several important guidelines were agreed. It was thus decided to integrate a European convergence objective into the mandate of national supervisors, which will be an engaging element for the entire supervisory community. Increased use of qualified majority voting should also help to improve the efficiency of the decision-making process of Level 3 committees. Finally, strengthening the functioning of colleges of supervisors is clearly a priority for the Committee of European Banking Supervisors, even though the Committee has already taken important steps in this area. General Assembly of the Office for Banking and Financial Coordination, by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France - 25 June 2008 - 4 Returning to more domestic work, I would like to add that the turbulence and, of course, the exceptional case of concealed risk-taking on the markets to which Socie9te9 Ge9ne9rale has been subjected, have shown the need to constantly strengthen internal control mechanisms and improve the flow of information, particularly to managers. This reinforcement could result in a revision of Regulation 97-02 on internal control, including provisions on operational risk control and a focus on the fight against fraud. This reform would also be in line with a greater formalization, provided for by legislation, of the involvement of governance bodies in the monitoring of internal control. On another subject of domestic concern, you are asking me, Mr President, about the mobility of banking staff, and more particularly between supervisors and the profession. In this respect, the first exchanges of personnel between the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission and the latter date back about twenty years. Initially of the order of one year, these provisions are now spread over two years. Nearly twenty-five employees of the SGCB and the Profession have benefited from such experiences in fields as diverse as risk management, banking studies or accounting. Currently four SGCB agents are seconded to several major French credit institutions. On a reciprocal basis, the SGCB simultaneously welcomes three employees from these establishments. Each return from detachment has shown how beneficial this type of operation is for both parties. It is certain that in the future these exchanges are destined to develop further. Finally, Mr President, you are asking me about the rise of sovereign wealth funds in the capital of international banks. From the point of view of financial stability, the contribution of sovereign wealth funds to an increase in solvency ratios can only be encouraged if it is accompanied by the maintenance or strengthening of good governance. Accordingly, it would be useful to define a code of conduct, which could be developed in international for a in order to establish minimum requirements for the adequate degree of disclosure by sovereign wealth funds. The G7 recently asked the IMF to examine the issue of good practices for sovereign wealth funds in terms of good governance, risk management, transparency, and accountability. For its part, the OECD is encouraged to identify good practices to be adopted from the point of view of the countries that host these investment flows. Further progress in these areas would significantly mitigate the risks of misallocation of capital as well as the negative externalities that the management of large international assets is likely to create in the macroeconomic sphere and in financial markets. * * * Mr President, thank you for the opportunity to share these thoughts with you. The Bank of France and the Banking Commission will ensure that the quality and richness of the relations between your association and the representatives of the authorities are maintained and deepened. Title: The lessons of a crisis some avenues for reflection
text: LESSONS FROM A CRISIS SOME FOOD FOR THOUGHT Jean-Paul Redouin Deputy Governor of the Bank of France Conference organized by the Toulouse School of Economics (TSE) in collaboration with the Ministry of the Economy, Industry and Employment and the Banque de France Paris, December 17, 2008 Ladies and Gentlemen, This conference is a privileged opportunity to exchange analyses between practitioners and theorists. I am convinced that, in the midst of the financial crisis, such an exchange is very useful. I also appreciate the difficulty of the task before me in introducing these reflections to eminent specialists in these issues. I will therefore start from my concrete experience, that of a central banker in charge of banking supervision. Over the past eighteen months, I have observed that three fundamental elements of the financial system have malfunctioned and that their simultaneous failure has in turn been a factor in aggravating the crisis: risks, liquidity and information. The roadmap set by the G20 will have to take this into account in its implementation: I will outline, in conclusion, some avenues to follow in this direction. NEW CHAINS OF RISKS ... This crisis removed the illusion that the market could allow an optimal spread of credit risk. The advantage sought by the techniques associated with securitization included their ability to "remove" credit risk from the balance sheets of certain institutions in order to increase the velocity of their capital. In addition, securitisation has been used extensively to finance complex and structured products in the short term. Such arrangements are inherently fragile: their complexity makes them difficult to negotiate and their financing, based on intensive transformation, makes them particularly vulnerable to large movements in interest rates. Once the crisis erupted, these risks quickly became concentrated in the hands of certain institutions, first and foremost the major investment banks. The development of securitized financing and investment banking activities has thus been accompanied by new risks. These new risks have not been sufficiently taken into account. I am thinking in particular of two phenomena. The first phenomenon is that the best risk allocation that was expected from new financial techniques has not taken place. In fact, the crisis has shown that the spread of risk has had the opposite effect to that expected. It has had an anxiety-provoking effect on market participants. The extreme difficulty in which they found themselves in knowing the location of the risks and the outstanding amounts concerned acted in the financial system like a virus, each one ending up distrusting his counterparties. In addition, the outsourcing of risks via financial arrangements has also shown its limits. We have seen that reputational risk, attached to the marketing of certain products, is a very real risk in times of crisis. We have also rediscovered the reality of liquidity risk, when institutions are exposed via credit lines open to off-balance-sheet vehicles. The second phenomenon is that the risk measurement itself has been distorted by two factors. Many financial intermediaries have lived under the illusion of being able to insure themselves against certain risks associated with new financial arrangements. However, experience shows that the agents providing these insurances, the monolines, could not be sufficiently capitalized in relation to the amounts insured. Finally, the crisis has highlighted the limits of risk analyses based essentially on probabilistic models, causing two adverse effects for financial stability: large and sudden jumps in product ratings and mimetic behaviour on the part of investors, confident in the overly simplistic "marketing" of rating agencies. ECLIPSE LIQUIDITY The crisis has revealed the complexity of liquidity dynamics and the speed with which they disappear. Whether it is market liquidity, that related to the negotiability of assets, or interbank funding liquidity, in both cases, with the crisis, we have rediscovered that liquidity is not acquired. It can 2 "The lessons of a crisis. Some food for thought" Speech by Jean-Paul Redouin, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France - Paris, December 17, 2008 suddenly and permanently disappear. This occurs in narrow, unregulated markets where illiquid construction products are traded; it can also happen, and this is a major issue in this crisis, in markets that are otherwise deep and, until recently, considered robust. The developments in the U.S. asset-backed commercial paper segment are a striking example. The sudden and lasting drying up of the interbank market, i.e. the heart of the financial system, is even more so. What happened? Without too much schematization, we can characterize the situation of certain market segments as having been, during the years preceding the crisis, in the illusion of liquidity. There are two main sources of liquidity that are interrelated. The one created by the ability to be able to trade an asset on a market at any time and the one that circulates between banking institutions and which is regulated at the margin by central banks. Two phenomena have disrupted liquidity supply systems. On the one hand, investors and financial intermediaries have discovered that few assets are actually tradable. Not very homogeneous, built to satisfy the needs of only one or a few investors, difficult to value, these assets could not access real secondary markets. Faced with the disappearance of this source of liquidity, we have seen a loss of confidence between financial intermediaries. This wave of mistrust put at risk those whose leverage was too high or who did not have direct access to central bank refinancing. FRAGMENTED INFORMATION The crisis has also highlighted the opacity of a large number of products and market mechanisms. Financial innovation and the rapid development of over-the-counter markets (especially on credit derivatives) have increased the imperfections of the financial system that the literature in banking and financial economics had long identified. In recent months, you will easily find examples illustrating these imperfections, whether in terms of inefficient capital allocation (overinvestment in real estate) or information asymmetry (disempowerment of credit distributors in the originate to distribute model). Finally, the opacity of certain mechanisms is aggravated by the closure of entire market segments due to the lack of adequate infrastructure. These findings call for the establishment of a more orderly and transparent management of market flows. The G20 called for support for recent initiatives to launch centralised clearing services for credit derivatives. Central banks must support these initiatives and encourage 3 "The lessons of a crisis. Some food for thought" Speech by Jean-Paul Redouin, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France - Paris, December 17, 2008 all developments that will tend to shift transactions towards better identified and organized market models. This necessarily involves the creation of exchange platforms identifying flows and counterparties. It is also necessary to think about the mechanisms to ensure the successful completion of these transactions by making the settlement process as robust as possible. The financial industry must equip itself with these tools and allocate the necessary resources to secure these essential phases of market operations. THE SYSTEMIC CHALLENGES OF REGULATION The first challenge is, of course, in the immediate future, to learn from these dysfunctions, but it is necessary to go further. Fundamentally, the experience of recent months highlights the limitation of current regulatory arrangements. The excessive use of leverage by financial institutions and the concentration of risks on an ultimately small number of banking institutions have not been well measured, captured or prevented by financial regulation. To contain the instability of the financial system, public interventions in recent months have been designed to stabilize the situation not of one institution but of the entire financial system. The scope of intervention of the public authorities has therefore ultimately exceeded that of regulated and supervised intermediaries. In other words, we must now ask ourselves whether, beyond the supervision of each banking institution linked to the public protection it enjoys, there is not a need to develop regulatory and prudential mechanisms that are the counterpart of the de facto protection granted by the authorities to all markets and institutions that appear "systemic". The issue was raised by the Heads of State and Government who, at the G20 summit, laid down the principle of a revision of the scope of regulation. It is a question of the competent authorities working to ensure that, and I quote, 'all markets, products and financial actors are subject to regulation or supervision as appropriate'. In other words, no actor in the financial system should remain completely outside the supervision of public authorities. In this perspective, a gradation in the regulation and requirements imposed on the actors of the financial system could be envisaged. A first minimum level of requirement would take the form of mandatory registration and a commitment to a code of practice. A second, more binding level would add to the registration and compliance with good practices obligations of transparency on activities and accounts. Hedge funds - in particular those exceeding a certain volume of activity - and, more generally, institutions pursuing strategies based mainly on leverage or risk-taking should meet these requirements. Finally, at the last stage of regulation, more restrictive regulation would cover activities and risk-taking. This supervision already exists, but it should be renovated. This is the whole field of reflection, in particular, of Basel 2. 4 "The lessons of a crisis. Some food for thought" Speech by Jean-Paul Redouin, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France - Paris, December 17, 2008 These principles should not be limited to prudential rules alone. They also apply to accounting rules, as it is essential that financial regulation, in all its forms, contributes to maintaining diversity in financial systems. Thus, seeking to value all the assets and liabilities of financial institutions in "fair value" has disadvantages, even risks, that will absolutely have to be taken into account. TO CONCLUDE, I would like to stress that it would be unrealistic to believe that financial regulation can do anything, including immunizing the risk of financial instability. Admittedly, macroeconomic imbalances have a share of responsibility for the magnitude of the crisis. However, this is largely due to problems with the internal management of financial institutions, some of which are themselves a reflection of the irrational confidence placed in certain quantitative tools. Prudential regulation is there to set new requirements in this area. However, risk management remains fundamentally the responsibility of the financial institutions themselves. Financial regulation must now allow a systemic approach to risks. It is to this monitoring mission and the duty of alert that attaches to it that regulators and central banks must now work. 5 "The lessons of a crisis. Some food for thought" Speech by Jean-Paul Redouin, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France - Paris, December 17, 2008

Title: Role and economic importance of consumer credit
text: Role and economic importance of consumer credit Speech by Jean-Paul REDOUIN, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France Symposium "Credit, consumption, growth and social emergency", at the National Assembly, 10 February 2009 I would like to thank Mr Delevoye, Ombudsman of the Republic, for convening this colloquium devoted to a very topical subject, consumer credit. The ultimate goal of economic activity, we must not forget, is to consume. Without consumption, there is no improvement in well-being and living standards, no investment, no innovation and no growth. In the current period, the dynamism of consumption is particularly important and I would like to say a few words about it before talking more specifically about the role of credit. The global economy, as you know, is facing a shock unprecedented in recent history. In the second half of 2008, there was a sharp synchronized decline in industrial production in all countries of the world, both developed and emerging. In the face of this shock, companies can be expected to become increasingly cautious about investment and employment. In addition, there are uncertainties about the financing of the economy that, in all countries, including our own, the public authorities are working to reduce or eliminate. This is why, in the coming months, the dynamism of consumption will determine the profile of economic activity. I would like to be relatively optimistic here. We are currently witnessing a powerful disinflation movement linked to the fall in oil and commodity prices. The reduction in oil prices alone from 140 to 40 per barrel will inject, in a full year, nearly 5% of the world's GNP in transfer to consumer countries. Less inflation also means more purchasing power and therefore more consumption. Households have understood this and, among the components of final demand, consumption is the one that is most resilient today. Even in the current climate, consumer confidence indices are best oriented. More significantly, purchase intentions at the end of a few months appear more positive than immediate intentions. I see this as a sign that households understand the benefits they can derive from the disinflation process. What about credit? I will first say a word about its justification before examining its main developments. In a modern economy, it is not desirable for households to be forced to pre-finance all their purchases of durable goods in advance. Such a situation, where, according to economists, households are "constrained in liquidity", is neither desirable nor optimal. It still prevails in some large emerging countries, where financial systems are poorly developed. We know the consequences: less well-being, the need to accumulate the cash necessary for any major purchase beforehand and, consequently, the structural surplus of savings. At the international level, this is reflected in the accumulation of external imbalances in current payments, with this paradoxical situation in which savers in poor countries finance the consumption of rich countries. According to some analysts, this surplus of savings in financially underdeveloped countries is one of the origins of the current crisis: failing to find a way to invest in safe and productive local financial assets, this savings has naturally turned to more speculative securities, thus fuelling the real estate bubble in some developed countries. On the other hand, excess credit in developed countries can be dangerous for the economic and social balance. Credit is healthy when it anticipates a sustainable and permanent evolution of incomes and helps to smooth temporary shocks over time. It becomes harmful when it is based on excessive extrapolation of asset values that reach speculative levels. This is what we have seen in many developed countries over the past 10 years. Through various techniques, households have been encouraged to extract value from their real estate assets and use it to pledge the expansion of their consumer credit. Most of its dynamism can be explained in recent years by such excesses. With the turnaround in the real estate market, the consequences are now immediate and negative. Fortunately, our country has protected itself from such excesses. Consumer credit has developed in a balanced way. While we have seen strong growth in house prices, overall household debt has remained contained. If I can say for a moment a certain pride, it is that the Bank of France has always fought against the pressures and against the intellectual fashions aimed at irrederatingly encouraging households to go into debt. I believe that we have been able to find in our country a good balance, sustainable in the long term, between savings and consumption, in which a steady development of credit naturally finds its place, at the service of economic and social balances. New consumer credit accounts for 5% of household consumption. In fact, only just over 30% of households use debt to finance their consumption, which means that for them about 15% of their consumption is financed by credit. Credits are most often used to finance durable goods (automobiles and housing equipment, the latter including microcomputers and hi-fi equipment), for which they represent 60% of expenses. The boom in consumer credit has been sustained over the past 10 years, but this trend has changed in 2008 as a result of the development of the financial crisis and its spread to the real economy. Thus, according to the latest available statistics on the distribution of credit in France, the cumulative flow of new consumer credit over 12 months has decreased slightly since February 2008 and it reached 53 billion euros for the whole year against 56 billion. As a result, outstanding consumer credit was almost stable at the end of 2008 in France (0.1% on an average monthly basis over the last three months). 2 "Role and economic importance of consumer credit" Speech by Jean-Paul REDOUIN, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France Colloquium at the National Assembly on February 10, 2009 Total household debt, particularly that linked to consumer credit, is below the EU average. Admittedly, for the total stock of consumer credit, France comes in third place behind the United Kingdom and Germany, but in terms of outstanding per capita at the end of 2007, the France reached 2,160 euros, a level below the EU average (2,320 euros per capita), the United Kingdom and Ireland exceeding 5,000 euros per capita. In recent years, outstanding consumer credit grew by an average of 5.4% per year in France from 2002 to 2007, compared with an EU average of more than 6.5% per year. The same can also be said in terms of total indebtedness, since the French appear much less indebted than other Europeans: their debt ratio, which amounts to 78.8% of their gross disposable income, is lower than that of Germany and the Eurozone (90%). The France is also a country where the household saving rate is relatively high compared to its main European partners; it is around 16%, as in Germany, but much higher than in Italy (14%), Spain (10%) and of course the United Kingdom (2.5%); this characteristic also probably explains, in part, the relatively smoother evolution of consumption. The French situation can therefore be characterized by three elements: a high savings rate, a fairly low short-term debt ratio and relatively limited fluctuations in consumer spending. However, the crisis has already impacted the most vulnerable households. Thus, the number of over-indebtedness cases filed in 2008 increased by 3% compared to 2007, whereas it had decreased by an average of 1% per year between 2005 and 2007. More worryingly, filings in the fourth quarter of 2008 were 10.5% higher than in the fourth quarter of 2007. It should also be remembered that in situations of over-indebtedness, consumer credit constitutes an important part of the loans subscribed. In this context, it remains very important to ensure that the development of consumer credit does not lead to unsustainable situations for borrowers and lenders alike. Conclusion Consumer credit in recent years has helped support demand for France, but it has not helped to accentuate the economic cycle as in some countries where mortgage credit is very widely used to finance household consumption. It can therefore be assumed that the current slowdown in this type of credit will not contribute to amplifying the recession we are facing. However, given the role played by consumer credit in certain sectors of activity and for certain segments of the population, the conditions for the responsible development of consumer credit must be maintained. A protective regulatory framework is essential, but it must be accompanied by responsible behaviour on the part of both lenders and borrowers. 3 "Role and economic importance of consumer credit" Speech by Jean-Paul REDOUIN, Deputy Governor of the Banque de France Colloquium at the National Assembly on February 10, 2009

Title: Middle school students at the Banque de France for an equal opportunities policy
text: Middle school students at the Banque de France: for an equal opportunities policy Christian Noyer Governor of the Bank of France Paris, 18 May 2009 Dear Minister, Dear friends, It is a great pleasure to welcome you today to the headquarters of the Bank of France as it was a pleasure to welcome many of you to our branches for an internship to discover the world of work. I will not make a long speech. I would just like to share with you a few thoughts that are close to my heart. First, you are here in a beautiful place, in a somewhat intimidating setting. I reassure you, the whole Bank of France does not look like this Golden Gallery. We have offices, as you have seen in our branches. These offices are more austere but also more functional. What I would like to tell you is that you are here at home. The Bank of France is an independent institution. But it is a great institution of the French Republic. Its heritage, its buildings belong to the Nation, that is to say to all of us, to all of you. We are in charge of it, we take great care of it, because it is a precious heritage. But it's yours. And that's why we wanted to welcome you here today. You spent a week with us. You have met or met very diverse people, very competent, passionate about their profession. We are proud of our teams. All of them, from the bottom up, have reached where they are through their work and efforts. Many have passed very difficult competitions and exams. We would very much like to develop and intensify our relations. To have you here today, Mr. Minister, with many eminent collaborators is a great encouragement to us. Thank you all. 2 "Middle school students at the Banque de France: for a policy of equal opportunities" Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France - Paris, 18 May 2009

Title: Annual report
text: Presentation of the Annual Report of the Banking Commission for 2008 Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France, President of the Banking Commission Paris, 26 June 2009 I welcome you to the press breakfast organised on the occasion of today's publication of the Banking Commission's 2008 Annual Report. On this occasion, I would like to return to the main developments that have marked the French banking sector over the past year, as well as the challenges that these have raised, both for banks and supervisors. In many ways, 2008 was an exceptional year: while it was the first year of full implementation of Basel 2 in France and Europe, it saw all banks suffer shocks of exceptional magnitude. Thus, who would have been able to predict the failure of a large American bank, internationally present on the derivatives market? But it was also in 2008 that fundamental initiatives were undertaken, in France and at the international level, to quickly remedy the effects of the crisis and, in the longer term, to create the conditions for a better functioning of the financial system. From this point of view, I would like to highlight the successes of the consultation implemented by governments, central banks and supervisors, to work to restore investor confidence in the financial system. In this context, what is the situation of French banks? The crisis has of course not spared them, but they, because of a comfortable financial base, have rather resisted better (1). However, significant challenges must be addressed, both by credit institutions (2) and by supervisors (3). Let me come back to these three points. 1. In 2008, French banking groups generally saw their profitability decline, but they continue to have a solid financial structure 1.1. The profitability of French banks has decreased, but remains positive The profitability of French banks, already affected in 2007 by the first effects of the subprime crisis, was severely impacted in 2008, both by the amplification of financial turbulence and the economic slowdown. Taken as a whole, the French banking system continued to generate profits. But these are in sharp decline. Thus, if we look at the eight main banking groups1, the net result, which reached 3.6 GEUR in 2008, is down 83% compared to 2007. What were the factors that led to this evolution? I see at least four: 3/4 First, the main explanatory factor, the banks have continued to see, for amounts significant impairments and value adjustments on so-called "toxic" financial products; from this point of view, the fragility of certain credit enhancers, who are supposed to protect banks against such an adverse development, has contributed to this deterioration. In addition, it has gradually spread to other segments of the financial market, in particular leveraged arrangements, such as LBOs, under which banks have had to note impairments linked to the increase in the cost of risk. 3/4 Secondly, the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, beyond its direct impact on the cost of risk of the institutions for which the US bank was the counterparty, resulted in a general crisis of confidence, particularly in the interbank market. This has had the effect of increasing the risk premiums paid by borrowing banks and, consequently, the cost of their financing. 3/4 Thirdly, in a context of high market volatility, corporate and investment banking activities suffered sometimes significant losses, particularly in the last quarter; for their part, asset management activities also saw their performance deteriorate, due in particular to a decline in inflows. 3/4 Finally, the increase in business insolvencies, in the wake of the economic downturn, has resulted in an increase in the cost of risk and therefore in allocations to provisions and lossovers. In this context, retail banking activities, which are one of the assets of the "economic model" developed by the major French banks, have generally continued to remain dynamic, both at home and abroad. Their GNP increased by 4% in 2008, while that of corporate and investment banking and that related to asset management decreased by 35% and 13% respectively. This dynamism, which confirms the stabilizing role of this business line, has concerned the various customer segments, small businesses or individuals, housing loans, as well as specialized financing. In total, given these contrasting developments, while the overall GNP of the main French banking groups is down compared to 2007, this 7% decline appears limited. This is different from the cost of risk, which recorded a sharp increase in 2008 (214%); this calls for greater vigilance on the part of the banks, a point to which I shall have the opportunity to return. 1 Groups: Cre9dit Agricole, BNP Paribas, Socie9te9 Ge9ne9rale, Caisses d'e9pargne, Banques populaires, Cre9dit Mutuel-CIC, HSBC France and DEXIA Cre9dit Local. 2 "Presentation of the Annual Report of the Banking Commission for 2008" by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Banking Commission - Paris, 26 June 2009 It is difficult to draw conclusions for 2009 from the analysis of the first quarter results. It shows particularly contrasting developments from one bank to another, particularly as regards corporate and investment banking activities. However, it shows that, although slightly lower than in the last quarter of 2008, the cost of risk remains at a high level. 1.2. The solvency of French banks is solid What are the effects of these developments on the financial situation of French banks? It would probably be a little simplifying to summarize the situation of the French banking system to the sole question of the level of the solvency ratio of its institutions. But the fact remains that, if we look at this key indicator, focusing on the most revealing calculation of solvency, i.e. the so-called "Tier one" ratio, which compares the amount of the most robust elements of own funds to the amount of risk-weighted risks, the situation at the end of 2008 is satisfactory. In fact, the Tier One ratio stands at 8.3% for the eight major groups, up 30 basis points from a year earlier. And, if we look at the situation of the four major groups that publish quarterly accounts, their Tier One ratio increased slightly between December 31, 2008 and March 31, 2009. This good level of solvency can be explained in particular by the capital strengthening policies put in place by the banks as part of the exchanges initiated by the Banking Commission, which has endeavoured to rigorously implement Pillar 2 of Basel 2. In addition to these policies, the measures taken by the French government to enable banks to continue to play an active role in financing the economy have been added, which have resulted in contributions of basic capital via the Socie9te9 de prise de participation de l'c9tat, the SPPE. However, as I have indicated, it would be simplifying to be satisfied with this "photograph". The Banking Commission has in fact endeavoured, throughout recent years, to develop the most forward-looking analysis possible of the risks borne by institutions, in particular in order to test the resilience of a bank or the French banking system to shocks, whether macroeconomic or more specific. From this point of view, the annual report published today presents, in one of its boxes (see Box 4), our way of building macroeconomic scenarios and simulating their effects on the solvency of French banks. In that regard, the various stress tests carried out in recent months seem to me likely to confirm my assessment of the soundness of French banks. Of course, the evolving nature of the environment in which they operate calls for a regular update of this type of analysis. My services are actively working on this; beyond that, an initiative has been launched by the European supervisors, to which we fully subscribe. As you know, I voted in favour of publishing the results of this exercise on a country-by-country basis. I now come to the second point of my speech. 3 "Presentation of the Annual Report of the Banking Commission for 2008" by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Banking Commission - Paris, 26 June 2009 2. Strengthening the organisation and risk management methods of banking institutions remains more necessary than ever 2.1. Great vigilance must remain essential Banks could seek to take advantage of the trend reversal that seems to be emerging for certain segments of the financial markets to develop the activities of their trading rooms and thus compensate for the decline in revenues that may affect the credit sector. This revival of market activities would be a good thing if, and only if, risk management and management processes develop at the same pace. We will be very vigilant on this point. Moreover, if this is not the case, the Banking Commission, under Pillar 2 of Basel 2, will require more capital and liquidity buffers. Beyond that, four specific risk factors are attracting attention. 95 First of all, the so-called "second round" effects of the crisis, if they concern all segments of banks' credit activity, could weaken bank commitments on CLOs and leveraged financing, and in particular LBOs. 95 Secondly, the risks arising from alternative management activities, in relation to hedge funds, which I had already highlighted last year, should remain at a high level. 95 In addition, even if banks have so far cautiously hedged the risks arising from so-called "toxic" assets, that is to say directly impacted by the subprime crisis, it is necessary to continue to follow carefully structured products underlying loans financing residential or commercial real estate (RMBS and CMBS), while real estate markets tend to weaken in several European countries, or even business loans. 95 In this regard, in general, the cyclical deterioration to which almost all countries are faced, to varying degrees, results in a significant increase in credit risk. This development concerns in particular the financing of companies which, due to the increase in insolvencies, could contribute to increasing the cost of risk for institutions. But the latter could also be fuelled by the defects likely to be found in international transactions. These, as you know, have been an important axis of development of French banks during the recent period; this is particularly the case for activities carried out in the countries of Eastern Europe, some of which are facing significant economic difficulties, weakening the borrowers of these countries. We are following this development very closely, even if it is not, of course, a question of making French banks give up maintaining their presence in these countries. 2.2. Two particular lessons from the crisis for banks Among the many lessons to be learned from the crisis in terms of risk management, two of them seem to me to be of particular importance. First, risk management can only be fully effective when it fits into and is embodied in strong corporate governance. It is indeed at the highest level of the hierarchy of institutions that it is necessary to ensure that the measurement and monitoring of risks are an integral part of the decision-making process of institutions and constitute tools for steering activities, both in the monitoring of cyclical development and, more upstream, during the strategy development phase. A topic 4 "Presentation of the Annual Report of the Banking Commission for 2008" by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Banking Commission - Paris, 26 June 2009 The major issue that illustrates the link between governance, risk-taking and strategies is that of remuneration policy: as you know, the Banking Commission ensures with great attention that the various commitments made in this area by the banking profession are respected. Second, banks need to further strengthen the conditions for their stress tests. The crisis has indeed shown that, unlikely as they may be, certain extreme events can occur there and when they are not always expected. Proof of this is the liquidity crisis, which reached an acute phase in the second half of 2008. Stress tests, while they are of course not intended to immunize against all risks, nevertheless help to prepare banks to better anticipate the consequences of crises, before they occur and to better manage them, if they do occur. Risk governance and stress tests are two topics that the Banking Commission is examining with particular attention as part of its analysis of the risk profile of each bank under Pillar 2 of Basel 2. Before concluding, I will address the third point of my presentation. 3. The crisis has also created significant challenges for supervisors It is, of course, too early to draw definitive lessons from the financial turbulence. However, as far as banking regulation and supervision are concerned, I believe that three points deserve to be highlighted. First of all, international cooperation, and in particular European cooperation, has never been so necessary. The cross-border dissemination of risks calls for more coordination. From this point of view, the Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS/CEBS) has, in recent years, played a pivotal role in strengthening this cooperation in Europe, in particular through colleges of supervisors, whose functioning it has helped to harmonise. Naturally, the General Secretariat of the Banking Commission has taken an active part in these developments, which it has, moreover, most often provoked. Moreover, without prejudging the solutions that will finally be decided, I believe that it can already be said that the path traced by the 'Larosie8re report' will lead to a significant strengthening of cooperation not only between supervisors, but also between them and the central banks. In the latter respect, I am referring to the European Systemic Risk Board, the name given today to this future forum where major macroprudential developments will be analysed and the general measures they call for will be decided. These European reflections reaffirm the fundamental nature of the links between supervisory and central banking functions. You will note, in this regard, that this is one of the strong points of the report submitted by Mr Deletre9 on the rapprochement between the Insurance and Mutual Insurance Supervisory Authority and the Banking Commission, since the future Prudential Control Authority would, like the latter, be backed by the Banque de France. The second point I would like to come back to is the strengthening of the banking prudential framework and the improvement of international accounting regulations. The year 2008 was marked by major initiatives, decided at the highest level (I am thinking in particular of the G20) and implemented under the aegis of the Basel Committee in particular. The European authorities are also particularly active. 5 "Presentation of the Annual Report of the Banking Commission for 2008" by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Banking Commission - Paris, 26 June 2009 Thus, in the prudential field: 95 The securitisation regime will be strengthened, in particular so that assets sold on the market are selected and then monitored as if they had remained on the balance sheets of the originator banks and sufficient capital is built up to protect against unexpected risks; 95 The quality of core capital, Tier One, will be enhanced and, above all, assessed more homogeneously, from one country to another; I have been a personal advocate for such a strengthening for a long time. 95 Similarly, the risks induced by market activities will give rise to more appropriate capital requirements and, let us be clear, "thanks to" the experience gained during the market turbulence of 2008, which are higher. 95 Finally, guidelines have been defined to develop best practices for liquidity risk management within cross-border groups. In the accounting field, enormous efforts are under way to obtain convergent accounting frameworks on both sides of the Atlantic with a very high level of quality. You know how committed I am to ensuring that these efforts are continued and strengthened, particularly so that the pro-cyclical effects of standards are combated, especially on the side of the international standard-setter, the IASB. On the latter point, I am on the side of those who are working in favour of "dynamic provisioning". Let me come back to liquidity risk management, to make it my last point of intervention. In 2007, the French authorities began discussions to renovate the prudential framework for monitoring that risk, which, in France, dated from 1988. Carried out in close consultation with the profession, this work, inspired by internationally agreed guidelines, has resulted in a regulatory text that will enter into force in 2010. It provides for the prudential recognition, after authorization by the Banking Commission, of the internal methods developed by the most advanced institutions. French banks must mobilize to succeed in the transition from old to new regulations and be at the global forefront of liquidity management. * * * To conclude, I would say that the year 2008, through the multiple shocks that have occurred, some of which have been systemic in nature, has tested the resilience of all banking systems. French banks were of course not spared by these events, as evidenced by a lower profitability in 2008, compared to that observed in 2007. However, with a good level of capital, continuing to benefit from the positive effects of an economic model based on diversification, less exposed than other international banks to so-called "toxic" assets, they have so far been able to overcome the crisis. They must thus be able to continue to ensure adequate financing of the French economy. But the economic situation cannot lead to an excess of optimism, which could lead to a relaxation of vigilance in the management of all the risks carried by credit institutions. It is necessary to develop banking activities with a long-term perspective. This is what is at stake for our banking system for years to come. 6 "Presentation of the Annual Report of the Banking Commission for 2008" by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Banking Commission - Paris, 26 June 2009

Title: Tribune Financial Times A strong structure to secure the CDS market
text: Op-ed by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Published on 20 October 2009 in the Financial Times A strong structure to secure the CDS market While financial innovation can make a key contribution to growth and prosperity, it is also likely to cause significant instability. To reap the full benefits of innovation while limiting its risks, we need robust and resilient financial systems and infrastructure. At the Pittsburgh summit, G20 leaders also called for further regulation. Credit default swaps (CDS) are a typical example in this regard. A recently published report by the ECB, the result of extensive quantitative and qualitative work carried out by the Eurosystem central banks1 with the contribution of the profession, highlights two important characteristics of this market. The first relates to the increasing concentration of the CDS market in the hands of a small number of institutions. In Europe, two-thirds of banks' exposures to CDS are concentrated on their top ten counterparties. Globally, five banks (one of which is headquartered in Europe) account for half of this market. This concentration has increased since the beginning of the financial crisis, with several important counterparties leaving the market. Non-bank players, such as hedge funds, now account for less than 10% of all transactions on the CDS compartment. Such a degree of concentration is a factor of vulnerability, a risk to market liquidity and the proper formation of prices. The second interesting feature is the strong interconnection that exists in the CDS market. Indeed, not only do the main operators on CDS essentially negotiate with each other, but they also increasingly exchange protections against their own default: of the ten most negotiated contracts concerning non-sovereign entities, six actually relate to these same operators. In other words, these operators insure their peers for a risk to their own community. This circularity implies that the transfer of risk has become more limited than expected. The combined effect of concentration and the "interconnectedness" of the market amplifies counterparty risk and the systemic consequences that may result from the failure of a significant operator. For this reason, the authorities have advocated for the clearing of CDS by CCPs. The final declaration of the G20 leaders at the end of the Pittsburgh Summit indicates a clear direction and sets a precise deadline: all normalized OTC derivative contracts will have to be traded on exchanges or via electronic trading platforms and cleared by central counterparties by the end of 2012 at the latest. Currently, most of the CDS market is organized around over-the-counter contracts through which buyers and sellers conclude the transaction and settle it bilaterally. The resilience of the market therefore depends on the strength of a dense and complex network of bilateral relations. Such a network is no stronger than its weakest link. On the other hand, the use of a CCP reduces counterparty risk through multilateral clearing. However, even in a central counterparty system, counterparty risk never disappears. Clearing houses concentrate risk and remain vulnerable to the failure of a major player. They must be subject to appropriate oversight to ensure that they are properly capitalised, use robust risk management practices and meet high standards of governance. In addition, they must not depend on other financial intermediaries for the provision of liquidity, which means that they must have access, at all times, to central bank liquidity. A sensitive issue relating to CCPs is their location. In this regard, two points can be made. First, the size of the market allows multiple CCPs to operate simultaneously with sufficient liquidity. The monopoly situation created by the existence of a single CCP would increase systemic risk and deprive the financial system of the benefits of healthy competition. Second, where a central bank is required to provide liquidity to a CCP, it is normal for it to wish to be directly responsible for the supervision of that infrastructure. Taken together, in view of the volume of CDS contracts denominated in euro, these two concerns explain why we consider it essential that CCPs be established in the euro area. The transparency of the CDS market also needs to be improved. Data warehouses, which keep a register of all positions, play a key role in this regard: regardless of their location, they must provide regulatory and supervisory authorities with access to all the data necessary for effective macro-prudential and micro-prudential supervision. With a more robust market infrastructure and greater transparency, we will be able to ensure that CDS make a more secure contribution to financing the economy. 1 Credit Default Swaps and Counterparty Risk, ECB, August 2009. The Bank of France contributed significantly to this report. Banque de France Direction de la Communication Press Service 48, rue Croix des Petits Champs 75049 PARIS CEDEX 01

Title: International financial stability
text: Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Paris-Europlace Financial Forum 29 November 29, Tokyo, "International financial stability" Although the financial crisis originated in one country, it soon became apparent that it was undeniably global in nature. It delivered a simple message: capital markets are closely interconnected around the world and, therefore, domestic financial stability is inseparable from international financial stability. These are really two sides of the same coin. Today I would like to reflect on international financial stability. The views expressed here are my own. However, as you know, the France is currently in charge of the G20 presidency and I will try to put my own thoughts in this perspective. International financial instability has increased in recent times. Whether it's exchange rates, international capital flows or commodity prices, signs of greater volatility abound. Volatility is not necessarily a bad thing. To a certain extent, it testifies to the proper functioning of the markets. Asset price movements allow the financial system to act as a buffer, to "absorb" exogenous economic shocks. This process increases well-being, insofar as it avoids, or at least limits, the adjustment of the more rigid markets for goods and labour. Volatility can also result from changes in fundamentals. For example, capital flows to emerging economies partly reflect very favourable long-term growth prospects and potentially strong return on capital. There is nothing wrong with that. At most, it may seem paradoxical that net capital flows are still directed upstream, from emerging to developed economies. This means that some of the world's poorest citizens lend money to the richest, allowing them to finance their consumption. The same applies to commodity prices. The functioning of commodity markets is increasingly comparable to that of asset markets, given that 1/4 the development of financial instruments based on baskets of raw materials. In fact, commodities have become an asset class per se, which requires special attention from the point of view of financial stability. On the other hand, there may be good reason to believe that "fundamentals"," such as robust growth in commodity-intensive countries, are driving the current behaviour of many commodity markets. Finally, financial volatility is likely the result of several specificities of the current environment. The concomitance of economic uncertainty, strong risk aversion and abundant liquidity globally is particularly conducive to a sharp reversal in market sentiment and sudden portfolio rearrangements. Volatility begins to be a problem when it results from government decisions and financial markets contribute to deepening shocks rather than mitigating them. Lasting instability then sets in and generates potential threats to the real economy. We may find ourselves in such a situation today, as the reciprocal coherence of the economic strategies followed by the major economies is questioned. At the same time, policies implemented to address volatility can sometimes cause further damage and distortions in capital markets. I will address both of these issues before turning briefly to the longer-term challenges. Global imbalances and financial stability There is a broad consensus on the need to rebalance aggregate demand around the world. This shared objective strengthened the cohesion shown by the G20 countries during the acute phase of the crisis. It played a key role in 2008 and 2009 in restoring confidence and charting the path to recovery. However, this concerted approach to global imbalances may have lost its strength recently. There is a real debate around two major and closely related issues: first, on the appropriate pace of rebalancing, with advanced countries giving it a greater degree of urgency; and, secondly, on the most effective strategies, particularly in the area of exchange rates. It would be a mistake to attribute responsibility for imbalances to a specific cause. All countries have legitimate concerns. In recent weeks, we have seen a propensity on the part of some countries to challenge the monetary policies of their partners. Nothing good can be expected from such an attitude. We must rely on three fundamental realities. First, countries are free to pursue such monetary policies as they deem appropriate. Indeed, when central banks are independent, they are legally obliged to do so. Monetary policy should be conducted solely on the basis of domestic objectives, but, as you have seen, all central banks have the same mandate: price stability. This applies to all countries, large or small. The world has benefited enormously from two decades of price stability resulting from monetary regimes based on central bank independence and the primacy of internal price stability. When external objectives have been allowed to influence monetary decisions, it has generally yielded very poor results and increased instability. 2/4 Second, under the IMF's Articles of Agreement, countries are free to choose their capital account and exchange rate regimes as long as they do not manipulate exchange rates. This is a fundamental pillar of our current system. This condition has proven to be very complex to define, and even more so to implement. The IMF has encountered difficulties in seeking to establish an effective and symmetrical process of multilateral surveillance. Third, and finally, we live in a world of increased interdependence and complexity. International capital flows have created a real interconnection between countries. The monetary and financial system has become "multipolar". An increasing number of countries, both developed and emerging, have become active players in international capital markets. Contagion effects have multiplied between national monetary and economic policies. And no country can be truly indifferent to the actions of others. In the current circumstances, it has become much more difficult to reconcile these three fundamental realities. Monetary policy divergences are inevitable given the erratic pace of recovery around the world. Moreover, for each country, it may be that currently the objectives of price stability do not coincide with the objectives of financial stability. In advanced economies, monetary easing and dampens to credit growth create the risk of new financial imbalances. In many emerging markets, inflationary pressures would require monetary tightening, but this would clearly risk triggering destabilizing capital inflows. In this context, macroprudential policies have a key role to play. In advanced economies, they should aim to encourage credit growth, while increasing the resilience of the financial sector. Supervisors must also be prepared to act in the event of bubble-like phenomena emerging on certain markets. For emerging economies, measures to stabilize capital inflows can ease stress on domestic financial conditions and prevent the formation of new asset bubbles. The international financial architecture In the longer term, however, we may need to work together to develop a more effective and stable international financial architecture. I would like to set out three possible avenues for progress. First, we can start thinking about ways to deal with the volatility of international capital flows. At the country level, capital controls can temporarily reduce stress on its capital account or even permanently limit the volatility of its exchange rate. For the international system as a whole, however, these controls may simply shift tensions onto other countries or asset classes and exacerbate overall volatility rather than reduce it. There must be ways to eliminate these negative effects by creating a predictable framework defining the circumstances, modalities and conditions for the implementation of temporary controls. 3/4 Second, it would be wise to find ways to disconnect the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves from exchange rate management and, more generally, from the balance of payments and monetary policies. Currently, the accumulation of reserves can only be achieved through the combination of a balance of payments surplus and a certain level of exchange rate interventions. Emerging market foreign exchange reserves have risen from 4% of GDP in 1990 to more than 20% on average today. The accumulation of precautionary reserves, however legitimate it may be, inevitably has side effects on domestic macroeconomic policies and spillovers to other countries. Stabilizing the demand for international reserves would therefore bring enormous benefits in terms of global well-being. The need for national reserves could be reduced if there were credible mechanisms to ensure the provision of official liquidity on a multilateral basis, hence the current search for global financial safety nets that has taken a prominent place in the G20. Finally, I would like to say a few words about financial development. The differences between countries are striking, whether in terms of capital account regimes, the size and indebtedness of national financial markets or, more generally, their ability to create a sufficient supply of safe and liquid assets locally. Some of these differences reflect real choices and preferences of social model that should be respected and taken into account. Others result from deliberate or unintentional distortions caused by the authorities that must be reduced or eliminated. Domestic financial imperfections and frictions on international capital flows interact to create and amplify imbalances. Financial instability, ultimately, is a product of this interaction. Some of this instability manifests itself in exchange rate movements. It is highly unlikely that a global financial market characterized by constant friction between vastly different national financial systems will lead to a stable (and fundamentals-based) equilibrium of foreign exchange markets. Full harmonisation and convergence of financial development is neither desirable nor feasible. But it is imperative that we ensure that our different financial systems interact harmoniously. Greater compatibility of approaches to financial regulation between advanced and emerging economies is within our reach. Important progress is being made. The institutional framework has adjusted to the new reality of the world. Emerging countries are now fully assuming their role in the constellation of committees in Basel that are working to define the fundamental principles of financial regulation. The most important of them sit as full members of the Financial Stability Board and its Steering Board. Finally, a historic agreement on IMF reform at the last G20 meeting fully recognized the role and place of these countries in the new financial environment. I am therefore convinced that we can and will make progress in addressing the difficult issues we face and build a better and safer global financial system. 4/4
