Title: G20 Roadmap how finance can help rebalance the world economy
text: PARIS EUROPLACE FINANCIAL FORUM Paris, July 6 & 7, 2010 G20 Roadmap: How Finance Can Help Rebalance the World Economy Introduction by Christian NOYER, governor of Banque de France Before I start let me thank the organizers for inviting me to this conference: they have managed to put together an outstanding program and it is a great pleasure for me to exchange views with the other participants in this round table. I was asked to introduce the discussion on G20 Roadmap: How Finance Can Help Rebalance the World Economy. The title of this session contains some of the most important concepts on the current policy agenda: finance, rebalancing the world economy and the G20 Roadmap. Let me take them in turn. Finance, first. Since 2008, the world is going through the deepest financial crisis since the second World War, and hence never before has the word finance been so crucial in the policy agenda. This financial crisis has had very high real costs: real output, industrial production, trade flows, to name just a few key variables, have contracted markedly during the crisis. In addition, the fiscal positions and the public debt of many countries have also deteriorated markedly in the past two years. Yet, it is important to recall that these real and fiscal problems largely stem from the financial issues that plagued our economies in the past decade. Indeed the financial sector, with the help of financial innovation and loose regulation fostered unsustainable growth and asset price bubbles, and if trade linkages have contributed to spread the crisis across countries, financial integration has fostered the contagion. So, yes finance matters and is the heart of the real economy. Rebalancing the world economy, next. In the years leading to the crisis, the global economy was growing at unprecedented speed: above 5% per annum in 2006 and 2007, far above the average recorded in the decade from 1992 to 2001, at 3.1%. Yet, this growth was unbalanced, both internally and across countries, such that it was, as it turned out, unsustainable. In fact, the global policy agenda in the mid- to late 2000s was dominated by the issue of global imbalances: current account positions widened to unprecedented amounts (at least by modern standards), reflecting strong saving-investment gaps: to many observers, household saving was strikingly low in the United States, while emerging Asia was characterized by a global saving glut, in the words of Chairman Bernanke. These global 1 imbalances have adjusted markedly in the wake of the financial crisis, but this rebalancing has been mostly cyclical and the issue remains. Let me now turn to the third important keyword of this session, the G20 Road map. With the intensification of the crisis, it has become obvious that the G20 was the right, -because the most legitimate- forum to prepare the policy response. And the G20 fulfilled the most optimistic anticipations as it reacted promptly and strongly to the crisis. Beyond this, the G20 has also agreed on an ambitious policy agenda, aiming for the long run. The G20 Roadmap does not only aim at one particular aspect of the global economy; it is very encompassing. One aspect of it is macrorebalancing, another is on financial regulation and global financial safety nets. The G20 agenda is focused on crisis prevention by coordination in order to avoid, or at least dampen overheating and boom/bust cycles. How are these issues related? First I will briefly tackle the important question of the link between the financial crisis and global imbalances. Second, I will go through the main implications of this link and outline the key features of the policy agenda of the G20. In this second part I will mostly focus on the so-called G20 Framework for a Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth and on financial safety nets. In the last section I will focus on financial regulation issues more specifically. Why and how do the financial crisis and global imbalances interact? An overwhelming body of research has established the clear relation between global imbalances and financial issues, some of which were behind the financial crisis. Indeed, global imbalances were not just the result of cyclical factors, such as business cycle fluctuations, changes in oil and other commodity prices, etc. They were also, and to a large extent, the result of deeper, structural factors, as illustrated by the link between global imbalances and asymmetries in financial development. Ricardo Caballero focuses for instance on the notion of asset shortage: as safe financial assets were not readily available in some regions of the world (emerging Asia noticeably), net savings in these regions were channeled to the United States, which, in lowering financial constraints, amplified the current account deficit of this country. One may actually wonder whether this also partly contributed to the development of a financial bubble in the United States. The key idea I would like to take from this literature is that finance most certainly played a key role in the emergence of global imbalances. How and why may the G20 Roadmap help financial soundness and global rebalancing As the global economy is recovering from the crisis, the G20 roadmap aims first at ensuring the transition to a strong, sustainable and balanced growth. By strong, we mean that growth should converge to the growth rate of potential output over the medium term whereas that potential is enhanced by the implementation of more effective structural policies. Sustainable growth should be consistent with public finance sustainability, price and financial stability, along with social and environmental policy goals. Finally, balanced growth implies a growth that is broadly based across all G20 countries and all regions in the world, and as I said earlier, that should not generate persistent and destabilizing internal or external imbalances. Balanced growth also implies to facilitate the catching up of developing countries (and the taking off of the poorest). Drawing the lessons from the 2 crisis, growth cannot be strong without being sustainable and cannot be sustainable if it is not balanced. The so-called Framework for Strong, Sustainable and Balanced Growth is the key mechanism by which G20 countries work together to achieve these objectives. With support from the IMF, G20 countries are going through a mutual assessment process by sharing their policy frameworks, programs and projections and assessing their consistency with the common objectives. This process will lead the G20 to recommend policy options to its members. Policy options obviously depend on national circumstances. Countries facing serious fiscal challenges need in particular to accelerate the pace of fiscal consolidation, while countries that have the capacity should expand domestic sources of growth and help cushion a decline in demand from other countries. Reforms of social safety nets will be essential in both cases and structural reforms of the product and labor markets will be key to foster stronger growth in the medium and long run. Policy options may also entail exchange rate adjustments consistent with smooth rebalancing. In search of global financial safety nets There is another side to rebalancing where finance matters. Starting with the Asian crisis of 1997-1998 and up until the global shortage of liquidity that took place in 2008, many emerging countries have experienced sudden stops of capital inflows on a recurrent basis. The international financial architecture as it was before the crisis lacked appropriate tools to deal with volatility in global capital flows and to prevent crisis contagion. This was an incentive for emerging countries to self-insure against global liquidity shocks by accumulating international reserves or protect themselves through capital flows control, both distortive types of protection. Reserve accumulation is costly to emerging economies as they have to restrain consumption and forego profitable investment opportunities in order to buy the low-yield assets that usually constitute reserves. It also has global consequences. For those emerging market economies that ran a current account surplus to accumulate reserves, the process has contributed to current account imbalances. This is why finance has an important role to play to help these economies effectively deal with capital volatility. A lot has already been done by G20 countries and international institutions since the beginning of the crisis. Central banks of large advanced countries have set up swap arrangements with some emerging countries. The International Monetary Fund has created a precautionary lending facility: the Flexible Credit Line. A general SDR allocation of USD 250 bn has been agreed in the London summit of April 2009 and out in place. However, there is still scope for improvement and further work is currently being done to improve global financial safety nets. In their meeting in Busan earlier this month, Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of the G20 have acknowledged a need for national, regional and multilateral efforts to deal with capital volatility. A Financial Safety Net Experts Group has been set up to work on the issue. The reform of financial regulation The financial crisis as taught us some very hard lessons. While there are many causes to the crisis, it is clear that it forces us to reconsider the way we regulate and supervise the financial system. That is what we have been doing since the November 2008 G20 meeting. 3 We entered this crisis with many unregulated entities playing a major role in the financial system. There were, therefore, huge "black holes", including what has been called a "shadow banking system" where most of the excesses of securitisation took place. The G20 has fostered coordinated efforts by industrialized and emerging countries alike to bring most important financial actors under the umbrella of supervision, with rating agencies and hedge funds receiving a larger degree of attention. Beyond these actors, the G20 and the Financial Stability Board (FSB) in particular have been instrumental in efforts aimed at enlarging the scope of financial regulation to make sure that the systemic importance and interconnectedness of institutions, markets, instruments no longer escape our vigilance. Naturally, the necessary reform of OTC derivatives markets has gained traction and the G20 has set a very clear roadmap on these matters. Efforts aimed at integrating these markets into regulated and supervised market infrastructures are indeed an essential policy response to risks accumulated in these markets. However, the crisis has not just shown us that we should expand the scope of regulation and supervision. In fact, two clear trends have emerged and are greatly affecting the very nature of regulation. The first observable trend is that we must complement micro-supervision with macrofinancial supervision: this macroprudential approach has in fact developed in many countries. The second trend is that regulation needs to become more global in response to the globalization of finance. In that respect, the commitment by all G20 jurisdictions to implement Basel II by 2011 and to finalize this year a new package aimed at strengthening bank capital and liquidity standards is a great achievement. We are confident that making tangible progress on each of these fronts is an essential response from policy makers to the roots of the global financial crisis. To some extent, the ultimate aim of financial regulation has to do with financing the real economy. Sound regulation should enable the stable provision of financial services to economic agents as they strive to finance their productive investments and consumption, which constitute the fuel for growth. Banks are central to the financing of economic activity because they perform maturity and liquidity transformation as well as a credit risk screening function. This is especially true in continental Europe, where they are responsible for more than 80% of financial intermediation. This is why the current focus on enhancing banking regulation is right and progress on key reforms to strengthen bank capital and liquidity standards remains a top priority. The recent reform package of the Basel Committee will lead to a much more robust and resilient banking system in the future, with both a stronger capital and liquidity base than before the crisis. The challenge, now, is to calibrate and phase in the new framework in a way that does not impede the recovery and does not contradict our macroeconomic objectives. The macroeconomic assessment of the reforms underway will help us strike the optimal balance. We must also reduce procyclicality. Some of the procyclicality can be trimmed through prudential regulation but I strongly believe that our first line of defense against procyclicality should be the accounting framework. I therefore support the current focus on reducing the scope of the mark-tomarket approach and moving from an incurred loss model to a forward-looking model for provisioning. Conclusions To conclude, the main challenge ahead of us is to find the right balance between all these measures and the short-run effects of the rebalancing. If the rebalancing process happens too fast, it might weaken the recovery; but if reforms are delayed too much, the longer-run growth prospects will be 4 affected negatively. One very important issue to focus on while analyzing this trade-off is that policy decisions need to be perfectly coordinated across countries. The crisis has demonstrated that it was necessary, and that it was possible. I am confident that the G20 Roadmap is the right approach to this coordination problem. We will, under the French leadership of the 2011 G20, pay due attention to the smooth implementation of this process. 5

Title: Monetary policy responses to recent financial market tensions
text: Monday, June 21, 2010 Remarks by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France - VIIIth Days of the Bank of France Foundation "Macroeconomic Policies in Times of Crisis" "Monetary policy responses to recent financial market tensions" Ladies and gentlemen It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you to the VIII days of the Banque de France Foundation. As you know, the purpose of this Foundation is to encourage research in monetary, financial and banking economics and to provide financial support for research projects. These Days are an opportunity for researchers who have received a grant from the Foundation to present the results of their work. Given the public policy challenges posed by the financial and economic crisis we have been experiencing since 2007, it is not surprising that most of these research projects focus on macroeconomic policies pursued since the beginning of the crisis. Central banks have made a major contribution to these policies and I would like to take this opportunity to review the latest developments in this area. From the beginning of the crisis, central banks had to act on several fronts. First of all, they have of course continued to fulfil their mission of maintaining stability. 1 prices. And their actions have been successful in this area. As far as the Eurosystem is concerned, at no point in the crisis have inflation expectations deviated significantly from our definition of price stability. This was very clear, and crucial, in the months when headline inflation remained negative, the output gap was itself strongly negative, and the risks of deflation could have materialized. With inflation expectations firmly anchored around 2%, the "zero rate floor" has never really been a problem. In the euro area, real short-term interest rates have been brought to negative levels fast enough to stabilise the economy despite an unprecedented shock following the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers. Central banks have also had to ensure that monetary policy transmission channels are not affected. There was a risk, in this context of high instability, that the dysfunction of the financial and credit markets would strongly disrupt their actions. Their intervention was therefore necessary, and it had to be adapted to the specificities of each economy. In the United States, where financial intermediation is heavily dependent on securitized credit markets, the central bank had to make substantial asset purchases from the outset (which have since been phased out). In the euro area, financial intermediation is mainly provided by the banking system. Most of the measures we took were therefore aimed at providing banks, through repo operations, with a sufficient amount of liquidity to prevent credit flows to the economy from being seriously disrupted. We were fortunate to approach the crisis with a very appropriate range of tools. From the beginning, our operating framework has been based on a wide range of counterparties and collaterals, and therefore did not require any significant changes. We have, however, never ruled out the possibility of asset purchases, if necessary, to address market dysfunction and ensure appropriate transmission of monetary policy impulses. Thus, in 2009, the Governing Council implemented a 2 covered bond purchase programme, which has now almost come to an end. Although of modest amount (8060 billion), this programme has been quite successful in reviving the covered bond market. I would note that the covered bond market was the most dynamic of all money and securities markets last month and provided valuable support to bank financing at a time when bond issuance is proving more difficult due to an environment of increased uncertainty. The recent decision to purchase government bonds is part of this same context. As we all know, market participants have carried out a sharp reassessment of sovereign risk. Tensions over Greece's public debt began to manifest themselves in December 2009. By early 2010, they had rapidly spread to other European countries. In recent weeks, despite the austerity measures implemented by all governments and supported, in the case of Greece, by significant financial aid, these tensions have increased and risk premiums have risen sharply. Disturbances have occurred in other market segments, in particular in the interbank and repo markets. Bank-referenced default swaps (CDS) increased in line with sovereign CDS premiums. Some banks have begun to face increasing funding problems. The euro area has been the epicentre of this phenomenon, but the consequences are being felt indirectly in other parts of the world, with indicators of money market tensions rising in some non-European countries. This reflects a climate of widespread uncertainty which, if left unchecked, could have significant consequences for financial stability and the real economy, as was the case at the end of 2008. This situation required a rapid response. From the Eurosystem's point of view, the transmission of monetary policy could be affected in several ways: 3 ? Through the price channel: Rising government bond yields are likely to be reflected in the cost of private sector financing. When bond markets are functioning normally, sovereign bonds represent a floor for private sector financing conditions. o Through the liquidity channel: government bonds are the main collateral used by banks. The dysfunction of the sovereign debt market reduces the role played by government securities as a liquidity buffer and thus hampers banks' ability to issue loans and refinance the real economy. o Through the balance sheet channel: lower bond prices lead to capital losses on the assets and balance sheets of financial and non-financial agents. In the case of banks, these losses reduce their capital base, thereby reducing their supply of loans to the economy. As for borrowers, capital losses on the assets they hold reduce their solvency and, therefore, their borrowing capacity. In addition, contagion effects on interbank markets have posed risks to financial stability, also involving possible chain effects, which are detrimental to the financing conditions of the economy. We therefore felt that further action was needed. It goes without saying that, although important governmental measures were subsequently adopted at European level in addition to ours, our decision was taken in complete independence and in fact preceded the deliberations of Ecofin. Firstly, the Governing Council reversed the abandonment of certain non-conventional measures: the fixed-rate tendering procedure - all tenders being served - was reinstated for refinancing operations at 4 Three months. These will be launched in May, June and July. Second, we decided to create a Securities Markets Programme. Through the purchase of government bonds, this programme aims to counter the sudden changes in the euro area bond markets and to guarantee the depth and liquidity of these markets in the short term, while helping to restore liquidity on the secondary market in the medium term. Due to the nature of the underlying instruments and the diversity of stakeholders, these transactions are not expected to have an immediate and dramatic impact. These measures, however, fulfil their role in mitigating the two threats we face, that of inefficient and inappropriate transmission of monetary policy and that of financial instability at the international level. These purchases of securities are not intended to change the stance of monetary policy. As a result, these operations have been sterilized through weekly liquidity recovery operations in the form of term deposits, which perfectly neutralizes their direct impact on overall bank liquidity. Of course, since purchases of securities are carried out exclusively on the secondary market, this intervention therefore fully respects the prohibition on the monetary financing of public debt laid down in the Treaty. It is clear, however, that these measures alone will not be enough. Doubts about the sustainability of public finances in many countries are the root cause of the current uncertainty. Therefore, for market tensions to ease, fiscal discipline must be rigorously enforced. The Securities Markets Programme was decided against the backdrop of the budgetary commitments made by the States concerned. It cannot and will not replace an effective and rapid process of fiscal consolidation. The credibility of budgetary commitments is therefore paramount. Thank you for your attention. 5

Title: How does the crisis lead to a reconsideration of economics
text: Introductory speech at the 12th days of the Book of Economics Intervention of Christian Noyer, Governor of the Bank of France "How does the crisis lead to a reconsideration of economics?" No one foresaw the crisis. No one had even imagined that it could occur in this form and with such magnitude. We can therefore doubt today the ability of economics to explain reality and its ability to help us understand the world. And, since the modern economy is largely based on market mechanisms, the crisis can also undermine confidence in the market economy for many of our fellow citizens. Faced with these questions and doubts, I will try today to present some personal reflections, without concealing the questions that arise and the uncertainties that we have to face. In the scientific debate and the public discussion, three questions must be clearly distinguished: (1) Is the market economy effective? (2) Is it stable? (3) Is it right? I leave aside the question of justice. Not because it is secondary: on the contrary, it is too important to be treated so quickly. I shall confine myself to the question of efficiency and stability, which are of a more macroeconomic nature. First, some definitions. The efficiency of an economy is measured by its ability to allocate resources well, to constantly identify the needs of economic agents and to satisfy them at the lowest cost. Stability is a different concept. An economy is stable if it returns to equilibrium after what economists 1 call for a shock. By shock, they actually mean largely unforeseen circumstances such as a sharp increase in the price of oil. The economy is unstable if it has mechanisms that amplify shocks, or even create shocks themselves within the economic system. The prosperity of an economy depends first and foremost on its efficiency. Making the right investments and technological choices, knowing how to optimize the organization of production, avoiding waste, all this creates jobs and promotes growth. But stability also matters: shocks that are too frequent and too violent create uncertainty, sometimes have irreversible effects and reduce consumption and production capacity. The current crisis is an illustration of this, which is reflected in a considerable loss of resources, a rise in unemployment and a downgrading of many investments. Markets are generally considered to be the most effective instrument for the proper allocation of resources. Of course, they have shortcomings that public action must correct. But, apart from North Korea and Cuba - two countries plunged into extreme poverty - there is no longer a command economy in the world. Everywhere, the market plays a vital role in setting prices and guiding the decisions of businesses and households. Overall, therefore, everyone agrees that market economies are effective. Are they also naturally stable? The crisis has proven the opposite. It has shown us that market economies are unstable, perhaps even fundamentally unstable. In a sense, we already knew that. After all, there have been, for thirty years, a period of great financial liberalization, other crises, probably less serious, but quite frequent. We had forgotten that. For almost two decades, we have been going through a phase of exceptional growth in its regularity, this in the absence of inflation. This phase, which has been described as "great moderation", may have anesthetized us. We thought we had found the recipes for economic policy that would guarantee us stability forever. Economics should have deceived us. On the contrary, it has reinforced our illusions. What happened? 2 For three decades, economic analysis has developed on a body of assumptions and principles based on the absolute rationality of economic agents and the total efficiency of financial markets. With these assumptions, efficiency and stability naturally coincide. In particular, there is no financial instability. Speculative activity is itself stabilizing because speculators have an interest in buying when prices are too low and selling when they are too high. They therefore bring prices and markets back to their fundamental equilibrium levels. For this reason, in an efficient market, there are no financial bubbles. Credit is correctly allocated because the creditworthiness of each economic agent can be accurately assessed. All creditworthy borrowers find financing. Liquidity is always present in sufficient quantities. Similarly, in such an environment, there is no economic volatility. Households and businesses are constantly making rational choices about consumption, saving and investment. There is no place in this approach for business cycles. Of course we see that these cycles exist, with phases of expansion and lower growth, or even recession. In part, these cycles are considered to stem from "shocks", for example a technological discovery that temporarily accelerates growth and investment; in part, they result from "frictions", i.e. from the imperfections of the markets themselves, for example the rigidity of prices and wages, which means that they adapt only gradually to imbalances between supply and demand. But the fundamental assumption is that, left to its own devices, a market economy does not experience crisis. Even hit by shocks, it returns to balance, after a more or less long delay. How did this vision gradually take hold? Over the past thirty years, macroeconomic and financial market analysis have gained much in intellectual rigour and formal coherence. They developed on very rigorous representations - and 3 advanced modelling - of the behaviour of economic agents and the functioning of markets. This modeling has been criticized for its formalism and its excessive use of very sophisticated mathematical tools. I do not share that criticism. I deeply believe that modelling is an indispensable aid to economic policy analysis and decision-making. My question is elsewhere. It is clear that, whatever their power, the available modelling techniques do not allow to give a faithful and complete representation of a complex economic reality. There is therefore a choice, an arbitration, between formal rigor and realism. Economic analysis has chosen total rigour. But this choice was accompanied by an extreme simplification in the description of individual behaviour and the functioning of markets. The modern economist reasoned on what are called "representative agents" (households, companies,) all identical, who form "rational" expectations, and for which there are "complete" financial markets. If these assumptions are accepted, all the evolution of the economy and financial markets can then be described on the assumption that these representative agents optimize their choice of consumption, investment and savings at all times without liquidity constraints. It is not even necessary to take into account the financial markets since their efficiency ensures that capital is well allocated in the economy. And, indeed, contemporary macroeconomic models largely ignore financial variables, the functioning of capital markets and the role and evolution of credit. This bias has, of course, played a big role in their inability to describe the crisis, or even to consider its eventuality. Experience has shown what the situation is. Over the two years of the crisis, we have seen cumulative chains, mimetic behaviour, liquidity drying up, total paralysis of certain markets, great uncertainty about valuations, opacity of structures and products, all phenomena that absolutely contradict the efficiency hypothesis. Overnight, banks that had been lending themselves their cash surpluses on the interbank market for decades on a day-to-day basis decided to stop doing so. We also know that the crisis followed a period of artificial euphoria, leading to a housing bubble in several countries and development. 4 excessive credit masked by an often fake financial innovation. Nothing in the theory of the efficient market sheds light on this reality. We had, of course, often brilliant references, illustrating market failures (such as bank panic patterns) or the fragility of financial systems. But they have never led to a fundamental questioning of the efficiency hypothesis. Economics is therefore facing an examination of conscience and a formidable challenge. On the one hand, it must aim to describe the world as it is, with all its complexity and corollary, uncertainty and diversity (and therefore, probably renounce the simplification of the representative agent). We must think of the economy and, in particular, the financial sphere as a complex system, which will make it possible to better account for the volatility, sudden changes and discontinuities that periodically appear in the form of more or less acute crises. But science must also maintain conceptual analytical rigour, otherwise economic analysis would be reduced to a collection of empirical descriptions with uncertain foundations and therefore difficult to exploit to guide economic policies. In describing complexity, reconciling rigor and realism will be a major challenge. To be frank, everyone today does not know how this dilemma and tension will be resolved. It will probably take many years. My intuition is that our theoretical approach to finance will be profoundly changed. Account will have to be taken of the incentives, uncertainty, effects of innovation and its links with system risk, i.e. the interdependence between individual decisions and their undesirable effects for all market participants. As for macroeconomic analysis itself, we will probably see the development of two opposing approaches: one based on the deepening of current assumptions and methods, hoping that the increasing sophistication of models will bring them closer to reality; the other, more empirical, close to other disciplines such as psychology and behavioral sciences. Despite this uncertainty, we must continue to conduct economic policies, drawing lessons from the crisis, if possible. I would like to make three points here. 5 We now know that the market economy is unstable. We must therefore draw lasting conclusions from this. One, which is needed, is that we need to strengthen our capacity to deal with instability, since it is part of our economic universe. We need more robust economies. To simplify, we must install, wherever we can, "cushions" to absorb shocks. This simple idea has multiple implications. Fiscal "buffers" should support activity in the event of a crisis without, as is the case today for all advanced economies, leading to unsustainable levels of debt. It is therefore a priority to consolidate our public finances and regain room for manoeuvre. In another area, we will build "buffers" in the financial system by increasing the capital requirements of banks. This leads to my second point. The impression prevails that the crisis has led to a lasting rehabilitation of state activism in economic policy. This is not always true. We have certainly made lasting changes to our approach to financial regulation. Implicitly, in many countries, the benchmark was that of the efficient market. Regulation, where it existed, should therefore simply aim to remove barriers to efficiency and get as close as possible to the ideal model. And therefore above all, do not interfere with the market. It was a "light touch" regulation. Today, the approach is the opposite. We postulate non-efficiency, and we draw the consequences: strengthening robustness, changing incentives (for example by rules on remuneration), supervision of non-bank actors. The evolution is less clear on the so-called macroeconomic policy. The crisis has led to a budgetary activism that is certainly justified, but which cannot be renewed given the weight of public debts which, according to assumptions, our fellow citizens "rationally" anticipate that they risk becoming unsustainable. My third point follows from that. In questioning economics, we must be careful not to throw the baby away with the water of the 6 Bath and deprive us of the considerable progress made over the past thirty years. I would take an important example: the so-called rational expectations hypothesis. Taken to the extreme, it is probably unrealistic. It is excessive to think that all economic agents can base their decisions on such expectations. But the fundamental intuition remains correct. Expectations play a big role in economic life: agents look to the future to make their decisions. They are not always and systematically mistaken. All contemporary monetary policy is built on this observation. We have known for thirty years that inflation is determined by expectations and that, in order to achieve price stability, it is necessary to be able to influence and stabilize (we say, in our jargon "anchor") these expectations. To this end, all countries have built institutional frameworks, based on the independence of Central Banks, which protect monetary policy from short-term constraints and pressures. The experiment was very successful and, in all the major countries, inflation now seemed defeated. Many of you are too young to have experienced it yourself, but your parents and grandparents experienced periods in the 1970s when inflation fluctuated by 5 to 15% per year. The crisis has certainly shown that price stability is not a sufficient condition for financial stability. But it is certainly a necessary condition. You will allow me to conclude these brief reflections with this modest plea in favor of the Central Banks, whose independence does not prevent them, as you know, from mobilizing very actively to fight the crisis and try to limit its effects. 7

Title: Greetings from the President of the CPA
text: Paris, 17 January 2011 WISHES FROM THE PRESIDENT OF THE ACP Presidents, Ladies and Gentlemen, dear friends, As we enter this new year, I would like to offer you my most sincere and warmest wishes for 2011! However, this year opens in an environment marked by great uncertainties. Concerns from some countries, whether sovereign debt or the banking sector, feed into each other. While this phase of the crisis seems more specifically European, it mainly reflects uncertainty and potential instability on a global scale. In all advanced economies, the adjustment of public and private balance sheets continues under difficult conditions. In Europe, we are facing a debt crisis in some countries today. But make no mistake, this is certainly not a Euro crisis. As you know, the specificity of the euro zone obviously lies in its organisation: integrated money and financial markets but public finances and national public debts. There is therefore a potential risk to the financial stability of the area that requires appropriate governance. This issue is now a priority for the states of the euro area. From my point of view, three things are essential: - Firstly, let us set ourselves ambitious objectives: let us stop considering that the objective is 3% deficit and finally respect the Stability and Growth Pact as it has existed since the beginning, that is to say, let us aim with determination at the balance of public finances on average over the cycle; - Secondly, adopt rigorous European procedures: while it is legitimate for each sovereign state to decide on the level and structure of its expenditure and revenue, the same is not true of the balance, which is a subject of common interest to the entire euro area; - Finally, Member States must put in place careful monitoring of their relative competitiveness and of the evolution in each country of unit costs of production, which must be based on the objective of price stability that the ECB is mandated to maintain, and will maintain no matter what. On the side of the Central Banks, these difficulties led us to assume extensive responsibilities because there was a great risk for the integrity of the financial markets, and therefore for the 1 SENSITIVITY WATER NIVSENSITIVITY mechanisms for the transmission of monetary policy, through the yield curve and the credit channel. This led to the implementation of the public securities purchase program, whose monetary impact was totally sterilized. This device is by definition temporary but it will work for as long as necessary. These very real difficulties should not mask the great success of the euro: price stability has been ensured for ten years; deflation has been avoided; our citizens have one of the world's two largest currencies; there is no visible change in the behaviour of holding foreign exchange reserves; and the overall financial situation of the area is better than that of many others. Let us not forget that the average budget deficit in the euro area is significantly lower than that of the United States, the United Kingdom or Japan, for example. That is why, provided that the necessary efforts are made, I believe that we can look to the future with optimism. This year 2011 must therefore be approached with determination and vigilance: - Resolution first of all because, with the work done in the last few years years, we can rely on a consolidated supervisory architecture, a framework stronger regulations and broadly cleaned balance sheets of financial institutions; - Vigilance too, because major financial stability issues remain ahead we. Major regulatory projects must be carried out while many risks must continue to be the focus of our attention. I. 2010, the year of the creation of the Prudential Control Authority, was a year of intense mobilization of all actors, First of all, I would like to remind you of the "roadmap" assigned to the ACP when it was set up on March 9, 2010: - Successful merger between several authorities in the service of the general interest; - Successfully exit from the crisis; - Participate in the reform of the international financial system; - Protecting consumers. A. Successful merger in the service of the general interest: The ACP has been able to put itself in working order since its creation. Today it is: - an authority composed of nearly 1000 employees, fully operational and monitoring risks across the financial sector, banking and insurance - a plenary college of 19 members that brings together multidisciplinary expertise in the highest level of requirement - A sanctions college of 6 members, totally separate from the College, which guarantees increased legal certainty Backed by the Bank of France, the ACP thus retains the supervisory system that proved its worth during the crisis and benefits from the economic and financial expertise of the Banque de France. This model of supervision backed by the central bank is now becoming THE model in Europe, the most spectacular evolution being obviously that decided by the United Kingdom. B. Successfully exiting the crisis: The ACP has strengthened its action in the service of financial stability by developing its activity of measuring and monitoring risks, in particular through its stress tests. And there are, of course, documentary and on-the-spot checks, a key task for the ACP, which in 2011 will be as supported and brought closer together as it was in 2010. 2 SENSITIVITY WATER NIVSENSITIVITY C. Participating in the reform of the international financial system I believe that we have been able to participate actively in the drafting of new European or international regulations by being a force for proposals and by defending the models that are ours and that have resisted well during the crisis. We will continue this action within the various European bodies that will be set up at the beginning of 2011, but I will come back to it at greater length in a moment. D - Protecting consumers: The CPA exercises with dynamism and vigilance more extensive responsibilities in terms of controlling the marketing of financial products. The ACP ensures not only compliance with the laws and regulations but also with the rules of good practice of each profession. On-the-spot checks have already taken place on these subjects in several insurance bodies and banking institutions and this action will be continued and amplified in 2011 with, in particular, the strengthening of monitoring actions on advertisements. To facilitate the procedures of clients in an increasingly complex context, the legislator has strengthened cooperation between the ACP and the AMF by creating a common pole that ensures the coordination of the actions of the two authorities. In addition, this division relies on the Banque de France network for the telephone reception of individuals via the "Banqueinfo - service" platform, which receives nearly 1000 calls per day. This MFA/ACP/Banque de France is working really well and I am delighted about that. II. Despite these successes, we must remain vigilant and be aware of the challenges we will face in 2011. Has. The challenges of the insurance sector We can only welcome the fact that French insurance organizations have been able to withstand the financial crisis well. They achieved generally satisfactory results, despite natural disasters and the greater number of disasters affecting the non-life business; life insurance inflows increased significantly, taking advantage in particular of the low level of interest rates, which makes short-term products less attractive to savers. However, the fact that long-term interest rates have also remained at a persistently low level is not without risk for the financial equilibrium of organizations in the medium to long term. Conversely, the recent rise in long-term rates shows the speed and magnitude of possible movements. Asset-liability management and investment choices must therefore continue to be monitored very closely by each organization and we will be attentive to this. Similarly, commercial policy must remain responsible and fair, and I therefore invite you to exercise a great deal of caution and vigilance in the choice of rates served to customers, which your establishments are proceeding with in the current period. In the field of non-life insurance, the adequacy of pricing with claims must be carefully managed; it must allow all commitments made to policyholders to be rigorously covered. But today our priority challenge is to adapt to the new Solvency II rules. This is a priority for the CPA, it must be a priority for insurers. French insurance bodies responded massively - and I thank them for this - to the latest impact study, known as "QIS5", the collection of which was completed in November 2010. An intensive phase of exploitation and in-depth analysis of these data is now underway, the results of which the CPA plans to present at the Place at a conference to be held in April 2011. This study is an opportunity to evaluate the operational reliability of the processes implemented in your companies for "Solvency II". In particular, I hope that the control of "Solvency II" will go beyond the circle of specialists within insurance bodies, because all operational functions are concerned, including systems 3 SENSITIVITY WATER NIVSENSITIVITY of information which will have to be fully operational when the reform enters into force on 1 January 2013. 2011 will be a crucial year for Solvency II with the monitoring of pre-application processes for organisations wishing to use internal templates, the publication of so-called level 2 implementing measures during the year and the transmission of the measures that will complete them (so-called level 3) to the European Commission before the end of the year. B. I now come to the challenges of 2011 for the banking sector. The year 2010 was marked by a marked improvement in the situation of the French banking system. The results generated by French banks for the first 9 months showed a sharp increase compared to the same period of the previous year, under the combined effect of revenue growth, lower operating expenses, but above all lower costs of risk. In addition, the major French banking groups have generally improved their solvency. This evolution is the result of the gradual reorientation of activities towards less risky sectors whose profitability is more sustainable. However, this improvement in the situation of the French banking system should not lead to a lower level of vigilance. In particular, the cost of risk remains at a high level, particularly for commercial and residential real estate in several geographical areas. Another challenge is adapting to regulatory and prudential developments. The strengthening of capital requirements, quality and quantity, was justified. It was necessary to strengthen the robustness of our financial systems and to shelter public finances: it will now be impossible, in the future, to solicit the taxpayer to face possible difficulties as was the case in some countries during the crisis. We have ensured that this development preserves the financing capacity of the economy, which in Europe is 80% based on banks. We have also been very careful that this does not call into question our proven universal banking model. Finally, we will be particularly vigilant in the parallel and equitable application of the provisions agreed in Basel III. Europe must ensure, in defining its own timetable, that its partners implement these agreements in parallel and unambiguously. We will also ensure that the "level playing field" is respected in a context where major international institutions still benefit from significant public support. In my view, States should impose the fastest possible repayment of such assistance (which means privatization, withdrawal of guarantees and further restructuring), because in the current period of recovery of the global economy and financial activity, the risk of a resurgence of risky market activities and questionable remuneration practices exists, and would be all the more shocking and dangerous if it were supported by the assistance provided by the taxpayer. That being the case, I ask you to work without delay to improve the level and quality of your own funds as quickly as possible, so as to anticipate the deadlines set out in Basel III. There is also a debate, as you know, about systemic institutions. It affects both banks and insurance companies. We will resist the temptation of simplism and arbitrariness. On this complex subject, I believe that it is necessary to preserve the supervisor's ability to judge, to avoid any blind and automatic device and to rely mainly on "pillar 2" which is a central element of our system. As you know, we will work towards the convergence of our bank resolution regimes and I invite you to participate actively in the reflection that is underway on the "bail in" and the "capital quota". These are complex subjects, the outcome of which is neither certain nor obvious, and for which the contribution of the profession is absolutely essential. 4 SENSITIVITY WATER NIVSENSITIVITY But the most difficult question concerns the liquidity ratios currently under discussion. This is a subject that directly affects the business models and financial structures of different countries. The introduction of these ratios raises important questions about the organisation of financial intermediation or the transformation of maturity. Admittedly, the degree of transformation in the system was excessive, especially since some countries did not have liquidity rules, unlike France. But the technical parameters of the proposed ratios were decided in some haste and would merit further consideration. Interactions with monetary policy implementation are potentially significant and need to be carefully analyzed. Finally, it is not desirable that prudential regulation should lead to bank financing being directed primarily towards covering the borrowing needs of the public sector, even though we saw in 2010 that certain segments of the sovereign debt market could experience brutal liquidity crises. For all these reasons, I hope that a reflection will be re-engaged on the structure of these ratios. A period of observation is open and the current patterns should not be considered fixed. For my part, I believe that significant changes are necessary and that they must be considered without delay, in order to remove as soon as possible an uncertainty that is detrimental to good management and creates instability. * Preparation of the transition to "Solvency II", gradual implementation of "Basel III", measures to strengthen financial stability will therefore be the main challenges of 2011. They impose a high level of demand on us, but I know that the French banking and insurance system is well equipped to deal with it. The CPA, for its part, will be fully mobilized to ensure that these major issues are carried out. In this perspective, on my own behalf and on behalf of the College of the Prudential Control Authority, I once again present to each of you, to your teams and to the people who are dear to you, my warmest wishes for 2011! 5

Title: Does the management of financial and banking crises call for exceptional procedures
text: Conference by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France c9cole Nationale de la Magistrature 17 January 2011 "Does the management of financial and banking crises require exceptional procedures?" I am particularly pleased to speak today before future judges. The work of jurists and economists has many fields of shared reflection and many economists began their studies by learning law - I am thinking for example of Marx or Hayek to take a very wide range -; Crisis management is one of those issues where the contribution of lawyers is fundamental because it often requires recourse to mechanisms derogating from ordinary law that must therefore be carefully framed and applied in a homogeneous way in space and time. However, the financial crisis we are experiencing has profoundly renewed this problem by requiring us to find new solutions and implement them in a homogeneous way within a perimeter that goes beyond our traditional national or European horizon. It is therefore this project, which is well under way but remains far from complete, that I would like to discuss with you today. In order to better understand the extent to which the management of financial and banking crises calls for exceptional procedures, I propose to mention first of all the specific role of banks and the financial system in our economies (I). Indeed, only the analysis of the singularity of the actors and structures of the contemporary financial system will allow us, in a second step, to understand why the very wide panoply of tools and modes of intervention of public authorities must continue to be enriched in order to respond effectively to the growing diversity of financial crises (II). I) The management of financial and banking crises calls for exceptional procedures because, on the one hand, the current financial system has irreducible specificities and, on the other hand, the crises it has recently gone through are incomparable. The current financial system has peculiarities that have continued to strengthen. The heart of this financial system is, of course, always money, a currency that has been able to supplant barter only to the extent that it has managed to satisfactorily fulfil its three functions of unit of account, store of value and instrument of exchange. Thus, the specificity of the financial sphere is therefore first of all linked to the trust that is attributed to money, and this, in all the forms it can take: - metallic money, - fiat money then, Page 1 of 8 - scriptural money finally in our cards, or even electronic in the wallets of the same name. All in all, money, which today retains its three functions and three forms in the current financial system, is a public good that public or private actors cannot consider as a banal good. In particular, the intermediation practised by the approximately 700 European credit institutions and branches authorised in France, the selection of the investment projects they finance and the transformation of the maturities they allow, by having jobs of maturity longer than that of their resources, are of even greater importance on our continent than in the United States, where the financing directly obtained by the markets is more significant than that granted. through bank counters. That this has very precise legal consequences, you can see it from the mere fact that the normal definition of cessation of payments, - provided for by Article L631-1 of the French Commercial Code, namely that a debtor is "unable to meet the liabilities due with his available assets" - is simply inapplicable to banks. In the strict sense of this article, all banks in France, like those around the world, could be placed in judicial reorganization, because of the transformation they operate and that they must operate to fulfill their specific economic function of feeding loans with deposits. They therefore hold only by the confidence that their outstanding liabilities are not required. This is why the role of central banks and banking and market regulators is crucial in order to perpetuate this confidence in money, which remains the main driver of economic exchanges and one of the vectors of societal enrichment. Today, moreover, the crises of the banking and financial system are of considerable complexity. Considerable complexity, in fact, for three main reasons: the masses, the actors and the innovations. ? The masses first: every day, on the foreign exchange market, 1/6th of the wealth that the world takes a year to produce is traded. These 4,000 billion dollars of daily transactions on the foreign exchange market today, this represents a multiplication by more than 20 in the space of 30 years, while the global economic wealth, measured by the gross domestic product, has been multiplied by 6 over the same period, a rate of growth 3 times less. The second example is that of OTC derivatives, i.e. concluded outside an organised market that allows appropriate control: their stock has increased 6-fold in just 10 years, so that this stock of OTC derivatives is now 9 times higher than global wealth. ? The actors then. It is impossible for the regulator today to be the "doctor of the Law" examining word for word the letter of the contracts. The profusion of ad hoc structures (Special Investment Vehicle or Special Purpose Entity) and unregulated entities called shadow banking sector (shadow banking sector), this emergence of entities created for many in the silence or insufficiency of texts in order to optimize a regulatory arbitrage that facilitates the internationalization of financial activities, all this can weaken supervisors, or even discourage their best will or escape them for reasons of too limited regulatory competence. ? To these two factors are added, finally, the effects of innovation: - innovation, first, with the rise of alternative platforms or networks, a dematerialization of flows that allows the massification and quasi-immediacy of exchanges, sometimes at the expense of their traceability; - but also innovation through the constantly renewed creation of new financial products and new and often highly profitable management methods for certain institutions, such as the Page 2 of 8 High-frequency trading, capable of placing tens of thousands of orders to sell or buy securities per second. In these eminently changing conditions, where mass effects, new or poorly regulated actors and continuous innovations are undermining the stability of the financial landscape, crises, whether financial or banking, have profoundly changed in nature and undoubtedly also gained in complexity and force for value destruction. Due to the interdependence of the actors and the interconnection of the circuits, if there can be an economic crisis without a banking crisis, there is always an economic crisis of great magnitude after a banking crisis. Of course, there is no general rule, but last year's work on banking regulatory reform by the Basel Committee showed that countries experienced on average one major banking crisis every 25 years and that the resulting loss of growth ranged from 20 to more than 100 per cent of annual GDP with a median of 60 per cent. That is why banking crises must be prevented at all costs and, when they occur, contained them as quickly as possible in order to prevent the entire financial system from collapsing and the loss of growth from being considerable. The relevance of the response to a multitude of different situations such as the speed in the use of available instruments are essential for effective crisis management. II) Therefore, if we understand the necessity and legitimacy, what are the exceptional procedures that can allow regulators to deal with such banking and financial crises? Let me first clarify the reasons why the ordinary legal tools for dealing with the difficulties of undertakings, namely collective proceedings, provided for in France by Book VI of the Commercial Code are not appropriate for these cases. These procedures are based on the assumption that the difficulties in question can be dealt with by the suspension by the judicial judge of the exigibility of the debts of a legal person in order to give it time to find a plan for the continuation of the activity (whether it is a safeguard or recovery plan) or, if this proves impossible, that the collective treatment of claims be ensured according to very precise legal rules governing the relative priority of creditors. But banking crises are crises of confidence, and trust can disappear instantly, in time and space. In time, the solution to a crisis cannot wait for the processing times of a request for legal action and even less the time necessary for the establishment of a plan "adopted by judgment at the end of a period of observation, with the necessary constitution of two committees of creditors" (Article L620-2 of the Commercial Code on safeguard plans). In space, the crisis spreads immediately, wherever a bank has creditors and counterparties, for example more than a hundred countries for Lehman Brothers, where more than fifty different legal entities were located. It is not really relevant to the effective management of the international effects of this type of failure to bring an application for exequatur before the other 99 courts with territorial jurisdiction in order to extend the effects of the main proceedings, the conformity of which, moreover, with public policy, will have to be examined. So what are the appropriate tools to manage this type of crisis? I will distinguish, first of all, those that are mobilized today or have been mobilized very recently, from those, then, that are still being developed or finalized. Page 3 of 8 With regard to the procedures that can already be used to deal with crisis situations, let us mention them, if you wish, in two stages, on the one hand the role of central banks and on the other hand the action of States. The division of roles is in principle simple: central banks deal with liquidity crises, states deal with solvency crises. The reality is more complex because the border between the two is not indisputable, in fact the banking crises all more or less mix the two aspects. ? Why, in the first place, central banks? Because it is often they, when the law entrusts them with a supervisory power or thanks to their function as provider of central money - that which the banks exchange with each other - who are in contact with the institutions and who are the first to be informed of the difficulties of the institutions. Central banks can mobilize several types of tools: - First, in their currency, central banks have no material limit in the amount of liquidity they make available to institutions that need it; except that the excessive provision of liquidity may reflect the support of an insolvent institution on a micro level and, on a macroeconomic level, may constitute an inflationary factor. Central banks therefore provide liquidity either by buying good quality assets or by lending to banks with good quality assets as collateral. In a normal situation, this provision of liquidity is limited to the net need of the banking system and is responsible for distributing the amount via the interbank market. In a crisis situation, the central bank is led to: o provide more liquidity overall than the simple net need because the interbank market does not function well and the allocation is not made; this is what we are currently doing through so-called fixed rate full allotment operations: any institution with good quality guarantees has unlimited refinancing with the Eurosystem at the rate of 1%; o to provide liquidity on an exceptional and in principle temporary basis to institutions in crisis against guarantees of lower quality, not eligible for normal refinancing operations. This Emergency Liquidity Provision (ELA) allows the institution to overcome its liquidity problems to enable it to restructure its business and regain market confidence; its rate is naturally penalizing, currently 2.25%. This is what the Central Bank of Ireland currently grants to some Irish banks. o When it comes to a liquidity problem in foreign currencies, the central bank is less well equipped to support institutions than in its national currency because, unlike the latter, it cannot create them itself. To solve this type of problem, a framework for enhanced cooperation between central banks has been developed. It most often works in the form of swap agreements - currency exchanges - between central banks, which then makes it possible to lend to the banks of its jurisdiction the currencies they need. It is clear that the agreements concluded by the US Federal Reserve System with central banks located on many continents, including the Eurosystem, play a decisive role in averting a global dollar liquidity crisis. Page 4 of 8 ? But very generally liquidity support is insufficient because, beyond a simple liquidity crisis, it is the solvency of the institution that is at stake and the action of the State is then essential to stop the panic. It can be declined from two angles: - Historically, public support is probably the oldest. It allows, as you know, an institution, in the event of systemic risk, not to be left in the grip of too great difficulties, in order to prevent the social cost of its eventual bankruptcy from being excessive for an economy. This public support can take place in two main ways: o First, recapitalize to strengthen equity. This was decided with the creation in France of the Socie9te9 de prise de participations de l'c9tat in 2008 and whose capital injections made it possible to improve the solvency ratio of the large banks concerned. This sometimes involves nationalisation, as governments have done, in the United Kingdom for Northern Rock Bank or in Belgium for Fortis Bank. o The second lever that can be used by States to consolidate banks' liabilities is to guarantee their debts: the France created the Socie9te9 de financement de l'e9conomie frane7aise for this purpose in 2008, issuing state-guaranteed bonds to finance medium- and long-term guaranteed loans to banks, but most other European countries and the United States have also embarked on it. Proof of the willingness of the public authorities to adapt the measures to the particularities of each institution, we even observed in 2008, for the benefit of the funding raised by Dexia, a guarantee shared by 3 States: France, Belgium and Luxembourg. The decision of the European Council taken last December, by which the European Financial Stability Mechanism will provide financial assistance to Ireland with the guarantee of the States of the Union, is based on the same desire to reduce the financing costs of an institution or a State in difficulty: in this case, it is a question of relieving Irish public finances and recapitalising some of its banks. - Second, more structural, angle of treatment for a State of financial crises, the cleaning of balance sheets. This long-term response logically comes after short-term aid, which is that of refinancing. Three options, in this context, are available to a State: o Provide a guarantee for a portfolio of assets: this loss sharing, which allows weakened financial institutions to reduce their exposure, was initiated during the last crisis by the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Belgium (and even the France, jointly with Belgium, for Dexia). o The second possible option is to confine the doubtful assets by outsourcing them to bad bank structures, as has been done under various modalities in Germany, Spain, Ireland and Switzerland to facilitate an orderly restructuring of certain banks. o Third possibility to deal with illiquid or toxic assets: their redemption. This solution was launched by the US Treasury in 2009 and is based on an action combining public and private intervention that allows private investors to benefit from the US state guarantee to finance the acquisition of bad loans from banks. These tools are therefore based on exceptional public intervention modalities, which provide rapid and comprehensive support to financial intermediaries, due to the importance for the public interest of crisis prevention. Page 5 of 8 But this type of intervention is potentially costly for public finances; Although in France this was not the case during the recent crisis, countries such as Ireland are experiencing a serious budgetary crisis as a result of public action to support a banking sector too deeply undermined by bad loans; it is also by construction derogatory to the normal competitive functioning of an economy; it must therefore remain as exceptional as possible. Instruments are therefore needed both to improve the prevention of these crises and their treatment, in particular to reduce their cost to public finances and the economy as a whole. That is why, after a quick examination of these tools mobilized by central banks and States to deal urgently with the most diverse financial crises, we will now discuss the measures currently under discussion or finalization. The crisis management measures that public authorities should be able to quickly adopt are both microprudential and macroprudential. ? In the area of individual supervision of financial intermediaries, which is called in our jargon microprudential, I will include two reforms undertaken, that of prudential regulation and that of remuneration methods. - First of all, the reform of prudential regulation: as validated by the Heads of State at the G20 summit in Seoul in November 2010 under the name of "Basel 3", it was quickly conducted, under the impetus of the Financial Stability Board and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. New capital and liquidity requirements will be introduced in the coming years to strengthen the resilience of the banking sector to possible future shocks. - I also welcome the very recent European and French rules (the French transposition decree dates from December) that govern bonuses: linking the remuneration of financial actors no longer only to short-term gains but to a fairer assessment of the risks they take is, without a doubt, a powerful prevention tool. ? Beyond the strict field of microprudential control, many regulatory projects should contribute to reducing the need for public action and strengthening its effectiveness. Let us briefly mention four areas where discussions already well underway could quickly lead to initiatives: - Recovery and resolution plans, first of all: first of all, institutions of a systemic nature must identify their vulnerabilities and prevent difficulties that may complicate rapid action in the event of a crisis. It also implies an upstream dialogue both between these institutions and all the authorities or institutions such as central banks that have a decisive role to play in the event of a crisis, but also between these authorities, so that problems of international coordination are not discovered just when action becomes necessary to avoid cross-border contagion of crises occurring in a country. Very concretely, the issues and points under discussion are particularly complex, and I will mention two of them by way of illustration: how can we immediately replace - without necessarily the legal guarantees of an adversarial procedure - the managers approved as responsible but who can no longer face the destiny of their establishment? Should we also be able to temporarily suspend shareholders' rights and interrupt the right one? Page 6 of 8 conduct of contracts to transfer assets and liabilities to a ring-fencing structure? But then what substantive and procedural guarantees should be provided for that the legitimate rights of stakeholders are ultimately respected? What exact role in this system for the judge guaranteeing freedoms and the right of property? How can we ensure the international recognition of measures so strongly marked by public order? - The second orientation of the initiatives under way is the development of mechanisms to strengthen what the Financial Stability Board calls the "loss-absorbing capacity" of systemic financial institutions. The aim is to limit as much as possible the use of public money to support institutions in difficulty. In general, the idea is to establish mechanisms that ensure that investors contribute to these losses in proportion to their investment and according to the nature of their claim on these institutions. In practice, intensive and complex work is underway to identify whether and how it is possible to convert debt securities into core equity, thereby absorbing going concern losses. The questions are numerous and mix major issues of law and financial stability. For example, should the conversion be done on a contractual basis or by decision of the public authorities? Should it be automatic and meet predefined criteria or should it allow discretionary action by the authorities to maximize the effectiveness of their intervention in circumstances that are difficult to predict? In this context, how can the fundamental legal principle of equal treatment of creditors of the same rank be ensured? How much of the liabilities of these institutions should be convertible? Should these mechanisms be restricted ex ante to subordinated debt alone or, on the contrary, should we not tie our hands? All these legal issues call for in-depth reflections that also take into account the economic effects of the options that would be chosen. Thus, for example, should we assess the effect of the various options on market dynamics in the event of stress or also on the cost of financing institutions in normal times? - The third orientation of the current projects is the possible creation of resolution funds and their articulation with deposit guarantee funds. The aim is to avoid that the cost of winding up a financial institution is borne by public finances alone. A dozen European countries, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, have set up a levy on the banking system as of this year, but its modalities (rate, base, scope of application) vary according to the States, as well as its purpose: to prevent defaults, improve the situation of public finances and / or strengthen the deposit guarantee system. In the run-up to a regulatory initiative by the European Commission expected in June, the risk for a banking group to be taxed twice must also be addressed. In addition, the establishment of such resolution funds must be appropriately coordinated with deposit guarantee funds. For my part, I hope that, as in France, they will be able to develop the preventive role that also makes it possible to minimize the cost of crises, since every judge knows that the assets of a bankrupt company do not sell at the same price as those of a company whose business continuity has been preserved. - Fourth and last point, the new European surveillance architecture born in 2011. As you know, since 1 January, in addition to the European Systemic Risk Board, three European supervisory authorities have been set up, covering banks, insurance and securities respectively. In cooperation with national authorities, they shall ensure that strict and consistent application of rules that are likely to contribute to the stability of the overall financial system are harmonised, and these rules will abound in the coming months, with proposals from the European Commission expected on the themes of Page 7 of 8 in particular: supervision of derivatives markets and market infrastructures, prevention of market abuse and short selling, reform of the governance of financial institutions and the supervision of credit rating agencies. In the area of crisis procedures, it is particularly important that a uniform framework applicable throughout the European Economic Area be defined at European level without legal uncertainties linked to the recognition of national measures. We will also be extremely vigilant to ensure that financial regulation continues to progress in two directions that we believe are essential: o First, to continue to strengthen the body of rules, so that no entity or market segment remains outside the regulatory framework; o secondly, to ensure that such regulation is appropriate, i.e. proportionate to the objectives to be achieved, and that it does not in any way result in distortions of competition or incentives to seek a form of regulatory arbitrage. * Let me conclude by stressing the twofold challenge we are currently facing. The world has gone through the worst peacetime crisis in 80 years in recent years. Therefore, the impressive will of the Heads of State and Government to reform the banking and financial system in depth should not be disappointed, to say nothing, of course, with the expectations of public opinion hit by crises. The G20 agenda, the European Commission's roadmap and the ambitions of the American Dodd-Frank law therefore represent progress that must be achieved before the reform momentum runs out of steam, and all the French authorities, particularly in the context of the G20 presidency, are putting their full determination into it. The second challenge is that financial crises, yes, call for exceptional procedures, derogating from the ordinary law of dealing with the difficulties of companies. But these exceptions are only intended to safeguard in particularly difficult circumstances two essential legal objectives, the preservation of business security and the pre-eminence of the general interest, which are also the conditions for financial stability. And this is not at the level of a single national legal area but by ensuring full international coordination. Moving forward together, in a convergent and harmonized manner among nations, is essential to ensure that international financial stability is best preserved in the interests of all. You are probably more familiar than I am with the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789, in particular its articles 5 ("The Law has the right to defend only actions harmful to the Society") and 15 ("The Society has the right to hold any public official accountable for its administration"). Believe me, in this delicate action of regulating a financial sector whose very engine of change is often imbalance, we too are working for proportionality, accountability and transparency. Thank you for your attention. Page 8 of 8
