Title: Debt and Foreign Exchange Professionals' Day
text: Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Bank of France Day of Debt and Foreign Exchange Professionals January 19, 2011 Ladies and gentlemen I am very happy to open this day of debt and foreign exchange professionals. This is a new illustration of the rich and constructive dialogue that we have been able to deepen together in recent years. This dialogue has been essential in helping us to take many delicate steps. It has now become indispensable to our reflection on monetary policy as well as on regulatory developments. The theme of your day, "The new challenges of the post-crisis period", is very timely and I would like to address it by developing three points that seem to me to be decisive for our near future: - First, the need for monetary policy to draw lasting lessons from the crisis - Secondly, the challenge of adapted banking regulation and better supervision of certain markets - Finally, the increased demand for in-depth international cooperation, particularly in this year of French presidency of the G20 I. The need for monetary policy to draw lasting lessons from the crisis Has. Monetary policy must be reactive and its operational framework flexible. First of all, I believe that the Eurosystem can be legitimately proud of its "framework" which has demonstrated its qualities during the crisis: by guaranteeing us a great capacity to adapt, it has given us the means to act quickly and effectively, for example by putting in place a new auction policy and extending the maturities of refinancing to one year. This focus on longer-term financing was also reflected in the implementation of the 8060 billion covered bonds programme between July 2009 and June 2010. It is undeniable that this programme has given a strong boost to the covered bond market and facilitated the return of investors. The Eurosystem has also shown pragmatism in the eligibility of collateral for monetary policy operations. In this area, it is important to emphasise that we take care to take into account the reality of the risks and not their appearance, using a range of assessment criteria as broad and precise as respect for equal treatment allows. The crisis has therefore demonstrated the need for a reactive monetary policy. 1 It has also reinforced the requirement for monetary policy to be attentive to the incentives it sends to the financial system, and I would like to say a few words about this, which I believe is crucial. In general, the implementation of monetary policy can and I would even say must encourage or encourage virtuous behaviour. For example, by denying collateral in the form of ABS to those made up of multiple opaque layers, the Eurosystem is promoting sound securitisation that is useful in the long term for economic development. We would like the market to set up a portal gathering key data on each of the loans underlying ABS, accessible directly to all market participants and allowing everyone to conduct a detailed analysis of the risks attached to these products. Our firm will here is to restore confidence in this important market for the financing of SMEs and households. B. Cooperation between central banks is essential Another lesson to be learned from the monetary policy crisis is the importance of cooperation between central banks. The various foreign exchange swap agreements are an example of this: after those concluded with the Fed and the Swiss National Bank in 2008, the ECB and the Bank of England recently announced the establishment of an agreement to mobilise up to a310 billion against euros to make available to the Central Bank of Ireland the books it would need. The interweaving of markets and the increasing use of third-currency financing by credit institutions make this cooperation between central banks an essential dimension of our monetary policy framework. II. The challenge of appropriate banking regulation and better supervision of certain markets I now come to my second point: the challenge of appropriate banking regulation and better supervision of certain markets. The Bank of France is very committed at the international level to develop regulations and tools to best prevent new crises. The reforms in which we are currently participating are organized around two main axes. On the one hand, the strengthening of the robustness of the banking system by the new Basel 3 standards and on the other hand the reduction of systemic risk on market activities through the establishment of adequate infrastructures. Has. Adapted banking regulations With regard to banking regulation, the measures recently adopted by the Basel Committee cover many aspects, including the implementation of a harmonised and more restrictive definition of regulatory capital, the raising of the minimum level of the solvency ratio, and the introduction of liquidity ratios. I want to develop a little this last aspect that directly interests the professionals that you are. The crisis has shown us how crucial and difficult it is to control liquidity in troubled times. Transformation, however, is the basis of the banker's profession; it must be preserved but framed by serious and homogeneous regulations. The Basel Committee, in a new exercise at the international level, quickly arrived at a system with two new ratios, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) over a one-month horizon and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) over a one-year horizon. The introduction of these ratios raises important questions. Admittedly, the degree of transformation in the system was excessive, especially since some countries did not have liquidity rules, unlike France. But the technical parameters of the 2 The proposed ratios were decided in some haste and would merit further consideration. With regard to the one-month ratio, I am particularly aware of the attention that must be paid to the definition of assets considered sufficiently liquid. We have heard comments from practitioners and analysts on the consequences of an overly narrow definition of the scope of eligible assets and have broadened the scope by introducing a "level 2" liquid asset class including covered bonds. We have also ensured that refinancing operations with central banks are properly taken into account since they are an effective source of liquidity, and you will have observed that those less than a month old are very widely considered to be stable. This progress is important, but there is still work to be done. In the light of the lessons of the sovereign debt crisis, it is necessary to see in particular whether these adjustments are sufficient and to ensure that we do not create too strong a bias in favour of covering the borrowing needs of the public sector. Similarly, I am aware of the questions about the one-year ratio, the NSFR, the introduction of which meets the objective of encouraging longer-term financing of banks by limiting the risk of excessive transformation. Here again, we know that the implications of this new standard must be analysed with the utmost attention, taking into account, in particular, the ability of the economy to finance and the capacity of the bond market to absorb a substantial amount of issues in the medium and long term. As you have understood, I hope that a reflection will be undertaken again on the structure of these ratios and we are particularly well placed, in France, to contribute to this reflection, since we benefit from more than twenty years of experience in measuring and prudential supervision of banks' liquidity, which has proven its effectiveness. A period of observation is open and the current patterns should not be considered fixed. For my part, I believe that significant changes are necessary and that they must be considered without delay, in order to remove as soon as possible an uncertainty that is detrimental to good management and creates instability. B. Reducing systemic risk by adapting market structures I want to share with you another lesson of the crisis: the quality of supervision is as important as that of regulation and the joint interest of public and private financial actors is that it be high. The need for a deeper knowledge of the different markets and the interactions that bind them is now undeniable. In particular, risk management related to otc derivatives needs to be improved and it was the conviction that led the G20 in Pittsburgh to adopt a common approach to better control these risks. Two orientations have been adopted: i) the central clearing by central counterparties (CCPs) of all products deemed sufficiently standardized and ii) the recording of these transactions by dedicated infrastructures (trade repositories). These requirements have several objectives: to increase the efficiency of these markets, to prevent fraud and abuse and, above all, to prevent the systemic risk generated by derivatives. The will of the regulatory bodies to implement the G20 guidelines in practice is strong. The United States passed the Dodd-Frank Act in July and enforcement measures are under negotiation. At European level, discussions are continuing on the draft EMIR regulation, which should be adopted by the summer. 3 Regarding the recording of information, the reform is already well advanced in the CDS market, where reporting to the trade repositories of the main players is already effective. These first steps are encouraging and must be continued so that all asset classes covered by TBTs achieve the level of transparency required by the G20. As for clearing houses, the Bank of France will pay particular attention to their risk management because, centralizing all positions, they can potentially be considered "super" systemic players. Strengthening their robustness requires the proper calibration of their obligations, such as the definition of guarantee funds, the segregation of these funds or the establishment of robust margin call mechanisms without unnecessary procyclicality. I also believe that the soundness of the system will be better ensured if these institutions have the status of credit institution as is the case in France; this ensures supervision consistent with that of the members of the chamber and allows them to have access to central bank facilities. III. Deepening international cooperation in this year of France's presidency of the G20 I would like to conclude with one last essential lesson of the crisis: while urgency has increased the need for in-depth international cooperation, it must now be sustained. The exact role played by the major global imbalances in triggering the crisis is still debated. Nevertheless, there is one certainty highlighted by the G20 Heads of State and Government: "inconsistent and poorly coordinated macroeconomic policies, inadequate structural reforms [...] have led to unsustainable overall macroeconomic outcomes." In Seoul, the Heads of State and Government therefore adopted an "action plan" including comprehensive and cooperative measures adapted to each country. Exchange rate flexibility is one of the instruments proposed, but it is indeed all cyclical and structural policies that must be able to be mobilized in a concerted and coherent manner to increase the growth potential of the world economy. Developments in the global economy also have important implications for the international monetary architecture. This is why the reform of the international monetary system is a priority at the centre of the French presidency of the G20 for 2011. The France wishes to open the debate. It is not a question of launching a great upheaval, but rather of taking the measure and drawing the consequences of the fundamental developments. Let me say it very clearly: the current monetary system has allowed us to get through the crisis, but it must be evolved so that it is better adapted to today's world. For example, it requires adjustments to reduce excessive volatility of capital flows and exchange rate misalignments; we also need to address the accumulation and excessive concentration of foreign exchange reserves in order to move towards a rebalancing of the world economy, which is necessary for lasting global stability. The France wants the G20 to establish an in-depth common diagnosis of the causes and consequences of the current dysfunctions of the international monetary system. On this basis, different reform options will be considered to provide the system with stronger rules. The cooperation of all our G20 partners, with the support of the International Monetary Fund, will be particularly important on this sensitive issue. Thank you for your attention. 4

Title: Q&A with journalists before G20
text: The G-20 is based on goodwill Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France, explains the key issues of the G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Paris Interview Le Monde, 18 february 2011 The Finance Ministers and central bank Governors of the worlds 20 leading economic powers are assembling on Friday 18 and Saturday 19 February for the first meeting under the French presidency. Their aim: to agree on a list of indicators to measure the main microeconomic imbalances. Five have already been identified in the following areas: current accounts, real exchange rates, foreign exchange reserves, public deficits and private savings. However, these indicators should not be target-based. Major exporting countries, such as China, Germany and Japan, continue to have strong reservations. Mr Noyer, do you not think that some countries might refuse to agree on a list of indicators that could stigmatise them by highlighting their imbalances? The idea is to come up with a sufficiently extensive list so as to not single out a small number of countries but to identify the main imbalances. Once the risk factors have been pinpointed, we can explore avenues for improvement and establish corrective economic policies to achieve stronger and above all more sustainable growth. Going forward, is it not essential that such indicators be accompanied by coercive measures? The G20 is not an institution endowed with coercive or regulatory powers. It is a forum based on consultation and goodwill. We will succeed if each and every participant is convinced that this exercise is in everybodys interest. For instance, countries running large surpluses, that is to say those whose savings substantially exceed investment, are fully aware that their major reliance on other countries domestic demand is a source of weakness. There are countries such as the United States that do not seem particularly willing to correct their imbalances No countries have voiced their disagreement with this exercise. Indeed, an agreement was reached at the G-20 Seoul Summit held on 11 and 12 November 2010, where the Americans themselves had raised the question of current account imbalances. But the devil is always in the details. Another of the G20s very ambitious priorities is the reform of the international monetary system. Can we expect concrete results during the French presidency? Such results can be achieved even though the aim of the French President, Nicolas Sarkozy, is not to resolve all matters in one year. We have already managed to table the question and now we will examine its different aspects. A series of problems and risks are posed by sudden capital inflows and outflows, the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves in some countries and exchange rate volatility. We do not claim to have all the answers. Problems relating to capital flow volatility are very difficult to resolve. The question is whether it is possible to design a toolbox with mechanisms capable of checking sudden capital flows, without bringing in foreign exchange controls that would be detrimental to the smooth functioning of the global economy. Do you think that the Chinese Yuan should be encouraged to be included in the special drawing right (SDR), the IMF's unit of account The SDR is based on a basket of major international currencies. If we had to redesign the SDR today, we would naturally include the yuan due to China's weight in the world economy. But all the currencies that comprise the SDR are freely convertible, which is not the case for the yuan. In fact, what we need to consider is a theoretical timetable for its inclusion. Are you in favour of a tax on financial transactions? I can understand the aim of it, but to make it feasible, such a tax would have to be applied in all countries, including in non-cooperative jurisdictions. If this were not the case, it would lead to a massive shift of financial transactions to tax havens, which would not be a satisfactory result. Are the solutions being put forward to prevent further debt crisis in the euro area adequate? Lessons have been learned. Everyone understands the importance of having rules and applying them. A competitiveness pact seems an excellent idea and was no doubt lacking at the outset. Convergence in the relative competitiveness of each Member State is a prerequisite to ensuring the smooth functioning of the monetary union. In a single currency zone, radical differences in unit production costs are unacceptable. A State that loses competitiveness because its production costs (wages, margins, etc.) increase faster than its productivity puts itself in a weak position. Since it cannot devalue, it must engage in painful wage and cost cutting. Are you concerned about inflation? The recent rise in inflation can chiefly be ascribed to commodity and energy prices. By the end of the year, prices should stabilise again. However, if wage-setters do not factor in such price stability in their demands, an inflationary spiral could be triggered. We therefore remain extremely vigilant. Are you optimistic about the outlook for French growth? Our business surveys show stronger growth at the end of last year and the start of this year. We can expect growth in 2011 to be closer to the governments forecast of 2% than to the consensus forecast of about 1.6%.

Title: International Risk Forum on Long-Term Risks
text: Le 10 mars 2011 Discours de Christian Noyer pour le Forum international du risque sur les risques de long terme (Paris Europlace)  Les themes dinteret et les initiatives de la Banque de France dans le domaine de la recherche en finance.  Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to take part in this fourth edition of the Financial Risks International Forum and I warmly thank the organizers for their kind invitation. This years forum is dedicated to the issue of long-term risks, and what academic research has to say in this regard is of primary importance to central banks. Since you kindly invited me to describe the research activities of the Banque de France in finance, I will first emphasize the reasons why a central bank should support financial and economic research. In particular I will show that promoting strong interactions between academia and central banks is key for the development and sharing of new ideas. In the second part of my address, I will focus more specifically on what research brings to the understanding of macro-finance modeling and longterm risks. 1. In-house research is essential to central banks policy assessment. The Banque de France has promoted research in economics for quite a long time. To my knowledge, the oldest piece of evidence of such interest dates back to the mid- 19th century. One of my predecessors, Charles Lebegue, who was Governor of the Banque de France between 1857 and 1863, opened the Banks archives to a young French economist of the time: Clement Juglar. He used the data he had access to to define what has been known since then as the Juglar cycle. The Banque de France has always been keen to share information with researchers and dedicate resources to their work. However, healthy intellectual emulation and cooperation within the Eurosystem over the last decade and the financial crisis have led to increasing significantly reliance on the contribution of well-staffed and highly qualified in-house research teams. By way of example, I need only mention the stimulating role of the successive Eurosystem Research networks, from the first one on monetary policy transmission in the early 2000s to still on-going ones on macroprudential policy and systemic risk analysis. 1 a) Why should a central bank produce its own research? - First, our own research may, in some cases, fill the gap between academics interests and policymaking issues. For example, research concerning the money market in the euro area was quite scarce in academia before the crisis. The assumption was widely held that banks, given a money market rate, would always be able to trade liquidity. From 2004 central banks researchers, at the ECB, the Fed and also the Banque de France, began therefore to focus on this research gap and to study the mechanisms governing the liquidity of the money market. They concluded at that time that, in some circumstances, liquidity may become scarce and volatility may increase on the money market due to asymmetric information between banks. They also pointed out that the impact of the design of our operational framework on money market dynamics was not neutral 1. In retrospect, the outcome of these efforts proved quite useful when we had to analyze the causes for the money market freezes of 2007-2008 and to react accordingly in a timely and appropriate manner. - Second, drawing on strong in-house research allows the central bank to track developments in methodologies, so that we constantly have state-of-the-art analytical toolboxes for assessing monetary and financial conditions and risks. For example, the research carried out at the Banque de France over several years in the area of stress tests2 helped us to calibrate the resilience of the French banking system at a high frequency well before the EU-wide exercises were carried out. - Last but not least, drawing on a strong research background is also essential for full credibility in the policy debate on the two leading functions of the Bank: monetary policy and financial stability. In short, central banks in-house research is essential to back up our policy tools, analyses and decisions on the most up-to-date and rigorous scientific basis. b) For these reasons, developing the Banque de Frances own research capacity has been a priority over the past few years The Banque de France, like other central banks in Europe, has continuously stepped up its investment into research. Since 2006, I have personally made policy-oriented research at the Bank one of our strategic priorities. I am confident that the result after 5 years is particularly striking. One benchmark is the number of articles published by our staff in high-level scientific journals - 51 in 2010, of which about a third in top academic journals- which has increased considerably. According to the quotation-based REPEC index, Banque de France now ranks in the top 20 central banks and international institutions, and in the top 5% of research institutions worldwide. This progress is also confirmed by the increasing participation of our economists in first-class international conferences and workshops like this one. Our strategy has not just been to increase the amount of resources allocated to internal research but also to consolidate our links with the academic world, research institutions, and research departments of other central banks and international institutions. For instance, over the last two years, the Bank has organized 16 international conferences and workshops featuring some of the most prominent experts in their respective fields. The "Asset Price Bubbles and Monetary Policy conference coorganized in Paris with the Chicago Fed, and the "Economic Linkages, Spillovers and the Financial Crisis" conference co-organized with the Paris School of Economics and the IMF are two recent examples of this commitment to stimulate the academic debate on important central banking topics. 1 See Ewerhart, Cassola, Ejerskov et Valla (2004) , Jardet et Le Fol (2007), Idier et Nardelli (2007). 2 De Bandt and Oung (2004), Coffinet, Lin and Martin (2009). 2 On the management side, we have diversified our pool of researchers by intensifying our recruitment of highly skilled economists, from young PhD candidates to experienced researchers. The Banque de France has notably been participating in the international Job Market for economists for three years now, and is identified by candidates as one attractive place in Europe to apply their technical skills to challenging real world issues, while still keeping in touch with academia and developing their own research agenda. Furthermore, we strongly encourage our staff to co-write papers and share ideas with academics. The Banque de France now benefits enormously from a rich network of highly experienced senior academic consultants, some of whom are in this audience and who give an invaluable impetus to new ambitious research projects. The Banque de France has also launched over the past three years partnerships with prominent universities, such as the Toulouse School of Economics and the Paris School of Economics, and research centers like the Cepremap. Finally, I would like to emphasize the key role of the Fondation Banque de France. Its numerous initiatives, including awarding prizes to promising young economists and providing financial support to visiting scholars, are also essential contributions to synergies with the academic community. 2. What financial research topics should a central bank focus on? Because we have limited time, I would like to consider just two issues from the current research agenda that are closely connected with the theme of this conference: macro-finance modeling and the measurement and consequences of long run risks. a) Macro-finance modeling Central banks are increasingly interested in theoretical and empirical research that explores the interlinkages between financial markets and the macro-economy. While monetary macroeconomists have long tended to neglect the veil of financial institutions and arrangements in their policy analyses, and financial econometricians have tended to neglect the role of macroeconomic variables in their purely financial models of asset prices, the recent crisis has shown that it is of utmost importance to bridge this gap and try to reconcile both analytical approaches. The new generation of macro-finance modelers - well represented in todays program - is thus more than welcome to investigate these issues. Contrary to pure financial models, which certainly do a good job in replicating the fluctuations of financial markets, macro-finance models aim by definition at investigating the important role of macroeconomic factors in the determination of asset prices. Macro-finance models, such as DSGE models with explicit sources of financial frictions3 or endogenous credit risk4, already help central banks in their everyday practice to better understand and anticipate the impact of policy shocks. However, banking and financial market components are still scarcely incorporated into these models, leaving room for further research. Affine term structure models of the yield curve with macroeconomic factors5 represent another approach that aims to explain the impact of economic news on asset prices. One recent application is the use of these models to reveal the actual value of inflation expectations. The last few months have been marked by increasing inflation expectations in the US and the euro area, as gauged by the rise 3 See for instance Beau, Clerc and Mojon (2011) and Antipa, Mengus and Mojon (2011) 4 Goodhart, Tsomocos and Vardoulakis (2010). 5 See e.g. Jardet, Monfort and Pegoraro (2011), Borgy, Laubach, Mesonnier, Renne (2011). 3 in breakeven rates on inflation-linked bonds. Affine term structure models have helped us to disentangle pure inflation expectations  that have been indeed quite stable - from inflation risk premia  that have been much more varying. b) Long run risks Let me now turn to the leading topic of this conference, the assessment and modeling of long run risks, which is one of the pervasive sources of uncertainty behind the fluctuations of both asset prices and macroeconomic variables. I really think that it is high time to focus again on long-term issues after three years of financial and economic turmoil during which most analyses reduced their time horizons to the short run. Climate change and the ageing populations, for instance, remain crucial topics, on which the expertise of the researchers is very welcome. Regarding the financial economics of climate change, we have to better understand how we could compare the short-run economic costs of environmental policies to the very long-term benefits that we expect to reap from them. This calls for an appropriate way of discounting the very long-term future, and I am very happy to observe the current development of this field of research, both inside6 and outside the Banque de France. Moreover, population ageing is one of the fundamental economic transformations that our European societies are faced with. For instance, the debate on a possible diversification in the funding sources of our retirement system is, as it should be, enlightened by the views of the academic community. In that regard, we do not only require good forecasts of the evolution of life expectancy in the future; we should also be able to assess the uncertainty surrounding these forecasts, the so-called longevity risk, by whom this longevity risk should be borne and at what price. Finally, let me suggest here a few avenues for further research that would be of particular interest for central banks in the current juncture. The development of new financial products with very long maturities raises new challenges for us, as central bankers and financial regulators. Research gives us the opportunity to better understand the risks that these new markets may create for financial stability and design adequate regulatory tools. If we think of our objective of maintaining financial stability as oriented towards the medium to long run, partly because booms in asset prices and financial imbalances in general often take a long time to develop, then we also need to identify which macroeconomic factors impinge on long-term financial developments. In spite of outstanding work on these issues since the outbreak of the recent crisis, we still need to improve our understanding of the long-run determinants of financial stability. Now, I am just opening the debate and hoping for your informed answers. Financial crises have at least the merit of blatantly revealing the extent of our current ignorance. In this respect, the bad times we have been through since 2008 have significantly reduced what Ricardo Caballero (2010) recently dubbed the economists Pretense of knowledge syndrome. However, retrospectively, I do not forget that insights gained from research during this period have proved a valuable input for decision-making and policy debates. This strongly suggests that central banks investment into research in finance and financial economics, be it in-house or through partnerships with academia, is a valuable asset. Let me reiterate my pleasure to be here and thank the organizers. I wish you all a fruitful and stimulating conference. 6 Dubecq and Gourieroux (2010) 4 References Antipa, P., Mengus, E. and Mojon, M., 2011, Would Macroprudential Policies have prevented the Great Recession?, mimeo. Title: ACPR Annual Report
text: PRESENTATION OF THE ANNUAL REPORT OF THE SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY FOR 2010 Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France, President of the Autorite9 de contrf4le prudentiel First of all, I would like to thank you for your presence today at this press conference organised on the occasion of the publication of the first Annual Activity Report of the Autorite9 de contrf4le prudentiel - ACP -. The ACP has just celebrated its first year of existence, since it was installed on March 9, 2010. One year later, this first activity report is the symbol of the successful merger of the previous authorities: you will find the results of the actions carried out on both the banking and insurance supervision sides. This very rich balance sheet reflects the diversity of challenges that the ACP has had to face throughout the year in its various areas of competence, whether it is financial stability, customer protection or international negotiations. What should we remember from the past year, from the point of view of prudential supervision? First, in 2010, the macroeconomic context in which banks and insurance companies in the broad sense operate changed significantly. The exceptional support measures for the financial sector taken in 2008 and 2009 in the wake of the "subprime" crisis have borne fruit in most European countries, particularly in France. Although still moderate, activity 1 the economy in France and Europe has recovered compared to 2009, contributing in particular to gradually improving the situation of industrial and commercial enterprises. These positive developments enabled French banking and insurance groups to post satisfactory results and thus consolidate their financial base. In the area of regulation, the round of negotiations, which began in 2009 under the aegis of the G20, led to the publication of a decisive agreement ("Basel 3") on capital enhancement and risk measurement at the end of 2010. In the insurance sector, 2010 was marked by the 5th quantitative impact study, intended in particular to calibrate the technical provisions of the Solvency 2 Directive. The CPA has played a leading role in advancing these issues. Finally, 2010 also marks the finalisation of the renewed institutional framework for European financial supervision, which enabled the establishment, in early 2011, of a European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS) and a new entity in charge of systemic risks (European Systemic Risk Board - ESRB). I would like to come back in more detail to some of these aspects as well as to the challenges that are emerging for 2011. I) The results and solvency of French banks and insurers improved significantly in 2010 (a) For credit institutions: the results of the five main banking groups1 thus show a net profit combined group share of 8022 billion, up 89% compared to the previous year. Several factors explain this good performance but three, in particular, seem important to me to highlight with: 1 BNP PARIBAS, SOCIETE GENERALE, GROUPE CREDIT AGRICOLE, BPCE, GROUPE CREDIT MUTUEL 2 - sustained commercial activity, particularly in retail banking and specialised financing, whose GNP grew by 9%; this increase is itself mainly due to activities in France, while those developed abroad are experiencing less favourable developments according to banks; - a marked fall in the cost of risk, which is down 36% across all business segments, although this development is mainly in corporate and investment banking. This must be seen in particular as the positive effect of a reduction in exposures considered sensitive (the "toxic assets" that the ACP today, the Banking Commission yesterday, has continued to monitor closely since the beginning of the crisis; - to a lesser extent, better operational efficiency, measured by the operating ratio, which has decreased by almost 3%. Thanks in particular to the setting aside of a significant part of their profits and the controlled evolution of risk-weighted risks, banks have seen their solvency ratio reach historically high levels, with the average ratio to core capital rising from 10% in 2009 to 10.6% in 2010. This positive development is part of the banks' necessary preparation for basel 3, to which I will return in a few moments. In this respect, I would like to stress that strict regulation and supervision, including on the issue of remuneration, will promote this preparation. From this point of view, I note, and this is a positive aspect in my opinion, that the profitability of investment in the banking sector has become of the same order as that in the non-financial sectors. (b) In the insurance, mutual and provident institutions sector, where numerous restructurings have taken place (the total number of companies subject to ACP supervision increased from 1 268 to 1 129 between 2009 and 2010). the first trends that are emerging are also positive. The results at the end of 2010 are thus profitable and the turnover is on the rise; on the basis of publications made by 4 French groups, this 3 which is certainly a partial sample from the point of view of the market, the turnover thus increased by nearly 5% and the net result excluding exceptionals by more than 20% However, the increase in non-life of the cost of the claim, under the effect in particular of climatic events, tends to weigh on profitability. Their solvency margins, well above 100%, have experienced contrasting trends depending on the group, but for some we observe a significant increase in the solvency margin expressed on average over 2010 stands at 162% for a sample of 3 major French groups] In total, I believe that it must be remembered from these developments that the major French banking and insurance groups have a good level of profitability and solvency. II) The persistence of potential sources of instability, however, calls for great vigilance on the part of all actors First of all, I think it is useful to recall that the companies subject to ACP control have shown good resilience since the beginning of the crisis. This resistance was confirmed by the European stress tests carried out in 2010 in the insurance and banking sectors, exercises which, as you know, will be renewed this year. Nevertheless, there are many potential sources of instability. Beyond the specific challenges of developments in the sovereign debt market and their effects on the real economy, several points seem to me to need to be highlighted: 1) The renewal of medium- and long-term liabilities that banks will have to or have begun to carry out takes place in a market context likely to lead to an increase in the cost of new resources; 2) If credit risk appears to be broadly under control, an economic recovery that is too weak could weaken the most vulnerable companies, particularly SMEs; 4 3) Increased volatility in financial markets could weigh on the results of large groups and on the liquidity of certain products; 4) With regard more specifically to the insurance sector, the risk, in non-life, of an increase in the cost of claims, in connection with the magnitude of climatic phenomena but also with the increase in the price of the elements taken into account for the compensation of the insured must be noted; in addition, the environment of persistently low long-term interest rates could adversely affect life insurance activity and results. 5) Finally, the real estate sector, particularly residential, calls for attention, since it has experienced a sharp rise in prices, to which, beyond the imbalances between the supply and demand for housing, particularly low credit rates are not unrelated. Faced with these challenges, banking and insurance institutions will have to maintain rigorous risk management. This requires the definition or continuation of an appropriate risk tolerance policy, as well as the maintenance of sufficient investments in information systems allowing a detailed analysis of exposures to various risks, and a demanding and permanent control of adequate risk limits. The ACP will continue to be particularly vigilant about the effectiveness of the measures taken by the establishments subject to its control on these various aspects, both in the context of permanent monitoring and on-site inspections carried out in each of the two sectors. In addition, the establishment of the new European architecture of financial supervision, in which the ACP and the Bank of France are naturally represented, will help to strengthen the effectiveness of actions taken at national level to address these various challenges. III) In this context, it is necessary for all stakeholders to continue their efforts to adapt to the ongoing reforms in the banking sector ("Basel 3") as well as in the insurance sector ("Solvency 2"). 5 As I mentioned earlier, the regulations of the banking and insurance sectors have been or will be profoundly revised. Let me return to their essential characteristics and the challenges they raise. (a) For credit institutions, these are the rules published by the Basel Committee on 16 December 2010, known as Basel 3. These new prudential requirements are a major step forward. They aim to strengthen the level and quality of capital, improve the measurement of risks involved, reduce the risk of cyclicality and establish quantitative and qualitative standards on the measurement of liquidity and transformation risks. They will lead to strengthening the resilience of banks to the vagaries of the financial markets and the economic situation and, therefore, to enable them to ensure their credit activity to households and businesses smoothly and thus to contribute to the financing of growth. The full success of these measures, however, rests on two conditions. The first is that credit institutions are making every effort to prepare for it. From this point of view, the gradual implementation of the scheme, from 2013 for those relating to the definition of capital and the measurement of risks, and from 2015 for liquidity arrangements, must be used to adopt all the necessary measures. I am thinking in particular of the consolidation of the banks' financial base and stock of liquid assets, as well as their short- and medium-term refinancing policy. I would like to point out that this is not contradictory to the idea I have already expressed of taking advantage of the observation period to correct, if necessary, certain aspects of the calibration of liquidity and transformation ratios. The second condition is based on the necessary synchronization, at international level, of the implementation of all these measures. It is important, for reasons of efficiency as well as equality of competition, that all the provisions relating to Basel 3 be implemented simultaneously according to the timetable set by the decision-making bodies in all countries, in 6 Europe as in other regions of the world. This is a point on which the French authorities will be very attentive, particularly in the context of the French Presidency of the G20. (b) in the insurance sector, the preparation of the technical measures necessary for the implementation of the Solvency 2 Directive is continuing. As with banks, this is a decisive development to improve capital adequacy for risk, the measurement of which will be significantly refined, including by offering the possibility of using internal models. As you know, the final calibration of the future prudential framework must continue and the ACP is fully committed to this. It seeks both to maintain a coherent overall vision and to deal with particularities, for example related to the specialization of certain organizations in the best conditions. Beyond that, it makes every effort to strengthen the technical preparation of the various actors. The strong participation of French bodies in the quantitative impact study that has just been completed, in which more than 500 of them took part, seems to me to be very encouraging from this point of view. Efforts in this regard must, of course, continue. c) Beyond these two major regulatory reforms for strengthening financial stability, I would also like to note the continuation of international work on the identification and supervision of systemic entities, in which the ACP and the Bank of France are actively participating. This is an important subject that must not be confined to the issue of systemic banks, as the G20 has also stressed. IV) Other aspects deserve our full attention I think it is useful to come back to two other issues that the French supervisor, and beyond that the French authorities, are keen to address. a) I am thinking in particular of customer protection. The CPA, in conjunction with the Autorite9 des marche9s financiers, has developed significant means to monitor the practices of 7 stakeholders. In this regard, numerous checks were carried out in 2010. They will continue in 2011. The ACP intends to scrupulously ensure compliance not only with the legislative and regulatory provisions but also with the rules of good practice of each profession. (b) On another note, I would also like to talk about the fight against money laundering and the financing of terrorism, which the French authorities have always considered central. As you are no doubt aware, the French system has been the subject of an in-depth evaluation by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The evaluation process, which lasted almost a year and a half, has just resulted in the publication of a synthesis report on 17 February, pending the full report to be published at a later date. It is already clear that the FATF recognises the high quality and overall effectiveness of the system established by the France. It is thus among the three highest-rated countries in the world. In particular, the report gives a very positive assessment of the supervision of financial institutions, stressing the high quality of the coordinated system of permanent checks on documents and on the spot. In conclusion, the French financial sector is robust, it is indisputable. In a world where there are multiple sources of vulnerability, I call for rigorous risk management to be maintained. First of all, it requires constant discipline on the part of banking and insurance groups. The strengthening of the regulatory framework goes in the same direction. We are in the process of finalising a new regulatory landscape and it is important that all actors, supervised entities and supervisory authorities, prepare for it. Rest assured that, for the France, the CPA is committed to it. 8

Title: Europe and the World in the face of the crisis challenges and prospects
text: Speech by Christian Noyer in Vannes on 25 March 2011 "Europe and the World in the face of the crisis: challenges and perspectives" Ladies and gentlemen I am very pleased to be able to speak to you this evening and I thank the Maison de l'Europe du Morbihan and Frane7ois-Xavier Camenen for organizing this conference and inviting me to it. I'm going to talk about economics - of course! -, but I would like to focus on current European and international issues. These issues are now at the heart of the main economic debates because the various crises we have experienced since 2007, even if they are not of the same nature, have one essential point in common: they have had international implications and have required cooperation between countries. I want to share with you this evening my conviction that one of the main challenges facing the world economy today is to transform this cooperation forced by the urgency of the crises into a proactive and sustainable cooperation, both in Europe and on a global scale, which alone will make it possible to look to the future in a more serene way. 1 I. [ Recent crises all have a strong international character ] To begin with, I would like briefly to recall the sequences of the various recent crises. 1. [The 2007-2008 Financial Crisis] When we talk about "the crisis", we are actually often talking about the crisis that revealed its magnitude on September 15, 2008 with the bankruptcy of the American bank Lehman Brothers. This crisis was initially of a financial nature, it stemmed from the collapse of the American real estate market and with it the system of loans to modest households, the subprimes. These subprimes were incorporated into many other highly sophisticated financial assets and the crisis of these products quickly turned into a global financial crisis. Financial markets had suddenly lost all confidence, banks refused to lend to each other, and the repercussions on the real economy were not long in coming. It is worth noting an element that distinguishes this crisis from previous ones: it has spread to all regions of the world at a speed and to an extent never seen before. So we had the concrete - and cruel - experience! - the extremely strong interdependence between the economies of the whole world. 2. [The Sovereign Debt Crisis] Another crisis has particularly affected the euro area since 2009: the so-called "sovereign debt" crisis. It began with the financial difficulties of Greece, whose public deficit had been largely underestimated by the Greek authorities, and which suddenly lost all the confidence of the financial markets. It has experienced a new episode in Ireland, where finances 2 Public policies have been severely degraded by the recapitalisation of the country's major banks. It is clear that these two crises, as well as the pressures exerted by the financial markets on other euro area countries, including Portugal at present, are not purely financial crises. They are above all and above all crises of economic governance in these countries and in the euro area as a whole. But we find the same international character as for the 2008 crisis: they were interpreted as a crisis of the euro itself, while they affected only a few of its members. This analysis is wrong, the sovereign debt crisis is not a euro crisis - we can come back to it in the questions if you wish - but it is based on an intuition that is right: the economies of the euro area are, more than any other, extraordinarily interdependent and the slippages in public finances of some members have repercussions on the area as a whole. These two crises, shared between countries, are contagious, transmissible, a bit like a bad virus. And this implies two important things: - on the one hand, their resolution required a collective commitment; - on the other hand, strengthening the resilience of economies is moving to the future through a deepening of this cooperation. This is what we are going to see now, first for the global case and then for the European case. II. [At the global level: moving from a G20 of crisis to a G20 of macroeconomic coordination] A. [The G20 Response to the Financial Crisis] 3 First, at the international level, the international nature of the 2007-2008 financial crisis has led to a real awareness of the need for a coordinated response. And it is the G20 that has taken the initiatives in this direction. As early as 15 November 2008, the heads of state of the world's 20 largest economies met in Washington and took note of the simultaneity of the crisis. They also expressed their belief that a rapid exit from the crisis would require in-depth macroeconomic cooperation, coordinated fiscal and monetary stimulus, and improved prudential and financial supervision rules. The G20 then met twice a year in 2009 and 2010 and achieved some quite remarkable results in my opinion, for example: - a list of tax havens; - bonus rules; - an increase in the IMF's resources and a greater place granted to emerging countries; - new prudential rules known as "Basel III". All these G20 actions were guided by one principle: shared crisis, shared responses. Global economic governance has emerged stronger, with a more legitimate G20 and emerging countries better represented in international financial institutions. B. [The success of the projects implemented by the G20 will depend on collective goodwill] Thanks to these collective measures combined with equally determined national actions, the international financial system has thus managed to overcome the subprime crisis. Are we safe from future crises? I think it would be dangerous to give in to that illusion. On the contrary, we must learn the lessons of the crisis, analyse as precisely as possible. 4 new risks can be made possible and the resilience of our economies to them. Two essential projects in this regard are underway at the G20. 1. [Le Framework for Growth] The first is what is called in G20 jargon the "Framework for Growth", and in better French the "framework for strong, sustainable and balanced growth". The idea is both very ambitious and completely relevant: it is a question of discussing collectively and in an organized way the external consequences of economic measures under the national sovereignty of the world's major economies. Countries announce their forecasts and policy measures and enter into a process of mutual evaluation, with the support of the IMF. The aim is to limit national attitudes that can contribute to increasing global imbalances, particularly between countries with large surpluses and countries with large deficits, which are known to contribute to weakening the stability of the economy. The first concrete step towards such a framework was taken at the G20 summit in Seoul late last year, where heads of state adopted a clear action plan. And it is now up to the French Presidency of the G20 to carry out the first of these actions: the definition of indicative guidelines to assess the impact of national policies on the major global balances. In this regard, the first summit of finance ministers and central bank governors, on 18 February in Paris, represents an important success: the countries agreed on a list of indicators that will be evaluated. These are public debt and deficits, the savings rate and private debt, and external imbalances. The next step is to agree on indicative guidelines for the evaluation of each of these indicators. 5 2. [The International Monetary System] The second major project undertaken by the G20 this year is the adaptation of the international monetary system to changes in the global economic environment. Our IMS has shown resilience during the crisis, but it is far from perfect. In particular, sudden capital inflows and outflows, the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves in some countries, exchange rate volatility present a series of disadvantages and risks. The French presidency of the G20 has chosen to put this problem on the negotiating table. We are well aware of the difficulties that this subject poses: it is not a question of stigmatizing countries or of putting in place rules that are too rigid and ultimately counterproductive. On the other hand, significant progress can be made, and the G20 Finance in February agreed on a work programme in this regard. Coping with potentially destabilizing capital flows and being better equipped in the event of a crisis requires, among other things, better management of international liquidity. Among the avenues mentioned, there is, for example, the idea of a system of "financial safety nets" or the strengthening of the role of the IMF's Special Drawing Rights. Work is underway and will feed into our next meetings. On these two major projects as on all the work of the G20, it is quite clear that the outcome is completely in the hands of the countries concerned: the G20 has no binding power, it depends 100% on the goodwill of its members. The challenge today is decisive: it is a question of moving from a G20 of crisis, which has proven its effectiveness, to a G20 of macroeconomic coordination, which the world economy needs so much. III. [At European level: improving economic governance] 6 At the European level, the situation in the face of the crisis is quite similar: countries first managed to strengthen their cooperation to overcome the difficulties and they must now find common solutions to improve their resilience. A. [European responses to the crisis, products of "de facto solidarity"] First, how has Europe responded to the crisis? There was a European response to the 2007 financial crisis, particularly from a monetary policy perspective. The ECB's action was extremely determined: it lowered its key rates from 4.5% to 1% in a few months and it allowed banks to refinance themselves very widely with it. The European response to the sovereign debt crisis has also been very innovative. The Member States first agreed to set up a one-off budgetary support for Greece of EUR 110 billion. Faced with the magnitude of the pressure from the financial markets and the spread of mistrust to other member countries and to the currency itself, countries understood that it was necessary to go further and demonstrate their determination. And that is what they have done by setting up the 80500 billion European Financial Stability Facility, which can borrow from a country in financial difficulty with the guarantee of the Member States. At the same time, the ECB, which is a completely supranational body of the euro area, set up an unprecedented programme of bond-buying states in difficulty and established currency exchange agreements with other central banks. In this crisis, the eurozone has finally re-experienced the "de facto solidarity" of which Robert Schuman spoke. The idea at the time, as you know, was to pool Franco-German coal and steel, which were so strategic for the 7 armament production and the functioning of economies, so that war in Europe becomes not only "unthinkable" but also "materially impossible". The Member States of the ECSC and then of the European Union would have no choice, in the event of difficulties, but to seek common solutions to shared problems. In my opinion, the establishment of monetary union is based on the same reasoning: by linking their monetary destiny, the Member States of the euro zone voluntarily withdrew a weapon (the currency and competitive devaluations) to deepen the common market. They also accepted the idea that in the event of a crisis, they should, in fact, show solidarity. [The creation of the EFSF was approved by the Heads of State on 9 May 2010, exactly 60 years after the Schuman Declaration. I think this is a very good example of how far we have come and how the spirit of Europe's founding fathers has been perpetuated! ] The combination of determined and cooperative actions of the States and the ECB has effectively enabled the euro area to overcome the difficulties caused by the crisis. We must salute this success... B. [The challenges ahead] ... But we must not be satisfied with it. Europe still has work to do if it is to be able to return to sustainable growth. In particular, two challenges lie ahead of us today: to equip ourselves with effective and credible crisis management mechanisms and to strengthen the resilience of the euro area through improved fiscal governance and competitiveness. Here, as at the G20 level, political will is absolutely key. 1. [An Effective Crisis Response Mechanism (ESM)] Europe has already repeatedly demonstrated its ability to resolve crises on a wide variety of subjects. We can remember the idea of Jean Monnet 8 that Europe has finally emerged grown from the successive crises it has gone through, that this is part of its construction process. The euro area must now prove that it still has this same capacity, especially for the resolution of financial crises. As I said, it has taken a decisive step in this direction with the establishment of the EFSF. But this mechanism is a temporary mechanism. The euro area countries have understood, after the financial market attacks on Ireland and other countries, that this response, while necessary and relevant, is not enough. Europe has understood that it must equip itself with a permanent crisis resolution tool that is sufficiently credible to calm market pressures in the long term: this is the idea of the mechanism called the European Stability Mechanism created at the end of 2010 and which will be operational from mid-2013. The eurozone's toolbox is becoming clearer - we are in the news: euro area heads of state took an important step at the March 11 summit by setting the Stability Mechanism's total lending capacity at 80500 billion and opening up the possibility of intervention in the primary public debt market. At the ECB, we have encouraged this movement, which strengthens the resilience of the euro area and thus also the effectiveness of our monetary policy. 2. [Improving economic governance through reform of the SGP and monitoring of competitiveness] Beyond crisis management, the euro area must also be able to better prevent the emergence of new difficulties. For this, it is imperative to act on the roots of the problem. It must be understood, as I have already said, that sovereign debt crises are first and foremost crises of economic governance, both in the countries concerned and at European level. The root of the problem lies there, and it is therefore at this level that progress must be made. 9 The plans for the recovery of public finances in the countries affected by the crisis are courageous and relevant. It is imperative that each country attach crucial importance to the development of its public finances if it is to avoid having to put in place such harsh plans. The European Union has a key role to play in this regard: it is its responsibility to strengthen its monitoring of these developments. Of course, the Union does not have to decide on the details or distribution of countries' public revenues and expenditures, this is a matter for national sovereignty. On the other hand, the budget balance is of common interest, as demonstrated by the sovereign debt crisis and must therefore be monitored by the Union. This is the purpose of the Stability and Growth Pact, which was designed precisely to compensate for the lack of European economic government. We have seen that this Pact has been gradually weakened and that it has not made it possible to avoid the slippages in public deficits that have contributed to the crisis. The Pact must therefore be strengthened and, here too, we are at the heart of the news, since proposals were made at the summit on 11 March - tightening of sanctions, budgetary rules at national level, conditionality of loans. On several occasions, the ECB has expressed its conviction that the automaticity of sanctions in the event of non-compliance with the Pact is an essential condition for its future effectiveness, but it is obviously up to the Heads of State to decide on this. It has also become clear that competitiveness gaps between euro area countries undermine its stability. I believe that competitiveness must be monitored according to precise rules with sanctions. In particular, the development of unit costs of production must absolutely be compatible with the ECB's price development objective. Strict rules on public finances and competitiveness are the prerequisite for the success of our monetary union. It seems to me that governments have become aware of this since the crisis; we will see whether the reforms decided in this direction will be sufficient. 10 To conclude, I cannot resist the pleasure of quoting Jean Monnet saying in his Memoirs that: "Men accept change only in necessity and they see necessity only in crisis." Indeed, the major economic powers have accepted important changes to get out of recent crises. These countries have changed some rules, they have made sacrifices, they have agreed to cooperate more. But I hope I have succeeded in conveying to you my hope that the future will prove Monnet wrong and that men, in Europe and in the world, will see the need to deepen these efforts today, without waiting for the next crisis. Thank you for your attention. 11
text_original: Intervention de Christian Noyer  Vannes le 25 mars 2011  LEurope et le Monde face  la crise : enjeux et perspectives  Mesdames et Messieurs, Je suis trs heureux de pouvoir intervenir devant vous ce soir et je remercie la maison de lEurope du Morbihan et Franois-Xavier Camenen davoir organis cette confrence et de my avoir invit. Je vais vous parler dconomie videmment ! -, mais je voudrais centrer mon propos sur les enjeux europens et internationaux actuels. Ces enjeux sont aujourdhui au cur des principaux dbats conomiques parce que les diffrentes crises que nous avons connues depuis 2007, mme si elles ne sont pas de mme nature, ont un point essentiel en commun : elles ont eu des implications internationales et ont ncessit une coopration entre les pays. Je veux partager ce soir avec vous ma conviction quun des principaux dfis  relever pour lconomie mondiale aujourdhui consiste  transformer cette coopration force par lurgence des crises en une coopration volontariste et durable, aussi bien en Europe qu lchelle mondiale, qui seule permettra denvisager lavenir dune faon plus sereine. 1 I. [ Les crises rcentes ont toutes un caractre international fort ] Pour commencer, je voudrais brivement rappeler les enchanements des diffrentes crises rcentes. 1. [La crise financire de 2007-2008] Quand on parle de  la crise , on parle en ralit souvent de la crise qui a rvl son ampleur le 15 septembre 2008 avec la faillite de la banque amricaine Lehman Brothers. Cette crise aura dabord t de nature financire, elle dcoulait de leffondrement du march immobilier amricain et avec lui du systme de prts aux mnages modestes, les subprimes. Ces subprimes taient incorpores dans de nombreux autres actifs financiers trs sophistiqus et la crise de ces produits sest rapidement transforme en une crise financire globale. Les marchs financiers avaient soudainement perdu toute confiance, les banques refusaient de se prter entre elles et les rpercussions sur lconomie relle nont pas tard. Il faut remarquer un lment qui distingue cette crise des prcdentes : elle sest propage dans toutes les rgions du monde  une vitesse et dans une mesure jamais observes jusque l. Nous avons donc fait lexprience concrte - et cruelle ! - de linterdpendance extrmement forte entre les conomies du monde entier. 2. [La crise de la dette souveraine] Une autre crise a touch plus particulirement la zone euro depuis 2009 : cest la crise dite  de la dette souveraine . Elle a dbut avec les difficults financires de la Grce, dont le dficit public avait t largement sous-estim par les autorits grecques, et qui a brusquement perdu toute la confiance des marchs financiers. Elle a connu un nouvel pisode en Irlande, o les finances 2 publiques ont t fortement dgrades par la recapitalisation de grandes banques du pays. Il est clair que ces deux crises, ainsi que les pressions exerces par les marchs financiers sur dautres pays de la zone euro dont le Portugal actuellement, ne sont pas purement des crises financires. Elles sont avant tout et surtout des crises de la gouvernance conomique dans ces pays et dans la zone euro dans son ensemble. Mais nous retrouvons le mme caractre international que pour la crise de 2008 : elles ont t interprtes comme une crise de leuro lui-mme, alors quelles ne touchaient que peu de ses membres. Cette analyse est fausse, la crise de la dette souveraine nest pas une crise de leuro nous pourrons y revenir dans les questions si vous le souhaitez  mais elle repose sur une intuition qui, elle, est juste : les conomies de la zone euro sont, plus que nimporte quelles autres, extraordinairement interdpendantes et les drapages des finances publiques de certains membres ont des rpercussions sur la zone dans son ensemble. Ces deux crises, partages entre les pays, sont contagieuses, transmissibles, un peu comme un mauvais virus. Et ceci implique deux choses importantes : - dune part, leur rsolution a ncessit un engagement collectif ; - dautre part, le renforcement de la rsilience des conomies passe  lavenir par un approfondissement de cette coopration. Cest ce que nous allons voir maintenant, dabord pour le cas mondial et puis pour le cas europen. II. [Au niveau mondial : passer dun G20 de crise  un G20 de coordination macroconomique] A. [La rponse du G20  la crise financire] 3 Au niveau international dabord, le caractre international de la crise financire de 2007-2008 a provoqu une vraie prise de conscience de la ncessit dune rponse coordonne. Et cest le G20 qui a pris les initiatives en ce sens. Ds le 15 novembre 2008, les chefs dtat des 20 plus grandes conomies mondiales se runissaient  Washington et prenaient acte de la simultanit de la crise. Ils exprimaient galement leur conviction quune sortie de crise rapide passerait par une coopration macroconomique approfondie, des mesures de relance budgtaire et montaire coordonnes ainsi quune amlioration des rgles prudentielles et de supervision financire. Le G20 sest ensuite runi deux fois par an en 2009 et 2010 et a obtenu des rsultats assez remarquables  mon sens, par exemple : - une liste de paradis fiscaux ; - des rgles sur les bonus ; - un accroissement des moyens du FMI et une plus grande place accorde aux mergents ; - de nouvelles rgles prudentielles dites de  Ble III . Toutes ces actions du G20 ont t guides par un principe :  crise partage, rponses partages. [Le succs des chantiers mis en uvre par le G20 dpendra de la bonne volont collective] Grce  ces mesures collectives combines  des actions nationales tout aussi dtermines, le systme financier international a donc russi  surmonter la crise des subprimes. Nous devons au contraire tirer les leons de la crise, analyser le plus prcisment 4 possible les nouveaux risques et renforcer la rsilience de nos conomies face  eux. Deux chantiers essentiels  cet gard sont en marche au G20. 1. [Le Framework for Growth] Le premier est ce quon appelle en jargon G20 le  Framework for Growth , et en meilleur franais le  cadre pour une croissance forte, durable et quilibre . Lide est  la fois trs ambitieuse et compltement pertinente : il sagit de discuter collectivement et de manire organise des consquences extrieures de mesures conomiques relevant de la souverainet nationale des principales conomies du monde. Les pays annoncent leurs prvisions et leurs mesures de politique conomique et ils entrent dans un processus dvaluation mutuelle, avec le soutien du FMI. Le but est de limiter les comportements nationaux qui peuvent contribuer  accrotre les dsquilibres mondiaux, notamment entre des pays trs excdentaires et des pays trs dficitaires, dont on sait quils contribuent  fragiliser la stabilit de lconomie. Le premier pas concret vers la mise en place dun tel cadre a t ralis au sommet du G20 de Soul en fin danne dernire au cours duquel les chefs dtat ont adopt un plan dactions prcises. Et il revient aujourdhui  la prsidence franaise du G20 de mener  bien la premire de ces actions : la dfinition de lignes directrices indicatives permettant dvaluer limpact des politiques nationales sur les grands quilibres mondiaux. A cet gard, le premier sommet des ministres des Finances et des gouverneurs de banques centrales, le 18 fvrier dernier  Paris, reprsente un succs important : les pays se sont mis daccord sur une liste des indicateurs qui feront lobjet dune valuation. Il sagit de la dette et des dficits publics, du taux dpargne et de lendettement priv et des dsquilibres extrieurs. La prochaine tape consiste  nous mettre daccord sur les lignes directrices indicatives pour lvaluation de chacun de ces indicateurs. 5 2. [Le systme montaire international] Le second grand chantier entrepris par le G20 cette anne est celui de ladaptation du systme montaire international aux volutions de lenvironnement conomique mondial. Notre SMI a fait preuve de rsilience pendant la crise, mais il est loin dtre parfait. En particulier, les entres et sorties brutales de capitaux, laccumulation de rserves de change dans certains pays, la volatilit des taux de change prsentent une srie dinconvnients et de risques. La prsidence franaise du G20 a choisi de poser ce problme sur la table des ngociations. Nous sommes bien conscients des difficults que ce sujet pose : il ne sagit pas de stigmatiser les pays ou de mettre en place des rgles trop rigides et in fine contreproductives. En revanche, des avances importantes peuvent tre ralises, et le G20 Finances de fvrier sest mis daccord sur un programme de travail  cet gard. Pour faire face aux flux de capitaux potentiellement dstabilisateurs et tre mieux arm en cas de crise, il faut notamment mieux grer la liquidit internationale. Parmi les pistes voques, il y a par exemple lide dun systme de  filets de scurit financire  ou le renforcement du rle des Droits de Tirage Spciaux du FMI. Des travaux sont en cours et viendront nourrir nos prochaines runions. Sur ces deux grands chantiers comme sur lensemble des travaux du G20, il est tout  fait clair que lissue est compltement entre les mains des pays concerns : le G20 na pas de pouvoir contraignant, il dpend  100% de la bonne volont de ses membres. Lenjeu est aujourdhui dcisif : il sagit de passer dun G20 de crise, qui a prouv son efficacit,  un G20 de coordination macroconomique, dont lconomie mondiale a tant besoin. III. [Au niveau europen : amliorer la gouvernance conomique] 6 Au niveau europen, la situation face  la crise est assez similaire : les pays sont dabord parvenus  renforcer leur coopration pour surmonter les difficults et ils doivent aujourdhui trouver des solutions communes pour amliorer leur rsilience. A. [Les rponses europennes  la crise, produits de la  solidarit de fait ] Dabord, comment lEurope a-t-elle rpondu  la crise ? Il y a eu une rponse europenne  la crise financire de 2007, en particulier du point de vue de la politique montaire. Laction de la BCE a t extrmement dtermine : elle a baiss ses taux directeurs de 4.5%  1% en quelques mois et elle a permis aux banques de se refinancer trs largement auprs delle. La raction europenne  la crise de la dette souveraine a en outre t trs innovante. Les tats ont dabord accept de mettre en place un soutien budgtaire ponctuel pour la Grce, de 110 milliards deuro. Face  lampleur de la pression des marchs financiers et  lextension de la dfiance  dautres pays membres et  la monnaie elle-mme, les pays ont compris quil fallait aller plus loin et dmontrer leur dtermination. Et cest ce quils ont fait en mettant en place le Fonds europen de stabilit financire, dot de 500 milliards deuros et pouvant contracter des emprunts en faveur dun pays rencontrant des difficults financires avec la garantie des tats membres. Dans le mme temps, la BCE, qui est un organe compltement supranational de la zone euro, mettait en place un programme indit dachat dobligations des tats en difficult et nouait des accords dchange de devises avec dautres banques centrales. Dans cette crise, la zone euro a finalement refait lexprience de la  solidarit de fait  dont parlait Robert Schuman. Lide  lpoque, vous le savez, tait de mutualiser le charbon et lacier franco-allemands, si stratgiques pour la 7 production darmement et le fonctionnement des conomies, de sorte que la guerre en Europe devienne non seulement  impensable  mais aussi  matriellement impossible . Les tats membres de la CECA puis de lUnion europenne nauraient pas dautre choix, en cas de difficults, que de rechercher des solutions communes  des problmes partags. A mon sens, la mise en place de lunion montaire repose sur le mme raisonnement : en liant leur destin montaire, les tats membres de la zone euro se retiraient volontairement une arme (la monnaie et les dvaluations comptitives) pour approfondir le march commun.
