[La cration du FESF a t approuve par les chefs dEtat le 9 mai 2010, soit exactement 60 ans aprs la dclaration Schuman. Je trouve que cest un trs bel exemple du chemin parcouru et de la perptuation de lesprit des pres fondateurs de lEurope ! ] La combinaison des actions dtermines et coopratives des Etats et de la BCE a effectivement permis  la zone euro de surmonter les difficults provoques par la crise. Il faut saluer cette russite... B. [Les dfis  venir]  Mais il ne faut pas sen contenter. LEurope a encore du travail si elle veut pouvoir retrouver une croissance durable. En particulier, deux dfis sont aujourdhui devant nous : nous doter de mcanismes efficaces et crdibles de gestion des crises et renforcer la rsilience de la zone euro grce  une amlioration de la gouvernance en matire budgtaire et de comptitivit. Ici comme au niveau du G20, la volont politique est absolument cl. 1. [Un mcanisme efficace de rponse aux crises (MES)] LEurope a dj  maintes reprises dmontr sa capacit  rsoudre des crises sur des sujets trs varis. On peut se rappeler lide de Jean Monnet 8 que lEurope est finalement sortie grandie des crises successives quelle a traverses, que cela fait partie de son processus de construction. La zone euro doit aujourdhui prouver quelle a toujours cette mme capacit, notamment pour la rsolution des crises financires. Comme je lai dit, elle a fait un pas dcisif dans cette direction avec la mise en place du FESF. Mais ce mcanisme est un mcanisme temporaire. Les pays de la zone euro ont bien compris, aprs les attaques des marchs financiers sur lIrlande et dautres pays, que cette rponse, bien que ncessaire et pertinente, ntait pas suffisante. LEurope a compris quelle devait se doter dun outil de rsolution des crises permanent et suffisamment crdible pour calmer durablement les pressions des marchs : cest lide du dispositif appel Mcanisme europen de Stabilit cr  la fin de 2010 et qui sera oprationnel  partir de mi-2013. La bote  outils de la zone euro est en train de se prciser  nous sommes en plein dans lactualit : les chefs dtat de la zone euro ont franchi une tape importante lors du sommet du 11 mars dernier en fixant la capacit totale de prts du Mcanisme de stabilit  500 milliards deuros et en ouvrant la possibilit dintervention sur le march primaire de la dette publique. A la BCE, nous avons encourag ce mouvement qui renforce la rsilience de la zone euro et de ce fait aussi lefficacit de notre politique montaire. 2. [Lamlioration de la gouvernance conomique par une rforme du PSC et une surveillance de la comptitivit] Au-del de la gestion des crises, la zone euro doit aussi parvenir  mieux prvenir lapparition de nouvelles difficults. Pour cela, il est impratif dagir sur les racines du problme. Il faut bien comprendre, comme je lai dj dit, que les crises de la dette souveraine sont dabord et avant tout des crises de la gouvernance conomique,  la fois dans les pays concerns et au niveau europen. La racine du problme se trouve bien l, et cest donc  ce niveau quil faut progresser. 9 Les plans de redressement des finances publiques des pays touchs par la crise sont courageux et pertinents. Chaque pays doit absolument accorder une importance cruciale  lvolution de ses finances publiques sil veut viter davoir  mettre en place des plans aussi rudes. LUnion europenne a un rle essentiel  jouer sur ce plan : il est de sa responsabilit de renforcer sa surveillance sur ces volutions. Bien sr, lUnion na pas  se prononcer sur le dtail ou la rpartition des recettes et des dpenses publiques des pays, ceci est du ressort de la souverainet nationale. En revanche, le solde budgtaire est dintrt commun comme le dmontre la crise de la dette souveraine et doit donc tre surveill par lUnion. Cest lobjet du Pacte de Stabilit et de Croissance, qui avait t prcisment conu pour pallier le dfaut de gouvernement conomique europen. On a vu que ce Pacte a t progressivement affaibli et quil na pas permis dviter les drapages des dficits publics qui ont contribu  la crise. Le Pacte doit donc tre renforc et, l aussi, nous sommes au cur de lactualit, puisque des propositions ont t faites lors du sommet du 11 mars  durcissement des sanctions, rgles budgtaires au niveau national, conditionnalit des prts. A plusieurs reprises, la BCE a exprim sa conviction que lautomaticit des sanctions en cas de non-respect du Pacte tait une condition essentielle de son efficacit future, mais il revient videmment aux chefs dtat den dcider. Il est galement devenu vident que les carts de comptitivit entre les pays de la zone euro fragilisent sa stabilit. Je pense que la comptitivit doit tre suivie selon des rgles prcises assorties de sanctions. En particulier, lvolution des cots unitaires de production doit absolument tre compatible avec lobjectif dvolution des prix de la BCE. Des rgles strictes concernant les finances publiques et la comptitivit sont la condition indispensable au succs de notre union montaire. Il me semble que les gouvernements en ont pris conscience depuis la crise ; nous verrons si les rformes dcides en ce sens seront suffisantes. 10 *************** Pour conclure, je ne rsiste pas au plaisir de citer Jean Monnet disant dans ses Mmoires que :  Les hommes nacceptent le changement que dans la ncessit et ils ne voient la ncessit que dans la crise . Effectivement, les grandes puissances conomiques ont accept des changements importants pour sortir des crises rcentes. Ces pays ont chang certaines rgles, ils ont fait des sacrifices, ils ont accept de cooprer davantage. Mais jespre avoir russi  vous transmettre mon espoir que lavenir donnera tort  Monnet et que les hommes, en Europe et dans le Monde, verront la ncessit dapprofondir ces efforts ds aujourdhui, sans attendre la prochaine crise. Je vous remercie de votre attention. 11

Title: The future for inflation
text: Euromoney Conference Real Return VIII  6 APRIL 2011 Panel 1: The Future for Inflation Speech by Robert Ophele, Director General of Operations It is a real pleasure to be part of this panel today. For central bank staff, being part of a conference of experts in inflation linked financial products is quite challenging. Because what is at stake is the core asset of central banks, their credibility in addressing its main duty: achieving price stability Let me be very humble and try to address some of the questions we face with regards inflation. These remarks are of course totally unofficial. First of all I have to observe that Central Bank credibility has a pivotal role at a time when we are facing mounting inflationary pressures. We have escaped the deflationary hole, limited the financial chaos, but, surprisingly, one can observe a negative evolution of the approval ratings for central banks; it is true for the US, true for the UK, true for the Euro Zone. Reasons for this decreasing support are probably very different from one country to another and I do not want to elaborate on them now but, taken as a given, it is all the more worrying that credibility is the most powerful asset of 1 central banks for fighting inflation. We all know that medium term inflation expectations are keys to the inflation process it-self and that credibility of central banks is key in order to maintain these expectations contained; it is The soft tyranny of inflation expectations recently highlighted by Adam Posen. We should all realize that a decrease in the credibility of central banks will clearly need to be accommodated by a larger shift in interest rates meaning the cost of keeping inflation on track would be higher in terms of output. As economists use to say, the Sacrifice Ratio would increase. Let me turn briefly to the current situation vis-a-vis inflationary pressures. There are many reasons not to be that worried: one could advocate that we are experiencing a set of one-off shocks in commodity prices triggered by political unrests or bad crops; one could consider that core inflation is almost everywhere very low, actually close to 1 % and that all this inflation story is in fact mainly a distortion in relative prices; one could also consider that output gaps are still broadly negatives, that growth it-self is not largely above potential and that large unemployment reduces the pressure for wage increases. Finally one can observe that inflation expectations either derived from financial markets or collected from professional forecasters remain both well contained. So the evilly second round effects are not part of the picture, and central banks could keep their accommodative monetary stance. Another way of looking at the same reality would be less buoyant. I will not elaborate on the commodities price trend but let us just keep for example in mind that the relationship between per capita energy consumption and per capita GDP is far from being linear and that the most rapidly growing economies still have an income elasticity with energy consumption close to 1. During the last decade the share of China in the world primary energy consumption has indeed doubled from 10 to 20 % according to the Internal 2 Energy Agency, meaning that China has now a largest consumption than Europe or the US, and the story is obviously not over. One can also doubt that inflation is completely under control in most emerging economies. They had globally a 6 % inflation rate at the beginning of this year, fully understandable when having in mind the large share of food in their basket, but they are clearly in dangerous territories. It means that prices for imported goods in our developed economies will increase if exchange rates dont adjust. And obviously it will not be fully the case. It would not be that problematic if the pass-through to domestic prices remains subdued as it has be the case in the past. But the contrary could occur. I was struck to understand that in the UK, according to the recent Inflation Report of the Bank of England, the pass-through could have been close to 100 % in the recent years. In that perspective, trend in commodity prices and inflation in emerging countries will certainly add a lot to inflation pressures in our developed economies. Turning to our domestic economies I would like to refer to the illuminating remarks made by Athanasios Orphanides at the recent Bank de France international symposium (The role of central banks: lessons from the crisis) in this very same room. He developed the idea that the output gap cant be of direct use for monetary policy purposes: on should first have in mind that the lag time for monetary decision to fully transmit to the real economy is between 12 and 24 months and that that a good measure of the output gap cant be available with a lower than 24 months delay. Real time output gap estimations have proven to be largely wrong with a strongly negative bias. During the first ten years of the Euro Are, every year, both the IMF and the European Commission have actually considered that the Euro Area had a negative output gap, even in 2006 before the outburst of the financial crisis. Nowadays experts have completely revisited their estimation and after having revised their data for potential output, they now think that at that time the Euro Area Economy was actually overheating. So do not rely too much on a contemporaneous negative output gap guestimation. 3 Another striking element is the recent evolution of the so called Beveridge Curve. This curve is a simple relationship between unemployment and a measure of difficulties to find work forces (be it the number of unsatisfied demand for workers coming from employers or a regular survey on bottleneck in the economy). Usually you have a close to linear and negative relationship between both factors, meaning that the more unemployment you have the less problem you have for finding working forces. By increasing the flexibility in the labor market and developing the training of the people you can shift the curve and decrease the unemployment rate for a given level of difficulties in covering the demand for workers. It is precisely what has been achieved in Germany with the so call Hartz reforms. But for the last couple of quarters, there is clear break in the Beveridge curves in most developed countries; they are becoming vertical as illustrated here in the curve for the Euro Area. It is strong indication that for some times, the Non-accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemplyment, the well known NAIRU, has increased. Last but not least from a central bank perspective one should consider the unintended consequences of maintaining very low interest rates for a long time. How it could foster an indiscriminate search for yield, encourage increasing leverage and facilitate the development of asset price bubbles be it in commodities, housing, and emerging market securities. Short term price expectations of all the economic agents are clearly going North, with the European Commission Survey showing a rare consensus between Manufacturers, Services, Retailers and consumers with expectations at historic heights. The same message is being delivered by the recent PMI data in the US with a rare unanimity in all the individual manufacturing and non-manufacturing sectors. In that perspective the current anchoring of medium term inflation expectation, the well known 5 years in 5 years ILS or break-even rate, seems to be a strong incentive to actually normalize relatively rapidly the monetary policy stance. 4 Will it be possible easily? One should probably make in distinction between central banks which have recourse to quantitative easing and the Eurosystem. The non-conventional tools of the ECB have not been targeting quantity. The fixed rate full allotment procedure provides liquidity to the banks which are no longer or not yet in a position to attract funding in the market provided they have adequate collateral, but, even if it could be associated with a persistent bidder component, one should recognize that the amount of excess central bank liquidity so distributed in the banking system is rather limited with, on average, only around 25 billion put at the deposit facility. Furthermore, the so called Securities Markets Programme, whose aim is to repair disfunctionning segments of the financial markets which are key for the transmission of the ECB monetary policy, has a rather limited size (currently 77 billion) and the liquidity provided through these purchases is fully sterilized. One could therefore fairly advocate that the monetary policy stance is separate from these unconventional monetary policy tools. The separation principle probably dont apply so easily to central banks implementing massive quantitative easing; they have weighted on the whole yield curve and have managed to avoid deflation at the lower bound of the policy rate spectrum; reversing this accommodative policy will certainly be quite a challenge but liquidity absorbing tools are ready to be implemented. To conclude I do think that central banks are ready to do the job of preventing inflation to spiral. Banks have failed and have been rescued by States; States have been in danger and to some extent they have been rescued by central banks. They have the immense advantage of having by definition no liquidity problem in their own currency, so they cant fail, but it is of utmost importance that they dont waste this privilege and be ready to apply the adequate monetary policy stance irrespective of course of their immediate financial interest; Bill Dudley was very clear on that point in a seminal speech delivered earlier this year at the Stern Business School. It is nevertheless evident in that 5 perspective that a strong financial position, which is also a prerequisite for their independence, is undoubtedly of help. Thank you for your attention. 6

Title: The next steps of Solvency II and the results of the 5th Impact Assessment
text: ACP CONFERENCE OF 27 APRIL 2011 THE NEXT STEPS OF SOLVENCY II AND THE RESULTS OF THE 5TH IMPACT STUDY (QIS 5) Introduction by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Autorite9 de Contrf4le Prudentiel Hello Ladies and Gentlemen, Thank you for coming in large numbers to this ACP conference on Solvency II. This morning will be specially dedicated to the next steps of Solvency II and the results of the 5th Impact Assessment ("QIS 5"). As an introduction, I would like to return to the main lessons of QIS5 before giving the floor to the eminent representatives of the various authorities involved as well as to the experts of the ACP General Secretariat who will present this morning, in more detail, the results of the impact study and its challenges. QIS 5 marks a crucial step in the process of developing the new regulations, a time when we are moving from the drawing board to the full-scale test, so to speak. I think it is indeed useful to recall that Solvency II is a long-term project, initiated more than 10 years ago, which has required effort and time because it aims to set up a regulatory framework of reference that must be able to apply durably, under normal economic conditions, but also in crisis situations. This new regulation will make it possible to harmonise the prudential regimes applying to insurance at european Union level as well as to improve risk management. Solvency II will have profound impacts both on the methods of calculating technical provisions and on the prudential valuation of other balance sheet items, the definition of own funds or the determination of the Solvency Capital Requirement - the "SCR" - of organizations, on an individual basis as well as at group level. It is important to keep in mind that this news regulation is based on a comprehensive approach to different risks. It would therefore not be relevant, or even possible, to try to draw conclusions from that impact assessment by comparing the specific treatment of a particular risk between Solvency I and Solvency II, since it is the entire reference framework that is being revised. It is therefore on the overall photography that we must look. Another key point I would like to emphasise is that the Solvency II reform is not limited to quantitative requirements alone, which are the first pillar of this new prudential framework. Solvency II also requires compliance with qualitative and internal control requirements within Pillar 2 and supervisory reporting and disclosure requirements under Pillar 3. The afternoon of this conference will thus be devoted to Pillar 2. The collection of the results of the 5th quantitative impact study was completed in November 2010. This was followed by an intensive phase of data exploitation. This impact assessment, which is expected to be the last of its kind, is also the first to take into account the lessons of the financial crisis. It is of particular importance for all stakeholders, as it provides a measure of quantitative impacts that will make it possible to determine the latest adjustments in terms of calibration. But, the interest of QIS5 is not only to collect numerical data. The impact study also made it possible to understand the preparation of the solvency II market. It was an opportunity for insurance and reinsurance organisations to assess the operational reliability of their processes and to disseminate knowledge of future regulations within their teams beyond the narrow circle of specialists. Participating in QIS5 has required organizations to form multidisciplinary teams including actuaries, accountants and information systems specialists. I now come to the main teachings of QIS5. I identify three major points. First lesson: French insurance organizations have massively participated in QIS5. 515 organizations responded on an individual basis, 253 more than in the previous study in 2008. At the group level, 31 participations were recorded compared to 29 in QIS4. This high number of responses places the France in 1st place in Europe among contributors! This in itself is a great success and I would like to salute the strong mobilization of local organizations. It was also made possible by the investment of the professional organizations that accompanied this work. I would also like to highlight the very strong investment of the teams of the Prudential Control Authority who prepared the exercise with the local bodies. The CPA teams then completed the in-depth analysis of the data in a tight period of time. The high participation rate observed makes it possible to ensure a good representativeness of the market at national level. Of the responses obtained, 62% come from mutual organizations (for a large majority of them the year was the first), 30% are corporate reinsurers anonymous and the remaining 8% from pension funds. The health sector is also well represented. I would also like to acknowledge the significant involvement of small organizations. Second major lesson: the QIS5 exercise confirms the overall solidity of the French market and its ability to move to Solvency II without major difficulties. The aggregate SCR of french participants in QIS 5 is widely covered. The aggregate Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) of the French participants amounts to approximately 101 GEUR. Its coverage shows a large surplus of EUR 82 billion, compared to a surplus of EUR 106 billion under Solvency I. For its part, the minimum capital requirement1 (MCR) aggregated for French participants in QIS 5 amounts to 39 GEUR. Its coverage shows a surplus of 135 GEUR. Of course, all of these results should be viewed with some caution. The novelty of the exercise, carried out in a rather limited time, for the first time for some organizations, did not always make it possible to obtain quality data. This is the third lesson that can be drawn from the exercise: for a number of individual organizations, significant efforts remain to be made, as their level of preparedness is not yet sufficient and the quality of the data is still very heterogeneous. An important source of change from the existing regime is the valuation of the prudential balance sheet, for which Solvency II adopts an economic approach close to that of IFRS. If the organizations that belong to groups and are experienced in the preparation of IFRS accounts have not encountered major difficulties in establishing their prudential balance sheets; on the other hand, the exercise proved to be more complex for the other agencies, although some improvement in data quality can be seen for those who had already responded to previous studies. In order to enhance accounting positions, some organizations have sometimes resorted to summary simplifications not provided for in the technical specifications. This observation leads the ACP to renew its position on the need to subject the Solvency II prudential balance sheet to an external audit. In addition, in terms of equity, a number of restatements have not always been well carried out by participants, such as the deduction of holdings in financial and credit institutions, or the treatment of ring-fenced funds. Finally, the classification of certain instruments as "tier" has sometimes been problematic, as illustrated by differences in the classification within the profession of subordinated debts with identical characteristics. In total, with regard to the qis5 teachings for French insurance organizations, I would mainly like to emphasize 2 messages: 1 The RCM refers to the level of own funds that the organisation must hold continuously under penalty of withdrawal of authorisation First message: it does not seem desirable that the entire quantitative "package" of Solvency II be put back on the table and discussed again in the very short time that separates us from the implementation of the new regime. We need to focus on the most important issues. The impact study showing that the aggregate SCR of French donors is covered by a large surplus of 82 GEUR, this result shows that we can approach the next steps of the Solvency II project with serenity, even if we must not abandon the necessary vigilance. On the elements of the QIS5 having demonstrated, either too much complexity of the exercise, or an inadequate calibration, the Prudential Control Authority has already resumed negotiations and work, in consultation with the other European supervisors within EIOPA as well as with the French Treasury or professional organizations and individual bodies. On other elements that deserve clarification, either at level 2 or level 3, the ACP will continue to put forward its proposals within EIOPA so that satisfactory solutions are found (I am thinking, for example, of the scope of consideration of future premiums, or the calculation of the adjustment for deferred taxes). The second message I would like to deliver is that the bodies must actively continue their preparation for the future regulation. We can welcome the high participation rate of French organizations in QIS 5, but we must also be attentive to the situation of those who did not participate in the exercise. In addition, the impact study highlighted the often perfectible nature of certain data. Agencies must therefore intensify their preparedness efforts. The operational reliability of data must be enhanced and processing processes must be industrialized. In conjunction with the provisions of Pillar 1, work must also be continued to meet the requirements of Pillar 2 and Pillar 3 of the future regulation. * 2011 will be a crucial year for Solvency II with the monitoring of the pre-application processes for organisations wishing to use internal templates, the publication of the so-called level 2 implementing measures and the finalisation by EIOPA of the measures that will complement them (so-called level 3), before transmission to the European Commission towards the end of the year. All organizations must continue to prepare; the ACP will be ready and present to accompany them. Thank you for your attention.

Title: The Euro Area Challenges and response
text: Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of Banque de France Tokyo, May 16th, 2011 The Euro Area : Challenges and Responses It is a great pleasure to be here today. It is also a privilege to address such a distinguished audience. I would like to take this opportunity to present my assessment of the situation in the euro area, particularly with respect to the difficulties we meet on sovereign debt. Three views on the sovereign crisis in Europe Broadly speaking, opinions and views expressed on the euro area by people outside the Eurozone, can be divided into three categories: hostility for, at least very few people, skepticism and support. First, outright hostility. It is unfortunately true that, in some circles, there is a spontaneous and deeply ingrained opposition to European integration. Since the euro is the most accomplished part of the integration project, it is only natural that it crystallizes those oppositions. Somber predictions about the imminent demise of the euro came predominantly from those deeply anti  European commentators. While those views, like all opinions, should be treated with respect, there is no point in trying to refute arguments which, in great part, are irrational and mainly reflect wishful thinking. 1 Second, skepticism. It emanates mainly, but not only, from academic circles. Prestigious and well respected economists have been pointing to the fact that the Euro is not an optimum currency area. They also underlined that, absent sufficient labor mobility, there was a need for some form of fiscal federalism that current arrangements failed to fulfill by a large measure. Those arguments have been made and discussed for some time and deserve careful consideration. Obviously, recent turbulences and disruptions in the articulation of national fiscal policies have given them a new relevance. I will come back to this debate in a moment. At this stage, I will simply remind you of some responses that have been consistently formulated over the last decade. The benefits of the euro cannot be assessed exclusively through the lenses of the optimum currency theory. The Euro has brought to more than 400 million European citizens unprecedented stability. Price stability, obviously, with inflation averaging 1.97% over the last decade. And also, yes, financial stability. It is always useful to think of counterfactual when assessing a situation. Looking beyond current fiscal turbulences, let us think, for instance, how Europe would have absorbed the crisis with fifteen different currencies, fluctuating internal exchange rates, and, as a consequence, much higher volatility, uncertainty, risk premia and interest rates. This experiment speaks for itself. In addition, numerous studies have shown that economic cycles are becoming more and more synchronized across the euro countries. After a spike in 2009, the standard deviation between national growth rates inside the Euro area has gone down to its lowest historical level ever. This convergence has eliminated one major asymmetry and is getting the eurozone closer to the canonical model of the optimum currency area. 2 The last observable reaction is support. It shows up in comments from a majority of observers and investors, especially in emerging economies: they praise the euro; they want it to succeed; but they sometimes wonder about our collective ability, in current circumstances, to do what is necessary, to make the right decisions or make them at the right time and to set in place the proper framework for the future. These are the concerns I want to address now. Where and how did it start? Most Euro area and EU countries entered the crisis with significantly deteriorated fiscal positions. We were very far away from the "structural balance objective" which was the basic pillar of our fiscal framework. So, all countries were severely hit, not so much by an increase in expenditures but essentially through a massive loss of revenues. The IMF has shown that, in all advanced countries, including the US and UK, those losses account for around two third of the deterioration in fiscal positions which have been observed during the crisis. Fiscal deterioration was compounded, in some countries, by the size of blanket guarantees given to the banking sector. Those implicit liabilities only became apparent when difficulties materialized. As in the US and UK, fragilities in the banking sector stemmed from risks mostly taken in - or related to - the housing sector. Let me note, by the way, that those problems unfortunately were not specific to the Euro area. Public debt jumped by around 30% of GDP in UK and in US. Structural deficits in those countries stand at similar or higher levels than those in most parts of the Euro area. 3 Overall, the crisis has put into light major deficiencies in the implementation of fiscal discipline and, more generally, in the economic governance of the Euro area. It is indeed demanding to operate a single currency with multiple fiscal and structural national policies. Given the insufficient market discipline, the founders of the Euro had seen the problem and put in place the Growth and Stability Pact. The principles were sound. The framework was adequate. The implementation has been extremely weak. Bluntly speaking, peer pressure failed to ensure consistent and rigorous respect of the principles which had been agreed upon. It was, and remains necessary to make a "quantum leap" in economic governance. What did we do? The governments are now trying to address those deficiencies. Significant progress has been made over the past year. At the national level, all Member States have embarked upon credible public finance consolidation plans that are already bearing fruit. At the EU level, a new framework has been agreed upon. The first pillar is a strengthening of the SGP with a much stronger preventive arm. Surveillance over budgetary policies has been reinforced with a more effective prevention/correction of excessive deficits. Government debt levels are being better taken into account and sanctions will become more automatic. Ideally those European disciplines should be now completed by the adoption, in each member states, of strong national fiscal rules. The second Pillar is a new process to monitor competitiveness and, in particular, unit production costs. Lastly, member states have agreed on a new euro area framework for crisis management. Experience has shown the need to provide temporary financial support to EA Member States facing impaired access to market financing, 4 As you know, a new facility, the EFSF, was created in May 2010 for a three year period. It has been used to support and finance the Irish program and will be used for the Portuguese program. Although nominally set at 440bn its effective lending capacity was in fact limited to 250bn, an amount which may have been insufficient to instill confidence in the markets. Last March, an agreement was reached to raise that capacity to an effective 440bn. Member states also agreed on a permanent crisis management framework due to be implemented in 2013 and mainly based on a European Stability Mechanism (ESM) with an effective lending capacity of EUR 500bn. That mechanism will have the possibility of exceptional interventions in sovereign debt primary markets. Identical and standardized Collective Action Clauses (CACs) will be included in all new euro area government securities, with maturity above one year, from July 2013. Their basis will be consistent with the CACs that are common in New York and English laws. Significantly, all those mechanisms associate the IMF and the European Commission "in consultation" with the ECB to avoid relying only on peer pressure between members states and ensure proper conditionality. As you know, the crisis has also led the Eurosytem to embark on a very limited program of bond purchases. It was our judgment that the transmission mechanism of monetary policy was severely impaired in some cases, as local bond markets were close to paralysis. That program has served us well. Monetary impact was instantly and fully sterilized. Where do we stand? Overall, those changes have been favorably received by the markets. Spreads and CDS on most sovereigns have been trending down since January. Nevertheless, the sense of crisis has not yet disappeared. Most recently, 5 Portugal has asked its European partners, as well as the IMF, for financial assistance. A joint IMF / EU program is currently being finalized. At the European level, we expect the 78 bn Portuguese program to be endorsed at the next meeting of Economic and Financial Ministers on May 17th. However, the persistence of the sense of crisis may also lay in the fact that the success of existing programs remains to be demonstrated. In that regard, one may consider the utmost importance of conditionality embedded in these programs. What does conditionality means? Conditionality means that countries under a joint EU/IMF financial assistance program are committed to make structural reforms, whose benefits and positive impact could not immediately be assessed. These programs pave the way for stronger and more sustainable growth in the near future. If you look at Eastern European countries who received conditional financial assistance from the EU and the IMF two or three years ago, you will conclude that these programs proved to be highly useful and successful. Hence, the assessment has to be careful before being definitive. The time of economic policy is not the time of market sentiment, and I am convinced that Japanese Authorities, recently confronted with unthinkable and painful challenges, share this view. To come back to the European situation, the very progressive elaboration of the new European framework has prevented outside analysts to see the big picture and measure the amplitude of the changes. To put it in a nutshell, in just one year, since May 2010, the EU has embarked on a radical overhaul of its economic governance, while managing the sovereign crisis. This is a great achievement, especially when considering the multiplicity of actors at stake and the creativity of the answer which had to be combined with the respect of public opinions. There is also a more diffuse concern about sustainability, which I would like to discuss. Looking at aggregate numbers, it is very difficult to understand many of the concerns expressed on the euro area. The Euro area is the only major currency zone with its external accounts in balance, and which therefore does not depend on external finance. This is an essential element of robustness 6 and, for outside investors, provides a strong guarantee of long term solvency. Its aggregate fiscal balance (with a 2010 deficit at 6,3% of GDP) is the most favorable of all advanced economies ( US is at 10,5%, UK at 9,6% and Japan at 7,7%). The same holds true for public debt which stands at 92% of GDP similar to 93% in the US versus 200% in Japan. But, of course, markets, and analysts do not look always at the euro area as a whole. Because fiscal policies remain national, they tend to assess separately the situation of public finances in each individual country. While most analysts would acknowledge the magnitude of the efforts undertaken, some tend to take a very pessimistic view about future outcomes. As I understand it, that pessimism can be articulated around two lines of argument. First, the amplitude of fiscal consolidation will negatively affect growth for a very long time making it impossible to service debt and leading unavoidably to some kind of restructuring. And second, this economic stagnation will trigger strong political reaction which, ultimately, would put the very existence of the euro area at risk. In short, the whole reasoning is based on the euro area, and more specifically, its periphery, being unable to return to normal growth anytime in the foreseeable future. This is a very dramatic assumption and it matters a lot because, as we all know, the dynamics of debt are extremely sensitive to forecasts about future growth. Small changes in projections can have a huge impact on sustainability. Some of the implicit assumptions underlying current negative judgments seem to me seriously misguided. Let's look first at the short run. As you know, we have been recently surprised on the upside with the dynamics of growth in the Euro area. Consumer confidence is almost back to pre crisis levels, PMI are at an all time high and GDP growth will almost certainly be above potential, on average, for the year 2011. Those developments take place at a moment where drastic fiscal consolidation programs are implemented in all countries. Those analysts who predicted that fiscal tightening would stifle growth in the Euro area are 7 currently being proven wrong. Positive confidence effects in the private sector are outweighing the negative impact of public expenditure reduction. In our economic jargon, we seem to be living to day in a "Ricardian" world. What about countries in the periphery? Spanish growth rate swung from  3.7% in 2009 to -0.1% in 2010, despite the fact that a major austerity plan was being implemented. Spanish exports are booming with an increase of 10% within the euro area in 2010 and 19% outside the euro area in 2010. This compares very favourably with performances of other countries both inside and outside the eurozone. Turning to the long run, it is essential, when looking at the inner workings of the euro area to make a distinction between real and nominal evolutions. Real convergence is occurring between various parts of the zone and I think this process will continue and support growth in the future, contrary to over simplistic descriptions One overlooked fact is the very fast productivity catch up in the periphery of the euro area. Between 2000 and 2008, cumulative labor productivity growth in Greece, as measured by the output per employee, was 14,7%, and 10,2% in Ireland. Both significantly outpaced Germany (6,1%). This is exactly what you would expect in an integrated economic and monetary area and this process should continue in the future, provided that appropriate policies are implemented. Economic convergence will therefore boost growth and support the return to debt sustainability. Now, looking at nominal evolutions, a very different picture emerges. During the same period nominal wages grew by a total of 42% in Ireland and 52% in Greece vs only 7,4 % in Germany. The nature of the challenge, therefore, is clear. There has to be a regime change in the way nominal wages and prices are set in some parts of the euro area. As Central Bankers, we have been making that argument for years. One benefit of the crisis has been that this message is now fully accepted by Governments and public opinions. Strong reforms are currently being pushed in labor markets legislation as well as wage determination in the public sector in many countries. 8 I'll end up with a few words about the banking sector. I have the privilege to be both a Central Banker and a supervisor. From that vantage point, I will make four remarks : 1/- Revenues for the twelve biggest European banks have grown, in aggregate, by 8.6% in 2010 (as compared, to 2.5% for the main US banks). As a result, European banks Core Tier 1 ratios stood at between 8.5% and 15.3% at the end of 2010 (corresponding numbers for US banks are between 8.4% and 13.3%). Our "universal banking model", based on a diversity of activities and sources of income is proving its resilience. 2/ - Obviously there is a circular causality between government debt and the banking sector. Spreads on public debt naturally act as floors for the funding costs of banks. And, conversely, doubts about banks solvency create expectations of public support and deterioration in public finances. This gives rise to multiple equilibria where sudden shifts in confidence can be self fulfilling and create difficulties which, previously, did not exist. This process has been at work in a number of cases in the Euro area during the last year. 3/ - The main purpose of the stress tests is to break that circularity. Our first european tests encompassed 81 banks vs only 19 for the US. The basic exercise was sound and taken as such by analysts when it was published. Somehow clumsily, however, a few banks were added at the last moment, with only limited investigation, and these are precisely the banks which proved problematic afterwards, which undermined the credibility of the whole exercise. That mistake won't be repeated. 4/ - A lot has been made of the fact that no sovereign stress was made on the banking book. And indeed, as regulators, we did not want to give any credibility to a scenario that we consider unacceptable. However, there was full, total, and transparent disclosure of exposures to sovereigns for each in individual bank. Everybody is free to make their own assumptions and calculations. With knowledge of the exposure, it does not take a rocket scientist to figure out some scenarios. It turns out that such calculations would 9 produce very reassuring numbers. But, for some reasons, they never were publically made by most analysts. Just as an illustration, the total exposure of French banks to sovereign debt in the southern part of Europe is 38% of total tier one (13% without Italy). I'll let you make your own conclusions. Even in an apocalyptic scenario, only a small fraction of French banks tier one ratio would be compromised. The same results apply, with some variations, to other countries. Conclusion Let me now conclude. Like all other major advanced economies, the euro area is facing big challenges in adjusting to the post-crisis environment. For all, those challenges relate to long term fiscal sustainability. They are neither bigger nor smaller for the euro area than for the US, UK or Japan. They may be more complicated to solve because, by nature, our governance is more complex and we face specific collective action problems. It may take us longer to deal with difficulties as they appear, and we are paying a price for this relative inertia. But problems are being tackled, reforms are being implemented and I am convinced that, at the end, the Euro area will emerge as a stronger and more robust entity than before the crisis. As for the European System of Central Banks, I can assure you that we stand ready to act as forcefully as necessary to ensure price stability and preserve the integrity of the euro, which is, today, our most precious common good. 10

Title: Annual report of the ACPR
text: AUTORITe DE CONTRoLE PRUDENTIEL (PRUDENTIAL SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY) - ANNUAL REPORT 2011 Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and Chairman of the Autorite de controle prudentiel Ladies and gentlemen, Let me say first of all how pleased I am to host this press conference which has been organised to coincide with the publication of this second annual report of the Autorite de controle prudentiel (ACP). The newness of this institution, which was officially set up in 2010, has no doubt contributed to the dynamism that it has shown during this crisis period. Independent, but operating under the aegis of the Banque de France, the ACP has acted efficiently and quickly to ensure financial stability and enhance the protection of customers and clients of banks and insurance companies. It has also effectively projected Frances voice in international negotiations concerning its domains of competence. Before saying a few words about the challenges facing the Authority in 2012, I would like to develop two points that in my view best characterise 2011: the solidity of our financial system in a period of severe crisis on the one hand, and the evolution of our prudential supervision methods and instruments on the other. Jean-Philippe Thierry, Vice-Chairman of the ACP, will continue this overview by talking more specifically about the insurance and mutual insurance segment. I) My first point: the French financial sector has demonstrated its robustness in a context of severe crisis. Whereas the 2008 crisis was above all a global crisis triggered by the rapid deflation of the US real estate bubble and its associated financing, the crisis that began to spread as of mid-2011 is focused on the euro area: a crisis of sovereign debt and financial institutions in the euro area. Because the French banks have 1 the broadest geographic coverage in Europe and because they have the most internationally open scope of activities, they have been particularly affected by the crisis. In just several weeks last summer, French banks lost nearly 250 billion dollars in US money market financing, their share prices fell to half or a third of their value and their capacity to pursue a sustained activity of financing the economy looked seriously compromised, especially as these events coincided with the tightening of regulatory constraints that put even more pressure on them. However, this was not the case. Of course, what we call the cost of risk increased considerably in 2011 with the need to provision the risk associated with Greek debt. But the distribution of credit remained buoyant and the net banking income of French banks remained stable (-1.5% for the five main banking groups). Their aggregated profit, down 36% compared with 2010 to 14 billion euro was substantially higher than the 2008 and 2009 level, and this allowed them to significantly bolster their own funds and to continue financing the French economy. The ACPs vigilance has been decisive in helping the banks to maintain a satisfactory liquidity and solvency situation. In 2011, the ACP conducted 136 on-site inspections; the risk profiles of 700 institutions were analysed according to a harmonised procedure with, notably, a sustained pace of meetings with the senior managers and heads of the main business lines, thereby allowing the ACP to draw up detailed maps of the main risks to which they are exposed. During 2011, the two principal dimensions of prudential supervision  monitoring credit institution liquidity and solvency  required particular vigilance by the ACP. Credit institutions' liquidity levels were monitored more closely, particularly in its dollar resources dimension; this is an area where the rationale behind the ACPs being placed under the aegis of the Banque de France  which is responsible for central bank refinancing  is clearly demonstrated. By ensuring that the adequate risk provisioning, the reduction of managements and market participants' compensation and the allocation of the bulk of profits to strengthen own funds, the ACP has managed to ensure  over the longer term  the solvency of the French banking sector. Today, all the major banking groups have Core Tier 1 own funds ratios above 9%. This confirms their capacity to meet the targets set for 30 June 2012 by the European Banking Authority (EBA), thereby contributing to their adaptation to the future Basel III regulatory framework and the fulfilment of the objectives announced to the market. Lastly, the ACP has resolutely placed its individual supervision within a macro-prudential perspective. Our Authority has been particularly attentive to the way banks fulfil their role in financing the economy via the extension of loans to non-financial companies and to households, in a context in which both regulatory changes and liquidity constraints, particularly in dollars, have prompted certain groups to deleverage. It has undertaken an in-depth analysis and published studies on developments in household credit as well as the reallocation of households' financial investments, particularly between bank savings products and insurance savings products. II) 2011  and this is my second point  was a year that saw the reinforcement of the methods used in prudential supervision. It was above all the year in which the process of merging banking and insurance supervision was completed. Having been set up in the midst of the crisis that we are going through, the ACP continually reviews the methods it uses to deal with new challenges. 2 On the one hand, the traditional activities of on- and off-site inspections have been enhanced by taking the best procedures and practices from each of the two sectors, leading to improved quality and comparability in the assessment of the situation of the different institutions being inspected. During the year, the ACP thus developed a more cross-functional mode of operating, thereby responding to the intention that led the Government to merge the former authorities in 2010. The ACP's College has set out priorities for the supervision of each of the two sectors in a coordinated manner, and the ACP has set up an autonomous and cross-functional research directorate. On the other hand, in line with international and European initiatives, the ACP's supervisory methods are complemented by the "stress test" approach to ever more complex scenarios and by the monitoring of the systemic nature of certain institutions. Organised by the European authorities (the EBA for banks and the EIOPA for insurance companies) and the Basel Committee respectively and implemented concretely in France by the ACP, these approaches supplement the individual supervision of banks and facilitate the macro-prudential supervision of the financial system. The ACP's supervision methods have also fully taken on board its remit with respect to consumer protection, which is an essential condition for maintaining consumer confidence in the French financial sector. The ACP's mandate is to promote, in coordination with the AMF  the report of our joint unit will be presented to you shortly  the sound conduct of market players' commercial practices without hampering responsible financial innovation that is suited to each category of customers. In 2011, the ACP thus took a whole range of measures, of which I will only mention the main ones. The ACP has put in place a system for monitoring advertising and contracts that enable it to analyse promotional material. By means of a survey conducted among over 300 institutions, the ACP also checked compliance with the provisions made by banks to facilitate banking mobility. In addition, in order to reinforce its activities at local level, the ACP works with the Banque de France branch network, which is mobilised to carry out inspections of insurance intermediaries. All of these actions have made it possible to identify good practices in the area of the marketing of banking and insurance products and five recommendations in the area of consumer protection were published during 2011. I may mention in particular the recommendation relating to the measures that insurance undertakings must implement to deal with conflicts of interest when consumers are offered unit-linked insurance policies composed of bonds and other debt securities from an issuer that is financially linked to the insurance undertaking. To conclude on this point, I will add that, although the legislation applicable to the revised sanctions procedure was only published in the middle of the year, the ACP began to exercise its power to impose sanctions with three decisions that mainly concern breaches in terms of internal control and anti-money laundering procedures. III) 2012 is a year of intense preparations for the forthcoming regulatory developments. Throughout 2011, the ACP actively participated in the preparation of the transposition of the "Basel III" agreements into European law which is due to be adopted in mid-2012 and in the negotiations preparing the entry into force of "Solvency II". At national level, the preparation of banks for the new "Basel 2.5" and "Basel III" regulations was one of the priorities of the on-site inspections and of the teams responsible for preparing authorisations for the use of internal models notably for market risk. 3 In 2012, the ACP will continue with its work helping the market to adjust to the new regulatory frameworks, notably by putting in place, in coordination with the supervised institutions, the new procedures for prudential reporting. With regard to banks, I also see a number of areas where decisive progress is expected in 2012. Without going into detail at this stage, I will just mention:  the work on the regulatory framework applicable to systemic banks, which will be pursued with the idea of taking into account that, owing to their size relative to a domestic market, certain banks can generate major systemic risk in a given country;  the finalisation of liquidity regulation, which must revisit the stress test scenarios applied to banks' assets and liabilities as well as the scope of assets deemed to be liquid;  the adaptation of the French regulatory framework for all of the institutions that are currently credit institutions according to our national definition but which will lose this status under the new European definition, which is much more restrictive;  the overhaul of the banking crisis resolution mechanism, with the French mechanism  in anticipation of the forthcoming European projects  not having been updated to integrate the more powerful crisis management instruments resulting from the G20 guidelines;  the deliberations, in both the European and French frameworks, about better organisation of banking activities and of the relationships between investment banking and retail banking. The ACP will ensure that there is coherence between these different initiatives so as to avoid any unanticipated negative impacts. * * * Before handing over to Jean-Philippe Thierry, I would like to stress that, although the difficult macroeconomic context persists, I remain confident about the robustness of the French financial sector. It has the necessary fundamentals to actively participate in the financing of the economy and in particular of SMEs and VSEs, whose activity is mainly financed by bank lending. The return of growth in France and the health of the financial sector depend on this. It is a fact that rigorous risk management in each institution is indispensable to ensure financial stability. These past few years have also shown the full scope of the role of the supervisory authorities and have proved that the interventionist nature of their activities is a crucial element that regulation, however exacting, cannot replace. The forthcoming developments in prudential regulation in the banking and insurance sectors will only be fully effective if the efforts made by the institutions in 2011 to prepare and adapt are followed through. One of the ACP's main tasks in 2012 will be to help them to do this. 4

Title: Why the euro Past present future
text: Intervention of Christian Noyer Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry in France July 18, 2011 Why the euro? Past, present, future. Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure and honour for me to be with you today and I thank you most sincerely for inviting me to speak before you. I thank the Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry in France for organizing this meeting and in particular its President Mr. Nakajima and its Secretary General Mr. Nagatsuka. I would also like to thank Mr. Suzuki of the Bank of Japan and Mr. Tsuruoka, President of Mitsubishi France who participated in its preparation. The links between the Bank of France and Japan are many and diverse, and I am personally delighted. We have very frequent and friendly exchanges with the Bank of Japan of course, but also with different actors of the Japanese economy, in France or in Japan. I always have great pleasure in these exchanges, all of which are very enriching. I would like to take this new opportunity for dialogue to talk about the single European currency, the euro. I imagine you already know a lot about that. But the news is very extensive - a little too much for my taste by the way... - and I have the impression that it can sometimes leave perplexing observers foreign to the area. You have to tell yourself that our system is incredibly complicated, between the surprising decision-making processes and the 1 cohabitation of federal policies and national issues. We are not a federation, but our states have voluntarily renounced certain attributes of their sovereignty, first and foremost the privilege of minting money. We have the only stateless currency in the world, and I am willing to believe that this is extremely difficult to conceive. The purpose of my remarks today is therefore to shed light on this European curiosity, which fascinates but also sometimes worries, as may be the case at present. To summarize its history and project us into its future, I want to compare the different phases that the euro has experienced to that of a human life: a thoughtful conception, a happy and carefree childhood, an eventful adolescence and, finally, I hope and I believe, a peaceful and solid adulthood. *************** 1. [Thoughtful and meaningful design] You know that the whole essence of the project of European integration is the reconciliation of the peoples of Europe after centuries of devastating struggles. Peace was therefore the primary objective, and even if the new generations tend to take it for granted, we must never forget that it is the basis of our union. The founding fathers of the European Union, after the Second World War, were aware of the fact that the construction of a political Europe was random and probably premature, and therefore chose to privilege the progress of economic integration, certain that Europe would be made "by concrete achievements creating first of all a de facto solidarity" in the words of Robert Schuman. This is Jean Monnet's famous "small steps" method. Little by little, integration is deepening, the Union is enlarging, and there is no turning back: this is called the "acquis communautaire". Since the creation of the Common Market in Rome in 1957, this logic has put the economy in motion. 2 in the service of a very political, and even moral, goal, that of making reconciliation between the peoples of Europe irreversible. The creation of the single currency was fully in line with this vision and it is its most profound outcome. The euro was not built in a day. It is also the result of a set of concrete achievements: - a founding and pioneering report, the Werner Report of 1970; - after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, a first attempt to regulate exchange rate fluctuations between European currencies with the monetary "snake". This system lasted only 6 years, from 1972 to 1978; - the European Monetary System takes its place from 1979. The fluctuations of one currency against all the others are limited. A prototype of a single currency is also being created: the European Currency Unit (ECU), which in fact represents a basket of different currencies weighted according to their importance in economic activity. The role of unit of account, one of the three functions of the currency, is thus, for the first time, devolved to a single currency; - but fluctuation limits tend to be often exceeded and the system eventually implodes in the early 1990s. Those responsible at the time understood that more had to be done and provided in the Maastricht Treaty of 1992 for the establishment of a genuine monetary union with the creation of a single currency managed by a system of central banks, the Eurosystem. This Treaty has been approved by all the peoples of Europe, who have thus shown their support for this new crucial stage of their integration. 2. [A happy and carefree childhood] By creating the single currency, the European Union naturally aimed to equip itself with a powerful instrument at the service of its economic prosperity. The euro 3 made it possible both to avoid intra-European exchange rate crises generating trade and political tensions, to eliminate the costs associated with managing foreign exchange risk and to simplify business management, to increase competition through better price comparability, to promote the free movement of citizens throughout the territory of the Union and ultimately to increase the ECONOMIC PERFORMANCE OF THE EU, through a convergence of the economic policies of its members. After 12 years of existence, the results are there: the mandate of the ECB, which like that of the Bank of Japan, has as its priority the maintenance of price stability, has been perfectly respected since average inflation has been very slightly below 2%. Europeans have developed great confidence in our ability to fulfil this mandate. This is an essential point for supporting economic activity. Moreover, the credibility of the euro internationally has lowered French public borrowing rates from 7.3% in the 1990s to 4% in the 2000s and this trend was proven for all members of the zone until the recent crisis. 14 million jobs have been created in 12 years, compared to 8 million in the United States. The economic stability and strength that resulted from the first twelve years of the euro's existence obviously protected the economies of the zone, if only via the foreign exchange market, from much greater destabilisations than it experienced after the 2007 financial crisis. The achievement of the euro therefore appears to be a major achievement of European economic integration. But the euro is far from being a mere instrument at the service of an integrated economic area. It is also, in itself, a producer of meaning and identity for Europeans. The iconographic evolution of monetary signs, banknotes and coins, circulating in Europe is significant in this respect. In the past, coins frequently depicted monarchs in arms. Today, for euro banknotes, the theme of European architecture has been retained, with doors and bridges as symbols, oh so peaceful, of openness and exchange. 4 3. [An eventful adolescence] The euro has therefore had a happy first ten years. Happy by the support of the peoples, by the success of its technical implementation, by the beneficial results that it very quickly obtained. Happy also because carefree. We can say today that this beautiful "childhood" ended with the beginning of the sovereign debt crisis at the end of 2009. At that time, monetary union entered an eventful phase, of which I would like to say a few words. First of all, I would like to challenge the idea that the current crisis is a 'euro crisis'. This interpretation is wrong. The crisis we are going through is a sovereign debt crisis, not a currency crisis. Where and how did it start? Most euro area countries and EU Member States entered the 2007 financial crisis with sharply deteriorated fiscal positions. We were a long way from the "structural balance objective" that was the fundamental pillar of our fiscal framework. As a result, countries have all been hit hard, not only by an increase in spending but also, and above all, by a substantial decrease in their revenues. The fiscal deterioration has been accentuated in some countries by the volume of comprehensive guarantees provided to the banking sector. I would point out, by the way, that these problems were unfortunately not specific to the euro area. Public debt has increased by about 30% of GDP in the United Kingdom and the United States, and you know better than anyone that it is a major problem of the Japanese economy, even though, and this is important, Japanese debt is held almost entirely by domestic savers. Overall, the crisis has highlighted major deficiencies in the implementation of budgetary discipline and, more generally, of the 5 economic governance in the euro area. Given the inadequacy of market discipline, the founders of the euro anticipated the problem and set up the Stability and Growth Pact. Its principles were solid, its framework adequate but its implementation was very insufficient. To put it plainly, peer pressure has not been able to ensure rigorous and consistent adherence to the principles that had been agreed. I believe that two major mistakes have been made: - First, the states - including France and Germany - have weakened the Pact by not respecting either its preventive arm (they were not in balance over the cycle but permanently close to the 3% deficit), nor its corrective component (they never complied with the sanctions provided for). Secondly, the euro area did not have a competitiveness monitoring instrument from the outset. The basic idea is important and simple: when one adheres to a monetary zone whose stated objective is inflation a little below 2%, one must align the evolution of its unit costs of production on this objective of the Central Bank. In all the countries that have not been subject to this calculation and discipline, year after year, there has been a loss of competitiveness. The bottom line is that, once the countries had passed the passing test to enter the eurozone, they considered that they were protected from market pressures simply by belonging to the single currency - and they were de facto protected for ten years! In the event of an imbalance in their balance of payments, they no longer had an immediate sanction in terms of downward pressure on their currency. They have therefore lost interest in this problem and this has weakened the stability of the area as a whole. This is what we see very clearly today with countries that, no longer able to use the weapon of devaluation, must make real adjustments, particularly on wages. 6 The current crisis is therefore not a euro crisis but a sovereign debt crisis, that was my first point. Secondly, I would like to stress the importance of differentiating the situations of the countries concerned. Obviously, we are a monetary union, so observers tend to extrapolate the difficulties of one country to the whole area. But this is not the case. The "core" countries are solid, they have sustained growth, fiscal positions in the process of consolidation. And they represent a very large proportion of the GDP of the zone! Looking at aggregate values, it is very difficult to understand many of the concerns expressed about the euro area. It is the only major monetary area with balanced external accounts and therefore not dependent on external sources of financing. This is a decisive robustness factor which represents a high guarantee of long-term solvency for external investors. The aggregate budget balance of the euro area (with a deficit of 6.3% of GDP in 2010) is the most favourable of all advanced economies (the United States is at 10.5%, the United Kingdom at 9.6% and Japan at 7.7%). The same goes for public debt. It is therefore necessary to differentiate the overall situation of the area from the specificities of certain countries. If we take a closer look, which countries are most affected? There is Ireland. Ireland has had very strong growth over the last ten years with a service-based model. It had exemplary fiscal management, having managed to go from 130% debt/GDP in the early 1990s to 30% before the crisis. But Ireland has made a double mistake: it has overdeveloped a banking sector that is very involved in Anglo-Saxon real estate assets and the State has guaranteed the quasi-integrity of this sector. In 2010, the country suffered the shock of the financial and real estate crisis of the United States, banks went bankrupt and the state had to intervene massively. As a result, the budget deficit has exploded, causing panic in the markets. But it is clear that this is a one-off crisis. The 7 the country reacted very quickly by making a very courageous fiscal adjustment supported by public opinion. Wages have been cut in the public sector by 10-15% and growth is back. I therefore have no doubt that the case of Ireland does not pose a major problem, despite the further downgrading of the Irish rating last week. The case of Portugal is very different. The Portuguese economy has performed poorly in recent years. Growth and productivity have been weak and budget management has been very lax. So it's typically a sovereign debt crisis. But the programme put in place by the IMF, the European Commission and the ECB is credible. The growth potential can be greatly increased if the structural reforms that Portugal has not undertaken so far are finally implemented. The public is committed to this plan and we are confident that it will bear fruit. Finally, Greece is the only truly critical case. This country has accumulated the bad points: it has not made structural reforms, it has increased wages much faster than productivity and to top it all, it has made up its public accounts. The cocktail was explosive, and it exploded in late 2009. So a lot of things need to be revisited, and that is the purpose of the programme accepted by Greece. I believe that the room for manoeuvre is proportional to the shortcomings that the country has accumulated: it is very large. In particular, if Greece manages to collect its taxes better, reduce its personnel costs, reform its labour market and carry out the privatizations that are long overdue, the country will regain growth, sound public finances and therefore market confidence. This will obviously take time and will require socially painful efforts. But this is the only solution that the entire Eurosystem sees to the problem of Greece. 8 Finally, I would like to say that the current crisis is not a purely European problem. Most major developed economies are under pressure on sovereign markets. And the ability of each of these parties to emerge from this crisis is decisive for the global economic future. We Europeans therefore have a complete interest in the American and Japanese economies restarting more sustainably; just as you Japanese have every interest in us finding solutions to our specific problems. This is why the G20 has established itself as an essential forum since 2008. 4. [A Demanding Transition to Adulthood] These difficulties of the peripheral countries of the euro area have reminded us that it is indeed difficult to steer a single currency in a context of multiplicity of national budgetary and structural policies. This crisis vindicates those who have always felt that the "economic" pillar of economic and monetary union was not sufficiently developed. Today, learning must take place. Considerable progress has been made over the past year. At national level, all Member States have embarked on credible plans for the consolidation of public finances that are already bearing fruit. At EU level, a new framework has been defined based on two pillars. The first pillar is a strengthening of the Stability and Growth Pact, which has a much stronger preventive arm. Fiscal policy surveillance has been strengthened by more effective prevention/correction of excessive deficits. Public debt levels are better taken into account and sanctions will become more automatic. The second pillar includes a new procedure for monitoring competitiveness and, in particular, unit costs of production. Finally, Member States have agreed on a new crisis management framework for the euro area. Experience has shown the 9 the need to provide temporary financial assistance to euro area member countries facing difficulties in accessing market finance. As you know, a new mechanism, the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), was created in May 2010 for a period of three years. It has been used to support and finance the Irish programme and will be used for the Portuguese programme. Last March, an agreement was reached to increase its real capacity to 440 billion euros. Member States also approved a permanent crisis management framework, scheduled to enter into force in 2013, based mainly on the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), with an effective intervention capacity of 80500 billion. The ESM will be able to carry out interventions on an exceptional basis on the primary sovereign debt markets. Standardised and identical collective action clauses (CACs) will be incorporated from July 2013 into all new issues of euro area government securities with a maturity of more than one year. Their legal basis will be in line with that of the CACs under English and American law. Significantly, all these mechanisms involve the IMF and the European Commission in a process of "consultation" with the ECB, so as not to rely solely on peer pressure from other Member States and to ensure satisfactory conditionality. As you know, the crisis has also led the Eurosystem to embark on a very limited bond-buying programme to ensure the effectiveness of monetary policy in a market that is close to paralysis. This program has a proven track record. Its monetary impact was immediately and fully sterilized. It is therefore clear that the euro area has been able to find in itself answers to the crisis. And, as has often been the case in its history, I am convinced that Europe will manage to emerge from its difficulties stronger and stronger. Once the particular cases of certain peripheral countries are dealt with, the euro area will be able to look to the future with confidence: 10 With healthier public finances and convergence of competitiveness, it should be less vulnerable to shocks and if it were nevertheless to suffer new ones, it will be well equipped to respond to them. In this crisis, the eurozone has finally re-experienced the "de facto solidarity" of which Robert Schuman spoke. The idea at the time, as you know, was to pool Franco-German coal and steel, so strategic for the production of armaments and the functioning of economies, so that war in Europe would become not only "unthinkable" but also "materially impossible". The Member States of the ECSC and then of the European Union would have no choice, in the event of difficulties, but to seek common solutions to shared problems. In my opinion, the establishment of monetary union is based on the same reasoning: by linking their monetary destiny, the Member States of the euro zone voluntarily withdrew a weapon (the currency and competitive devaluations) to deepen the common market. They also accepted the idea that in the event of a crisis, they should, in fact, show solidarity. It seems to me that it is this very powerful dynamic that is currently being implemented for Greece and that it is the key to the future of us all. I hope that this presentation has completed your understanding of our single currency. I recognize that this is a complex, ambitious and still recent experience that can therefore raise questions. But I hope I have shown you that it has very solid foundations and that it is progressing little by little, crisis after crisis, towards maturity. It is, I believe, our most precious common good in Europe and an asset to the global economy. And as for its future, I will conclude with a formula of one of the fathers of the European project, Jean Monnet: "what is important is neither to be optimistic nor pessimistic, but determined". Believe 11 although I, like all European leaders, are completely so. Thank you for your attention. 12

Title: Tribune JDD The euro, remarkable success
text: "The euro, a remarkable success" Op-ed by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France - Le Journal du Dimanche - 1 January 2012 The euro is the culmination of half a century of desire to live together and the expression of a very strong democratic will. So strong that we made an irreversible monetary choice by voting for the Treaty. We are now 332 million Europeans who share the same currency. The euro is also, despite the recurrent criticism, the best insurance to protect our purchasing power. Over the past decade, our independent monetary policy has contained inflation at an average of 2% per year in the euro area and at 1.7% in France. Let us remember that prices rose by 9% per year in the 1970s and by 7% in the 1980s. Despite this historic success, there is a feeling of rising prices. In reality, it is everyday goods that have increased, due in particular to the surge in raw materials and taxes on gasoline and tobacco. Conversely, durable goods, such as automobiles and household appliances, have fallen significantly and total inflation has been stable and moderate. A currency recognized all over the planet Finally, for the economy, the euro has facilitated trade, the mobility of people and competitiveness between countries. Not to mention our interest rates, which have fallen a lot in the last ten years. If growth and job creation have not been as strong as we would have liked, it is not because of the euro. We have not attacked our structural rigidities head-on, unlike Germany. On arrival, the euro is undeniably a remarkable success. In ten years, it has become the world's second largest reserve currency after the US dollar. Few people today still count in francs or in their original currency. Eurosceptics are mostly outside Europe. If we implement the decisions taken at the Brussels Summit, we will emerge strengthened. And in ten years, the euro may be the world's leading currency.

Title: New Year's Greetings
text: Paris, Monday, January 16, 2012 Greetings from Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the Autorite9 de Contrf4le Prudentiel Ladies and gentlemen, today I wished to extend my most sincere wishes for a Happy New Year to each and every one of you, to your staff and to your institutions.
