Perhaps more than ever, the Banque de France is counting on the Place as a whole to meet them and contribute to the proper functioning of the French economy: we will ensure this and we will help you. The decision that has just been taken by one of the main rating agencies with regard to the countries of the euro area is obviously an additional challenge. However, the strategy of the Member States seems to me to be the right one. It is based on three inseparable components: strong actions to restore public finances, with progressive consolidation measures such as pension reforms; structural reforms to strengthen potential growth and competitiveness; a reform of governance so that these various actions are resolutely maintained in the long term. The ECB and the Eurosystem more generally will continue their determined action to counter abnormal market developments and ensure the best possible transmission of monetary policy. I see three main challenges for the coming year: - continue to ensure the proper financing of the economy - control risks and adapt to new regulations - promote the Place de Paris 1 Ensuring the proper financing of the economy First, the good financing of the economy is undeniably one of the keys to activity in 2012. In France, access to bank credit is essential, even more so than in other European countries. It is therefore imperative that credit institutions show a resolute dynamism in the granting of loans, in particular to VSEs, SMEs and mid-caps that have almost no direct access to the market. I know how complex the environment is for you: the markets have been very nervous, you have had to deal with dollar financing restrictions and you have to adapt to important regulatory reforms. But I urge you not to give in to the temptation of restriction. It would only create difficulties for businesses, curb consumption, and quickly undermine the very quality of your commitments and risks. I particularly urge you not to be late in covering the needs of businesses. An overly cautious attitude on the part of banks in access to credit could only lead to a deterioration in the economic situation and therefore to an increase in risks, when that is precisely what you are trying to avoid. Banks are at the very heart of financing the economy and states. That is your fundamental role. You were the first to suffer from market mistrust and you are now in the best position to help restore confidence. You must participate in the virtuous circle that brings back trust. I am therefore counting on you to ensure that outstanding loans do not decrease in the first months of 2012, especially those of cash flow for SMEs, which may be in great need of this support to make this start to the year less easy than last year. The Bank of France, the Eurosystem, and all the major central banks of the world support you in your action in the service of the good financing of the economy. It is also for this reason that my expectations in this regard are so high. 2 On 30 November, the central banking community reduced the cost of the liquidity they provide through dollar facilities. The ECB lowered the main policy rate from 1.5% to 1.25% in November 2011 and then to 1% in December 2011. Following the re-emergence of strong market tensions during the summer, the Eurosystem has also taken very strong decisions aimed at strengthening banks' liquidity positions, both in the short term and in the medium and long term. In terms of short-term needs, we have extended until a minimum of July 2012 the fixed-rate tendering procedures with full bidding service. and we reduced the minimum reserve ratio from 2% to 1% as of 18 January 2012, freeing up around 80100 billion of liquidity across the euro area, including 8020 billion for the French banking system; With regard to medium- and long-term needs: we first decided to reactivate the covered bank bond purchase programme; we then set up, for the first time, three-year refinancing operations. The first of these operations took place on 21 December and enabled 523 institutions to borrow 80489 billion. This is an operation of unprecedented magnitude. It should make it possible to cover a large part of the banks' financing needs and, above all, to ensure banking support for our economy. In addition, our decision to relax the eligibility criteria for collateral for refinancing operations also shows our firm determination to support the financing of the economy. Certain categories of ABS - those whose underlying assets are mortgages or loans to SMEs - have seen their eligibility extended to lower ratings; in addition, we want to promote the use of private debt as collateral for refinancing operations. In addition to the encouragement provided by 3 the Governing Council to use this type of collateral more systematically; it will be possible to relax, temporarily, the eligibility rules of these claims, at the risk of each NCB, and according to modalities that are being defined: opening to dollar receivables, lowering the minimum rating required in order to go up to a probability of default from 1% to 1 year, taking into account residential mortgages .... Of course this enlargement will be done in a prudent way with adapted haircuts. I would like to point out that the Bank of France has been very active in the preparation of all these decisions and will continue to be so in 2012. In addition to the initiatives implemented at Eurosystem level, it also initiated in 2011 a reflection on the securitisation of "small" private receivables (i.e. less than 80500,000), in close collaboration with the Groupe Infrastructures de Place (GIP). It will be completed in 2012 by a reflection on the development of the use of private receivables in market financing, in the form of repo. Controlling risks and adapting to new regulations The second major challenge for 2012 is, in my opinion, the proper adaptation of banks and insurance companies to the new regulations. The Autorite9 de Contrf4le Prudentiel will monitor these developments closely; it is certain that the markets will also be very interested in it. For banks, June 30, 2012 will be an important event. By that date, they will have to display a "Core Tier One" ratio of 9%, in accordance with what was required by the European Banking Authority at the end of 2011. For the four French banks subject to the financial year - BNP Paribas, Groupe BPCE, Groupe Cre9dit Agricole and Socie9te9 Ge9ne9rale; the total additional capital requirement was estimated at 807.3 billion, compared for example to the 8050 billion of additional equity accumulated since the end of 2008. I consider that they are well equipped to do so, relying in particular on their internal capacity to generate equity by setting aside results and by an adequate dividend distribution policy. Unlike your AMERICAN counterparts, you have already integrated the new Basel 2.5 ratios, which significantly strengthen fund requirements. 4 market risks - on average a 3-fold increase. The strengthening of capital will have to continue beyond these years in view of the transition to Basel III. This year, you will also focus on other regulatory developments, including liquidity management and corporate governance. There is no doubt that, in the latter area, exemplary remuneration behaviour and rigour in risk management remain essential objectives. For insurance, the challenge is called "Solvency 2". In 2011, the fifth impact study confirmed the overall strength of the French market and its ability to move to new standards in good conditions. The preparation must now go crescendo. As organizations enter the operational phase of implementation, it is a question, after having identified all the necessary information with the appropriate level of granularity, to prepare the processing chains in order to ensure the reliability of the data and the audit trail. Under Pillar 2, the definition and formalisation of procedures must also be completed. Similarly, the adaptation of governance and the strengthening of the integration of risk management into the general organization must be resolutely pursued. In addition, I want to draw your attention to various risks that we will be monitoring particularly this year. First, in 2012, credit institutions and insurance organizations will have to be cautious in their search for customer resources. In 2011, I drew the attention of the institutions of the Place, through the French Banking Federation, to the conditions of competition that some were engaged in in the collection of deposits from customers. This trend had indeed led some institutions to promote offers of remuneration for deposits on terms that sometimes appeared to be significantly disconnected from market rates. Such divergence could weaken the expected effects of our monetary policy on the cost of credit and could also weigh on the overall stability of the banking system. 5 On the occasion of these wishes, I would therefore like to once again strongly call on the institutions of the Place to show great responsibility in the implementation of the measures they are taking to prepare for the next international liquidity standards. It is important that each institution takes due account of market conditions when setting the conditions for remunerating the resources collected from its customers. In the same way, while it is true that in the last months of 2011, there was a decollection in life insurance, which nevertheless remains the preferred savings product of the French, I would remind you that too strong a revaluation of contracts in relation to the return on assets cannot be a response to such a development. It is also necessary to call for caution and to avoid committing to guaranteed rates of remuneration that would not reflect the reasonably foreseeable profitability of assets in support of contracts in Euros. I would also like to draw the attention of insurers to the fact that, more than ever, they must ensure the good governance of their asset management and pursue an investment policy in line with their liabilities. Although portfolios are generally of good quality and the French insurance sector remains globally resilient - notably property insurance and health insurance, which are dynamic - several factors make the environment difficult. In particular, a possible further decline in unrealised capital gains on investments in 2011 or low interest rates since the beginning of the crisis, which are generally penalising life insurance in the long term. In this context, it appears necessary to maintain a diversified investment policy, including good quality sovereign debt as well as other assets, bearing in mind that the benefits of diversification will be taken into account when determining market risks under Solvency 2. At the level of liabilities, the phenomenon of outflow in life insurance occurs in a context of tensions on liquidity in the banking system. The ACP will be particularly vigilant to ensure that developments that may occur, particularly within bank-insurers, do not pose increased risks to the stability of the French financial system. 6 Promoting the Place de Paris I would like to end these wishes by insisting on the fact that, despite or perhaps even because of the complexity of the environment you are facing, it seems important to me that you also take into account in your decisions the collective dimension and support of the Place de Paris. A strong and dynamic place is undoubtedly an asset for your establishments. Paris has areas of excellence that have nothing to envy to London or Frankfurt. This is particularly the case for our equity market and related activities, such as custody of securities or fund management in which French banks are leaders at European level. It is to be hoped that a possible financial transaction tax will not affect this excellence. Two elements seem to me to be essential in this respect: firstly, the reflection must obviously be European; secondly, the Commission's current draft raises many problems that deserve in-depth consideration. The support of the Place includes that of market infrastructures, which must be strong, efficient and cover a wide spectrum of activities. I believe that the determination of infrastructure objectives and strategy cannot be left to operational managers alone. The financial institutions that are the users, and most often the shareholders, must play a decisive role in their governance. This implies that you are ready to mobilize your best skills in the various areas concerned and probably also to act if it seems appropriate at the capital level. It can be observed that such efforts are being made in London or Frankfurt. I would like to mention three areas to which the establishments of the Place seem to me to have to pay particular attention. First of all, it is the euro equity markets which, whatever the outcome of the ongoing project between Nyse Euronext and Deutsche Bf6rse, should remain managed from Paris in line with the tradition of excellence that the Place has always been able to demonstrate in this field. 7 Then it is that of our clearing house LCH. Clearnet, which has demonstrated its ability to cope with the shocks resulting from the financial crisis and which has the necessary assets to develop its activities in its areas of excellence. Its role must be strengthened. In particular, the clearing of credit derivatives (CSD) which was launched in 2010 by Clearnet will be able to experience very significant developments in the coming months following the approval obtained in September by the British authorities and that expected by the American authorities (CFTC). Finally, the third area is the management of collateral and the development of the euro repo market. I would like to recall the recent launch in Paris of tripartite collateral management services for repo transactions delivered in euro, with or without the use of a central counterparty. Developed as part of a marketplace project involving the Bank of France, Euroclear France, Clearnet and banks, these services are intended to enable efficient and secure collateral management while facilitating trade-offs in collateral management between refinancing with the Eurosystem and market placement. The upcoming implementation of Target2 Securities (T2S), for which the support of the Place has been flawless, should give even more interest to this tripartite system by facilitating the circulation of securities and therefore by increasing the depth of the deposit, which seems to me to be of particular importance in the current context. *** As you know, 2012 is going to be a decisive year. I am counting on you, my expectations are high; but you can also count on the Bank of France to best serve, together, our common cause: the good health of our economy. I renew my best wishes for you. 8

Title: Senate hearing on the credibility of credit rating agencies
text: JOINT TASK OF PROVIDING INFORMATION ON THE FUNCTIONING, METHODOLOGY AND CREDIBILITY OF CREDIT RATING AGENCIES Hearing of 27 March 2012 at the Senate Robert Ophe8le, Second Deputy Governor of the Bank of France The role of credit rating agencies is at the heart of many of the processes that affect financial stability and, as such, challenge central banks. This afternoon it is neither their influence on the functioning of the markets nor their place in prudential regulation that will be the subject of my remarks, but their role in the very operations of central banks, in this case those of the Eurosystem. I will therefore deal more specifically with the place of agency ratings in our acceptance of assets to guarantee refinancing to banks and intraday overdrafts in the euro area's large payment system, Target, which we administer. However, it must be borne in mind that the eligibility of an asset for central bank operations has consequences that go far beyond mere operations with the central bank. In many financial transactions it is necessary to provide assets as collateral and whether or not these assets are eligible for central bank operations is decisive. On the other hand, this eligibility will no longer be a criterion used in the context of the future liquidity regulation, and I regret that. After the 2008 crisis, partly due to the agencies' overly favourable ratings on the quality of financial products backed by US housing loans, the G20 decided to reduce the dependence of the financial sphere on rating agencies and set among its priorities, the reform of their regulation and supervision the Financial Stability Committee (FSB) and it declined in October 2010 a dozen principles for ensure the reduction of this 1 dependency. In particular, the FSB invited central banks to develop their own risk analyses in order to avoid automatic consideration of agency ratings. What is the status of the Bank of France and the Eurosystem? I think we can make 2 observations: ? In the case of marketable securities, we make extensive use of agency ratings but with controls and corrections, ? For private debt, we favour internal bank ratings and central bank ratings; of course, the extent of the effective use of these ratings depends on the degree of maturity of the banks in their risk measurement and the involvement of the national central banks in the rating activity. First, a few details on negotiable securities. For this asset class, agency ratings remain essential references and there is no existing or in-preparation central bank-specific rating. But this dependence is limited by the following: ? For non-asset-backed securities (ABS, Covered) only the best rating is used, which makes eligibility less sensitive to possible downgrades decided by one or two agencies. ? Rating is not the only criterion used: o thus ABS with a complex structure are not eligible, even when they have the best rating, o conversely, sovereign bonds of programme countries have remained eligible even though their rating fell below the thresholds of common law. ? Gradually we are trying to favour products whose quality is not only the central bank but above all the market players are able to judge for themselves without mechanical recourse to agency ratings; this is the case for collateralised securities whose characteristics of the underlying assets will have to be tracked via dedicated infrastructures in order to be eligible for Eurosystem operations. Turning now to non-marketable assets, what we call private debt, their importance in pools of mobilizable or "usable" assets depends largely on the ability of central banks to value companies. This approach has always been at the heart of the Bank of France's policy, which based its refinancing of banks on their financing of the real economy. We have thus moved into France prior rediscount agreements, post-performance control and rating of companies by deploying a very important system in terms of human resources and information systems. The Bank of France is a rating agency and, to set the 2 Orders of magnitude, we note about 260,000 French companies and to do this we directly mobilize a thousand "eatp" on the territory. As a result, about half of the assets deposited as collateral at the Bank of France for central banking operations are private receivables. This proportion is less than 20 % in the rest of the Eurosystem. This reflects first of all the absence of a central bank rating mechanism in most other members of the Eurosystem, since only the Bundesbank, the Bank of Austria and the Bank of Spain have it and their tool is more modest than ours: only 30,000 companies are rated at the Bundesbank, for example. However, the role of private debt in refinancing is tending to increase as banks can rely on their internal risk assessment tools when these tools have been validated by banking supervisors as part of the implementation of their solvency regulation (CRD). Regardless of the type of asset mobilised, it is finally necessary to highlight an important development in the Eurosystem's practice which has the effect of limiting the dependence of our operations on ratings, whether from agencies, central banks or internal banks; it is the broadening of the range of accepted ratings. Before the 2008 crisis, we only accepted excellence ratings with a very low discount (haircut); we have since lowered our threshold of acceptability but increasing the associated reductions. This makes it possible to reduce the effects of thresholds and therefore the cut-off effects of rating downgrades while ensuring controlled risk-taking for the central bank in the event of non-repayment of loans. The Eurosystem did not wish to replace the rating agencies by engaging in a rating approach for sovereign or bank issues; Asked on this point by the Commission last year, the Governing Council of the ECB declined due in particular to the potential conflicts of interest that this would generate. However, the Eurosystem is moving cautiously but resolutely towards reducing the role of agency ratings in its operational system and the Bank of France is one of the driving forces behind this development. Title: Rebalancing Rigour and Economic Growth in Europe
text: Paris Europlace International Financial Forum July 3rd 2012 Roundtable 2: Rebalancing Rigour and Economic Growth in Europe Introduction by Christian Noyer Ladies and gentlemen, It is, as usual, a great privilege and a great pleasure for me to participate in the Paris Europlace International Financial Forum and I want to congratulate all the Paris Europlace team for the organisation. The theme of this roundtable is very topical: rebalancing rigour and economic growth in Europe. Indeed, the current combination of unprecedented levels of public debt and sluggish activity in the euro area poses numerous policy challenges to the governments. In particular, the challenge of finding the right balance between fiscal consolidation and growth-enhancing measures is crucial. But let me be clear: I see no trade-off, no contradiction between the two objectives. On the contrary, I believe that the two are mutually reinforcing and absolutely necessary. And I must add one other element that is essential to building a durably stronger euro area: the creation of a financial union to complete the monetary union. Let me say a few words on these three  as I said, completely interlinked  topics. 1. The fiscal consolidation efforts need to be pursued 1 The crisis of the euro area is rooted in the individual and collective inability to have followed a fiscal discipline during the first decade of existence of the single currency. Thus, the cure begins with fiscal consolidation and a more credible fiscal discipline framework. The efforts already made on the fiscal front by the individual countries of the euro area are already bearing fruit: not only is the absolute level of the euro areas deficit half that in the other major economies, but also the pace of fiscal consolidation is actually much greater. This is clearly an asset for us today and an element of confidence both for the markets and economic agents, which needs to be further enhanced. Beyond these national efforts, a more powerful common discipline framework has been put in place, representing significant progress towards a more integrated economic union. The legislative package (the so-called "Six Pack") entered into force in December and considerably reinforces the Stability and Growth Pact: the surveillance powers of the European Commission over national budgets have been enhanced, sanctions have become quasi-automatic, the criteria for public debt and public spending are being more closely scrutinised. In addition, the Treaty on Stability, Coordination and Governance establishes a comprehensive new fiscal compact. It includes in particular a requirement for the annual structural government deficit not to exceed 0.5% of GDP. At current debt levels, economic agents would react to fiscal permissiveness by delaying their own private expenditure. Financial markets would continue to impose very punitive interest rates on our countries to compensate for the uncertainty in the fiscal outlook. Overall, the confidence and financial benefits of fiscal consolidation far outweigh its negative effects on effective demand in the short run. It is of the essence that all the efforts on this side be decisively pursued. 2. Growth-enhancing measures are needed Another major explanation of the crisis is the development of competitiveness gaps between the euro area countries throughout the last decade. The economic rationale is easy to understand: when joining a monetary area whose goal is to achieve a rate of inflation of just below 2%, changes in its unit production costs must be in line with this central bank objective, modulo the productivity gains. In all the countries that did not abide by this calculation and discipline, year after year, there was a loss of competitiveness that the market did not take into account until the crisis. The new Stability 2 and Growth Pact now provides a framework for the surveillance of macroeconomic imbalances and competitiveness developments. Competitiveness is one of the major factors for long-term growth and that is why it is so important that we succeed in boosting it today. How? Through structural reforms of the goods and services and labour markets, for instance. Here, as well, the progress already made in many countries is impressive. In recent history, European economies have never reformed so extensively in such a brief period of time. I could cite many examples: the labour market reform in Spain and now in Italy, the pension reforms in Italy and France. Such reforms are a necessary foundation for dynamic and sustainable growth in the future and they must be vigorously pursued. Despite the constrained fiscal situation, there is also some room for direct public support for growth, which is all the more efficient if it targets long-term growth-enhancing projects. I believe this is precisely the idea of the EUR 120-billion package adopted at the European Summit last week. 3. Institutions matter: the need for a financial union in the euro area I believe that there is a third very important reason why the euro area has been so badly hit by the crisis; it is because we are a very highly integrated economic area but do not have the appropriate institutional mechanisms for this integration. In particular, this shortcoming explains the contagion effects and the negative feedback loops between banks and States, which have made matters much worse in the area. Obviously, the good and coherent functioning of the banking sector is absolutely vital for the euro area to become more stable, resilient and efficient. This conviction is based on some fundamental observations: Appropriate financing is essential for our economies to achieve strong and sustainable growth. In Europe, the banking system is the main source of financing, and hence its strength is of crucial importance; As long as the euro areas financial health is vulnerable to problems in one country, negative feedback loops between sovereign and banking risks can materialise. Besides, in a monetary union, capital is free to move very quickly from one country to another, thereby augmenting the potential incidence of bank runs if no supranational deposit guarantee mechanism is in place. These are significant threats to financial stability in the area; 3 Financial stability is critical not just for creating the right conditions for the appropriate financing of the economy. It is also an extremely valuable asset in fostering confidence, which has been severely lacking in recent years and is another key condition for growth. In addition, given the links between banks and sovereigns and the potential impact of a financial crisis on a countrys fiscal position, financial stability makes a major contribution to fiscal stability; As monetary policy transmits to the real economy mainly through banks and credit, it is of the utmost importance that the banking sector is not dysfunctioning in one part of the area if we want an efficient single monetary policy. For all these fundamental reasons, the euro area needs a new and concrete leap towards stronger financial integration. We need a consistent financial union entrusted with three main powers: A unified supervision of all the euro area banks (with the same kind of structure as the Eurosystem with one head -the European Central Bank- and decentralised implementation through national central banks as the crisis showed the importance of maintaining banking supervision close to the central bank); A deposit guarantee scheme, with massive firepower, provided that it could collect an annual contribution on all euro area banks and could borrow on the markets with a supranational guarantee; A banking resolution scheme (crisis management), with a resolution fund that could be either separate or mixed with the deposit guarantee fund. Of course, such a leap will require numerous steps and the elimination of a large number of substantial obstacles. But what it requires most is an unfailing political will from all euro area members to progress towards a stronger and more coherent economic and monetary union. I think that we saw a demonstration of this will during the Summit of last week: the work on the financial union has now started and we are determined to make it successful. Thank you for your attention. 4

Title: Oublic and private debt imbalances of global savings
text: Aix-en-Provence Economic Forum- 6 July 2012 Session 3  Public and private debt: imbalances of global savings Introduction by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France In introduction to this session, I would like to make seven remarks. 1  My first remark is inspired by the very title of this session. In advanced countries, the average public debt to GNP ratio is 100%. In emerging countries, the figure is 30%. This is a very wide gap, and it represents one of the global economys largest imbalances. And one of the least mentioned. It also represents a complete reversal of the situation compared with just over twenty years ago. At that time, I remember well, I was chairman of the Paris Club, and emerging countries came to ask for the rescheduling of their debt. 2  Second remark, global demand is still fairly concentrated on the advanced countries. Not only is their debt higher, but their savings (as a ratio of GNP) are lower. The G7 countries alone still account for 56% of global consumption. The problem is clear. How can we hope to raise our level of consumption if we need to reduce our level of debt and increase our savings? And if the advanced countries consumption stops growing, what will happen to global economic growth and particularly that of emerging countries with entirely export-oriented economies? 3  Which brings me to my third remark: we need the emerging countries to continue investing their savings in advanced countries. We therefore need properly functioning international financial markets. In a world where the savings and financing needs are so geographically dislocated, properly functioning financial markets are a prerequisite for economic growth. But, today the capital markets appear very unsettled and full of anomalies, and not just in Europe.  For example, certain sovereigns (the USA and UK for example) borrow today at historically very low nominal interest rates and at negative real interest rates despite the fact that their deficits are around 10% of GNP and that doubts exist regarding the future evolution of their debt levels.  Another anomaly: large corporations have accumulated unprecedented cash reserves (several trillions of dollars) despite numerous highly profitable and unexploited investment opportunities around the world, unsatisfied infrastructure needs and investment bottlenecks in commodities production. 1 4  Fourth remark. We can identify two reasons for this situation:  The first is the general and exceptional uncertainty weighing on the global economy. Uncertainty makes liquid and safe assets more attractive. It makes investment less attractive. It can therefore partly explain the phenomena that I have mentioned.  The second reason is more structural: a malfunctioning of our financial intermediation mechanisms. There are doubts about the solidity of banks in numerous countries. Debt markets are profoundly disrupted and international movements of capital have been highly volatile over the last two years. 5  Fifth remark. The intervention capacities of central banks are of course limited. They can remedy temporary market disruptions and situations of illiquidity caused by uncertainty. Recently they have intervened to an unprecedented extent, as reflected in their balance sheets. But they cannot permanently substitute financial markets and banks when financial intermediation malfunctions. Likewise, low or zero interest rates can contribute to stabilising the economy in periods of crisis, but if maintained over a protracted period, they can create distortions, encourage the formation of bubbles and create risk for long-term investors. Indeed, on this topic, I would like to make one observation. The question of monetary financing of deficits was raised by David Thesmar. Such financing cannot in any way resolve the problem of the dislocation between savings and investment, either at the national level or at the global level. Some central banks have developed large-scale public debt acquisition programmes. They have done so for reasons relating to immediate macroeconomic stabilisation... to go beyond the zero-interest rate limit. The Eurosystem as well intervened on a much smaller scale when malfunctioning debt markets prevented the effective transmission of monetary policy impulses. There is not a single central bank that is seriously considering the monetisation of deficits with the more or less declared intention of reducing the weight of debt via inflation. In my view, this notion is nothing more than a financial analysts fantasy. In fact, over the last six months, we have seen constant confirmation of the antiinflationary stance of monetary policy with, for example, the FED actually establishing a quantitative definition of price stability for the first time (in fact, identical to the one used by the Eurosystem). 6 - Sixth remark. Our immediate priority is therefore to construct or reconstruct the mechanisms and structures of a sound and efficient financial intermediation framework. That is why, at the euro area level, the financial union project is fundamental. At the global level, the FSBs role is crucial in developing a robust technical, regulatory and prudential architecture, adapted to the interconnection of our economies. 7  Seventh and last remark: fiscal policy and debt management. Here, I would say that we are all guilty of a certain degree of ambiguity, both at the market level and at the political level:  on the one hand we want public debt markets that are broad, deep and liquid, because they form the base on which our entire financial system is built. In particular, government bonds are the safest and the most liquid assets. They act as reserves of value for a large number of investors, starting with the central banks themselves which hold them as foreign currency reserves or as monetary policy collateral.  And on the other hand we want solvent States, i.e. with perfectly controlled deficits and levels of public debt, which logically places limits on the growth of public debt markets. 2 This contradiction is known by economists as the Triffin dilemma. It was first identified in relation to the U.S. balance of payments deficits and the value of the dollar, but it can also be applied to fiscal equilibrium. The economy needs a growing volume of risk-free assets, but the more they are issued, the more risky they become. We cannot totally side-step this dilemma, but we can avoid making it worse. It is clearly not good for major developed countries to find themselves in a situation where their solvency is put into question, or to allow markets to think that under certain circumstances, they may be unable to honour all their commitments. But this is what we have done in Europe, against the better judgement of the ECB, by introducing the principle of private sector involvement. The idea is attractive in theory. However, its consequences for financial stability are extremely negative. There has never been any doubt about whether the United Kingdom or the United States would honour their debts. Today they are enjoying very favourable interest rates compared with Spain and Italy even though the latters fiscal fundamentals are better. I know that some attribute this difference in borrowing conditions to the actions of the UK and U.S. central banks. I do not agree. I believe that Europe has a major project ahead of it to recreate a broad, deep and liquid public debt market that is completely and unambiguously free from insolvency risk. 3

Title: Tribune WSJ The next step for the euro area is the financial union
text: The next step for the Eurozone is the financial union Wall Street journal, 12 June 2012 By Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France The crisis has revealed that economic and monetary union is not complete: the single currency must be supported by a financial union. Our banks are now banks in the euro zone, they are no longer German, Spanish or French banks. They can borrow from the European Central Bank anywhere; they can lend to any citizen or company in the euro area. Depositors can easily transfer money from one country to another. We are all part of the same financial system. We are all winners when things are going well and we are all losers when something goes wrong. Yet Europe's banking supervision and deposit guarantee schemes are fragmented and remain country-specific, and banks are still considered "national" by markets and investors. This situation is the 1 source of many difficulties. We cannot, and must not, prevent capital movements from being selective within the European Union; there will always be differentiation based on investor preferences. But it is not logical, as we are currently seeing, for some banks to be heavily penalized in their financing and activities for the sole reason that "their" government has behaved, in the past, in a fiscally irresponsible manner, which weighs on their rating. This in turn hampers the transmission mechanisms of the single monetary policy, as credit conditions differ from one region of the euro area to another, despite the single key interest rate set by the central bank. As long as the financial health of the euro area as a whole is vulnerable to the problems encountered in a country, the negative interactions between sovereign and banking risks can materialise. We must break this link between sovereign and banking risks in order to avoid seeing the dangerous spirals and contagion that are at the heart of the crisis renewed in the future. For this to happen, we need a structure for the euro area that is responsible for deposit insurance, banking supervision and crisis resolution. Capitalizing on the success of the single monetary policy, we must now put in place a single supervisory system, organized according to the same principles: centralization of decision-making and decentralization of implementation. The ECB and the national central banks are well equipped to form the backbone of the financial union. This is another lesson from the crisis. Keeping banks supervised close to the central bank has many advantages. 2 The United Kingdom is returning to this organizational principle, having departed from it. In the United States, the Federal Reserve System has become the "systemic supervisor" that can designate any institution it deems to be of sufficient systemic importance to require its oversight. The ECB and the seventeen national central banks of the Eurosystem should also be empowered to monitor and supervise institutions with a significant cross-border presence or activities. But a true financial union must extend to all banking institutions, regardless of their size. This is all the more necessary as some medium-sized and regionally important banks have encountered far more difficulties during the crisis than more global institutions. This federalisation of banking supervision is a prerequisite for the creation of the single deposit guarantee fund, which is ultimately necessary to break the link between banking and sovereign risks. This fund would have massive firepower, since it could collect a tax on every bank in the euro zone and borrow on the markets. Finally, to be comprehensive, the financial union needs a single bankruptcy regime and a bank resolution system. As in the United States, the federalization of bank resolution must include all the necessary instruments: full harmonization of rules, of course, but also all operational tools such as recapitalization, restructuring, dismantling, the transfer of assets and liabilities to solid institutions and the ability to intervene to manage a bank in difficulty. These developments will require time, courage and determination. Harmonizing legislation and deciding on the division of responsibilities is a complicated process by nature. 3 But this is the raison d'eatre of the whole process of European integration. We have always been able to overcome crises and design appropriate responses. The current situation requires decisive progress on our part. We need to get to work now. 4

Enfin, pour tre complte, lunion financire a besoin dun rgime de faillite unique et dun systme de rsolution des dfaillances bancaires. Comme aux tats-Unis, la fdralisation de la rsolution des dfaillances bancaires doit comporter tous les instruments ncessaires : une harmonisation intgrale des rgles, videmment, mais galement lensemble des outils oprationnels tels que la recapitalisation, la restructuration, le dmantlement, le transfert des actifs et des passifs vers des institutions solides et la capacit dintervenir pour grer une banque en difficult. Ces volutions vont ncessiter du temps, du courage et de la dtermination. Harmoniser la lgislation et dcider du partage des responsabilits est un processus compliqu par nature. 3 Mais il sagit de la raison dtre de tout le processus dintgration europenne. Title: General Assembly of the ASF
text: Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France ASF General Meeting 13 June 2012 I am very honoured to speak at this new General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies (ASF). I am all the more pleased to take part in this exercise as it gives me the opportunity to present the actions and positions of the Autorite9 de Contrf4le Prudentiel (ACP) and the Banque de France, in a regulatory environment that will undergo major changes very quickly. In this regard, I will focus my speech on the developments expected in the context of CRD IV but will also address the issues surrounding consumer protection, subjects which, both, I am aware, represent an important issue for the members of the ASF. 1) Regulatory developments related to CRD IV As you know, the so-called CRD IV European reform has entered its final phase of negotiations with the publication in mid-May of the positions of the ECOFIN Council and the European Parliament's Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs (ECON). It should be stabilised in the summer of 2012, with entry into force at this stage set for 1 January 2013. This reform aims above all to integrate into European law the prudential reform of the Basel Committee ("Basel 3"). It also has another major objective: the effective harmonisation of management standards, which will make it possible to ensure that credit institutions are subject to the same rules regardless of their country of establishment in the European Union. This should not, of course, preclude any national flexibility, provided that it is strongly regulated; this is a point on which we must be very vigilant in the context of the current 'trilogue'. In practice, however, maximum harmonisation will require all credit institutions to be subject to future liquidity standards, even if they are clearly not suitable for all specialised institutions, in particular those that do not have a significant deposit-taking activity. Maximum harmonisation also involves the exercise of both activities, of receiving repayable funds from the public and granting credit, as provided for authorisation as a credit institution. . From a purely legal point of view, the approval of French financial companies has these two dimensions, since they can receive funds from the public on an ancillary basis. This approval is not 1 therefore not in law called into question by the entry into force of the future regime, but in view of the constraints it will impose, it could prove to be inappropriate. It therefore seems to me desirable, in accordance with European law, to introduce in France a special status, as already exists in other Member States, for companies that would like to specialise in certain types of credit activity, without having to collect deposits or then comply with the new liquidity rules. The members of the ASF could then choose between two options, depending on the contours that will be decided for this status: - either they would remain a credit institution and would therefore be automatically subject to CRD IV standards; - or they would renounce the status of credit institution and apply to benefit from the new status. In the first case, I would point out that the concept of receipt of repayable funds from the public would include, according to draft CRD IV directive, the proceeds of the continuous issue of bonds or equivalent securities. This makes it possible to receive funds from the public other than individual deposits. In the second case, the question arises of the contours of the prudential regime that would be put in place for these specialized institutions. On this complex and multidimensional issue, which has given rise to intense reflections in recent months between your members, the Directorate-General of the Treasury and my services, the final choices are naturally the responsibility of the Minister of the Economy, Finance and Foreign Trade. These choices also depend on the outcome of the "trilogue". I shall therefore confine myself to providing preliminary lines of thought from the point of view of the ACP and the Bank of France. In general, the possibility that institutions developing a major credit activity will no longer be subject to prudential regulation and fall outside the scope of the ACP's supervision seems to me to be totally excluded. The French approach that has prevailed so far has proved its worth and calling it into question would not be self-evident, especially in a context marked by the intensification of reflections on shadow banking at international and European level - as evidenced by the recent publication of the Commission's Green Paper. On the other hand, the question of which body of regulations should be applied is more open. In my opinion, several aspects must be taken into account, including: the preservation of financial stability, customer protection and a level playing field. This is an aspect to which I am very attentive, because it is fundamental to preserve the ability of the French financial system to finance the economy. Another important point is that we must ensure that the future rules that will ultimately be adopted are in line with the nature of the risks and activities developed by the different categories of financial companies. These elements call for a balanced solution, proportionate to the stakes and adapted to the different economic models of financial companies. Differentiated regimes may therefore appear useful depending in particular on the challenges to financial stability. It seems important to me, in any event, that the elements that make up the quality of today's financial companies should be as close as possible to the future characteristics of companies which, 2 tomorrow, will no longer be credit institutions. I am thinking here in particular of the definition of capital, the approaches applicable to credit and operational risk, as well as more generally governance. However, as we know, there are clearly requirements in the CRD IV project that are not easily applicable to undertakings with a different business model than credit institutions. I have already mentioned the liquidity ratios, the one-month one, the LCR, and the one-year ratio, the NSFR. Particularly in view of the absence of deposits and the nature of the credit activities carried out, it is far from certain that these ratios constitute in all cases the most appropriate regulatory response. In some cases, the solution of maintaining the rules in force in France seems to me to have to be explored, provided, as I said earlier, that this does not have an impact on the conditions of competition. Beyond these general questions, some more technical, but equally important, issues must be taken into account. This is the case for surety companies, which may, in the future, no longer be considered as credit institutions. The subject, of course, is the recognition of guarantee funds in equity. The problem is well known and well identified: a fund covering only credit risk cannot be assimilated to own funds, which are in essence called upon to cover all types of risks. Proposals for changes to the funds in place had to be carried out. They will be carefully examined. These guarantee funds are now subject to different prudential recognitions depending on their characteristics: the only certainty to date is that they will not be subject to uniform treatment tomorrow. The status quo is not a satisfactory option. The objective to be pursued is clear: the loss-absorbing capacity of these funds must be improved. This is the condition for improving, where appropriate, their prudential consideration. I would now like to turn to the second point of my speech, consumer protection. 2) Consumer protection The financial crisis has increased the need for consumer protection within the European Union and shown the importance of mutual trust between the customer and his bank for the maintenance of economic activity and financial stability. Designed in this direction, the 2008 Consumer Credit Agreements Directive, which is of maximum harmonisation, included provisions on advertising and pre-contractual information by credit intermediaries. These provisions have been included in the Lagarde law and supplemented by various regulatory texts aimed at defining and framing, on the one hand, intermediation in banking operations and, on the other hand, at giving the criteria defining intermediaries in banking operations and payment services (IOBSP). Clearer and more detailed regulations do not mean increased difficulties in their application. Financial companies, which use merchants, large distribution chains or equipment sellers to market their credits, generally know who they are working with. They monitor the turnover provided by their intermediaries and detect, in particular through the examination of the quality of the credit file or claims, those of them who pose a problem or do not apply the bases of the partnership agreement well. 3 They can then revoke this agreement. The commissions paid to these intermediaries are an important criterion in the monitoring of IOBSPs by the financial companies that mandate them. The entry into contact with customers, the presentation of credit agreements, the evaluation of the customer's knowledge and experience as well as his solvency are services that contribute directly to the execution of banking operations. They are also practiced daily in bank branches. Entrusting them to a third party on a lasting basis and on a regular basis obviously amounts to outsourcing them within the meaning of Regulation No. 97-02. When establishing a mandate to delegate to an IOBSP, the financial company therefore remains fully responsible for compliance with its obligations. Integrating intermediation in banking operations and payment services into the scope of the financial company's internal control does not mean delegating to it the control carried out by the ACP. It is simply signing a written contract, ensuring the quality and continuity of the service provided, the protection of confidentiality rules, the follow-up of the procedures defined by its establishment and being able to realize it on the spot. This is the well-understood interest of the financial company. And that the new regulation leads to a clarification of the roles and responsibilities of each can only have positive impacts on the functioning of the market. The CPA carries out its own checks on the proper application of the regulations and its own recommendations. She intends to develop them in the coming years at the IOBSP. There are certainly many IOBSPs, and the CPA cannot subject them all to its control every year. Nevertheless, its controls can be targeted through its action of verification of advertising, exploitation of complaints and all sources of information at its disposal. I therefore hope that I have dispelled your doubts and have also reassured you about the usefulness of this new regulation and the diligence that is incumbent on your respective institutions. * * * In total, the members of the ASF, who have played and continue to play a central role in the financing of the French economy, will be profoundly impacted by CRD IV, like all credit institutions for that matter. The extent of the changes will depend on the solutions that are finally adopted in terms of the statute and prudential regimes. At this stage, the precise and definitive outline of the latter is not known, as you can see, but I hope that I have today helped to clarify what, from the point of view of the ACP and the Bank of France, seems to have to be taken into account. However, I have no doubt that the continued mobilization of all stakeholders, the profession and the public authorities, will make it possible to quickly bring out a solution. 4

Title: Introduction Finding a new balance between rigour and economic growth in Europe
text: July 3, 2012 Paris Europlace International Financial Forum Round table 2: Finding a new balance between rigour and economic growth in Europe Introduction by Christian Noyer Ladies and gentlemen It is, as always, a great privilege and pleasure for me to participate in the Paris Europlace International Financial Forum and I would like to thank the entire team in charge of organizing this Forum. The theme of this round table is at the heart of the news: "finding a new balance between rigour and economic growth in Europe". Indeed, the current situation combining unprecedented levels of public debt and sluggish activity in the euro area poses many challenges for governments. In particular, striking the right balance between fiscal consolidation and growth support measures is crucial. But let us be clear, I see no dilemma, no contradiction between these two objectives. On the contrary, I think they are mutually reinforcing and are both absolutely necessary. I must add another element that is essential to build a sustainably stronger euro area: the creation of a financial union to complete the monetary union. Let me say a few words about these three subjects which are, as I have pointed out, totally interconnected. 1 1. Fiscal consolidation efforts must be continued The eurozone crisis has its roots in the individual and collective inability to maintain fiscal discipline during the first ten years of the single currency's existence. Therefore, the remedy lies first in fiscal consolidation and a more credible fiscal discipline framework. The fiscal efforts already made by the various euro area countries are already bearing fruit: not only is the absolute level of the euro area deficit twice as low as elsewhere, but the pace of fiscal consolidation is indeed much faster. This is, of course, at present an asset for us and a factor of confidence both for the markets and for economic agents, which needs to be further strengthened. Beyond these efforts at national level, a strengthened framework of common discipline has been put in place, which is an important step towards a more integrated economic union. The legislative package (known as the six-pack), which entered into force in December, significantly strengthens the Stability and Growth Pact: the European Commission's supervisory powers over national budgets have been increased, sanctions are now almost automatic, and the criteria for public debt and public spending are being monitored more closely. In addition, the Treaty on Stability, Coordination and Governance establishes a new "fiscal compact" including the requirement that the annual structural government deficit should not exceed 0.5% of GDP. At the levels of debt we are currently experiencing, economic agents would react to fiscal laxity by deferring their own private spending. Financial markets would continue to impose very penalizing interest rates on our countries to take into account the uncertainty surrounding the fiscal outlook. Overall, the confidence generated and the financial benefits of fiscal consolidation far outweigh its negative effects on effective demand in the short term. It is essential that all efforts in this area be pursued resolutely. 2. Measures to promote growth are needed 2 The widening of competitiveness gaps between euro area countries over the past decade is another fundamental explanation for the crisis. The economic reasoning is easy to understand: when you join a monetary zone that aims for an inflation rate of just below 2%, the evolution of unit costs of production must be in line with this objective set by the central bank, modulo productivity gains. All the countries that did not respect, year after year, this calculation and this discipline suffered a loss of competitiveness that the market did not take into account until the crisis. The new Stability and Growth Pact now provides a framework for monitoring macroeconomic imbalances and competitiveness developments. Competitiveness is one of the key drivers of long-term growth and that is why it is so important that we succeed in strengthening it today. How? Through structural reforms of the market for goods and services and the labour market, for example. Again, the progress already made in many countries is impressive. In the recent past, European economies have never reformed so much in such a short period of time. I could cite many examples: the reform of the labour market in Spain and Italy, the pension reform in Italy and France. These reforms are the foundations for dynamic and sustainable future growth and must be vigorously pursued. Despite fiscal constraints, there is also some scope for direct public support for growth, which will be all the more effective if it targets projects aimed at stimulating long-term growth. This, in my view, is precisely the idea of the EUR 120 billion 'Growth Pact' adopted at last week's European Summit. 3 3. Institutions matter: the need for a financial union within the euro area In my opinion, there is a third very important factor that explains why the crisis is hitting the euro area so hard: it is the fact that we are a very highly integrated economic area without having the appropriate institutional mechanisms to accompany this integration. This gap explains in particular the contagion effects and the negative interactions between sovereign and banking risks, which have greatly aggravated the difficulties of this area. Clearly, a smooth and coherent functioning of the banking sector is absolutely essential to increase the stability, resilience and efficiency of the euro area. This conviction is based on several fundamental observations: adequate financing is essential for our economies to grow strongly and sustainably. In Europe, the banking system is the main source of financing, and its soundness is therefore of crucial importance; as long as the financial health of the euro area as a whole is at the mercy of the problems faced by only one of the member countries, negative interactions between sovereign and banking risks can materialise. Moreover, in a monetary union, capital can move freely and very quickly from one country to another, which increases the potential impact of "bank runs" in the absence of a supranational deposit guarantee mechanism. These are all major threats to the financial stability of the euro area; 4 financial stability is essential, not only to create the conditions for adequate financing of the economy. It is also an invaluable asset for fostering confidence, which has been sorely lacking in recent years and is another key condition for growth. In addition, given the interactions between banks and sovereign borrowers and the potential impact of a financial crisis on a country's fiscal position, financial stability makes a major contribution to fiscal stability; Since the transmission of monetary policy to the real economy is mainly through banks and credit, it is of the utmost importance that the banking sector does not malfunction in any part of the area if we want an effective single monetary policy. For all these fundamental reasons, the euro area needs further concrete progress towards closer financial integration. We need a coherent financial union with three essential powers: unified supervision of all banks in the euro area (with the same type of structure as the Eurosystem, i.e. with a body at its head - the ECB - and decentralised implementation through the national central banks, as the crisis has demonstrated the importance of keeping banking supervision close to the central bank); deposit insurance, with massive firepower, insofar as this body could collect a contribution from each bank in the euro area and borrow if necessary on the markets with a supranational guarantee; bank resolution (crisis management), with a resolution fund that could either be separated or linked to the deposit guarantee fund. 5 Of course, such a breakthrough involves many steps and the removal of a large number of important obstacles. But what it requires above all is an unwavering political will on the part of all the members of the euro area to move towards a stronger and more coherent economic and monetary union. I believe that we saw a demonstration of this will at last week's summit: work on a financial union has now begun and we are determined to make it a success. Thank you for your attention. 6
text_original: Le 3 juillet 2012 Paris Europlace Forum financier international Table ronde 2 : Trouver un nouvel quilibre entre rigueur et croissance conomique en Europe Introduction par Christian Noyer Mesdames et Messieurs, Cest, comme toujours, un grand privilge et un grand plaisir pour moi de participer au Forum financier international Paris Europlace et je souhaite remercier toute lquipe en charge de lorganisation de ce Forum. Le thme de cette table ronde est au cur de lactualit :  trouver un nouvel quilibre entre rigueur et croissance conomique en Europe . En effet, la situation actuelle associant des niveaux de dette publique sans prcdent et une activit morose dans la zone euro pose de nombreux dfis aux gouvernements. Les efforts en matire dassainissement budgtaire doivent tre poursuivis La crise de la zone euro trouve ses racines dans lincapacit individuelle et collective  suivre une discipline budgtaire durant les dix premires annes dexistence de la monnaie unique. Au-del de ces efforts au niveau national, un cadre renforc de discipline commune a t mis en place, ce qui constitue une avance importante vers une union conomique plus intgre. Par le biais de rformes structurelles du march des biens et des services et du march du travail, par exemple. L encore, les progrs dj raliss dans de nombreux pays sont impressionnants. Ces rformes constituent les fondements ncessaires  une croissance future  la fois dynamique et durable et elles doivent tre vigoureusement poursuivies. Les institutions ont de limportance : la ncessit dune union financire au sein de la zone euro Selon moi, il existe un troisime facteur trs important qui explique pourquoi la crise frappe si durement la zone euro : cest le fait que nous sommes une zone conomique trs fortement intgre sans disposer pour autant des mcanismes institutionnels appropris pour accompagner cette intgration. Cette lacune explique notamment les effets de contagion et les interactions ngatives entre risques souverains et risques bancaires, qui ont largement aggrav les difficults de cette zone.  lvidence, un fonctionnement harmonieux et cohrent du secteur bancaire est absolument essentiel pour permettre daccrotre la stabilit, la rsilience et lefficacit de la zone euro. Title: Colloquium on 40 years of the franc zone
text: Colloquium of 5 October 2012 "Crossed views on 40 years of the Franc Zone" Closing speech by Mr. Noyer, Governor of the Bank of France Ministers, Governors, Colleagues and Friends, It is a great honour that you have done me by inviting me to deliver the closing speech on the 40th anniversary of the monetary cooperation agreements of the Franc Zone, which have consolidated a system that has actually existed for much longer. Without pretending to summarize these debates, I would like to retain three ideas, important to me and characteristic, I think, of the system of the Franc Zone which is at the same time effective, robust and modern: 1) It is an effective system in terms of its objective: to guarantee price stability. Indeed, it is necessary to recall forcefully what the Franc Zone has brought for more than 50 years to member countries: a price stability particularly remarkable for developing countries, for example if we compare this result to the rest of sub-Saharan Africa. This comparative advantage has been maintained over the most recent period, this low inflation preserving the purchasing power of the populations. Price stability is largely due to the fixed exchange rate vis-e0-vis the euro. Price stability and fixed exchange rates also provide a secure environment for economic operators, favouring investment and the conduct of economic policies and structural reforms. The fixed exchange rate has often been criticised for being likely to lead to an overvaluation of the currency, which would hamper growth. However, in terms of growth, the performance of the Franc Zone over a long period has nothing to envy to that of most other African countries. 1 The Franc Zone has also been a framework for gradually improving economic policies, particularly fiscal policies. On the one hand, the implementation of the limitation of the monetary financing of the States, which is one of the basic rules of these unions, creates a strong and salutary constraint on the budgets of the States. On the other hand, beginning in the mid-1990s, multilateral surveillance prompted greater discipline in public financial management. Efforts in the formulation and conduct of economic policies must, of course, continue and the multilateral surveillance framework strengthened. 2) It is also an extraordinarily robust system, which is the oldest fixed exchange rate system in the world. It has resisted drastic changes in the context: independence, the break-up of the Bretton Woods system, trade liberalisation and the integration of France into the European monetary union. It has also withstood an incredible succession of shocks, both political, economic and social. The political and social crises experienced in recent years by the Central African Republic, Chad, Togo, the Congo and, more recently, Cf4te d'Ivoire have perfectly illustrated the stabilizing role played by the mechanisms of the Franc Zone. In these periods of extremely serious turmoil, these mechanisms have preserved the credibility and value of the currency and have played an effective protective role in preventing the spread of the crisis and hyperinflation or dollarization that would have aggravated it. Similarly, in countries that are highly vulnerable to changes in commodity prices, the pegging of the CFA and Comorian francs provides protection against external shocks, in particular to avoid the second-round effects that could have been caused by the depreciation of the exchange rate of the national currency. Thus, during the multiple food crises caused by drought or other natural disasters or when commodity prices rose sharply in 2008 and again in 2011, the anchoring provided by the Franc Zone system helped to limit the rise in the prices of food and energy imports from member countries. Despite the questions, as well as the criticisms, that the Franc Zone can sometimes arouse, it is therefore necessary to recognize and emphasize the ability of this system to overcome the trials and crises that have not been lacking in the past decades. If this system has withstood so many changes, it is not because it has adapted but because it is by nature adapted to very different contexts. Neither its principles, nor even its fundamental mechanisms have changed because it is a pragmatic construct based on 2 on simple principles and rules: a fixed exchange rate, a guarantee of unlimited convertibility and a credible external guarantor. The commitment of all parties to these rules and principles has ensured their robustness, during drastic changes in the political or economic situation or in sometimes acute crisis situations. The 1994 devaluation also showed that this system could incorporate an adjustment when necessary. The human factor must also be taken into account. As all the participants pointed out, the Franc Zone has forged very strong human relations. It is also the closeness and depth of these links that have allowed this system to show a great capacity for resistance in unstable or uncertain contexts. 3) Finally, the Franc Zone system is a resolutely modern system. If some have been able to judge or rather "prejudge" that it was a colonial relic, it seems to me on the contrary to be the precursor of the regional fire protection devices that we are now seeking precisely to promote, particularly in the euro zone. The guarantee given by the French State allows each monetary zone to face a balance of payments shock such that it would deplete foreign exchange reserves. The opening of an unlimited appropriation in this case to the operating account makes it possible to continue to finance the necessary external expenditure. In return, the monetary authorities must take the necessary steps to rebuild foreign exchange reserves. Combined with the centralization of export earnings, these mechanisms therefore function as a "financial safety net" to protect economies from balance-of-payments shocks. Here are the three main lessons inspired by the exchanges we have just attended and which have also given us the measure of the interest of the history of the Franc Zone. In this respect, it seemed to me, particularly in reviewing the book commemorating the 40th anniversary of the Franc Zone that the Banque de France is publishing today with the Directorate-General for the Treasury, that while some episodes of this history are well known to us, other parts of it would certainly deserve to be explored further. This is why the Bank of France wanted to launch a research program on the history of the Franc Zone, which aims to involve all interested parties, I am thinking in particular of the central banks of the Franc Zone, but also universities, research centers and development institutions, in France and Africa. To conclude, even an efficient, robust and modern system alone cannot solve all the problems and ensure that the countries that benefit from them succeed in their long-term development. In this respect, the monetary cooperation mechanisms of the Franc Zone would benefit from 3 in my opinion, to be supplemented by three pillars: (i) as I mentioned, monetary unions must be consolidated by closer multilateral surveillance of economic policies, in particular budgetary policies, and the example of the euro area shows this amply; (ii) the implementation of structural reforms, in particular with regard to improving the business environment and the management of public enterprises, is certainly essential to enhance the growth potential of the economies of the Franc Zone and contribute to improving their competitiveness, bearing in mind that the fixity of the exchange rate does not allow us to indulge in the ease of devaluations; (iii) the deepening of regional economic and financial integration in the Franc Zone is, finally, a major challenge in the medium and long term, even more so than in the euro area, because it generates the scale effects essential for integration into the world economy. The last fifty years have shown that the Franc Zone is a factor favourable to development. However, this was neither a necessary condition nor, a fortiori, a sufficient condition. The good economic performance of other countries in Africa shows this. The sustainability of the Franc Zone will therefore depend on the dynamics of the development model chosen by the Member States and the willingness of the French partner to support this development. I have no doubts about either. 4
