Title: Synopsium of the 40th anniversary of the BEAC
text: BEAC Malabo 40th Anniversary Symposium, 23 November 2012 Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France First of all, I would like to thank the Governor of the BEAC for organizing this symposium, which brilliantly marks the 40th anniversary of the Bank of Central African States. I would also like to take advantage of the privilege of the presidency of this session to share with you some reflections drawn from the very particular experience of the Bank of France, both a privileged observer and an actor of three monetary unions: the Central African Monetary Union (WBU), the West African Monetary Union (WAMU) and the euro area. As a preliminary point, I would like to point out that it is in Africa that monetary integration projects are most numerous. If this flowering of monetary integration projects was inspired by the European experience, it is also and above all the consequence of the success of the two African monetary unions: the UMAC and the WAMU. I would therefore like to return to this success, without concealing its shortcomings. In the light of recent European experience, I would then like to share with you my thoughts on the conditions for the sustainability of monetary unions in a context of deepening regional integration. 1) The two African monetary unions are a source of stability and a catalyst for regional integration These two examples of monetary union are first and foremost a source of price stability: inflation is significantly lower than the rest of sub-Saharan Africa: this is a real comparative advantage, which has been maintained over the most recent period. Admittedly, this stability is primarily due to the system of the Franc Zone and the power of the nominal anchor provided by the fixed exchange rate. of the two single currencies vis-e0-vis the euro. But if both the BEAC and the BCEAO have been able to maintain this anchorage, it is largely because their multinational character has given them independence from States that has facilitated the achievement of this objective. These two African monetary unions are then a source of economic and social stability: more fundamentally, the monetary union has protected the currency from the economic and social crises that have erupted in different member countries. Finally, they are a source of resilience to balance of payments crises. The pooling of foreign exchange reserves, which is one of the key elements of both UMAC and WAMU, allows for great regional solidarity to deal with external shocks, to which member countries are particularly vulnerable because of the structure of their economies. These two unions are also a catalyst for regional integration. In UMAC and WAMU, monetary union preceded economic union and even customs union. This sequence, very heterodox in terms of economic theory, makes monetary union a catalyst for regional integration through three channels. First, through institutional dialogue: it was within the framework of monetary unions that the new States began, and then deepened the learning of regional coordination mechanisms. It is also a monetary phenomenon, the devaluation of the CFA francs, which precipitated the institutional creation of real economic unions: the CEMAC and the UEMOA. Then, by the development of multilateral budgetary surveillance which was built on a rule: the strict limitation, then the prohibition of monetary financing of States. Finally, by the need for integration of capital, goods and people markets: monetary integration has been a factor in integrating into the world economy and stimulating growth through gains in scale that are particularly profitable for small markets. However, as recalled in a recent report presented at the meeting of finance ministers of the Franc Zone on 5 October, regional integration is less advanced than could be hoped for and as the institutional arrangements suggest. Indeed, the member countries of the two monetary unions have not, over a long period, had a better performance in terms of growth than other African countries. sub-Saharan. However, the gains from deepening integration have been estimated, for example, for the Franc Zone at 1 or 2 additional growth points per year in this report. It is therefore desirable that the process continue and accelerate in both CEMAC and WAEMU. This will strengthen monetary unions but, as the experience of the euro area shows, will also test their strength and resilience, as it increases the risk of contagion within unions. 2) To prevent and limit these risks, monetary unions will have to be strengthened in the future by three major developments: Firstly, enhanced coordination of fiscal policies is the sine qua non for ensuring the compatibility of a monetary union with still national fiscal policies. Such coordination must be based on an effective supervisory framework, including in particular effective sanction mechanisms, which can complement market discipline. Secondly, mechanisms must also be provided for within monetary unions for the mutual surveillance of national macroeconomic imbalances, in particular balance of payments, competitiveness or credit developments. As we have learned from recent crises, the reciprocal return effects between the real and financial spheres can exert cumulative effects that can aggravate crises. Thirdly, in order to deal with asymmetric exogenous shocks, which could threaten the financial stability of monetary unions in the short term, increasing monetary and financial integration also requires the establishment of financial crisis management mechanisms, which must strike the right balance between solidarity and the prevention of moral hazard. The financial integration generated by monetary unions also implies, as a longer-term target in UMAC and WAMU, the establishment of a banking union. This will make it possible to prevent any risk of a vicious circle between public finances and the banking sector at national level and to better manage the increased risks of regional financial contagion. With a single banking supervisor and uniform prudential rules, both UMAC and WAMU already have the first pillar of a banking union. To take full advantage of it, we must push the logic to its conclusion at the regulatory level. It will also be necessary to set up coordinated mechanisms for the resolution of banking crises and to set up deposit guarantee and/or resolution funds at union level. * * * Finally, whether monetary unions precede or aim to consolidate and deepen economic integration, they induce a multifaceted and favourable dynamic of regional integration. The lesson that can be drawn from the experience of the euro area is that, in order to prevent the risks of instability that this dynamic can engender, it must be accompanied by a change in the institutions that jointly strengthen the discipline and solidarity of the Member States.

Ces deux unions montaires africaines sont ensuite une source de stabilit conomique et sociale : plus fondamentalement en effet, lunion montaire a protg la monnaie des crises conomiques et sociales qui ont clat dans diffrents pays membres. La mutualisation des rserves de change qui est un des lments cls tant de lUMAC que de lUMOA permet en effet une grande solidarit rgionale pour faire face aux chocs externes, auxquels les pays membres sont particulirement vulnrables du fait de la structure de leurs conomies. Title: Speech for the Economics Book Prize
text: Robert OPHELE Economics Book Prize Deputy Governor of the Bank of France ----------------- Paris, 6 December 2012 Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear friends, It is a great pleasure for me to be present among you to open this 14th Economics Book Day; the participation of the Banque de France shows our willingness and commitment to contribute to spreading the economic and financial culture to our fellow citizens in general and young people in particular. The theme of this Day is the competitiveness of the French economy. I'm not going to talk to you about it directly because I don't want to anticipate the great panels we have this morning; I will tell you about the lack of knowledge of the French in economics. The French are said to have only very vague notions of economics and a Nobel laureate in economics, Edmund Phelps, would have concluded that by raising the level of economic culture of the French the growth potential of our economy would be significantly increased, by 1%. In fact, as part of a recent survey on the French and the economy, conducted by TNS-SOFRES for the Banque de France, we 1 asked "How would you judge the level of knowledge of the French in economics?". Answer: only 7% of our fellow citizens consider it good, 59% average, 32% weak or very weak. From the same survey, it appears that 60% of French people consider that economic information is not understandable. This mediocre level, however, is the result of self-evaluation and we know the natural tendency to self-flagellation in this type of exercise; I also note that dissatisfaction increases with the level of education of the respondents: if overall 32% consider that their level of knowledge is low or very low, this rate rises to 44% for higher education graduates. This is a good sign; in fact, the more you learn, the more you realize that you know little. Let us therefore be careful not to conclude too quickly and overestimate our shortcomings. But let's be aware. In 2010, CODICE (Conseil par la diffusion de la culture e9conomique) had carried out a quiz that included questions of reasoning, knowledge and practical economy. The average score obtained was 8.3/20 and the average rate of correct responses was 41%; for higher education graduates the average score rose to only 9.8/20. More prosaically, at the Banque de France, we receive more than 200,000 cases of over-indebtedness per year and in many cases there is a lack of knowledge of the basic financial mechanisms, useful for managing a family budget, and which would certainly have reduced the extent of the problems encountered. This gap in economics, which probably results from a multitude of sociological, philosophical or even religious reasons, is in fact combined with an almost congenital distrust of the French towards their fellow citizens, public authorities and markets; this was excellently highlighted by a very stimulating book awarded here a few years ago ("The Society of Defiance, How the French Social Model Self-Destructs" by Yann Algan and Pierre Cahuc) - I really recommend reading this 2 book that is short, simple and very enlightening - ; the result is consequences that I believe are disastrous for our economic growth, as this is a formidable obstacle to the implementation of reforms; it is the society blocked to use the expression popularized by Crozier in his time but found 50 years ago by an American researcher to characterize the France. We do not accept reforms whose economic usefulness we do not understand and which are proposed by people or institutions in which we do not trust. But these reforms, the crisis - financial crisis and economic crisis - reminds us cruelly of their indispensable nature. This crisis was caused by excesses and excesses in the world of banking and finance. We are making sure that it does not happen again. That is why, together with the government and our foreign counterparts, we are working to reform and strengthen the regulation and supervision of financial activities. But we also need the "right" finance, the one that makes it possible France to create, to undertake, to acquire one's home, to insure oneself against the risks of life, to finance companies. Our country has gone through a crisis, unprecedented, it seems essential in this context to work of pedagogy and to give the French a real economic and financial culture; for the reforms necessary for our boost to competitiveness to be implemented effectively and serenely, they must be fully understood and accepted by economic agents. I don't know if Phelps was right when he said that by raising the level of economic culture of the French the growth potential of the economy would have increased by 1%, but it is clear that human capital explains an important part of the growth. It is the economies where agents are best trained that are among the most competitive economies. The relationship between education and economic growth is well established. A high level of education also makes it easier to adapt 3 to new technologies and to innovate and innovation is a key to the competitiveness of tomorrow. To be interested in the economy, to read the economy, is to give ourselves keys to better understand the uncertain environment in which we live, to better analyze the trends of the contemporary world, the risks and the opportunities. This will allow you as an individual but also as a French and European citizen to be better prepared to face the challenges of global economic competition. You see what you have to do! I therefore wish you stimulating debates and enriching readings! 4

Title: Symposium on accompanied microcredit
text: Paris, 12 December 2012 SYMPOSIUM ON ACCOMPANIED MICROCREDIT Introductory speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Bank of France It is with great pleasure and interest that I open this Symposium on Accompanied Microcredit, which will provide a better understanding of its main aspects and the role in financial inclusion. This subject is at the heart of the concerns of the public authorities, and at the heart of the news, since you certainly know that the Prime Minister announced yesterday future measures in this area. I warmly thank the academics, leaders, representatives of associations and banks, who agreed to speak at this event. This will cover both personal and professional micro-credits, as long as both have been selected or monitored by a support structure. As you know, the Banque de France has been working steadily for several years to promote banking and financial accessibility. 1. It acts first of all in the context of the right to an account procedure, which has no equivalent to our knowledge in Europe. The system consists in the Bank of France designating to any natural or legal person who has been refused an account opening, a bank that will be required to open one. Basic banking services are associated with it, which make it possible to make the account work concretely. In 2011, nearly 40,000 designations, 36,700 to be exact, were made. The Financial Sector Advisory Committee has also organised a consultation with all stakeholders, which has made it possible to develop a range of alternative payments to cheques, in particular through the payment card with systematic authorization, a secure means of payment for both the holder and his banker, and thus an effective tool for financial inclusion. From 2013, further progress will be made thanks to a more precise monitoring of the right to the account. We will have, within the framework of the Observatory of Regulated Savings, which I have the honour to chair, additional data on how the exercise of the right to an account is 1 concretely implemented. We will thus list the number of payment cards with systematic authorization issued when opening the right to the account. We will also gradually measure, with the help of credit institutions, what happens to the right to the account in the year following its implementation. 2. The Bank of France is also very active in the fight against over-indebtedness. Its branches receive over-indebted people, and prepare the files that will be presented to the specialized commissions. This represents considerable work in the service of the community, which a single figure is enough to illustrate: in each of the last five years, more than 200,000 cases have been registered by over-indebtedness commissions. This figure should not hide the fact that over-indebtedness is too often still a partially repetitive phenomenon: nearly 40% of cases are submitted by people who had already been over-indebted previously. It is therefore also and above all necessary to implement preventive measures. In this regard, I am encouraged by the first results of the law of 1 July 2010 on consumer credit. The consumer loan rate monitoring committee, which recently submitted its first report to the government and parliament, provides a clear observation: revolving credit, often present in over-indebtedness cases, is being reduced, to the benefit of depreciable loans. In fact, the latter, by making the lender and the borrower responsible throughout the life of the credit, present less risk of leading to over-indebtedness. Statistics tell us that over the last twelve months the number of over-indebtedness filings has decreased by 5%, even though the economic situation was less favorable than before. I am therefore convinced that prevention is one of the most effective ways of combating excess debt, and therefore deserves to be continued. But I would also like to stress that over-indebtedness is not only of financial origin. It is increasingly rooted in the difficulty of some households in meeting the regulations of basic consumer goods. Remedies should therefore not be sought exclusively from credit institutions, which it would be unfair to reproach them with both, or in turn, for lending too much or too little. It is upstream, in the causes of over-indebtedness, that I also think it is useful to look for remedies. 3. Accompanied microcredit is also one of the ways to promote financial inclusion. As early as 2006, the Microfinance Observatory, whose presence this afternoon I welcome from its president, Michel Camdessus, included it in its reflections and analyses. In fact, it is a particularly welcome instrument in our country, for at least three reasons. ? First of all, while the population is very largely banked - at 99%- the most modest households do not have as much access to credit. However, living without any loans, even of a very modest amount, is a real handicap for a whole part of the population who nevertheless needs to transport, to find housing and to equip themselves to obtain employment, the income that will then allow them to provide for their needs independently. ? Accompanied microcredit is also a concrete form of economic and financial education for the population, especially those who have not had the opportunity to access a high level of education. Thanks to the microcredit support networks, which play a remarkable role with a constancy and dedication to which I pay tribute here, people, modest households, apprentice entrepreneurs, learn concretely 2 what a loan means, a useful investment, a cash flow to manage, repayment deadlines to honor. ? Finally, it is a modest but nevertheless valuable way of preserving the social fabric and developing entrepreneurship. It is also often a welcome opportunity for credit institutions and social networks to work together to achieve the objectives I have just mentioned. Despite all its merits, accompanied microcredit is still little known and recognized. That is why the Bank of France wants to help promote it. ? First of all, by ensuring better visibility of its characteristics. As an extension of the work of the National Council for Statistical Information, the Banque de France has set up from the end of 2011, with the help of the Social Cohesion Fund, an ambitious collection of quantitative data. Many associations are already contributing to this, and I appreciate the particular effort that this represents for them. This exercise will ultimately allow a complete knowledge of microcredits, their purpose, their cost and their performance. I am convinced that this information will significantly help the reflection and action of all stakeholders. ? I have also decided to show our support for this particularly courageous and responsible form of financing by awarding, each year from autumn 2013, two prizes intended to reward and publicly recognize for the exemplarity and quality of their projects an individual beneficiary of a personal microcredit and a micro-entrepreneur accompanied by a professional microcredit. The choice of the beneficiaries of these prizes, amounting to 3000 and 5000 euros respectively, will be made by a selection committee including associations and banks that I will have the honour of chairing. This afternoon's work will be concluded by Frane7ois Bourguignon, Director of the Paris School of Economics, who will be very pleased to share his thoughts on this theme, even though the economic model of accompanied microcredit is probably still to be specified. Previously, three round tables were held to better understand the different facets. I shall therefore give the floor without delay to Ms. Catherine Barbaroux, President of the Association du droit e0 l'initiative e9conomique, who was kind enough to chair the first round table. I wish you a very fruitful afternoon of work. Thank you for your attention. 3

Title: New banking regulations, consequences for companies
text: Association Frane7aise des Tre9soriers d'Entreprise Paris, February 28, 2013 Speech by Robert Ophe8le, Second Deputy Governor "New banking regulations, consequences for companies." Hello, I will mention this morning some issues of the financing of French companies in the light of the regulatory changes underway in the financial sphere. My main point is this: currently the demand for financing is limited due to the weakness of economic activity - some say the opposite: economic activity would be limited due to a lack of financing; this is not my analysis - this limited demand is generally satisfied but when this demand increases again with the economic cycle that will not fail to turn around, it is not certain that our banking system can cope with it due to a lack of customer deposits: this means that we must prepare either to reintermediate deposits in bank balance sheets, either to activate alternative channels of market financing, I am thinking in particular of securitisation, or, probably the wisest, to do a little of both. If you will, I will first make a brief inventory: French companies are largely indebted but the flow of new credits is essentially drying up for lack of demand. In a second step, I will mention why, in the new regulatory and institutional context, the banking sector would find it difficult to support a recovery in demand for credit. We will then see how to complement these bank financings with market financing, in particular via securitization. I will conclude on the actions taken by the Bank of France to facilitate corporate financing. First a brief inventory. We are currently seeing a moderate decline in the funding flows of non-financial corporations but a rapid decline in their investment flows, which brings us to an exceptionally high net flow of funding. Quite a bit 1 classic these developments accompany with a little delay the evolution of the GDP; investments are the most reactive, financing is a little more staggered as you can see on these graphs on the right (see slide 1) which bring the growth over one year closer to the investment and financing flows of NFCs as a percentage of GDP over one year by shifting the growth rate by 2 and 4 quarters respectively. This moderate decline in financing covers a rapid decline in credits offset by an increase in debt through the issuance of securities, with share issues remaining symbolic (see slide 2). In fact, the decline in credit, like the decline in investments, is an almost coincidental indicator of the growth failure that the French economy is experiencing. But this must be placed in a context where French companies, like the entire economy, are characterized by a relatively high level of debt; none of the major categories of economic agents are heavily indebted, but all are significantly indebted. It may therefore be interesting to compare the French economy with the German economy (see slide 3): the German economy has had, basically, a stable debt ratio since the creation of the euro zone with a tendency to deleverage companies and especially households offset by growing public debt while in France all economic agents have increased their indebtedness and, even if that of companies has grown less rapidly than that of households and APUs, it now represents 67% of GDP against 43% for German companies. However, for more than a year we have had almost zero credit flows with a compensation between positive investment credit flows and negative cash credit flows. And this despite interest rates that are particularly low, even for SMEs, you see on this graph on the right (see slide 4) the rate of new loans of less than 80 1 million at 1/5 years in France, at less than 4%, close to German rates and at an all-time low. In fact, surveys show a sharp decline in the demand for credit both in investment and cash even though the responses of banks remain largely positive. To establish this diagnosis, we have our survey of banks and our survey of companies; since I am at AFTE this morning I will refer to this second survey that we conduct every quarter among SMEs and mid-caps on their access to credit. You can see the latest results (see slide 5): a decline in the number of SMEs applying for new credit, almost systematic acceptance of demand by banks, but an inflection is observed on cash loans to SMEs. I therefore believe that there is currently no rationing of companies on their access to finance, either on the markets for large companies or via bank credit for SMEs and mid-caps. The real question is, in fact, the ability of these channels, markets or banks, to meet the increased demand for financing that is sure to manifest itself when the economic cycle reverses. The quality of this response will determine the strength of the 2 recovery because it is it that will allow companies to invest, to carry the production cycle, to create jobs and value. Nothing seems to me to be a given. I shall refer successively to the issues of solvency, liquidity and profitability. I will be very brief on solvency because the French banks are in a very good position in this regard. At the beginning of 2013, most of the major French establishments have Core tier 1 above 9% Full CDR4 and by the end of 2013 all will be clearly above. Admittedly, this is a subject that is never closed, with today a questioning of the weightings determined by the internal models of the institutions to calculate the solvency ratios, but I believe that our banks do not have much to fear in this regard. It is therefore not the problems of solvency ratio that will hinder the distribution of credit to companies, since, and I believe he is making this mention, the profitability of their operations and therefore in fact the profitability of retail banking, which represents about two thirds of net banking income, will be maintained. The issue of liquidity is more delicate. We know that future liquidity regulation revolves around a short-term ratio, at 30 days, and a long-term ratio, at more than one year. The first should be respected gradually from 2015, the second should enter into force in 2019. These ratios favour the stable resources of retail customers, but French banks are handicapped in this respect because their "retail clientele" resources have been, via tax incentives, siphoned off by life insurance on the one hand and regulated savings, largely centralized at the Caisse des De9pf4ts, on the other. Life insurance, which accounted for 20% of household financial savings in 1995, accounted for 37% 15 years later, while bank deposits rose from 37% to 30%. This decline in bank deposits has been halted, but it is regulated savings - which now represent (livrets A, livrets Bleu, LDD and LEP) more than 30% of total deposits - which has benefited, therefore, for the most part the Caisse des de9pf4ts. The movement, illustrated on this graph at the bottom right (see slide 6), will continue all other things being equal with the announced continuation of the increase in the ceiling of the booklet A. Liquidity ratios will therefore be "biting", especially since the current situation is improved by the way monetary policy is conducted. The fixed rate full allotment liquidity allocation system and the two 3-year operations conducted a little over a year ago result in a significant liquidity surplus that singularly improves the LCR ratio (and the nfSR long ratio) since resources are more than 30 days (and more than a year) and excess liquidity is a liquid asset for those who hold them. But 3-year operations will fall mechanically in 2015 and a policy cannot be based on the permanent maintenance of the mechanism of unlimited liquidity allocation. I will not dwell at this stage on the long-term ratio that must be reviewed, but we must be aware that for institutions lacking deposit, it leads to 3 a reverse transformation by forcing short credits to be financed by long expired resources. What conclusions should be drawn from this in terms of financing the economy in general and companies in particular? This seems to me to be extremely simple in principle: either the banking system can reintermediate a larger share of households' financial savings, or the financing will have to be provided by the institutions that benefit from this savings, namely the Caisse des De9pf4ts and the life insurance institutions. And in fact, there is a strong appetite of both for credit activities. If you will allow me, I will come back more specifically to the prospects for the financing of credits by insurance bodies. Indeed, while the Insurance Code explicitly authorises insurance undertakings to hold loans in representation of their regulated liabilities, such holding is strictly limited, in particular with regard to loans to undertakings, ? Only loans to companies, whose shares are traded on a recognised market, as well as to public undertakings are widely admitted and without any particular guarantee in representation of regulated liabilities; they fall into the broad asset class, which in total must not exceed 65% of commitments. ? Shares in securitisation undertakings are only allowed if they are traded on a recognised market and within the limit of assets whose overall envelope is capped at 5 % of regulated liabilities. However, the concept of a recognised market in the Insurance Code refers to the regulated markets of the States of the European Economic Area as well as to the markets of other OECD countries in so-called regular operation which have defined conditions of operation, access to the market, admission to trading and which comply with reporting and transparency obligations. This is in fact a very restrictive definition for the French side since a market like Alternext is not a recognized market even though it meets the criteria imposed on markets in regular operation. The direct purchase of loans to companies can therefore only concern loans to large companies, and, as for the others, we are led to go through FCTs whose assembly constitutes regulatory avoidance with a passage in Ireland and a listing in Luxembourg which makes them eligible under the 5% envelope. It is clear that if we want to move further in this direction, we need to promote simple securitisation mechanisms that avoid the mistakes of the 2000s and we also need to re-examine the regulatory treatment of the corporate-lending asset class in insurance companies in the broad sense. These observations on the concept of a recognised market and on securitisation highlight the importance that the use of market financing cannot fail to take. 4 Making the importance of a good mastery of the market chain that goes from listing to settlement through trading and clearing. From this point of view, we can only welcome the maintenance of market-making activities within the perimeter of the universal bank as provided for in the text of the banking law under discussion in Parliament - this is also the case in the German banking bill - ; but it is clear that the financing of the French economy will also require the maintenance or even strengthening of French influence in the market infrastructures that deal with our values; this concerns financial intermediaries but, ultimately, especially issuing companies. The future of Euronext is as important for the financing of our economy as the maintenance of market making activity by French banks. At the Banque de France, we believe that corporate finance is at the heart of our missions. We are therefore resolutely proactive in this area. Beyond our statistical apparatus, the basis of our intervention is our business rating activity with a resolutely SME-ETI orientation; we currently note 280,000 companies; this rating, which is for the exclusive attention of the rated company and the banking system, can be used in particular to refinance "well" rated loans or to calculate the risk weighting for solvency ratios. This very granular system actually makes it possible to refinance loans to medium-quality companies since the ECB extended its eligibility criteria from rating 3 to rating 4 in 2008 and then accepted, at the beginning of 2011, that the Bank of France refinance at its own risk the loans associated with rating 4, which corresponds roughly to a probability of default of 1% over the 1-year horizon. As shown in the graph (see slide 7), this eligibility currently covers a total of 55% of loans to SMEs. In fact, today in the pool of mobilizable assets deposited by banks at the Bank of France, private receivables represent 50% of the total. Through this system, we exert a very strong incentive to grant credit to companies. But we want this deposit of good quality assets to be better exploited and made more liquid. With the Place de Paris, we are conducting a reflection on the implementation of a system that would allow banks, via a securitization vehicle, to house some of their private claims within an instrument that can be mobilized in bilateral repo transactions and with the Eurosystem. The underlyings envisaged would be exclusively loans to non-financial corporations in order to exclude any "cannibalization" of the ABS market, the underlying of which are mainly loans to households. The Bank of France would be a stakeholder in the scheme since it would evaluate the underlying assets and could rate the securities - unslicensed bonds - issued by the securitisation structures. At the same time, the Banque de France has taken steps with the Eurosystem to ensure that this mechanism, which is similar to a securitisation vehicle of Place, is accepted on a long-term basis and to promote its use in the other countries of the euro area. Indeed, private debt deposits are now under-exploited in many euro area countries, for legal or operational reasons. 5 This approach is also part of a broader desire to make loans on banks' balance sheets more liquid. Thus, in parallel, the Banque de France has initiated a reflection on the possibility of assigning to each line of loans, as is practiced for negotiable securities, the equivalent of an ISIN code. The advantage of such a system would be twofold: it would make it much simpler to manipulate and mobilise private claims, particularly in the context of bilateral or tripartite repo operations; it would reduce the risk of double mobilization as collateral for loans. If we want to be at the rendezvous of economic recovery, we must start these reforms now; the Banque de France is working on this with all economic actors. Thank you for your attention and support. 6

text: Presentation of the Best Financial Article Award Speech by Christian Noyer June 18, 2013 ------------ Ladies and gentlemen members of the jury, Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Friends, It is a great pleasure for me to be here with you to conclude this presentation of the Best Financial Article Award 2013. But we also need the "right" finance, the one that makes it possible to create, to undertake, to acquire one's home, to insure oneself against the risks of life, to finance companies.) I am pleased for the Bank of France that it is sponsoring this award and I am pleased that you will continue to enlighten your readers, which every citizen can welcome.

Title: press conference on payment card security
text: Press conference of 2 July 2013 Introductory remarks by the President Ladies and Gentlemen, I am pleased to present to you today the tenth annual report of the Payment Card Security Observatory. I would like to begin by commenting on our findings and recommendations regarding the security of card payments on the Internet in France. The findings are encouraging for two reasons: - The share of payments on the Internet secured by strong authentication of the bearer is increasing. It now accounts for 27.5% of card payment transactions on the Internet in value terms, up from 23.5% in 2011. As a result, these devices benefit from increased notoriety among carriers, who are more regularly confronted with them. Nine out of ten online shoppers now say they know of such a device in addition to the card number and visual cryptogram requested during an online transaction and two out of three online shoppers confirm that they have already used strong authentication. - for the first time since 2008, we are seeing a decrease in the rate of fraud on payments on the Internet (0.290% compared to 0.341% in 2011), which is of course positive and the Observatory welcomes these first encouraging results. Press conference of 02 July 2013 1/5 But for all that, the nominal amount of fraud continues to grow on this channel (109.4 million euros against 104.2 million euros in 2011). Thus, all distance payments, which continue to grow at a steady pace (13% in 2012), represent 9.2% of the value of national transactions but account for 61% of the amount of fraud. This is why I call on all stakeholders, in particular the online merchants most exposed to fraud (in amount or rate), to resolutely pursue in 2013 the actions taken to better secure payments on the Internet by deploying solutions allowing the reinforced authentication of holders. If we now look at all card payments, the overall fraud rate is up slightly from 2011 to 0.080% (up from 0.077% in 2011). This is explained by a significant increase in fraud at the international level (11.2%), due to an upsurge in cases of card theft and data compromise during stays abroad, but also to the increase in fraud on international transactions via the Internet (37%). On this channel, we can see a partial transfer of national fraud to the international sphere. The gradual adoption of payment security devices on French websites is leading fraudsters to turn to websites that are less well protected abroad. The shift from fraud to international transactions makes it clear that the fight against fraud cannot stop at the national level. At the European level, this observation is widely shared and has led to the creation of the European forum "SecuRe Pay", which brings together central bankers and European supervisors, and to an effort to coordinate their actions. This resulted in january 2013 in the publication of joint recommendations, in particular the implementation of enhanced authentication of cardholders whenever possible and relevant whenever possible and relevant, by 1 February 2015. This is an important first step for a harmonised approach at European level to securing means of payment, including card payments on the Internet. As such, I plan to organize a major event in 2014. Press conference of 02 July 2013 2/5 in order to bring together all stakeholders around the security of payments on the Internet, a crucial issue to preserve users' confidence in the means of card payment. As far as card payments are concerned, fraud remains stable again this year and at a very low level (0.015%), which I welcome. This is of course the result of significant and constant efforts, undertaken in France and Europe in recent years, to combat fraud on these payments, and in particular by generalizing the use of smart cards to the EMV standard. The fraud rates of international transactions carried out in Europe (SEPA zone) compared to those carried out outside Europe (outside the SEPA zone) show in passing that regions that have not adopted EMV are victims of a very significant postponement of fraud (the rate of fraud on payments is about twice as high at 0.687% compared to 0.372% within the SEPA zone). In this context, the announcement last year by Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Discover (Diners Club International) of a set of measures to encourage the adoption of the EMV standard in the United States by 2015 is welcome. The expected benefits, in particular in the fight against magnetic stripe counterfeiting, will concern both French cards for proximity payments and withdrawals made in the United States, and American cards for proximity transactions carried out in France. However, I call on carriers to be extremely vigilant, on the Internet of course, but also when making a payment or withdrawal in France or abroad: in 2012 we are seeing a very significant increase in attacks on ATMs and points of sale, which have become prime targets for organized fraud networks. Very attentive to this targeted evolution of fraud, I would like to remind all cardholders of the need to remain vigilant. Being vigilant means in particular using your credit card with caution, at any place and on any occasion and not disclosing your identifiers on unknown websites or to unidentified telephone interlocutors. Before a trip abroad, this means contacting Press conference of 02 July 2013 3/5 his bank, in particular to inquire about the precautions to be taken and to bring the international telephone numbers of opposition of his card. I would now like to make a few comments on the Observatory's technology watch work. In 2012, these focused in particular on the security of contactless payments. Following the significant increase in the number of contactless cards and payment terminals, the Observatory wished to update its analyses for 2007 and 2009. It shows that the risks associated with the fraudulent capture of contactless transaction data and the non-legitimate remote activation of the card remain low, as the technical implementation of this fraud is particularly difficult. The financial interest for a fraudster also remains very limited given the small amounts of contactless payments that can be made without entering the PIN. Based on these findings, the Observatory considers that the main risk associated with contactless card payments is image risk. However, the need to maintain users' confidence in this means of payment leads the Observatory to reiterate its previous recommendations aimed at preventing the fraudulent capture of contactless transaction data. In this context, the issuers have undertaken to make available to their holders devices to prevent the use of contactless mode: this involves the use of protective cases or the deactivation of this method of payment by sending remote scripts, or finally the issuance of cards without this function at the request of the holders. I would also like to point out that, in France, the contactless cards now issued no longer allow the bearer's name or transaction history to be captured since they are no longer accessible during a possible eavesdropping. This data does not allow a fraudulent payment transaction to be carried out anyway. In conclusion, I would like to stress the high level of security of payment cards today in France. Fraud on card transactions, remains well Press conference of 02 July 2013 4/5 controlled and is even at a particularly low level for local national payments and withdrawals. In addition, and for the first time, we are seeing a shift in the rate of fraud on the Internet, which is positive: it is therefore necessary to maintain the efforts and actions undertaken in order to confirm and amplify the movement to reduce the rate of fraud on the Internet that has begun thanks to the spread of strong authentication methods. In this perspective, the work, which is now well under way at European level, in particular through the recommendations of the "SecuRe Pay" forum, should provide particularly useful support. Thank you for your attention. Press conference of 02 July 2013 5/5

Title: Do banks still have a role to play in financing companies?
text: Dinner of the think tank Etienne Marcel "Do banks still have a role to play in financing companies?" Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Salons du Se9nat - Monday, September 23, 2013 Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, I am very pleased to be with you this evening to talk about a crucial subject for the economic growth of our country and which is at the heart of many of the Bank of France's concerns: the financing of companies, and more particularly smEs since your think tank is dedicated to them. As a preliminary point, I would like to quickly give you some background and possibly launch some avenues that can be included in the discussion. I will then of course be at your disposal to answer all your questions and debate together. 1. To begin with, a simple answer to your question: yes, banks still play a considerable role in the financing of companies: ? They still cover 64% of companies' financing needs, i.e. around 80820 billion, compared to 36% for market financing; ? Of course, this figure has been declining since the beginning of the financial crisis: in 2008, bank loans accounted for 73% of corporate financing compared to 27% in the market; ? But this decrease is mainly due to large companies that can and have massively resorted to securities issues on the market (7.7% in 2011; 12.5% in 2012); ? This substitution has a very simple explanation: financing costs on the market have been lower than bank credit costs since 2011, in particular due to the fall in ECB interest rates to historically low levels which has a more direct impact on market rates than on credit rates (on average monthly, financing costs for French companies were 2.7% in July against 2.2% on the market); ? The latest figures for July 2013 confirm this trend: while the outstanding loans mobilised by large companies are down 10.3% compared to July 2012, the stock of loans mobilised by SMEs is growing by 0.4% compared to last year. 2. Although credit to SMEs has continued to grow since the crisis, there has undeniably been a sharp deceleration, especially in the last year, which partly explains your concern: ? However, what we see at the Banque de France is that this phenomenon is not due to a decline in the supply of bank loans: - the granting criteria have not significantly tightened for SMEs and credit applications are very largely satisfied (84% of SMEs have obtained in full or at least 3/4 the credit requested in Q2 2013); - rates have fallen significantly (from a peak of 6% on average in mid-2008 to less than 3% today); ? The decline (small, I insist, especially compared to all our European neighbours) in loans to SMEs is in fact mainly attributable to a drop in demand, itself resulting from a bearish economic context and marked by uncertainty. We have recently seen this demand rise slightly, accompanying the rather positive news about the state of our economy; ? Only one sector showed a tightening of supply that caught our attention: it was cash loans, whose rate of obtaining by SMEs had fallen to 63% in the last quarter of 2012. It has since risen to 72%, but we continue to remain vigilant on this point. 3. I also believe that concerns about the sustainability of intermediated financing of SMEs are linked to the new regulatory context. On this point, I believe I can reassure you somewhat, even if efforts will still be necessary: ? The Basel Committee took into account the potentially harmful consequences for the financing of companies of these new solvency and liquidity ratios: - the calibration of solvency arrangements was reviewed in order to correct certain rules on capital charges and liquidity lines that penalized companies. French banks have managed to meet these new solvency requirements without any significant impact on bank credit; - the liquidity ratio was also thoroughly reviewed at the beginning of the year to limit the counterproductive effects on the financing of the economy. The situation for French banks is less comfortable on this point: their liquidity ratios are relatively good but dependent on very accommodative monetary policy conditions that are not intended to last forever. In addition, French banks remain structurally disadvantaged in terms of liquidity by the UCITS/life insurance/regulated savings trio. 4. To ensure that a recovery of the French economy can be supported by adequate financing of companies, several avenues seem to me important to explore: ? We must maintain our efforts to ensure that the new regulatory standards do not have an impact on intermediated financing and, more specifically, continue our actions to avoid tensions on the liquidity of French banks (an update will be made in the autumn on the impact of the reform of regulated savings, in particular on the provision to banks of part of the centralized funds); ? The situation requires creativity and boldness in this area, as in many others. I want to mention here the Place project, led by the Bank of France, to collateralize private debts that you have probably already heard about. The idea is quite simple, it consists in exploiting the large deposits of good quality private debt that are not so today. Banks that wish to do so will be able, via a Place vehicle, to back these claims with a bond, itself negotiable and allowing banks to raise resources in the medium / long term. We are also ensuring that these bonds can be mobilised, subject of course to fulfilling the eligibility conditions, as collateral for Eurosystem refinancing. This system will have the double advantage of allowing banks to diversify their sources of financing and to encourage lending to SMEs. Work with the Place has already progressed well and we hope that a first issue can take place before the end of the year. Discours de Christian Noyer, Gouverneur de la Banque de France Salons du Snat  Lundi 23 septembre 2013 Monsieur le Prsident, Mesdames, Messieurs, Je suis trs heureux dtre parmi vous ce soir pour parler dun sujet crucial pour la croissance conomique de notre pays et qui est au cur de nombreuses proccupations de la Banque de France : le financement des entreprises, et plus particulirement des PME puisque votre think tank leur est consacr. Title: Speech on SEPA migration
text: Speech by Christian Noyer at the press conference of the Minister of the Economy and the Governor of the Banque de France on migration to SEPA 23 September 2013 Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to thank the Minister for associating me with this press conference, which aims to highlight the importance of migration to SEPA means of payment for French companies and to recall the simple but urgent actions to be taken to seize this opportunity. As the Minister points out, by providing Europe with a harmonised area for non-cash payments, SEPA will enable our companies to settle and receive their payments identically and under significantly improved economic and technical conditions, regardless of the country of origin or destination of the payment. The adoption of SEPA credit transfer and direct debit represents an opportunity for our companies because it is a source of simplification and optimization of processing chains and allows access to a wider range of services. 1 The adoption of sepa credit transfers and direct debits is also a mandatory development: in accordance with the European regulation of 14 March 2012, SEPA credit transfers and direct debits will definitively replace the old domestic models on 1 February 2014. Less than 5 months before this deadline, the proportion of French companies that have successfully migrated to SEPA payment methods is insufficient: - The migration to SEPA credit transfers has started well but, as the Minister notes, in August 2013 only half of the transfers made were SEPA compliant. - The migration to SEPA direct debit is to be initiated as soon as possible: in August 2013, sepa direct debit represented only 3% of the total volumes of direct debits made. In these circumstances, it is essential that French companies take the necessary actions to adopt SEPA means of payment as of today and actually use them as soon as possible. It is not too late to complete this migration on time, especially for the benefit of smaller companies. But to do this, simple actions must be resolutely taken now. They consist for companies: - To ensure the ability of their treasury software to manage the data formats of SEPA payment orders; - To obtain the bank details of their supplier customers in BIC and IBAN format. Companies wishing to issue SEPA direct debit orders will also need to ensure their ability to retain mandates signed by their debtor clients. Unlike the national levy, which was based on a double mandate held by both the creditor and the bank of the 2 Debtor, companies will now be solely responsible for the archiving of SEPA direct debit mandates and it will be up to them to provide their banks with proof of the existence of these mandates in the event of a dispute of a SEPA direct debit order by one of their debtor customers. Given the technical nature of these developments, it is important that companies are supported in their migration to SEPA. I am thinking here of all the privileged interlocutors of companies such as banks, professional associations, accountants or chambers of commerce. These players, who are already supporting companies in this migration to SEPA payment methods, will intensify their communication actions. The Banque de France actively participates in this awareness-raising and support effort. As co-chair of the SEPA National Committee, the Banque de France played a central role in organizing more than forty SEPA information meetings in the regions. These meetings made it possible to recall the legal obligations that weigh on companies as a result of the SEPA project, but above all to provide concrete advice on the actions to be taken to comply with them. The Bank of France also sent 160,000 brochures, real practical user manuals for companies to successfully migrate to SEPA. The Bank of France will intensify its efforts in the coming months, building on the strong action of its branches which, benefiting from the confidence of local economic actors, are valuable relays to raise awareness of SEPA payment methods among all stakeholders concerned by migration. Of course, the Bank of France will also fully support all awareness-raising actions undertaken by the various stakeholders. 3 Switching to SEPA is a legal obligation with a deadline of 1 February 2014. It also represents an opportunity for our companies that they must seize now. The success of French migration requires the mobilization of all. Less than 5 months away, we must redouble our efforts. I therefore call on all stakeholders to step up their actions to ensure the successful transition to SEPA means of payment. 4

Title: Europlace International Forum
text: Europlace International Forum Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Bank of France Beijing, 26 November 2013 Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to be able to speak here today. I would like to thank and congratulate the entire Paris Europlace team for organizing this Forum, which is a valuable opportunity every year for direct dialogue with Asian economic and financial leaders and investors. Before exchanging directly with you, I would like to focus my introduction on the following three themes: ? Progress on the recovery in the euro area; ? Progress in the European Banking Union; ? The Eurosystem's monetary policy strategy. These three topics are inseparable for analysing the euro area at the moment and for understanding the path it is taking towards solid and sustainable growth. ********* First of all, let me use a few figures to shed light on the current economic and financial situation in the euro area: 95 The second quarter of 2013 marked the end of a six-quarter period of recession. The euro area thus returned to positive growth of 0.3% per 1/5 report to the previous quarter. The improvement is certainly modest, but it is indisputable and reflects a much better overall dynamic and, despite the volatility and the persistent fragility of this recovery, it was confirmed by growth of 0.1% in the third quarter; 95 In recent months, PMIs have returned to above their long-term average in the euro area, confirming a rebound in economic activity. In October, for example, the euro area PMI was 51.9 (with a positive development common to the services sector - 51.6 - and the manufacturing sector - 52.9); 95 On the financial front, there has been a significant normalization of the situation: (i) peripheral bond markets continue to stabilize and have returned to sustainable interest rate conditions; (ii) fragmentation within the euro area is decreasing - as evidenced for example by the decline in excess liquidity or Target 2 balances. As we had expected, we have therefore been in a recovery dynamic since the middle of the year. But this recovery is still weak and fragile, especially because it starts from very low levels. Why are we starting from such low levels of growth? For two reasons: 95 The euro area has gone through a very severe and complex financial, economic and institutional crisis; 95 And, to get out of it, it didn't just deal with the surface of the problems; it has undertaken fundamental projects to act on the root of the difficulties. These projects concerned all the causes of the crisis. Public finances have been strongly recovered, the banking system has been thoroughly cleaned up, structural reforms are being undertaken to improve the competitiveness of economies and the economic governance of the euro area has been strengthened. Naturally, these developments, carried out simultaneously and rapidly in most countries of the zone, have weighed on domestic demand and growth. It is the ransom of courage. But these measures also pave the way for sustainable and robust future growth, as the euro area has significantly strengthened its fundamentals since then. In budgetary terms, we have the smallest government deficit in the developed areas and a primary balance that is almost in balance, and our competitiveness is growing as well as our balance of payments surplus. 2/5 Currently, we are carrying out another reform project that is particularly crucial for the future growth and stability of the euro area: the establishment of the European Banking Union. The crisis has revealed that a uniformly sound financial system is essential for the stability of the euro area as a whole and for a good transmission of the single monetary policy. Once this reasoning was completed, it was necessary to think of the concrete solution. The key to the whole banking union could be summed up in this sentence: we must ensure that the banks of the euro zone are considered as such, as "euro zone" banks and more as "Irish", "German" or "Italian" banks. And for this, three things must be put in place: 1) federal supervision of institutions, ensuring that the same rules and control methods are applied everywhere; 2) a unified mechanism for the resolution of banking crises, to avoid that the management of a major crisis depends on a single State; 3) a unified deposit guarantee system, to avoid the phenomena of bank run. Over the past year, ideas and words have turned into concrete actions. Let me give you an update on the current state of play. 1. The principle of creating a single supervisory mechanism was endorsed by the Heads of State at the end of last year and we are currently preparing for its implementation. In a year's time, the main banks in the euro area will be controlled by a federalised system under the aegis of the ECB and based on national teams and expertise. In addition, the entire European banking system - including in Great Britain - will be supervised on the basis of a single rulebook. As indicated by the ECB on 23 October, we are now actively working on the preparation of a comprehensive balance sheet assessment to which European banks will be subjected before the establishment of the SSM in November 2014. This exercise will be unprecedented: around 130 participating banks, representing 85% of the total assets of European banks, will be subjected simultaneously to a comprehensive asset quality review, which will be conducted according to a common methodology. The objective is threefold: to promote greater transparency on the situation of the European banking system, to take the necessary corrective actions and finally, to restore confidence. 3/5 This is a great opportunity for banks to show that they have cleaned up their balance sheets and are trustworthy. 2. Like my colleagues at the ECB, I consider the Single Resolution Mechanism to be another key pillar of the Banking Union, together with the SSM. The SRM should consist of three main elements: a single system, a single authority and a single fund, and it should be in place by the time the SSM becomes operational. At the last EU summit on 22 October, all countries expressed their willingness to reach an agreement before the end of the year on the Directive on the recovery and resolution of banking crises, so that the SRM is in place by 2015. I would like to stress once again: the implementation of the banking union is a decisive step in building a stronger euro area: ? It will strengthen the stability of the European banking system; ? This stability and confidence regained should help boost production bank loans that will be necessary for the recovery; ? It will enhance the effectiveness of the transmission of our single monetary policy by strengthening our main transmission belt: the banking system. Finally, let me say a word about the Eurosystem's monetary policy strategy. Since the beginning of the crisis, we have used all the means at our disposal, in accordance with our mandate, to ensure our mission - to maintain price stability - and to support economic and financial adjustment in the euro area. I would like to return to our most recent decisions: ? With the announcement of the OMTs last year, we managed to put away the speculations of the break-up of the area. We have convinced of our infallible commitment to defend the single currency and have thus dried up a source of extreme and unjustified concern; ? We have provided constant support for bank refinancing, to compensate for the drying up of interbank markets and avoid a worsening of the financial crisis. At the last Governing Council, we reiterated our commitment to this effect: we decided to continue to carry out the main refinancing operations in the form of fixed-rate tenders, with all tenders being served, for as long as necessary and at least until July 2015 (i.e. beyond the maturity of our three-year long-term refinancing operations); 4/5 ? We have a very accommodative "conventional" interest rate policy, as evidenced by the recent reduction of our main refinancing rate to 0.25% and the continuation of our Forward guidance policy. We do this to ensure our mission of keeping inflation below but close to 2% over the medium term. This mandate is very clearly symmetrical: inflation must not be too high or too low in the euro area, for fundamental reasons, especially in this period of reforms, of the proper functioning of the economy. Even if inflation expectations remain well anchored in the euro area, several indicators have convinced us that inflation is likely to remain very low for an extended period of time, hence the need for a clear and rapid response. Our monetary policy strategy is therefore extremely clear: we are determined to ensure price stability in the euro area; we are determined to combat the financial fragmentation of the area so that our policy can be effectively transmitted. That being said, of course, monetary policy cannot and must not replace the substantive efforts of individual States. I am thinking in particular of fiscal recovery efforts calibrated so as not to run upside down the recovery and of structural reforms that alone will ensure future competitiveness and growth. Thank you for your attention. 5/5

Mais ces mesures ouvrent galement la voie  une croissance future durable et robuste, car la zone euro a considrablement renforc ses fondamentaux depuis lors.
