Title: Regulatory repression and monetary policy
text: Conference of Macro-Finance Caisse des De9pf4ts / Dauphine University Paris "The long-term challenges of the Eurozone" Tuesday, 17 December 2013 "Regulatory Repression and Monetary Policy" Speech by Robert Ophe8le, Second Deputy Governor bank of France "My purpose this morning is to explore the extent to which the far-reaching regulatory change applying to financial institutions and more specifically to banks - and it is because of the importance that I believe is largely underestimated in the opinion of these regulatory changes that I have used the provocative term 'regulatory repression' - to what extent, therefore, this change is likely to affect monetary policy, whether it is the "big" decisions that determine the more or less accommodative nature of this monetary policy - the "stance" - or the more technical ones that fix the instruments used by the central bank to implement this monetary policy. The regulatory proliferation that followed the G20 summits in London and Pittsburgh in 2009, both in terms of strengthening banks' capital, putting in place rules concerning their liquidity and transformation, and orderly management of banking crises with, in particular, the participation of creditors in covering losses, and finally the regulation of derivatives transactions via their clearing by chambers and for over-the-counter transactions by the imposition of initial margins, all this has singularly modified the framework for the exercise of the activity of banks by modifying the regulatory incentives and therefore the financial circuits. Naturally, the impact of these reforms is more or less strong depending on the characteristics of each banking system (whether the reforms bite or not), according to the financing structure of each economy (intermediation by financial institutions versus market financing; financing by debt or by equity) and according to the position of each country in the macroeconomic cycle (demand). 1 of funding is it strong or not). I will therefore focus my remarks on the case of the euro area and, to stick to the consequences that monetary policy must take into account, will structure my presentation this morning around two ideas: ? the regulatory changes in progress mechanically lead, all other things being equal, to a reduction in the supply of credit by banks with a particular decrease in very long-term loans and an increase in the price of all these credits; this should therefore lead the central bank to conduct a more accommodative policy than would be justified by the macroeconomic context; but the calibration of this specific factor is difficult to carry out because of the heterogeneity of the euro area; ? the modalities of intervention of the central bank, which ensure the proper transmission of monetary policy decisions, could also be reconsidered due to two types of factors: o the new regulations profoundly modify the microstructure of the money market, the usual vector of the transmission of monetary policy in the euro area: incentive for arbitrage between collateral HQLA and not HQLA, incentive to refinance more than a month, penalization of intermediation on the money market; all this could lead the central bank to change its methods of intervention; o regulatory changes also encourage disintermediation of the financing of the economy, it would be tempting to move from a model of providing central bank liquidity through bank refinancing via the repo of good quality assets to a model giving more importance to the purchase of securities; but in the euro area the selection of these securities obviously poses specific problems. The following graph (slide 1) illustrates the general reasoning: we have an accumulation of new regulations that profoundly modify the framework for the exercise of the banking profession, which has effects on monetary policy: 1) From the beginning of the process of developing the new prudential standards in 2009, regulators have tried to integrate the measurement of the likely macroeconomic effects of the envisaged reforms even though it was clear that the precise quantification of these effects was particularly uncertain with studies with very divergent results. In fact, all the potentially negative effects of these reforms have been crushed by the prospect of reducing, with the implementation of the new regulations, the probability of occurrence of a major financial crisis whose economic cost is, as we have experienced, very high. I am not going to dwell on this point, which has no direct interaction with monetary policy in the years to come, but I believe that we must all bear in mind both the quantitatively decisive importance of this positive factor and its very uncertain nature. 2 ? Quantitatively dominant because the discounted average cost of an economic crisis triggered by a financial crisis is considered to be around 60% of annual GDP1 so that any reform that reduces, even marginally, the probability of crisis is beneficial because its macroeconomic cost is unlikely to be higher. Thus, even an a priori anecdotal risk such as the annual crisis risk resulting from the current treatment of OTC derivatives transactions, estimated at 0.26% (i.e. one crisis every 400 years!) 2, if it is abolished by regulatory reform, "reports" nearly 20 points of GDP (0.0026x0.63); ? But all this is largely uncertain because we combine uncertainty about the probability of crisis, that of the effect of reforms on this probability and that on the actual cost of a crisis; in the latter register estimates range from 19% of annual GDP to 153% of annual GDP depending on whether or not the loss of GDP related to a crisis is considered to be definitive. As a result, the estimate of GDP gain corresponding to the implementation of Basel 3 regulations can vary considerably (slide 2). The massive nature of the expected long-term gains should not, however, overshadow the short-term negative impacts through the reduction in private sector bank financing that will weigh on growth: ? the very sharp increase in capital requirements leads to a reduction in the credits shown on the balance sheet: either because it is easier to reduce the distribution of credit than to raise equity, or because their profitability must be higher to ensure normal ROE ? The longest loans, which in the case of ALM management must be hedged on the derivatives markets, will be particularly penalised in view of the increase in capital charges on market operations. ? Within banking assets, low-risk assets - in fact sovereign debt as opposed to loans to private non-financial agents - and therefore not very demanding in capital will be all the more privileged as they will allow compliance with LCR regulations. ? In general, the cost of the resource will increase because the beneficial effect of an increase in equity is offset by increased competition on deposits from retail customers and the risk premium that will have to be paid to cover the risk of bail-in. In most models, the impact of these reforms involves an increase in the credit spread, which reduces the demand for credit and ultimately weighs on growth. 1 The median of the various estimates of crisis-induced GDP loss is 63% ("An assessment of the long-term economic impact of stronger capital and liquidity requirements" August 2010; ). 2 " Macroeconomic impact asssessment of OTC derivatives regulatory reforms" aofbt 2013 3 The impact depends on how long it takes for banks to adapt; the faster the adaptation and therefore concentrated in time, the greater the shock. The increase in spreads was estimated by the Macroeconomic Assessment Group, mandated by the FSB and the BCBS to assess the impact of the measures envisaged, at approximately 13 basis points per weighted solvency ratio point: In fact ? Basel 3 was supposed to result in an increase in the capital ratio of 130 basis points, which, implemented over 4 years, implied an increase in credit spreads of just over 30 bp and a one-off maximum decline in annual GDP growth of 0.19%; ? The SIFIs layer would result in an increase in the capital ratio of 200 basis points for this category of banks, which, implemented over 4 years, would imply an increase in credit spreads of nearly 35 bp and a one-off maximum decrease in annual growth of 12 bp Of course, it was necessary to add to this the effect of liquidity regulation; i.e. 25 points estimated under the NFSR. The combined effect on spreads could, however, be reduced by a substitution within banks' assets between loans associated with high RWA and high-quality liquid securities with very low RWA. But in the end the estimate of the total impact of the regulation was between 50 and 75 basis points. These approaches, which are very "macro", even if they use for some of the DSGE, must however be compared with more micro approaches that tend to highlight the effects of stronger regulations on the distribution of credit than what emerges from "macro" approaches. ? Thus, based on data covering the period when the EBA requested the recapitalisation of part of the European banking system, namely October 2011 - June 2012, work conducted at the Bank of France (Mesonnier and Monks "Did the EBA Capital Exercise lead to a Credit Crunch in the Euro Area?" 2013 working paper to be published) show that for every 1 point of ratio to be filled, the banks concerned reduced their credit distribution by 1.3%. ? Similarly Brun, Fraisse and Thesmar in a recent paper3 measuring the effect on credit distribution induced by the transition from Basel 2 compared to Basel 1 from individual data on loans to French companies and internal models of banks, suggests that a tightening (reduction) of 1 point in capital requirements, results in a reduction (increase) of 3 to 8% in the distribution of credit to non-financial corporations. Naturally, macro models incorporate a central bank reaction function; faced with this exogenous shock on the supply of credit and the associated rise in rates, banks 3 The Real Effects of bank Capital Requirement, Juillet 2013 4 Centrals are expected to conduct a more accommodative monetary policy. That is, to have lower policy rates than normally necessary. The difficulty of the exercise lies in the extent of the phenomenon; this varies according to the place of financing intermediated by banking systems and the degree of bite of new regulations, but it is clear that these are very different within the euro area. With regard to the financing structure, we first see that the indebtedness of NFCs varies from single (Germany) to more than double (Italy and Spain) with quite different trajectories (decrease in Spain, increase in France). In addition, while the issuance of negotiable debt securities, i.e. market financing, covers less than 3% of the debt needs of non-financial corporations in Spain, it covers nearly 40% in France, which is from this point of view the country in the most "advanced" zone - I put it in quotation marks -, because of the important place of very large companies in the French economy. Penalizing bank financing will therefore have a much stronger impact in Spain than in France (slide 3). With regard to the impact of regulatory changes, the breakdown by country of the efforts to be made is not public, but reference can be made here to the follow-up made by EBA4, which illustrates the dispersion of situations (slide 4): ? With regard to weighted solvency ratios, if the 4.50% CET1 low is reached by almost all banks, there is still a long way to go for all institutions to constitute their conservation buffer by the end of the ramp-up period of the scheme (2019); on June 30, 2012 it was "missing" nearly 80 400 billion, without integrating the buffer of systemic banks which I recall can go up to 2.50%, nor counter-cyclical buffer. ? With regard to the leverage ratio, it can be seen that roughly only half of the institutions would respect it on a "full Basel 3" capital basis. ? As for the transformation ratio, which should not be implemented before 2018, the situation is simpler since almost no one would respect it; the lack of long-term resources is estimated at EUR 1 230 billion, but here again the dispersion of situations is great. ? Finally, with regard to the short-term liquidity ratio, the LCR, the analysis conducted by the EBA at the end of December 2012, which will be published, highlights the magnitude finally reduced in absolute terms of the gap to be filled to reach a ratio of 100% which is the minimum target in 2019 but still with a third of the institutions covered by the financial year that are concerned. But these figures are obviously minors of the situation because of the exceptional nature of the situation at the end of 2012 with a particularly high central bank liquidity surplus that is not intended to last either in the euro zone (more than 80600 billion at the end of 2012) in the United Kingdom (nearly a3300 billion) or in the United States (1500 billion). We must also take into account the distribution by country of this insufficiency, which is very concentrated in certain countries and it is no secret to recall that if French banks are well placed in terms of solvency they are less well positioned in terms of liquidity. 4 5 Naturally, the consequences of the heterogeneity of the situations I have just mentioned are mirrored by the financial fragmentation that the euro area is also experiencing with the absence of a single credit market fuelled by a fluid movement of capital within the area. Monetary policy is therefore facing a singular difficulty, reacting to a regulatory shock whose effects are very different from one country to another. Even though the key rates are already very close to the famous Zero Lower Bound, it is more on the duration of the accommodative policy that we will have to play than on its level. Indeed, the heterogeneity of national situations in the context of a monetary union without a banking union singularly slows down the transmission of monetary policy decisions in the real economy. I draw your attention to this aspect of the slowdown, which is very important for understanding the current reaction function of the ECB, which I believe is well characterised by one of President Draghi's answers at his last press conference: The final point I would like to make is that it would be wrong to think that we determine our monetary policy on the basis of a single figure for inflation. It would also be wrong to think that the effects of our monetary policy are instantaneous. They are anything but that. It takes time for the full effects to materialize and the amount of time it takes depends on many factors, in particular two. What is the state of banks' balance sheets? And what is the state of the private sector's balance sheets? The greater the deleveraging process that needs to be undertaken by both banks and corporates, the longer it will take for our monetary policy to have its full impact. That is why the asset quality review is so important, because it could actually shorten this period of time. 2) I now come to my second point, which concerns monetary policy instruments. All these new regulations singularly modify the general regime of incentives that control the financial decisions of economic agents; ? first, there are strong incentives for bank disintermediation that will reduce the place of the bank credit channel, the "bank lending chanel" of monetary theory, in the transmission mechanisms of monetary policy; ? and then there are incentives that affect the microstructure of the money market and therefore the traditional channels of monetary policy intervention. Let us first discuss the possible consequences of disintermediation, a development that the Eurosystem must prepare, support and which, in the long term, will lead to the adaptation of monetary policy instruments. We know that this disintermediation movement goes through three main channels: public offering, private placement and securitization; for this securitization to have a regulatory effect, it must be deconsolidating. The Banque de France contributes to its developments through its action as a Market, but, as far as monetary policy is concerned, these major developments could point to a monetary policy that would make its liquidity injections no longer via the refinancing of banks but by purchases of securities on the market; a classic monetary policy in anglo-Saxon countries, as illustrated (cf. 6 slide 5) putting into perspective the assets of the US federal system (4 trillion in securities acquired under monetary policy) and the Eurosystem (less than 80250 billion acquired under the SMP and CBPP programs). Such a prospect, however, comes up against the classic technical difficulties of the euro area; in the absence of strong financial and institutional integration, there is, unlike the United States, no significant issuer covering the entire zone, so there is no real pool of eurozone securities to buy. The European Commission (via the balance of payments and macro-financial assistance mechanisms) or the EIB have a perimeter that goes beyond the euro area; the institutions properly euro zone have a limited debt: the EFSF has a debt of 80 175 billion and a total commitment of 80 192 billion, the ESM has a maximum intervention capacity of 80 500 billion but only 80 50 billion are mobilized at this stage. Moreover, there are no securitisation structures such as Fanny Mae or Freddy Mac covering the whole area in the euro area. Therefore, the purchase of securities amounts to purchases of national securities, sovereign or not. For sovereign bonds it could be a question of buying baskets of securities, each country being weighted according to its weight in the key of the ECB capital, but it is clear that the differences in the quality of the signatures, which are currently taken into account by haircut grids adapted to the rating of the issuers and the duration of the papers, would pose formidable problems of political acceptance. The solution adopted in the covered bond purchase programmes (CBPP1 and 2), which left the credit risk to the NCBs, clearly could not be adopted in a normal framework for the implementation of monetary policy, which can only be based on revenue and risk sharing within the Eurosystem. It therefore seems that the refinancing of banks will remain for many years, the preferred mode of supplying liquidity central bank; this therefore makes it really crucial to adapt our instruments to take into account the evolution of the money market microstructure that will result from regulatory reforms. However, these reforms are likely to have a profound impact on the money market. ? It is clear that the LCR, by introducing a difference in treatment between operations with less than one month to run, will in the first place lead to a disaffection for the shortest operations and an increase in the price of operations in the 1/3 month segment. As a result, the ECB's monetary policy, which, via its one-week operations (MROs), focuses on the shortest part of the yield curve could lose its readability and therefore its effectiveness. One can therefore wonder about a possible extension of the main operations. ? Secondly, the favourable treatment accorded by the LCR and probably by the NFSR to central bank refinancing compared to market refinancing will encourage banks to refinance themselves primarily to the central bank and as a priority by repurchasering assets that do not have the best category under the LCR. I would point out, for example, that central bank refinancing does not give rise to any leakage under the LCR regardless of the collateral provided, whereas repurchase agreements in the market give rise to an outflow of funds within 30 days if the collateral is not in the best category (level 1 HQLAs, headlines 7 State). This will therefore encourage institutions to finance themselves primarily at the central bank with non-HQLA collateral, which already represents a growing fraction of the assets deposited as collateral for monetary policy operations and intra-day debit balances in Target (see slide 6). There is therefore a risk that the central bank will gradually become no longer the lender of last resort in the literature but, to use the recent word of Benoit Coeure9, the lender of first resort. In the current fixed rate full allocation refinancing scheme, this means that central bank refinancing can only be used to meet its LCR ratio; which is the exact opposite of what was sought by this regulation: to make banks less dependent on central bank intervention. If the ECB were to return to a quota feed according to the actual need for liquidity central bank of the consolidated banking system of the euro area, the usual Dutch-style auction system would automatically result in an increase in the price of liquidity since the traditional requests for cash management will be added for some banks a request of a purely regulatory nature.5 ? In fact, it is not certain that the return to a mode of feeding according to a net need for liquidity is easily conceivable because it only works if liquidity actually circulates in the banking system which requires banks active in the money market. The combination of a leverage ratio, a short-term liquidity ratio and a long-term NFSR ratio could be devastating for money market intermediation activity. Indeed, such an activity increases the size of the balance sheet (bad for the leverage ratio), penalizes the transformation less than a month / more than a month while stumbling in any case on the capping of inflows of funds at less than a month to 75% of cash outflows at more than a month (bad for the LCR), and is not admissible, in the case of funding of less than one year for a backing of jobs of less than one year (bad for the NFSR). The magnitude of these effects depends, however, on the final outcome of the ongoing negotiation on the precise definition of the leverage ratio and in particular on the acceptance or not of compensation where netting agreements exist as well as the finalisation of the NFSR scheme. On these two points, easing decisions are expected next January. Since the refinancing of banks will remain for many years, the preferred mode of liquidity supply central bank of the euro area, the adaptation of our instruments to the evolution of the microstructure of the money market is therefore essential; definition of the eligible collateral, maturity of the main operations, target market rate, width of the corridor ... all of these elements are likely to be revisited once regulatory frameworks are stabilized. Thank you for your attention. Le foisonnement rglementaire qui a suivi les sommets du G20 de Londres et de Pittsburgh en 2009, tant en matire de renforcement des fonds propres des banques, de mise en place de rgles concernant leur liquidit et leur transformation, de gestion ordonne des crises bancaires avec en particulier la participation des cranciers  la couverture des pertes, et enfin dencadrement des oprations sur drivs via leur compensation par des chambres et pour les oprations de gr  gr par limposition de marges initiales, tout cela a singulirement modifi le cadre dexercice de lactivit des banques en modifiant les incitations rglementaires donc les circuits financiers. That is why the asset quality review is so important, because it could actually shorten this period of time. 2) Jen viens  mon second point qui concerne les instruments de la politique montaire. Toutes ces nouvelles rglementations modifient singulirement le rgime gnral des incitations qui commandent les dcisions financires des agents conomiques ;  il y a dabord des incitations fortes  la dsintermdiation bancaire qui vont rduire la place du canal du crdit bancaire, le  bank lending chanel  de la thorie montaire, dans les mcanismes de transmission de la politique montaire ;  et puis il y a des incitations qui affectent la microstructure du march montaire donc les canaux traditionnels dintervention de la politique montaire. Evoquons dabord les consquences possible de la dsintermdiation, volution que lEurosystme doit prparer, accompagner et qui,  terme, conduira  adapter les instruments de la politique montaire. On sait que ce mouvement de dsintermdiation passe par trois canaux principaux : lappel public  lpargne, le placement priv et la titrisation ; pour que cette titrisation ait un effet rglementaire il faut quelle soit dconsolidante. La Banque de France contribue  ses volutions par son action de Place, mais, sagissant de politique montaire, ces volutions lourdes pourraient pointer vers une politique montaire qui effectuerait ses injections de liquidit non plus via le refinancement des banques mais par des achats de titres sur le march ; une politique montaire classique dans les pays anglo-saxons, comme lillustre (cf. 6 diapo 5) la mise en perspective des actifs du systme fdral US (4000 Md$ de titres acquis dans le cadre de la politique montaire) et de lEurosystme (moins de 250 Md acquis dans le cadre des programmes SMP et CBPP). Par ailleurs il ny a pas en zone euro de structures de titrisation de type Fanny Mae ou Freddy Mac couvrant lensemble de la zone. Ds lors, lachat de titres revient  des achats de titres nationaux, souverains ou non. Pour les titres souverains il pourrait sagir dacheter des paniers de titres, chaque pays tant pondr en fonction de son poids dans la clef du capital BCE, mais on voit bien que les diffrences dans la qualit des signatures, qui sont actuellement prises en compte par des grilles de haircuts adaptes  la notation des metteurs et  la duration des papiers, poserait de redoutables problmes dacceptation politique. Il est clair que le LCR, en introduisant une diffrence de traitement entre les oprations  moins et  plus dun mois restant  courir, va en premier lieu entraner une dsaffection pour les oprations les plus courtes et un renchrissement des oprations sur le segment 1/3 mois. On peut donc sinterroger sur un ventuel rallongement des oprations principales.  En second lieu, le traitement favorable accord par le LCR et probablement par le NFSR au refinancement banque centrale par rapport au refinancement de march va inciter les banques  se refinancer en priorit  la banque centrale et en priorit en mettant en pension des actifs qui nont pas de la meilleure catgorie au titre du LCR. Je rappelle par exemple que les refinancements de banque centrale ne donnent lieu  aucune fuite au titre du LCR quel que soit le collatral apport alors que les mises en pension dans le march donnent lieu  une sortie de fonds sous 30 jours si le collatral nest pas de la meilleure catgorie (les HQLA de niveau 1, en gros les titres 7 dtat). Cela incitera donc les tablissements  se financer en priorit  la banque centrale avec du collatral non HQLA qui dailleurs reprsente dj une fraction grandissante des actifs dposs en garantie des oprations de politique montaire et des soldes dbiteurs intra-day dans Target (cf. diapo 6). Il y a donc un risque que la banque centrale devienne progressivement non plus le prteur de dernier ressort de la littrature mais, pour reprendre le mot rcent de Benoit Coeur, le prteur de premier ressort. Dans le dispositif actuel de refinancement fixed rate full allotment, cela signifie en effet quon peut utiliser le refinancement banque centrale uniquement pour respecter son ratio de LCR ; ce qui est lexact oppos de ce qui tait recherch par cette rglementation : rendre les banques moins dpendantes de lintervention des banques centrales. Si la BCE devait revenir  une alimentation contingente en fonction du besoin effectif en liquidit banque centrale du systme bancaire consolid de la zone euro, le systme habituel dadjudication  la hollandaise se traduirait mcaniquement par une hausse du prix de la liquidit puisquaux demandes classiques de gestion de trsorerie sajoutera pour certaines banques une demande de nature purement rglementaire.5  En fait, il nest pas certain que le retour  un mode dalimentation en fonction dun besoin net de liquidit soit facilement envisageable car cela ne fonctionne que si la liquidit circule effectivement dans le systme bancaire ce qui ncessite des banques actives sur le march montaire. Or la combinaison dun ratio de levier, dun ratio de liquidit  court terme et dun ratio  long terme NFSR pourrait tre dvastatrice pour lactivit dintermdiation sur le march montaire. En effet, une telle activit accrot la taille du bilan (mauvais pour le ratio de levier), pnalise la transformation moins dun mois / plus dun mois tout en butant en tout tat de cause sur le plafonnement des entres de fonds  moins dun mois  75 % des sorties de fonds  plus dun mois (mauvais pour le LCR), et nest pas recevable, sagissant des financement  moins dun an pour un adossement demplois  moins dun an (mauvais pour le NFSR). Lampleur de ces effets dpend toutefois du rsultat final de la ngociation en cours sur la dfinition prcise du ratio de levier et en particulier de lacceptation ou non des compensations lorsque des accords de netting existent ainsi que de la finalisation du dispositif NFSR. Sur ces deux points des dcisions dassouplissement sont attendues en janvier prochain. Title: EMU and peace in Europe
text: "Economic and Monetary Union and peace in Europe" Speech by Anne Le Lorier, Senior Deputy Governor of the Bank of France in front of French and German students Saarbrfccken (Germany), 15 January 2014 "First of all, I would like to thank Carl-Ludwig Thiele1 and Yves Mersch2 for inviting me to participate in this conference, I am particularly happy to speak to young people. I have to deal with a subject that is a bit original for a central banker, which is stimulating and which I appreciate. The subject, as you know, is "Economic and Monetary Union and Peace in Europe". I will try to elaborate on three points. The first is that economic and financial integration and monetary union were conceived as an instrument in the service of peace, and I will remind you of a few steps. The second point is that the process and standards that govern Economic and Monetary Union could be a model or a source of inspiration for global governance. The third point is the conditions for the continued success of Monetary Union and the strengthening of European cohesion. First, I would like to take a quick look back. Why did you finally conceive of the economy and money as tools in the service of peace? For a very simple reason: a very long time ago, eminent philosophers, thinkers, imagined solutions for peace in Europe. At the beginning of the eighteenth century, the abbot of Saint-Pierre in France had a project to make peace perpetual in Europe. At the end of the eighteenth century, Kant, another eminent philosopher, had a European state project bringing together all countries. You know the rest, it is not brilliant from the point of view of peace. After the trauma of the 1st World War, there were again proposals for a pacified Europe, in particular, Aristide Briand and Gustav Stresemann spoke before the League of Nations for a European State. Then there was the 2nd World War. Finally we found ourselves in the situation where Europe had been at the origin of the two most serious world conflicts of the twentieth century. Fortunately, a number of people, after the 2nd 1 Member of the Executive Board of the Deutsche Bundesbank 2 Member of the Executive Board of the European Central Bank War, have shown great voluntarism and great foresight, and rather than relaunching exclusively political projects, they have developed an economic and monetary project. You know that they succeeded, that the Coal and Steel Community and then the Treaty of the European Economic Community made it possible, in particular, to completely transform relations between France and Germany. You know that the same dynamic made it possible to succeed in the transition after the fall of the Berlin Wall. So today, in a way, we have proof that the economy and money are extraordinarily powerful instruments in the service of peace. Make no mistake, I am not advocating the economy and the currency, it is not a question of being attached to a purely financial Europe. It is simply a question of noting that in the face of a political objective, which was peace in Europe, the most effective tool has been economic and monetary integration in contrast to many other projects. I remind you, for example, that it was not possible after the 2nd World War to set up a European Defence Community. And yet, there were good reasons to do so. Let me refer to one of the fathers of the euro. Being in Germany, I cannot fail to quote him: Helmut Kohl said that the achievement of Monetary Union was the condition for peace for the twenty-first century. We are in the twenty-first century: he was right, it seems to me. What more can we say about the euro? I know that it has not always been very well received in Germany. But today it is accepted in Germany. What ultimately matters is what a currency really is. When you are a child, you learn to count, you understand that a candy is not free, you have to buy it, you have a piggy bank. What is the first support for learning? It is the currency. For you, for your children, it's the euro. There is a very interesting point in the evolution of the iconography of money. CarlLudwig (Thiele) would talk about it better than I do, because he is very knowledgeable about monetary signs, and Yves (Mersch) who is also responsible for fiduciary activity at the ECB. Look at what is on euro banknotes today: there are bridges, there are buildings, there are European symbols. When I was a child, on the banknotes, there were French historical men who do not always have a good reputation in the field of peace. I remember for example a note with the portrait of Napoleon Bonaparte. Today, on the other hand, on the euro banknotes, there are doors and bridges and the mythical incarnation of Europe, the goddess Europa. This is not neutral knowing that one of the most precious values we share today is peace. Turning to more institutional or legal issues, let me remind you that, in the economic and monetary field, between the two world wars, European countries suffered from considerable monetary disorder, competitive devaluations, loss of value of the currency. This has been a real trauma in Germany. It was very important to protect oneself against the repetition of such phenomena. And again, it's not just about finances, it's about democracy. When a currency collapses, the state is generally not very strong, extremism is not far away and neither is war. So the subject is not only to have a single currency, it is to have a stable currency. And this, as you know, is the priority of Monetary Union and is enshrined in the Treaty. The mission and permanent work of the European Central Bank is to ensure the stability of the euro. Here too, democracy and political objectives are not far away. What makes it possible to be confident that the European Central Bank, and with them the Eurosystem, will fulfil their missions? I know that in Germany there are many fears on this subject that are expressed very often. Why do you have reason to be confident? For very simple reasons. In the first place, there is a treaty, this treaty is binding on all the States of the European Union and in particular on those who are now members of the euro zone with regard to the mission of the European Central Bank. The second reason why you are right to have confidence is that the governors and members of the Executive Board of the European Central Bank are not national representatives and they are forbidden to reason according to their national interests. This is written in black and white in the treaty and they are committed to respecting it. This group of leaders, eminent experts, decide collegially on the decisions to be taken. Obviously, they do not always spontaneously agree, obviously, they debate, but obviously they are responsible, reach decisions and these decisions are perfectly in line with the objective of stability of the currency. I will give you two figures to show you that the results obtained are not so bad: what has been the inflation in the euro area since the creation of the euro? The answer is simple: 1.9%. What is the target in the Treaty: 2%. We cannot say that we are far from the target. Second example: what was the share of European currencies in international currency reserves? Depending on the currency - it's very uneven - at most for one of them, we will say 15%. What is the share of the euro today? Between 24 and 25% of the world's foreign exchange reserves. The euro has had a good run, it has credibility. All this has been achieved in a set of standards that are not specific to the euro area, that are European standards, that have been the tool for building Europe and that have something of interest to the world community. There are two principles in a way: the legitimacy of the law, an essential point here in Germany and there is a total support of all European countries for this approach. The second principle is subsidiarity. I know that the reality of its application is often disputed and that regulations are often cited that are a little technical, a little surprising in their level of detail. The fact remains that in the case of monetary union, we are really in a federal system with federal decisions taken by the body in charge, the Governing Council and deconcentrated implementation. It is a system on which, in a way, German culture has shown the way. Last but not least, communication is that communication takes place in all European languages. If you go to the ECB's website, you will see that all the languages of the euro area can be used there. This means very concretely that citizens have access to all the information of the European Central Bank, to the explanation of all its decisions. This is an interesting example of governance. On Europe's place and role in the world, you have certainly read a lot. There have been two somewhat extreme reactions that have proved to be wrong, and that is why we can confidently say that monetary integration is at the service of peace. The first reaction was to say that Europe was going to be a fortress and that this fortress was going to be hostile to the rest of the world. Exactly the opposite has happened, Europe has succeeded, as Carl-Ludwig (Thiele) pointed out, it is the world's leading economic hub. It can also be said that it is the first set of States that are working so hard to make the notion of international negotiations and norms prevail. International. The second adverse reaction was to say: the European Union is made because Europe is so weak that it can only get out of it like this. Here too, the answer is Europe's success. A former German minister summed up the fact that neither of these criticisms was right: Joschka Fischer, your foreign minister for many years, explained that at the heart of Europe's success would always be the rejection of the treaties of yesteryear that divided the world and reflected hegemonic ambitions. This is also the European example, it is not only an economic and financial example, it is an example of a body of standards for the whole world. Looking to the future, what are the conditions for continuing in the success of Monetary Union? We have gone through strong turbulence, there have been these fears of "redenomination" that is to say exits from the euro zone. What are the answers? Yves (Mersch) reminded you of them: there is the response of the Banking Union, there is also the answer on macroeconomic discipline, and it is important to stress that it is not simply budgetary. Of course it is budgetary, of course it is very reinforced on the budgetary aspects, but there is also a surveillance of all macroeconomic indicators. I would remind you that one of the developments that has been wrongly ignored by the markets and by the authorities has been the evolution of the current account balance of each of the countries in the zone. That should have been addressed. Behind the deterioration or improvement of these balances was, of course, the evolution of unit labour costs and competitiveness. Monitoring now carries a wide spectrum of indicators and includes cumbersome procedures that will not allow much indiscipline. However, we are not at the last state of completion of Economic and Monetary Union. What can make us confident that this is a sustainable Union? Here again, there are two extreme theses. There is a cynical thesis that says: Economic and Monetary Europe where the euro zone cannot change its contours because the cost would be considerable and excessive. No one in the world has an interest in the failure of the eurozone. It is true that when we imagine the number of billions involved in a theoretical scenario of return to other currencies, there is certainly a fairly strong deterrent. But this is not enough. The other aspect is, of course, beyond economic reasoning the ideal and the objective of peace, and I believe that the younger generations can be trusted to continue on this path. Are there still subjects of misunderstanding or concern in the various countries of the euro zone, among our fellow citizens? Of course but at the same time, common sense is a fairly widespread value. What I mean by that is that the crisis is not there entirely by chance and that there are a number of people who have understood very well that excessive debts, for example, cannot persist for long. There can and should be debates about how to deal with the crisis, but there is not much debate about the origin of the crisis. Awareness is now collective. An example is that of Spain: the causes of the crisis were obvious, they have been identified, dealt with at the cost of considerable efforts and now Spain is reaping the first fruits. This is an example that makes it possible to understand that the way out of the crisis is not only a matter of monetary policy, it is also a matter of governments, a matter of reforms and also, and above all, a matter for citizens. To try to conclude, three points: The first one that still baffles the outside world, the countries outside Europe: Europe is made in crisis. We have the impression that we know how to progress when we are faced with a great difficulty. It's a bit frustrating, you could say that we could make progress without a crisis. At the same time, it is in a way a factor of robustness since each time, the crisis is different and each time we find adapted answers. The second is the relationship between the European Union and peace. Just a remark: we are now in the situation where Croatia has just become a member of the European Union and Serbia is a candidate to be a member of the European Union. I think if you had asked yourself the question of this possibility five years ago, you would have considered it impossible. This means that Europe is capable not only of preserving peace between its member countries but also of being an example of peace. Another example but which did not succeed. When the euro was created, there was a project in the Middle East, one of the most conflicting areas on earth, an attempt to set up a monetary union. Unfortunately it did not succeed, maybe it was too difficult economically. However, this shows that monetary union is not a universe of "financiers", it is a universe carrying much more important values. The third last point concerns you more directly: I am sorry not to speak German but I know that many of you are bilingual French and German and probably master other languages. We have greatly developed student exchanges. Perhaps you are familiar with the Erasmus programme, perhaps you have been or will be members of it. The German Chancellor recently proposed that there should be a sort of Erasmus for apprentices, and I fully support this idea as a citizen. The mobility of people within Europe and in particular within the euro area, not just for tourism but for professional projects, is certainly an extraordinarily powerful driver of unity. It's in your hands, it's up to you to play. "

Title: Greeting speech at the Square
text: Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Wishes at the Place - 16 January 2014 Ladies and Gentlemen, I wished, as has become tradition, to bring you together this evening to present you with my best wishes for the year 2014. These wishes are of course addressed to you but also to all the employees of your establishments. The past year has once again been very dense. It has certainly not lacked critical episodes - let us remember the case of Cyprus, the US shutdown or the difficulties encountered by certain emerging countries. But 2013 marked, above all, a turning point towards a gradual "normalization" of the economic and financial environment, particularly in the euro zone. Significant progress has indeed been made in strengthening the stability and coherence of the economic and monetary union - in particular the progress of the banking union to which I will return. For your establishments, 2013 will also have seen a determined continuation of the efforts made to prepare for the entry into force of the new regulations and to remain competitive in a world that is constantly evolving. 2014 will, I am sure, be the year of the confirmation of these advances and the affirmation of a robust French and European financial system, capable of supporting more dynamic growth. Adequate financing of the economic recovery will indeed be absolutely key in 2014. And I hope that the reforms announced - which are crucial for our economy and for employment - can be implemented quickly and start to bear fruit as early as this year. Let me detail more precisely the various axes that I believe will be priorities in 2014. *** 1 As I told you, a major step forward in 2013 in my opinion was the realisation of the project of a European banking union. Words and ideas very quickly turned into deeds. And it's a performance worth highlighting. In less than a year now, the main French banking groups will be supervised by the Single Supervisory Mechanism, under the aegis of the ECB and in close cooperation with the Autorite9 de Contrf4le Prudentiel et de Re9solution. By then, a particularly ambitious challenge will have to be met: that of the prior review of bank assets. You know the idea behind it: to get the single supervision started on a transparent and robust basis and thus restore investor and market confidence in the European banking system. This is an unprecedented project, which requires an enormous commitment on the part of both the "controllers" and the "controlled". I know that I can count on your full cooperation in 2014 to ensure the success of this challenge which, in my opinion, is also a unique opportunity for you to demonstrate to the world the extent of the efforts you have already made and the quality of your institutions. A regulatory and economic environment still demanding for banks and insurance For banks, a new era opened on January 1, 2014 with the official entry into force of the CRD4 "package". You have largely prepared for this beforehand, in terms of solvency and liquidity in particular. But these adaptations must, of course, be continued this year and throughout the planned timetable. In this perspective, it seems particularly essential that we give ourselves the means to develop a deconsolidating securitization of residential real estate loans, which will lead to revisiting the economic balance of this activity, marked today in France by a particularly low level of rates. The normative work does not stop with CRD4 and many projects are still in progress. All in all, the adaptation efforts on your part therefore remain considerable. I am well aware of this, and we are ensuring as much as possible that the abundance of new regulations fulfils its primary objective, which is to strike the right balance between the robustness of the financial sector and its ability to finance the economy effectively. The adjustments made in Basel last weekend, which concern not only the leverage ratio but also the liquidity and transformation ratios, reflect, I believe, this concern. For the insurance sector, the agreement of the trialogue on Solvency 2 last November clarified matters. The coming months should be marked by the finalisation of level 2 measures, the publication of the Omnibus II Directive, and then its transposition into French law. 2 The priority for 2014 is therefore obvious: we must continue the preparation. The ACPR will also ensure very concretely: ? Following on from what was done in 2013, all bodies subject to the future prudential regime will be asked to participate in a collection exercise for Solvency II reporting statements, in XBRL format from this year; ? A preparatory exercise for Solvency II will also be conducted, during which insurers will assess, inter alia, their compliance with solvency requirements, on the date of application of the new regime (2016); ? In terms of governance, the submission to the supervisory authority of a preparatory ORSA (own risk and solvency assessment) in 2014 will allow you to set up a risk analysis process in line with EIOPA's recommendations. But the most important thing is before us with the strengthening of the body of rules governing the governance of institutions, a point on which the France is very out of step with the requirements of Solvency 2 and far behind compared to other countries; ? Similarly, work on internal models should continue to move forward even though applications will only be considered in 2015; ? These devices will be complemented by stress tests orchestrated by EIOPA in spring 2014. Beyond these regulatory aspects, the environment of persistently low interest rates and persistent risks, linked in particular to the level of recovery in the main economies, will remain demanding for banks and insurance companies in 2014. In this context, it is therefore necessary to remain vigilant. Title: The orientation and mobilization of savings in 2014
text: 23rd Parliamentary Meetings on Savings - 29 January 2014 Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France The orientation and mobilization of savings in 2014 Thank you for inviting me to this morning of reflection on savings, a very key subject for the French and European economy at the moment. I would like to give you some framing elements and some food for thought before answering your questions. As you know, the household saving rate in France is one of the highest in the euro area, at 16% of gross household disposable income, compared to an average of 13% in the euro area. Where does this money go? Most of it is invested in real estate. The rest - just under 804 trillion - is divided between three main types of financial investments: life insurance contracts (about 801,500 billion), bank investments (801,300 billion) and securities (801,150 billion). EUR 4 000 billion, so twice the annual GDP of the France, is obviously huge and is a major source of funding that banks and other financial intermediaries must be able to put at the service of the economy, in the most efficient way possible. Let me provide an update on each of these investments. Life insurance, first of all, which within the financial wealth of households, is therefore the preferred investment of the French. Between January and September 2013, the holding of these contracts increased by 8032 billion, 8012 billion more than in 2012 as a whole. It is the only financial investment whose growth in 2013 was stronger than in 2012. From 2014, savers will be able to access new products created as part of the life insurance reform adopted last December. These should drain part of household savings towards financing the economy through holding shares. The new "life-generation" contract, in particular, aims to finance SMEs and mid-caps. Nevertheless, the contribution of funds that these new contracts will provide will satisfy only a small part of the financing needs of French companies because, in France, SMEs are mainly financed by banks. This is why it is essential that banks have cheap resources to be able to benefit their borrowers, even more so in the current situation of fragile economic recovery. The ECB's extremely accommodative monetary policy must be reflected in the lending rate. This brings me to the second set, bank investments. With more than 1,240 billion euros, they represent a source of funds a priori very important for banks. But in reality, these resources are often too expensive in France. This is due to the fact that three quarters of these investments consist of deposits whose rates of remuneration are regulated: livret A, sustainable development booklet, accounts and home savings plans, etc. For example, as you know, the rate of remuneration of Livret A and LDD, which alone account for more than 80360 billion held by households at the end of December 2013, stands at the beginning of the year at 1.25%, a level well above that of Eurosystem refinancing, 0.25%. In addition, this rate largely determines those of freely remunerated booklets, for obvious commercial reasons. Its high level therefore actually contributes to the increase in the cost of bank resources and, ultimately, has an impact on the cost of credit. Households also hold term deposits, mainly in the form of home savings plans. The latter, whose remuneration is regulated at least 2.5%, regardless of the market cost of resources of comparable duration, attracted more household savings in 2013. Including the capitalization of interest, their outstanding amount increased by 809.5 billion over the past year. This is not surprising, as funds deposited on PELs are frozen for only two years and not subject to income tax, while bond interest is and the 10-year OAT rate averaged 2.2% in 2013. Finally, households hold securities, mainly in the form of units of non-monetary UCITS or unlisted shares, for a total outstanding amount of just over 801,150 billion in the third quarter of 2013. The creation on 1 January 2014 of the PEA PME and the increase in the ceiling of the PEA could attract part of the savings of households towards the financing of the economy and this is a development that must be supported. These initiatives, together with others such as the CICE and the New National Pact for Growth, Competitiveness and Jobs, should facilitate business financing and contribute to a rebound in investment if necessary for more robust growth. Indeed, in addition to the beneficial effect on labour costs and therefore the competitiveness of enterprises, these measures can help to restore the margin of enterprises, therefore their savings (self-financing capacity) and therefore their ability to invest. In this global context, which is quite specific to France, it seems useful to continue thinking about the allocation of savings and the conditions for a balance between four objectives: - direct a greater proportion of household investments towards financing innovation and investment that will help French companies to be more competitive on a global scale; - enable the banking system to fulfil its role of intermediation in the financing of the economy in the years to come, in the context of international standards leading them to improve the ratio between loans and deposits; - ensure, after taking into account taxation, a fair remuneration of household savings, which depends on the duration of the investments and the risk incurred, as is the case in all the major European countries. With the ageing of the population, a good allocation of savings will be one of the keys to growth tomorrow; - To allow a normal transmission of the ECB's monetary policy, by reducing the obstacles to this transmission constituted by state regulations on interest rates, which it is questionable whether they are in line with the rules of monetary union laid down in the Treaty. Reconciling these objectives seems to me to be both possible and desirable. Thank you for your attention and I am ready to answer your questions.

Avec le vieillissement de la population, une bonne affectation de lpargne sera demain lune des cls de la croissance ; - Permettre une transmission normale de la politique montaire de la BCE, en rduisant les entraves  cette transmission que constituent les rglementations tatiques des taux dintrt dont on peut dailleurs se demander si elles sont bien conformes aux rgles de lUnion montaire fixes par le trait. Concilier ces objectifs me semble  la fois possible et souhaitable. Je vous remercie de votre attention et suis prt  rpondre  vos questions.

Title: Economic Value Interview
text: Interview with Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Published in Valor Economico, January 29, 2014 "I have confidence in Brazil," says the Governor of the Bank of France After a great movement of euphoria for emerging countries, which has resulted in considerable capital flows to these countries, we are now in a situation of market rebalancing and there is no reason to be pessimistic about Brazil. This is what the Governor of the Bank of France and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS, the Bank of Central Banks), Christian Noyer, one of the most influential personalities in the field of international finance, says in an interview with Valor. He recalled that Brazil itself, at one time, had complained of excessive capital inflows and, as a result, the country was concerned about the consequences of such large capital outflows. For Christian Noyer, the current volatility is above all the expression of heterogeneous developments between countries at the rate of adjustment of foundations or reforms. Christian Noyer was Vice-President of the European Central Bank (ECB) from 1998 to 2002. Since 2003 he has been Governor of the Bank of France. Below are excerpts from the interview: Valor: What is the real risk of reduced capital flows for emerging countries? Christian Noyer: The Federal Reserve's announcement has created concerns about the possible effects of tapering. But, in reality, capital flows from emerging markets have remained relatively limited and even some countries have not been affected. He 1 It should be remembered that, at the height of the crisis, there were significant capital flows to emerging markets, in a great movement of euphoria, some said too much. Today, we are witnessing a rebalancing. Emerging markets with strong imbalances may suffer from capital outflows, but this will not be the case for those with healthy fundamentals. We know that emerging markets continue to be a stronger source of growth than advanced economies and will remain so in the coming years. They have a stronger growth potential because they will achieve productivity gains, moving to a highly liberalized economy, because they have labour reserves at very competitive costs. So when the fundamentals of these countries are good, when they conduct good economic policy, there is no reason why capital flows should not become sustainable investments. Therefore, I continue to be confident. Valor: How do you see the situation in Brazil in this context? Christian Noyer: Brazil is a country that has typically seen an excessive inflow of capital and, as such, is worried about the consequences of large outflows. For me, Brazil remains fundamentally an economy with strong growth potential and I am rather optimistic about it. Brazil may need to re-examine all the structural conditions of its growth, do what may be necessary, and have a monetary policy that is well adapted to the country's conditions, but there is no reason why Brazil should experience a period of difficulties. On the contrary, Brazil must rather progress, have results as good as Mexico, but with a larger territory and therefore offering more capacity. Valor: The global economy is recovering a bit, but several analysts are talking about high volatility. Why is that this year? Christian Noyer: I think it's because we went through a period of great uncertainty, which caused violent pendulum movements in the markets. First, the slowdown in advanced economies, then the end of euphoria in emerging economies, and finally some countries, such as China, that have had to readjust their overall macroeconomic policy, which is necessary and welcome, but a source of uncertainty. We have limited the development of shadow banking. All of this created volatility in growth rates, but it was necessary. Today, the dominant impression is that things are starting to stabilize. The slowdown in India is linked to structural, infrastructure and logistical problems, but these difficulties are well identified. Personally, I think that the current volatility corresponds above all to a differentiation of countries according to their pace of adjustment of fundamentals or the pace of necessary reforms. 2 We are moving from an economy that is emerging from the crisis to, I hope, an economy of more steady and sustainable growth. In this period of adjustment, more or less significant movements may occur, but I do not think it is extreme volatility that would see a quarter of recession succeed a quarter of growth. Valor: At the G20 Finance, will tapering dominate the agenda? Christian Noyer: Oh, no. I don't think so. First of all, we need to finalise the regulations for the banking and financial sectors, which need to be put in place in all countries. Secondly, we must address the essential issue of financing long-term investment. We must ensure that savings, which are abundant in the world, are well directed towards long-term investments, industrial investments, infrastructure investments. I believe that the financing of investment, the restart of investment, will make it possible to have sustainable and balanced growth. Valor: What role will central banks have in long-term financing? Christian Noyer: Central banks have done their job so far. But long-term financing is not their responsibility. This is the responsibility of governments, institutional investors, insurance companies, pension funds. What should be done so that pension funds, which have significant liquidity, can finance infrastructure around the world, including emerging countries, provide long-term financing for companies or industrial investment, etc. That's the kind of thing to look at, but it's not the responsibility of central banks. Valor: For emerging countries, it's important... Christian Noyer: Long-term financing, infrastructure financing... This is what emerging countries, like Brazil, need to be sure that the capital flows that will come will not be short-term capital flows, but long-term financing, infrastructure. For which, of course, we need a reception capacity with a solid, protective legal system, but there must also be good regulations in advanced countries that have additional savings to invest. Valor: What regulatory themes should the G20 bring to a successful conclusion in 2014? Christian Noyer: We need to finalise the regulation on derivatives, finalise the latest liquidity "ratios" and ensure that in national and European legislation, these new "ratios" and new rules have been transcribed. The most important measures have been taken and are gradually being implemented. The last point on which we must make progress is that of shadow banking. 3 Valor: Generally speaking, there are no big risks for this year? Christian Noyer: We are all very vigilant, because we are coming out of a very serious crisis, but it is true that, in most areas, the turn signals are green. Valor: But will the eurozone still take time to recover from the crisis? Christian Noyer: The euro zone is emerging from recession but, as long as we are not on a stronger, steady growth slope, we must remain very cautious. For my part, I am confident because I think all the signs we have in most countries are encouraging and, even though growth is at low levels, sentiment about the euro area is changing. Business and consumer confidence is starting to turn around. And experience shows that, in general, that's when you're heading for a period of stronger growth. The challenge for the euro area is to continue to carry out the structural reforms that will allow us to find strong growth. I have little doubt that we will return to 1% or 2% growth fairly quickly everywhere, but we need to go beyond that, in a few years' time, to reduce unemployment. So this presupposes that we are able to pursue structural reforms in the area of the labour market, goods and services, in order to return to strong growth. 4
text_original: Interview de Christian Noyer, Gouverneur de la Banque de France Paru dans Valor Economico, le 29 janvier 2014  Jai confiance dans le Brsil , dclare le gouverneur de la Banque de France Aprs un grand mouvement deuphorie pour les pays mergents, qui sest traduit par des flux de capitaux considrables vers ces pays, nous nous trouvons dsormais dans une situation de rquilibrage du march et il nexiste aucune raison pour tre pessimiste en ce qui concerne le Brsil.
