Title: General Assembly of the ASF
text: ASF General Assembly Tuesday, June 24, 2014 Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France It is always with great pleasure that I speak at the General Assembly of the French Association of Financial Companies. This is an opportunity for me to present the actions and positions of the Banque de France and the Autorite9 de Contrf4le Prudentiel et de Re9solution, in a regulatory environment that has undergone major changes in 2013 at European level, as part of the CRD IV reform. The work to transpose CRD IV strongly mobilized the supervisory authorities and the banking profession in the second half of 2013, in particular with the introduction into French law of a new status of establishment: that of finance company. This work continued in 2014 with the adoption last February of the transposition ordinance and the forthcoming publication of the implementing decrees. In this regard, I would like to thank the professionals in the sector, and in particular the ASF and its members, who participated very actively in the consultation meetings on the draft texts, in an economic context that is also difficult for many specialized institutions, as President Dumont also pointed out in his introduction. My speech will first focus on (I) the reform of the articles of association, in particular the status of finance company, under which a significant part of you now carry out its activities. I will then return (II) to regulatory points, which have just been introduced or are in the process of being introduced, and which constitute an important issue for the members of the ASF. 1) The reform of the statutes As you know, financial companies have been able, since 1 January 2014, the date of entry into force of the Ordinance of 27 June 2013, to carry out their activities under the status of credit institution, within the meaning of the new European texts, or under the national status of finance company. - The status of specialised credit institution was automatically conferred on financial companies. It allows for the receipt of repayable funds from the public, as well as for other banking operations, within the limits of the licence received. These institutions are obviously subject to all the provisions of CRR-CRD IV and they have all the rights attached to the status of credit institution, in particular the European passport. - The purely national status of finance company makes it possible to carry out credit operations under the conditions defined by the authorisation, as well as to offer related services that are not regulated, without being able to receive repayable funds from the public. 1 The prudential regime for finance companies has been developed in line as much as possible with that of credit institutions. The decree of 23 December 2013, which defines the prudential rules applicable to finance companies, refers to a large extent to the CRR regulation. In particular, a broad alignment of the prudential regime of finance companies with that of credit institutions was essential for such companies to be treated as bank counterparties by credit institutions. Risks relating to finance companies will thus be treated in the same way as those relating to credit institutions, for the application of prudential regulation. However, I would like to point out that, beyond this alignment, taking into account the specificities of finance companies has led to the adaptation of their prudential regime, particularly as regards liquidity and the recognition of own funds. In this regard, with regard to your concerns regarding the taking into account of the minority interests of regulated entities that are not credit institutions, the provisions of the CRR will have to be clarified by interpretations of the competent European bodies (European Commission and EBA) to allow a homogeneous application of these texts by national supervisors and therefore equality with regard to competition. I note that many institutions have already opted for this new status. Out of 215 financial companies at the end of 2013, the ACPR received 102 requests for options for finance company status. These requests come from institutions with diversified profiles, representing all the activities of financial companies: factoring, specialized credits, leasing, surety, which shows the adequacy of this status vis-e0-vis the different professions of asf members. More than half of the applications have already been granted. I would like to highlight here the quality of the exchanges conducted with the professionals, which contributed to the smooth running of the option procedure for the new status. Two delicate issues have emerged in recent months, to which I would like to return: access to Eurosystem refinancing and access to payment systems. As you know, the concept of a credit institution is a structuring element of the Eurosystem's monetary policy framework. It defines the eligibility conditions for monetary policy counterparties and is taken into account in collateral policy. On the one hand, entities subject to minimum reserves are eligible for monetary policy operations, which are by definition credit institutions. On the other hand, the only credits that can be mobilized as collateral for monetary policy are loans granted by a credit institution. These rules respond to fundamental considerations. The main one being that, in a euro area economy dominated by bank credit, credit institutions are the natural vehicle for the transmission of monetary policy impulses. Financial companies that lose their status as a Credit Institution by becoming a finance company can no longer be counterparties to monetary policy. Furthermore, under the European legal framework, access to payment and settlement systems is limited to credit institutions and investment firms. Finance companies that do not have a licence to offer investment services can therefore no longer participate in these schemes. This is why the Bank of France has made finance companies aware of the consequences of the new status in terms of access to payment systems and has supported them in the search for a solution. In particular, the exchanges between the Banque de France, the ACPR and your association have made it possible to clarify how finance companies can continue to benefit from payment and settlement systems, by becoming customers of a participant. The second consequence induced by the new status of finance company concerns the mobilization of assets as collateral for monetary policy. I understand that this point is the subject of some concern on the part of professionals. On this subject, the implications of the 2 The choice of the status of finance company, to which we drew the attention of financial companies very early on, are of two kinds. First implication: as funding companies are no longer counterparties to monetary policy, they can no longer obtain credit from the Eurosystem and their assets can no longer be mobilised directly from the Eurosystem. However, assets held by finance companies remain eligible, as long as they meet the Eurosystem criteria. Clearly, the change in the status of the institution has no consequence on the intrinsic eligibility of the collateral. The choice to become a finance company nevertheless has a second consequence on the indirect mobilization of private debts. Indeed, the Eurosystem accepts as collateral only private claims representing a debt to a credit institution. In order to be effectively mobilised, these claims must therefore be contributed by a monetary policy counterparty to which they have been transferred in full ownership. This condition of transfer in full ownership excludes the flexibility offered by the use of the transfer mechanism as collateral provided for in Article L.21138 of the Monetary and Financial Code. I would stress that these mobilisation conditions are the result of rules that the Eurosystem applies uniformly throughout the euro area, in order to ensure equal treatment of all counterparties. My teams are of course at the disposal of institutions that would like to meet us on one or the other of these subjects. I would now like to take advantage of the invitation to address you in an attempt to shed light on certain aspects of the implementation of the CRD4/CRR package about which you have expressed legitimate concerns. 2) Regulatory points In this regard, I would like to address the issues of governance and internal control, as well as liquidity. The Order of 20 February 2014 transposed into French law several important provisions of CRD IV, which concern not only credit institutions but also finance companies. These texts include a "governance" component that introduces new rules relating to managers, the organisation of institutions and their internal control, remuneration and specialised committees. I would like to highlight here the challenge of implementing these new provisions, which aim to ensure that institutions have a clear organisational structure, with a well-defined, transparent and coherent division of responsibilities, adequate internal control and remuneration mechanisms, which allow for sound and prudent risk management. The Directive stresses the importance of checks and balances in governance. This is based in particular on the separation of executive and supervisory functions. Directive CRD4 thus enshrined this principle of separation of functions, by providing that the chairmanship of the Management Board, the body responsible for supervising the action of the Directorate-General, may not be exercised by the Director-General. The importance given by CRD4 to governance issues has also led the Directive to entrust the supervisory authorities with the task of verifying that the members of the Management Board and senior management have the experience, competence and good repute required for the performance of their duties. The ACPR now has the power to oppose the appointment or retention of a member of the board of directors or senior management if he or she does not meet or no longer meets the required requirements. This shows how much the people in charge of the 3 oversight is considered to play a critical role in balancing governance, which is of direct interest to the supervisor. Furthermore, the Directive leads to the management of an establishment being an activity carried out on a full-time basis, or at least on a principal basis. It thus strictly limits the accumulation of functions. The rules are precise: no more than one executive mandate and two non-executive mandates for the same person; not more than four terms as a member of the Management Board, the Supervisory Board or any other body performing equivalent functions. This strengthening of the governance rules has raised questions among you as to the implementation of the principle of proportionality for the application of the above-mentioned rules. I would like to clarify this point. Thus, the law opens the possibility for the ACPR to authorize a combination of the functions of chairman of the board of directors and chief executive officer in the light of the justifications produced by the credit institution or the finance company. The principles governing such a derogation have been specified in position 2014-P-02 of the ACPR, with criteria of size, nature and complexity of the activities carried out. In addition, the rules on the cumulation of mandates apply only to institutions of significant importance because of their size, internal organisation and the nature, scale and complexity of their activities. The consultation currently being conducted by the authorities aims to define thresholds of significance taking into account the specific structure of the French banking sector, without calling into question the final objectives of the Directive. It will soon lead to the publication of a decree, which will allow each company to clearly assess the impact of the new rules on the mandates of its directors. For the application of the new governance rules, institutions will be able to rely on the way in which they had declined the principle of proportionality in application of the provisions of Regulation 97-02, which is now registered at the legislative level. To conclude on the regulatory aspects, I would like to recall the timetable of the texts relating to liquidity. - The final text defining the LCR ratio at Basel level was published in January 2014. Discussions are ongoing at European level on the content of the Delegated Act of the European Commission, which is expected to be adopted by the end of June 2014 and which will define the final requirements of the CRL. - The NFSR ratio is currently under discussion at Basel level and should be published in its final version in January 2015, for implementation in January 2018. After a first publication of the standard in December 2010, a revised version was published in January 2014; it was subject to a public consultation which ended in April. The rules that will apply to French banks will be defined at European level. We cannot therefore commit to the outcome of the requests made in order to adapt these rules according to the nature of the establishments. For my part, I am in favour of provisions promoting efficient financing of the economy, particularly with regard to the needs of SMEs. Nevertheless, those provisions must not be contrary to the prudential objective otherwise pursued, which must make it possible to ensure that lenders have sound management of their liquidity risk, and that they are in particular able to continue to lend when refinancing conditions are tightening. A final word on over-indebtedness, a matter of concern for the Bank of France and for you. 4 I share your feeling that governments, and parliament, have tended to change the rules too often, sometimes without the previous reform having borne all its effects, and thus making it difficult to adapt procedures. I therefore call for a period of legislative stability. As far as the files are concerned, the positive file has disappeared from the landscape since the decision of the Constitutional Council. We ourselves had always expressed the greatest doubts about the feasibility of a file that was both acceptable vis-e0-vis the main principles of law and operable. Even for the version submitted to the Constitutional Council, it was far from obvious. I welcome the work you have launched. Enriching existing files seems to me the only possible option, and it is indeed important to show the outside world that we can get the most out of our traditional files, and that this is the only way forward. Thank you for your attention. 5

Title: ACPR Conference on the Control of Commercial Practices of Financial Actors
text: ACPR Conference on the Control of Commercial Practices of Financial Actors Tuesday, November 4, 2014 Speech by Christian Noyer Governor of the Bank of France and Chairman of the Prudential Supervision and Resolution Authority Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to welcome you today for this new conference of the Prudential Control and Resolution Authority, and thank you for your presence. This day of 4 November 2014, which also marks the establishment of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) for banks in the euro area, is for me an excellent opportunity to deepen our exchanges on missions that continue to fall entirely within the purview of the ACPR, such as the control of commercial practices in insurance and banking, theme of the morning, and payment and electronic money services, theme of the afternoon. Customer protection and the control of the commercial practices of financial players have now become essential subjects, at national, European and international levels. Let me dwell on that a little bit. Reflections at global and European level will have a very concrete impact on national regulations in the years to come, and thus on the ACPR. The next G20 summit is expected to present the OECD's finalised work on the 10 financial consumer protection principles that are intended to be 1 introduced in the regulations of the Member States. These principles reflect the notion of responsible behaviour of professionals and their intermediaries. At the European level, regulations are significantly changing the traditional French banking and insurance normative landscape. These changes will be all the more rapid as they are accompanied by a significant change in the way European standards are produced, with an increase in delegated acts and guidelines issued directly by the European Supervisory Authorities. These regulations and guidelines on marketing are increasingly applied across sectors, with the aim of harmonising obligations between the banking, insurance and financial instruments sectors. Stemming from miFID on markets in financial instruments, many concepts such as the management of conflicts of interest, the obligation to act in the best interests of the client or the transparency of distributors' remuneration, serve as a reference for ongoing discussions on the distribution of insurance products and credit. These regulations and guidelines tend to objectify the requirements imposed on professionals: what content for pre-contractual information? What materialization of the advice? How to ensure the creditworthiness of a borrower, from what elements? What is a conflict of interest and how to deal with it in practice? The answers to these questions all have a direct impact on the organisation of institutions and their intermediaries. I would like to illustrate my point by evoking three themes common to the 3 sectors related to the sales environment and currently dealt with in different European working groups: advice, the remuneration of advisors and the process of placing financial products on the market. These three topics represent an opportunity to evolve practices towards better customer protection. On the one hand, it is a question of avoiding structural situations of conflict of interest between an advisor and a client. On the other hand, it is a question of supporting financial innovation so that it meets the expectations of customers without being detrimental to them. In terms of advice, the European trend is to distinguish an autonomous consulting service from the deed of sale itself, and paid as such by the customer. This scheme, far removed from the French conception in banking and insurance, could present a regression in the field of customer protection. The ACPR, in favour of maintaining the advice integrated into the sale, ensures to maintain a base of requirements that cannot be detached from the product itself in order to avoid the generalization of non-recommended sales. 2 With regard to remuneration, the financial markets were the first to adopt a framework for remuneration policies and practices. This system deals with both the remuneration of employees in relation to customers and the commission of intermediaries. The banking and insurance sector is now following this trend. Remuneration is an important element that should not call into question the neutrality of the advice given. While a framework seems necessary, if only to rule out situations of conflict of interest, it must not have the effect of creating artificial arbitrations between the different modes of distribution. When it comes to deciding to place a financial product on the market, the concept of product governance is relatively new on the European scene. It aims to put in place, upstream of the marketing of products, customer protection systems that rely on producers. Framing "product governance" aims to make producers more accountable to customers for the products they launch on the market. More specifically, it is a question of reserving the products considered to a previously targeted clientele. This is the European answer to unadvised selling. However, this new system must not be built in opposition to the council. An intelligent articulation can be organized between the two approaches, both protective of the clientele, in order to make them complementary. These three topics attest to the rapid progress of European thinking on customer protection and will soon constitute a new challenge for the ACPR, which will have to apply all these new concepts. Another challenge for the ACPR will come from the new channels and modes of distribution in the financial sector. Here too, the landscape is changing. Mainly due to new patterns of "consumption" in the broad sense and the widespread application of new technologies to everyday life. The ACPR already sees this in its controls: marketing channels are multiplying in terms of actors, whether they are insurance or bank intermediaries, brokers, wholesalers or agents, platforms, comparators, not to mention the multiple players in the payments industry. The recent ordinance of 30 May 2014 on crowdfunding has thus introduced new actors entitled to finance projects under certain conditions, by exception. 3 the banking monopoly, via loan or donation platforms, with the new status of crowdfunding intermediaries. These different players are modifying or will modify the market: what will be the commercial stakes? And with what responsibility towards customers? For what articulation between these new distributors, and with the producers? These channels are also changing at the technical level: digital banking, distance selling, new payment methods, and more generally the use of customer data in the world of artificial intelligence and its multiple applications to offer solutions to customers. These developments must integrate - and not call into question - the principle on which European regulation is built, that of a singular relationship between a professional in the financial sector and a customer - in principle less technical, less informed. This is the second challenge of the ACPR: to ensure that these new distribution channels and methods comply with customer protection rules. In this constantly changing environment, the ACPR has a complete range of instruments at its disposal to fulfill its mission of customer protection. Since its establishment in March 2010, the ACPR has developed methodologies for the control of commercial practices and consequent means to ensure its mission of protecting the customers of banking institutions, insurance organizations and financial intermediaries. Firstly, documentary and on-the-spot checks are intended to verify compliance with and compliance with the applicable rules, and to have errors corrected before they have harmful consequences for customers. Faced with serious breaches of legal and regulatory obligations and significant consequences for customers, sanctions may be imposed. This repressive approach is legitimate; it is necessary to sanction past breaches. And the ACPR Sanctions Commission does not fail, when necessary, to sanction. It did so recently when it noted a failure to apply the terms of the right to the account, a substantial element of the banking inclusion of vulnerable clienteles to which institutions have strongly committed. It also did so when it found that the now old requirements of the duty of insurance advice were still not being met. Finally, it did so, most recently, in life insurance, when it found that the system for identifying deceased insured persons, 4 of finding beneficiaries and payment of capital to insured or beneficiary clients was not properly implemented. While sanctions are also useful for their exemplary value, they must not overshadow all the other tools and instruments, more focused on prevention, available to the ACPR. With regard to soft law, the power to issue recommendations was expressly conferred on the ACPR by the legislator in order to take advantage of the observation of good and bad practices and thus guide the market. With a very operational aim, the ACPR's recommendations help the profession to identify and take into account in a more concrete way what is expected in the context of the implementation of the customer protection regulations. Their purpose is to modify or guide the behaviour of professionals, they form a very useful preventive instrument that complements the repressive approach. Finally, communication, pedagogy and dialogue, particularly with professionals, are a determining element of the supervision policy to which the ACPR is very attached - and this conference is one of its highlights. I would like to take advantage of this conference to recall the ACPR's particular vigilance on the level of revaluation rates that will be paid to insured persons for 2014. Interest rates in bond markets, in which insurers have a very large presence, have been on a downward trend for several years and this low interest rate environment could continue for many years to come. Insurers must adapt to the current context by relying on an adapted performance of insurance contracts. This may include smoothing the distribution of results to policyholders over time, by providing the provision for profit-sharing at a sufficiently high level. In the past, good management of revaluation rates and provisions has allowed French insurers to weather several crises much better than others. Questioning the security of the market, by taking reckless decisions to upgrade to the detriment of reserves, would reduce the resilience of certain actors in the event of a crisis. This is why all the players in the insurance market concerned must apply a revaluation of contracts adapted both to the real performance of their assets and to the characteristics of their liabilities. I will now give the floor to Fabrice Pesin and the ACPR teams to come back to some of the aspects I briefly mentioned and wish you an excellent conference. 5

text: Interview with Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France "Real simplification measures must be implemented" Radio Classique - Nicolas Pierron - 14 November 2014 Nicolas Pierron: It is the governor of the Banque de France who is therefore the guest of the Economy on this Friday morning on Radio Classique, hello Christian Noyer. Christian Noyer: Hello. N. P.: Thank you for accepting our invitation, this weekend a G20 is being held in Australia, Europe is getting there weakened, growth is weaker, weaker than elsewhere, especially in the United States, is this weak European growth not also the failure of a monetary policy that has been extraordinarily generous for several years now? C. N.: No, I don't think we can say that because, if monetary policy could do everything, on its own, it would be known. Why did things start again in the United States? Of course, because there has been a very accommodative and very vigorous monetary policy, but also because the economic structures are such that the economy naturally recovers quite easily. That is to say, there are very few constraints to supply, there is a situation of competition that is very broad. We can easily start activities, grow activities, the labour market is very flexible, very flexible, relatively unprotected, which means that there is an objective interest of people to look for a job at all costs, to embark on activities even less remunerative than the old job we had because we absolutely need a job. 1 find a job. Gradually, the market is consolidated and we find a job with a remuneration and an interest more in line with what we have, with our skills, with what we have exercised in the past. So this very high flexibility helps to restart and accelerate the economy, it's not just monetary policy. Obviously in Europe, we have a very different situation. N. P. : Yet Germany now has somewhat the same model as the United States, after the Schrf6der reforms on the labour market, all things considered, we see today that it is itself in a situation of increasingly weak growth. C. N.: Yes, Germany, of course, has more flexibility, even if it is not at the American level anyway, we must not exaggerate. But Germany has a growth model that was very largely export-oriented, the dynamism of exports. And Germany is indeed affected, it is quite natural, first of all by a slowdown in the dynamism of consumption in the euro area as a whole, demand and investment in the euro area as a whole. And it had also enormously increased its market share and the importance for it of customers from emerging countries, but we have a slowdown at least in some emerging countries, China which has taken an investment path let's say a little more balanced, a little more reasonable, more attention to consumption, a little less strong growth, and some Latin American countries such as Brazil, which I hope have had a temporary fall in growth as well. So, we can see that there is a slightly less buoyant market that can explain this. However, conversely, consumption is trying to maintain itself well in Germany, the level of domestic demand is sustained. N. P. : Nevertheless, would it not be in the interest of Germany, as several voices call it, IMF, but also European Central Bank, the France is a partner, it is a partner of Germany, to revive its economy in its own interest this time and not only in that of the whole of Europe? C. N.: Of course, I believe that Germany must not and cannot be satisfied with growth that could reach around 1.2% this year according to IMF estimates, and therefore Germany needs to have a more dynamic domestic demand, which does not mean damaging its external competitiveness. We need a Germany that continues to export to the whole world. But to have a better balance between supply and demand in order to strengthen both the labour market and the dynamism of its consumption. This is the path it is taking, the level of wage increase this year should be of the order of 3%, and moreover there is indeed a problem of investment in infrastructure in Germany, I believe that this is recognized by most experts. 2 N. P.: Christian Noyer, the France precisely, we have had a significant decline in the euro for several months, a spectacular drop in oil prices, which therefore allows us to consume energy a little cheaper, despite everything growth will be zero, almost zero for the third consecutive year in 2014. We also have employers' organizations that are dissatisfied despite the supply policy, despite the reductions in charges, they will demonstrate at the beginning of December, is there a failure of the supply policy, has it not gone far enough in France or is it polluted by other measures that finally neutralize it? C. N.: I think there are two things that must be kept in mind, there is one which is that the policy of reducing expenses which, in my opinion, is essential and essential, it does not take effect in a day, it is only this year that we began to see the effects of the CICE and it is next year that we will begin to see the effects of the reductions in charges on contributions Social. And so it's a gradual effect, you can't expect measures that haven't come into force yet to have an effect. So, again this is not a criticism but for reasons of budgetary constraints, all this is gradual, it should improve the climate, the confidence of entrepreneurs, and that's what is important, but hey the effect is obviously gradual. And then secondly, there is indeed probably first of all an extreme sensitivity to the tax which has come from the fact that, in recent years the tax burden has increased significantly, so there is a lot of sensitivity as soon as we agitate, even for amounts that are quite marginal, the possibility of a certain increase in taxation, it is clear that there is a rejection reaction that occurs. And then, perhaps, the feeling that we are not moving fast enough in simplification, we have simplification measures that have been announced and which are quite nice and symbolic, but finally we see that it is in areas that are most important for business leaders, labour law, Social Security law, or taxation, we cannot say that there has been simplification, it continues to be more and more complex. So, here too, if there could be real measures of simplification, of reduction of the size of the codes that are implemented, I think that it would have a huge impact on the morale of business leaders, incidentally consumers as well. N. P.: Thank you Christian Noyer for being this morning the guest of the economy of Radio Classique. C. N.: Thank you for the invitation. 3

Title: Year of financial professions
text: Year of Financial Professions November 24, 2014 Introduction by Robert Ophe8le, Deputy Governor of the Bank of France Welcome everyone to this auditorium of the Bank of France. By way of introduction, before mentioning the prospects for financing our economy, I would like to give some elements of the state of play which are, I believe, extremely encouraging. The France shows that it can rely on an efficient financing system for its economy: 95 French companies have easy and very cheap bank financing; all intra-euro area comparisons are favourable to France, 95 Large companies have easy access to market finance and can rely on large national IFBs, 95 Non-residents finance our public sector without restriction, as well as the equity of our large listed companies, 95 We have a developed market ecosystem: a stock exchange now largely focused on covering our needs, a clearing house with EMIR standards, numerous and diversified asset managers, large securities custodians with proven efficiency. And in fact, the France is thus a country where the indebtedness of all economic agents is increasing. Whether households, businesses or public administrations, all have increased their indebtedness, through the issuance of securities or by bank credit. The situation of general government is well known with the debt in the sense of Maastricht which has increased by 4% in one year and now exceeds 95% of GDP. For its part, the bank debt of individuals increased by 2.8% over the last 12 months, that of non-financial companies by 1.8%; and, for the latter, when we add the issuance of securities, we have a debt that increases by about 4.5%. In relation to GDP, while the indebtedness of private economic agents is falling everywhere, and when I say everywhere it is in Spain, in Italy or Germany, but also in the United Kingdom, the United States or Japan; it increases in France. This evolution is naturally not without challenging us since we have countries that combine growth and deleveraging while others combine stagnation and increase in debt; this illustrates the fact that debt is not the only key to growth; especially when it does not finance the investment. I recall that in France private investment is currently 12.5% lower in volume than its pre-crisis level in Q1 2008. This ability to respond positively to credit requests is largely explained by the strength of our banking system. The recent evaluation exercise of the banking system, conducted under the authority of the ECB, has indeed shown: ? that the prudential situation of French banks at the end of 2013 was reliable, the corrections made under the AQR are extremely low: less than 20 bp CET1 ratio when the rest of the zone is at more than 40bp; ? their solvency, measured to be comparable from the fully loaded capital ratio (CRR), was the highest in the euro area, 100 bp higher than that of banks in the rest of the euro area. And yet, our financial system is caught in a strong zone of turbulence resulting from the conjunction of three phenomena: ? a regulatory avalanche, ? a technological breakthrough with the irruption of digital technology and the generalization of the Internet in the finance, ? a very accommodative monetary policy with risk-free rates, negative up to 4 years. I will not, of course, go into detail about these three factors, but I would like to stress that they are sustainable and affect all financial professions; paraphrasing the fabulist one could say that not all will die but that all will be affected and are therefore invited to revisit their strategic positioning. These three phenomena undoubtedly have at least one thing in common: all three of them lead to questioning our usual notion of financial intermediation. We know that most of the new - and future - banking regulations encourage banks to reduce their balance sheet size, but it is clear that all the work on bank resolution is also part of a logic of developing alternative financing methods to bank financing: to no longer be "too big to fail", you have to be smaller, and not be essential to finance the economy; market financing must be ready to replace bank financing. At the same time, Solvency 2 will open up the spectrum of insurers' investments more widely as long as they respect the "prudent person" principle, a vast programme, and the implementation of the AIFM Directive organises alternative management. This avalanche of new regulations reshuffles the cards and revives regulatory arbitrage; all of them push for bank disintermediation. The technological breakthrough is the now proven rise of investment and financing solutions accessible via the Internet. This profoundly modifies the relationship between the bank and its customers and leads to a review of the organization of retail banking, but above all it leads to a revisit of the very notion of intermediation: marketplaces are multiplying, suggesting that the interposition of banks' balance sheets, which is no longer technically essential, would be useless. Finally, the accommodative monetary policy with persistently very low interest rates also pushes for disintermediation: it paradoxically increases the banks' fundamental resource, the "retail" deposits that cannot be applied negative rates under penalty of suffering a massive leak, especially in the form of notes. It also encourages investors to seek yield and some may in this perspective be able to do without banks and keep the intermediation margin to their advantage. This disintermediation movement is therefore powerful; I tried to show in the paper I wrote for the Year of the Financial Professions how dangerous it would be for everyone to do without bank intermediation: dangerous for borrowers who would have great difficulty in renegotiating their credits, dangerous for investors subject to a formidable information asymmetry, dangerous for the economy that would risk more instability and a misallocation of means of financing. Our challenge is therefore to resolutely but carefully organize this disintermediation and to organize it with the banking system and not against it. It is in this sense that the Banque de France and the supervisory authorities intend to work with the Place and I believe that the 2014 delivery of the Year of Financial Professions clearly traces this path. Thank you for your attention and pass the floor to Mrs. Denise Flouzat who will present this book.

La situation des administrations publiques est bien connue avec la dette au sens de Maastricht qui a progress de 4 % en un an et dpasse dsormais 95 % du PIB. De son ct lendettement bancaire des particuliers progresse de 2,8 % sur les 12 derniers mois, celui des socits non-financires de 1,8 % ; et, pour ces dernires, quand on ajoute les missions de titres, on a un endettement qui augmente denviron 4,5 %. Par rapport au PIB, alors que lendettement des agents conomiques privs baisse partout, et quand je dis partout cest en Espagne, en Italie ou en Allemagne, mais galement au Royaume-Uni, aux tats-Unis ou au Japon ; il augmente en France. Cette volution nest naturellement pas sans nous interpeller puisquon a ainsi des pays qui combinent croissance et dsendettement alors que dautres combinent stagnation et augmentation de lendettement ; cela illustre le fait que lendettement nest pas la clef unique de la croissance ; surtout lorsquil ne finance pas linvestissement. Je rappelle quen France linvestissement priv est actuellement infrieur en volume de 12,5 %  son niveau pr-crise du T1 2008. Cette capacit  rpondre positivement aux demandes de crdit sexplique largement par la solidit de notre systme bancaire. Le rcent exercice dvaluation du systme bancaire, conduit sous lautorit de la BCE, a en effet montr :  que la situation prudentielle des banques franaises  fin 2013 tait fiable, les corrections faites dans le cadre de lAQR sont extrmement faibles : moins de 20 bp de ratio CET1 quand le reste de la zone est  plus de 40bp ;  que leur solvabilit, mesure pour tre comparable  partir du ratio de fonds propres cible (CRR  fully loaded ), tait la plus forte de la zone euro, suprieure de 100 bp  celle des banques du reste de la zone euro. Et pourtant, notre systme financier est pris dans une forte zone de turbulences rsultant de la conjonction de trois phnomnes :  une avalanche rglementaire,  une rupture technologique avec lirruption du numrique et la gnralisation dInternet dans la finance,  une politique montaire trs accommodante avec des taux sans risques, ngatifs jusqu 4 ans. Je ne vais naturellement pas reprendre dans le dtail ces trois facteurs mais je voudrais souligner quils sont durables et touchent toutes les professions financires ; en paraphrasant le fabuliste on pourrait dire que toutes ne mourront pas mais que toutes seront affectes et sont donc invites  revisiter leur positionnement stratgique. Ces trois phnomnes ont sans doute au moins un point commun : ils conduisent tous les trois  remettre en cause notre notion habituelle dintermdiation financire. On sait que la plupart des nouvelles  et futures - rglementations bancaires incitent les banques  rduire leur taille de bilan mais il est clair que tous les travaux sur la rsolution des banques sinscrivent galement dans une logique de dveloppement de modes de financement alternatifs au financement bancaire : pour ne plus tre  too big to fail , il faut tre plus petit, et ne pas tre incontournable pour financer lconomie ; les financements de march doivent tre prts  se substituer aux financements bancaires. Paralllement, Solvabilit 2 va ouvrir plus largement le spectre des investissements des assureurs ds lors quils respecteront le principe de la  personne prudente , vaste programme, et la mise en uvre de la directive AIFM organise la gestion alternative. Cette avalanche de nouvelles rglementations rebat les cartes et relance larbitrage rglementaire ; toutes poussent  une dsintermdiation bancaire. La rupture technologique, cest lessor dsormais avr des solutions de placement et de financement accessibles par Internet. Cela modifie en profondeur la relation entre la banque et ses clients et conduit  revoir lorganisation de la banque de dtail mais cela conduit surtout  revisiter la notion mme dintermdiation : les places de march se multiplient laissant  penser que linterposition du bilan des banques, qui nest plus techniquement indispensable, serait inutile. Enfin, la politique montaire accommodante avec des taux dintrt durablement trs bas pousse galement  la dsintermdiation : elle renchrit paradoxalement la ressource fondamentale des banques, les dpts  retail  qui ne peuvent se voir appliquer des taux ngatifs sous peine de subir une fuite massive, en particulier sous forme de billets. Elle incite galement les investisseurs  rechercher du rendement et certains peuvent dans cette perspective pouvoir se passer des banques et garder  leur profit la marge dintermdiation. Ce mouvement de dsintermdiation est donc puissant ; jai essay de montrer dans le papier que jai crit pour lAnne des Professions Financires  quel point il serait dangereux pour tous de se passer de lintermdiation bancaire : dangereux pour les emprunteurs qui auraient de grandes difficults  rengocier leurs crdits, dangereux pour les investisseurs soumis  une asymtrie dinformation redoutable, dangereux pour lconomie qui risquerait plus dinstabilit et une mauvaise allocation des moyens de financement. Notre dfi, cest donc dorganiser rsolument mais prudemment cette dsintermdiation et de lorganiser avec le systme bancaire et non pas contre lui. Cest en ce sens que la Banque de France et les autorits de supervision comptent uvrer avec la Place et je crois que la livraison 2014 de lAnne des Professions Financires trace clairement ce chemin. Je vous remercie de votre attention et passe la parole  Madame Denise Flouzat qui va nous prsenter cet ouvrage.

Title: Introductory speech presentation of the Banque de France microcredit awards
text: PRESENTATION OF THE BANQUE DE FRANCE AWARDS OF MICROCREDIT ACCOMPANIES 2014 JANUARY 20, 2015 CHRISTIAN NOYER, GOVERNOR INTRODUCTORY SPEECH Ladies and gentlemen, it is with great pleasure that I chair today the second presentation of the "Accompanied Microcredit Awards" organized by the Banque de France. As you know, the Banque de France has been working constantly for many years to promote banking and financial accessibility, in particular through the right to an account and the promotion of accompanied microcredit. The right to the account allows any person who has been refused a bank account to apply to the Banque de France to designate a bank that will be required to open one. In 2013, 41,000 applicants were able to benefit from this procedure and there were about 50,000 in 2014. The Bank of France also plays a crucial role in dealing with over-indebtedness. On an annual average over recent years, 225,000 files have been submitted to the secretariats of the over-indebtedness commissions. The law of 26 July 2013 strengthened the role of the Banque de France in terms of affordability by entrusting it with the presidency of the Observatory of Banking Inclusion (OIB), created as part of the implementation of the multiannual plan against poverty and for social inclusion. It will be up to the Observatory to propose to the government ways to strengthen knowledge of banking inclusion and the progress made in 1 this area. Accompanied microcredit is clearly one of the ways to promote the financial inclusion of vulnerable populations. The OIB will therefore continue, particularly in this area, the action carried out in recent years by the Observatory of Regulated Savings. As you know, accompanied microcredit is the result of an exemplary partnership between borrowers, associations and credit institutions. It benefits borrowers who would not have or would have difficult access to traditional credit. It is inherently for small amounts: less than 3,000 euros when the credit is for personal use and, in general, less than 25,000 euros when it finances professional needs. This is proof that this device is successful. The overall stock of accompanied microcredits exceeded one billion euros for the first time in 2013, while the number of microcredits granted increased by 13%. Finally, this type of microcredit is based on the support of specialized associations to which I would like to pay tribute today. These associations, which are on the front line in the fight against banking exclusion, do a remarkable job in terms of selection, support and advice to borrowers. The volunteer work of thousands of local representatives and teams that structure and harmonize their action at the regional and national levels is exemplary. It allows people in situations of fragility, whether for personal reasons - such as accidents in life - or for professional reasons - insufficient training, lack of means of transport, collective or individual redundancies - to regain through work a dignity and sustainable means of subsistence. I would like to stress this point for a few moments: microcredit accompanied, beyond its purely technical aspects, by its various modalities, is above all a way of working at the service of the least advantaged people, allowing them to be citizens and economic actors in their own right. It is also an act of solidarity whose usefulness is well established. Finally, for fragile populations, it is a mechanism that offers them an attentive listening to their difficulties, but also to their projects. Respect, solidarity and listening are essential values, the events that have plunged us into mourning at the beginning of the year have reminded us of the urgent need. 2 Thus, while the amounts at issue may be considered modest at the macroeconomic level, the individual effect and the economic and social impact of accompanied microcredit remain very important. The individual stories told in the nominations for the microcredit awards are an exemplary, vivid testimony to the effectiveness of this formula. They show that appropriate financing can lead to remarkable economic and social successes, even though borrowers would not have had access to the usual credit. The winners who will be rewarded today offer a vivid illustration of this, but many other nominations also provide a similar testimony. They also indicate that the financial education carried out by the accompanying associations as well as by the banks allows certain projects, whose success was uncertain at the beginning, to develop gradually under correct financial conditions. This sometimes even leads to the creation of relatively large VSEs, which in turn hire and thus help other people to look to the future with confidence. When it comes to personal microcredits, financial education allows everyone to make reasoned choices in terms of banking services. Finally, these individual stories confirm, if it were necessary, that it is possible to mobilize actors from different cultures and backgrounds - borrowers, associations, banks - to create together the conditions for success and allow the realization of a project. I would now like to warmly thank the selection committee that brought together associations - ADIE, Initiative France and Secours catholique -, banks - BNP PARIBAS and Cre9dit Agricole -, the CCSF as well as the services of the Banque de France, for having made it possible to award these prizes. As I indicated, we have received many great applications that reflect the diversity of personal backgrounds and individual situations. The candidates showed an unalterable dynamism in sometimes socially difficult situations. So the choice was again tricky. As in the previous award, we have chosen not only to reward two of them, but also to present 'nominees'. I therefore extend my warmest congratulations to all the candidates who have been proposed for the award of the prizes. Their personal determination, effort and tenacity have been 3 essential in the success of their project and, ultimately, of this event. I wish them every success in their future endeavours. Finally, in a few moments, I will have the pleasure of congratulating the two laureates more directly and personally. But I do not want to prolong these introductory remarks excessively and it is time for Emmanuel Constans, President of the CCSF, and Jacques Fournier, Director General of Statistics at the Banque de France, to introduce us to the nominees, whose projects will then be presented by their accompanying associations. I propose to start with the personal credits, of which I will give the prize to the winner, before proceeding in the same way for the professional credits. 4

Title: Presentation of the award for the best financial article 2015
text: Presentation of the Best Financial Article Award 2015 April 8, 2015 Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Ladies and Gentlemen, When in 2012 the association Lire la Socie9te9 and that of economic and financial journalists proposed to the Bank of France to sponsor the Prize for the best economic and financial article, this House did not hesitate. It is indeed the responsibility of a central bank to contribute to the development of the economic and financial education of the public. This is a task for which much remains to be done. If a majority of French people say they are interested in the economy (61%, according to a survey we had carried out last autumn as part of the Journe9es de l'c9conomie), this base would benefit from expanding further. If this interest is increasing (by 6% over one year), it remains a function - increasing - of age. Thus, 52% of respondents under the age of 35 said they were "not interested" in the economy. In addition, 58% of respondents of all ages disagreed with the statement that "economic information [would be] understandable". So there is a wide audience to reach, to conquer. To arouse a greater interest in the economy, to make understandable concepts that can sometimes seem obscure or abstract, this is the challenge that we at the Bank of France have set ourselves. We noted it, I hope, with some success, during the exhibition "The Economy, crash, boom, moult?" held at the Cite9 des Sciences et de l'Industrie in 2013. This exhibition, which prefigures the educational ambition of the future Cite9 de l'c9conomie et de la Monnaie, for the creation of which the Banque de France is working, is now "turning" in the provinces: it is currently installed in Marseille until June 7; she will be in Bordeaux next year. In Marseille at this time as in Paris last year, we could see that the public - and in particular the younger generations - was at the rendezvous. Simply explaining a complex subject is therefore possible. This is particularly the case in writing. Translating facts and mechanisms into understandable language in order to give everyone tools to decipher the major current issues is the objective of the various authors selected for the Best Economic and Financial Article award. It can be done in many ways, in many styles. This is what I was able to see with the winners of this 2015 edition. Fifty-two competitors, six finalists, two winners; the choice of the jury was difficult. And all the more so since quality and originality were at the rendezvous. The six titles in which your articles have appeared are representative of the diversity of the press, general or specialized, national or regional, but also of the extent of the audiences that can be reached, the variety of subjects that can be treated. Yes, the economy and finance can be found in a chocolate bar as in a generic drug, in a potato field as in an auction house, in new activities developed in Silicon Valley or in Israel as in a small town in the Loire. And we are all concerned by the French economy. You will have recognized in this table too brief the topics presented by the finalists. It was just enough for it to be explained clearly, simply and - which does not spoil anything - pleasantly. These are the requirements of the prize, which favors the qualities of analysis, synthesis and writing. But, for the first time, the jury was confronted with new forms of presentation of information. Until now, the economy has been illustrated by tables, "pie charts", graphs, histograms. All these supports based on numbers. Now it's time for computer graphics which, unlike the simple organized presentation of data, puts concepts in images, but also uses text, which we want to value. And, today, it's time for comics, when it is based on investigative work and demonstrates certain pedagogical qualities. All means of reaching the public in the respect of rigorous information are good when they are the work of journalists whose role is to make a complicated subject simple, to explain to the reader notions or facts sometimes technical and complex. Young or experienced journalists, you successfully complete this demanding task. To arouse the curiosity of the French for these subjects, and to advance them in the knowledge they have, it is a salutary work in an omnipresent economy, part of a globalized environment. It is also to do civic work, in enlightening citizens who have to make sometimes difficult choices between different economic policy options. Ladies and gentlemen journalists, this prize rewards you. The Banque de France, in this year 2015, so tragically started for the freedom of the press, dedicates it to Bernard Maris, member of its General Council, iconoclastic economist, writer, columnist and journalist, but above all - in the noblest sense of the term - popularizer of great talent.
