Title: Presentation of the ACPR 2014 report
text: PRESENTATION OF THE ACTIVITY REPORT OF THE AUTORITc9 DE CONTRd4LE PRUDENTIEL ET DE Rc9SOLUTION FOR 2014 Press conference of Tuesday, 26 May 2015 Speech by Christian Noyer Chairman of the Prudential Supervision and Resolution Authority Governor of the Bank of France Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to welcome you today for this press conference to present the 5th activity report of the Prudential Control and Resolution Authority, the ACPR. I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the work of Jean-Marie Levaux, who recently left office at the end of his term as Vice-President. During its five years of existence, the ACPR, an independent administrative authority backed by the Banque de France, has federated the cultures stemming from the licensing and supervisory authorities of the banking and insurance sectors and developed its new missions both in the field of customer protection and resolution. It has evolved to integrate into the new European supervisory landscape. Relying on the staff of its General Secretariat - a little more than a thousand -, the complementarity of its five colleges and its Sanctions Commission, the ACPR has made progress on all the major missions entrusted to it by the legislator. To contribute to the stability of the financial system, the ACPR carries out three types of actions. It issues the authorisations and authorisations necessary for the exercise of banking or insurance activity. It shall ensure the permanent supervision of the institutions under its control and shall ensure the development and implementation of the measures necessary to prevent and resolve financial crises. 2014 was a key year. In the banking sector, it saw the entry into force of European and national texts transposing the Basel III agreements, the practical establishment of the single supervisory mechanism, the SSM, under the aegis of the ECB and the adoption of the new European resolution framework. In the field of insurance, it was a new stage in the transformations that precede the entry into force of Solvency II. To protect customers, the ACPR General Secretariat continued to mobilize multidisciplinary control teams during 2014. Customer protection has been at the heart of several highly commented decisions of the Sanctions Commission, particularly with regard to life insurance contracts in escrow, a point that Will be developed by Re9mi Bouchez, the Chairman of this committee, in a few moments. To represent French supervision and its expertise on the international and European scenes, the ACPR continued to participate in more than 250 groups of 1/9 European and international work that discuss legal developments, supervisory practices and the consideration of risks to the institutions under its control. In order to present this activity report, I will comment on the progress of the European integration of banking supervision and the evolution of the ACPR in this context. Then I would like to highlight, in the insurance sector, the strengthening of supervisory actions and the completion of efforts to prepare for Solvency II. Finally, I will return to the results of the two sectors before drawing up some perspectives for the ACPR's action in 2015. Then, Re9mi Bouchez will present the activity of the Sanctions Commission. I - The European dimension of supervision was strongly strengthened in 2014 2014 was a key step in strengthening the European character of banking supervision. In terms of regulation, we have had the establishment of a new common framework for banking supervision resulting from the so-called "Bale III" international agreements and the adoption of a common resolution regime. At the institutional level, the Banking Union has become a reality with the effective start of the Single Supervisory Mechanism and the launch of the Single Resolution Mechanism. These are subjects that you know well but I have to come back to them as they will structure our activities in the future. The new common framework for banking supervision is first, as I mentioned in the introduction, the "CRD IV package", including the so-called "CRD4" directive and the so-called "CRR" regulation, which entered into force on 1 January 2014. In addition to these so-called level 1 texts, the European Commission has also adopted, on a proposal from the European Banking Authority, delegated acts specifying the modalities for the effective implementation of the leverage ratio and the short-term liquidity ratio (LCR). We therefore have an almost complete banking supervision framework, much more demanding than the previous one. It has given rise to a number of reservations which, I believe, must be put into perspective. Today I would like to mention two of them: firstly, the fact that it was found to be significantly non-compliant with the requirements of Bale III and secondly the fact that it leaves a significant part to national options. The negative judgment made by the Basel Committee on the European version of Bale III should not be overestimated; it stems from our more favourable treatment of SME financing as well as from exemptions granted to the benefit of exposure to certain non-financial counterparties in derivatives and uncleared SFTs with a central counterparty (CVA). The first reflects an economic choice to promote the financing of SMEs and the second will see its importance reduced with the development of cleared transactions with a central counterparty. The debate on the relevance of national options resurfaced last year during the EBA's stress test and the ECB's Comprehensive Assessment. It is first nourished by the different choices made by member countries regarding the pace of implementation of certain CRR treatments and which does not allow direct comparison of 2014 data from different banks. These transitional measures will expire on their own, most of them in 2018, and the comparability of the data is ensured by the publication, in addition to the 2/9 regulatory data of data calculated according to the target regime (full CRD4/CRR). More complex is the subject of so-called permanent national options, which are intended to take into account structural differences in savings circuits. From this point of view, France is concerned by its regulated savings circuit around the Livret A and by the importance of banking-insurance, which corresponds to the continuum of savings products of French households. It is clear that equivalent situations must be treated in the same way in Europe and especially in the Banking Union, but it is also clear that banking regulation is not intended to be deployed to the direct detriment of proven savings circuits or the good capitalisation of other financial intermediaries. I would also remind you that, beyond the siloed supervision of intermediaries, we call for a strengthening of the approach of financial conglomerates. The second major regulatory breakthrough is the finalisation of the common European bank resolution framework with the BRRD Directive. The France had largely anticipated this regulation with its law of July 2013 and the addition of a Resolution responsibility to the ACP, but there remains an important exercise of transposition into French law to be done in particular to implement the use of unsubmitted debts to cover losses ("bail-in"). More generally, it is necessary to be able to coordinate the European system as well as possible with future international standards for loss absorption (TLAC). Beyond the regulatory advances, the other major event is obviously on 4 November 2014, when the SSM became fully operational within the euro area. In fact, the European Central Bank (ECB) has set up four new Directorates-General dedicated to banking supervision, and a Supervisory Board where representatives of national authorities, such as the ACPR, sit. The establishment of this package, bringing together the national authorities and the ECB in a unified supervisory system, now guarantees the homogeneity of supervisory practices in the euro area, which is a major step forward, both to support the financial integration of the monetary area and to ensure the soundness of the European banking system. Since then, the ECB has provided direct supervision to the 123 banking groups deemed "significant" and the 4,900 entities that make up these groups. This designation of significant banks shall be based in particular on their size, their weight in the economy of the Union or of a Member State, or on the intensity of their cross-border activities. This direct supervision of the ECB, supported by the local teams of the national authorities, takes place within "joint supervisory teams" (JSTs) to which I will return in a moment. In contrast to these "important" banks, the approximately 3,500 so-called "less important" banks remain under the direct supervision of the national supervisory authorities, with the ECB exercising indirect control over these entities, always with a view to harmonising supervisory practices. The launch of the SSM was preceded by an unprecedented and ambitious exercise to comprehensively assess the balance sheets of 130 European groups, including the 13 main French banking groups, including a phase of review of the quality of the assets held by these institutions (Asset Quality Review - AQR), followed by a phase of stress tests of these institutions. This exercise largely mobilized the ACPR teams in 2014 and required the support of external firms. Once again, I would like to express my thanks for the exceptional involvement shown by all the stakeholders in this exercise. Up to 800 people have 3/9 were mobilized at certain times for the realization of this extraordinary project which required a total of more than 50,000 man-days. These considerable resources made it possible to carry out an in-depth audit of the 120 most significant credit portfolios, covering more than half of the credit risks of the banking groups inspected. On the basis of these "combed-through" balance sheets, stress scenarios could be tested to ensure the resilience of the European banking system to adverse macroeconomic shocks. These stress tests were conducted according to a common methodology developed by the national supervisory authorities and the European Banking Authority (EBA) based on scenarios established by the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB). Two scenarios were applied: a "baseline scenario" and a particularly severe "adverse scenario". Starting from an aggregate level of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio, after taking into account the AQR, of 11.3% at the end of 2013, the ratio of French banks returned to 9% by 2016 in the adverse scenario for the CRD4 benchmark with transitional measures, and to 8.6% in full CRD4 benchmark, well above European averages. When the results of these stress tests were published by the ECB on 26 October, no French bank had to provide a recapitalisation plan. These good results support the universal model of French banks and show that the diversification of their activities, combined with rigorous risk management, is a valuable asset for strong balance sheets and proven resilience to severe shocks. II - The ACPR's activity has evolved within this changing environment In order to take its place within the single European supervisory mechanism and to play its full role there, the ACPR had to partially review its organisation. The separation between documentary and on-the-spot checks was adopted by the SSM on a model similar to the practice in force at the ACPR. On the other hand, the establishment of the "joint control teams" (the "JSTs") that I mentioned earlier led the ACPR to adapt the portfolios of its control services on the basis of documents. Indeed, until recently, certain subsidiaries of large banking groups were grouped together and monitored by specialized control services on certain activities. Conversely, the logic adopted by the SSM consists in favouring the entities belonging to the same group. Thus, a JST is therefore formed for each of the 123 banking groups now directly under the supervision of the ECB. This new logic has led to a reallocation of portfolios between the ACPR's documentary control services, in order to allow the establishment of these JSTs and to ensure that the Authority is fully operational in the European mechanism. As I indicated, the conduct of the comprehensive assessment of the balance sheets largely mobilized the banking supervision teams, both on the spot and on the basis of documents, until September 2014, when the control programme defined by the ACPR Supervisory Board was able to resume. The priorities of the latter focused in particular on market activities and the preparation of institutions for the implementation of the law on the separation of banking activities. Within the institutions, the structures responsible for monitoring risks and internal control mechanisms were examined. Finally, the management of the overall interest rate risk was closely monitored by the control teams. The year 2014 also saw various changes in the status of entities in the banking sector. As such, the CRD IV Directive notably restricted the definition of credit institutions, leading the ACPR to introduce a new status of 4/9 "finance company" from the end of 2013. Over the past year, no less than 134 entities have opted for this new type of approval. In addition, two new statutes of "participatory investment advisor" and "crowdfunding intermediary" have been created to promote the growth of crowdfunding, while providing more legal certainty for individuals by specifying the obligations of these new players. The control exercised by the ACPR in 2014 in terms of customer protection once again focused on compliance with the right to the account and also focused on issues relating to revolving credit, assigned credit and credit consolidation. But emphasis was also placed on the training of professionals, identified as one of the main levers for improving consumer protection. In this context, the ACPR took part, at the request of the National Education, in the redesign of the BTS bank "customer advisor" so that the themes related to banking inclusion, the treatment of sensitive customers and the absence of unfair commercial practices, are naturally integrated into the training program. Finally, the ACPR maintained its action to combat money laundering and the financing of terrorism. In a context where expectations in this area vis-e0-vis the financial system can only increase, the ACPR insists to all players in the banking sector, as well as to life insurance organizations, on the need to set up or strengthen effective internal control mechanisms to counter these risks. III - In the insurance sector, the ACPR has strengthened its supervisory efforts and supported regulatory changes 122 authorisation or authorisation decisions have been taken by the ACPR in the insurance sector. This important figure can be explained in particular by the preparation of Solvency II, whose approach has contributed to the continued concentration of bodies subject to the Mutual Insurance Code and, more broadly, to a rationalization of groups around structures recognized as prudential groups. This trend is expected to continue in 2015. The permanent monitoring has continued its efforts to ensure regular and in-depth monitoring of the bodies subject to the ACPR's control. 97.1% of organisations with a turnover of more than 805 million have undergone a comprehensive risk profile assessment. Supplementary supervision of groups has also been strengthened in anticipation of Solvency II, relying on the 15 colleges of supervisors run by the ACPR for international groups. More than 90 on-site missions made it possible to check compliance with the regulations in the organizations but also, and this was one of the very first objectives of the year, to follow their preparation for Solvency II, whether they have undertaken the development of an internal risk measurement model, or whether they use the so-called "standard" basic formula. Finally, the control of commercial practices has carried out diversified actions. While continuing to monitor contracts and advertising, the Directorate for the Control of Commercial Practices carried out desk and on-the-spot checks with organizations and intermediaries on certain priority themes. These include the duty to advise, the management of legal expenses insurance and the operation of borrower insurance in the context of compliance with the so-called AERAS agreement. 5/9 These classic supervisory actions have been complemented by other tools such as stress tests, or stress tests, carried out under the aegis of EIOPA. During these tests, we wanted to test the solidity and identify possible weaknesses of French and European insurers, but also, once again, to verify the compatibility of their profiles with a measure of prudential risks close to the Solvency II framework. The results published on 30 November 2014 are very encouraging. The eleven participating French groups respect the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) in a basic situation, while 14% of European groups do not. Among the conclusions, we note that the scenario of a fall in equity markets would have an impact on French groups comparable to that observed on their European counterparts. Finally, as I mentioned just now, a complementary exercise called "satellite" made it possible to test in an exploratory way the impact that would have a persistence of the low interest rate environment. Measures targeting global systemically important insurance groups were another innovative focus of the ACPR's action during 2014. As group supervisor (for AXA) or as supervisor of notable subsidiaries (for Allianz, Aviva and Generali), the ACPR participated in the regular meetings of the "Crisis Management Groups" (CMGs) responsible for coordinating the supervision of these groups and validating their recovery and resolution plans. The main regulatory developments of the year focused on life insurance. The law on inactive bank accounts and dormant life insurance contracts, known as the Eckert law, of 13 June 2014, set new obligations for bodies and strengthened the powers of the ACPR in order to put an end to the issue of unclaimed life insurance contracts, which this year gave rise to three decisions of the Sanctions Commission. In 2015, the ACPR will ensure that insurers effectively implement the action plans leading to the payment of capital to beneficiaries. Following the report of the Berger-Lefebvre parliamentary mission, and in order to improve the financing of the economy, new life insurance supports and contracts were put on the market in 2014. These new products, known as "Euro-growth" and "generation life", have been designed to develop life insurance products that contribute more to the equity of non-financial companies. Euro-growth supports include a guarantee in euros at maturity and diversification provision shares. They therefore require particular attention both from a prudential point of view and from a point of view of the control of commercial practices. The ACPR will therefore closely monitor the development of these new products, which in any case remains moderate in the period of very low current rates, which does not allow significant diversification margins to be made while ensuring a capital guarantee over a reasonable horizon. But, of course, the main regulatory issue remained the preparation of Solvency II. IV - During 2014, the insurance bodies and the ACPR made decisive progress in preparing for the entry into force of the provisions of Solvency II This progress was made possible by the adoption of the Omnibus II Directive by the European Parliament and the Council in March 2014. This text amended the original directive and introduced many provisions that, in particular, facilitate the implementation of Solvency II: the principle of application on 1 January 2016 and the establishment of specific rules, in particular those applying to so-called "long branch" activities. Throughout 2014, EIOPA and then the Commission worked on delegated acts (the "Level 2 texts") which were published in January 2015. In this final stretch, 6/9 voices are raised to question this or that aspect of this regulation: weightings granted to this or that type of asset, annual risk calculation horizon, governance rules ... no regulation is perfect, and any regulation is intended to be regularly reviewed and amended, but it is now time to implement what has been decided. Throughout 2014, the ACPR has multiplied its actions to support organizations in their efforts to prepare for Solvency II. Two conferences were organized with the profession, one in June and the other in December, and numerous technical meetings were held throughout the year between the services of the ACPR and representatives of the profession. In addition, preparation for Solvency II was in 2014, and remains in 2015, one of the major priorities in the context of the supervision of the bodies concerned. The ACPR has also chosen to take advantage of all the opportunities offered by the calendar to put this preparation into practice. In addition to their Solvency I obligations, the bodies concerned by Solvency II thus calculated provisions and submitted prudential statements in 2014 in accordance with Solvency II rules. About half of the 400 participating bodies have already been able to use the electronic remittance format that will be the standard for prudential remittances under Solvency II. Finally, the organizations drafted and submitted a pilot version of the internal risk and solvency assessment reports, the "ORSA" reports to designate them by their English acronym. The assessment of the preparation for Solvency II, drawn up by the ACPR following an investigation, confirmed this clear progress but nevertheless made it possible to underline the need to continue the efforts undertaken, in particular to make progress on the work of communicating information to the public and the supervisor, so-called "pillar 3" issues. Changes in governance, known as "pillar 2", must also be the subject of increased and continued attention on the part of the organizations. The analysis at aggregate level of the Solvency II data submitted by the bodies and the results of this survey are available in the series of "analyses and summaries" in which the work of the ACPR is published. V - The French banking sector and the insurance sector demonstrated their strength in 2014 In 2014, the six main French banking groups generated a net income group share (RNPG) of 8014.3 billion, down 20% compared to 2013. However, it was affected by various exceptional items of fairly substantial magnitude, in particular the settlement of BNP Paribas' fine imposed by the US authorities. Excluding these exceptional items, there was a slight increase in profitability, which stemmed from both an increase in net banking income (GNP) of 1.8%, which exceeded that of operating expenses (1%), and a contraction in the cost of risk of nearly 18%. These results further support the solvency situation of French banks, which is already satisfactory, as demonstrated by the results of the AQR and the stress- 7/9 tests that I reminded you just now. The situation in terms of leverage is also correct insofar as all the major institutions in the market have published leverage ratios above the 3% threshold recommended by the Basel Committee. The same applies to the liquidity situation as all institutions have published short-term ratios (LCRs) above the 100% standard. These improvements come at a time when various risks weighed on the financial system in 2014, and still weigh to this day, requiring particular vigilance. I am thinking in particular of the volatility observed in the markets in a context where their liquidity is in many cases limited, as well as the context of very low market interest rates in euros over the entire curve. This rate configuration mechanically reduces bank margins but has an all the more significant effect in France as the fall in the cost of resources does not affect regulated savings and as renegotiations of fixed-rate housing loans multiply. This particularly affects the margins of retail banking and provides an incentive to reduce collection costs. Vigilance therefore remains necessary for this year 2015 and the ACPR will be able to show particular attention to these risks, as well as to those that are emerging, such as the development of cybercrime. As for the French insurance market, in 2014 it experienced, on the one hand, a confirmation of the recovery of premiums and contributions, both in insurance of persons and in property and liability insurance, and on the other hand a fairly high stability of benefits. This development is particularly noticeable for life insurance. Thus, according to ACPR figures, on redeemable media alone, net inflows amounted to more than 8019.5 billion after 8012 billion in 2013. Within the latter, net inflows in units of account (UA) amounted to nearly 806 billion in 2014. It has continued at an even faster pace since the beginning of the year and reached nearly 804 billion in the first quarter of 2015. The main insurance groups active in France reported improved results: the good performance of the technical account was supported by rising financial results, and the stock of unrealised capital gains of insurers increased further in 2014. Regarding the financial results, it should be noted that the fall in interest rates has mechanically increased the unrealised capital gains on their previous investments. On the other hand, in the medium term, the low interest rate environment we are going through entails risks for the insurance sector. The flattening of the yield curve leads to a gradual and lasting decline in the return on assets, which particularly penalizes life insurers. The latter would also be negatively impacted by a sharp rise in rates, if it were to take place, because such a situation would expose them both to a depreciation of the market value of their fixed-rate assets and to a significant risk of outflow, leading institutions to sell assets in unrealised capital losses. Such scenarios have been analysed by the ACPR and the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA). These have shown that, even if the current situation does not pose an immediate threat to insurance institutions, vigilance is required with regard to the quality of the investments made and the rates offered to life insurance savers, as I have stressed on many occasions in recent months. 8/9 As you can see, the ACPR's news was particularly busy in 2014 and many projects still await it for this year 2015. The year 2015 will be in many aspects marked by this theme of the resolution. Some adjustments to French law are necessary to finalise the transposition of the BRRD Directive. In addition, the European Union adopted at the same time as the Directive a regulation establishing a Single Resolution Board (SRB), which exercises its powers under the Single Resolution Mechanism, the second pillar of the Banking Union. Based in Brussels and operational since this year, it is responsible for drawing up and adopting the resolution plans of the groups that fall under the SRM, including all those considered important under the SSM. In addition, beyond the European framework, international discussions are continuing, in particular to further strengthen the total loss absorbency capacity (TLAC). In the insurance sector, preparation for Solvency II is coming to an end. All prudential statements in Solvency II format will be submitted in electronic form via the single, secure portal that was tested in 2014. As of 15 July, the first consolidated annual rebates will be collected according to the scope of the prudential groups. Starting With the September 30, 2015 deadline, quarterly statements will be added to the annual rebates. They will be submitted before 25 November for individual data. Finally, individual and group "ORSA" reports must be sent to the ACPR by 18 September at the latest. The ACPR will also have to decide on numerous authorisation procedures during the current year. The aim is to allow the use of an internal model, parameters specific to the organism or transitional regimes. The authority will be able to rely on the dialogue and exchanges carried out in 2014 in order to deal with these requests under the best conditions before the effective entry into force of the Directive. Faced with these multiple deadlines that are coming, I have no doubt that the acpr's organizations and agents will be able to work together to achieve these objectives. Finally, in line with previous years, the ACPR will remain strongly mobilized in 2015 in the many European and international working groups in which it takes an active part. Present in 255 groups and sub-groups, and chairing 24 of them, acpr representatives are recognized for their expertise and involvement in the preparation of future regulations, whether in the field of banking, insurance, or customer protection. I now give the floor to Re9mi Bouchez, President of the ACPR Sanctions Committee, who will present the Authority's recent disciplinary activity. Thank you for your attention. 9/9

Title: Financing the economy of new channels for growth
text: Research seminar Banque de France - Sciences Po Tuesday, June 16, 2015 Financing the economy: new channels for growth Introduction by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France Ladies and gentlemen, I am very pleased to host, here at Sciences Po, this seminar on the channels for financing economic growth in the new regulatory environment. This theme is precisely that of the latest issue of the Bank of France's Financial Stability Review. In the background, there is the question of a transition to more market-based financing, especially in economies that traditionally rely on bank financing, as is the case in France. The new edition of our Financial Stability Review, like previous ones, brings together contributions from leading academics, industry professionals and policymakers from around the world. I warmly thank all the authors. These contributions are very diverse, and sometimes even divergent, in terms of analyses and proposals. That is precisely what we want. It is clear that we do not necessarily share the opinions expressed in the articles, but we believe in the debate of ideas. The financial crisis has exacerbated the risk aversion of investors, both individual and professional, and their reluctance to make a long-term commitment. At the same time, a new regulatory paradigm has been developed to strengthen the financial system. In particular, it has resulted in a strengthening of requirements for banks, of course, but also for other components of the financial system: systemic non-banking institutions, OTC derivatives markets, Shadow Banking. These developments are likely to profoundly change the features of financial intermediation, the financing of the economy, the distribution of credit and the role of banks. In particular, the new Financial Stability Review focuses on three aspects: - Regulatory requirements have and will continue to have a significant influence on the behaviour and strategies of financial intermediaries and market participants. - The transition to a more balanced financing profile between intermediate and direct financing must be supported by government intervention. - Much remains to be done to drain resources more efficiently and ensure an adequate long-term flow of funding. This is not only a prerequisite for recovery but also an imperative to return to the path of strong and balanced growth. Before we start the discussion, I would like to share with you some personal thoughts on this topic. 1/ In my opinion, the problems of financing the economy are essentially of two kinds: - On the one hand, certain sectors of the economy, for example SMEs and infrastructure, are highly dependent on bank financing, in particular because of the existence of high fixed costs and significant information asymmetries that banks are better able to handle than the markets. For these compartments, it is necessary to unlock the bank credit. - On the other hand, and this concerns the whole economy, it is essential to promote the development of market financing in addition to bank financing. Although this evolution has already begun, its speed and magnitude vary across countries and sectors. Developing a more balanced funding structure is a necessarily lengthy process, requiring strong commitment and government intervention. In Europe, a series of initiatives, led by the authorities, are underway to revive the securitisation market, which has suffered unduly from the negative experience of the United States, and to develop the private placement market. More broadly, the European Commission's Capital Markets Union project aims to support increased funding flows, better allocation of resources and diversification of risks. This is an initiative that I fully welcome and support, but which will only produce the expected benefits if a number of conditions are met: - This project must be part of a clearly defined conceptual framework and aim at a limited number of operationally realistic objectives. - Market financing should be seen as a complement to and not a substitute for bank financing. - The rebalancing in favour of market financing must be done primarily through the issuance of equity securities (shares) rather than debt securities (bonds). At the same time, the use of debt must be accompanied by the development of private placements and quality securitization. - To support the development of market financing, the underlying risk assessment schemes and, more broadly, the information available to investors need to be expanded and improved. - Finally, possible risks to financial stability must be identified and controlled. 2/ Indeed, this move towards more market financing has two main consequences, from the point of view of financial stability: 2 - First, the proliferation of regulation creates a form of uncertainty for market participants. The analysis of the cumulative impact of regulations and their interactions has only recently begun, but it needs to be continued and deepened. Vigilance is indeed essential to ensure that the implementation of reforms does not lead to a reduction in activities essential for the financing of investments and enterprises. I am thinking in particular of market making activity, which is showing signs of decline, in part due to regulatory costs, even though it is crucial for issuers, investors and market liquidity. - Secondly, the development of sources of financing outside the banking system brings a necessary diversification. However, the risks associated with disintermediation are difficult to assess and manage. In addition, the increasing use of non-bank financing raises issues of equal treatment between banking and non-banking institutions related to differences in regulation and supervision across sectors or countries. To discuss these important topics, we have the privilege of convening today an exceptional panel of eminent representatives from the financial industry and academia, whom I thank for being with us today. I propose that each speaker make a 10-minute presentation before starting the discussion in the panel. Then we will turn to the audience. 3

Title: Launch of Citco
text: Launch of "Cite9co" September 22, 2015 Speech by Christian Noyer, Governor of the Banque de France "The fate of a country depends on education," Disraeli said. However, France is perceived to be lagging behind in economic education. It has been measured on various occasions, whether in the PISA tests conducted by the OECD and the National Education, for 15-year-old students, or through the successive TNS SOFRES / Banque de France surveys, for adults. These polls show that the need and demand for better access to economic culture are strong on the part of the citizen: he is an economic actor on a daily basis and he wants to decipher the debates of experts in the media, decipher the economic policy proposals of this or that political party and, finally, have the means to make informed choices, for himself or his country. The Bank of France is fully aware of this; in addition, understanding the economic, financial and monetary mechanisms is one of the keys to the effectiveness of the policies it mobilizes. For example, to speak as an economist, the channels of transmission from monetary policy to the real sphere reach maximum effectiveness only if they are understood by everyone. Take the case of the interest rate channel. As a transmission belt for monetary policy, it will be all the more effective if borrowers understand the implications of a change in key rates on their future monthly loan payments - new or renegotiated - or on the evolution of the price of assets, real estate or financial. The same applies to credit and exchange rate channels or so-called unconventional measures used by central banks when the zero rate limit is reached by interest rates. It is because they will be better understood that such mechanisms will act effectively on demand. From this point of view, participating in the economic and financial education of the public is a natural mission for a central bank, an actor of economic policy in general and a guarantor of monetary and financial stability in particular. This is a task carried out by many other central banks. You are certainly aware that the Bank of France is already present in this area. The Bank designs and distributes a variety of educational materials (brochures, briefing notes, videos). She answers questions from the public on her telephone platform and on the internet. It hosts school groups, organizes educational visits, training and conferences. His involvement is old with the academies of Paris and Cre9teil and he expands more and more to other academies in the regions. In addition to its traditional activities as a central bank, it also carries out missions complementary to education. For example, it investigates cases of over-indebtedness, ensures that the right to an account is respected and keeps the large files of the financial services consumer. Finally, the Autorite9 de contrf4le prudentiel et de re9solution (ACPR) plays a specific role in protecting the customers of banks and insurance companies. The Bank of France's response to this need and demand for economic culture is already strong. But it has taken on a new dimension with the City of Economy and Money. While waiting for the opening of a physical location, the Hotel Gaillard, which will open its doors in Paris in 2018, the Cite9 is already present throughout the France in particular via its website, its social networks, its travelling exhibition and its conferences. Before summarizing the content of its 2015-2016 program, I am pleased to announce today the birth of its visual identity and logo with a clip that I hope will please you and make you want to know more. [One-minute clip]. Why this name CITECO? CITECO is first and foremost a short, readable, memorable name, highlighting the civic and educational character of the project. The logo, with its "e-globe", unites the City with the Economy. Both a letter and a pictographic symbol, the "e-globe" illustrates by its appearance of world map the economic exchanges carried out on a global scale, while evoking a face in profile, emphasizing the human character of the economy. The visuals of Cite9co's first information campaign, which you will see in the lobby or in your file, underline that with appropriate educational means, especially those made available by Cite9co, everyone can take an interest in the economy and get a taste for it. 2 In short, this new identity conveys Cite9co's values: modernity, proximity, accessibility, simplicity, pedagogy, citizenship. Cite9co is above all a City already in action, whose content and main vectors I would now like to recall, aimed at offering teachers, to illustrate their courses, young people and the general public an ever greater set of educational resources. 1/ A new website has just replaced the old one, as of today. Beyond its graphic adaptation, which further reinforces the clarity, recognized, of the old site, its main novelty is to be now accessible in a more adapted way for all those, especially young people, who use nomadic media (tablet, mobile). The site's homepage is also getting more into the age of social networks, with an integrated application to see Cite9co's latest tweets and subscribe to its Twitter feed. Citeco.fr is a site that offers a wide variety of content and gathers more than 200,000 visitors this year. In particular, the following are proposed: - 1,200 articles, - about thirty videos, as many dynamic statistical presentations and bibliographies, - games on sustainable development and others on economics and management, - dossiers and debates, as well as teacher dossiers, each for a twenty, but also a filmography and an interactive historical chronology - "10,000 years of economy" - of 200 commented dates, which was awarded by an international jury. Among the new content for 2015/2016 are a filmography on finance after that on the company, a market game with providers and applicants that was a great success in workshops with young people, animated videos on money creation, conventional and unconventional monetary policies, a quiz on innovations developed with the National Audiovisual Institute (INA), interviews with experts for a debate, or an interactive fresco on the history of economic thought. 2/ "Cite9co" is also a travelling exhibition. The exhibition "The economy: crash, boom, moult?", presented with Universcience in Paris in 2013-14, attracted more than 150,000 visitors. It would have been a shame not to present it elsewhere. After Marseille in 2015, she will be in Bordeaux, at Cap Sciences, in the spring of 2016. Pedagogical conferences 3 accompany this City in action during travelling exhibitions and during local or national events (Rencontres des Sciences c9conomiques et Sociales - SES - in Paris, Rendez-vous de l'Histoire de Blois, Journe9es de l'e9conomie - Je9co - de Lyon). You will find the details of the 2015 - 2016 programming of Cite9co's activities in the brochure that has been given to you. 3/ Cite9co is finally a network of partners to reach audiences, co-produce content, co-organize events. These partners are mobilized and loyal. Among them, National Education has a special place. Our first operations were organized thanks to the general inspectorates, the General Directorate of School Education, the rectorats, the teachers of Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux, in Canope9. As part of this partnership, teachers help us in particular in the development of new pedagogical tools and during tests with their classes. I would like to mention, of course, Universcience (for the co-production of the exhibition "Economy: crash, boom, moult?") and the National Library of France (for its loans of exceptional gold coins). They are represented here by Presidents Bruno Maquart and Bruno Racine. I would also like to underline our sympathy for the teams at the Cite9 des sciences who are facing the consequences of the recent fire. Other major partners contributing to the current and future content of de Cite9co are the Monnaie de Paris, the Muse9e des Arts et Me9tiers, the INA, the INSEE, the OECD, Bercy, the IEFP, also represented here. In Paris, and beyond Paris, I would like to mention the City Hall of the 17th arrondissement, the Ile de France Region and, during key events for Cite9co, the Journe9es de l'e9conomie de Lyon, the City of Marseille, Cap Sciences in Bordeaux and the Rendez-vous de l'Histoire in Blois; and abroad, the network of central bank museums of the European Union and the Museo interactivo de economia of the Central Bank of Mexico. In fact, it is a whole community of scientists, museographers, pedagogues, media professionals, who contribute to Cite9co, whether they are specialists in economics or other social sciences. Some have agreed to invest in our governance, participating in the Scientific Council. I thank them and I appreciate the variety of backgrounds from which they come. All these actions therefore prefigure the opening to the public of the Hotel Gaillard, in the 17th arrondissement of Paris, planned in 2018 to accommodate the museographic elements of Cite9co. 4 Thank you all for having marked, today, this important step of Cite9co and the advent of a major player in economic pedagogy for an audience that we expect ever more numerous. In this way, we hope to succeed in making Oscar Wilde lie, according to whom "education is an admirable thing, but nothing worthy of being known can be taught". Well, for us, not only is economics worthy of being known, but it can - and must - be taught, in the classroom and then throughout life. This is precisely Cite9co's credo. Thank you for your presence and your attention. 5
