Title: Wholesale Central Bank Money in Digital Times
text: OMFIF DMI Conference 29th April 2021 Wholesale Central Bank Money in Digital Times Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor * * * Ladies and gentlemen, The health crisis has sped up the transition towards more digital ways to consume and pay and it has shown the ability of the ecosystem for retail payments to adapt. Less apparent changes have taken place so far for wholesale payments. This does not mean that wholesale payments cannot be faced with the digital push underway in the retail space and will not be confronted with their associated challenges such as safety, accessibility, competition or sovereignty. New tradable assets have emerged, such as security tokens, stablecoins or utility tokens, based on the use of new technologies such as Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLTs) which may alter the functioning of market infrastructures through which wholesale payments flow. For central banks, as providers of the dominant settlement asset in wholesale transactions, addressing those issues means questioning and possibly reconsidering the way they actually make available their settlement asset for wholesale payments. In other words, at the digital age should we provide central bank money to financial intermediaries, and possibly to other players for wholesale payments, in new ways and forms, including in the form of a wholesale CBDC, to ensure that central bank money keeps it dominant and stabilizing role in this critical payment market segment for financial stability? To share with you a few thoughts on the answer to this question, I will focus my remarks on (I) the opportunities and challenges I see for a wholesale CBDC and (II) the first lessons I draw from experiments we have been running at the Banque de France with market participants in this area. I - Opportunities and challenges associated with the provision of CBDC in the wholesale space It is not a matter of controversy that digital innovation in the financial sector and the use of DLTbased innovative technologies are creating a wealth of opportunities to improve the functioning of market infrastructures. In that context the provision of a digital form of central bank money could provide positive contributions and help materialize those opportunities, in supporting efficient and safe settlement processes in two ways: - First, facilitate integration and STP of clearing and settlement activities: It is indeed essential that asset tokenization does not halt the trend of the integration of financial markets by leading to disorderly approaches and heterogeneous adaptations of market infrastructures and their clearing and settlement activities. Furthermore, we could face a situation where liquidity becomes insulated thus threatening the settlement finality of transactions and complicating liquidity management. In front of these risks, a wholesale CBDC could play a unifying role for various systems just as TARGET services did for the current European market infrastructures landscape. This would obviously be valid within a single currency zone, but also for cross border payments, one of the G20 priorities. - Second, minimize settlement risk: the tokenization of financial instruments raises the question of the tokenization of the settlement asset, the so-called cash leg. Such a question should not lead to downgrade the requirements vis-a-vis the safety of settlement but on the contrary it should invite us to revisit the form in which the most liquid and risk-free asset to settle financial transactions, central bank money, is made available. From that perspective, a wholesale CBDC is a way to put tokenised central bank money on the ledger, protecting beneficiaries of transfer orders notably against counterparty risk, which had been nearly eliminated from current securities settlement procedures. It could also be an answer to the risks associated with the use of private assets for settlement, in particular stablecoins backed at par with central bank money, which may expose central banks to a possible loss of control over central bank money issuance and management. The observation that a wholesale CBDC would be clearly beneficial from an integration and settlement risk perspective may explain why central banks have expressed so far fewer concerns for providing it to the market, compared to a retail CBDC; but this does not mean that its implementation would be straightforward. Actually, such a move requires addressing a number of issues. And I would like to stress two of them of significant importance, from the public policy standpoint of a central bank. 2 The first challenge relates to the choice of the technology that would support the deployment of wholesale CBDC and to its scalability features. Blockchain technologies are evolving rapidly: distributed ledgers can be permissioned or public, account-based or token-based which has consequences from an operational, interoperability and control perspective. DLTs remain yet to be tested for large-scale applications in order to be mature enough to be used in a financial context, which would imply to ensure interoperability, with both conventional systems and other DLT systems. When designing a wholesale CBDC, central banks should also, and by any means, guarantee technological neutrality and make sure that the DLT-based solution is underpinned by strong governance and includes adequate processes conducive to the proper production of information data through the consensus mechanism. Operational resilience, cybersecurity, protection of data confidentiality are also key dimensions. The second challenge relates to the access conditions to central bank accounts for settlement purposes, which is currently restricted to entities subject to specific and stringent regulatory requirements. A wholesale CBDC could trigger a demand from other financial actors which do not currently have access to central bank money to become eligible to settle in CBDC, in order to enhance their settlement. In a broader wholesale CBDC access scenario, even if these actors would be subject to similar regulatory requirements, the role of large banks in the settlement of transfer orders in central bank money would be challenged. Conversely, central banks may be confronted with the dilution of their control over the monetary policy transmission. Putting central bank money on the ledger for the purpose of settling payments is therefore not straightforward. But it could make a crucial contribution to the digitalisation of financial markets, which calls for experiments. II - A few lessons drawn from our experiments Therefore, since 2020, we at the Banque de France have launched an experimentation program, with interested market participants, to explore the risks and opportunities triggered by the availability of CBDC for clearing and settlement procedures of tokenized financial assets. Our ongoing program constitutes a tangible evidence of our support to innovation as well as our willingness to take into account the needs of different stakeholders. Two experiments have already been completed in 2020 and the remaining ones  there will be eight of them- should end by this summer. This program has three singular features. First, the program follows a learning by doing approach, as a needed complement to the conceptual and economic considerations to help us acquire the necessary expertise and confidence to inform future decisions. Second, it takes place in a secure and controlled environment, verifying a proper enforcement of the existing regulation: 3 in other words, this is not a sandbox. Third, it embarks a wide range of both domestic and international private partners around a variety of use cases over a wider array of asset classes, with different technologies, in a domestic as well as cross-border and cross-currency setup. Most of our experiments are still under way, but let me already share with you four main lessons learned at the current juncture: 1. Wholesale CBDC could prove instrumental in improving the efficiency of crossborder payments. It is well-known that there are numerous impediments and frictions that hamper their efficiency, in terms of costs, delays, transparency and accessibility. Experiments show that performing interbank payments on DLT could optimize reconciliation efforts and reporting costs for intermediaries and improve information flows. In particular, this opens an avenue to multi-CBDC arrangements1, formed by interoperable CBDCs in different jurisdictions, that would mirror the current approach used to interoperate traditional payment systems  namely the correspondent banking model -, but adapted to the technology supporting CBDC. The three arrangements identified by the BIS offer different levels of accessibility frameworks and degree of interoperability to mitigate cross-border and cross-currency frictions: the first offers compatibility between CBDC systems, the second the interlinking of multi-CBDC systems and the third the integration of multiple CBDCs into a singlecurrency CBDC system. The Banque de France is currently experimenting these 3 arrangements, leveraging on successful pilot operationalizing interoperability between blockchains. But interoperability also calls for international cooperation: to commit to common technical standards, to revamp legal and policy frameworks, to mitigate macro financial implications on the International Monetary System and global capital flows. 2. While CBDC used for retail and wholesale payments are conceptually distinguished, there is actually a complementarity between the two. To support optimal circulation of a CBDC for retail payments, in a domestic or a cross-border context, a wholesale CBDC arrangement is proven necessary. First, a wholesale CBDC, by minimising cross-border frictions, improves retail payments by retroaction. Second, at domestic level, the issuance of a so-called all-purpose CBDC, which would cover both retail and wholesale uses and smoothen circulation between both, would minimizes risks of deposit funding loss for the banking sector through ex-ante measures (in its design) rather than rely solely on ex-post mechanisms (deleveraging, increased central 1 Source: Multi-CBDC arrangements and the future of cross-border payments, Raphael Auer, Philipp Haene, Henry Holden, BIS paper 115, 19 March 2021 4 bank funding). For instance, such a link could prove necessary to allow retail market participants to purchase or sell (tokenized or not) financial instruments, or to settle any subsequent cash flows. 3. Interoperability between conventional systems and DLT-based arrangements is required. All the new use cases referred to as decentralized finance raise the question of the safe and efficient coexistence of different types of architectures to support innovation while maintaining an integrated market for post-trade infrastructures and services. To this end, the Banque de France is testing the settlement of financial transactions, using both securities collateralized in a centralised system and CBDC tokens issued on a DLT, relying on a conditional settlement procedure. Issuing a wholesale CBDC could also complement the current offer by making central bank money available to settle payments on a 24/7/365 basis, which would be particularly interesting when RTGS systems are closed. Decentralized finance and CBDCs will not substitute centralized systems overnight, therefore interoperability by design is key. 4. The underlying technology of wholesale CBDC offers to central banks new ways to keep control over their settlement asset. In a centralized setup, only the central bank as owner and operator of a system exercises control over its settlement asset. The first experiments have shown that central banks do not have to be themselves operators of the DLT and that owning a node and a smart contract could suffice for exercising an appropriate control over their settlement asset, even potentially located outside the Central Bank jurisdiction. The upcoming experiments will contribute to demonstrate how the risk of outsourcing the management of settlement accounts in central bank money, that the use of distributed ledgers to process and validate transactions might imply, can be mitigated. To this end, the Banque de France will analyse the usability of public blockchain technology, including from a safety perspective and determine whether such use would be pertinent or not. * * * In conclusion, with the ongoing tokenization of financial markets and the emergence of new settlement assets, central banks must make sure they continue to safeguard financial stability and help leveraging technological progress for a more efficient financial system. To fulfil this dual mandate, there is a case for a wholesale CBDC, which may not take pre-eminence over the case for a retail CBDC, but which is related to it and which therefore calls for a thorough analysis of all its consequences. Banque de France is definitely engaged in this journey. Thank you for your attention. * * * 5

Title: Housing Credit: The Chicken, the Egg and the Price of Eggs
text: EUROSYSTEM Rostrum (Deputy Governors J) Home credit: the chicken, the egg and the price of eggs Published on June 22, 2023 Op-ed by Agnes Benassy-Quere, Second Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Image Chicken and eggs It's no secret that the days of free money are over. Since July 2022, the European Central Bank has raised its key interest rates seven times. A year ago, banks were happy to lend you at less than 2% because they could hardly find anything better to do on the market. But today, the least risky borrower in the country - the state - borrows at around 3% (compared to negative rates only a year ago). All rates have shifted upwards. Even if they are always happy to recruit new customers, banks will no longer lend at 2% and even less at 1%. The rise in rates is particularly affecting households wishing to own a home. It is general in all euro area countries, although less pronounced in France than in the other three major euro area countries (Chart 1). Chart 1: Interest rate on new housing loans (annual percentage rate* in annual percentage) * including fees and insurance. Source: ECB, Banque de France calculations.Last update: April 2023. Image GraDhiaue 1: interest rate on new housing loans This rapid rise in interest rates is intended to curb inflation, which has made a sudden and pronounced return in Europe and around the world. If it becomes more expensive to borrow, then households and businesses will slow down their investment and consumer spending, and companies that provide goods and services will be forced to moderate their prices to find customers. This inflation-fighting strategy has led to a normalisation of the production of new housing loans since the second half of 2022. However, the decline in volumes raises three questions: (1) is it excessive in relation to the need for access to housing? (2) Is it unfair, penalising young and/or low-income households in particular? (3) Is it recessionary for the construction sector? Is the decline in housing credit excessive? In April 2023, excluding renegotiations, just over 12 billion in new housing loans were granted by banks in France, down from the peaks of 20 billion per month in 2021, but at a level that seems to be stabilising well above the amounts observed during the decade 2005-2014 (9 billion on average, Chart 2). The near doubling of housing credit between 2005-2014 and 2015-2022, correlated with changes in real estate prices, must be put into perspective with a 49% increase in nominal GDP between 2005 and 2022. Graph 2: New housing loans for individuals (seasonally adjusted, in billion) Source: Banque de France - Statlnfo Loans to individuals. Last update: April 2023. Image Graph 2: New housing loans for individuals Is the right level of credit production 5, 10, 12 or 20 billion per month? There are several ways to look at the subject. The first is to note that with 12 billion in new loans in April, France is above Germany (9 billion, a very sharp decline over one year), and well above Italy and Spain (each at less than 4 billion). So far, the development of credit has essentially resembled a normalisation after the exuberant years of very low interest rates. A second way of approaching the issue of housing credit is to examine its impact on "real estate purchasing power", i.e. on the ability of households to acquire a given surface area: all other things being equal, rising interest rates reduce households' ability to borrow, and therefore to finance their purchases. Conversely, the fall in interest rates was a powerful factor in increasing real estate purchasing power until 2017 (Chart 3). However, it is important to emphasize the "all other things being equal": after 2017, the continued decline in interest rates combined with the increase in incomes ues empruiiieuib a aie pius que uumpeiieee pai the rise in prices, as a result of the fact that purchasing power would have decreased if the banks had not extended the duration of loans. Chart 3 shows that real estate purchasing power decreased in 2020 and 2021, even before interest rates rose. A general law in finance is that asset prices move inversely to interest rates. In the real estate sector, rising interest rates are making buyers scarce and eventually driving prices down. This phenomenon is already at work in Germany, the Nordic countries and, outside the European Union, in Canada and Korea (see OECD data). This is a powerful reminder for real estate purchasing power, even if there may be a delay between the rise in rates and the fall in prices. Figure 3. Cumulative change in real estate purchasing power since January 2008, in % Source: Banque de France calculations. Last update: March 2023. Image Figure 3. Cumulative change in real estate purchasing power since January 2008, in % A third way to judge the level of credit is to look at the household debt ratio. At 65% of GDP (and 101% of gross disposable income) at the end of 2022, French household debt is the heaviest of the four major countries in the euro area, whereas it was among the lowest ten years ago. Even if this debt is almost always at a fixed rate, it poses a risk to households whose repayment burden (interest and principal) represents a significant part of their income. Is the decline in housing credit unfair? Faced with the continuous extension of the duration of loans and the increase in the repayment costs borne by borrowing households (as a % of their income, which is known as the effort ratio), the High Council for Financial Stability recommended (in December 2019), recalibrated in January 2021, and then imposed (in January 2022) a limit on both the duration of loans (25 years) and the borrowers' effort rate (35%). The aim was to put an end to the excesses observed in housing credit practices in terms of effort rate and loan duration, while preserving access to credit, particularly in the context of access to property. This objective has been achieved, as the share of loans involving an effort ratio of more than 35% has rapidly fallen below the threshold of the permitted flexibilities (Chart 4). However, credit did not slow down (Chart 2), nor was that the purpose of the measure. Figure 4. Breakdown of the production of new appropriations according to the effort ratio (in %) Image Figure 4. Breakdown of the production of new appropriations by effort ratio (in %) With rising interest rates, there is a temptation to extend the term of loans again or to increase repayment costs. However, it can be observed that, despite the limits imposed, first-time buyers (those most dependent on credit) have not been squeezed out of the market: their share in the production of housing loans is increasing, to the detriment of buyers who are already homeowners, with the share of loans for rental investment being stable (Chart 5). Figure 5. Share of different types of borrowers in the production of housing loans, in % Image Figure 5. Share of the different types of borrowers in the production of housing loans, in % The recent evolution of housing credit does not seem to have ousted the youngest from the market either. According to data from Credit Logement (a financing company granting guarantees on real estate loans), the share of people under 35 in housing loans has been on the rise since 2019 and has not decreased in 2022-23, as has the share of households with incomes below three times the minimum wage. Of course, we must remain vigilant, but inequality of access to property does not seem to have increased significantly to date. However, it could be objected that, among the 10% of the poorest households, 65% are tenants and not owners (Graph 6). Tenants could suffer from the credit crunch not directly, through restricted access to homeownership, but indirectly, through attrition of the supply of rental housing. Whatever possible technical adjustments that could be considered by the HCSF on this subject, rental investment remains above all hampered by its low profitability, particularly in tense areas (Madec, 2023). Between 2015 and 2022, investors in the rental market were paid more by the capital gain on the resale of the property than by the rents received during the holding period, which are sometimes capped. This hope of surplus value has disappeared. If rising interest rates lead to a fall in prices without an equivalent decrease in rents (see for example, Bove, Dees and Thubin, 2020 ; Terra Nova. 2023). then the profitability of rental investment will recover and we can hope, in the long term, for an increase in the supply of rental housing. Multi-owner households are clearly concentrated in the tenths, hundredths and thousandths of the highest standards of living (Chart 6). The purchase of second homes and the rapid development of furnished tourist rentals may have partly crowded out the supply of long-term rentals (see for example Duso et al. (2021) on the case of Berlin, and the Paris Habitat Institute (2023) on the case of Paris). Thus, it is possible that the same volume of credit excluding primary residences will feed the long-term rental market less than was the case in the past. The solution to this problem is primarily through the reduction of regulatory and fiscal distortions. Figure 6. Number of dwellings owned by standard of living, year 2017 Source : Insee (2021). Image Figure 6. Number of dwellings owned by standard of living, year 2017 Home loans and housing construction A third way to analyze the slowdown in housing credit is to take into account its repercussions on construction. In fact, the construction of new homes began to decline in the second half of 2022, and bookings are also down. However, with 431,800 authorised constructions (and 354,200 started) between May 2022 and April 2023, the overall volume remains close to the pre-pandemic level (460,100 authorised constructions and 385,200 started between March 2019 and February 2020), and in the order of magnitude of the projection of needs carried out by the General Commission for Sustainable Development - between 300,000 and 350,000 housing units per year. If the feeling is clearly that of a shortage, it is partly due to the large stock that is not devoted to the main residence and because new housing is not sufficiently located in areas where demand is high, due in particular to a persistent difficulty in densifying cities (see Tardiveau. 2020). It should be remembered here that the volume and price of housing loans are not the only determinants of activity in the construction sector. Other elements, such as labour shortages, the slowness of the authorisation processes for collective housing or the decline in household confidence, are also likely to slow down projects. While construction costs are difficult to adjust in the short term, a drop in land prices could temporarily help support households' real estate purchasing power. The normalization of housing credit could ultimately contribute to a form of rationalization of the supply of new housing in France by limiting the burgeoning of second homes and furnished tourist accommodation, by making investors aware of the risk of vacancy and by reducing the price of land. Updated on November 21, 2023

Les locataires pourraient souffrir du resserrement du crdit non pas de faon directe, par restriction de laccs  la proprit, mais de manire indirecte, par attrition de loffre de logements locatifs. Quelques soient dventuels ajustements techniques qui pourraient tre envisags par le HCSF sur ce sujet, linvestissement locatif reste avant tout frein par sa faible rentabilit notamment en zone tendue (Madec, 2023). Entre 2015 et 2022, les investisseurs sur le march locatif se sont rmunrs davantage par la plus- value  la revente du bien que via les loyers perus pendant la priode de dtention, lesquels sont parfois plafonns. Si le ressenti est clairement celui dune pnurie, cest en partie en raison de limportance du parc qui nest pas dvolu  la rsidence principale et parce que les nouveaux logements ne se situent pas suffisamment dans les zones o la demande est forte, du fait notamment dune difficult persistante  densifier les villes (voir Tardiveau. 2020). Si les cots de construction peuvent difficilement sajuster  court terme, une baisse des prix du foncier pourrait temporairement contribuer  soutenir le pouvoir dachat immobilier des mnages. La normalisation du crdit  lhabitat pourrait finalement contribuer  une forme de rationalisation de loffre de nouveaux logements en France en limitant le bourgeonnement de rsidences secondaires et meubls touristiques, en sensibilisant les investisseurs au risque de vacance et en rduisant le prix du foncier. Title: Margins at a snail's pace?
text: EUROSYSTEM Tribune (Deputy Governors J) Margins at a fast pace? Published on June 23, 2023 Op-ed by Agnes Benassy-Quere, Second Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Image A rise in profits in the eurozone, which may have contributed to the rise in prices in 2022 The European Central Bank (ECB), through its President, Chief Economist and Director-General for the Economy (and colleagues), have warned of rising profits in the euro area, which may have contributed to the rise in prices in 2022. While wages have, on average, risen less rapidly than prices last year, one can legitimately wonder about the respective contributions of wages and profits to the rise in prices. At the beginning of the energy crisis, the state took on most of the loss of household income due to higher import prices (see Claveres. 2022 : Villerov de Galhau. 2022). However, companies have been able to gradually pass on the increase in their costs, so that households and companies have begun the ping-pong game that Guillaume Claveres and I described in February on Telos, and of which Guido Lorenzoni and Ivan Werning have recently proposed an elegant model: workers are asking for wage increases to preserve their purchasing power; but companies are asking for their own in turn pass on wage increases in their prices; workers must again ask for wage increases, etc. Inflation then depends on the relative aspirations of workers (in terms of purchasing power, wages) and companies (in terms of margins). The incompatibility of their aspirations can lead to self-perpetuating inflation. This is why central banks are concerned about it. Sharing added value Let's start from the ground up: the wealth created by the productive sector during a quarter or a year is distributed to the two factors of production, labour and capital, as well as to the state via taxes on production and products. Since the mid-1980s, France has shown a relatively stable recovery in the value of the asset  a development yes in contrast to the decline in the labour share observed in the United States (Chart 1). The share of labour is even stable in France over a very long period when we exclude real estate services which, by definition, essentially remunerate capital via real or imputed rents. Image Share of labour in value added In the most recent period, wages, with the exception of the minimum wage (SMIC), have risen less quickly than inflation, so that the purchasing power of wages has declined in France. However, employment has risen sharply, so that the wage bill has grown more or less at the same rate as value added. Gross operating surplus (EBITDA), which in national accounts represents the return on capital, also increased as did value added. Between the beginning of 2018 and the beginning of 2023, the wage bill, EBITDA and value added all increased by around 20% for all market branches (Chart 2). There is indeed an acceleration in EBITDA in 2022, but this compensates for a drop in the second half of 2021. In other words, the ratio between EBITDA and nominal value added has returned to its 2018 level (see INSEE's March 2023 Economic Outlook). Image Evolution of the wage bill and gross operating surplus in France - Branches of the market There seems to be a significant gap between this cold statistical observation and the "feeling" of a clear increase in company margins, to the detriment of workers. This difference can be explained in many ways:  We tend to extrapolate the evolution of the purchasing power of wages to the evolution of purchasing power in general. As we have seen above, the increase in employment has made a significant contribution to purchasing power since 2018.  We read in the newspapers that some companies have made windfall profits, which we extrapolate to all companies. However, these large profits were generally made in certain specific sectors such as freight transport, while other companies saw their profits fall without necessarily being reported in the press, for example in construction or market services (in particular hotels and restaurants). In addition, the profits of large French companies such as those of the CAC40, which are highly internationalized, particularly in the energy sector, are largely made outside France and are therefore not taken into account to calculate the distribution of added value on the national territory (in the sense of the Gross Domestic Product).  We are particularly sensitive to the agri-food sector, for which the share of EBITDA in value added was, at the end of 2022, according to INSEE, 5 percentage points above its level at the beginning of 2018.  In connection with the previous point, the price index used to calculate the value of the value is the value of This increased less quickly over the period than the consumer price index due to the sharp increase in the prices of imported goods (especially energy).  And finally, it is normal for corporate profits to increase with inflation. The question is whether they are rising faster than wages, and whether they are growing in a sustainable way. Contribution of margins to inflation To what extent has the recent increase in the unit margin (gross operating surplus in current euros per unit of value added in volume) contributed to the rise in prices? We will stick here to the price of value added, i.e. the price invoiced by companies, corrected for the price of their inputs. This price gives the value of a unit of added value. It is the sum of the labour cost of a unit of value added (the unit labour cost) and the capital cost of the same unit of VA (the unit margin). In times of inflation, all costs per unit of output increase. Assuming that the share of labour in value added is 2/3 and that of capital is 1/3, if all unit quantities increase at the same rate, say 4%, the contribution of unit labour costs is 4%x2/32.6% while that of the unit margin is 4%x1/31.3%. Have unit margins contributed more than their share over the recent period? Figure 3 answers this question for the euro area and for France. In order to allow comparison, the graph is plotted for the economy as a whole and not just for the market sector. It is therefore the price (or "deflator") of GDP and not the price of market value added. In the second half of 2022, the contribution of the unit margin to inflation was higher than that of the unit labour cost in the euro area. In France, however, the contribution of the unit margin is lower than that of the unit labour cost, after being negative in the first half of 2022. The graph also shows the contribution of net indirect taxes, which, in accounting terms, make it possible to move from a concept of value added to the concept of gross domestic product (GDP). Image Year-on-year change in GDP deflator and contributions of unit labour cost and unit margin This overall diagnosis masks a strong sectoral heterogeneity. For example, in France, the agri-food and other manufacturing industries appear to have driven unit margins upwards in recent quarters, while these sectors had contributed little to the decline in the aggregate margin at the beginning of 2022 (Chart 4). Other sectors, such as accommodation and catering or other market services, saw their margins fall during the period. Despite its low weight in GDP, the agricultural sector contributed positively to the revolution in the aggregate unit margin in 2021-2022. However, the very sharp increase in input prices for this sector makes it difficult to interpret this contribution (see Colonna. Torrini and Viviano. 2023). Image Another way of looking at the issue is to calculate not the unit margin (margin per unit of value added) but the margin rate (price in relation to unit labour cost). If the price of value added increases at the same rate as the unit labour cost, then the margin rate remains constant and its contribution to inflation is zero (the price of value added increases as does the unit labour cost). Figure 5 shows that in the euro area, the margin rate increased over the years 2021 and 2022, partly by catching up after the decline recorded in 2020, and that this contributed to the rise in prices. In the case of France, the aggregate margin rate evolved more bumpily due to the massive support received by companies in the second half of 2020 and the first half of 2021, with a backlash afterwards, to finally return to the level of early 2018 at the end of 2022. Image Year-on-year change in GDP deflator and contributions of unit labour cost and margin rate In the first quarter of 2023, according to INSEE's first estimate, the margin rate of non-financial corporations increased by 0.4 percentage points compared to the previous quarter in France, mainly due to the decrease in the contribution on the added value of companies (CVAE) and an increase in aid for the payment of energy bills. In terms of level, the margin rate remains around 32%, its medium-term value. Micro contre macro A microeconomist would probably dispute the above margin measures. In principle, a company sets its price not in relation to its average cost (the unit wage cost), but in relation to its marginal cost (the cost of the last unit produced): if the company is alive, it is because it makes a sufficient commercial margin on its variable costs to cover its fixed costs. The price itself is not determined by fixed costs, but by marginal cost and market structures. Based on this principle, De Loecker and Warzvnski (2012) proposed a simple formula to calculate the markup of each firm, and Bauer and Boussard (2020) applied it to French firms between 1984 and 2016. In line with the national accounts approach, they find a stable aggregate markup over this period. But this stability is the combined result of a decrease in markup at the individual firm level and a reallocation of output towards companies with a high makup (composition effect). Unfortunately, the individual data needed to update this work are only available two years late. Given all these methodological difficulties, it is prudent to cross-reference different measures of margins and to observe them over sufficiently long periods. In addition, there are difficulties of interpretation when the price of imported inputs rises sharply. Updated on November 21, 2023

Mise en ligne le 23 Juin 2023 Tribune d'Agns Bnassy-Qur, Seconde sous-gouverneure de la Banque de France. Image Une hausse des profits en zone euro, qui pourrait avoir contribu  la hausse des prix en 2022 La Banque centrale europenne (BCE), par la voix notamment de sa Prsidente, de son Chef-conomiste et de son Directeur gnral pour lconomie (et collgues), ont alert sur la hausse des profits en zone euro, qui pourrait avoir contribu  la hausse des prix en 2022. Alors que les salaires ont, en moyenne, augment moins vite que les prix lan dernier, on peut lgitimement sinterroger sur les contributions respectives des salaires et des profits  la hausse des prix. Au dbut de la crise nergtique, ltat a pris  sa charge lessentiel de la perte de revenu des mnages lie au renchrissement des importations (voir Clavres. 2022 : Villerov de Galhau. 2022). Toutefois, les entreprises ont pu progressivement rpercuter le renchrissement de leurs cots, de sorte que les mnages et les entreprises ont commenc la partie de ping-pong que Guillaume Clavres et moi dcrivions en fvrier sur Telos, et dont Guido Lorenzoni et Ivn Werning ont rcemment propos une lgante modlisation : les travailleurs demandent des augmentations de salaires pour prserver leur pouvoir dachat ; mais les entreprises  leur tour rpercutent les hausses de salaires dans leurs prix ; les travailleurs doivent de nouveau demander des hausses de salaires, etc. Linflation dpend alors des aspirations relatives des travailleurs (en termes de pouvoir dachat du salaire) et des entreprises (en termes de marges). Lincompatibilit de leurs aspirations peut conduire  une inflation auto-entretenue. Cest pourquoi les banques centrales sen proccupent. Partage de la valeur ajoute Repartons de la base : la richesse cre par le secteur productif au cours dun trimestre ou dune anne est distribue aux deux facteurs de production que sont le travail et le capital, ainsi qu ltat via les impts sur la production et les produits. Depuis le milieu des annes 1980, la France affiche une rnartition relativement stable de la valeur aioute  une volution oui contraste avec la baisse de la part du travail observe aux tats-Unis (graphique 1). La part du travail est mme stable en France sur trs longue priode lorsquon exclut les services immobiliers qui, par dfinition, rmunrent essentiellement le capital via des loyers rels ou imputs. Image Part du travail dans la valeur ajoute Sur la priode la plus rcente, les salaires ont,  lexception du salaire minimum (Smic), augment moins vite que linflation, si bien que le pouvoir dachat du salaire a recul en France. Cependant, lemploi a fortement augment, de sorte que la masse salariale a cr peu ou prou au mme rythme que la valeur ajoute. Lexcdent brut dexploitation (EBE), qui en comptabilit nationale reprsente la rmunration du capital, a augment lui aussi comme la valeur ajoute. Entre dbut 2018 et dbut 2023, la masse salariale, lEBE et la valeur ajoute ont tous augment denviron 20% pour lensemble des branches marchandes (graphique 2). On observe bien une acclration de lEBE sur lanne 2022, mais cela vient compenser un dcrochage au second semestre 2021. Autrement dit, le rapport entre EBE et valeur ajoute nominale est revenu  son niveau de 2018 (voir la Note de conjoncture de lInsee de mars 2023). Image Evolution de la masse salariale et de l'excdent brut d'exploitation en France - Branches marchandes Il semble exister un cart important entre ce froid constat statistique et le  ressenti  dune nette hausse des marges des entreprises, au dtriment des travailleurs. Cet cart peut sexpliquer de multiples manires :  Nous avons tendance  extrapoler lvolution du pouvoir dachat du salaire  lvolution du pouvoir dachat en gnral. Comme on la vu plus haut, la hausse de lemploi a fortement contribu au pouvoir dachat depuis 2018.  Nous lisons dans les journaux que certaines entreprises ont ralis des profits exceptionnels, que nous extrapolons  lensemble des entreprises. Or, ces profits importants ont en gnral t raliss dans certains secteurs spcifiques comme le transport de marchandises, tandis que dautres entreprises voyaient leurs profits diminuer sans que la presse sen fasse ncessairement lcho, par exemple dans la construction ou les services marchands (notamment l'htellerie-restauration). Par ailleurs, les profits des grandes entreprises franaises comme celles du CAC40, trs internationalises, notamment dans le secteur nergtique, sont pour une large part raliss hors de France et ne sont donc pas pris en compte pour calculer le partage de la valeur ajoute sur le territoire national (au sens du Produit Intrieur Brut).  Nous sommes particulirement sensibles au secteur agro-alimentaire pour lequel la part de lEBE dans la valeur ajoute tait, fin 2022, selon lInsee, 5 points de pourcentage au-dessus de son niveau de dbut 2018.  En lien avec le point prcdent, lindice de prix utilis pour calculer le nartanc rla la valeur aimitaa aQt Innimiamant la nriv rla la valaiir aimitaa lequel a augment moins vite sur la priode que lindice des prix  la consommation du fait de la forte augmentation des prix des biens imports (notamment lnergie).  Et finalement, il est normal que les profits des entreprises augmentent avec linflation. Toute la question est de savoir sils augmentent plus vite que les salaires, et ce de manire durable. Contribution des marges  linflation Dans quelle mesure la hausse rcente de la marge unitaire (excdent brut dexploitation en euros courants par unit de valeur ajoute en volume) a-t-elle contribu  la hausse des prix ? On va sen tenir ici au prix de la valeur ajoute, cest--dire au prix factur par les entreprises, corrig du prix de leurs intrants. Ce prix donne la valeur dune unit de valeur ajoute. Cest la somme du cot en travail dune unit de valeur ajoute (le cot salarial unitaire) et du cot en capital de cette mme unit de VA (la marge unitaire). En priode dinflation, tous les cots par unit produite augmentent. En supposant que la part du travail dans la valeur ajoute soit de 2/3 et celle du capital de 1/3, si toutes les grandeurs unitaires augmentent au mme rythme, disons +4%, la contribution du cot salarial unitaire est de 4%x2/3=2,6% tandis que celle de la marge unitaire est de 4%x1/3=1,3%. Les marges unitaires ont-elles contribu pour plus que leur part sur la priode rcente ? Le graphique 3 rpond  cette question pour la zone euro et pour la France. Afin de permettre la comparaison, le graphique est trac pour lensemble de lconomie et non pas pour le seul secteur marchand. Il sagit donc du prix (ou  dflateur ) du PIB et non du prix de la valeur ajoute marchande. Au second semestre 2022, la contribution de la marge unitaire  linflation est suprieure  celle du cot salarial unitaire en zone euro. En France, toutefois, la contribution de la marge unitaire est infrieure  celle du cot salarial unitaire, aprs avoir t ngative au premier semestre 2022. Le graphique indique aussi la contribution des taxes indirectes nettes qui, comptablement, permettent de passer dune notion de valeur ajoute  la notion de produit intrieur brut (PIB). Image Glissement annuel du dflateur du PIB et contributions du cot salarial unitaire et de la marge unitaire Ce diagnostic densemble masque une forte htrognit sectorielle. Ainsi, en France, les industries agro-alimentaires et les autres industries manufacturires semblent avoir tir les marges unitaires vers le haut au cours des derniers trimestres, tandis que ces secteurs avaient peu contribu  la baisse de la marge agrge au dbut de lanne 2022 (graphique 4). Dautres secteurs, tels que lhbergement-restauration ou les autres services marchands, ont, eux, vu leurs marges baisser au cours de la priode. En dpit de son faible poids dans le PIB, le secteur agricole a contribu positivement  rvolution de la marge unitaire agrge en 2021-2022. Toutefois, la trs forte augmentation des prix des intrants pour ce secteur rend difficile linterprtation de cette contribution (voir Colonna. Torrini et Viviano. 2023). Si le prix de la valeur ajoute augmente au mme rythme que le cot salarial unitaire, alors le taux de marge reste constant et sa contribution  linflation est nulle (le prix de la valeur ajoute augmente comme le cot salarial unitaire). Le graphique 5 montre quen zone euro, le taux de marge a augment au cours des annes 2021 et 2022, en partie par rattrapage aprs la baisse enregistre en 2020, et que cela a contribu  la hausse des prix. Dans le cas de la France, le taux de marge agrg a volu de faon plus heurte du fait des soutiens massifs reus par les entreprises au second semestre 2020 et au premier semestre 2021, avec un contrecoup ensuite, pour finalement revenir fin 2022 au niveau de dbut 2018. Image Glissement annuel du dflateur du PIB et contributions du cot salarial unitaire et du taux de marge Au premier trimestre 2023, selon la premire estimation de lInsee, le taux de marge des socits non financires a progress de 0,4 point de pourcentage par rapport au trimestre prcdent en France, principalement du fait de la diminution de la cotisation sur la valeur ajoute des entreprises (CVAE) et dune hausse des aides au paiement des factures dnergie. En niveau, le taux de marge reste autour de 32%, sa valeur de moyen terme. Micro contre macro Un microconomiste contesterait probablement les mesures de marges qui prcdent. En effet, une entreprise fixe en principe son prix non par rapport  son cot moyen (le cot salarial unitaire), mais par rapport  son cot marginal (le cot de la dernire unit produite) : si lentreprise est vivante, cest quelle ralise une marge commerciale suffisante sur ses cots variables pour couvrir ses cots fixes. Le prix lui-mme nest pas dtermin par les cots fixes, mais par le cot marginal et les structures du march. Sur ce principe, De Loecker and Warzvnski (2012) ont propos une formule simple pour calculer la marge commerciale, ou markup, de chaque entreprise, et Bauer et Boussard (2020) lont applique aux entreprises franaises entre 1984 et 2016. En cohrence avec lapproche de comptabilit nationale, ils trouvent un markup agrg stable sur cette priode. Mais cette stabilit est le rsultat combin dune baisse du markup au niveau de lentreprise individuellement et dune rallocation de la production vers les entreprises  makup lev (effet de composition). Malheureusement, les donnes individuelles ncessaires pour mettre  jour ce travail ne sont disponibles quavec deux ans de retard. Compte tenu de toutes ces difficults mthodologiques, il est prudent de croiser diffrentes mesures des marges et de les observer sur des priodes suffisamment longues.  cela sajoute des difficults dinterprtation lorsque le prix des intrants imports augmente fortement. Title: The banking crisis that didn't happen
text: EUROSYSTEM Rostrum (Deputy Governors J) The banking crisis that did not take place Published on July 3, 2023 Op-ed by Agnes Benassy-Quere, Second Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. After the health crisis, after the energy crisis, we could have suffered a banking crisis in March. In fact, the banking world has shaken with the successive bankruptcies of several US regional banks and the emergency takeover of Credit Switzerland, a global systemic bank, by UBS (Chart 1). Bank share prices were affected in both the euro area and the United States, but they recovered quickly, although they did not reach the levels seen before March. How was the domino effect, so often seen during financial crises, stopped As reported in the latest report on the Banque de France's Risk Assessment of the French Financial System (June 2023), the contagion did not occur for two main reasons: (1) an extremely rapid handling of the crisis by the US and Swiss authorities, and (2) a European banking system that was well prepared to face turbulence, following the major regulatory and supervisory reforms made since the global financial crisis. Figure 1. Difficult spring for some American and Swiss banks Source: Banque de France, Risk assessment of the French financial system, June 2023. Curative: a high level of responsiveness by the authorities in the United States and Switzerland Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and Signature Bank each recorded a fiiitn rlp nlii.c: rlp 20% rlp IpiirQ rlpnntQ on iinp qpiiIp iniirnpp Ipq PiiitnritPQ put them into "resolution" the next day. Bank resolution covers a set of instruments designed to preserve the continuity of the bank's critical functions and to avoid contagion to other institutions. It can take the form of business sessions, a balance sheet restructuring, an asset transfer or a bailout, usually a combination. In the United States, the resolution is carried out by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), which is also in charge of deposit insurance. The vast majority of deposits in these two banks were made by very large clients, often private equity funds or Silicon Valley start-ups, waiting to be used. Many deposits were above 250,000, and therefore uninsured for the portion above this limit. However, on the basis of a systemic risk exception, the FDIC announced on March 12, jointly with the Federal Reserve and the Treasury, that all SVB and Signature Bank deposits would benefit from the deposit insurance scheme. The Federal Reserve has also put in place temporary measures to strengthen the liquidity of the entire US banking sector. In Switzerland, the authorities also intervened quickly to limit the risk of contagion from a bankruptcy of Credit Switzerland. First, on 16 March, they granted it a credit line of 50 billion Swiss francs. Faced with persistent investor mistrust, the Swiss authorities then supported its takeover by UBS on March 19 by guaranteeing a substantial part of the potential losses and granting additional liquidity lines. On the occasion of this buyback, the holders of convertible bonds on Credit Switzerland lost their entire investment. To avoid contagion on the convertible debt markets, the European authorities and the Bank of England quickly clarified that, in their respective jurisdictions, losses would always be borne as a priority by shareholders. Prevention: the benefits of regulation and supervision in the euro area The failures of US regional banks are mainly due to unsustainable imbalances in interest rate and liquidity risk management. Neither SVB nor the other failing regional banks were subject to the international rules set out after the Great Financial Crisis (Basel 3) to make banks more resilient to these risks. Conversely, all banks in the European Union, including the smallest, apply these requirements. But a robust regulatory framework must also be accompanied by strong supervision. This is the case in the euro area, with active and intrusive supervision within the Single Supervisory Mechanism. French banks have comfortable liquidity ratios. In particular, their eligible assets are all valued at their market value for the determination of these ratios, so there are no possible unpleasant surprises. In addition, the share of uninsured deposits is only 29% of all liabilities in France, compared to 85% in the case of SVB. In France, unrealised losses on securities not already recognised in banks' income or equity amounted to 8.4 billion at the end of 2022, or 2.2% of the narrow equity (CET1) of the 6 French banking groups taken together. Assuming that the banks concerned were obliged to sell these securities at the same time, their CET1 ratio  the ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets  would fall by 33 basis points (0.33 percentage points) overall. The aggregate capital ratio of the major French banks, which was 15.55% at the end of March 2023, would therefore remain well above the minimum requirements. In addition, French banks, like their European counterparts, must assess the sensitivity of their economic value to an interest rate shock: if, assuming a 200 point rise in the entire interest rate curve, the bank's economic value decreases by more than 15% of CET1 capital, an alert is triggered. No French bank would have been in such a situation based on the assessment carried out at the end of March 2023. French banks and rising interest rates If you are a borrower, you may have the feeling that the banks are benefiting from the rise in interest rates, since you pay them higher interest while your current account is not interested. This is partly true. However, banks do not only finance themselves via our current accounts, but also on the markets, in particular via bond loans. They also distribute regulated savings accounts and offer term deposits, the interest rate of which has increased with the rise in rates, which makes their financial resources more expensive. Conversely, they have in their portfolios and assets loans or long-term bonds acquired in recent years at interest rates that are most often fixed and very low. The remuneration of these assets is insensitive to rising market rates. Of course, banks can now improve the return on their assets as loans to customers mature and are replaced by new loans, and by gradually renewing their portfolios of financial securities. However, this process is slow. The result is that their net interest margins (the difference between the average rate at which they lend and the average rate at which they borrow) increase with interest rates, but less rapidly in France than in other European countries (see Chart 2). Figure 2. Net interest margins, France and international comparison Thus, French banks are not threatened by the same type of catastrophic chain of events that led to the bankruptcy of SVB, but they must manage their profitability so that it does not appear insufficient for the markets, compared to competing banks abroad. Similarly, life insurers, whose weight is significant in France (see table below), must manage a risk of divergence between the profitability of their assets, largely determined by the financial securities acquired in recent years, when rates were very low, and the remuneration expected by their policyholders, which is rising. In the short to medium term, however, they will be able to draw on their profit-sharing provisions to improve the returns served. In addition, their liabilities are relatively stable, despite a slight increase in policy redemptions. Other segments of non-bank finance do not benefit from this stability. Scan areas without street lights It is customary to mock the tendency of economists to "look for their keys under the street lamps": to focus their research on areas where they have reliable data. This bias is one of the reasons for the global financial crisis of 2008, as the development of "shadow finance" was neglected. Today, we no longer speak of "shadow finance" but of non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) because these institutions are not only legal and also partly regulated. At the end of 2021, this non-bank finance held nearly half of total financial assets worldwide, and a third at the French level (table). Financial stability is increasingly dependent on these institutions, including investment funds that can be pension funds, money market funds, real estate funds, hedge funds, etc. Knowledge of these different segments, and their link with banks, is still imperfect, but this is no reason to neglect them, this potential source of systemic risk. Table. Share of non-bank finance in total global financial assets at end-2021 * financial intermediaries exposed to risks similar to those of banks (e.g. maturity transformation). Source: Financial Stability Board. Indeed, some of these funds are exposed to high liquidity risks, which cannot be insured by the lender of last resort, the central bank, which is only aimed at banks. In the event of an urgent need for unmet liquidity, a fund has no choice but to sell part of its assets in a hurry, with a possible loss for savers-investors if the sale takes place at the wrong time or if the assets are illiquid (real estate, private equity in particular). Insofar as various funds are simultaneously selling, the fall in prices could exacerbate the phenomenon through two channels:  An exit of savers from these products, for fear of greater losses;  An unrealised capital loss for all the holders of these assets, which could trigger sales in other assets. The risk is particularly high at a time when equity and real estate prices are considered high relative to their economic fundamentals. It is also important in times of market volatility due to the increase in margin calls from central clearing houses (as was the case during the so-called "mini-budget" crisis in the UK in the autumn of 2022). The most exposed funds are those that offer perfect liquidity to their clients, who can enter and exit without delay and without fees. The regulation of financial institutions excluding banking and insurance needs to be completed to better integrate their possible impact on overall financial stability. Because of their size and their interconnections with the rest of the financial system, these institutions play an important role in the smooth functioning of international financial markets, but they are particularly sensitive to liquidity imbalances between assets and liabilities. Their assets are often invested in financial and real products such as real estate or long-term so-called "private" financing, which are not very liquid, while their liabilities are liquid if their clients can exit freely. Regulation must allow them to meet the demand for liquidity of investor-savers without generating negative externalities on other financial market participants (including banks). It is nothing more or less than acknowledging the systemic dimension of these financial players, as was done for banks after the 2008 financial crisis. Updated on November 21, 2023

Title: Non-bank finance: blurred contours, growing risks, incomplete regulatory framework
text: BANK OF FRANCE EUROSYSTEM Speech Financial stability Non-bank finance: blurred contours, growing risks, a deficient regulatory framework Published on November 21, 2023 BANK OF FRANCE ''W EUROSYSTEM non-bank finance as part of a morning session of the Association Europe Finances Regulation (AEFR). The exact title of his speech was " Non-bank finance: blurred contours, growing risks, a deficient regulatory framework". While non-bank finance accounts for almost half of the world's total financial assets and contributes significantly to the financing of the real economy, knowledge of this sector is still very imperfect and its connections with the traditional banking system are sometimes poorly identified. Defining by negation (non-bank) is a first step, but it is necessary to categorize and analyze more precisely this vast group grouped under the English name of Non-bank financial institutions or intermediaries (NBFI). Some of these players are already regulated, generally in a logic of investor protection (insurance, pension funds, collective investment vehicles). From a financial stability perspective, it is imperative to deepen our understanding of the interactions between these different actors and their interconnections with the rest of the financial system (in particular banking). Recent shocks (Covid-19, the collapse of the Archegos family office, dysfunctions in liability-driven funds in the United Kingdom, etc.) have highlighted significant vulnerabilities in this sector. The excessive use of leverage, inadequate liquidity risk management, and strong interconnections within the financial system largely explain how NBFI players have been able to amplify and transmit these tensions. Existing regulatory tools have not been able to adequately contain these shocks. Since March In 2020, a lot of work was undertaken at the international (FSB, IOSCO, etc.) and European (ESMA, ESRB, European Commission) levels to fill the gaps identified in the regulatory framework. However, the work carried out so far has focused on measures focused on investor protection or BANK OF FRANCE ''W EUROSYSTEM Given the growth of non-bank finance in recent years and the scale of the financial assets involved, the risks to overall financial stability must now be considered systemic. The need to better regulate them is all the more obvious, while taking into account the heterogeneity of the activities grouped within this sector and the sometimes significant differences between jurisdictions. Title: High Council for Financial Stability: an unexpected notoriety
text: EUROSYSTEM Rostrum (Financial stability High Council for Financial Stability: an unexpected notoriety Published on December 4, 2023 Op-ed by Agnes Benassy-Quere, Second Deputy Governor of the Bank of France. For some time now, the High Council for Financial Stability (HCSF), whose 2023 Annual Report was published on 25 October, has enjoyed unprecedented notoriety (see Chart 1). It is true that it has just celebrated its 10th anniversary. Created by the Banking Law of 26 July 2013. its mission is to "prevent systemic risk, i.e. a dysfunction of the financial system as a whole (or in a large part) leading to a deterioration in its ability to ensure its fundamental function of financing the economy" (see the HCSF website). It is chaired by the Minister of Finance and includes five ex officio members (including the Governor of the Banque de France, who proposes the so-called "macroprudential" measures) and three qualified personalities from the academic world and appointed respectively by the President of the Senate, the President of the National Assembly and the Minister of the Economy and Finance. If the term "HCSF" is becoming part of everyday language, it seems to be less because of its decisions on "countercyclical buffers" - additional capital that banks must accumulate to cushion subsequent reversals in the supply of credit - than because of the "HCSF standards" relating to the conditions for granting real estate loans. Introduced in December 2019 in the form of recommendations, they were recalibrated in January 2021 and then transformed into binding standards to be applied from 1 January 2022. The objective was, and remains, to put an end to the drift observed in loan terms and effort ratios (monthly repayments and interest in relation to disposable income) likely to weaken the French model of real estate financing. This model is based on the granting of fixed-rate loans that protects borrowers by making banks bear the interest rate risk - a risk that increases with the extension of maturities - while credit risk, which is normally well controlled, increases with the increase in borrowers' effort ratios. This point was raised by the International Monetary Fund in October 2019 during its periodic analysis of financial vulnerabilities in France, and it also prompted an alert from the European Systemic Risk Board in June 2019. Image Source: Google trends, an index based on keyword searches on the search engine. Last update: November 2023. The "HCSF standards" limit the maximum duration of housing loans to 25 years and the maximum effort rate weighing on borrowers to 35%. However, the HCSF has provided for a margin of flexibility, which was itself readjusted in June 2023 : 20% of new loans granted may deviate from the standards. The HCSF wanted this flexibility to benefit first-time buyers and households taking on debt to acquire their main residence. Thus, it reserved 70% of the 20% (i.e. 14% of total loan production) for the acquisition of a main residence, including 30% (still of the 20%, i.e. 6% of total production) for first-time buyers (see Table 1). The standards are applied on a quarterly basis and compliance with them is assessed with certain flexibility in order to accommodate the delays in the approval of credit files and the seasonality of certain transactions. They are intended to serve atypical cases, for example for wealthy households wishing to make a rental investment, and for whom the maximum effort rate of 35% could appear too restrictive in the eyes of the lending bank. Image Table 1 Source: HCSF, Decision of 29 June 2023 ; Credithab, ACPR calculations. The last two columns of Table 1 show the rate of use of flexibilities in the second and third quarters of 2023 (September was the first month of application of the adjusted mechanism, announced in June 2023). They show an under-use of existing flexibilities: in the summer of 2023, the "HCSF standards" in no way prevented French banks, collectively, from granting loans that did not respect the limits of effort rate (35%) or duration (25 years). The sharp decline in housing credit compared to the peaks reached in 2021 and early 2022 (see Chart 2) can be explained by the decline in demand linked to the rise in interest rates and the decline in transactions (in a context where price developments are uncertain despite a downward trend); not by the constraints imposed by the HCSF. Banks therefore have room to increase their credit offer - up to 6% in total if they use all the flexibilities. However, managing these margins has proven to be complex for banking networks whose granting choices are decentralized at branch level. In its decision of 4 December 2023, the HCSF specified that their use would be assessed on average over three rolling quarters not only for the sub-envelopes, but also for the overall margin of 20%. This will allow the banking networks to no longer fear a one-off excess. In addition, the HCSF has lowered the threshold for work opening up the possibility to 10% (instead of 25% previously) a deferral of repayment for a period of up to two years, it being understood that major renovation work makes it impossible to use the premises immediately, which leads to a duplication of housing expenses during their duration. Finally, the rules for granting bridging loans have been simplified, with the corresponding interest no longer being taken into account in the calculation of the effort ratio, provided that the amount of the loan does not exceed 80% of the value of the property. To accompany these measures, a mechanism for re-examining files will be put in place by the banks so that a second look can be taken at solvent files that have been rejected. These adjustment measures should, without risking causing household over-indebtedness, encourage a revival of housing credit, which is already showing some signs of stabilisation. Image Chart 2 Source: Banque de France, Stat Info. November 3, 2023. Last update: September 2023 Macrocaution on housing credit Of course, France is not the only country to have introduced housing credit standards. According to a report to be published in December and carried out under the aegis of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), eight of the fourteen countries surveyed, including France, impose limits on effort ratios (debt service in relation to disposable income); three limit the debt ratio (debt in relation to disposable income); and eleven limit the amount of the loan in proportion to the value of the property. At the same time, seven countries (including France) impose limits on the duration of loans (see Table 2). Image Source: CGFS survey (2023, to be published in December 2023) from Australia (AU), Belgium (BE), Canada (CA), France (FR), Hong Kong (HK), Ireland (IE), Israel (IL), India (IN), Luxembourg (LU), New Zealand (NZ), South Africa (SA), Singapore (SG), United Kingdom (UK). In the European Union, according to the European Systemic Risk Board, 13 out of 27 countries impose limits on borrowers' effort ratios. Among them, only France does not also constrain the loan-to-value ratio of the property. As a result, France has traditionally been singled out as a relatively non-restrictive country in terms of housing credit (EBRD, 2021). What is the purpose of these measures? According to the same report to be published in December, the idea is not to restrict access to property, but to protect borrowers (14 out of 14 countries) and, to a lesser extent (9 out of 14 countries), lending banks. In only five countries (and not in France), the objective is also to limit the upward and downward cycles of credit and/or real estate prices. In short, it is essentially a structural measure of prudence and not of cycle smoothing. This is why macroprudential authorities (in France as elsewhere) are reluctant to relax these measures in order to revive the market and support construction. It would be a bit like relaxing housing safety standards to revive the construction industry. Starting from a fairly low level, the household debt ratio has risen steadily in France over the past 25 years, and it is now higher than the levels observed in the other major European countries (see Chart 3). Admittedly, the cases of over-indebtedness of households with the Banque de France primarily concern commercial and tax debts and not real estate loans. This procedure is used by households that are generally very modest, while it is rather the middle and upper classes who have access to property. However, high loan maturities can put a household in difficulty in the event of a personal unforeseen event, and force it, for example, to resell its property in an emergency. Creditor insurance and guarantees, which are almost systematically requested by lending banks in France, cover only part of life's hazards. Default rates on real estate loans are low in France (around 1% of the outstanding amount for the gross rate, cf. ACPR, 2023). But banks are sensitive to this because they traditionally make very little margin on these loans. This allows French borrowers to benefit from interest rates that are significantly lower than in other European countries, in exchange for guarantees on their ability to repay. However, the claims experience is directly linked to the effort ratios: between 2008 and In 2015, the doubling of the default rate was driven by the cohorts of borrowers for whom lending conditions had eased the most during the previous rate hike (Banque de France. 2021). In a phase of rising interest rates, pressure is increasing to ease up on the criteria of prudence in the granting of credit. But it is precisely these criteria that make borrowers and lenders more resilient at the individual level as well as at the level of the economy as a whole (resilience of consumption, investment, less fall in the prices of financial assets, etc.). Image Chart 3 Sources: HCSF (2019) and Banque de France (2023). Finely calibrated instruments The "HCSF standards" do not come out of nowhere. They were introduced in the form of simple recommendations in December 2019, to put an end to the drift observed gradually in relation to the traditional prudential practices of banks. A simultaneous increase in effort rates and loan terms had been observed for several years. In 2018, nearly 25% of new loans had a loan ratio of more than 35%, for an average term of 20 years (HCSF. 2019). Now, the combination of a high rate of effort and a high level of effort can be a combination of a high level of effort. Chart 4 shows how the HCSF recommendation, which later became a binding standard, has halted the drift in effort rates. The share of loans granted with an effort ratio of more than 35% has fallen to 12% from 2022. It then stabilised despite the rise in interest rates. Image Source: ACPR. Last update: March 2023. Break in series in January 2020. The HCSF could, as in Ireland or New Zealand, have limited the loan-to-value ratio of the property. He preferred to focus on the ratio of debt repayment to income (the effort ratio) for two reasons:  the effort ratio is more favourable to first-time buyer households that have not yet made a significant personal contribution; it corresponds to the practice of banks when granting loans in France;  A constant limit on the rate of effort has the advantage of not amplifying the dynamics of real estate prices up or down. The precise calibration of the measure was based on micro-simulations carried out from a sample of real estate transactions carried out between 2015 and 2017, calculating the impact of the measure on the real estate purchasing power of different categories of households, simulating the pairings between buyers and sellers in this new configuration and, finally, simulating the evolution of prices according to different adjustment rules. The aim was in particular to verify that the measure would not exclude from the market certain categories of borrowers such as first-time buyers, the most dependent on credit (cf. CGFS, 2023, forthcoming, as well as Bauer and Krakovitch. 2019). As shown in Figure 5, the share of first-time buyers increased after 2020 to reach 41.9% of loans granted in March 2023, and more than 50% of loans were granted for the purchase of a primary residence. Image Chart 5 Source: HCSF. Annual Report 2023. Nearly four years after the first HCSF recommendation on the granting of housing credit, the results of the "HCSF standards" are positive: without having influenced the total volume of credit either upwards (until 2022) or downwards (since mid-2022), they have helped to limit the risk-taking of borrowers and lenders, including since the recent rise in interest rates, All this without squeezing out first-time buyers, who are the most dependent on credit, from the market. The decline in credit today is due to weak demand in connection with rising interest rates. The banks' lending interest rates are gradually passing on the increase in the cost of their liabilities (term deposits, Livret A savings accounts whose rate has now stabilised, market financing, with sight deposits remaining uninterested). The average interest rate on new housing loans to households (percentage rate including fees and insurance) has at this stage only included part of the rise in the ECB's key rates: it was "only" 3.73% for new loans (excluding renegotiations) in September 2023 (Banque de France figure). this is less than the deposit facility rate, which is currently 4% (the rate at which commercial banks' deposits with the Eurosystem are remunerated), but more than the Livret A rate, which has been 3% since 1 August 2023. Lending rates could continue to rise slightly for a few months before stabilizing. The good news is that house prices are starting to fall in France (see INSEE). The continuation of this movement, combined with an expected rise in real wages, will offset the rise in interest rates to restore purchasing power to buyers, while encouraging sellers to put their properties on the market, as time is not necessarily on their side. Public policies have a central role to play in promoting market fluidity, supply incentives and cost reduction. There is no shortage of avenues, from the bill aimed at reducing the tax advantage linked to tourist rentals compared to traditional furnished accommodation to the recommendations of the Competition Authority (2023) on real estate brokerage, including regulatory simplifications and taxation of transactions and capital gains, incentives for urban densification, productivity gains in construction, etc. Home loans are not dysfunctional in France and they alone cannot compensate for the multiple distortions of the real estate market.
