Title: European bank supervision and its new challenges
text: European bank supervision and its new challenges Editorial by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France, and Joachim Wuermeling, Member of the Executive Board of Deutsche Bundesbank Page 1 sur 2 Five years ago, in a short press release, the ECB opened up a new era by announcing that it was officially taking over the responsibility of banking supervision within the euro area. The Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) was born. Drawing an important lesson from the financial crisis, Europe was thus providing an essential response that Member States alone could never have supplied in an interconnected European financial system. What has become of the SSM and what will its next objectives be? Here are a few Franco-German thoughts on this subject. Over the past five years, 1,200 ECB supervisors and around 5,000 bank supervisors from France, Germany and the 17 other euro area countries have worked daily to enhance the stability and soundness of our banks. All decisions are taken by the Supervisory Board, a joint body where all competent national authorities are represented. The transition from national supervision to European supervision proved rapidly successful. An example of this success is the reduction in non-performing loans. During the financial crisis, they totalled approximately EUR 1 trillion in the balance sheets of European banks, compared to EUR 600 billion today. This amount is no doubt still too high, but it has declined very significantly and continues to do so. The success of this European approach is based on a joint supervisory strategy and a firm implementation. The SSM brings together the experience and expertise of the supervisory authorities of the euro area countries. It supervises many more banks  including 116 large-sized ones!  than national authorities, which are entrusted with overseeing small and medium-sized institutions, under the control of the SSM. Thanks to this wide scope of supervision, risks can be detected earlier, better assessed and contained in a more targeted manner. Our priority is to ensure the stability of the whole of Europe. This is an essential achievement of the SSM: national interests have been relegated to the background in the context of European decisions. And tomorrow, what will be the challenges facing the SSM? According to us, there are three essential ones: first, we need to develop instruments to manage the new risks in the financial sector. The digitalisation of banking transactions, the tokenisation of money and securities, the use of blockchains, etc. represent as many opportunities as new risks! However, regulation and supervision must also enable banks to innovate in the digital field and facilitate their management and consolidation at the European level. Our second challenge consists in capitalising on digitisation to better identify risks and optimise banking oversight. We need to use our resources more efficiently, and generalise our digital approaches! Our instruments and indicators must be constantly reviewed with pragmatism, in terms both of their costs and their efficiency. Finally, the SSM must place ever greater emphasis on supervisors assessment and on the understanding of the specificities of national banking markets, within the framework of a body of common rules and practices which guarantees an exacting and fair supervision, vector of healthy competition. Following the 2008 financial crisis, the banking sector entered a phase of transformation as it faced new economic models. Traditional institutions are subject to sharp competition from "BigTechs" which Page 2 sur 2 are engaging in financial services, and "FinTechs" which are shaking up traditional patterns. The competitiveness of the traditional banking sector could be durably challenged. Lets hope that we wont have to face another crisis in the next few years. However, even without a shock, banks must rise to a large number of challenges, whether they are posed by their new competitors, or whether they result from a series of vulnerabilities that we are closely monitoring: a cyclical downturn could increase losses on loans, a sudden rise in interest rates could result in losses on market activities. Not to mention that continental banks will have to take on new tasks after Brexit The first five years of the SSM have shown that European cooperation can work for the general interest. Everyone benefits from stable and sound banks, be they households, businesses, investors and government. While our track record is positive and instructive, one thing is certain: the challenges facing banks and their supervisors are increasing rather than decreasing. Given this fact, the future of supervision will be European or will not be.

Title: Les Echos et Handelsblatt : Build the future of European payments now
text: 30.06.2020 Build the future of European payments now Burkhard Balz, Mitglied des Vorstands der Deutschen Bundesbank Sylvie Goulard, Sous Gouverneur, Banque de France The way we work, learn, do business and shop has dramatically changed during recent months. Various aspects of our daily lives have become much more digital throughout the COVID19 pandemic, thus amplifying already existing trends: Among others, it appears that consumers use cash less and less, paying instead with debit or credit cards but also with smartphones, even at bakeries. Frequently, shopkeepers started asking for contactless card or mobile payments as a precautionary measure to prevent infections. Moreover, new behavioural rules such as stay home and keep distance have accelerated online shopping which leads to additional e- and m-payments. As of today, payment behaviour post-Corona will not completely return to pre-pandemic levels. Alongside their better-known responsibilities for monetary policy and financial stability, central Banks are also tasked with keeping means of payment efficient and safe. Not only in times of crisis, we ensure innovative, user friendly digital solutions while  at the same time  provide sufficient cash for the society. Today, the majority of card, mobile and online payments made by Europeans already rely on technology platforms by global providers and international card schemes. The ongoing changes in payment behaviour and the rapidly progressing digitalisation of our lives will further amplify this development resulting in a number of challenges for European societies as a whole as well as for regulators and authorities. During the pandemic, it became more obvious that the EU needs to safeguard the uninterrupted functioning of essential infrastructures and the continuous supply of crucial services. Stand-alone payment systems are part of these. Solely reliance on non-European providers could put European sovereignty at stake here. Moreover, as Big Techs continue to gain market share and become increasingly dominant by offering a comprehensive range of services to a global customer base, consumer choice is becoming limited. They might end up tied to such a proprietary platform. Other areas of concern relate to data protection, as the European Union has adopted one of the most stringent legal frameworks. Moreover, digital payment solution providers are often riding on the infrastructure and regulatory compliance provided by banks. Banks, in turn, face the risk of being disintermediated by BigTechs as they lose the direct links to their customers. There are some stand-alone, successful domestic payment systems in Europe, such as the card schemes of Germany and France or digital solutions for e- and m-payments as well as for payments from person-to-person. They serve a broad range of users and enjoy significant market share, but only in their national markets. In contrast, global players offer availability all over Europe. They sustain and grow based on vast network, scale and scope effects as well as a strong branding. Overall, the developments stated diminish the competitiveness of European markets in an increasingly digitalized world  to the detriment of its citizens. European providers cannot leave this challenge unanswered. Therefore, a number of large banks from the North sea to the Mediterranean have proposed the European Payment Initiative (EPI). Through this initiative, consumers would be able to pay in a uniform, convenient, safe and efficient manner throughout Europe using different onand offline- channels. Trusted European banks and payment providers would bring this solution to payers and payees. Instant payments, the new service allowing bank transfers all over Europe within seconds, would form an integral part of this service. Later on, consumers could use it globally as well, thus weakening dependency from non-European actors. EPI could be an inclusive nucleus to pool European interests and to regain autonomy, while being open to other players from national markets. For a successful implementation, all important stakeholders from the supply side as well as payers and payees need to join in. Without a doubt, such a reorganisation of the European payments landscape requires significant investment in times when resources of banks are scarce and priority is rightly given to recovery. Nevertheless, it is obvious that continuous investment into the payments business is inevitable , not least to safeguard resilience. It is important that the work of building a compelling pan European payment solution continues, with high strategic priority. This would also be in line with the current work of the EU Commission to define a retail payments strategy for Europe and the leadership shown by the ECB while digitalisation is high on the agenda of the German Presidency of the EU. European authorities and central banks are willing to support respective initiatives within the reach of their mandates. This includes more clarity on business models and a certain level of regulatory predictability. Obviously, payments are not a free lunch and respective investments need a return to it. The EPI digital wallet will be the first step in offering digital payment services to all European consumers and businesses paving the way to programmable money. It is of utmost importance that European banks and payment providers use this momentum, stay committed and deliver a convincing solution that supports European sovereignty and competitiveness while fulfilling the needs of consumers and businesses.

Title: Statement, Bitcoin
text: 1 Statement of Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France Beijing 1st December 2017 Bitcoin  I would just like to say a few words on bitcoin, a subject which is attracting a great deal of attention here in China. It is associated with a useful form of technology, the blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technology. Like other market participants, the Banque of France is experimenting with this innovative technology. But beyond that, we need to be clear: bitcoin is in no way a currency, or even a cryptocurrency. It is a speculative asset. Its value and extreme volatility have no economic basis, and they are nobodys responsibility. The Banque of France reminds those investing in bitcoin that they do so entirely at their own risk. We have also noted with interest the measures taken by the Chinese authorities regarding ICOs.

Title: Financing companies at the end of the crisis: where do we stand?
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) Financing companies emerging from the crisis: where do we stand? Published on April 20, 2022 OFEM Annual Conference April 20, 2022 Opening speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Madam President, dear Agnes, Ladies and gentlemen, dear friends, It is with great pleasure that I speak to you today for an annual meeting that is now well established. An appointment that is an opportunity to take a step aside to re-examine the situation of business financing. Last year, we discussed the structural changes that we could discern before the health crisis, drew up an initial assessment of the impact of the crisis and underlined the need for an "economy of equity", within the European framework of the Capital Markets Union. Last year, the economy was catching up to its pre-crisis level and we were wondering about the conditions for a stronger, faster and more sustainable recovery. One year later, where do we stand? From my point of view as a central banker, I would articulate a diagnosis on the basis of three observations that I would like to share with you this morning: while it has been confirmed that companies have resisted the crisis well, in parallel with the rise in inflation, the war in Ukraine has made the economic outlook less favourable, while the challenges to be met remain very present and have even increased. 1.1a hnnnA rpsistancA cIa Companies during the crisis [slide 2] The rebound in 2021: a global trend... Starting from a rather healthy situation in 2019 and with the support of particularly large public measures (around 250 billion since March 2020), it is clear that NFCs have generally held up rather well during the crisis. For this, non-financial companies took on debt, but 2021 was a year of return to normality. After the exceptional amounts of 2020, gross debt flows (52 billion in 2021 compared to 218 billion in 2020) and cash flows (25 billion in 2021 compared to 204 billion in 2020) normalised. Net debt has thus hardly increased as a percentage of GDP compared to the pre-crisis period: 41.4% at the end of 2021, compared to 40.6% at the end of 2019.1 ... and heterogeneous situations [slide 3] However, the overall observation should not mask the heterogeneity of the shock to activity and financial structures. Regarding the latter, SMEs are structurally more dependent on bank credit than mid-caps and GEs. The share of bank credit in total debt (banking, bonds, leasing) averaged 86% between 2005 and 2019 for SMEs, compared with 76% for mid-caps and 33% for LEs. Thus, in the face of the health crisis, SMEs have had massive and rapid recourse to state-guaranteed loans. Conversely, mid-caps and GEs first drew on their credit lines that could be mobilized before resorting to state-guaranteed loans and have, moreover, largely mobilized market financing, to which they have relatively easier access. Finally, while the strengthening of cash flow has been a widespread phenomenon (3 out of 4 companies have strengthened their cash flow in 2020 compared to 56% in 2019), it should be noted that the companies that have taken on the most debt are not necessarily those that have accumulated cash. Companies have thus emerged from the crisis weakened. The Banque de France has decided to monitor it closely. Nearly 2,364 companies have been brought to the attention of the departmental councils at the end of the crisis by the Banque de France and 500 support meetings have already been held by its network. In this respect, the Banque de France actively participates in this capacity, and more generally, in the mechanisms for detecting and supporting companies in difficulty emerging from the crisis. 2. From one crisis to another [slide 4] At the end of 2021, the good resilience of companies in the crisis gave hope that a robust recovery would continue and that support measures would be lifted as the health situation normalised. However, during 2021, headwinds arose and weighed on this recovery. Inflation rose from 0% year-on-year in the first quarter to nearly 4% at the end of the year. One of the first factors of this increase was the increase in energy prices and first and foremost gas prices from the end of summer 2021. However, this increase is lower in France than in other countries, with a powerful "tariff shield" that brings two points less inflation. But there were also supply and recruitment difficulties. These difficulties were present before the war in Ukraine with a persistent disruption of production chains and a deterioration of the situation in China. In parallel with rising inflation, the war in Ukraine has reinforced economic uncertainty and risks to financial stability. In terms of economic activity, we have just conducted a business survey of more than 8,000 entrepreneurs and SMEs in all regions and sectors. They confirm that after a good post-Covid recovery, our environment is now more uncertain, The first quarter should still record growth of around 0.25%, but we are seeing the first effects of the shock induced by the war. For companies, the market shock linked to the war in Ukraine is expected to be relatively moderate, and concentrated on some of them only. The supply shock is likely to be more pronounced and broad-based, and complicated by the resumption of the pandemic in China. The rise in energy prices affects all activities, as does the increase in costs and supply difficulties. However, some sectors are more exposed, as evidenced by our latest monthly economic survey (EMC), where supply difficulties appear to be greater for the agri-food industry (increase of 14 points in the balance of opinion), which is very exposed to Ukraine and Russia, but also for other industrial products (12 points) and the automotive industry (10 points). On the financial stability side, the immediate impacts were limited given the low direct exposure of the French economy and financial sector to Russia and Ukraine. Indeed, not only is trade with Russia and Ukraine relatively small, but, although sometimes with a fairly high sectoral concentration, direct investment by French companies, loans granted and securities held by French financial institutions also represent a very limited share of the assets of the various sectors. At the same time, the adjustments and volatility observed in the markets since the beginning of the conflict have been absorbed without these tensions degenerating. Nevertheless, both financial and economic second-round effects cannot be excluded. From this point of view, the epicentre of the shock is in the commodity markets (gas and oil, but also food and mineral commodities). In other words, the shock caused by the war in Ukraine is much less brutal than the Covid shock of two years ago, but it could last longer, weigh on our growth rate and maintain inflation in France at 4 or 5% for many months. 3. The challenges faced by companies and their funders The situation we are facing is therefore much less favourable than the one we were hoping for last year, while the challenges remain major. Allow me to mention three in particular to which companies will have to respond. A possible sustained rise in interest rates [slide 5] In the current environment of high inflation and high uncertainty about the evolution of inflation and the economic situation (including geopolitics) over the medium term, financing conditions have so far tightened only very moderately, with the vast majority of high-rated companies, for example, trading below 2%. However, the ECB specified in April that it will retain all optionality, gradualness and flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy: it will therefore adjust the stance of its monetary policy according to the data ("data-driven"), gradually and with full optionality to stabilise inflation at 2% in the medium term. And it confirmed its intention to end its net purchases of securities, most likely in the third quarter. Thus, after a long period of very low interest rates and an even longer period of falling rates, financial markets are now anticipating a new phase of normalization of monetary policy and financing conditions, while companies are significantly more indebted than they were fifteen years ago. The rise in interest rates does not appear to be a short-term threat to companies. The refinancing they carried out just before the Covid crisis and, sometimes, even more recently, offers them space, while the structure of their debt, two-thirds at a fixed rate, protects them in the short term. Nevertheless, the possibility of an increase in interest rates must be anticipated so that the increase in the debt burden does not lead to trade-offs that are detrimental to investment and preparation for the future. A rise in interest rates will also be a test of the robustness of the market-based debt financing ecosystem, which has been gradually built up over the past ten years. While the fall in interest rates was particularly conducive to a form of disintermediation of the financing of mid-caps, I have often indicated that such a development was only sustainable and desirable if it was not just a question of opportunistic arbitrage but of the construction of a financing offer that would be able to demonstrate its added value and its ability to withstand both default and interest rate cycles. Strengthening the external capital supply to overcome the slowdown in internal capital generation [slide 6] The supply of external equity, which was fundamental yesterday for the recovery, is critical, while a rise in interest rates could make the situation of the most indebted companies more precarious and a slowdown in activity will constrain the generation of equity capital by setting aside profits, which is and remains the most common method of equity financing. From this point of view, 2021 was rather a good, if not very good, surprise: good valuations, a remarkable year in terms of IPOs, record inflows for private equity funds, proven success of the adjustments made to make it easier for individuals to invest in these funds, etc. These developments sometimes call for a nuanced comment and, from this point of view, the end of the phenomenon of SPACs, which presented many of the symptoms of obvious exuberance, is very welcome, as is the good performance of equity risk premiums which, without guarding against a price correction, suggest that high valuations are somewhat less precarious than Price Earnings Ratios suggest. But, beyond the caution that we cannot depart from, we can see here the signs that we hope are heralds of this "capital economy" that we are calling for at the Banque de France. If one swallow does not make a spring, and although we have not reached the end of this project, at least we must welcome this progress and make the most of these promising circumstances. Don't lose sight of the long-term challenges: climate transition and digital transition fslide 7] The third challenge is to prepare for long-term issues, whether it is the transition to a carbon-neutral or fully digitalized economy. I say long-term issues because these are phenomena that will leave a very lasting mark on our modes of production, consumption and, more generally, our lifestyles. But make no mistake: the change they imply is an immediate challenge. On the climate front, the IPCC has recalled that it is essential to keep climate change around 1.5C. Essential and possible - provided we do not wait: at the current rate, we have less than five years of carbon budget left before reaching this objective becomes very uncertain. From this point of view, the energy crisis amplified by the war in Ukraine presents us with a brutal alternative: it may be an unexpected opportunity to accelerate the climate transition as the cause of a dramatic delay. Similarly, in terms of the digital transition of our economies, the health crisis and the rise of teleworking have forced an acceleration of the transformation of our working methods, our purchasing behaviour, and digital equipment. At the same time, a movement towards reindustrialisation is taking shape but remains conditioned by the deployment of solutions (in particular, robotisation) that make it possible not to reduce trade-offs to the sole question of labour costs. While digitization was slow to take place, it has begun and can accelerate. However, in either case, and I will conclude my remarks on this point, the response to these challenges requires strategic thinking on business models and organizations, as well as funding to implement the necessary investments. Whether it is a question of strategic thinking or investment financing, financiers, first and foremost equity investors, have an important role to play in supporting them.  /sites/default/files/media/2022/03/03/impact crise covid mars-2022.pdf 2 - france.fr/sites/default/files/medias/documents/820281 BDF232- 7 credits vf.pdf Updated on November 21, 2023

Title: Les Echos: "The Banque de France and the opening of financial services"
text: EUROSYSTEM Rostrum (Deputy Governors J) Les Echos: "The Banque de France and the opening up of financial services" Published on April 27, 2022 Op-ed by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Such an alignment of the planets is rare. The strong acceleration in the pace of technological innovation has been accompanied in recent years by a rise in the supply and demand for new financial services. This combination of factors is profoundly transforming the banking, insurance and savings landscape. New players are appearing on the market, bold and agile in the exploitation of data. The opening up is broadening from banking to finance. "Open banking" is evolving into "open finance." In order for these transformations to contribute to more efficient, accessible and less costly banking and financial services in the long term, they must be part of a framework of trust, to which we are particularly attentive at the Banque de France and the ACPR, as part of our monetary and financial stability missions. Such a framework requires, in particular, reconciling open access to data and security, innovation and integration, competition and sovereignty. To meet these challenges, a first lever is the creation of appropriate statuses. In the field of payments, the evolution of the status of service providers or agents has allowed for a gradual and proportional application of the regulatory framework, which is favourable to market entry and the very rapid development of fintechs: more than half of the 62 electronic money institutions and payment institutions currently operating in France were approved after 2018. However, promoting the opening up of the market must not be at the expense of coherence and simplicity: the same rules must apply to the same risks. On the other hand, differentiation is possible when the uses and risks are different: for example, the rules applicable to stablecoins must be different depending on whether they are investment vehicles or tokens intended for payment functions Promoting open access to the market, and in particular to data, must also be accompanied by appropriate security requirements and measures to prevent the risk of fragmentation between incompatible offers. The experience of the payments market has shown the usefulness of clear definitions of shareable data, a precise allocation of responsibilities and the promotion of standardized technical tools (such as APIs). In addition, to prevent fragmentation, central banks could usefully offer new services to financial intermediaries. It is with this in mind that the Banque de France is conducting a programme of experiments with a central bank digital currency (CBDC) for interbank use. Experiments show in particular that an interbank CBDC would make it possible to secure and optimize the interbank settlement of tokenized assets on distributed ledgers, including for cross-border settlements. Finally, the development of open banking and its extension to open finance in France and Europe calls for vigilance with regard to the risk of excessive concentration of offers and the preservation of our strategic autonomy. Eurosystem central banks can also make a contribution here by making a digital currency available to the general public. But other levers will be necessary to reconcile competition and sovereignty. First of all, the regulatory lever. Secondly, the industrial lever. While our market is and must remain open, it is no less essential to encourage innovation on the part of European players. The Banque de France and the ACPR are fully committed, in the exercise of their missions, to help meet these challenges, in favour of the development of ever more accessible, efficient and innovative financial services, in a framework of trust. Updated on November 21, 2023

Title: Economic and financial situation and outlook in the context of the war in Ukraine
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) Economic and financial situation and outlook in the context of the war in Ukraine Published on June 17, 2022 OCBF General Assembly June 17, 2022 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Ladies and gentlemen, I am delighted to be with you today for your Annual General Meeting. Last year, I spoke here about our prospects for emerging from the health crisis. Since then, new lockdown measures in China and especially the war in Ukraine have created new shocks for the European economy and financial system. Today, I would like to share with you our analysis, at the Banque de France and the ACPR, of the resulting short-term macroeconomic and macro-financial prospects and risks, which guide our actions as central banks and supervisors in the service of monetary and financial stability. I will conclude my remarks with the longer-term challenges that we collectively face, associated with climate change and the digitalisation of finance, which the war in Ukraine and its consequences must not make a secondary concern. These challenges still require resolute and immediate action from all of us, and in this context I will say a few words about the role we can play as supervisors and central bankers to help banks on the paths of transition to a sustainable economy and digitalized finance.  Macroeconomic outlook and risks The war in Ukraine and the lockdown measures in China have taken a heavy toll on the weighed on the rebound in activity in Europe, and particularly in France, which had developed in the second half of last year. They have also greatly amplified, extended and diffused to consumer prices the rise in producer prices, initially fuelled by the rise in energy and raw material prices. In other words, we are now facing a "slow-flationary" shock, the extent and duration of which remain very uncertain at this stage. Nevertheless, the central scenario for all euro area countries, as shown in the forecasts just published by the ECB, remains that of continued growth, but at a more moderate pace of 2.8% in 2022 and 2.1% in 2023, with growth revised upwards to 2.1% in 2024. This central scenario also includes higher and more persistent inflation, at 6.8% in 2022, 3.5% in 2023 and 2.1% in 2024. The risk in relation to this central scenario is clearly oriented towards less growth and more inflation. For France, we will publish our new forecasts on 21 June and I cannot give you the first details today. It is clear, however, in view of the latest business surveys that we have just conducted, that the growth outlook at CT should be comparable to the European dynamic, and a little less unfavourable in terms of inflation. Thus, on the basis of our business survey conducted in mid-May, early June, we expect GDP to increase by around a quarter of a point in Q2, after -0.2% in Q2. So, from my point of view as a central banker responsible for monitoring price stability in the medium term, the major risk has changed radically in recent months: it is no longer that inflation is too low for too long, but that inflation is too high for too long. Hence the need to initiate an immediate normalisation of monetary policy decided by the ECB's Governing Council and which it has begun to implement by reversing exceptionally accommodative measures that had been designed to deal with the risk of inflation being too low for too long. But the ECB's commitment is clear: the Governing Council will do what is necessary to bring inflation back and stabilise at 2% over the medium term. The ongoing normalisation of monetary policy is expected to follow a clearly defined order. Last December, the ECB announced the gradual reduction of net purchases under the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP). These net purchases have been stopped since last March. In March and April, it announced the reduction of monthly net purchases under the Asset Purchase Programme (APP). At the last Governing Council, the ECB announced the end of net purchases as of 1 July 2022, and its intention to increase the ECB's key interest rate package by 25 basis points at its July monetary policy meeting. The ECB also expects a further increase in key interest rates in September, the calibration of which will depend on the updated medium-term inflation outlook. Beyond September, based on its current assessment, the Governing Council anticipates that a gradual but sustained sequence of additional interest rate hikes would be appropriate. Finally, the reduction in the size of the Eurosystem's balance sheet will only take place at a later stage, probably as soon as the need not only for normalisation but for a tightening of monetary policy becomes necessary. As part of this gradual normalisation process, the ECB's Governing Council has made it clear that it will not rule out any options, in particular to act against fragmentation within the euro area, and will maintain progressiveness and flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy.  Macro outlook and risks Financial In this context marked by the multiplication of external shocks, a high degree of uncertainty about the extent of their impact and their duration, and a change in the interest rate environment with the end of the prospect of very low or even negative rates for a long time, we can collectively rejoice that for more than two years, the banking sector has held up well; it has helped to mitigate the shocks and not to amplify them. This ability to absorb shocks is an asset that must be maintained or even strengthened. This involves two vectors, supervision and regulation. In particular, the macroeconomic outlook and risks support the need to maintain banks' monitoring of their credit and market risks at the top of the supervisory priorities, those of the ACPR and the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM). The immediate impact of the war in Ukraine on financial stability has been adequately absorbed so far, as the financial sector's direct exposures to Russia have been low. However, risks to banks and financial stability may materialize through second-round effects and indirect channels from pre-existing vulnerabilities, including those associated with (i) the sectors most dependent on energy commodities, (ii) the development of leveraged finance, and (iii) exposure to cyber-attacks. In this regard, particular attention should be paid to potentially sharp repricing of risky asset prices. The same is true of rising prices and volatility in commodity markets and the considerable increase in margin calls on derivatives, particularly for energy and agricultural products. These have already led to liquidity pressures on commodity market participants. Very vigilant monitoring of credit and liquidity risks in the energy commodities sector is therefore required, in particular to ensure that any possible default (e.g. of a trader) remains contained and does not lead to systemic contagion. Our second lever for action to maintain and strengthen banks' ability to absorb shocks, after supervision, is through regulation. This is an opportunity for me to reiterate the importance of effective, fair and final implementation of the Basel III agreement, in its final version of 2017. I told you last year when quoting the Governor, and it is even more true today in light of the crises we are facing: the Basel III rules represent the best possible agreement to promote financial stability at the international level. The Commission's proposal (CRR3/CRD6) to finalise the implementation of these rules is a decisive and very balanced step forward. This balance must be preserved in the context of the discussions that are in full swing at Council and Parliament level, and which will continue under the Czech Presidency. In this regard, I would first like to mention two major issues that you are well aware of. First, we continue to call for the implementation of a output floor" at the highest level of consolidation in the European Union, which is the only level consistent with the spirit of the Banking Union, which is now almost complete. Secondly, we need targeted adjustments to critical and strategic exposures for the financing of the EU economy, but they must remain temporary in nature to reflect the spirit of the European Union. In the current context, in addition to complementing microprudential regulation, it is also desirable to maintain a comprehensive and consistent macroprudential backstop, to enable banks to absorb new shocks while continuing to provide essential services for the real economy. This takes several forms, ranging from the counter-cyclical capital buffer, which the authority At its meeting last March, with an implementation period of 12 months, the French macroprudential authority restored the measures applicable to borrowers to 0.5%. In this regard, the High Council for Financial Stability has transformed its recommendation advocating a maximum effort rate of 35% and a maximum maturity of 25 years for new real estate loans into a legally binding standard since 1 January 2022, while maintaining the margin of flexibility for 20% of quarterly production. This measure aims to prevent excessive household debt in a context where the production of housing loans remains strong, while preserving the French model of financing access to property. In conjunction with the predominance of fixed-rate loans in France, which borders on exclusivity, it has strengthened the financial resilience of households in the face of the prospect of rising interest rates. Attention to the solvency of non-financial players also involves the standard, adopted in May 2018 and extended until 2023, limiting the exposures of systemic banks to the most indebted large companies resident in France to 5% of equity. Finally, the strengthening of financial stability in Europe requires the completion of the Banking Union. The approach put forward by the President of the Eurogroup last May envisages a reasoned progress on the four main areas (management of banking crises, protection of depositors, diversification of sovereign exposures and provision of banking services within the single market). This step-by-step approach prioritizes trust and realism. We see this as an asset for obtaining a political agreement that is necessary to move towards a more complete and resilient Banking Union, but which does not lose momentum or capacity for innovation.  Challenges associated with climate change and the digitalisation of finance To conclude these remarks, I would like to say a few words about the role we can play as supervisors and central bankers in helping banks on the paths of the transition to a sustainable economy and the digitalization of finance. Regarding the first component, the recent publication of the latest contribution to the IPCC's 6th Assessment Report1 reminds us of the need for an urgent transition to carbon neutrality Supervisors have already started to assess the exposure of financial institutions to transition risksto encourage them to identify, assess and manage these risks in the same way as traditional risks - and the ACPR played a pioneering role with the first stress test on climate risks. Climate risks will be progressively integrated into the prudential framework, starting with Pillar 2 and Pillar 3 requirements. I-UO MCIIIVMC7O UUIVUIIl OU pi Upai Ul YES lUOpUVl VIC bUO IULUIC3 UAIJUI IVUO regulatory measures, including those relating to climate risk stress testing and transition plans. The latter are part of the CRD6 proposal currently under negotiation. On the Pillar 1 framework, the integration of climate risks continues to be a hotly debated topic and I hope that the publication of an EBA consultation paper will allow us to move forward. Before implementing new requirements, however, many methodological and data shortcomings will need to be addressed. In any case, I would like to emphasise that, from my point of view as a supervisor, Pillar 1 should remain risk-based and that we should go beyond the somewhat artificial opposition between green and brown exposures, by assessing transition risk more on the basis of transition plans. Regarding the digitalization of finance, in addition to supporting the development of regulations, such as DORA (Digital Operationai Resilience Acf) and MiCA (Markets in crypto-assets), which aim to facilitate the development of innovations in a framework that enhances confidence and financial stability, As a central bank, we can play a positive role from an operational point of view by reviewing our money services offer. It is with this in mind that the Banque de France has successfully conducted 9 central bank digital currency (CBDC) experiments over the past two years for interbank settlement, corporate actions or cross-border payments. They will continue in 2022 on two major axes:  The first axis concerns the settlement in central bank money of securities issued on new distributed ledger platforms, which will be governed by the pilot regime from 2023. New technologies offer opportunities to facilitate the exchange of financial securities and improve the functioning of markets. However, central banks are careful not to lead to market and liquidity fragmentation. As a result, the Eurosystem, as was done for TARGET2-Securities, could change the terms of access to its settlement asset to secure the exchange of tokenised assets.  The second axis is the improvement of cross-border payments, which international bodies have - rightly - made a priority. Last year, we demonstrated the advantages of a CBDC, to optimize the payment chain by reducing the number of intermediaries and improving the security of payments. In parallel with these reflections on the interbank CBDC, investigations are underway into the issuance of a retail CBDC. The launch of a possible digital euro by the Eurosystem would meet several objectives:  Reaffirming the anchoring role of central money in the universe digital, like the role that the banknote plays today in the physical world.  To contribute to strengthening European strategic autonomy in the field of payments, in a public-private partnership logic. We are aware of the impacts that a digital euro could have on financial intermediation and monetary and financial stability. This means addressing these issues from the design stage of a digital euro, for example by introducing holding limits or by favouring a model in which intermediaries play a central role in the distribution of the digital euro and in the management of user relationships. That is why we are now setting up a dialogue with stakeholders, which should be intensified in the weeks and months to come. But there should be no doubt that, in addition to regulators and central banks, the private sector also has a key role to play in digital innovation. From this point of view, I would like to highlight the strategic importance of the pan-European payment service project (European Payments Initiative, EPI), which currently represents the only project for a solution under a common brand rather than an interoperability of heterogeneous domestic solutions. We at the Banque de France therefore hope that the launch of the first PPE solutions, scheduled for 2023, will convince other banks to join this initiative, which offers Europe a great opportunity to build the independence of the European payments market for the future. To conclude, in the face of short- and medium-term risks and challenges, I want to share with you, the members of the OCBF and more broadly the players in our banking system, a message of confidence but also of great vigilance. The reforms of regulators and the efforts of banks over the past decade have borne fruit and the European banking system has demonstrated its great resilience during the health crisis and then in the face of the war in Ukraine. The banking sector has also managed to support the efforts of the public authorities in the crisis and for the recovery. But these developments should encourage us collectively to remain highly vigilant in an environment of increasing shocks and high levels of uncertainty, and to continue our efforts to build resilience to successfully address current and future challenges. 1 IPCC Working Group III contribution published on 4 April 2022 Updated on November 21, 2023

Title: Macroeconomic situation, monetary policy stance and impact on the financial sector
text: Macroeconomic situation, monetary policy orientation and impact on the financial sector Stakeholder Published on October 13, 2022 University of Artois Wednesday, October 12, 2022 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Dear students, ladies and gentlemen, I am delighted to be here with you today to talk about the evolution of the macroeconomic and financial situation and the conduct of the policies that we are pursuing at the Banque de France to ensure our monetary and financial stability missions. The economic and financial impact of the war in Ukraine has profoundly changed the outlook for the end of the Covid crisis as it was understood at the beginning of the year for the countries of the euro area, and France in particular, and subjected our economic and financial system to new major shocks. After presenting the macroeconomic situation and outlook as we are analysing them today at the Banque de France, I will tell you what consequences we draw from them for the conduct of monetary policy and for financial stability.  Macroeconomic situation in the euro area As for the macroeconomic situation in the euro area, the deterioration in the economic outlook throughout the year is due in particular to the war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China, which fuelled a "slow-flation shock. This shock now threatens to turn into a shock "stagflationary". The most recent data show a significant slowdown in economic growth in the euro area. There are several reasons for this. The negative terms-of-trade shock resulting from very high energy prices, which affects the real income of households and businesses. Supply and recruitment bottlenecks, even if they are easing, continue to constrain economic activity. Finally, the harmful geopolitical environment, with in particular the unjustifiable war waged by Russia in Ukraine weighing on the confidence of business leaders and consumers. As a result, the projections for economic growth have been revised significantly downwards for the remainder of 2022 and for the whole of 2023 [slide 2], In the ECB's September projections, the baseline now assumes growth of 3.1% in 2022, 0.9% in 2023 and 1.9% in 2024. The expected improvement in euro area countries is based on the assumption that gas supply disruptions would cease to be a significant constraint on activity as temperatures rise and alternative sources of supply are gradually put in place. Real GDP growth is expected to pick up in the course of 2023, driven by several factors: easing inflationary pressures, which should reduce downward pressure on real disposable income; bottlenecks are expected to disappear, external demand is expected to recover, and export price competitiveness is expected to improve vis-a-vis major trading partners such as the United States. In this context, as far as the French economy is concerned, activity is expected to be marked by a cycle in three "Rs": Resilience-Slowdown-Recovery, [slide 3] The Bank of France's in-depth analysis of the French economic cycle [which is presented in detail in our macroeconomic projections published every quarter] can be summarised in three stages, around three "R:  Resilience first of all in 2022, because the French economy is resilient to recent shocks better than expected: we have even revised our forecasts for this year slightly upwards, which now stand at 2.6% (compared to 2.3% in June).  Slowdown from winter onwards. The Banque de France's reference scenario is GDP growth of 0.5% in 2023. Nevertheless, given the extent of the uncertainties surrounding gas supplies and their price, we have decided to present a forecast range for 2023 between 0.8% and -0.5%. A recession cannot therefore be ruled out, but if it were to occur, it would be limited and temporary.  Economic recovery by 2024. In a context of gradual easing of tensions on the energy markets, the French economy is expected to return to more sustained growth. I now come to our assessment of recent inflation developments, [slide 4] In the euro area, consumer price inflation has increased in recent months, reaching 10% in September according to the provisional results of the harmonised index of consumer prices. In France, inflation was 6.2%, the lowest level in the euro area, thanks in particular to the price shield, but it remains well above the Eurosystem's inflation target. We at the Banque de France, like our colleagues in the other Eurosystem central banks, believe that the current sharp acceleration in inflation is fundamentally due not to excess liquidity, but to the bottlenecks resulting from the faster-than-expected rebound in activity following the pandemic and the sharp rise in energy and food prices. largely exacerbated by the war in Ukraine. The inflation we are seeing at the moment is mainly imported and is largely the result - about two-thirds for the euro area - of energy and food prices. The recent sharp rise in international gas prices has led the ECB to forecast a peak in inflation by the end of 2022, beginning of 2023. However, inflation in the euro area is also starting to take on a more "internal and "broad-based character, with all other components of inflation rising: according to the preliminary results for September, core inflation (which excludes energy and food) now stands at 4.8% in the euro area (and 3.7% in France), and price increases are spreading to goods and services - which account for the other half of total inflation. It is this more "internal" inflation for which central banks are responsible, and which they must not let slip out of control or persist. This is the critical objective and commitment underpinning the actions taken by the ECB's Governing Council. Therefore, there should be no doubt whatsoever about its willingness and ability to bring inflation in the eurozone down to 2% over the next two to three years.  Implications for monetary policy So what are the implications of the current situation for monetary policy in the euro area? [slide 5] The fundamental shift in the risk to price stability that we face from "too low for too long" to "too high for too long" inflation clearly implies a normalisation of monetary policy, which means dismantling the measures adopted to combat the risk of deflation and quickly moving to at least a neutral stance. As far as the ECB's key interest rates are concerned, this has resulted in a rapid return to positive territory, towards what is known as the "neutral rate. As a reminder, the neutral rate refers to the theoretical equilibrium level at which there is neither a new monetary acceleration nor a slowdown in inflation. It is therefore an unobservable variable and its estimate is surrounded by uncertainty. At the Banque de France, we estimate that the neutral rate is at or near 2% in nominal terms in the euro area. Regarding the speed at which this move towards a neutral rate should occur, I would like to recall the words used by Francois Villeroy de Galhau in a recent public communication on monetary policy: "As long as we take our foot off the accelerator, it is certain that we must act, in a determined but orderly manner, and we should reach our objective by the end of the year." On this point, I would only add that, in the current context, it is particularly important to be agile and to be ready to adapt the pace of normalization to the changing situation. A second important issue regarding the ongoing normalisation of monetary policy in the euro area concerns the destination of the trip, i.e . terminal interest rates. On this point, I would like to give a typical economist's answer, I fear: it depends! Indeed, it is important to keep in mind that it is only beyond the neutral rate that tightening will really begin. In my view, the ECB's Governing Council will then have to discuss and decide, based on its assessment of observed inflation and the outlook for inflation, focusing in particular on its underlying component and on wage developments. In the context I have just described, an important role for monetary policy is to ensure that inflation expectations remain anchored, especially when inflation is high. So far, inflation expectations remain relatively well anchored in the euro area. In particular, there is no sign that a possible wage-price loop is at work. This imperative to anchor inflation expectations helps explain why the ECB has raised key interest rates by a total of 125 basis points at the last two monetary policy meetings. As indicated by Christine Lagarde, the appropriate pace of future rate hikes will be decided on a meeting-by-meeting basis. Indeed, as she has repeatedly pointed out, the decision will remain data-driven across scenarios. Inflation is expected to slow to 2 per cent as its current drivers fade and monetary policy normalization affects the economy and pricing mechanisms. When will this happen? Will it be necessary for the Eurosystem to tighten monetary policy significantly? To provide some answers to this difficult question, I would like to point out firstly that ECB staff revised their inflation projections significantly upwards in September, with price increases now expected to average 8.1% in 2022, 5.5% in 2023, but are projected to decline to 2.3% in 2024. Second, market participants do not expect the ECB to tighten its key interest rates significantly at the moment, with central expectations for the interest rate at the end of the period being just below 3%. [slide 6]  I would now like to discuss with you the Consequences of environmental change The immediate impact of the war in Ukraine on financial stability has certainly been properly absorbed so far because the direct exposures of French financial players to Russia were low. However, risks for financial intermediaries, and thus financial stability, can materialize through second-round effects and indirect channels from pre-existing vulnerabilities, notably those associated with the sectors most dependent on energy commodities, and the development of leveraged finance. Hence the strong attention we are paying to rising prices, volatility in commodity markets and the considerable increase in margin calls on derivatives, in particular for energy and agricultural products [slide 7], which have already led to liquidity pressures on commodity market participants. Very vigilant monitoring of credit and liquidity risks in the energy commodities sector is therefore required, in particular to ensure that any possible default (e.g. of a trader) remains contained and does not lead to systemic contagion. Beyond the energy derivatives markets, the financial markets in general have also been subject to very high volatility since the beginning of the year, with significant corrections on the main equity and bond indices and are therefore also a strong point of attention. Valuations are now more subdued than at the beginning of the year, but the risk of a further and, above all, disorderly correction cannot be ruled out. As illustrated by recent episodes of market stress, the materialization of such a shock could uncover vulnerabilities in important non-bank financial actors subject to liquidity risk, and if necessary, amplify corrective movements on the financial markets, [slide 8] The third major point of attention for the assessment of financial stability is the evolution of the debt sustainability of non-financial agents, households, companies and the State, in the macroeconomic context that I have described and the change in the regime undertaken in terms of the interest rate environment, [slide 9] In France, households are at the forefront of the real economy. The risk of default on mortgage loans - which make up more than 80% of household debt - is on the rise, but remains moderate given the characteristics of these loans. On the one hand, the public authorities have put in place support measures for the households most affected by inflation. On the other hand, while they may have been contested at the time of their implementation, the standards issued by the High Council for Financial Stability, which aim to ensure sustainable debt levels, now make sense: they protect households against over-indebtedness associated with access to property and ensure that these expenses are limited to a reasonable proportion of their income. Finally, it should be remembered that structurally households in France take on debt at a fixed rate, unlike the practices in force in some European countries, and are protected against a rise in interest rates, which also promotes their resilience. In addition, at this stage, mortgage rates have only risen moderately. Non-financial companies, on the other hand, approached the economic downturn in a good situation: at the end of 2021, there was an improvement in turnover and net income compared to 2019 in most sectors. In 2022, activity has been resilient so far, but their cash flow and margins are starting to erode as a result of higher supply prices, as the ability to pass on higher costs to selling prices may be limited. Secondly, the downward revision of growth prospects in France and abroad is likely to reduce their outlets, and therefore their level of activity. Finally, rising interest rates are increasing the cost of financing them. As a large majority of the debt of non-financial corporations is at a fixed rate and over long maturities, the increase will only be gradual, when debt renewals are made. Despite this, average rates for non-financial corporations are now higher than their average over the past decade. All this contributes to the gradual increase in credit risk, which weighs on corporate debts. Finally, it is important to note that the current circumstances are having a negative impact on public finances and the public debt market. The counter-cyclical measures to support the economy, made necessary by the situation, are widening the public deficit even further, at the very moment when the rise in interest rates is beginning to increase the interest charges paid by the State. All of these vulnerabilities are now at a high level, which requires our full attention. This observation is shared by our peers in the euro area, and led the European Systemic Risk Board to issue an "alert in September, inviting all supervisory and regulatory bodies to work closely together to prevent the occurrence of a potential crisis. To make a good diagnosis of financial stability, it is nevertheless essential to compare the vulnerabilities likely to materialize under the effect of shocks, the resilience and absorption capacity of the financial system. However, the resilience that the French financial system has been able to demonstrate, through the various crises that have followed one another for more than two years now, must be underlined and is therefore an important asset for the stability of our financial system, [slide 10] French banks are entering this new financial cycle with a solid financial and prudential situation. Their solvency ratios are close to historical highs of 14.8% for the main French banks and the results for the first half of 2022 were up after an already excellent year in 2021. Moreover, in terms of profitability prospects, banks should benefit from rising rates, at least in the medium term. An analysis of the structure of their balance sheet shows that they receive more income than they pay out, both on fixed-rate and variable-rate products, because they have non-interest-bearing resources on their liabilities, our deposits. This situation is likely to increase their interest margin in a context of an orderly rate increase. Even with unfavourable assumptions, such as a sharp decline in loan volumes or an accelerated increase in the deposit interest charge, this margin would remain on an upward trend in the medium term. However, they are exposed to a potential increase in defaults on loans granted to individuals and businesses, due to the increase in the cost of refinancing and the slowdown in growth. It should be noted that this risk has not materialized for the time being, with the default rate of French non-financial companies remaining 30% below its 2019 level. The insurance sector is also resilient as a whole, with different challenges between life and non-life insurers. Life insurers could benefit from the rise in rates over the medium term, if it were gradual, and if there are no massive arbitrages from euro funds to other investment vehicles, which could offer more attractive returns from the outset. However, the impact in terms of improving the return on assets will be very gradual, with assets remunerated at low or even negative rates maturing only gradually and gradually being replaced by better-yielding investments. This may also vary depending on the risk profile of each institution and the respective duration of its assets and liabilities. Non-life insurers are exposed to inflation because it increases the cost of claims: compensation is simply more expensive than what was envisaged when the insurance contract was set up and insurance premiums were calculated. Traditionally, this is particularly pronounced for long-term risks, where payments can be made several years after the premiums have been collected. However, when short-term inflation is also very high, it is the entire activity that can potentially be affected. In the current context, this shock-absorbing capacity is an asset that must be maintained and maintained. Caution is therefore required in the management of the capital of financial institutions so as not to weaken the solidity of these players. In line with this prudential approach, the High Council for Financial Stability increased the counter-cyclical capital buffer to 0.5% in March 2022. It plans to raise it at its next meeting in December 2022 to 1.0% unless the banking system's ability to meet the financing needs of the economy declines sharply and unexpectedly. In this horizon, the structural supply problems of the French economy remain and call for the implementation of policies to strengthen our productive capacity. To achieve this, we will have to succeed in three major transformations: o Ecological and energy transformation o Digital transformation o Increasing the supply of labour and skills. Thank you for your attention.

Title: The World of Crypto Assets: The Litmus Test
text: EUROSYSTEM Rostrum (Deputy Governors J) The world of crypto assets: the test of truth Published on January 10, 2023 Op-ed by Denis Beau, Senior Deputy Governor of the Bank of France. Will 2022 go down in history as the year that marked the "beginning of the end" of crypto assets and decentralized finance (DEFI)? Indeed, their very dynamic and creative development has had as a corollary a rise in risks and losses for their players and customers, some of which have materialized in a spectacular way, with the collapse of the third largest "stablecoin" system (obviously misnamed), Terra-Luna, the bankruptcy of FTX, one of the world's largest platforms for exchanging crypto assets, and the undermining of other players in their ecosystem, including liquidity providers like Genesis or BlockFi. They were accompanied by a nearly 70% reduction in the capitalization of all crypto assets, which returned to its level at the beginning of 2021. While these violent tremors have probably not yet produced all their effects in a chain, they are already rich in lessons. An important lesson is related to the general principles of organization and means, in particular in terms of governance, internal control, protection of client assets, separation of activities and prevention of conflicts of interest with affiliated entities, accounting, transparency, etc. that apply to traditional financial players, given the risks inherent in financial activities. Until now, the scope of these principles has been very limited, their content undemanding and uneven from one jurisdiction to another for players in the world of crypto-assets, on the grounds that the dissemination of the innovations they carry should not be unduly slowed down. The difficulties encountered by certain players, the effects of contagion regardless of borders, the losses and thefts suffered by their customers, now make it necessary to reconsider this policy and to evolve rapidly at the national, European and international levels towards broader, more robust and harmonised regulatory requirements, in line with the rncnmmonrlninnr innr rli i rlii DQD mniArn rli i I'm in the second place in the second place in the second Cl MU I xJLJ In the case of the U.S. financial stability or anti-money laundering. At the Banque de France and the ACPR, based on our experience as supervisor of traditional players in finance and the financial system as a whole, we are convinced that the world of crypto assets and decentralized finance will only develop again, usefully and sustainably, with a an appropriate regulatory framework, a vector of trust. Its objective should be to allow all competitors to be placed on an equal footing, without suffering the damaging consequences of "rogue" actors as has been the case until now. It should also aim to ensure an appropriate balance between the objectives of protecting customers and maintaining financial stability on the one hand, and operational realities on the other. Europe has been a pioneer in this direction, defining a new regulatory framework, known as MICA (Markets in crypto assets regulation), which should come into force in the first quarter of 2023, and come into force at the end of the first half of 2024. In this perspective, the implementation in France, rather than the simple registration, of a mandatory approval of DASPs (Digital Asset Service Providers) before the entry into force of MICA, currently under discussion, is desirable. It should facilitate and accelerate the adaptation of players, whether established or setting up in France, to a regulatory environment that will allow them to evolve in a framework of trust for all on the path to innovation.
