Title: The return of inflation in the euro area and monetary policy responses
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) The return of inflation in the euro area and monetary policy responses Published on February 2, 2023 Conference in partnership With the Faculty of Economics and Management of Orleans 1er fevrier 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Dear students, ladies and gentlemen, I am delighted to be here with you today to talk to you about the evolution of the macroeconomic and financial situation in the euro area and the conduct of the policies that we are pursuing at the Banque de France and in the Eurosystem to ensure our monetary stability missions. The economic and financial impact of the war in Ukraine has profoundly changed the prospects for emerging from the Covid crisis as it was a year ago, and subjected our economic and financial system to new major supply and demand shocks, which have resulted in a sharp acceleration in inflation. After presenting the macroeconomic situation and outlook as we are analysing them today at the Banque de France, I will tell you what consequences we draw from this in terms of monetary policy, in order to bring inflation back to 2%.  Macroeconomic situation and outlook As regards the macroeconomic situation, the euro area economy has been affected by a series of unprecedented shocks in recent years. The deterioration of the economic outlook since the beginning of 2022. yes has resulted in revisions made to the The rise in inflation forecasts and the downward trend in growth forecasts [slide 2] is due in particular to the war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China, which have fuelled a "slow-flation" shock. This shock now threatens to turn into a "stagflationary" shock. The most recent data show a significant slowdown in economic growth in the euro area. There are several reasons for this. In particular, and first and foremost, the negative terms-of-trade shock resulting from very high energy prices, which affects the real income of households and firms. For France, this shock to the terms of trade could be the second largest since the first oil shock in 1974. It implies a decrease in real income for the euro area economy of -2.3% of GDP (-1.8% for France) year-on-year at the end of the 3rd quarter of 2022. Supply bottlenecks in terms of supply and recruitment are also at play. Even if they are abating, they continue to constrain economic activity. The harmful geopolitical environment is finally playing a role, in particular with Russia's unjustifiable war in Ukraine, which is weighing on the confidence of business leaders and consumers. As a result, the projections for economic growth have been revised significantly downwards for the end of 2022 and for the whole of 2023. In the Eurosystem's December projections, the baseline now assumes growth of 3.4% in 2022, 0.5% in 2023, 1.9% in 2024 and 1.8% in 2025 [slide 3]. The combination of supply and demand shocks at the sector level has also resulted in a sharp acceleration in inflation. Inflation is expected to reach 8.4% in 2022 in the euro area. According to the Eurosystem's December projections, inflation is expected to slow only gradually and return to 2% by the end of 2024 and in 2025.La inflation forecast for the euro area is thus 6.3% in 2023, 3.4% in 2024 and 2.3% in 2025. In its monetary policy statement (statemenf) of 15 December, the Governing Council stressed that the risks to the economic growth outlook were tilted to the downside. Risks to the inflation outlook were mainly tilted to the upside. Economic data released since then, however, suggest that these downside risks have narrowed overall. In particular, a relaxation in wholesale oil and gas prices has occurred in recent weeks compared to the assumptions made in the December forecast, [slide 4] This decline in energy costs could reduce price pressures. In addition, a number of recently published economic indicators seem to indicate that the risk of recession in the winter of 2023 has diminished in favour of temporary stagnation: I am thinking in particular of the latest business surveys in Germany and France. [slide 5] In this context, with regard to the French economy, our December forecast reflects macroeconomic dynamics marked by a three-phase cycle, which can be summarised by three "R's" for growth: Resilience in 2022 -Slowdown at the end of the year 2022, early 2023-Resumption in 2024. Regarding inflation, it is expected to be 6.0% on average per year and also in 2023. However, after peaking in the first half of 2023, it is expected to gradually decrease to 4% at the end of 2023, then 2.5% in 2024 and 2.1% in 2025. The forecasts are based on the outlook for household consumption, which is expected to remain positive, based on the observation that consumer price increases are already partly transmitted to nominal wages, which in turn feed price increases in a usual price-wage relationship [slide 6]. In addition, the impact of the shock on the terms of trade, and in particular on the energy bill, on real incomes is largely cushioned by the numerous budgetary measures to support purchasing power put in place1 SUP" . At the Banque de France, we estimate that this levy linked to the energy bill will be around 60 billion or 2.5% of GDP for the year 2022. As a result of the compensatory budgetary measures put in place by the Government, it can be estimated that the share of this levy ultimately borne by households is around 6%; that borne by enterprises by about 50% and that borne by general government by 35% (This assessment does not, however, take into account all the macroeconomic adjustments that are at work, and in particular the transmission by enterprises of cost increases to their selling prices and the reaction of wages to prices). However, given the high inflation, the per capita purchasing power of households is expected to decline slightly in 2022 (-0.6%) and in 2022. 2023 (-0.4%), although less than the increase observed in 2021 (2.0%). As far as companies are concerned, their investment plans are expected to be moderately affected over the forecast horizon. The increase in energy costs, the acceleration of nominal wages and the weakness of productivity gains, due in particular to the rise in work-study programmes and labour retention behaviour to prepare for the subsequent rebound in activity, should weigh on margins and therefore their profitability. However, the margin rate of non-financial corporations, which was exceptionally supported in 2020 and 2021 by the various measures put in place to deal with the Covid crisis, is expected to be around 1 point below its 2018 level over the period 2023-2024, around 30.5%. Then, the margin rate would return to its pre-crisis level, at 31.4%. At the same time, the upward trend in the investment rate is expected to come to a halt over the forecast horizon, as a result of the slowdown in activity, wait-and-see behaviour linked to macroeconomic uncertainty and the normalisation of financial conditions. Over the entire forecast horizon, the investment rate of non-financial corporations is expected to stabilise at around 25.5% of their value added. A final word to close this presentation, on the situation and outlook for inflation, [slide 7] In the euro area, consumer price inflation has accelerated in recent months, reaching 9.2% in December. In France, according to the results of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, inflation stood at 6.7%, the lowest level in the euro area, thanks in particular to the price shield, but it remains well above the Eurosystem's inflation target. We at the Banque de France, like our colleagues in the other Eurosystem central banks, believe that the current sharp acceleration in inflation is fundamentally due not to excess liquidity, but to the bottlenecks resulting from the faster-than-expected rebound in activity following the pandemic and the sharp rise in energy and food prices. widely pyarprhpp nar Iq riiiprrp en I ikrainp In 2022, the surge in energy prices on international markets was the main inflationary shock for the French economy. This shock had a limited impact on retail energy prices in 2022, due in particular to the price shield, but it was also transmitted indirectly and with a delay of a few months to the other components of inflation, via the repercussions of the increase in producer costs. Thus, inflation in France and the euro area has spread very widely and is now "internal" and "generalized" in nature, with an increase in all the other components of inflation: according to the December results, core inflation (which excludes energy and food) now stands at 5.2% in the euro area (and 4.2% in France), and price increases are spreading to goods and services - which account for the other half of total inflation. It is this more "internal" inflation for which central banks are responsible, and which they must not allow to persist. According to our December forecast, inflation is expected to peak in the first half of the year, before easing to 2% in late 2024 and 2025. This decline in inflation over the forecast horizon would result from the combined effect of several factors: the stabilisation in 2023 commodity prices, with the dissipation of the base effects associated with their previous rise, the effects of the change in monetary policy stance decided by the ECB Governing Council to bring inflation down to 2%, on which I will now focus my remarks, and, correlatively, the maintenance of the anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations in the vicinity of the ECB's inflation target.  Implications for monetary policy So what are the implications of the change in macroeconomic situation and outlook that I have just described for monetary policy in the euro area? [slide 8] From a monetary policy perspective, this shift has had the effect of changing the nature of the main risk it needs to reduce: the risk to price stability we face is no longer one of inflation that is "too low for too long" but that of inflation that is "too high for too long". This fundamental change called for a change in monetary policy stance. This is why, as a first step, the Governing Council decided to dismantle the measures adopted to combat the risk of deflation. Thus, with regard to the ECB's key interest rates, the ECB's Governing Council decided to increase them at an accelerated pace, by a total of 250 basis points in 6 months between July and December 2022. With these decisions, monetary policy has reached the neutral rate. As a reminder, the neutral rate refers to the theoretical equilibrium level at which there is neither a new monetary acceleration nor a slowdown in inflation. It is therefore an unobservable variable and its estimate is surrounded by uncertainty. At the Banque de France, we estimate that the neutral rate is close to 2% in nominal terms in the euro area, the level reached by the key rates at the end of the December Governing Council. It is important to keep in mind that the reduction of the Central Bank's balance sheet is expected to begin during this second stage. The important questions now are the extent, speed and duration of this tightening of monetary policy. At her last press conference, the ECB President made it clear that key rates had to go beyond the neutral rate, and that the market's expectations at the time about the so-called "terminal" rate, i.e. the rate at the peak of the increase, were just under 3%, which were incorporated into the ECB's forecasts, would not be sufficient to bring inflation back to the 2 per cent target over time. Further rate hikes will therefore be necessary in 2023, to bring inflation back to 2%. However, it is too early to predict the level and date at which the "terminal" rate will be reached, and how long it will be maintained at this level. As Francois Villeroy stressed during his hearing before the Senate's Finance Committee in mid-January, pragmatism will govern these decisions, and will be guided by the observed data, with the aim of bringing inflation back to 2% within two years, which is the time frame for monetary policy to act. To recall the words used by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, " the speed race of rate hikes in 2022 is becoming more of a race of and the duration will count at least as much as the level". With regard to the "terminal" rate, I would simply like to point out that market participants do not currently expect the ECB to tighten its key interest rates sharply, as central expectations for the interest rate at the end of the period are now slightly above 3% [slide 9]. In addition, they anticipate that the end of the rate hike cycle should be reached in the summer of 2023. According to the markets, it should give way to the start of a decline in the 1st half of 2024 in line with its expectations of a return to 2% of inflation in the first part of 2024. However, it seems reasonable to me to say that in the context of high uncertainty in which we operate, these expectations are fragile and volatile. Indeed, many factors are likely to influence the path of monetary policy in this context, whether or not they contribute to the persistence of core inflation (excluding volatile components) significantly above the 2% target. Hence the indication given by Christine Lagarde in December that "our future decisions will remain dependent on data and will continue to be taken meeting by meeting". In the context I have just described, an important role for monetary policy will be to ensure that inflation expectations remain anchored, particularly as long as inflation remains high. So far, this is the case and there is no sign that a possible wage-price loop is at work. But vigilance must remain the order of the day, [slide 10] The Governing Council's forecast and commitment is that inflation is expected to slow to close to 2% in 2025 as its current drivers fade and the normalisation of monetary policy takes its toll on the economy and in pricing mechanisms.  Conclusion [slide 11] To conclude, I would like to draw three lessons from this rapid review of the evolution of the economic and monetary situation for France:  The good resilience of our economy and financial system to shocks so far  The regime change in the interest rate environment that these shocks have caused by pushing for a normalisation of monetary policy  The importance, beyond immediate actions to maintain monetary and financial stability, objectives to which the Banque de France is resolutely committed by virtue of its mandates, to focus on the project over a longer horizon. In this regard, the structural supply problems of the French economy remain and call for the implementation of policies to strengthen our productive capacity. To achieve this, we will need to succeed in three major transformations: o The ecological and energy transformation o Digital transformation o Increasing the supply of labour and skills. Thank you for your attention. - The total amount of these measures for households could thus reach around 50 billion in 2023. o -This final distribution after the final macroeconomic adjustments in prices and quantities is much more difficult to assess. Updated on November 21, 2023

Il devrait selon les marchs, laisser place  l'enclenchement d'une baisse au 1er semestre 2024 en cohrence avec ses anticipations dun retour  2 % de l'inflation dans la premire partie de l'anne 2024. Toutefois, il me semble raisonnable de dire que dans le contexte de forte incertitude dans lequel nous voluons, ces anticipations sont fragiles et volatiles. De nombreux facteurs sont en effet susceptibles dinfluer sur la trajectoire de la politique montaire dans ce contexte, en alimentant ou pas la persistance dune inflation sous-jacente (hors composantes volatiles) significativement au-dessus de la cible de 2 %. D'o l'indication donne par Christine Lagarde en dcembre que  nos futures dcisions resteront dpendantes des donnes et continueront d'tre prises runion par runion . Dans le contexte que je viens de dcrire, un rle important pour la politique montaire sera de veiller  ce que les anticipations d'inflation restent ancres, en particulier tant que l'inflation demeure leve. Pour y parvenir, il nous faudra russir trois grandes transformations : o La transformation cologique et nergtique o La transformation numrique o Laugmentation de loffre de travail et des comptences. Title: Payments in the Digital Age: Towards a Turning Point?
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) Payments in the digital age: towards a turning point? Published on February 16, 2023 Pay Tech Day de France Payments Forum February 16, 2023 Payments in the digital age: towards a turning point? Opening speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. It is a pleasure to speak to you again on the occasion of the Pay Tech Day of France Payments Forum. Thank you to Herve and Nicolas for giving me the opportunity to open your conference on a subject that is at the heart of our concerns as a central bank responsible for ensuring the efficiency and security of our payment system. I think that each and every one of you will agree that the payments ecosystem that we use on a daily basis is a microcosm in the etymological sense of the term, that is to say a condensation, a reflection of our society. An open and dynamic microcosm, however, driven by the growth of trade, and moreover in an intangible form. Nearly 15 billion cashless transactions were recorded in the first half of last year in France, an increase of 6% compared to the same period in 2021. The European Central Bank's recent SPACE 1 study on payment habits confirms this trend, since half of point-of-sale transactions in France now involve cashless payments, and in particular cards. These developments are sources of opportunities and risks for service providers and users alike. As the impact of digitalization on everyday payments amplifies and takes a new turn with the development of tokenized and decentralized finance, I would like to share with you some lessons that we at the Banque de France have learned from the challenges we have already collectively faced, how we see the evolution of these challenges with the amplification and turning point of digitalization underway, and the contributions we are committed to making under our monetary and financial stability mandates to meet them. 1/ We are now used to dematerialized, real-time exchanges. The growth of e-commerce has been made possible by the existence of digitized means of payment, first and foremost the bank card, or payment applications in emerging countries. The mobile phone is also making a place for itself in Europe, both to initiate and receive payments: it helps to facilitate our mobility, but also increases our dependence on non-European technologies and equipment. In this context, both private players and regulators had to face a first major challenge: that of preserving and even strengthening the dynamism of our market, by preserving and strengthening the safety of users. Because fraudsters and hackers have also invested in the digital world, and that is why legislation must evolve with new technologies. The second Payment Services Directive, or PSD2, is a good example of this: by introducing strong authentication, it reduced fraud on remote payments by 20% in 2021, while supporting e-commerce growth of more than 20%. Another challenge has been related to the interconnection between actors made possible by APIs. By breaking down the barriers between databases, these interfaces have opened up new service opportunities and encouraged cooperation between actors; But they have also exposed infrastructure to new attacks, and raised questions about personal data protection and a viable business model. It is to meet this challenge that PSD2 has once again laid the groundwork for a banking data sharing framework. This framework is intended to be extended more widely: this is the objective pursued by the European Commission with its open finance strategy, but also by the EPC through the work of the SEPA Account Access scheme. What lessons can be learned from these first experiences? For my part, I retain the need for agile regulation, in a market that is changing very quickly, and regulation that offers a framework of trust for the development of innovation. These experiences have also shown the importance of supporting the various stakeholders in the implementation of standards, and of promoting dialogue: this is the role played in particular by the National Committee for Payment Methods in France, but also by private bodies such as the France Payments Forum. H/ iaes first lessons ooivern us eciairer oans i learning about the new challenges we face, as the impact of digitalization on everyday payments amplifies and takes a new turn with the development of tokenized and decentralized finance, driven by new players at the crossroads of IT and finance, new assets, crypto assets, and new exchange and settlement infrastructure. Without addressing all the facets of this subject, I would like to highlight three major issues: sovereignty, security and accessibility. We can congratulate ourselves on being an open and attractive market for many non-European players, but this interest has a risk: that of limiting our strategic autonomy and threatening our sovereignty. The illustrations are numerous. For example, because of the refusal to fully comply with European regulations: beyond the restriction on access to the NFC antennas of Apple phones, which has been widely commented on by the press, we can also mention the difficulties of the supervisory authorities in convincing certain major technical service providers to set up a governance structure on European soil. Foreign heavyweights are also entering into agreements that can limit competition, for example by imposing single-brand or closed-loop payment solutions. When it comes to security, payment experts are faced with increasingly sophisticated fraud techniques. Faced with substantial advances in cybersecurity standards, scammers are now targeting the human factor through social engineering mechanisms. These issues are all the more sensitive in the context of the rise of instant transfers. Moreover, by attempting to replicate some of the functions performed by the traditional financial system, the crypto-asset ecosystem inherits vulnerabilities from the latter and could amplify them with potentially systemic consequences. At present, it is fortunately not large and interconnected enough to threaten the stability of our entire financial system, as the limited impact of the collapse of Terra-Luna and crypto asset conglomerate FTX has shown. Finally, I want to highlight the challenges of including digital means of payment, particularly for the elderly and those with disabilities. But accessibility must also take into account the dimension of the cost of payment services: the study conducted by the Observatory on banking tariffs last year highlighted an overall increase in fees over the last ten years, particularly for basic services such as account maintenance. 111/ To meet these challenges, we believe that our contribution as a central bank must develop in various complementary directions, ranging from contributing to the development of a regulatory framework conducive to both innovation and security, to careful and demanding supervision, to support the fight against fraud, to the accessibility of payments and to the commitment to defend the freedom of choice of means of payment. In the limited time allotted to me for these remarks in the introduction to your conference, I would simply like to illustrate the actions we are taking to guarantee our freedom of choice in terms of daily means of payment, in a context where our strategic autonomy is becoming a central subject of attention. First and foremost, we are committed to supporting and encouraging the payment ecosystem and players to develop innovative and pan-European payment methods: in this respect, the EPI initiative has benefited from the support of the Banque de France and the Eurosystem from the outset, and we are looking forward to the market launch of its diqital solution. Guaranteeing freedom of choice also means preserving access to fiat money: while its use at the point of sale is tending to decrease, the SPACE study that I mentioned in the introduction nevertheless confirms the attachment of French and European consumers to cash. It is also essential to anticipate the evolution of uses by considering the introduction of central money in digital form. This is the subject of the current reflections carried out by the Eurosystem as part of the investigation phase on the digital euro. This would aim (i) on the one hand to preserve the anchor role of central money, without which our monetary system could be destabilized, like the historical precedent of free banking; (ii) and on the other hand, to strengthen the strategic autonomy of the European continent, by facilitating the emergence of pan-European payment solutions developed by PSPs and harmonised thanks to a new "scheme" designed for the digital euro, the development of which has just begun, in close cooperation with market players. I would like to emphasise this again very clearly to you: a digital euro would not replace cash or other electronic means of payment, but would complement them, in particular in compliance with very important concepts, such as the confidentiality of our fellow citizens' personal data. Finally, the Banque de France is also contributing to the Eurosystem's discussions on the possibility of settling assets circulating on distributed technologies (DLTs) in central money, possibly tokenised. This would allow the use of the safest and most liquid settlement asset for the settlement of tokenized financial securities. It is time for me to conclude, with a simple message: as we reach a turning point in the digitalization of our payment system, you can count on the Banque de France's commitment to keep it on the right trajectory of efficiency in security, but it is only together, with the help of all the players in the payments ecosystem, that we will actually take this path. Thank you for your attention and have a good conference. 1 Study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area (SPACE) Updated on November 2, 2023

Title: Financing companies in the face of crises
text: Crisis financing Stakeholder Published on April 25, 2023 OFEM Annual Conference April 25, 2023 Opening speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. The theme, as always, is important: the economic and financial impact of the war in Ukraine has profoundly changed the prospects for emerging from the Covid crisis as it was understood a little over a year ago, and subjected our economic and financial system to new supply and demand shocks. This has resulted in a sharp acceleration in inflation and a major change in the interest rate environment, pushing for a rapid reorientation of monetary policy. What impact on business financing? A review of the year 2022 is necessary and clear prospects are to be drawn for the financing of companies in 2023, to which I propose to contribute in these introductory remarks to your conference. 1. A few observations first on the change in the macro-economic and macro-financial context to highlight two points that seem to me to be structuring for taking stock and outlining prospects for the financing of companies: has. The risk of "stagflation" has receded in favor of a "soft landing" scenario. The economic outlook since the beginning of 2022 has deteriorated significantly, due in particular to the war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China, causing shocks that resulted in less growth and more inflation and threatened to lead to a period of "stagflation". This threat did not materialize. Instead, the most recent data and surveys point to a significant slowdown in economic growth in the euro area, followed by a recovery. According to the ECB's macroeconomic projections published on 16 March, the average annual growth of real GDP in the euro area is expected to slow to 1.0% in 2023 (from 3.6% in 2022), before rising to 1.6% in 2024 and 2025. For the French economy, the outlook is broadly similar. GDP is expected to grow by 0.6% in 20231, then by 1.2% in 2024 and 1.7% in 2025. We should therefore effectively escape recession in France as in the euro area as a whole. Regarding price developments [slide 2], after its resurgence in 2021, inflation continued to rise in 2022 at a pace not seen since the 1980s. However, in 2023, against a backdrop of lower energy prices, inflation in the euro area started to decline to 6.9% at the end of the month of March. In France [slide 3], according to the results of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, inflation stood at 6.7%, the lowest level in the euro area, thanks in particular to the price shield. We at the Banque de France, like our colleagues in the other central banks of the Eurosystem, believe that the sharp acceleration in inflation is fundamentally due not to excess liquidity, but to the bottlenecks resulting from the faster-than-expected rebound in activity at the end of the pandemic and the sharp rise in energy and food prices. largely exacerbated by the war in Ukraine. Thus, inflation in France and the euro area has spread very widely and is now "internal" and "generalized", with an increase in all the other components of inflation. It is this more "internal inflation for which central banks are responsible, and which they must not allow to persist. And the Governing Council has already acted quickly and strongly over the past year to avoid this prospect. As early as the end of 2021 [slide 4], the Eurosystem reacted to the inflationary shock by changing the stance of its monetary policy. With the interest rate increases decided in January and March, which brought the increase in key rates to 350 basis points between July 2022 and March 2023, monetary policy has now entered "restrictive" territory in the technical sense of the term, with the "neutral rate having been reached at the end of last year. We are now in a more open phase in which the high level of uncertainty reinforces the importance of a data-dependent approach to the Governing Council's policy rate decisions. According to the Governing Council's forecasts and commitment, inflation is expected to slow to close to 2% in 2025 as the current drivers fade and the effects of monetary policy normalisation affect the economy and pricing mechanisms. These forecasts are based on an improved outlook for household consumption from 2024 onwards in line with the rebound in purchasing power and the investment outlook for companies, which are expected to be moderately affected by the slowdown in activity, wait-and-see behaviour linked to macroeconomic uncertainty and the normalisation of financial conditions. In other words, we should avoid recession in France as in the euro area as a whole, while winning the fight against inflation. This is what we call a "soft landing". And I would like to refer you to the Annual Letter from the Governor of the Bank of France to the President of the Republic, which was published yesterday, for a more in-depth presentation of the causes and symptoms of inflation and how this economic and social disease can and will be defeated. b- Our financial system is an asset to ensure this "soft landing" The second structuring point for the financing of companies that I would like to emphasize concerning the evolution of the macro-economic and macro-financial context is the resilience of our financial system. By reorienting its monetary policy, the Governing Council, in an international environment that is nevertheless marked by turbulence on the financial front, has sent a strong signal of confidence in its ability to support and promote the achievement of the "soft landing that we anticipate. The two recent crises at SVB and Credit Switzerland have shaken investor confidence and led to increased volatility on the financial markets. But our financial system has absorbed this phase of volatility that has come from outside the euro area. We are confident in the resilience of the European banking system, and in particular of French banks. Their high level of solvency and liquidity has not been affected by this turbulence. In addition, all European banks are subject to the strong Basel 3 requirements and the vast majority of them are also subject to a single supervision within the Banking Union  which is a big difference from the US banking sector. In addition, unlike SVB, French and European banks benefit from a diversified and profitable business model, whether on the deposit or loan side, and from the management of their risks, and in particular interest rate risk, which is the subject of sustained and permanent attention by their supervisor. Finally, I would like to point out that the objectives of price stability and financial stability are not incompatible and that in the euro area we use separate instruments to achieve them. For the vast majority of European banks, higher interest rates are beneficial. If, however, we were to intervene on financial stability, it would be mainly through temporary liquidity support instruments, which would not conflict with the interest rate hikes needed to ensure price stability. 2. I now come to the consequences of this environment for the financing of companies with three observations: has. Access to finance for companies has been well ensured [slide 5]. On a quantitative level, bank credit to companies remained very dynamic in France for all sizes of companies and reached more than 1,300 GEUR at the end of February 2023, i.e. a growth of 5.5% on average over the period January 2022 - February 2023, supported by demand that remained on the rise. In terms of bond issuance, which I think you will discuss in more detail during the conference, the stock has stabilised at around 700 GEUR since December 2021 with a first downward trend recently, correlated with the tightening of monetary policy. As a reminder, the size of companies (in the LME sense) influences the structure of their liabilities. Thus, about 70% of the debt of large companies is made up of bond and similar debts, while 85% of the debt of SMEs comes from bank loans (proportions stable over 10 years). To complete this panorama of companies' liabilities, the weight of equity continued to represent almost half of their resources2. I also note that part of these resources have been added to a cash flow that remained significant in 2022, even if it has declined overall: after the PGE effect, which is being repaid well, NFCs had a significant amount of outstanding cash at the beginning of 2023, of nearly 900 GEUR, up 30% compared to the end of 2019, before the COVID crisis. b. A financing cost that remained favourable In terms of prices, or the cost of financing for companies, the reorientation of monetary policy has obviously had a significant impact on average conditions. The magnitude of the increase differed, however, between bank credit and market financing, the latter increasing on average faster to reach 4.3% in February 2023 compared to 3.7% for bank credit, with of course a differentiation according to the quality of the signature. In addition, despite an increase in nominal rates, the real cost of credit (deflated by medium- to long-term inflation expectations) remained favourable for companies. In addition, in France at the end of 2022, around 25% of outstanding corporate debt is at a variable rate or a fixed rate with a maturity of less than 1 year. As a result, the financial costs of companies, from an aggregate point of view, are expected to increase moderately in 2023 and French companies are thus financing themselves at rates that are the lowest in Europe. c- The importance of the Capital Markets Union for the development of a competitive and diversified financial system The difference in cost between bank credit and market financing has led to a re-intermediation of financing for companies with access to both sources of financing in the recent period. However, for the time being, this appears to be largely cyclical and limited in scope. It did not call into question the rebalancing of financing between banks and markets that took place between 2012 and 2016 [slide 6]: banks represent just under 40% of the total assets of the European financial sector, whereas NBFI players continue to represent 55% of the total assets of the European financial sector. In a context where different liabilities finance different needs for different companies, this rebalancing is an asset that must be maintained because it is likely to promote adapted, diversified and resilient financing to the shocks of our economy, even more so in the current context of the dual digital and climate transition. This is why we strongly support the reform programme of the Capital Markets Union at the Banque de France. The action plan thus provides for a simplification of access to listing for companies, especially the smallest. The work of European legislators on adapting the rules on "SME growth markets" is also encouraging. The revision of the ELTIF3 Funds Regulation may also help to facilitate equity financing for companies, especially for smaller companies. Even if progress is still needed - venture capital is absent from the 2020 action plan - the CMU is thus starting to produce visible results, such as the growth of SME IPOs in 20224. We will see if they are a harbinger of the "capital economy" that we are calling for at the Banque de France. In conclusion, despite an economic and financial context that has changed significantly, and which is marked by uncertainty and turbulence, the balance sheet and the financing outlook for companies appear favourable. With a view to a "soft landing" of the euro area economies, which is our central scenario, the maintenance of good financing conditions for French companies for all their needs should be able to benefit from the continued evolution of our financial system, in the direction of better integration and complementarity between bank and non-bank financing. in the context of the realization of the Capital Markets Union. Our financial centre is now unique in the network of European financial centres in terms of the range of its activities. This is an asset that we must maintain and develop to help our companies and more broadly our economic players to successfully meet the challenges they face, particularly in the context of the ecological and digital transitions underway. Title: After the crypto winter, the spring of crypto-asset regulation and supervision
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) After the crypto winter, the spring of crypto-asset regulation and supervision Published on May 26, 2023 World Bank Global Payments Week 2023: The Future of Payments May 18, 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Dear colleagues from the World Bank, ladies and gentlemen, According to some commentators, in a context of cascading bankruptcies (Terra/Luna, Celsius, Three Arrows, Genesis, BlockFi, FTX), the crypto-asset ecosystem may have entered what is known as a " crypto winter". I don't know if this winter will last, but I think it should be considered a "spring" by regulators and supervisors, whose initiatives should be abundant. Recently, many countries have accelerated regulatory work within their jurisdiction. However, we also found differences in the combination of three regulatory approaches: prohibiting crypto-asset activities; containing and isolating them from traditional finance and the real economy, which implies prohibiting certain specific aspects and practices (e.g. advertising); regulate the market for crypto-assets, either by assimilating them to traditional financial assets and applying the corresponding regulatory regimes that exist, or by adopting dedicated regulations (e.g. on stablecoins). With the exception of China, the world's major economies and currency areas have developed, or are in the process of adopting, a combination of the latter two approaches, based on the principle of "same activities, same risks, same rules". With an outright ban on crypto-asset activities not an option for most countries, for a number of reasons, including the belief in France that this would likely lead to regulatory arbitrage between jurisdictions, both domestically and internationally, the focus has largely been on the "what?" (what activities and risks) and the "how?" (by what means) regulate. In my short keynote speech today, and as the organizers of this Global Payments Week conference have kindly suggested, I would like, speaking from the perspective of a central bank in charge of ensuring financial stability, to share with you my thoughts on the types of risks associated with crypto-activities that particularly need to be taken into account for regulation and supervision. and the importance of a convergent and coordinated regulatory approach to crypto-assets at the international level. I. What risks should be taken into account for the Regulation and supervision of the crypto-asset ecosystem 1) Traditional and new risks associated with the development of the crypto-asset ecosystem The November 2022 bankruptcy of FTX, one of the largest crypto-asset exchanges, and the repercussions on its users and other market participants, dramatically showed the instability of the crypto-asset ecosystem. Within the regulatory and supervisory community, the root cause of this instability is well identified. At present, crypto-asset infrastructure and activities generate risks comparable to those of traditional financial services, which are inherent in the provision of financial services, including credit, liquidity and market risks. However, they do not have the same regulatory safeguards to limit these risks and ensure that they are properly identified, tracked and managed. In addition, crypto-asset infrastructures and activities, in addition to expanding outside the regulatory perimeter, have expanded to include products, services and practices that present certain Qnorifir'itoQ D'un nnint rlo \/i io du ricmio roc rarartorictini ipq cnorifim ioc Wl I I VI LV\J IZ Mil JVII II V V4\r V4 IIVVW; KJVVJ VMI MVIV I l\J II V M MM VJ JJ V VJ I I I V V V VJ could either amplify traditional vulnerabilities or create new ones, and should fall within the scope of regulation and supervision. Let me illustrate this point with two examples: The first is financial integrity risk. This risk should be paid attention to for two reasons: firstly, because, as our supervisory experience at the ACPR shows, AML/CFT controls by service providers are difficult to understand and control, and are sometimes not implemented in the crypto-asset ecosystem, and secondly, because investors have the possibility to use and hold crypto-assets under a pseudonym. The second concerns cyber risk. Cyber risk is currently the first operational risk for financial players, and it has the potential to compromise the stability of the financial system as a whole. The exposure of the crypto-asset ecosystem to this risk could be exacerbated by its technical specificities, including the use of blockchains, and the introduction of new points of vulnerability such as bridges between blockchains or the so-called "oracles" that power blockchains in data. In my opinion, the success of several cyberattacks targeting crypto actors is a warning signal that should attract the attention of regulators and supervisors. 2) The specific case of "stablecoins" In addition, within the crypto-asset market, stablecoins pose very specific risks. In particular, a false sense of security, largely abusive, induced by their name, as it turned out that they were not so stable, as illustrated by the collapse of Terra USD. At the heart of their instability is the lack of transparency on the nature and appropriateness of their reserves or on the limits of their stabilisation mechanism, which exposes their holders to limitations and risks with regard to their redemption rights. The lack of any legal recourse is also a concern, as many countries, with the exception of the EU in a few months, have yet to adopt a legal framework, dedicated or not, to regulate stablecoin issuance activity . It is a European regulatory orientation and The importance of a regulatory response convergent and coordinated 1) European regulatory guidance In this context, several countries, such as the United Kingdom, Singapore and Japan, have accelerated their regulatory work within their jurisdictions. But I think it's fair to say that the European Union is leading the way, with the adoption of the Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation by the European Parliament last month. The MiCA regulation is an important regulatory and supervisory milestone for the crypto-asset ecosystem, as it will provide a strict regulatory framework for issuers and service providers of crypto-assets and stablecoins, while addressing a number of major risks. However, while MiCA is an important step in the regulations, it should be supplemented in the coming years with additional requirements. This is because MiCA partially covers service providers for crypto-assets that combine multiple functions and activities in different jurisdictions, the so-called crypto conglomerates. To improve this coverage, it is essential to limit and control the concentration of activities in these conglomerates through strict governance requirements and to improve investor protection by addressing conflicts of interest and strengthening buy-back rights and reserve protection. In addition, MiCA does not cover the DeFi ecosystem and does not address the challenges that its specifics present in terms of regulation. To do this, I think we should not try to replicate existing financial regulations at all costs, but draw inspiration from the regulations of other sectors to regulate, for example, "products" even when their "producers" or "emitters" are not clearly identified. In addition, we need to recognize the technical specifics and pay close attention to the three layers that schematically make up DeFi (infrastructure, applications, and access points). In order to contribute to the development of this extension of MiCA, we have recently published a working document defining possible regulatory avenues. This document, available on the ACPR website, is subject to public consultation and we encourage industry players to contribute to it. 2) The challenge of international coordination for an effective and comprehensive regulatory framework That said, these regulatory issues are global, which means that we need to ensure that national regimes are consistent with each other to avoid any risk of regulatory arbitrage. To this end, we need to accelerate international work under the aegis of the FSB. The highest priority should be given to finalising the FSB's recommendations on stablecoins and other crypto-assets, in cooperation with other international standard-setting bodies (CPMI, CBBS, FATF). The second priority should be to regulate the interconnection between the traditional financial system and the crypto-asset market in a secure manner. The swift and faithful implementation of the Basel Standards on the prudential treatment of banks' exposures to crypto-assets, published in December 2022, will be essential from this perspective. The development of crypto-asset-based services offered by banks must be part of a prudent framework that limits risks to financial stability. Therefore, the application of prudential standards should strictly take into account the evolution of the interconnections between crypto-assets and regulated entities, such as banks. Finally, two new questions will require a global regulatory response. DeFi is the first: its use of public blockchains and global reach make it difficult to assign responsibilities and impose strong regulatory requirements as in MiCA. The FSB is working on it, however: it has already published a report on DeFi vulnerabilities and work is underway. Second, we need to address the challenges posed by crypto conglomerates globally. The FSB has also begun work on this type of crypto-acms service provider and monitor the risks associated with the concentration of their activities. To conclude, let me emphasize that I don't know exactly what the future of the crypto-asset ecosystem will be or what form of financial landscape will ultimately result from it. Market forces will decide. But what is clear to me is that, in order for the crypto-asset ecosystem to overcome the crisis of confidence that is currently affecting it and to develop on a sustainable basis, it is necessary to implement a regulatory and prudential framework that promotes trust. Central banks have an important role to play in contributing to the development of this framework and in facilitating the establishment of a convergent and coordinated framework, which is urgently needed, at the international level. Thank you for your attention. Updated on November 21, 2023

Title: Inflation, monetary policy and financial stability: balance sheet and outlook for France and the euro area
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors ") Inflation, monetary policy and Financial stability: balance sheet and outlook for France and the euro area Published on May 30, 2023 Conference CCI Le Havre May 26, 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Ladies and gentlemen, I am delighted to be here with you today to talk to you about the evolution of the macroeconomic and financial situation in the euro area and in France and the conduct of the policies that we are pursuing at the Banque de France and in the Eurosystem to ensure our monetary and financial stability missions. The economic and financial impact of the war in Ukraine has profoundly changed the prospects for emerging from the Covid crisis as it was a year ago, and subjected our economic and financial system to new major supply and demand shocks, which have resulted in a sharp acceleration in inflation. After presenting the macroeconomic situation and outlook as we are analysing them today at the Banque de France, I will tell you what conclusions we draw from them in terms of monetary policy. Finally, I will present to you the consequences of the change in the economic and monetary environment on financial stability.  Macroeconomic situation and outlook In terms of the macroeconomic situation, the euro area economy has been affected by a series of unprecedented shocks over the past few years. Years. [slide 2], The deterioration in the economic outlook since the beginning of 2022 is due in particular to the war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China, which have fuelled a "slow-flation" shock. This shock threatened to turn into a "stagflationary" shock. This threat has not materialized so far. Instead, the most recent data and surveys point to a significant slowdown in economic growth in the euro area, followed by a recovery. Several factors have contributed to this slowdown. Elements of explanation include, in particular and first and foremost, the negative shock to the terms of trade resulting from very high energy prices, which affects the real income of households and firms. For France, this shock to the terms of trade could be the second largest since the first oil shock in 1974 (around 1.4% of GDP). The economic cost of this shock is expected to fall by 2/3 in 2023 and remain limited in 2024 and 2025. Supply bottlenecks in terms of supply and recruitment operations also had a negative impact on activity. Even if they are abating, in particular the difficulties supply chains, they continue to constrain economic activity. The geopolitical environment is the third major factor in the slowdown at work, in particular with the unjustifiable war waged by Russia in Ukraine. It weighs on the confidence of business leaders and consumers. [slide 3]. As a result, according to the ECB's March macroeconomic projections, average annual GDP growth in the euro area is expected to slow to 1.0% in 2023 (from 3.6% in 2022), before rising to 1.6% in 2024 and 2025. Regarding inflation, it is expected to slow down only gradually and return to 2% at the end of 2024 and in 2025. The ECB's inflation forecast for the euro area is 5.3% in 2023, 2.9% in 2024 and 2.1% in 2025. [slide 4] For the French economy, the outlook is broadly similar. Economic activity is expected to grow at a limited pace in 2023, before recovering in 2024 and 2025. GDP is expected to grow by 0.6% in 2023, then by 1.2% in 2024 and 1.7% in 2025. So we should effectively escape recession in France as in the whole of the euro zone. These forecasts are based on the outlook for household consumption, which is expected to grow slightly in 2023 (0.4%) and then accelerate in 2024 (1.5%) and 2025 (1.6%) with the rebound in purchasing power. These forecasts are based on the observation that consumer price increases are already partly transmitted to nominal wages, which in turn feed price increases according to a nriy-QAlAirpq h a hiti ipI I p Fn mitrp.t the imnpp.t of the shock qiir Ipq tprmpc dp Trade, and in particular that of the energy bill, on real incomes is largely cushioned by the numerous budgetary measures to support purchasing power put in place1. At the Banque de France, we estimate that this levy linked to the energy bill will be around 60 billion or 2.5% of GDP for the year 2022. As far as companies are concerned, their investment plans are expected to be moderately affected over the forecast horizon. The increase in energy costs, the acceleration of nominal wages and the weakness of productivity gains, due in particular to the rise in work-study programmes and labour retention behaviour to prepare for the subsequent rebound in activity, should weigh on margins and therefore their profitability. However, the margin rate of non-financial corporations, which was exceptionally supported in 2020 and 2021 by the various measures put in place to deal with the Covid crisis, is expected to be close to its pre-crisis level (around 31.5%) over the period 2023-2024. Then, the margin rate would rise slightly to nearly 32% in 2025. At the same time, the upward trend in the investment rate is expected to come to a halt over the forecast horizon, as a result of the slowdown in activity, wait-and-see behaviour linked to macroeconomic uncertainty and the normalisation of financial conditions. Over the entire forecast horizon, the investment rate of non-financial corporations is expected to stabilise at around 25.5% of their value added. A final word to close this presentation of the situation and outlook for inflation, [slide 5] Since its resurgence in 2021, inflation has continued to rise in 2022 at a pace not seen since the 1980s. In 2023, against a backdrop of lower energy prices, inflation in the euro area started to decline to 7.0% at the end of April. In France, according to the results of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, inflation stood at 6.9%, thanks in particular to the price shield, but it remains well above the Eurosystem's inflation target. We at the Banque de France, like our colleagues in the other central banks of the Eurosystem, believe that the sharp acceleration in inflation is fundamentally due not to excess liquidity, but to the bottlenecks resulting from the faster-than-expected rebound in activity at the end of the pandemic and the sharp rise in energy and food prices. largely exacerbated by the war in Ukraine. In 2022, the surge in energy prices on international markets was the main inflationary shock for the French economy. Admittedly, this shock had a limited impact on retail energy prices in 2022, in particular because of the price shield, but it was also transmitted indirectly and with a delay of a few months to the other components of inflation, via the repercussions of the increase in producers' costs. Thus, inflation in France and the euro area has spread very widely and is now "internal" and "generalized" in nature, with an increase in all the other components of inflation: according to the April results, core inflation (which excludes energy and food) now stands at 5.6% in the euro area and 4.7% in France, and the rise in prices is spreading to goods and services - which account for the other half of total inflation. It is this more "internal" inflation for which central banks are responsible, and which they must not allow to persist. According to our March forecast, inflation is expected to peak in the first half of the year, before easing to 2% in late 2024 and 2025. This decline in inflation over the forecast horizon would result from the combined effect of several factors: the stabilisation of commodity prices in 2023, leading to the dissipation of the base effects associated with their previous rise, the effects of the change in monetary policy stance decided by the ECB's Governing Council to bring inflation down to 2%, which I'm going on now focus my remarks, and, correlatively, the maintenance of the anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations in the vicinity of the ECB's inflation target.  Implications for monetary policy So what are the implications of the change in macroeconomic situation and outlook that I have just described for monetary policy in the euro area? [slide 6] From a monetary policy perspective, this shift has had the effect of changing the nature of the main risk it needs to reduce: the risk to price stability we face is no longer one of inflation that is "too low for too long" but that of inflation that is "too high for too long". This fundamental change called for a change in monetary policy stance. This is why, as a first step, the Governing Council decided to dismantle the measures adopted to combat the risk of deflation. Thus, with regard to the ECB's key interest rates, the ECB's Governing Council decided to increase them at an accelerated pace, by a total of 250 basis points in 6 months between July and December 2022 to bring them back to the neutral rate, which refers to the theoretical equilibrium level at which there is neither a new monetary acceleration nor a slowdown in inflation. At the Banque de France, we estimate that the neutral rate is close to 2% in nominal terms in the euro area. It is clear that with the interest rate increases decided in January, March and May, the ECB's Governing Council has gone further and pushed monetary policy into "restrictive" territory in the technical sense of the term. The important questions now concern the extent and duration of this tightening of monetary policy. In the monetary policy statement of 4 May, Christine Lagarde reiterated that future monetary policy decisions will have to ensure that key rates are reduced to levels that are sufficiently restrictive to allow inflation to return quickly to our medium-term objective of 2% and that they will be kept at these levels for as long as necessary. In this context, the Governing Council will continue to follow a data-dependent approach to determining the appropriate level and duration of the maintenance of interest rates rlpnc ne tnrritnirn a rpqtrirtif  nn qp fnnrlpnt qi ir trniq 4\/li iptinnq   that of the inflation outlook in the light of economic and financial data;  that of the dynamics of core inflation;  and that of the transmission of monetary policy. Headline inflation has declined in recent months, but underlying price pressures remain high. At the same time, past interest rate hikes are gradually but fully being transmitted to financing and monetary conditions within euro area countries. However, the timing and strength of transmission to the real economy remain uncertain. Regarding the "terminal" rate, I would simply like to stress here that market participants do not currently expect a further sharp tightening of the ECB's key rates, with expectations now slightly above 3.5% [slide 7]. especially as long as inflation remains high. So far, this is the case and there is no sign that a possible price-wage loop is at work. But vigilance must remain the order of the day, [slide 8] The Governing Council's forecast and commitment is that inflation is expected to slow to close to 2% in 2025 as its current drivers fade and monetary policy normalization spills over into the economy and pricing mechanisms.  Consequences of environmental change Economic and Monetary Policy on Financial Stability [Slide 9] I now come to the consequences for financial stability, starting with the observation that the European financial system has been resilient in the face of recent shocks: Covid-19, invasion of Ukraine, and more recently, the difficulties encountered by some American regional banks (Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank, First Republic), as well as a Swiss systemic bank (Credit Switzerland). Among the factors that help explain this resilience, the difficulties encountered by US banks have highlighted the role of the Basel prudential framework, which was strengthened after the Great Financial Crisis of 2007-2008. Within the European Union, nearly 4700 banking institutions are subject to the Basel framework (including about 1200 under the direct control of the ECB), compared to only thirteen in the United States, following the implementation in 2019 of lighter rules (the " tailoring approach ") for the benefit of so-called regional banks whose balance sheet total was less than 250 billion. For example, SVB, whose exposure and lack of liquidity and interest rate risk management in its business model were fatal, did not apply the Basel liquidity ratios (LCR and NSFR), and the Fed's post-mortem report published on 28 April 2012 notes that SVB had not complied with the LCR ratio for several months. Ld ueuui imui e ue uvd pidiue diiibi uduuiu ei dvdin iuui puui une mibe eu full implementation of the Basel III requirements, and reinforces our commitment to the ACPR and the Banque de France to the transposition of the latest contributions of the Basel III Agreement, by the end of June 2023, I hope. At the international level, we will campaign to clarify that any simpler prudential regime that would be defined for a subset of banks, in the name of proportionality, should systematically comply with a requirement of overall consistency with Basel standards. SVB's bankruptcy has also highlighted the importance of demanding, intrusive and responsive supervision by supervisory authorities. The Fed, in its post-mortem report already cited, uncompromisingly acknowledges its own shortcomings in the field of supervision, both in terms of identifying risks and taking action to remedy these risks. This importance of supervision is also a lesson that can be learned from UBS's takeover of Credit Switzerland, whose fall cannot be explained by the non-application of Basel rules: while good regulation is necessary, it is never enough. The risks generated by the weaknesses identified over several years in Credit Switzerland's governance should have led to higher supervisory requirements. I sometimes hear doubts about the modalities of the supervision of supervisors, which, for some, should be considered as a legal dialogue, cautious in its form and slow in its effects. No, supervision can and should be intrusive - including on-site - rapid in its response, carried out by highly qualified practitioners. This is not wishful thinking: it has been our experience for decades with the ACPR, and now for almost ten years, with the Single European Supervisory Mechanism. These observations on the robustness of the current banking regulatory framework and the importance of its deployment as a contribution to the resilience of banks do not mean, however, that it cannot still be improved, of course, [slide 10] In this respect, in terms of liquidity risk monitoring, for example, recent events call for reflection on regulatory assumptions regarding deposit flight - in the age of digitalisation, has easier access to information and bank accounts fundamentally changed banks' liquidity risk, so that regulatory ratios should be radically tightened? However, this reflection should be based on the principle that these standardised Basel ratios, LCR and NSFR, are not supposed to prevent the occurrence of bank runs on their own; they are not intended to protect against all dimensions of liquidity and funding risk, including situations where liquidity stress is more severe and materialises more quickly than expected. Our feeling at the ACPR is that the tools already provided by Basel as part of the supervisory process, Pillar 2, already allow the supervisor to have a detailed view of each bank's risks, in particular with regard to liquidity; Basel thus provides for monitoring the level of concentration of liabilities, by products and by counterparty - which would have been particularly useful in the case of SVB, one of the problems of which came from the excessive level of concentration of liabilities. One avenue for reflection could therefore be the strengthening and systematization of the use of these Pillar 2 tools. In the cases of SVB and Credit Switzerland, we are also thinking about ways to Improvements to the crisis management framework to make it more operational and reliable in the face of the risk of faster bank runs. First of all, it is necessary to be able to provide a significant amount of liquidity in times of crisis, when a bank enters resolution. To this end, existing sources of financing in the European Union must be complemented by a credible liquidity mechanism that protects public funds and is predictable for all market participants. This mechanism is currently lacking. Second, the authorities must be better prepared to use all the resolution tools at their disposal. Since 2016 and the implementation of the directive that created the European Banking Crisis Resolution Regime (BRRD), the focus has been on preparing for the use of bail-in, a cornerstone of resolution ensuring the fair contribution of shareholders and creditors in the event of a crisis. Recent episodes of banking crises confirm that business transfer tools deserve to be mobilised in addition to bail-in. The crises of SVB and Credit Switzerland, in particular, were managed by divestments of activities, on the sidelines of the resolution for the latter. Finally, resolution remains the only harmonised crisis management tool we have, beyond the borders of Europe, but this international coordination is so far limited to global systemic banks (GSIBs). Recent events lead us to believe that more banks, including small and medium-sized ones, should prepare for this. At the international level, it is the Financial Stability Board (FSB) that identifies systemic banks by comparing the size, international activity, interconnections and substitutability of large banks. Better preparation for resolution must involve a review of the international standards developed by the FSB, in particular in order to assess whether it would be appropriate to impose the constitution of loss-absorbing capacity (through the issuance of debt) on more banks. This possible extension is also reflected in the European Commission's recent proposal for a revised framework for crisis management and deposit insurance (CMDI). In conclusion, I would like to draw three lessons from this rapid review of our economic and financial situation:  The good resilience of our economy and financial system to shocks so far;  The change in the regime of the interest rate environment that these shocks have caused by necessitating, in order to curb inflation that has become too high after having been too low for a long time, a normalisation of monetary policy;  The importance, in order to maintain financial stability, an objective to which the Banque de France is resolutely committed, to continue to learn from each episode of stress in the financial sector, and to draw lessons from it in terms of deployment and homogeneous application or improvement of standards. These lessons to be learned in terms of the regulation of the banking system should not, however, distract us from the need to also strengthen the regulatory framework for the non-bank financial sector, highlighted by the shocks generated in 2020 following the containment measures linked to the Covid 19 pandemic, and more recently, in 2022, the bankruptcy of the Archegos Family Office and the problems encountered by United Kingdom pension funds in 2022.
