Title: Growth and inflation: the main forecasts
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) Growth and inflation: the main forecasts Published on September 7, 2023 Breton Economic Forum September 7, 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Ladies and gentlemen, I am delighted to be here with you today to talk to you about the revolution in the macroeconomic situation in the euro area and in France and the conduct of the monetary policy that we are conducting at the Banque de France and in the Eurosystem, as part of our monetary stability mission. The economic and financial impact of the war in Ukraine has profoundly changed the outlook for emerging from the Covid crisis in which we were 18 months ago, and subjected our economic and financial system to new significant supply and demand shocks, which have resulted in a sharp acceleration in inflation. After presenting the macroeconomic situation and outlook as we are analysing them today at the Banque de France, based in particular on our forecasting exercises, I will tell you what consequences we draw from them for the conduct of monetary policy. 1 Macroeconomic situation and outlook Regarding the macroeconomic situation, I would like to start by recalling that the euro area economy has been affected by a series of unprecedented shocks in recent years, [slide 2] This has resulted in a deterioration in the economic outlook from the beginning Hnnnnn 9A99 l'illi icfrn Hrnnhiniin riii mrinfrn lr\r rn\/ic'ir\ro uu i a i 11 i c; c; z_?z_z_, luiiiuoiiu y i a pi iiy uc yui 11101 111 c; ICO icvioiuiio successive to the increase in inflation forecasts and the downward growth forecasts for 2023 for the euro area. These shocks, linked in particular to the war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China, have had the effect of slowing growth and accelerating inflation. Will this effect, known as "slow-flation", turn into a "stagflationary" effect, i.e. lead to a recession? This threat has not materialized so far. Instead, the most recent data and surveys point to a significant slowdown in economic growth in the euro area, followed by a recovery. Three main factors have contributed to this slowdown, the negative terms-of-trade shock resulting from very high energy prices, the economic cost of which for 2022 is estimated at 1.3% of GDP, supply constraints in terms of supply and recruitment and the geopolitical environment, with in particular the unjustifiable war waged by Russia in Ukraine weighing on business and consumer confidence, [slide 3]. As a result, according to the ECB's macroeconomic projections, the latest of which was in June, average annual GDP growth in the euro area is expected to slow to 0.9% in 2023 (from 3.5% in 2022), before rising to 1.5% in 2024 and 1.6% in 2025. As for inflation, it is expected to slow only gradually and return to 2% by the end of 2025. The ECB's inflation forecast for the euro area is 5.4% in 2023, 3.0% in 2024 and 2.2% in 2025. [slide 4] For the French economy, the outlook is broadly similar. Economic activity is expected to grow at a limited pace in 2023, before recovering in 2024 and 2025. GDP is expected to grow by 0.7% in 2023, then by 1.0% in 2024 and 1.5% in 2025. In other words, the central scenario of our forecast is that the French economy would succeed in gradually emerging from inflation without recession, even if the economic slowdown is marked. The forecasts of the Eurosystem and the Banque de France are based on the outlook for household consumption, which is expected to decline slightly in 2023 (-0.1%) as a result of the slowdown in purchasing power [in 2022 and 2023] and then accelerate in 2024 (1.5%) and 2025 (1.5%) with the rebound in purchasing power, while on the business side, investment plans are expected to be moderately affected. [slide 5] These forecasts are based on the observation that consumer price increases are already partly transmitted to nominal wages, which in turn feed price increases according to a usual price-wage relationship that has not gotten out of hand. In addition, the impact of the shock on the terms of trade, and in particular on the energy bill, on real incomes is largely cushioned by the Numerous budgetary measures to support purchasing power put in place1. As far as companies are concerned, the increase in energy costs, the acceleration of nominal wages and the weakness of productivity gains, due in particular to the rise in work-study programmes and labour retention behaviour to prepare for the subsequent rebound in activity, are expected to weigh on margins and therefore their profitability. The margin rate of non-financial corporations, PYCpntinnnpIlpmpnt sniitAmi pn 9O9O Pt 9091 nar Ias rtiffarpntpp mpiirpp put in place to deal with the Covid crisis, has not contributed globally to inflation in France, unlike in other countries. These margins are expected to decrease slightly over the period 2023-2024, before recovering in 2025 to 32%, a level slightly higher than its pre-crisis level (2018). [slide 6] Our monthly business survey published at the beginning of August broadly confirms the central scenario I have just described for activity, which increased in July in industry, services and construction, and the slowdown is less pronounced than expected in the previous month. Supply difficulties continue to decrease in construction and industry. Based on the survey results, complemented by a set of other indicators, we estimate that GDP growth in the third quarter of 2023 would be slightly positive compared to the previous quarter. As for inflation, it has started to decline after a peak in the euro area in October 2022. It stood at 5.3% at the end of August. [slide 7] In France, according to the results of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, inflation reached 5.7% in August. According to our latest economic survey, for the fourth consecutive month, manufacturers believe that prices are down sharply for raw materials, and are stabilising for finished products. Nevertheless, inflation remains well above the Eurosystem's inflation target. In 2022, the surge in energy prices on international markets was the main inflationary shock for the French economy. This shock had a limited impact on retail energy prices in 2022, due in particular to the price shield, but it was also transmitted indirectly and with a delay of a few months to the other components of inflation, via the repercussions of the increase in producer costs. [slide 8] Thus, inflation in France, and in the euro area, has spread very widely and is now "internal" and "generalized", with an increase in all the other components of inflation. This is shown in the graph on the left on the evolution of the components of inflation in France. It is this more "internal" inflation for which central banks are responsible, and which they must not allow to persist. In the absence of a new shock, our forecast is that inflation in France as in the euro area will gradually return to 2% in 2025. This decline in inflation over the forecast horizon would result from the combined effect of several factors: the stabilisation of commodity prices in 2023, leading to the dissipation of the base effects associated with their previous rise, the effects of the change in monetary policy stance decided by the ECB's Governing Council to bring inflation down to 2%, on which I will now focus my remarks, and, correlatively, the maintenance of the anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations in the vicinity of the inflation target lo DPC 2 Implications for monetary policy So what are the implications of the change in macroeconomic situation and outlook that I have just described for monetary policy in the euro area? [slide 9] From a monetary policy perspective, this shift has had the effect of changing the nature of the main risk it needs to reduce: the risk to price stability we face is no longer one of inflation that is "too low for too long" but that of inflation that is "too high for too long". This fundamental change called for a change in monetary policy stance. This is why, as a first step, the ECB's Governing Council decided to dismantle the measures adopted to combat the risk of deflation. Thus, with regard to the ECB's key interest rates, the ECB's Governing Council decided to increase them at an accelerated pace, by a total of 250 basis points in 6 months between July and December 2022 to bring them back to the neutral rate, which refers to the theoretical equilibrium level at which there is neither a new monetary acceleration nor a slowdown in inflation. At the Banque de France, we estimate that the neutral rate is close to 2% in nominal terms in the euro area. It is clear that with the interest rate increases decided between January and July 2023, the Governing Council has gone further and pushed monetary policy into "restrictive" territory in the technical sense of the term. The important questions now concern the extent and duration of this tightening of monetary policy. In the monetary policy statement of 27 July, Christine Lagarde reiterated that future monetary policy decisions will have to ensure that key rates are set at sufficiently restrictive levels for as long as necessary to allow a rapid return of inflation to our medium-term objective of 2%. In this context, the Governing Council said it will continue to follow a data-driven approach to determining the appropriate level and duration of holding rates in this "restrictive" territory based on three assessments:  that of the inflation outlook in the light of economic and financial data;  that of the dynamics of core inflation;  and that of the transmission of monetary policy. In this context, it can be observed that headline inflation has declined in recent months, but underlying price pressures remain high. According to the first results in August, core inflation, which excludes energy and food, stands at 5.3% for the euro zone as a whole and 4% in France. At the same time, past interest rate hikes are being transmitted gradually, but financing and monetary conditions within euro area countries2. However, the timing and strength of transmission to the real economy remain uncertain. We will therefore see what consequences the ECB Governing Council draws from these developments at its meeting scheduled for next week. [slide 10] In any case, in the context I have just described, an important role for monetary policy will be to ensure that inflation expectations remain anchored, especially as long as inflation remains high. So far, this is the case and there is no sign that a possible wage-price loop is at work. But vigilance must remain the order of the day. The Governing Council's forecast and commitment is that inflation is expected to slow to close to 2% in 2025 as its current drivers fade and monetary policy normalization spills over into the economy and pricing mechanisms. 1 The total amount of these measures for households could thus reach around 50 billion in 2023. o The results of the latest Bank Lending Survey illustrate this point. Title: How to keep SupTech future-proof
text: How to keep SupTech fulure-proof Stakeholder Published on September 20, 2023 Innovators Conference Supervision September 20, 2023 Initial remarks proposed by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. The digitalisation of finance, the emergence of new players and new technologies, as well as the emergence of associated risks, in particular cyber risks: all these trends are prompting the urgent development of an augmented approach to financial supervision. How are we meeting this challenge at the ACPR and the Banque de France? I. First of all, by adopting a proactive innovation approach focused on business needs, which resulted in the launch of a "SupTech" program in 2019. This aims to strengthen the ACPR's supervisory capacities by relying on new data processing and artificial intelligence technologies. A/ All projects identified, developed and deployed since 2019 are the result of a structured process based on a number of incentives and filters. I would like to mention two in particular, which play a decisive role. The strong impetus given by the highest level of the hierarchy, as well as its involvement in the selection and monitoring of the investigation, implementation and deployment phases of projects, is a powerful incentive. This impetus and involvement helps to overcome the inevitable  and understandable  resistance generated by the transformation of well-established business processes. In order to sustain this momentum, the SupTech programme has been included in the Banque de France's 2019-2024 strategic plan, and is high on the list of priority actions monitored by the Management Committee. Among the filters used, one of the most important is that projects must contribute to solving the day-to-day operational problems faced by ACPR staff in the performance of their duties. In other words, our approach is demand-driven, rather than supply-driven, to avoid the classic situation of problem-seeking solutions that end up sitting on the shelf. As we know that it is difficult to imagine an innovative solution without knowing what technology can and cannot do, we now have monitoring experts and IT departments work together in project-oriented teams that combine creativity and know-how. In addition to these incentives and filters, senior management has a role to play in promoting more effective and less costly approaches, paying particular attention to the results of each project. This means in particular favouring agile methods in the management of projects, which make it possible to correct problems as they arise, and therefore to gain in productivity. It also means following the project from start to finish, right up to the industrialisation phases. Finally, it means promoting "feedback" on the difficulties encountered during a project, in order to be able to progress collectively for subsequent projects. B/ This approach feeds into and is integrated into an overall reflection on the evolution of computer systems, putting the question of data and its exploitation at the heart. Indeed, structured or not, data is the key element of the ACPR's analyses and controls, and it is growing exponentially. The SupTech projects all aim to facilitate the management, access and visualization of this data, in order to enable better targeted analysis and controls , in order to support our risk-based supervision and improve its effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, the SupTech approach cannot afford to neglect the technical problems related to the management, evolution or decommissioning of existing systems. The integration of new tools into the existing environment cannot be improvised, and on the contrary must be thought of in coherence with the evolution of the information system as a whole. In addition, the decommissioning of old applications - which can be one of the objectives of the deployment of new tools - must also be integrated into the strategy of data valorization: very often, old applications contain a large heritage of data, the richness of which should not be neglected. II. To be effective, this approach must also be carried out in a spirit of anticipation and openness. A/ We must first anticipate the profound upheavals in our uses and our organizations that certain new technologies are likely to cause. Generative AI , for example, opens up exciting prospects, particularly in terms of synthesizing, extracting and classifying information, or generating text or computer code. At the same time, it raises a large number of concerns, in terms of reliability, data confidentiality or intellectual property. To anticipate the effects of these new technologies, we need to go through the learning curve as quickly as possible, in order to have the most complete view possible of their potential contributions, but also of their risks. The experimentation approach can in particular promote this accelerated learning. In May 2023, the Banque de France, through the innovation platform operated by its Lab, launched a call for contributions on the uses and impacts of generative AI on its activities. Aimed at the innovative ecosystem, it aims, on the one hand, to refine our understanding of this technology and, on the other hand, to accelerate its potential use, through the proposal of concrete use cases, or even operational solutions. Anticipation must also focus on the human resources needed to adapt to new modes of supervision. In particular, it is a question of diversifying the experience and profiles of supervisors, by promoting the recruitment and development of specialized skills, particularly in data science and artificial intelligence. B/ We must also be open because, in a field where solutions have yet to be invented, cooperation and co-construction can bring many common benefits. As we have seen, cooperation with the innovative ecosystem can be very fertile; similarly, it is in our interest to maintain sustained links with academic circles. But I would like to emphasise here in particular the interest of establishing enhanced cooperation with other authorities (memoranda of understanding, multi-authority supervisory committees, etc.), in order to develop shared analyses on themes of common interest (the benefits and risks of a new technology, for example) or with a view to jointly developing tools for the supervision of the financial sector. The Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM), a forum for cooperation par excellence between national and European supervisory authorities, is the ideal field for organising such cooperative mechanisms. In this respect, the ACPR and the Banque de France are fully committed to providing all European partners with a "SupTech Centre" that will offer, for example, an advanced analysis interface for supervisors, likely to integrate analysis modules developed by other authorities or SSM players.

Title: Staying the course in bad weather: confidence in support of innovation
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) Staying the Course in Bad Weather: Confidence in Support of Innovation Published on October 19, 2023 FINTECH DEVOLUTION 2023 Paris, 19 October 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. Ladies and gentlemen I would like to start by thanking the France Fintech association, and its president Alain Clot, for their invitation to participate once again in this major event for the French fintech ecosystem. The current context is clearly less conducive to fundraising for young companies. This turbulence in the fintech ecosystem is a reflection of a recently deteriorating economic and financial environment. Indeed, the euro area economy has been affected by a series of unprecedented shocks. These shocks, linked in particular to Russia's unjustifiable war in Ukraine and the lockdown in China, have slowed growth and accelerated inflation. However, in France, this configuration, known as "slow-flation", has not yet turned into "stagflation", i.e. a recession. According to our most recent forecasts, economic activity in our country is expected to grow at a limited pace in 2023, before recovering in 2024 and 2025. In other words, the central scenario of our forecast is that the French economy would manage to gradually emerge from inflation without recession, even if the economic slowdown would be marked. If times are gloomy, there is therefore reason to remain confident about the medium-term outlook. And I would like to tell you this morning that trust is built on a daily basis, by consolidating the foundations to strengthen the resilience of the ecosystem, on the one hand, and by anticipating the future to develop an efficient and innovative financial sector on sound foundations, on the other hand. 1/ Consolidating the foundations means preparing as well as possible for the many operational risks that lie in wait for fintechs, and which will be subject to a more extensive regulatory framework in the near future. 1/ Cyber risk is a good example of these risks, as well as the need to prepare. The European financial sector is increasingly targeted by cyber attacks, so cyber risk has become the number one operational risk for financial companies. In this context, the European DORA regulation (published in December 2022) aims to strengthen the resilience of the sector; It will apply to all financial entities from January 2025. In addition to the current requirements for good governance of the information system, institutions will be required to conduct regular operational resilience testing, and report major incidents. Despite many new elements, DORA reaffirms a principle that is as old as it is fundamental: financial institutions remain responsible for their risks. They must therefore retain control of the entire subcontracting chain, audit their IT service providers, and have exit strategies. The adaptation period to DORA is short, so we need to collectively prepare. For the institutions, this means reviewing all existing service contracts, renegotiating some of them, and launching as quickly as possible the developments necessary for the production of the new reports, in order to finalize compliance with DORA before January 2025. The ACPR, for its part, will continue to maintain its dialogue with the financial centre in order to identify any operational difficulties that may arise. In this respect, I encourage you to participate in the new public consultation on the DORA implementing texts, which should open before the end of the year. 2/ With regard to digital assets, it is obviously the gradual entry into force of the provisions of the MiCA regulation (between December 2023 and December 2024) that guides the necessary consolidation work. In this regard, my main message is that we must anticipate the entry into force of MiCA. For players planning to issue stablecoins, anticipating means contacting the ACPR and I invite them to do so now. You can apply for the status of electronic money institution (EME), which will allow you to start issuing digital assets as soon as MiCA comes into force, in a secure environment. This is all the more important as there will be no transition phase here: as of 30 June 2024, the provisions of the regulation relating to token issues will apply immediately. Secondly, to the current crypto-asset service providers (DASPs) and to the players who plan to provide such services in the future, I say that it is time to seek approval. This allows most of the provisions of MiCA to be met in advance. Above all, in a context that has recently been troubled by the increase in bankruptcies, it is the best way to regain the confidence of consumers and investors. 3/ Still in the field of crypto-assets, it is also necessary to consolidate the anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) mechanisms, in particular In the current European Remittance Regulation, or TFR, which will take effect at the same time as MiCA. The traceability of funds and transactions made possible by blockchain technology is weakened by the ease of creating new addresses - sometimes without identity verification or control of the origin of the funds deposited - as well as by various concealment techniques. In this respect, innovation could play a favourable role. Digital identity solutions, based on advances in cryptographic proof techniques, could facilitate the direct implementation of Know Your Customer (KYC) obligations on the blockchain. They could thus make it possible to reconcile the identification of persons involved in blockchain transactions, for the purposes of AML/CFT, with privacy protection requirements. 11/ As we can see with this last example: efforts to strengthen operational resilience, while necessary, do not prevent us from designing the business models and technological solutions of tomorrow. A/ In this area, as in others, the Banque de France and the ACPR stand by the fintech ecosystem, first and foremost by contributing to the development of a regulatory framework that promotes innovation while protecting consumers. A good example is "open finance". The so-called FIDA (Financial Data Access) proposal, published on 28 June by the European Commission, aims to promote access to financial data. This is obviously an opportunity for fintechs to deploy their creativity and agility, in order to offer consumers innovative financial services in a secure environment. A first element of satisfaction, for both the Banque de France and the ACPR, is that lessons have been learned from the mixed results of the implementation of the open banking policy provided for in PSD2. Thus, the core of the proposal lies in the data sharing schemes, which data holders and users will have to develop together, and to which they will then be obliged to adhere. Title: Crisis prevention and management in the era of digitalization of financial services
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Deputy Governors J) Crisis prevention and management at the heart of the digitalisation of financial services Published on November 9, 2023 University of Rennes - November 9, 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, Senior Deputy Governor Introduction (slide 2) The international financial system has been confronted with significant turbulence over the past 18 months, which has affected both traditional finance banking players in the wake of the SVB bankruptcy, and new digitized finance players in the wake of the FTX bankruptcy. This turbulence is the consequence of the materialization of traditional risks to which financial actors are usually exposed, but whose impact has been amplified and spread within the financial system fueled by the increasing digitalization of banking and financial activities. This amplification is clearly apparent when we look at the case of SVB and its consequences: the fall of this bank was first of all the result of poor governance and the deficient management of traditional liquidity and interest rate risks, but it was accelerated due to the digitalization of finance, which facilitated massive withdrawals in record time of its customers' sight deposits mainly made up of tech players. They have withdrawn them all the more massively and in record time - one could say "in one click", because they constitute a financially and digitally educated clientele. This role of diffusion through the financial system, via the emerging bridges between traditional finance and an alternative "finance" that is based in particular on new tokenized assets (crypto-assets) issued on a blockchain, also appears when examining the chain consequences of the collapse of the FTX platform, which brought down the banks Signature and Silvergate. In the opposite direction, the failure of SVB - again, threatened the reserves of Circle (the issuer of the USD Coin) that were placed there. The effects of these turbulences have not ultimately had a systemic impact, they have not had a strong and lasting impact on the financial system as a whole or the real economy, and this is to be welcomed. Their occurrence nevertheless illustrates the emergence of new vulnerabilities in the financial system, fuelled by its ongoing digital transition, which raises questions about how to prevent their materialisation and limit their consequences. From the point of view of institutions such as the Banque de France and the ACPR, which are responsible for ensuring the stability of our financial system, these new vulnerabilities raise the question of the adequacy of the prevention tools (regulation and supervision of financial intermediaries), and crisis management tools (provision of liquidity and resolution tools), which we use to ensure financial stability. both in traditional finance and in decentralized, or disintermediated, finance. From my point of view, the first lessons that can be drawn from the turbulence of recent months encourage us to provide a cautious and differentiated response to this question of the adequacy of crisis prevention and management frameworks, in the era of the digitalisation of financial services, depending on whether we consider traditional finance or so-called decentralised finance. For traditional finance, the priority seems to me to be to better implement this framework and adapt it, whereas for decentralized finance, it would be appropriate to develop and apply it in a homogeneous way. I. A framework for the prevention and crisis management of traditional finance to be better implemented and adapted (sude 3) K- Priority to the implementation of the regulatory framework and the strengthening of the supervision Regarding the crisis prevention framework for traditional finance, based on regulation and individual supervision of financial intermediaries, known as micro-prudential, the priority should be better implementation, due to the following lessons that can be drawn in particular from the case of the "one-click" bank run of which SVB was a victim in the United States. Firstly, this framework, which is based on the rules laid down by the Basel Committee of Banking Supervisors (BCBS) for banks, has not been invalidated by the bankruptcy of SVB. On the contrary, the fall of SVB illustrates more the consequences of a lack of implementation than a lack of effectiveness of this framework, for at least 2 reasons: Lzuui i ici 11 ie uu le oeuii uciiciic i ciciui a ia oci loiumie au i ioiuc uc idUA defined in the Basel regime. Several lights would have turned red and alerted his supervisor if they had been put in place. However, these observations do not mean that it would not be appropriate to draw lessons from the role of new technologies and social networks in accelerating the liquidity stress that SVB has suffered. Avenues for reflection have been identified by the Basel Committee in this perspective, for example with regard to the leakage rate of certain deposits, such as large deposits not covered by guarantee mechanisms, (sude 4) In short, when it comes to the crisis prevention framework, we don't need another framework, we need more of it! Banks considered to be less significant cannot be exempted from this on the sole grounds of their size, given the multiple interconnections that make up the financial system. It should be noted that this is the path that the Fed has just embarked on, which in its recent proposal on the implementation of the so-called Basel 3 rules advocates a wider application of this prudential framework. Fortunately, in this area, the European situation is radically different and reassuring. The Basel rules are fully applied to all banks in Europe. I would add in passing that Europe is about to finalise the transposition into European law of the latest reinforcements of the Basel III agreements. As for supervision, the Eurozone benefits from a single supervisor, the European Central Bank, which has extensive supervisory powers, such as stress tests, or on-site inspections, which it knows how to mobilise in a reactive and intrusive manner. Because it is also a fundamental aspect that is important to remember: good regulation implemented globally is a necessary condition, but not sufficient to guarantee the stability of a banking system. It would not be able to give the best of itself without demanding, rigorous and responsive supervision, which, by the Fed's own admission, was lacking in the bankruptcy of SVB. The so-called "Pillar 2" framework and the tools provided for in this respect by the Basel Committee establish the principle and allow the implementation of such supervision: complementary to "Pillar 1" which defines harmonized and automatic requirements and "Pillar 3" which includes the rules of transparency and disclosure of financial information, "Pillar 2" allows supervision based on an analysis of all of a bank's risks. The supervisor thus has the means to impose additional requirements on a case-by-case basis. Could they be strengthened by introducing, for example, new alert thresholds, in particular in terms of liquidity risk management? I think so. Work is also under way in this direction within the Basel Committee. B- Priority to adaptation for the crisis management framework (slide 5) Prudential regulation, combined with rigorous supervision, can anticipate and prevent the majority of crises, but they cannot prevent them all. Hence the importance of crisis management tools, to limit their impacts. Among these tools, the recent crises have shown us the importance of exceptional mechanisms for providing liquidity to banks in difficulty, by central banks, in a context of a very strong acceleration in the materialization of liquidity stresses that promotes the development of digitized services, which make it possible to manage accounts and obtain banking services remotely, online, very fast or even immediate and continuous. In the midst of the crisis of their regional banks or Credit Switzerland, the American and Swiss authorities activated this type of mechanism. They have been decisive for the return to financial stability. Within the euro area, we also have these mechanisms of last resort, but we still lack a single mechanism, adopted by all the central banks of the Eurosystem, that would make it possible to deal very quickly with the liquidity needs of a failing bank subject to resolution. It is therefore necessary to adapt the European system, by supplementing it and making it operational quickly if a crisis were to occur. In my view, this is a priority that the development of the digitalisation of financial services can only help to strengthen. Another lesson that can be learned from recent crises is that the authorities need to be better prepared to use all the resolution tools at their disposal. Since 2016 and the implementation of the directive that created the European Banking Crisis Resolution Regime (BRRD), the focus has been on preparing for the use of bail-in. This is the cornerstone of the resolution guaranteeing the fair contribution of shareholders and creditors in the event of a crisis. However, recent episodes of banking crises confirm that transfer tools (sale of institutions, subsidiaries or assets) must be able to be mobilised quickly in addition to bail-in, including for large banks. In the case of Credit Switzerland, for example, the Swiss authorities ultimately considered that bail-in was not the best option in terms of financial stability - one of the reasons why they preferred to set aside the resolution procedure and impose a sale of Credit Switzerland to its competitor UBS. A final lesson concerns the scope of banking crisis management frameworks. International standards currently apply to the thirty or so so-called systemic banks at the global level (G-SIBs). In Europe, we have chosen to apply these rules more broadly, targeting around a hundred major banking groups. But this is not the case, for example, in the United States. However, the crises of the American "regional" banks, which are not classified as systemic, have nevertheless had repercussions throughout the world, and in particular in Switzerland, reinforcing depositors' mistrust of Credit Switzerland, which has already been destabilized for several months. We therefore have a collective interest in ensuring that banks, even if they do not fall into this category of systemicity, have sufficient capacity to absorb losses in resolution, which can then be used to recapitalise them through the bail-in mechanism. The American authorities want to move in this direction, and we approve of it. It is in this context that the EU Member States and the European parliamentarians are currently discussing a proposal to reform the European banking crisis management framework: the CMDI (crisis management and deposit insurance) package. From the point of view of the Bank of France and the ACPR, this reform should be an opportunity to extend the application of the European resolution procedure, which should be the reference method for managing crises udiiudiieb, iiuii beuieiiiein puui iet pius yidiiub yiuupes udiiudiieb iiidib also for small and medium-sized banks. Since its entry into force in 2015, we have too often seen this procedure circumvented in favour of national approaches that are less demanding in terms of controlling moral hazard, and often more costly for public funds. In summary, the tools for managing banking crises are already well established, in Europe and around the world. Recent crises have not called them into question, but have demonstrated the importance of adapting them by complementing them and extending their scope, while preserving the authorities' room for manoeuvre at the heart of the crisis. II. The evolution of finance under the effect of new technologies calls for regulation that must be extended and deployed in a more homogeneous way (slide 6) h- The transformation of the financial landscape calls for an extension of regulation I now come to the transformations that new technologies are bringing about in finance and the regulatory issues that they raise. New forms of finance and the technological innovations on which they are based occupy an important place in our reflections at the Banque de France and the ACPR, from the point of view of our financial stability mandate, because their very dynamic and creative development can have as a corollary an increase in risks and losses for their players and clients. In tokenized finance, for example, some of these risks have materialized very dramatically, with the collapse in the last 18 months of the third largest stablecoin system, Terra-Luna, the bankruptcy of FTX, one of the world's largest crypto-asset exchange platforms, and the undermining of other players in their ecosystem. including liquidity providers. Beyond these individual cases, and the particular case of "tokenized" finance, our attention is based on the observation that this emerging finance is likely to introduce instabilities at least two levels: by disrupting existing business models, by reconfiguring value chains, technological innovations can first quickly lead to a reconfiguration of the competitive landscape and this "creative destruction" can result in bankruptcies, harmful concentration movements or even strengthening the dependence of certain players on their technical service providers. In addition, and more prosaically, the technologies and innovative tools used by financial players can carry increased risks in themselves: cyber risks, for example, but also risks for consumer protection - whether in terms of access to financial services, if we think of online distribution, or in terms of non-discrimination, if we think of AI. However, these innovations are of course beneficial, benefits in terms of efficiency in the financial sector, benefits in terms of services provided to the customer. To capture these benefits without compromising financial stability, the Banque de France and the ACPR believe that it is important to build an appropriate regulatory framework, at the national level, but also at the European and international level. By creating an environment where competitors are put on an equal footing - without fear of competition from "rogue" actors - by clarifying the obligations that innovative players must follow, by limiting risks, the can be a tremendous vector of trust. To illustrate the form and the path that this adaptation of the regulations must take, allow me to take two examples: one very concrete, the other more forward-looking. In terms of financial data sharing, the European Commission recently published a proposal for a regulation called FIDA (Financial Data Access). This text, which is currently being negotiated, is a good example of the legislator's efforts to build a regulatory framework that allows fintechs to deploy their creativity to offer consumers innovative financial services in a secure environment. IFAD is learning from the mixed results of the Payment Services Directive (the starting point for Open Banking) while maintaining a very protective framework for consumers. The heart of the proposal thus lies in the data sharing schemes, which data holders and users will have to develop together, and to which they will then be obliged to adhere. The system introduces the principle of remuneration for the use of data - which should encourage the players to work together - while providing a framework for the pricing of this remuneration. At the same time, IFAD sets a protective framework for customers. This will allow consumers to choose whether or not to share their data, and will have a dashboard to more easily view and manage the rights granted. Similarly, in order to secure the sharing of data, the " open finance " players who will use this data will have to have authorizations. The second important example is decentralized finance, "DeFi" - which we prefer to describe at the Banque de France and the ACPR as "disintermediated" - and which is based on distributed ledger technology (DLT, or to put it simply, blockchain). Blockchain technology is a way to store and share information in a decentralized, secure, and transparent way, without the need for a central control body. In this area, the work of regulators is more forward-looking: the Banque de France is at the forefront of thinking on the subject, with the publication by the ACPR, in April, of a document exploring avenues for regulatory frameworks for DeFi. From the public consultation that followed, we drew a summary document, which we have just published, which specifies the regulatory paths that are taking shape on the three "levels" of DeFi: (1) ensuring the resilience of the blockchain infrastructure, even if it is public, through security standards (2) certifying smart contracts, even though it stems from many operational issues (3) regulate entry points to DeFi in order to protect users. For digital asset and DeFi innovation as with other innovations, our approach remains consistent; This innovation is welcome, but it cannot be achieved at the cost of less regulation, which would - as we see elsewhere - go against the interests of the players themselves. B- This transformation also calls for a review of banks' service offerings Centrales (slide 7) New distributed ledger technologies, in particular blockchains, allow the creation of new financial services, based in particular on tokenization. Tokenization is a process that consists of issuing a financial security on a blockchain. It is attracting growing interest from traditional investors and issuers as well as new players, such as BigTechs and Fintechs, as it holds the promise of improving the settlement and delivery processes of financial assets by making them faster, cheaper and more transparent. While tokenization currently represents only a marginal part of the capitalization of financial markets, its development could nevertheless lead to the emergence of counterparty, liquidity and liquidity fragmentation risks that could become systemic. This is why central banks must remain vigilant. We must anticipate such a development and secure it so that players can fully benefit from the potential of tokenization. How? By continuing to ensure at the very least that the most sensitive transactions from the point of view of financial stability, i.e. between financial intermediaries, are settled in central bank money, the safest and most liquid settlement asset available. However, while central bank money is currently made available to commercial banks in digital form in our centralized payment systems (in the Eurozone this is the TARGET2 system), it is currently not available on blockchain. In other words, central money cannot be used to buy and settle tokenized assets (shares, bonds, fund shares registered on the blockchain) directly on the blockchain. However, if we do not adapt central bank money to the tokenized world, players could turn to other less secure settlement assets, inducing both counterparty and liquidity risk and therefore ultimately a risk to financial stability. If this were the case, it would be a real regression in terms of financial stability. Indeed, these other settlement assets - first-generation crypto-assets such as Bitcoin, or second-generation crypto-assets, also known as stablecoins - do not have the three attributes of a currency (unit of account, instrument of exchange, store of value) and cannot be qualified as such. They also present specific risks, such as money laundering, liquidity, market and operational risks in particular, which can take on a systemic scope and raise questions of monetary sovereignty for so-called global stablecoins, such as the one in the launch phase of PayPal. Faced with these risks, and to ensure financial stability, establishing a clear and appropriate regulatory framework is essential: the European MiCA regulation governing the issuance and provision of financial services on cryptoassets and stablecoins, which came into force in June 2023, is a major step forward. However, regulation is only one floor of the edifice to be built: central banks must appropriate these new technologies and innovate to offer central bank money services adapted to a financial system in digital transition, both for exchanges between financial intermediaries, which have the greatest impact in terms of financial stability, and for everyday payments to citizens, both domestically and cross-border. II. Lvolution de la finance sous l'effet des nouvelles technologique appelle une rgulation qui doit tre tendue et dploye de faon plus homogne (slide 6) h- La transformation du paysage financier appelle  une extension de la rglementation J'en viens maintenant aux transformations que les nouvelles technologies induisent dans la finance et aux enjeux rglementaires que celles-ci soulvent. Les nouvelles formes de la finance et les innovations technologiques sur lesquelles elles s'appuient occupent une place importante dans nos rflexions  la Banque de France et  lACPR, du point de vue de notre mandat de stabilit financire, car leur dveloppement trs dynamique et cratif peut avoir pour corollaire une monte des risques et des pertes pour leurs acteurs et leurs clients. Pour linnovation lies aux actifs numriques et  la DeFi comme pour les autres innovations, notre approche demeure constante ; cette innovation est la bienvenue mais elle ne saurait se faire au prix d'une moindre rgulation qui irait - on le voit ailleurs - contre l'intrt des acteurs eux- mmes. B- Cette transformation appelle galement une revue des offres de services des banques centrales (slide 7) Les nouvelles technologies de registres distribus en particulier les blockchains permettent la cration de nouveaux services financiers, reposant notamment sur la tokenisation. La tokenisation est un processus qui consiste  mettre un titre financier sur une blockchain. Elle suscite un intrt croissant des investisseurs et metteurs traditionnels comme des nouveaux acteurs, tels que les BigTechs et les Fintechs car elle porte la promesse damliorer les processus de rglement et de livraison des actifs financiers en les rendant plus rapides, moins coteux et plus transparents. Toutefois la rglementation n'est qu'un tage de l'difice  btir : les banques centrales doivent s'approprier ces nouvelles technologies et innover pour offrir des services en monnaie de banque centrale adapts  un systme financier en transition numrique, tant pour les changes entre intermdiaires financiers dont la porte en matire de stabilit financire est la plus forte que pour paiements des citoyens au quotidien  la fois sur le plan domestique et transfrontire. C'est en particulier le cas pour les usages entre intermdiaires financiers pour lesquels nous conduisons depuis 2020 des exprimentations, qui visent  mettre  disposition la monnaie centrale directement sur blockchain. Nous avons ainsi ralis douze exprimentations avec des acteurs privs comme publics, et nous participons activement aux travaux exploratoires lancs par l'Eurosystme sur ce sujet. Conclusion Les turbulences que nous avons connues ces derniers mois montrent que la transition numrique en cours des services financiers qui a contribu  les alimenter, est  la fois une opportunit pour la sphre financire, mais galement un risque. Cette transition ne sera donc une aubaine durable que si et seulement si elle se dveloppe dans un cadre de prvention et de gestion des crises qui doit tre adapt, pour le bnfice de toutes et tous, tant pour la finance traditionnelle que pour la finance dite dcentralise, selon des modalits diffrencies. Les banques centrales et superviseurs ont un rle majeur  jouer dans cet effort d'adaptation que nous devons mener, et les nouveaux talents, et je pense  vous, seront les bienvenus pour contribuer  rpondre  ces attentes, chez les acteurs de la transformation numrique eux-mmes, comme chez les banques centrales et les superviseurs comme la Banque de France et lACPR. text: Digital Money and Payments Published on November 10, 2023 University of Southern Brittany - November 10, 2023 Speech by Denis Beau, Senior Deputy Governor [SHde 1] Thank you first of all for this invitation. It is a pleasure to be able to discuss with you money and payments, which are undergoing profound transformations in the digital age. Whether it is fiat money - which refers to banknotes and coins - or all other means of payment, which are called "cashless means of payment", supporting their transformations resulting from technological innovations and societal developments to ensure their availability, security and freedom of choice is an integral part of our mission as a central bank. and is at the heart of our concerns at the Banque de France. How are payment methods evolving with the times and what challenges does this evolution raise? [Slide 2 - Transition: Title I. Trends and Challenges] I. What are the trends that can be observed today within the ecosystem particularly dynamic that is the Retail payments? A- General trends in the evolution of the payments ecosystem [Slide 3: Decline in the use of cash]  Species have been experiencing a sharp decline in their use for several years. Admittedly, they are still the leading payment method, still representing 50% of point-of-sale transactions in France in 2022 and 59% in the euro zone.1 However, this figure has fallen sharply, down 7 percentage points over the last three years in France and 14 points in the euro area.  This decline is part of a long-standing trend: as a result of changes in consumption patterns and technological innovations in payment, there has been a continuous decline in the use of fiat money in transactions in favour of electronic means of payment.  The health crisis may also have contributed to this erosion; Individuals then preferred to use cashless means of payment, which require less handling or physical contact. The increase in the contactless payment limit from 30 to 50 in May 2020 has facilitated this, and has made contactless the main way to use the card today. Lockdowns and travel restrictions have also favoured online commerce, with some of the purchases usually made in stores having been transferred to this distribution channel due to the closure or non-accessibility of physical points of sale. [Slide 4: The use of payment methods in FR in 2022]  The year 2022 confirmed the general increase in the use of cashless means of payment (8%) observed since the health crisis.  Among these, the bank card is at the top of the list of French people's favourite cashless payments, with more than 60% of these transactions being carried out by card, at the point of sale (contactless or contactless) or online. Moreover, more and more French people are using a 'virtual' card, available on their mobile phone in an electronic wallet , which illustrates the growing dematerialization observed in payments: for example, mobile payment jumped by 137% last year, to reach nearly 6% of transactions by proximity card. Special payment vouchers (e.g. transport tickets, restaurant vouchers, gift vouchers, etc.) but also invoices, receipts, tips, etc. follow the same trend, as you see on a daily basis. The use of digital means of payment is thus becoming part of the new payment habits of individuals and professionals. [Slide 5: Diversification of players and supply]  This trend is the result of the development of new technologies that have modernized payments. To name but a few: NFC (Near-Field-Communication) technology or QR code have made it possible to deploy contactless payments; tokenisation2 of sensitive payment data, i.e. the transformation of bank data into a non-reusable digital token (or token) during the payment process, makes it possible to better secure transactions on the Internet; the use of biometric data (fingerprint, retina, palm of the hand, etc.) to identify the paying consumer is also particularly innovative.  At the same time, in recent years, there have been a myriad of new players in the payments industry, whose added value is mainly based on technology. These have come to compete with the traditional 'traditional' financial players that are the banks: we are talking about FinTechs of course but also about 'non-financial' players, namely telecom operators, technical service providers (specialising in tokenisation, for example), subsidiaries of mass distribution and finally BigTechs (these tech giants that we all know, in particular the American GAFAM - ApplePay, GooglePay - which dominate the mobile payments market, but also Chinese and Korean platforms such as AliPay or WeChatPay).  All these players, who are now involved in one or more links in the payment value chain, maintain the dynamism of the payments ecosystem.  The payment offer has therefore diversified greatly in recent years, to the point that there are now many alternatives to 'traditional' means of payment such as cash, card and cheque. New payment methods allow for faster and faster use: for example, an instant transfer allows you to transfer funds in the space of a few seconds. Similarly, the development of contactless credit cards and mobile phone payments have made it possible to speed up and streamline our daily payment procedures.  In this changing landscape, we have also seen the emergence of crypto-assets. Although originally imagined to be used as a currency and sometimes wrongly called "crypto-currencies", crypto-assets do not fulfil the three functions: they are really neither an instrument of exchange (allowing easy buying and selling in everyday life), nor a unit of account (allowing the prices of different goods and services to be easily compared), nor a store of value. Their use as a payment instrument remains marginal, although this may change with the adoption of the Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation. This is an important step for the crypto-asset ecosystem, as it will provide a European regulatory framework for crypto-asset issuers and service providers, intended to address a number of major risks and provide more confidence to users.  In the end, innovation and digitalization, carried out in a controlled framework, have contributed to bringing many benefits, with more secure, faster, more convenient and easy-to-use means of payment. [Slide 6: Issues and challenges for the European payments sector] B- The digitalisation of the economy: issues and challenges for the Europe of payments  While the benefits of the evolution of payments are numerous, the dynamics observed and the The increasing fragmentation of the accompanying payment chain raises challenges far beyond our borders.  Species characteristics, in particular privacy, universal acceptance, and accessibility, are not currently available in the digital space. The increase in the use of payments via the digital space therefore raises the question of how, in the future, to guarantee the sustainability of these essential characteristics for citizens.  In addition, the growing use of dematerialized solutions has gradually increased our dependence on non-European players (particularly in the United States) who already benefit from significant network effects, thanks in particular to the exploitation of large databases and customers, and who hold certain widely used proprietary standards (Visa, MasterCard). Beyond operational resilience, this situation raises issues of competition, strategic autonomy and data protection.  Finally, the development of online payments has been accompanied by the implementation of strong authentication, driven by European regulations. Strong authentication is an authentication that is based on at least two of the following three factors: possession of an object, knowledge (for example of a password), or a biometric factor, such as a fingerprint. While the widespread use of this strong authentication has made it possible to ensure a high level of technological security throughout the payment chain, it makes it all the more necessary to strengthen the vigilance of users, who are increasingly targeted by fraudsters. The year 2022 confirmed the rapid growth of fraud and payer manipulation fraud techniques, including those based on a phone call to the victim by impersonating bank staff. The Observatory for the Security of Payment Methods has noted in this regard that, while the proportion of fraudulent payments with strong authentication has remained contained in 2021, this proportion has become significant in 2022 (30% of the total amount of fraudulent card payments made on the internet).  All these aspects related to the digitization of payments pose challenges in terms of regulation and supervision. However, over the years, we have observed a fragmentation of the payment value chain linked to the multiplication of players, more or less specialised, operating in different segments and offering an increasingly diversified offer but sometimes with limited interoperability. In this context, it is becoming increasingly difficult for regulators to develop a "holistic" view of the risks and interdependencies of the sector. In addition, the role of certain unregulated - or poorly regulated - players in the security of means of payment has become crucial, such as that of mobile phone manufacturers and telephone operators. [Slide 7: Transition - Our ambitions for the future] Are regulators able to respond to these challenges? II. How do we see our ambitions for The future? [Slide 8: Transition - 2 complementary answers: supervise/support and innovate.] By providing complementary responses: coaching, supporting and innovating. A- Actions in the regulation of means of payment [Slide 9: Strengthening financial regulation at the national and international levels]  In terms of financial regulation: it is a question of continuously adapting our regulatory frameworks, both nationally and internationally, in order to offer a framework of trust conducive to innovation while ensuring: o the maintenance of a " level playing field between players, following the principle of "same activity, same risk, same regulation, o consumer protection, and o Neutrality with respect to technological developments, which are constantly transforming the retail payments landscape. In this way, an effort is made to regulate the ways in which they are used, and not the technology itself, which is constantly changing.  The multi-year strategies for retail payment methods, which are also applied at different geographical levels, make it possible to identify and implement priority orientations over the medium term, if necessary with communication actions and quantified objectives to measure progress. [Slide 10: Supporting targeted initiatives and actions]  At the same time, the authorities are supporting the actors by mobilizing for certain initiatives (public, private, or public-private partnerships) that work towards the development of an autonomous and competitive European payment market. In particular, the Banque de France and the Eurosystem actively support the future pan-European EPI payment solution . It is a new payment method that will allow you to pay from account to account by instant transfer via a QR code, both between individuals and to professionals. This payment method will be integrated into a digital wallet (called "wero ") that will be able to host other payment methods and allow the provision of associated services (e.g. digital identity services or access to merchant loyalty programs). This solution will contribute to strengthening the sovereignty of the European payments market, providing an alternative to the use of international networks such as MasterCard and Visa, and ensuring that the processing of payments and associated data is carried out by European players. It is in the same spirit that the Banque de France has supported the Groupement Cartes Bancaires since 1984 and Paylib since 2013. We are convinced that EPI will make it possible to promote European know-how in the field of payments, by helping to diversify the uses of SEPA instant transfer. More broadly, the development of instant credit transfers goes hand in hand with the enrichment of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA), which makes it possible to make payments under the same conditions throughout the European area. This is a key lever for successful European integration towards a single market for payments.  Finally, promoting targeted, very concrete actions makes it possible to raise consumer awareness. The National Committee for Payment Methods, of which the Banque de France is the secretary, has for example drawn up a charter for better accessibility of payment services for people with disabilities. For its part, the Observatory for the Supervision of Payment Methods (OSMP), also set up under the aegis of the Banque de France, develops recommendations in close collaboration with the French financial centre to constantly strengthen the security of payment methods in the face of increasingly sophisticated fraud techniques. B- Innovating with the digital euro  Central banks are not only supporting innovation, they are also a key driver of innovation. This dimension is fully embodied by the digital euro project, which is a public response to the challenges I outlined earlier. [Slide 11: Digital Euro: motivations and characteristics]  The digital euro will be a new form of central money, issued by the Eurosystem, and accessible to the general public. It will complement cash and other means of payment, not replace them.  The digital euro will first of all make it possible to perpetuate the unique characteristics of cash in the digital space, making it a true "digital banknote". The legal tender it should have made it usable anywhere in the euro zone, in all contexts - including e-commerce. Its offline mechanism will offer cash-like privacy and will be a guarantee of resilience. It will be free to use for individuals. Its features will be conducive to financial and digital inclusion, including for the unbanked or those who do not have a smartphone.  These unique features will enable the digital euro to enhance individuals' freedom of choice. I would like to respond here to some unfounded fears that are circulating about this project. First, the central bank will never be able to see the personal data of users of the digital euro: it is not a question of creating a European " big brother" but, on the contrary, of offering a new means of payment that will offer a level of privacy that is still unequalled in the digital space. Moreover, the digital euro will never be a "programmable currency, i.e. the central bank will never be able to restrict its use  neither in the long term, nor in the goods and services that can be purchased. The digital euro will also not be remunerated - neither positively nor negatively, like the banknote. Finally, the digital euro will not replace cash: the Eurosystem is committed3 to ensuring that cash remains widely accessible and accepted and is considering4 designing a new series of banknotes. The European Commission has published a proposal for a regulation that reinforces the legal tender status of cash within the EU. Finally, the Banque de France announced the construction of a new banknote printing plant in the Puy-de-Dome region, which is set to become the most modern, efficient and environmentally friendly public banknote production centre in Europe. Our commitment is clear: cash will remain widely accessible, everywhere in the euro area.  In addition to offering these unique features and enhancing the freedom of choice of individuals, the digital euro will also support sovereignty, competition, innovation and European integration in the payments sector. Its distribution will be entrusted to private intermediaries, and governed by a set of rules defined by the Eurosystem. These rules will require the emergence of open and harmonised acceptance standards, which will reduce our dependence on non-European players and allow private players to offer their services anywhere in the euro area. As a result, the digital euro will promote the development of private solutions, under European governance, that can be used anywhere in the euro area and in all contexts (in stores, e-commerce, between individuals) - whereas most solutions are currently confined to certain countries or use cases. Finally, the digital euro will build, as much as possible, on existing infrastructure (e.g. terminals and payment cards) to facilitate its integration into the payments ecosystem. [Slide 12: Digital Euro: next steps]  While the digital euro project is well advanced, we still have a long way to go before we consider paying in digital euro. The ECB's Governing Council recently announced the launch of a "preparation phase", which follows the "investigation phase that was opened in 2021. This new phase will allow us to (i) finalize the design, (ii) experiment with certain features and (iii) prepare for the development of the architecture, by selecting potential vendors. We will also continue to engage actively with market participants, merchant and consumer representatives, to ensure that the digital euro meets their expectations.  At the same time, the European Commission published a proposal for a regulation last June, which must now be debated by the Parliament and the Member States, and which has made it possible to open an essential democratic debate on this project. I would like to stress that the decision to issue a digital euro has not yet been taken, and that it cannot be taken until the co-legislator has finalised and voted on this text. In conclusion, money and payments are of strategic importance, which in the digital age brings with it new challenges. As guarantors of monetary and financial stability, central banks must be able to anticipate and respond to the risks and vulnerabilities inherent in these developments. Within a dynamic payments ecosystem, made up of a plurality and a wide variety of players, it is a question of finding a delicate balance between supporting innovation, maintaining a high level of payment security and competitiveness. All these ingredients are necessary to give users the greatest freedom of choice among payment methods that are modern, secure, reliable, accessible and efficient - both economically and environmentally. Thank you for your attention and I suggest that you devote a few minutes to your questions. [Slide 13: Thank you for your attention]  Based on card payments alone, the number of point-of-sale payments accounted for 81% of flows, compared to 19% for remote payments (compared to 84% and 16% respectively in 2019). Including the estimate of cash payments from the European SPACE surveys, the share of internet payments was 10% in 2022 (compared to less than 8% in 2019), and the share of cash in all retail consumer payments was around 45% (compared to 53% in 2019). Title: Challenges and new opportunities for CBDCs
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Monnaie J) ( 1 ") Challenges and new perspectives for CBDCs Published on November 16, 2023 6th Financial Technology Conference November 16, 2023 Speech by Denis BEAU, First Deputy Governor of the Banque de France [Slide 1 : introduction] Ladies and gentlemen Thank you for allowing me to open this sixth edition of the Assises des Technologies Financieres. This edition is timely, as the Eurosystem has recently made important announcements to support our monetary sovereignty, of which central bank money is the best embodiment, and more specifically in payments. I am referring here to the work we are doing on central bank digital currencies: one for financial players (the interbank CBDC), the other for the general public (the digital euro). These projects, which are being carried out in parallel, and which I propose to take stock of in my introductory remarks to this conference, are two sides of the same strategy in the service of monetary and financial sovereignty and stability; objectives that are intimately linked, and at the heart of the missions of the Banque de France and the Eurosystem. [Slide 2: "interbank face" transition] I. The "interbank" side: adapting central money to the tokenization of finance ot amolinror Ioq noiomontc cross-border [Slide 3: Interbank CBDC: Supporting Asset Tokenization] In the era of the tokenization of financial assets and the possible development of decentralized blockchain-like infrastructures to exchange them, we need to ensure that central bank money remains the preferred settlement asset for transactions between financial institutions. To do this, central money must follow the tokenization movement of finance, and even better: it must accompany it to help build a secure innovation environment. To do this, the central currency must be adapted to the settlement of market transactions involving tokenised assets such as tokenised shares or bonds, i.e. bonds issued on distributed ledgers ( DLT). Hence the experiments carried out by the Banque de France since 2020 on interbank CBDC. Interbank CBDC, as we are experimenting at the Banque de France, is an innovative form of central money directly issued in the form of tokens on DLT. These experiments were extended by the launch by the Eurosystem of an exploratory phase in April 2023, for the settlement of tokenised assets in central money. The Banque de France's interbank CBDC solution, based on the use of its own blockchain, is one of the solutions that will be tested in this context during 2024. The entry into force of the European Pilot Regime in March 2023, for a minimum period of three years, and probably renewed, is an essential element of this exploratory phase, since it also creates a new regulatory framework, a "regulatory sandbox". It is this derogatory framework that will allow us to identify the necessary adjustments to the current regulatory framework, in order to facilitate the functioning of market infrastructures based on distributed ledger technology (DLT), while preserving investor protection, market integrity and financial stability. The Paris financial centre has been significantly mobilised around the issues of tokenisation: this makes it one of the most dynamic centres in Europe. However, the challenge today is to maintain this leadership, by gradually moving from a phase of experimentation to a phase of industrialization. The Eurosystem's exploratory work and the Pilot Regime are essential milestones on this path, and I therefore strongly encourage market players to include these steps in their roadmap and participate in them. [Slide 4: Interbank CBDC: Improving Cross-Border Uses] Interbank CBDC can also help address the challenge of cross-border payments, acting as a catalyst. Currently, cross-border payments are expensive, slow, inaccessible and lack transparency, but in a differentiated way according to "corridors" and currencies. The G20 is strongly committed to meeting this challenge and is determined to make tangible improvements by 2027. In the short term, this can be achieved through the interconnection of instant payment systems, such as the Nexus project where the Eurosystem is involved with its instant payment system TIPS. In the longer term, interbank CBDC can pave the way for even more innovative solutions. To do this, we must work on the development of common standards and work on interoperability between CBDC trading systems for interbank use, but also with existing systems. This is why the Banque de France is working with other international players, such as the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Singapore Monetary Authority (MAS) and SWIFT to explore the modalities of this interoperability between CBDCs. But we also need to take a step back, and consider the longer-term development of regional or even global technical platforms. There is a need for exploratory work on such platforms, which could enable us to overcome the need for interoperability between national systems. To conclude on this aspect, I would simply like to tell you that we at the Banque de France are determined to continue these experiments in order to better understand the needs of the market and meet its expectations. And we will not succeed without the participation of financial market participants, whether issuers or investors, on whom our experiments are based. [Slide 5: "Face detail" transition] This approach of experimentation and cooperation with the private sector is also a marker of the digital euro project, which brings me to the second "face" of our strategy concerning CBDC, the digital euro. II. The "detail" side: perpetuating the characteristics of the banknote in the digital space [Slide 6: Features and Timeline] As economic and financial exchanges become more digital, we want to develop a new form of digital central currency for the general public, together with private players, adapted to these exchanges. The features envisaged for this digital euro will make it comparable to a "digital banknote": usable anywhere in the euro area, free of charge for individuals, it will offer cash-like privacy and high resilience via its "offline" mechanism, and it will be distributed via banks and other payment service providers. The Governing Council recently approved the launch of a new phase, known as the "preparation" phase, in the conduct of the project to create and deploy a digital euro issued by the Eurosystem's central banks. Initially, this phase will allow us to (i) finalize certain analyses, for example the design of the scheme, i.e. the framework of rules that will govern the issuance and distribution of the digital euro; (ii) experiment with several functionalities and (iii) prepare to develop the digital euro architecture. This new state in the conduct of the Droiet does not however sianify Das aue The decision to issue a digital euro has been taken. This decision can only be a collective one, involving the Eurosystem and European legislators, at the end of a real democratic debate. This debate was opened by the presentation of a draft regulation by the Commission, and is set to continue in parallel with the preparatory work carried out by the Eurosystem. [Slide 7: Enhanced freedom of choice for individuals] While it is experiencing a growing media echo, the digital euro raises many legitimate questions. But it is also the subject of unfounded fears. I would like to make it clear here that the digital euro is not a dangerous and liberticidal project that does not speak its name, if I understand correctly some of the comments that the digital euro could become an instrument of "mass surveillance" by the authorities, a European " Big Brother". We thus understand that the digital euro would allow the central bank (i) to trace the payment data of individuals; (ii) restrict their purchases; (iii) to impose a negative remuneration on them; (iv) or even to eliminate cash. The digital euro will obviously not allow for any of this. First, the digital euro, as conceived and prepared by the Eurosystem, will offer an unrivalled level of privacy in dematerialised payments. The Eurosystem will never be able to see the personal information of digital euro users, nor will it be able to link payment information to an individual. The "offline" payment mechanism, which will be usable for payments below a certain threshold, will offer cash-like privacy. Second, the digital euro will never be a "programmable currency". The Eurosystem issues currency, not vouchers. The digital euro will therefore be convertible "one for one" at any time with the other forms of money in circulation. And the Eurosystem will never be able to prevent users of the digital euro from buying certain goods or services. The Eurosystem will also not be able to restrict the validity period of digital euro holdings; Here again, the parallel with banknotes remains. Thirdly, the digital euro will not be remunerated - neither positively nor negatively - like the banknote. It will be a means of payment, not an investment asset. Fourth, the digital euro will not replace cash. On the contrary, it aims to perpetuate their characteristics in the digital space. In addition, public actors have made strong commitments to preserve the availability of species. The Eurosystem is committed1 to ensuring that cash remains widely accessible and accepted and is considering2 the design of a new series of banknotes. The European Commission has published a proposal for a regulation that reinforces the legal tender status of cash within the EU. Finally, the Banque de France announced the construction of a new banknote printing plant in the Puy-de-Dome region, which is set to become the most modern, efficient and environmentally friendly public banknote production centre in Europe. Our commitment is clear: cash will remain widely accessible, everywhere in the euro area. Conclusion [Slide 8: Banque de France logo] As I said in my introduction, the interbank CBDC and the digital euro are two sides of the same strategy in the service of our sovereignty and monetary and financial stability. These initiatives are essential to preserve confidence in our single currency, the euro. The democratic debate that has begun on the digital euro must enable us to answer the questions, to build strong support around this essential social issue that is the currency, this collective good, this public good. At the same time, although it attracts less media interest, the work on interbank CBDC is no less central, and you can count on the commitment of Banque de France employees to innovate and secure the transition to the financial system of tomorrow. 1 See the Eurosystem's fiduciary strategy o See the process for defining a new series of notes.
