A final word on monetary transmission: while its first part (transmission to financial conditions) is obviously rapid, we are less clear at this stage about its second part (transmission of financial conditions to the economy) [VIJ. Second thought: we clearly have one main objective, which is our destination, to bring inflation back to 2% by 2025. There can be no doubt about our determination and commitment. We are increasingly confident that we will achieve this  see our latest inflation forecast for 2025. And so, subject to this main objective, we can now incorporate a secondary objective concerning the trajectory: if we can reach our destination with a soft landing, rather than a hard landing, it is a much better path, for the economy, for our fellow European citizens and for the sound conduct of fiscal policies. The risk of doing too much must be weighed against the risk of not doing enough. In my view, these risks are now at least symmetrical. In the second case, inflation would remain persistently above its target and inflation expectations could become de-anchored. This is a manageable risk, because we can always do more if that risk materializes. But when it comes to the risk of doing too much, with an economy going into recession, leading to a sharp deceleration in inflation, we would be forced to reverse course quickly. Therefore, "testing to the breaking point" is not a reasonable way to calibrate monetary policy. This suggests that we should now focus on monetary policy persistence rather than on constantly raising rates  the year rather than the level. Patience and persistence in monetary policy do not mean inaction. Our current stance is restrictive  the real implied rates extracted from the markets are higher than our estimates of the neutral rate  so maintaining its current level will reduce inflation. Just as there is a risk of doing too much in the future, there is the opposite risk of easing too soon. If markets fully price in our persistent strategy, they should not expect rate cuts for a long enough period; In this case, markets will endogenously extend the duration of high rates, thus contributing to the appropriate calibration of the monetary policy stance. In all cases, our policy must continue to be data-driven. In particular, we need to closely monitor the recent rebound in oil prices. At the moment, it is far from being a general shock on commodities as in 2021-2022; But we need to monitor its possible effects on inflation expectations and wages: core inflation remains our main indicator. A persistent strategy is not a forward guidance that rates will never rise again. This remains a pragmatic strategy: and as a pragmatist, I am clearly emphasising today that "on the basis of our current assessment, we consider that the ECB's key interest rates have reached levels which, maintained over a sufficiently long period", are broadly consistent with the return of inflation to our target in 2025. To conclude, over the past three years, we have had to navigate through unprecedented uncertainty. It would be ridiculous to claim that we were always 100% right, but overall, we handled the data and surprises as best we could. We now know that we are on the right track, we are increasingly confident that we will return to our 2% inflation target. However, continuing to accept this uncertainty, which is not usually the prerogative of science, may at least be what rationality requires. As the British mathematician and philosopher Bertrand Russell wrote, " not being absolutely certain [is] one of the essential things of rationality " [Vllj. Title: Wholesale CBDC: just as decisive as retail CBDC, and actively tested
text: Speech Governor Wholesale CBDC: just as decisive as retail CBDC, and actively Experienced Published on October 3, 2023 Conference "Unlocking the potential of wholesale CBDCs: what lessons and what perspectives?" - Paris, October 3 2023 Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to welcome you to this conference organized by the Banque de France. I would also like to welcome the distinguished speakers here today, from both the community of central banks and the private sector. I am convinced that only a broad and deep cooperation between all of us will "unlock the potential of digital currency in the world". wholesale central bank (CBDC)", which is the theme of our conference. We are currently witnessing a wave of technological disruptions driven by blockchain and tokenization: our ambition, as a central bank and supervisor, is to explore their potential, which is extremely promising, as soon as possible. This explains why no less than 93% of central banks are currently exploring the possibilities of issuing a CBDC1. Wholesale CBDC garners less attention and passion than retail CBDC, but it is nonetheless Important. The purpose of this currency (the question of "why") is probably even better perceived by market participants than that of retail CBDC, so I will start with its two very interesting areas of application, namely asset tokenisation and cross-border payments (I). I will then come to the the question of "how", i.e. the technical aspects of how it could work. The Banque de France leads the way experiments at all levels to develop such a system (II). I. The double potential of a wholesale CBDC a. Maintaining your central currency as a "security pivot" in a tokenized world The tokenization of finance is a new trend that is attracting growing interest from the financial sector and its players. Distributed ledger technologies (DLTs) could indeed improve the automated processing of market and back-office activities, resulting in significant cost savings for the financial sector and end-users. To do this, new private settlement assets, such as stablecoins, are popping up in this tokenized ecosystem. PayPal's plan to create a global stablecoin for retail payments is a stark reminder that if we don't take the initiative, someone else will do it for us. The need for a safe settlement asset on DLT has become apparent. To date, tokenized finance lacks the anchor provided by central bank money, which reduces counterparty and liquidity risks, and inherently guarantees the finality of payments. By acting as a monetary anchor, tokenized central bank money would enable convertibility between tokenized assets, just as central banks currently provide convertibility between commercial bank currencies. In short, tokenized central bank money would constitute a "security pivot" and serve as a reliable foundation of trust on which these new technologies could deploy their full potential. This is why it is in the interest of European commercial banks and the public sector to work together towards a framework for a tokenized European Union. On the public sector side, this means moving forward with a wholesale CBDC. The Eurosystem began studying new technologies relating to settlement in central bank money in April, including the issuance of a first type of tokenised CBDC. Eligibility criteria and the call for expressions will be released in the coming weeks, and the will be carried out in the course of 2024, including In this regard, the BIS has strongly advocated for the concept of "tokenized deposits": recorded on the liabilities side of the issuer's balance sheet, they differ from stablecoins, which are backed by a specific stock of assets and mainly issued by Bigtechs, not banks. I invite European commercial banks to take ownership of "tokenised deposits" and to experiment with their implementation. The actors cannot be left behind: on the one hand, to remain spectators of the emergence of stablecoins, issued by Bigtechs, none of which are European; and on the other hand, not to explore the field of tokenized deposits, on which American and Asian banks seem to be innovating faster. Private providers of tokenized currency could complement the issuance of a wholesale CBDC; Such a framework would replicate the two-tiered monetary system, ensuring that commercial banks have a critical role in the tokenized world. B. Improving cross-border payments Improving cross-border payments has been identified as one of the G20's priorities: a roadmap was dedicated to it in 2020, then updated to revive the momentum in this area, prioritising actions that have the most impact. In fact, some projects could be implemented quickly with the aim of achieving short- and medium-term results, such as Project Nexus. This is intended to allow individuals to make payments Instant cross-border payments, connecting fast payment systems around the world, made interoperable via Nexus gateway software. This ongoing interconnection of national payment systems* could form the basis for a longer-term approach based on the use of wholesale CBDCs: indeed, the emergence of DLT has been identified as a promising channel for improving cross-border payments. The use of wholesale CBDCs has the potential to address a number of costs and common friction issues based on common standards. Let us not repeat the mistakes of the past so that we do not end up with different standards, as has happened with real-time gross settlement systems. Ex-ante interoperability is always easier than ex-post interoperability : as we are in the early stages of tokenisation, there is still scope to develop international standards and ensure the future interoperability of wholesale CBDCs. Let me now combine these two objectives (tokenisation and cross-border payments). International bodies such as the BIS' and the IMFiv are actively considering integrated platforms, which would bring together tokenised central bank money, tokenised deposits and tokenised financial assets such as bonds and tokenised securities. This could make domestic CBDCs inherently interoperable, making cross-border payments much easier and avoiding further fragmentation. Because Europe must build its digital monetary sovereignty and because it is committed to building a more multilateral monetary system, the Eurosystem should and could display a new ambition here to enrich its financial services offer. I would like to invite all of you, representatives of both public and private entities, to go further in your reflection and to consider the construction of an integrated European platform. This would provide European players with the most efficient settlement system, while helping to strengthen the international role of the euro. A European platform would be subject to standards and rules of European governance, but interconnected from the outset with other regional or global platforms. Combined with a As a wholesale and/or retail CBDC, this infrastructure could make the euro more attractive for trade finance or foreign exchange activities. II. The technical contribution of the A. 12 experiments conducted by the Banque de France The Banque de France has in fact been very proactive by conducting twelve wholesale CBDC experiments since November 2020. We explored all the use cases identified for all types of DLT (public and private) with a wide range of public and private partners. We strongly believe in this learning-by-doing approach as a way to develop an operational framework for a wholesale CBDC, and here are three of the practical lessons we've learned so far. First, the experiments have shown that central banks will be able to steer the supply of wholesale CBDC money  which is a fundamental requirement for its eventual deployment. A permissioned network coupled with smart contracts would allow central banks to maintain their oversight of the network and even improve their ability to control the use and circulation of its CBDC. The control of central bank money is not an objective in itself, but it is essential to ensure the anchor value of central bank money and thus for financial stability. Second, in moving towards CBDC, it is important not to prematurely favor a particular technology or type of DLT. Continuing the path initiated in 2020, the Banque de France is committed to continuing to test different technologies during its experiments. In fact, while continuing to improve our own DLT [DLS3], we are also exploring other protocols and blockchains, both private and public, in parallel. On governance, the focus should be on the development of common standards and protocols for DLT platforms and wholesale CBDCs, following an assessment of all existing traditional features and options. Third, the development of wholesale CBDCs must now take into account climate-related concerns. I think sincerely that the tokenization of finance could make a valid and effective contribution to the challenge of climate change, as it should make it possible to streamline the intermediation chain and save energy-consuming processes. In this In this field, the design of wholesale CBDCs must be exemplary in order to promote the development of energy-efficient financial markets. In addition, financial actors must rely on the transparency and automation enabled by DLT to foster the development of green finance, for example by integrating ESG criteria into smart contracts. B. We will continue our experiments at Eurosystem level and at the level of the international The Banque de France is now actively involved in the Eurosystem's exploratory work on the settlement of tokenised assets in central bank money, which was launched last April. We are behind one of the three solutions that will be used in 2024 for experiments and trials with actual transactions. The particularity of this solution is that it is a true CBDC, based on a proprietary DLT, called DL3S, developed by the Banque de France. Major financial entities have already successfully tested the DL3S in our past 12 experiments. Thanks to the Eurosystem's exploratory work, I invite the All European market participants have been testing this solution with real transactions. In the longer term, the Banque de France is working internationally, in particular with the BIS Innovation Hub and the IMF, as well as with other central banks, in particular the Automated Market Maker ( AMM) Monetary Demonstration Authority that we developed as part of the Mariana project. To conclude, let me quote this wonderful poem by the Spanish writer Antonio Machado: "Traveller, the path // is the footprints of your footsteps, that's all; Traveller, there is no path, // The path is made by walking". Let's continue to move forward and experiment together. One thing we can be sure of: if we don't pave the way for a future payments infrastructure, others will. And we are determined to "chart" a European path . Discussions during the upcoming roundtables on cross-border payments and the tokenization of finance will contribute to this journey. Discours de Franois Villeroy de Galhau, Gouverneur de la Banque de France Mesdames, Messieurs, C'est un grand plaisir de vous accueillir  cette confrence organise par la Banque de France. Pour ce faire, de nouveaux actifs de rglement privs, tels que les stablecoins, font leur apparition dans cet cosystme tokenis. Amliorer les paiements transfrontires L'amlioration des paiements transfrontires a t identifie comme l'une des priorits du G20 : une feuille de route y a t consacre en 2020, puis mise  jour pour relancer la dynamique dans ce domaine, en donnant la priorit aux actions qui ont le plus d'impact. Une plateforme europenne serait soumise  des normes et  des rgles de gouvernance europennes spcifiques, mais interconnecte ds l'origine avec d'autres plateformes rgionales ou mondiales. Associe  une MNBC de gros et/ou de dtail, cette infrastructure pourrait rendre l'euro plus attractif pour les activits de financement des changes commerciaux ou sur le march des changes. II. La contribution technique de la MNBC de gros : tout aussi dcisive que la M... A. 12 exprimentations menes par la Banque de France La Banque de France s'est de fait montre trs proactive en conduisant douze exprimentations de MNBC de gros depuis novembre 2020. Nous avons explor tous les cas d'usage identifis pour tous les types de DLT (publiques et prives) avec un large ventail de partenaires publics et privs. Nous croyons fermement en cette approche d'apprentissage par la pratique comme moyen de dvelopper un cadre oprationnel pour une MNBC de gros, et voici trois des enseignements pratiques que nous en avons tirs jusqu' prsent . Premirement, les exprimentations ont montr que les banques centrales seront en mesure de piloter l'offre de monnaie de MNBC de gros - ce qui constitue une exigence fondamentale pour son ventuel dploiement. Un rseau permissionn coupl  des contrats intelligents (smart contracts) permettrait aux banques centrales de maintenir leur surveillance du rseau et mme d'amliorer leur capacit  contrler l'utilisation et la circulation de sa MNBC. Le contrle de la monnaie de banque centrale n'est pas un objectif en soi, mais il est essentiel pour garantir la valeur d'ancrage de la monnaie de banque centrale et donc pour la stabilit financire. Deuximement, en progressant vers une MNBC, il est important de ne pas favoriser prmaturment une technologie ou un type de DLT en particulier. Poursuivant la voie initie en 2020, la Banque de France s'r engage  continuer de tester diffrentes technologies lors de ses exprimentations. De fait, tout en continuant  amliorer notre propre DLT [DLS3], nous explorons galement en parallle d'autres protocoles et blockchains, qu'ils soient privs ou publics. S'agissant de la gouvernance, l'accent devrait tre mis sur la dfinition de normes et de protocoles communs pour les plateformes DLT et les MNBC de gros, aprs une valuation de l'ensemble des caractristiques et des options MNBC de gros : tout aussi dcisive que la M... classiques existantes. Troisimement, le dveloppement des MNBC de gros doit  prsent prendre en compte les proccupations lies au climat. Je crois sincrement que la tokenisation de la finance pourrait apporter une contribution valable et efficace face au dfi du changement climatique, car elle devrait permettre de rationaliser la chane d'intermdiation et d'conomiser des processus consommateurs d'nergie. Dans ce domaine, la conception des MNBC de gros doit tre exemplaire pour favoriser le dveloppement de marchs financiers efficaces du point de vue nergtique. En outre, les acteurs financiers doivent s'appuyer sur la transparence et l'automatisation rendues possibles par la DLT pour favoriser le dveloppement de la finance verte, par exemple en intgrant les critres ESG dans les contrats intelligents. B. Nous poursuivrons nos exprimentations au niveau de l'Eurosystme et au niveau international La Banque de France est dsormais activement implique dans les travaux exploratoires de l'Eurosystme concernant le rglement des actifs tokeniss en monnaie de banque centrale, qui a t lanc en avril dernier. Nous sommes  l'origine de l'une des trois solutions qui seront utilises en 2024 pour les exprimentations et les essais avec des transactions relles. Title: The Future of Multilateralism: Three Facts, Three Demands and One Conviction
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Governor ''J The future of multilateralism: three concrete facts, three demands and one conviction Published on October 11, 2023 Emerging Markets Forum Global Meeting 2023 - Marrakech, 11 October 2023 Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Bank of France. Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to be here with you for this global meeting of the 2023 Emerging Markets Forum, which we were honoured to host last year in Paris. Before I begin, I would like to express my great solidarity with the Moroccan people after the terrible earthquake that has hit the country. We all stand with Morocco. The theme of my speech is not a cause for celebration either. We are collectively witnessing a growing crisis of multilateralism, which could lead to an increasingly fragmented world. As a convinced  but not a Eurocentric  European, I firmly believe that multilateralism is our overriding public interest. Therefore, we must first recognize that its current form is more than imperfect, and that it needs to be adapted to new international realities. Today, I would like to share with you some personal views (without claiming to be France's official views) on three concrete facts (A), three requirements to respond to them (B) and one hope for the future of multilateralism (C). 331 equals seven and I don't pretend to compare myself to the great T.E. Lawrence and his "Seven Pillars of Wisdom"... But let's try to plant some seeds of wisdom in this world turned upside down.  Let me start with the three hard facts. Ly. The Disease of Nationalism Spreads and it is often associated with populism, power politics and protectionism. Its most extreme expression is, of course, Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It has also spread to other countries around the world and, in particular, has underpinned China's rise. But let's recognize that we are all contaminated to varying degrees, with the examples of India's assertiveness, or the "America First " policy in the United States fueling a trade war. It has acted as a driving force for Brexit in Europe, while testing Franco-German unity. A month ago, The Economist headlined " Howparanoid nationalisai corrupts " [he- If we are not careful, the 2020s could bring us back to a situation reminiscent of the darkest hours of European history in the 1930s. The tragic events that have taken place in Israel since Saturday are a sad reminder of this. A2. The disease of nationalism threatens international cooperation precisely at a time when we need it most. This is what I call the paradox of "goods" global audiences". Let me explain. More likely than ever, the global community must preserve and provide essential  even existential  public goods: green transition to combat climate change, pandemic preparedness, digital transformation and cybersecurity, financial stability in the face of rising global debt, to name but four. These problems can only be solved collectively and in a concerted manner: none of us can face them alone. However, multilateralism is experiencing an unprecedented crisis. Once a symbol of great progress, the G20 is clearly underperforming given the international challenges we face. Despite the growing impact of climate change, I fear that this priority is fading, as we are seeing in our latest international discussions and at the G20, also due to the increased polarisation of political debates around climate and environmental issues in the United States. Europe is ahead; the rest of the world must not be left behind - this is a hope, a call for the agenda of the next few days in Marrakech. As geopolitical dissension deepens and trust erodes, it is becoming increasingly difficult for international forums, including the IMF and multilateral development banks, to carry out their missions. But let's face it: multilateralism is first and foremost a victim of Russia's war, but also in part a backlash against the dominance of the Global North and the post-World War II international order. Only a system in which each country considers itself legitimately represented will be viable in the long term. We must find pragmatic ways of moving forward: I will come back to this point. A3. Some lessons learned from European cooperation. However imperfect it may be, the European Union is a historic experiment showing that decades of nationalist rivalry can be overcome, from which we can draw three useful lessons in responding to today's multilateral challenges. The first lesson relates to the objectives of cooperation. To achieve results and cement solidarity, multilateral action must be based precisely on the spirit of Europe's founding fathers, as illustrated by the Schuman Declaration of 1950: "[Europe] will be built by concrete achievements creating first of all de facto solidarity". It all started with the creation of the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) - it wasn't very glamorous, but it was concrete - followed by the Common Agricultural Policy (1957), the single market (1993), and then the advent of the euro (1999)... and now the Green Deal (2030-2050). We should adopt a similar strategy at the international level: rather than pursuing unrealistic ambitions, we need to focus multilateral efforts on a selection of a few global issues, which have clear common interests  this is what I call "targeted" or "pragmatic" multilateralism. A second lesson concerns governance. Europe is a unique initiative of shared governance among sovereign states, with several interesting features: a) a powerful secretariat in the form of the European Commission; (b) a change in its rules for voting by qualified unanimity on most subjects in the Council of the European Union - a decision-making body that brings together the ministers of the Member States - which means that no country has a right of veto; and (c) a clear hierarchy of legal norms - with European law taking precedence over the national laws of the Member States - guaranteed by the European Court of Justice. The third lesson relates to its geography. The European Union has adapted and evolved through successive enlargements to include new Member States: it has gone from the six founding countries to the current Union with 27 members. In the process, the Union has undergone profound changes, with a notable rebalancing in favour of Eastern Europe. The Union has gone through these changes thanks to its flexibility, introducing possibilities for participation (opt-iri) or non-participation ( opt-out), and allowing for smaller circles of cooperation - of which the euro area is the prime example. The Bretton Woods institutions could draw inspiration from it in order to remain a central forum where the Global North and the Global South meet and cooperate effectively.  To respond to these three concrete facts, three requirements must be met. B1. The first step is to honour our commitments with regard to the reforms of the Bretton Woods international financial institutions. Some of these are already on the table, and reform has already been completed: the global community has delivered on its commitment to redirect at least 100 billion of SDRs to countries that need it most. The majority of these reallocations will be redirected to the Resitience and Sustainability Trust (RST) and the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PGRT), for the benefit of low-income countries. Still on the subject of the IMF, progress can, I hope, be made on two fronts. First, we still need to find additional resources to fund the PRGT subsidy account in a context of growing demand and rising interest rates. Second, the 16th Quota Review, which is currently underway, is expected to strengthen the Fund's firepower, leading to an increase of at least 35% in overall quotas. In addition, the governance of the Fund would be improved if, as is currently under discussion, a 25th seat on the Executive Board for African countries were created. Beyond the IMF, we must act to modernize the multilateral development banks (MDBs) as quickly as possible. The G20 Leaders' Declaration [iii] rightly called for increasing the World Bank's financial capacity and, more generally, working to "improve, consolidate and make the MDBs more effective". The G20 has approved a dedicated Roadmap that could provide MDBs with additional lending space of around 200 billion over the next decade: progress will need to be closely monitored to ensure concrete implementation of the Capital Adequacy Framework's recommendations to maximize the leverage of potential capital increases. These advances must be implemented effectively and as soon as possible: there have been too many broken promises in the past. Restoring confidence in multilateralism to all, and especially in the South, means first of all, today, and finally, moving from words to action. B2. The next step is to go beyond these measures to truly revitalize multilateral cooperation and address the shortcomings of the current system. Multilateralism is at a crossroads, or let's say at a "Darwinian" moment : it must evolve in order to survive, otherwise it could disappear. To do this, why not start by creating an ad hoc working group, which would be an amplifier of the 2017 Panel of Eminent Persons, with a balanced representation of the international community. This independent group would be tasked with proposing more ambitious ways to reform the international financial system. Let me dream a little and give food for thought, based on the lessons learned from the European experience. First, we must move towards indisputable fairness in the governance of the international financial institutions, as also advocated by the French President, Emmanuel Macron . This means ensuring a fairer seat at the table for emerging and developing countries. In the long term, a revision of the distribution of IMF quotas will be inevitable. But the emerging countries that will benefit from it - including China - will have to accept common rules of the game; This includes their fair share in debt restructuring and in the financing of global public goods, starting with the climate. This revision could also be an opportunity to create new interest groups on the Governing Council. We must also consider adjusting the majority voting rules at the IMF in order to limit the right of veto: in 2011, the initiative of the Palais Royal [vi] led by Michel Camdessus had already recommended lowering the majority rule from the current 85%. Second, global economic governance should be formalized and given a strong political impetus, building on the key role played by the G20 in this area. For example, some suggested the activation of a "Board" already enshrined in the IMF's Articles of Agreement, which would bring together the 24 members of the IMF's International Monetary and Financial Committee and G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors [vii]: l'nrnano nui on roQiiltomit Qorait rhorno rlo nronrlro Hoq rlaricinnc ctratonim ioc I wi VAI IW Wl I I VMMIIVI Mil Wl Vil l Wl I VA I y W WW I VI IMI W MW WWWIWIWI I VJ VU VAlVyiVMVV for the international financial system. In operational terms, this revitalised G20 or G24 could have formal rules of governance, including qualified majority voting in some areas, while a permanent secretariat could be provided by renewed international financial institutions (IMF and World Bank). To achieve concrete results, it should build on what I have called "pragmatic multilateralism" and stick to a limited agenda with a medium-term horizon (e.g. 2030). Global issues towards which interests and goals could converge include climate change mitigation  as a canonical global public good  debt restructuring and pandemic preparedness. B3. The third requirement relates to the How the monetary system works international (SMI). Despite the end of the Bretton Woods system in the 1970s, the US dollar still plays a major role. However, the decline - even very gradual - in its share in world foreign exchange reserves and the current geopolitical situation are reviving the debate on maintaining the dollar as the anchor of the international monetary system. But it would be worse than anything to move from a dollar-based system to a confrontational "non-system." Fragmentation, especially if disorderly, would generate instability and inefficiency, especially from a crisis management perspective: a fragmented global financial safety net (GFSN) is an ineffective one. This would compromise the convertibility of reserves and lead to inefficient and costly excessive accumulation of reserves. That said, let us be more positive and focus our efforts on the "creative frontier" of a resilient and truly balanced multipolar system. The international community would be well advised to discuss the evolution of the IMS in a coordinated international dialogue based on a few practical guiding principles:  Foster cross-border payments and digitalization to achieve a more efficient international payments system, as this could be an important lever to increase trade, reduce costs, and promote integration between countries.  Design a coherent regulatory and supervisory framework that ensures that the development of crypto-assets and private stablecoins does not undermine public confidence in the financial system.  The currencies of this multipolar system - including of course the euro, and probably to begin with those in the SDR basket - should all commit to rules of convertibility and stability: I am thinking in particular of a common "inflation anchor", as exists in fact between the euro, the dollar, the yen and the pound at around 2%. Jean-Claude Trichet has often pointed this out.fviii].  Revitalize our crisis prevention capacity, in line with the principles of the IMF's Integrated Policy Framework, which enables a a balanced mix of tools including foreign exchange intervention as well as macroprudential and capital flow management measures.  The last point I would like to share with you  let's call it the Seventh pillar of wisdom - is A strong conviction. In the face of the current turbulence on the international stage, a strong Europe is essential for international cooperation. It represents a unique endeavour in which countries have freely and peacefully decided to join forces, based on the values of freedom, democracy and the rule of law[ix], so there can be no doubt about which side we are on in the face of Russian aggression. Europe is supported by a so/Zpoiver based on respect for international rules, the highest official development assistance in the world and openness to the South. In a context of growing rivalry between the United States and China, the European Union is setting up a model of power that is not hegemonic, but endowed with strong values: Europe was a pioneering model of social progress in the twentieth century, combining lower levels of inequality with a higher level of public services, and with a social security system. It is now forging a pioneering environmental model for the twenty-first century. The fragmented international environment certainly requires new institutional skills... and to quote Robert Schuman again, "the contribution that an organised and living Europe can make to civilisation is indispensable to the maintenance of peaceful relations" [xl. We are living in a decade of decisive choices. The world order is facing a destructive triangle of "fragmentation/isolation/confrontation". Let us open up a more promising perspective with an alternative triangle "competition/solidarity/cooperation"; in the words of Jacques Delors, "we need competition that stimulates, cooperation that strengthens, and solidarity that unites" [xi], Europe has shown that this triangle can become a reality, despite its history of rivalries and  yes  imperfections. Thank you for listening to these personal reflections that I wanted to share with you here in Marrakech. [il The Economist, How paranoid nationalism corrupts. 2 septembre 2023. Title: Fintechs, at the forefront of the "new frontiers"
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Governor ''J Fintechs, at the forefront of the "new frontiers" Published on October 16, 2023 ACPR-AMF Fintech Forum - Paris, Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France, Chairman of the Autorite de Controle Prudentiel et de Resolution Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to welcome you to the Banque de France for this fourth edition of the Fintech Forum, jointly organised by the ACPR and the AMF: I would like to greet Marie-Anne Barbat-Layani, Chairwoman of the AMF, with friendship. Today, all insurance companies and banks work in partnership with one or more innovative players, and therefore operate in a more open architecture. Once again, this is to be welcomed: if existing players and Fintechs did not know how to innovate, and innovate together, it is the Bigtechs that would ultimately "win the day". I am aware that the French Fintech Week, which includes our Forum, is taking place this year in a context that is undoubtedly less buoyant than in previous years; the Banque de France and the ACPR remain all the more mobilized alongside the innovative financial ecosystem (I), in particular to help them better master these "new frontiers" that constitute crypto-assets and climate risk (II). I. The Banque de France and the ACPR remain firmly at the side of the innovative ecosystem 1. A less easy economic context for the financing and creation of Fintechs As I said earlier, the context is less easy this year for Fintechs, with this eloquent figure: their fundraising fell by around 60% in the first half of 2023 compared to the first half of 2022 1 , which was certainly an exceptional record in the equally exceptional context of ultra-low rates. This is a slightly more marked decline although that of all venture capital in France, of the order of 50% 11. While Fintechs are no longer on the podium of the largest fundraisers, they are still as numerous, if not more, to benefit from investments. This trend, similar to that observed in Germany and the United Kingdom, is interpreted by professional associations as a possible sign of maturity. The Fintech-Innovation Cluster, the ACPR's "one-stop shop" for project leaders, has logically observed a decrease in the number of requests this year (63 from January to August, compared to a hundred over the same period in 2022). However, the ACPR remains fully committed to providing the best possible support for innovative projects and making their regulatory process even more fluid. In 96% of cases (compared to 90% last year), a response was given within two weeks at the first contact. And once the authorisation process was really underway, our compliance with the deadlines of the Fintech Charter improved again, with, for example, an average response time of 10 days to exchanges (compared to 12 days last year... and compared to 19 on the applicants' side). In addition, we have undertaken to improve the "Fintech Journey" site to make regulations ever more accessible and understandable. This will help in particular the most "novice" project leaders to prepare their applications in good conditions. 2. However, the economic situation should not mask the underlying trends Cyclical factors should not mask underlying trends, in particular important structural strengths. Our Fintechs continue to grow; in France, they benefit from both a pool of recognized talent and an attractive and dynamic financial center. The continuous development of new technologies, and in particular the current trends in artificial intelligence (AI), opens up new perspectives 111. This is evidenced by the exceptionally rapid adoption of new generative AI tools, some of which have gained 1 million users in just 5 days. At the Banque de France, in order to understand and take advantage of this new situation, we have adopted an experimental approach, which encourages rapid learning. In May 2023, through the Lab, our Open Innovation Center, we launched a call for contributions on generative AI addressed to the innovative ecosystem, to perfect our understanding of this tool and accelerate its potential use through the proposal of concrete use cases - or even operational solutions. Closed on September 21st, it led to the selection of 3 French companies among the 25 quality applications we had received. A generative AI platform, a specialized conversational assistant, and a tool for auditing generative AI will allow us to develop solutions adapted to our missions. II. The application at two new frontiers: tokenized finance, and the climate To conquer these new frontiers, you have to know how to play as a team. In this context, the ACPR, the Banque de France and the AMF are full partners. I would like to illustrate this in two areas "at the frontiers": crypto-assets, and climate risk.  Tokenized finance, crypto-assets, and the DeFI ecosystem The first "frontier", and perhaps the most obvious for our Fintechs, is that of tokenised finance. The biockchain technology, born in the crypto-asset ecosystem, could bring undeniable benefits to the functioning of financial markets in terms of transparency or immediacy. We are therefore supporting private actors in the implementation of the Vl Pilot Regime, not only as competent authorities, but also by carrying out work at the Banque de France with a view to an interbank central bank digital currency (CBDC)". And we are mobilizing to wish for and prepare a future "MiCA 2" regulation, after the adoption of MiCA, this pioneering regulation in Europe. We must deal with at least two subjects. On the one hand, "crypto conglomerates" - groups with multiple subsidiaries, activities and geographical locations - which should be subject to transparency rules, in particular the presentation of consolidated accounts. The sharing of information between jurisdictions appears to be an essential element in understanding their overall structure, the interdependencies between entities and the associated risks. On the other hand, DeFI, or "disintermediated finance" which seems a much more appropriate qualifier than "decentralized finance" (due to the absence of intermediaries, and the high level of centralization observed in practice). The MiCA regulation provides for a report by the end of 2024 on these new services, which already have 2 million Vl users". It is estimated that by value, DeFi accounts for less than 5% of the lx crypto market : the value of DeFi assets has risen from around 180 billion at the end of 2021 to around 40 billion today, on the heels of the bankruptcy of several crypto players. Its size is therefore reduced. In addition, its use cases are currently limited. So why should we be interested in this subject? For at least two reasons: DeFi presents many risks, especially for individuals (for example, it concentrates 80% of crypto-asset thefts according to some estimates); above all, it could foreshadow some of the transformations to come in finance Xl. It is with this in mind that the ACPR, last spring, submitted a discussion paper for public consultation outlining the first regulatory avenues. This consultation was widely received and resulted in some forty high-quality responses, which often confirmed, sometimes nuanced or enriched the ACPR's analyses. A summary of this feedback was published on October 12x". We are convinced that it is possible and desirable to build a regulatory framework adapted to DeFi, with three main axes:  enact measures relating to the reliability of biockchain infrastructures on which DeFi - or other activities related to the tokenization of finance - would be developed;  develop rules, for example certification , adapted to the nature and operation of Smart contracts Xl";  Define governance and operations management to ensure adequate protection of users against these complex and volatile crypto-assets. Of course, these first avenues will have to be the subject of further reflection and debate in a European context; some of them also deserve to be explored in greater depth at the technical level. This is why, under the aegis of this Fintech Forum, the ACPR and the AMF have decided to launch a working group dedicated to the certification of smart contracts in the coming weeks , an avenue that is attracting strong interest from respondents.  Climate risk I come to the second "frontier" - which is by far the first in terms of issues at stake - that of climate risk - I would like to thank Valerie Masson-Delmotte for the insight she will provide during our morning. The importance of this risk is well established, with consequences that will be decisive for the financial sector and the central banks XIV. After being a pioneer in 2017 by creating the Network for the Greening of the Financial System xv (NGFS), the Banque de France - recognised by NGOs as the greenest central bank in the G20 - is currently carrying out a large-scale project: that of a climate indicator that will complement the financial rating of French companies. This indicator will make it possible to measure their degree of preparedness and consideration of physical and transition risks, with a quantitative but also qualitative dimension. It is being built gradually with field tests, then applied to samples of increasing size (550 companies this year), and will be expanded in the longer term in consultation with the companies themselves and their representatives. Its interest is twofold. For companies, this single, objective metric based on recognized methodologies will make it possible to avoid a multiplication of reports, and to situate their transition over time and in relation to the average of their sector. For banks, it will be an additional, reliable and independent source of information. Our contribution to greener finance calls for others, those of all the innovative players in the ecosystem - Fintechs or Greentechs - who will be able to develop tools that facilitate information, decision-making and, ultimately, the emergence of finance that is equal to our environmental challenges. *** I will conclude this speech with Rene Magritte, a Belgian painter who was certainly not a specialist in finance: "To be a surrealist is to banish from the mind the 'deja vu' and to look for the not yet seen". You, Fintechs, are fully rooted in the real world, but you are definitely participating in its transformation, going beyond established models. We, the ACPR and the AMF, are realists but also focused on the "not yet seen". It is up to all of us, collectively, to make the most of technological innovations. Thank you for your attention. Title: Monetary Sovereignty in the Twenty-First Century
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Governor ''J Monetary sovereignty in the twenty-first century Published on November 14, 2023 Conference at the Council of State "Monetary sovereignty in the twenty-first century" - Paris, 14 November 2023 Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France Mr. President of the Constitutional Council [ Laurent Fabius], Vice-President of the Council of State [ Didier-Roland Tabuteau], General [Andre Lanata], Madam President of the section [Martine de Boisdeffre], Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very honoured by your invitation to this symposium on sovereignty. I realize, however, that it has little to do with my person, but a lot with the object I represent: money is a natural, almost obvious participant here. It is a classic attribute of sovereignty theorized since the sixteenth century by Jean Bodin: "only he who has the power to make the law, who can give law to money". This power to mint money was embodied for a long time in the person of the King: Philip IV the Fair (1285-1314) was the first in France to put gold coins in his effigy. But it was Louis XIII who gave them his own name in 1640: the term "Louis d'or" even partially spanned the Revolution, and then gradually gave way to the "Napoleon". By metonymy, the " sovereign" [sovereigri) is the name of a British gold coin minted since 1489. This equivalence is therefore several centuries old; Nevertheless, I would like to revisit it this evening under two headings: (i) first, that of the relationship between monetary sovereignty and political sovereignty, with two of its contemporary metamorphoses, (ii) secondly, the most acute challenge of the day, but perhaps less perceived, which is - with the help of technology - the revived competition of private "currencies" with regard to public money. I. Monetary sovereignty and Political sovereignty The assertion of monetary sovereignty has certainly been one of the most powerful instruments in the construction of national unity and state sovereignty. The gradual centralization of the minting monopoly - which has been at work for France since the Middle Ages - and the promotion of national currencies have been a vector of national economic integration. The aim was thus twofold: to materialize the borders of the domestic market, and to face competition from international foreign currencies such as the guilder or the ducat. Coins were also used for their symbolic function to forge a sense of national unity, and served as a medium for national imagery. It was in this context of joint assertion of monetary and national sovereignty that central banks were created between the sixteenth and twentieth centuries." Their history is strongly marked by their respective national experiences: some were created to meet the financing needs of states, such as the Bank of England (1694), others to facilitate payments, such as the Bank of the States of Sweden (1668). The Banque de France was founded in 1800 under the Consulate - just a few weeks after the Council of State... - in a broader movement to build French institutions, these "granite masses" capable of unifying the "grains of sand" of the nation. Autonomous, but allied with the government, the Banque de France obtained the privilege of issuing banknotes (1803, 1848), and participated in the consolidation of national unity in the territory, in particular through the development of its network of branches. Overall, the functions of central banks converged from the nineteenth century onwards to gradually arrive at their modern version: operators of monetary policy, managers of payment systems, and guarantors of financial stability... but no more, I must repeat, state financiers. This historical heritage has resulted in a still very "Westphalian"111 vision of monetary sovereignty, according to which the issuance of money and the management of monetary policy are sovereign prerogatives managed by nation-states. It is here, however, that I would like to come to two potential contemporary metamorphoses. a) The euro, a currency without a state... Or do you start a European sovereignty? For the Westphalian vision, the project of European monetary union wanted in particular by Francois Mitterrand and Helmut Kohl from 1989-90 is undoubtedly a shake-up, to the point of a pure and simple loss of sovereignty for the member countries. The founding fathers of the euro responded to this by freely choosing greater effective sovereignty, and here I quote Jacques Delors: "It is by sharing our national sovereignty that we can better defend our common interests"IV. Let us be clear: the monetary policy of many was previously largely anchored in practice to that of the Deutsche Mark in the framework of the European Monetary System, a necessary but not sufficient step. The Westphalian order was in danger of becoming a German monetary order. The advent of the euro has made it possible to ensure collegiality in monetary policy decisions within the Governing Council. The ECB has also become one of the most influential central banks in the world - the euro being the second international reserve and exchange currency - which gives it a better capacity to absorb shocks, coupled with greater agility and autonomy in its decisions, including in relation to the US Federal Reserve. In the words of Mario Draghi, Europe has gained a "capacity to influence its destiny"VI. Is it a stable, self-sufficient stage? American economists strongly doubted it thirty years ago: a currency without a unitary state could not work. And yet, the euro has continued to grow stronger through the harsh crises of our twenty-first century, thanks to strong institutions and an unwavering common will of Europeans. For the federalists, too, monetary union imperatively calls for political union: the answer here is not mine. I would simply point out, through all the international meetings in which I participate, that Europe has invented a form of monetary sovereignty that is recognised - and sometimes envied - by the whole world. b) The independence of the central bank, but under two political conditions The second metamorphosis lies in an institutional evolution: during the twentieth century, central banks were gradually given independence from political power again. This pragmatic movement became widespread in developed countries from the 1980s onwards, in reaction in particular to the great inflationary wave of the 1960s and 70s and to two temptations: that of monetary financing of public debt; that of the rise in interest rates that is too late because it is still unpopular. This year also sees the 30th anniversary of the 1993 law marking the independence of the Banque de France7", the ECB also benefits from a strong independence under the European treaties7111. But "independence" does not mean "isolation", and can only be the result of two very clear political conditions: (i) An ex ante condition : independence is obviously not self-conferred, but granted by the democratic power for a specific mandate, that of price stability, fixed by the European treaties and ratified in France by the 1992 referendum. The ECB has clarified the definition, refined in 2021 during the strategic review: maintaining inflation at 2% over the medium term. Faced with the surge in inflation during 2022, the ECB has raised its key rates accordingly: the remedy is not always pleasant, but it is effective; Inflation is now falling to 2.9% in October, and we are confident that we will return to the 2% target by 2025. (ii) An exposed condition : the essential counterpart is to be accountable to elected officials and citizens for the proper accomplishment of this mandate. The ECB is regularly heard by European parliamentarians, as is the Banque de France in the National Assembly and the Senate. We are constantly developing our communication with the general public, for example through the annual monetary policy meetings in all regions. Monetary policy may seem austere, but it doesn't have to be abstruse. If we did not have results on our mandate, if we did not know how to account for them to our fellow citizens, then our independence would lose its very raison d'etre. Fortunately, this is not the case: the Eurosystem's long-term results allow the euro to benefit from a very high degree of confidence (78%) - and one that has been steadily increasing over the past 20 years - from the 350 million Europeans who share it. II. Public and private money I would now like to revisit sovereignty through another approach, that of the articulation between public and private money. This distinction is rarely perceived by the general public, and yet it is as old as money: in the words of Fernand Braudel, "when commodities are exchanged, a monetary stammering is immediately heard. A more desired or more abundant commodity plays the role of money"XI. Similarly, bills of exchange between merchants at fairs in the Middle Ages were used as instruments of private payment. They were at the origin of the first bank credit activities, notably by the Lombard bankers. The gradual introduction of "public" central bank money as a common and safe settlement asset has since become the rule. It is now a public good taken for granted, at least in advanced economies. However, the existence of private currencies does not belong in the history books. Only a fraction of money is currently held in its public or "fiduciary" form, which are central bank coins and notes . With the dematerialization of means of payment - transfers, cards, mobile phones - the vast majority of the money we hold is "scriptural" commercial bank money . The de facto equivalence between the two types of money is not an identity in law; it is based on the de facto guarantee of their convertibility at par by the public authorities: the money of the various commercial banks therefore benefits from the collective "anchor of trust" of public money. These challenges are now renewed by technological developments. There are new mediums: the tokenization of finance, i.e. the representation in digital form of money, but also of financial assets and contracts integrated into autonomous blockchains. And there are obviously new players to drive these developments: the globalized digital Bigtechs, American or Chinese, but none of which is European or public, in a context where the European payments market is already dominated by international operators. The conjunction of these media and these actors could give rise to private quasi-"currencies" with a global reach, without public anchoring: Meta's Libra/Diem project in 2019 was an example of this. The abandonment of Libra should not be deceived: the real threat to monetary sovereignty seems to me to lie here today, in the privatisation and "de-Europeanisation" of payments. Such a threat can and must fortunately provoke a twofold reaction from the public authorities:  Regulating these private assets in order to limit their intrinsic risks (money laundering, customer protection, etc.) and their misuse, while promoting innovation: Europe has been a pioneer in this area, by adopting dedicated regulation (Market In Crypto-Assets); the United States has unfortunately not yet done so.  In addition, central bank public money, which has been in paper form for several centuries, has no reason to remain aloof from the technological breakthrough of digitalization and tokenization. That's why together with the ECB, to expand the choice beyond banknotes, we are currently exploring both sides of digital currency, both in its use as a retail payment, but also as a "wholesale" settlement asset. The potential issuance of a digital euro must be done in partnership with private banks in order to pursue the complementarity between the two types of money. But the very legitimacy of central banks, in the name of public authorities, remains the ability to mint money, whatever form it takes. And I am betting in front of you that a digital euro will see the light of day in this decade, to guarantee European monetary sovereignty in the long term. I would like to conclude with our common founder, Napoleon Bonaparte, who said that "money has no country." Yes, but the fatherland needs a currency, and the currency needs a sovereign. The European monetary success certainly modifies the conditions for its exercise, but not the principle. Defending our monetary sovereignty today means further strengthening the euro in a world marked by a new situation: digitalisation, geopolitical tensions, and great economic uncertainty. Rest assured that we, the central bankers, are mobilized in this fight. Thank you for your attention. U. Bodin, The Six Books of the Republic, 1576. Title: Building the payments of tomorrow, for Europe and beyond
text: Speech Payment methods Building the payments of tomorrow, for Europe and beyond Published on November 16, 2023 Singapore Fintech Festival -November 16, 2023 Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Bank of France BANK OF FRANCE ''FF EUROSYSTEM Menon for inviting me to speak at the Singapore Fintech Festival. Allow me to pay tribute to your twelve years as Director-General of the Monetary Authority of Canada. Singapore (MAS), as well as to your excellent chairmanship of the NGFS. Two years ago, Ravi gave one of his remarkable speeches here, focusing on three characters from Greco-Roman mythology: Juno, Plutus, and Mercury. Today, I'll talk about another part of this mythology, starting with Daedalus, the architect of a masterpiece built for a specific purpose: to imprison and remove the Minotaur - a half-man, half-bull, bloodthirsty monster. Central banks are similar to Daedalus: they are the main architects of our current monetary and financial system. This system was designed to give the private sector room for manoeuvre to innovate and develop activities that fit well into this overall framework, from an operational and regulatory point of view. This is why we, the central banks, can be considered the main architect, but not the only architect. Our architecture is not set in stone: it has never stopped evolving, and is destined to continue to evolve, at the pace of the most recent technologies. And so far, we have been able to do so while avoiding monetary and financial instability, which is "our" Minotaur. His mere existence had even been more or less forgotten. But the monster has recently woken up, with, in particular, the rise of innovations independent and insufficiently regulated financial institutions. First-generation cryptoassets, so-called " stablecoins " and DeFI protocols have emerged one after the other; these wild constructs (albeit to varying degrees) have already led to excessive volatility, insufficient consumer protection, vulnerabilities bankruptcies and insolvencies, among others, which could spread to the entire financial system. Should the principal architect order the destruction of these constructions, and prohibit them from now on? It would be better if not, BANK OF FRANCE ''W EUROSYSTEM To shape our construction accordingly, so that it remains state-of-the-art, fluid and consistent with its environment. Central banks are thus also, so to speak, doubly responsible for the Ariadne's thread, by ensuring trust and creating new bridges, so that everyone can find their way. It is well known that Asia is open to technology and that MAS in particular is proactive in this area. It may be less well known, but Europe and France are just as proactive. I will illustrate this concretely by recalling what the Banque de France and the Eurosystem have achieved so far, and our new projects, many of which are related to the exploratory work on central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). I will start with the interbank CBDC, for which the Banque de France has been a pioneer by conducting twelve experiments since November 2020. We explored all the use cases identified for all types of DLT (public and private) with a wide range of public and private partners3. These experiments have shown that central banks will be able to steer the supply of interbank CBDC money  which is essential to anchor the supply of the central bank money and, therefore, financial stability in the field of tokenization. We test different technologies in our experiments: we improve our DLT [DLS3] and, in parallel, we are exploring other protocols and blockchains, both private and public. The Banque de France is now also actively involved in the Eurosystem's exploratory work on the settlement of tokenised assets in central bank money, which was launched last April4. With our DL3S technology, we are originally one of the three solutions that will be used during 2024 for experiments and trials, the latter involving real transactions. The Eurosystem has already published the envisaged eligibility criteria and a survey5, ahead of a formal call for applications that will be launched in Building the payments of tomorrow, for the future of the Eurosystem. BANK OF FRANCE ''W EUROSYSTEM differ significantly from stablecoins, and could potentially complement the issuance of an interbank CBDC. This brings me to the detailed CBDC: after having conducted a phase After a two-year investigation, the Eurosystem recently launched the preparatory phase that will lay the foundations for a possible digital euro6. This "digital banknote" will have the same features as the Current cash equivalents: it will be accepted throughout the euro area thanks to its legal tender7 and will meet the highest standards in terms of Privacy protection and its basic features will be free for individuals8. In addition, the digital euro will bring additional advantages over banknotes: it will allow the use of central bank money in e-commerce, for peer-to-peer payments, as well as for conditional payments, and will promote financial inclusion in the digital age. Similarly, the digital euro will be distributed through banks: we are not and will not become competitors of commercial banks. Once again, the currency will remain a public-private partnership. But the confidence that commercial bank money inspires is anchored by its full equivalence and permanent convertibility, 1:1, to central bank money. Loosening this public anchorage would sooner or later mean compromising trust; tokenized central bank money will be the necessary "security pivot", and will also serve as an "innovation platform"9. The payments ecosystem as a whole will therefore benefit: the digital euro system we are developing will enable the emergence of open acceptance standards, fostering convergence and providing a common basis from which to pursue innovations. With its pan-European digital wallet payment solution called "v The European Payments Initiative (EPI), led by the private sector, will be able to take full advantage of this. From a more global perspective, we are actively working to BANK OF FRANCE ''W EUROSYSTEM remedy these problems and thus improve payments cross-border.  In the short and medium term, we are studying the creation of bridges between payment systems. Some projects could be implemented quickly, such as the BIS Nexus platform, which aims to enable individuals to make instant cross-border payments by connecting fast payment systems around the world (including the Eurosystem's TIPS service).  Longer-term projects with a more global reach could open up new avenues. The BIS10 and the IMF11 reflect Actively to integrated platforms, which would bring together tokenized central bank money, tokenized deposits, and tokenized financial assets. In particular, the BIS project for a unified ledger is very promising, as it would make CBDCs inherently interoperable and significantly facilitate cross-border payments. We look forward to contributing to this project." At the same time, we are continuing our experiments, by collaboration with the BIS, the IMF and the national central banks. After the Mariana project conducted under the aegis of the BIS Innovation Hub, I am pleased to announce that the Banque de France will soon participate in the MAS Guardian project. Our joint experiment, "The Guardians", will focus on multi-CBDCs and potentially tokenized deposits in cross-border repo and cross-currency transactions. I will conclude with one of our contemporary architects, Frank Gehry, who was one of the very first to use the potential of computers to design iconic buildings. He once said that "architecture should speak of its time and place, but aspires to be timeless." This is precisely what we, the central banks, are doing to We are striving to realize once again, together with private partners. Thank you for your attention.
