Title: The current solidity of banks and insurance companies, for the proper financing of the French economy
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Financements "'J ( 3 The current soundness of banks and Insurance, for the sake of Financing the French economy Published on November 17, 2023 Conference of the French Prudential Supervision and Resolution Authority (ACPR) - Paris, Palais Brongniart, 17 November 2023 Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France and President of the ACPR Ladies and Gentlemen, I am very pleased to welcome you to this new edition of the ACPR Conference. Its theme this year was "The financial sector facing the new situation of inflation and rising interest rates". Without wanting to kill the suspense at the outset, I can already say that this rise in interest rates is generally benefiting both banks and insurance companies. More broadly, in a year 2023 that is still tinged with high uncertainty, the French financial sector has confirmed its great resilience (I). These forces should enable it, in a period of slowdown, to ensure sound financing of the French economy (II). I. In a year of strong uncertainties, the financial sector French has confirmed great resilience The year 2023 was once again marked by an exceptional level of uncertainty: the geopolitical context - from Ukraine to Israel, unfortunately - a source of instability and economic and financial volatility; banking turbulence in the United States and Switzerland at the beginning of the year; and inflation remained too high. Eurosystem policy rates have increased by 450 basis points since July 2022, raising the deposit facility rate to 4% in September, in the face of inflation that had peaked at 10.6% in the euro area in October 2022. At 2.9% last month, inflation has been significantly reduced. Energy prices certainly contribute to this, but core inflation (excluding energy and food) also continues to decline: at 4.2% in the euro area and even less in France (3.5%), it has clearly passed its peak in the spring. This is proof of the effectiveness of monetary policy, which fully justifies the end of the sequence of rate hikes decided by the Governing Council on 26 October. Our monetary policy must now be guided by confidence and patience: confidence that we are moving resolutely on the path of inflation falling back to 2% by 2025; patience on the stabilisation of interest rates at their current level, for the time still proportionate to their full transmission.  Profitability and solvency Reinforced There can be no doubt: European banks are generally benefiting from the past increase in key rates, although there is a certain time lag for French banks due to their business model. Interest rates that are mostly fixed to their assets (97% of outstanding mortgage loans are at a fixed rate), and regulated savings to liabilities lead to a slower adaptation of financial conditions in France. A mechanical catch-up is expected in the coming quarters, with the continued renewal of French banks' assets and liabilities. This temporary delay has been mitigated by the decision to stabilise the Livret A rate, which was maintained at 3% on 1 August and is expected to remain stable at this level until at least 1 February 2025. This is a very favourable decision for the banks' interest margin; it has as its counterpart, I would remind you, an accelerated development of the LEP (Livret d'epargne Populaire) - which reached 10.3 million holders in September 2023, and should exceed 12.5 million next summer. This stabilisation of the Livret A rate is also aimed at ensuring a sound financing of the French economy, as we will come back to later. The financial results of the French banking sector have already remained very solid, with pre-tax income of the 6 largest groups of 21.7 billion in the 1st half of 2023, up 2.5% compared to the 1st half of 2022, and a trending increase in net banking income (NBI) since the beginning of 2022. The solvency ratio of French banks improved again as a result, reaching 15.6% at the end of the 1st half of the year compared to 15.1% at the end of 2022, well above regulatory requirements. In the third quarter of 2023, the results published by the four main French banking groups2 show more contrasted performances, with revenues from retail activities in France sometimes weighed down by interest rate hedging strategies that may have proved costly in the current interest rate environment3. The rise in interest rates also improves the profitability of the insurance sector: as the duration of liabilities is greater than that of assets, this has a positive impact on the balance sheet and, therefore, on the solvency of insurance companies. Thus, the coverage rate of the Solvency Capital Required (CSR) of insurance companies increased from 247% in the 4th quarter of 2022 to 255% in the 2nd quarter of 2023. More prospectively, the rise in interest rates opens up the possibility of changing the composition of portfolios towards more remunerative assets. This also leads to customer arbitrage, with life insurance policy redemptions of up to 62 billion on npiif nrpmiprQ mni.c; rlp 1'annep 202.3 Mnnt 47 billionc: on Ipq rnntmt.c: pn euro funds); The buyback-to-premium ratio nevertheless remains relatively contained at 73% in Q3 2023, well below the historical peak of 100% at the end of 2011. We remain attentive to the slowdown in net inflows from life insurance, and to reallocations to other savings products insofar as they induce more risk of capital losses and liquidity risk. Another strong point: despite the economic slowdown, the cost of risk for banks has not risen significantly, and even remains at a moderate level. The quality of assets is indeed maintained: the rate of non-performing loans on households remains stable, and that on corporate loans is marginally upwards, approaching 4% at the end of June 2023. This is due in particular to the high proportion of fixed rates in business loans. The solidity of French banks in this regard is attested by the results of the European stress tests published at the end of July. We do not expect a general deterioration in the cost of risk in the short or medium term, but we remain attentive to the creditworthiness of borrowers. In particular, some commercial real estate players are already weakened by structural changes in their business segment as well as by their high level of debt, which makes them more vulnerable to rising financing costs.  Liquidity generally preserved Liquidity is a subject on which real fears have been expressed after the failures of Silicon Valley Bank in the United States and Credit Switzerland, in particular. Eight months later, however, French banks benefit from a high degree of stability in total deposits, and liquidity coverage ratios (LCRs ) that remain well above 100%. What we are seeing with the rise in interest rates is therefore not a global "flight of deposits" - on the contrary - but trade-offs: a shift from sight deposits to interest-bearing deposits, not only by households but also by companies, which have increased their holdings of term deposits and savings accounts since mid-2022. Overall, since July 2022, households have increased their deposits more (63 billion) than companies have reduced them (-40 billion) in favour of money market funds. And this follows, for the record, a period of historic increase in deposits between 2011 and 2022, a period during which deposits from non-financial customers grew by 6.4% per year on average. These aggregate figures largely reflect intra-group reallocations of savings products, as evidenced by the stability of each banking group's shares in the total deposits collected from households and businesses over the same period. I want to say it clearly: there is therefore no reason for deposits to be the subject of a "war"; Nor is there any reason for banks to seek to target "excess liquidity" individually. Especially since monetary policy will result in a high level of bank liquidity for a long time. It currently stands at around 3,600 billion, and market analysts anticipate, for example, that this excess liquidity will only decrease gradually, and would only be halved by the end of 2026. These good results of the French financial sector are not due to chance: they can be explained by the good management of the institutions, and by the very reassuring "European couple" of demanding regulations (transposition of Basel 3, the equivalent of which is now expected in the United States for the majority of banks) and a unilateral and effective supervision of the SSM established on the recognised model of the ACPR. However, one subject in particular remains to be completed in Europe: the resolution. The framework already in force for large groups must be deepened, to allow for greater use of this mechanism. Europe is better at preventing banking crises ex-ante than the United States; however, it is not a given that it will be able to deal with them ex-post as well . Recent events have shown that the availability of liquidity in times of stress, potentially for significant amounts, is a key problem. While the framework for the ECB to provide "Eurosystem liquidity for resolution" remains to be built, we also need to think carefully about how to ensure the effective availability of existing sources of funding, including deposit guarantee funds. II. These forces must enable the financial sector to ensure a Healthy financing of the French economy, in a period of slowdown In other countries, the banking sector is even more profitable and profitable than it is currently in France. These record profits are the subject of criticism and circumstantial surcharges elsewhere: it is fortunate, in my opinion, that this is not the case in France. But the counterpart of the solidity of the banking system must be the good financing of our economy.  Financing of companies still well assured On the business side (including SMEs and VSEs), access to credit seems to remain well preserved. Driven by investment loans, outstanding loans continued to grow for all sizes of companies at a pace that gradually moderated (3.0% year-on-year in September), in line with lower demand for credit from non-financial corporations. Compared to our European neighbours, access to bank credit also remains more favourable in France: interest rates on new loans are on average lower (4.6% in France in September compared to 5.05% in the euro zone); The share of accepted financing requests remained stable, both in investment and in cash, according to our quarterly survey published yesterday evening. The Credit Mediation, which is present in all the departmental branches of the Banque de France, remains relatively little used with, on average, just over a hundred cases per month over the past year. However, the steady deceleration in outstanding loans to companies invites us to remain attentive.  A more sensitive subject on real estate loans On the side of households and real estate loans, the subject is more sensitive. Output excluding renegotiations fell to a low of 9.2 billion in September, almost identical to the monthly average observed before 2015 and the implementation of ultra-accommodative monetary policy. This slowdown in the production of housing credit makes sense given the point at which we are in the interest rate cycle. Households, after having made massive use of mortgage loans until mid-2022, are taking a wait-and-see approach in the face of higher interest rates - even if they remain lower in France than those observed in our European neighbours - and, above all, with property prices which, correspondingly, have only begun to fall since the beginning of the year at the national level. But beyond a wait-and-see demand, there is still a widespread question about supply, and the fact that "banks would no longer lend". This suspicion, even if it is exaggerated, is not good for anyone: neither for the banks and their image; nor for the housing sector, because it can contribute to self-censorship by borrowers; nor for the quality of the overall economic diagnosis. The excessive "halo" around real estate loans undoubtedly prevents us from calmly shedding light on other levers of action necessary in the sector: the supply of land; the proliferation of regulatory standards; an interweaving of tax incentives and subsidies of a complexity rarely equalled elsewhere in Europe. Progress is being made on these various subjects, but this morning I want to examine with you two questions: The HCSF (High Council for Financial Stability) standards are an easy and recurrent candidate for criticism, but - need we say it again? - the HCSF is not the result of the Banque de France but of the law of the Republic, namely the 2013 banking law. In recent years, it has unanimously fulfilled its mission of risk prevention in the face of the continuous and singular increase in household debt, and the marked drift in loan terms and repayment burden. In addition, its standards are not biting today, since banks have the capacity to produce more on all the flexibilities offered by the HCSF decision within the 20% margin. The total flexibility of 20% on the main parameters, effort rate and duration of loans (currently set at 35% and 25 years maximum), was only used at an average of 14.3% in the 3rd quarter of 2023. In particular, the 6% flexibility on rental investment is only used at 2.6%. Making more use of flexibilities, rather than contesting them, is the best way for banks to produce more loans... provided, of course, that the volume of production of "compliant" loans is maintained: we will ensure this, so that longer and riskier loans do not replace safer loans. That being said, as indicated in its press release of 26 September4, the HCSF will study any new technical adjustments, provided that they do not lead to an increase in the risk of over-indebtedness.  The refusal rate of banks, at the same risk, is not expected to increase. This rate is not precisely measured, but there is a diffuse feeling that it has risen. In view of the diagnosis I made in the first part, there would be no justification for this: neither on profitability - margins have recovered, thanks in particular to the accelerated increase in the exceptional usury rate in 2023; nor on liquidity, where an "overadjustment" of networks on the ground would be counterproductive, for example by seeking a much increased coverage of loans by deposits. In any case, it seems necessary and in the collective interest to better monitor these refusal rates. Among our initial internal reflections, I would like to mention two non-exclusive avenues:  The collection of data from various sources, including the Eurosystem's quarterly bank lending survey (BLS ). We are vigilant after the increase in Q3 in the evolution of refusal rates and balance sheet constraints put forward by French banks.  I believe that it would be in the common interest to consider, between banking players and public authorities, and temporarily for the current phase of the cycle, opening an amicable procedure: this would target mortgage loans that appear to be solvent and which have given rise to refusal, as exists for business loans. We will continue the enhanced individual dialogue between the banks and the ACPR on mortgage lending policies, which is of course part of the more general dialogue conducted within the framework of the Single Supervisory Mechanism. Let me conclude by broadening the perspective even further. Major structural challenges, including digitalization in the field of payments, lie ahead. French and European banks are strong enough to respond in an offensive and innovative way. In parallel with the EPI project and a tokenization of bank deposits, the central bank digital currency (CBDC), retail or interbank project, is an example. Title: "The Franco-German couple is necessary": the appeal of the governor of the Bank of France and the president of the Bundesbank
text: "The Franco-German couple ": the appeal of the Bank of Francs, President of the Bundes Stakeholder Published on November 20, 2023 Le Figaro: In the face of inflation and strong geopolitical tensions, Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France, and Joachim Nagel, President of the Bundesbank, call on Europe to rely on Franco-German friendship. By speaking with one voice, we will have more weight in the world, they argue. What does friendship mean? This does not always mean seeing things the same way, but rather having the ability to establish a common foundation. France and Germany are effective friends. By working together, our two countries have helped move Europe forward. In this article, we wish to illustrate the essence and strength of the Franco-German friendship through two themes that are at the heart of our daily work: the economy and the currency. More than 60 years have passed since President Charles de Gaulle and Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed the elysee Treaty. But the close cooperation between our two countries had begun long before: in 1950, the French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman proposed the Coal and Steel Community, intended to unite French and German heavy industries and guarantee peace. The alliance forged between our two countries was a first step on the road to European integration: Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Italy later joined the Coal and Steel Community. In 1993, the economic integration of our continent led to a common internal market. At the turn of the millennium, it reached a further stage with monetary union. Today, the euro is a currency used by more than 340 million people in 20 countries. From 2009 onwards, the global financial crisis evolved into a sovereign debt crisis in the euro area. Some highly indebted euro area Member States faced the prospect of losing access to capital markets and the euro area faced the danger of a break-up. Conversely, Europe has become more solid: the Member States have established a rescue shield, created the European Stability Mechanism and the Banking Union. The resolution of the crisis was achieved thanks to the efforts of many. At the same time, it testifies to the strength of the Franco-German friendship. Our countries had different opinions. France was in favour of greater debt mutualisation, while Germany insisted on the individual responsibility of the Member States. But in a dialogue based on trust, our governments have managed to find compromises. France and Germany once again reached a successful compromise in 2020 when, in the face of the coronavirus crisis, it was decided to create the 750 billion Next Generation EU fund and invest in the future of Europe. We  the governors of the twenty national central banks of the euro area and the members of the ECB's Executive Board, alongside Christine Lagarde  show respect and trust in each other in the ECB's Governing Council, the body in which we take monetary policy decisions. Our objective is price stability, i.e. an inflation target of 2% over the medium term. With an inflation rate of 2.9%, but declining rapidly at the time of going to press, we have not yet reached that target. Inflation is hitting the weakest members of society particularly hard, and it is also making it more difficult to make the long-term investments needed to ensure the future viability of our economies. There are several reasons why inflation is too high. Has our expansionary monetary policy of previous years contributed to the rise in prices? Between 2013 and 2020, we saw that inflation was too low, sometimes even negative. Until recently, therefore, it was our responsibility to ensure that prices rose more sharply. What matters is that today, too, our actions are aligned with the 2% inflation target  and that's what we're doing: in the space of 14 months, we've raised interest rates by 450 basis points, faster and harder than ever before. Both of us have not always fully agreed on all the measures that have been taken, but together with our colleagues in the ECB's Governing Council, we have been able to reach a decision. And inflation is falling significantly. The challenges facing Europe and the euro are intensifying and becoming more complex. In addition to the long-term tasks related to climate change, our ageing population and digitalisation, we have to deal with geopolitical crises. Actors representing different parts of the globe are making their voices heard. In this context, the Franco-German friendship is not losing its importance, quite the contrary. To divide us would be to condemn us, and to condemn Europe. If, on the other hand, we speak with one voice, our words will carry more weight. And if Europe manages to speak with one voice, perhaps by relying on the Franco-German core, it will have an important role to play in the world. Economic integration led to the unification of Europe. We still have a lot of progress to make in this area: a real Capital Markets Union to finance the green transition  for which we advocated together a year ago; common and balanced rules on fiscal policy  the euro area needs a stability framework; A Digital Single Market, which would combine regulation, funding and talent development so that the unique advantage of our European size benefits European innovation. But Russia's war against Ukraine brutally shows us that integration does not guarantee peace. A stable Europe benefits greatly from close coordination between France and Germany, beyond economic policy. It is true that our countries sometimes have divergent opinions in areas such as foreign affairs, security and energy. We welcome the compromise reached in October to reform the EU electricity market. This is just one example among many others of the constant ability of France and Germany to find common ground. If our friendship maintains this quality, we can continue to help Europe move forward. We are both fully dedicated to achieving this essential goal. Updated on November 21, 2023

Nous - les gouverneurs des vingt banques centrales nationales de la zone euro et les membres du directoire de la BCE, aux cts de Christine Lagarde - faisons preuve de respect et de confiance les uns envers les autres au sein du Conseil des gouverneurs de la BCE, cette instance au sein de laquelle nous prenons les dcisions de politique montaire. Ce qui importe, c'est qu'aujourd'hui aussi, nos actions s'alignent sur la cible d'inflation de 2 % - et c'est ce que nous faisons : en l'espace de 14 mois, nous avons augment les taux d'intrt de 450 points de base, plus rapidement et plus fortement que jamais. Tous les deux, nous n'avons pas toujours t pleinement d'accord sur toutes les mesures qui ont t prises, mais avec nos collgues au sein du Conseil des gouverneurs de la BCE, nous avons pu parvenir  une dcision. Et l'inflation diminue significativement. Les dfis auxquels sont confronts l'Europe et l'euro s'intensifient et se complexifient. Outre les missions  long terme lies au changement climatique, au vieillissement de notre population et  la numrisation, nous devons faire face  des crises gopolitiques. Des acteurs reprsentant diffrentes parties du globe font entendre leur voix. Dans ce contexte, l'amiti franco-allemande ne perd pas de son importance, bien au contraire. Nous diviser, ce serait nous condamner, et condamner l'Europe. Si, au contraire, nous parlons d'une seule voix, nos mots auront plus de poids. Et si l'Europe parvient  parler d'une seule voix, peut-tre en s'appuyant sur le noyau franco-allemand, elle aura un rle important  jouer dans le monde. L'intgration conomique a conduit  l'unification de l'Europe. Nous avons encore beaucoup de progrs  faire dans ce domaine : une vritable union des marchs des capitaux pour financer la transition verte - pour laquelle nous avions plaid ensemble il y a un an ; des rgles communes et quilibres en matire de politique budgtaire - la zone euro a besoin d'un cadre de stabilit ; un march unique numrique, qui combinerait la rglementation, le financement et le dveloppement des talents afin que l'avantage unique que constitue notre taille europenne bnficie  l'innovation europenne. Mais la guerre mene par la Russie contre l'Ukraine nous montre avec brutalit que l'intgration ne garantit pas la paix. Une Europe stable bnficie grandement d'une coordination troite entre la France et l'Allemagne au- del de la politique conomique. Il est vrai que nos pays ont parfois des opinions divergentes dans des domaines tels que les affaires trangres, la scurit et l'nergie. Nous saluons le compromis obtenu en octobre pour rformer le march de l'lectricit de l'UE. Il s'agit d'un exemple parmi tant d'autres de la capacit constante de la France et de l'Allemagne  trouver un terrain d'entente. Si notre amiti conserve cette qualit, nous pouvons continuer d'aider l'Europe  aller de l'avant. Nous nous consacrons tous deux pleinement  l'atteinte de cet objectif essentiel. Title: Monetary Policy in Times of Conflict
text: BANK OF FRANCE EUROSYSTEM Speeches Monetary Policy Monetary policy in times of conflict Published on November 20, 2023 SPE Annual Dinner - London, 20 November 2023 Good evening It is a pleasure for me to be in London today, and in particular at the invitation of the Society of Professional Economists. London evokes many things for the French. French economists appreciate the concentration of excellent economic research in London  tonight's list of participants is particularly impressive in this regard. But for French citizens, London also reminds us of an important page in our history: let's not forget that during the Second World War, London welcomed the government in exile of General de Gaulle and Free France. It may seem surprising that I mention this historical episode, as central bankers generally talk about recent economic developments. But today, I'd like to take a longer perspective and focus on a key aspect of our current environment: conflict. In retrospect, the Great Moderation, which began shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall, was a period of peace, rapid economic development and globalization, stability and relative political consensus. Economists were not the only ones to delude themselves that this could be a new permanent regime, the "End of History" or, more modestly, the end of crises and inflation. While the situation had already deteriorated slightly over the last decade, it has deteriorated sharply in a few years, due to global tensions and fragmentation as well as the increase in political conflicts in our countries or groups of countries. What are the implications of this situation for central bankers? I will first try to describe what is "almost indescribable": the nature of these shocks and their economic consequences, before presenting how I think central banks should chart their way through this turbulent new landscape. 1. A new, more confrontational environment  A multiplication of exogenous shocks with far-reaching consequences Shocks are inevitable. However, in recent years, we have seen an increase in their multiplication, as evidenced by an anthology of new words, such as "polycrises" and "megathreats". Today's shocks no longer come "from within" the economic and financial cycles themselves; They are exogenous, with major negative impacts: the worst pandemic since the Spanish flu of 1918, the increase in extreme natural disasters due to climate change, the accentuation of domestic political tensions and "geopolitical tensions"  a euphemism for this word that we hoped would disappear from our vocabulary: war. Let me illustrate these rapid changes with a few graphs. Slide 2 focuses on geopolitical risk. Researchers have developed a synthetic index; This is based on news coverage. After a relatively calm twenty years, the issue of geopolitical tensions is back in the spotlight. Image Geopolitical risk is back Slide 3 presents different metrics of climate change - a very complex and multifaceted phenomenon. On all these charts, 2023 stands out in red: regardless of the metric used, this year is expected to be the worst, by far. Climate change can no longer be denied and it seems to be accelerating. It carries the seeds of potential conflicts: between countries, and between generations, because of the famous "tragedy of the horizon". Image Climate anomalies in 2023: uncharted territory The economic consequences of these global developments are paramount, and I will focus this evening on geopolitical conflicts. The most immediate channel is that of commodity prices. These prices are a major determinant of inflation and therefore play a key role in central bank projections. They are notoriously difficult to predict, as shown in slide 4, which presents historical and forecasted oil prices from several data series in the IMF's World Economic Outlook. Image Oil prices are more difficult to predict Sharp swings in oil prices have been underestimated in the past; in future it could be even more difficult to predict them. Indeed, the prices of materials Former are reacting strongly to geopolitical events, as shown in the following slide (slide 5), which illustrates the volatility of gas prices before and after the invasion of Ukraine. A world where geopolitical tensions are heightened is not only more dangerous, it is also much more uncertain. Image Sharp increase in the volatility of gas prices Secondly, conflicts also mean increased strains on public finances: governments are forced to increase defence spending, but also to protect their citizens from the negative consequences of these shocks, as "insurers of first resort": for example, after the Covid measures, various costly "energy shields" have been deployed in Europe  and the United Kingdom  over the past two years. A third channel is fragmentation. On slide 6, the first graph shows the number of sanctions, by type, and the second focuses on sanctions Commercial: Both charts show a strong increase. The third chart shows global trade and financial flows, which are currently stagnating after a long period of growth: while it is too early to talk about deglobalization, the golden age of globalization is clearly over. Image A more fragmented world Finally, another consequence of geopolitical tensions and conflicts is that multilateralism is going through a crisis unprecedented since 1945: at the WTO of course, but also at the G20 and even at the IMF despite the welcome agreement recently reached on the increase in quotas. This is both a paradox and a problem, as more issues than ever are global and require international cooperation: climate change, pandemic preparedness, digital finance, and crypto-assets, to name just a few themes of what I call "pragmatic multilateralism"1U . More uncertainty and more inflationary shocks, more public spending, more fragmentation and less multilateralism: these are the global economic risks induced by these "periods of conflict". Before I turn to possible responses, let me mention the domestic dimension of conflict  although more peaceful, it also has significant effects.  The response of economic actors and decision-makers is itself increasingly conflictual In many countries, political decision-making has become more confrontational. Brexit is of course the first example that comes to mind. But in the United States, too, it is becoming increasingly difficult to achieve bipartisan solutions. And within EU member states, a government majority is more difficult to achieve, due to the decline of traditional political parties and increased political fragmentation. The Economic Policy Uncertainty Index is a practical way to summarize these developments. Slide 7 shows the global index, but the country indices also show an upward trend. Image Economie policy is more incertain We know that risk-sensitive economic agents respond quickly to increased uncertainty by reducing their investments and purchases of durable goods and hoarding liquidity. But there is also an important indirect effect, which is that necessary structural reforms tend to be postponed when the political landscape is more divided. This is particularly detrimental when the economic challenges are on the supply side  as is the case with the the case now - and no longer on the demand side. This is particularly the case for public finances. Slide 8 shows the level of general government debt in the G7 countries. Image Government net debt at unprecedented levels Public debt has never been so high. This situation is the result of various factors, including of course the Covid pandemic, but it should not hide deeper difficulties. Weaker governments can hardly resist the "contradictory injunctions" to increase spending and reduce taxes: increasing deficits is often the too easy answer to these conflicting objectives. This complicates the mission of central banks against inflation in too many countries today - including arguably the most important - monetary tightening is not sufficiently supported by fiscal tightening. We regularly recall in our Monetary Policy Statement that this inconsistency could "call for an even tighter monetary policy". Let me cite another possible dimension of domestic "conflicts". Inflation has an inherent conflictual component, as recalled in a recent article by Guido Lorenzoni and Ivan Werning v, which echoes previous work by Olivier Blanchard. Conflicts between incompatible aspirations in terms of margins and wages can arise between companies and employees, and potentially lead to an inflationary spiral. Inflation is potentially a conflict of distribution: we have known this since the 1970s. And we've recently seen episodes of greedflation in certain countries or certain sectors, or wage demands that are too high. That said, from a macroeconomic perspective, the recent surge in inflation has not been significantly fueled by a wage-price spiral, nor by a profit-price spiral. Several factors have limited the magnitude of these spirals. First, the prevalence of automatic wage indexation has decreased and wage negotiations are more decentralized. Second, government policies have directly or indirectly limited the impact of sharply rising energy costs on households and businesses, albeit at the expense of higher public debt. Last but not least, the credibility of central banks, coupled with their swift responses, has helped to anchor and coordinate employers' and employees' inflation expectations. This last consideration naturally brings me to the second part of my speech, and so I now come to how central banks should navigate this new turbulent landscape. 2. Central banks are showing more humility, but are not disarmed In today's highly complex environment, it must be admitted, central banks are showing more humility, but they are not disarmed. The word "conflict" being the common thread of my remarks, allow me to borrow from Clausewitz the concept of the "fog of war": " War is the domain of uncertainty; three-quarters of the elements on which the action is based remain in the mists of greater or lesser uncertainty. More than in any other field, a subtle and penetrating intelligence must know how to discern and instinctively appreciate the truth." This comment could, to a large extent, apply to the actions of a central bank (albeit more peacefully!). Let me present in more detail three possible characteristics of this "subtle intelligence": humility; pragmatism; and nevertheless confidence. a) Central banks must show humility 1 V7C11 VV7111111V11W , JV VVFU. VLLCLAO VI V111L7AW O V U.g,llV Cl 11 pVFAllL, Cil CCUV ClU. 1 V111CVL VU.CLL7V Christine Lagarde's speech at Jackson Hole vn: central banks must show humility. The current environment is particularly difficult to predict. Moreover, current shocks - and probably future shocks - are no longer driven by demand - for which monetary policy is most appropriate - but by supply. Addressing the causes and consequences of these supply shocks is primarily a matter for public policy, as well as the private sector. And for a central bank, it is more difficult to control inflation when it results from mainly supply factors. Inflationary supply shocks tend to put downward pressure on real incomes: a monetary policy response that is too quick can increase the volatility of inflation, while ultimately causing a recession if transmission delays are not properly accounted for. On the other hand, when supply shocks are persistent and threaten to cause inflation expectations to lose anchorage, the central bank must respond to keep underlying inflationary pressures under control and prevent so-called second-round effects. But central banks should not give up, quite the contrary. Humility means being clear about what we, the central banks, can or cannot achieve, and what we know and don't know. In this regard, let me suggest a few "rules of conduct":  Focus on our core mandate of price stability. I remain a strong supporter of the role of central banks in the fight against climate change: but climate change has such a significant effect on activity and prices that it must of course be taken into account in order to guarantee price stability. In the face of other legitimate challenges, such as inequality and unemployment, tackling inflation is currently the most effective way to foster inclusive and strong growth.  Focus on actual data, at least as much as on models. Listening to companies and our fellow citizens at the "micro" level is at least as important as modelling at the "macro" level, which remains useful, but cannot claim to be totally accurate in the current context of multiple and unprecedented shocks interacting.  And to learn from some past excesses when it comes to /jforward guidance: our use of forward guidance for interest rates has probably been excessive in principle in the face of exceptionally large and unexpected shocks, and too rigid in its content. We can't totally tie our hands in advance with rules, and should retain some discretion to deal with unexpected V1U data or events . Central banks must be predictable, but they must not be predetermined. In the future, I do not rule out a return to some form of forwardguidance, but considered more indicative, more dependent on the economic situation... and more modest - that is to say, less powerful as an instrument. The aim of this forward-guidance must be to reduce volatility, not to claim to "forge the economic order" for the future: that would be arrogant. b) Be pragmatic in the face of the challenge of more volatile long-term interest rates Central banks are currently facing an additional challenge as regards the "weapons" at their disposal. When they reached their effective floor for short-term policy rates after the global financial crisis, they increasingly lowered long-term interest rates. The combination of the dampening effect of the effective rate floor, the compression of term premiums resulting from asset purchases and endogenous stabilisation through the monetary policy reaction function  through forwardguidance  means that long-term interest rates have been strongly influenced by monetary policies. This process has now been reversed as policy rates have moved significantly away from the effective floor (slide 9) and central banks have signalled that short-term rates are the active monetary policy instrument, with a gradual normalisation of the balance sheet. As a result, long-term interest rates are rising more and more by the price and the premiums in the long term are rising, as you can see in slide 10. Image Policy interest rates in the euro and in the US Image Long yields in the euro area: the role of the term premia Why is that? According to some, the natural rate of interest seems to be rising. Even more likely, high and rising sovereign debt, as well as uncertainty about the future path of public finances, as discussed above, are contributing to the rise in real and nominal risk premiums. This is another reason to plead for a coherent policy mix, with sound fiscal policies. In the euro area, the rise in long-term rates observed until the recent correction seemed to have been largely the result of contagion from the United States (in this respect, there is no deglobalisation). It is too early to say whether these upward pressures on long-term bond yields will resume. But we should expect more volatility in global bond markets, a greater decoupling of short-term and long-term interest rates, and we will need to take pragmatically into account the implications for our domestic monetary policy. The simplest option would be to incorporate this factor into the future path of our main short-term policy rate: further increases in long-term rates would further tighten financial conditions and would be an additional reason not to continue raising short-term interest rates. As for balance sheet policies, we will have to stop our PEPP reinvestments in due course  and perhaps before the end of 2024. But I see no reason today to tie our hands on a specific sequence between our future first cut in key rates and the end of full reinvestments under the PEPP. As long as our rates are in restrictive territory  which will clearly remain the case  reversing the previous balance sheet expansion may be consistent with our overall monetary stance.  Confidence: central banks play an effective anchoring role In the current environment, central banks must and can play the role of anchor more than ever, to reduce uncertainty. The closer we are to the 2% target for average inflation, the less persistent and disruptive relative price shocks will be for the economy  and such supply shocks are likely to be more frequent than in the past. With average inflation If low enough, we could return to "rational inattention" on the part of consumers and businesses and thus reduce the risk of inflationary conflicts. Internal work carried out at the Banque de France highlights a non-linear relationship between the level of inflation and the attention it receives, with a threshold of around 2.5% in the case of France. Therefore, in this very uncertain context, let me mention two reasons for being confident:  We, the ECB, will bring inflation back to 2% by 2025. This includes some judgment: I'm not a 2.0% fetishist to one decimal place; and I am not Inflation , as some economists suggest, would risk clouding expectations, and we would not be able to fulfil our mandate. There can be no doubt about our determination to achieve our target: we have already made significant progress, reducing headline inflation from 10.6% to 2.9% in one year, and core inflation from 5.7% to 4.2% in six months. There could be There will be some jolts in the coming months, but the disinflationary trend is solid and relatively faster than expected on both sides of the Atlantic: look in particular at the encouraging figures in services (where it is estimated at 4.6% in October in the euro area, after a peak of 5.6% in July). The latest developments in Israel and the oil market are not expected to significantly change this trend: we are moving away from a general shock on commodities every day as in 2021-2022.  As we are confident about our target, we can be patient on our instrument. A "smart patience", if I may say so, quite different from stubborn stubbornness: we will adapt to the data, especially the data on economic activity  and I continue to think that we should and can avoid recession, preferring a soft landing trajectory. But the question has shifted too quickly from "when will you stop raising rates?" to "when will you start cutting rates?" In a mountainous environment, there are not only peaks and descents: there are also plateaus, to appreciate the effects of altitude and to look at the view. That's what we're probably going to do, for at least several boards and for the next few quarters. As early as last January, I said that we would probably have finished the hikes "by the summer of 2023" - and we have done so -; Today, I will not give a date for the first reduction in rate. Rather than a timetable, I believe, for the passage of this coming "lock" x, in a key criterion: the return to an inflation outlook compatible with our 2% target, solidly and sustainably. Solidly, that is, supported by actual data on headline inflation, as well as core inflation and wages. Sustainably, i.e. forecasting 2% sufficiently before the end of our projection horizon, and including a decline towards 2% in household and business inflation expectations". Let me conclude by quoting the famous words of Winston Churchill, who said in the House of Commons in 1940: "We will not falter and we will not waver." will not fail (...). We will fight with ever more confidence and growing strength." In a world marked by growing conflict, rest assured that we, as central bankers, will never lay down our arms in the face of inflation, and that in this way we will do our part to reduce what I call "domestic conflicts." We must do so with humility, focusing on our core mandate and on the actual data, rather than pretending to shape the future of the economy in general; and with pragmatism, particularly in the face of more volatile long-term interest rates. But we need to succeed by 2025 with increased confidence: expect, as I said, that our next meetings will be a little more boring. But if that means slightly reduced uncertainty and smart patience before future rate cuts, no one will regret it. Thank you for your attention.  F. Title: Europe's awakening and the Franco-German engine
text: EUROSYSTEM Speech (Banque de France The awakening of Europe and the Franco-German engine Published on December 12, 2023 Frankfurt School of Finance and Management - 12 December 2023 Speech by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, Governor of the Banque de France Dear students, dear professors, ladies and gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to be here with you today and I would like to warmly thank the former President of the Bundesbank, Jens Weidmann, and Professor Emanuel Monch for their invitation. Lieber Jens, I am very pleased to be with you this evening, albeit in circumstances different from those we have experienced for six years here in Frankfurt, when the alphabetical placement in the Governing Council of the ECB led us to sit almost side by side at meetings. We shared a lot of things, while forging our mutual understanding and, more importantly, our friendship. Tonight, we are on the eve of a monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council and in a "reserve period". In other words, in this speech I will not mention monetary policy. Let me just reiterate that after peaking at 10.6% in October 2022, inflation slowed significantly to 2.4% in the euro area last month1. In hindsight, the euro has proven to be remarkably stable over time, with inflation averaging 2.1% since its introduction in 1999,11 compared with 4.9% in the previous two decades. And the single currency has made it possible to protect the purchasing power of European citizens, which has increased by almost 17% since 1999. The euro inspires confidence, the fundamental value of a currency, and has proved to be a popular success. According to the latest flash Eurobarometer poll, conducted in October, 79% of eurozone citizens (and 80% in Germany) are in favour of the euro, up from 63% a decade ago. The euro represents "Europe in the pocket of the citizens", and the most concrete and advanced form of European integration. This evening, I would like to focus on Europe and the These aspects are particularly close to my heart since I am 100% French, but also 100% from Saarland, where my family has its roots... and, therefore, 100% European. Together with Joachim Nagel, who succeeded Jens as President of the Bundesbank, we recently published a joint op-ed 111 calling for a revival of the European engine, 60 years after the elysee Treaty. And let's be clear: neither Europe nor the Franco-German couple is in the best shape today. European weakness is the result of at least three crises: the geopolitical crisis, obviously, with the return of war on our continent or in its very Middle East. Then there is the democratic crisis: in each of our Western countries, citizens are in distrust, political leadership appears to be diminished, populism is on the rise with each election - including recently in the Netherlands, despite the fact that it is the most successful economy in Europe. And finally, the economic and social crisis: even if we have escaped the black scenario of the European recession, our fellow citizens - starting with the poorest - feel that inflation has severely affected their standard of living. The figures are improving significantly, the negative perception remains. The upcoming European elections in June could act as a revelation of this European crisis, or even as a detonator, according to a more pessimistic view. In every country, the temptation for public opinion, and for each of our weakened governments - starting with the German and French - is to fall back on its own domestic problems , and I do not deny their weight. But I firmly believe that this would be a mistake: the European crisis can only be resolved from the top, and not from the bottom. This is what I would like to develop this evening, in my economic order: (I) because our challenges are more common than ever (II) because we also have the solutions, if and only if we act together. I. Europe must succeed in its three Economic transformations As some of the crises of our recent past  including inflation  gradually fade, let us free ourselves from the tyranny of urgency to better grasp the three structural challenges that lie ahead. They are all of direct importance to you, the younger generation: the transformation of work, and the digital and green transformations. And they all imply less dependence on other continents, and greater reliance on our own resources  let's call it having greater "strategic autonomy" to manage the geopolitical tensions of 2023.  The transformation of work Germany is known for its remarkable employment record: for two decades until 2019, the employment rate grew twice as fast as that of France, for example, leading to a considerable gap. In recent years, however, France has begun to close this gap, thanks to reforms of labour legislation, unemployment insurance and the apprenticeship system. Despite these recent improvements, and the creation of more than one million jobs since the end of 2019, the unemployment rate is still at 7.4%, far from full employment, while recruitment difficulties continue to affect nearly half (45%) of French companies. In order to close this gap, a high priority must be given to the rapid development of skills  especially scientific skills. As you all know, there is a very strong correlation between economic growth and education. In Europe, we have some of the best education structures. However, as the scores of the latest PISA survey published last week show, the Covid crisis has had a negative impact on teaching and performance in many OECD countries: results in mathematics, reading and science have all fallen in Germany and France compared to 2018. But from a long-term perspective, southern Europe  including my country  can draw inspiration from northern Europe, which has generally been able to maintain higher standards of educational achievement. Vocational training is another factor in growth, because the jobs of tomorrow will fluctuate even more than today. Take digital specialists as an example: in 2022, their number stood at 9.4 million, up from 7.8 million in 2019, but still well below our target of 20 million by 2030 Vl. In addition, the transformation of work will increasingly lead to common requirements for our two countries. The first mutation is psychological and managerial. Beyond the necessary collective enrichment through work, we must find the way to enriching work. I do not believe - contrary to what we often hear - that young people - your generation - or Europeans in general, "no longer want to work" after Covid; but let us recognise that Covid has acted as a revealer, and an amplifier, of a change in motivations for work. The popular emergence of teleworking, a great demand for autonomy and professional mobility as well as the strong inspiration for a sense of work are all possible levers: none of them is obvious to employers, but they too will have to change. The second mutation today is the scarcity of the supply of labour, after the era of its excess of high unemployment. European countries will soon be directly confronted with demographic ageing: the tipping point, where the working-age population will start to decline, is expected as early as 2024 in Germany and 2028 in France". This quantitative problem also raises qualitative questions, particularly about how women (and men) can more effectively reconcile their work with other imperatives, drawing on research by Claudia Goldin, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics this year. This transformation of work would be decisive because it would allow Europe to increase its potential growth rate. More broadly, the issue of productivity is once again at the centre, which brings me to our second transformation  digital transformation.  Digital transformation We must catch up technologically with the United States and, now, China as well. In terms of innovation, the number of patents relating to ICT (information and communication technologies) is evidenced, which was almost twice as high in the United States as in Europe between 2014 and 2018. Obviously, all the major Bigtechs are American or Chinese, not European. This is also true in terms of adoption: companies, especially SMEs, tend to have lower levels of digitalization compared to the United States, and thus lower total factor productivity growth. The continuous evolution of new technologies, and in particular the o nntiinllno nn rmiArn o rif i/izl In (IA) m i\/rnn here im ai icco aciuciico ci i 11 ta uci c m iii liiii vc ai 1111 v i c 11 c K 7 / uuvicm as for them new perspectives Vl". Many are concerned about how generative AI will impact certain professions and disrupt labor markets. Indeed, for some tasks, it is likely that AI will allow capital to replace labour in the short term. But AI will boost productivity, thereby lowering the prices of goods and increasing demand. This is why I tend to be a cautious "techno-optimist": the wisest approach, drawn from economic history, is to see AI as a potential new technological revolution traditionally leading to "creative destruction", to quote Joseph Schumpeter, and therefore as an opportunity rather than a threat. It is a question of both regulating AI and developing it, rather than fearing it. The challenge is therefore how we can help European digital services scale up to become global players. A prerequisite for this is the rise of venture capital in the EU, which remains five times less developed than in North America lx  Green transformation We have learned difficult lessons from our past dependence on Russian hydrocarbons: the imperative of strategic autonomy is added to the proven threat of global warming. This means that we need to reduce our consumption of fossil and imported fuels. Europe has made strong commitments in this area, firstly with the ongoing reform of the EU electricity market, which encourages investment in renewable energy through long-term contracts, and secondly with the objective of carbon neutrality by 2050. This path is set out in a very concrete way by the EU's 'Fit for 55' package, which aims to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030. France and Germany obviously share the same objective of a decarbonised, independent and competitive energy mix. But they differ on the means to achieve this: France will not give up nuclear energy and will use renewable energies as a complement, while Germany has begun its definitive exit from nuclear energy. As we will not be able to overcome these differences, we must accept them, rather than export them to the rest of Europe. Achieving a radical energy transformation requires considerable adaptation by all economic agents. The provision of appropriate market incentives is essential. I must remind you here of an economic fact, even if it is politically unpopular: a higher carbon price is essential. Joe Biden's United States has taken a different path: its efforts in terms of regulation and public subsidies - the famous IRA (Inflation Reduction Act) - are going in the right direction, but will not be enough. Whatever form it takes - paid emission allowances, taxation, etc. - carbon pricing should be global - not just national - and socially equitable: Europe must tirelessly advocate for this "new frontier". Carbon pricing is needed to align corporate behaviour, but also to develop private financing, via attractive returns on green investments. This brings me to our shared European solutions. II. Europe has the solutions to rnimrir where 11 imin On the challenges, Europeans are probably in agreement. But when it comes to solutions, a feeling of powerlessness threatens, as Europe is a prisoner of its agendas that are too domestic and too short-termist. This European numbness is all the more unbearable in the face of American speed x , and Chinese assertiveness. But it is by no means inevitable: from the end of the 19th century, Europe has constructed a single political narrative, reconciling economic growth and social justice within a pioneering "European social model" - or " soziale Marktwirtschaft ". The European narrative of the 21st century  for our citizens as well as for the rest of the world  should be to find a way to reconcile growth and sustainability, prosperity and ecology. And to deliver on this promise, I firmly believe that we need to activate the full potential of two powerful economic levers: the Single Market and the Financing Union. (a) The single market The single market is often seen as a thing of the past, a great economic legacy of Jacques Delors. On the contrary, the single market is clearly a subject for the future: it is one of the largest markets in the world, but it has not yet been fully exploited. A deeper single market would make use of the EU's unique combination of innovation and manufacturing production forces, strengthening growth and resilience in a fragmented world. In a recent study, the IMF estimates that reducing internal barriers and frictions, for example by harmonizing taxes and subsidies across countries, would have a significant impact on welfare, in the order of 7 percent of GDP. This would benefit both producing and innovative countries, and countries of the North as well as the countries of the South. On this basis, Gita Gopinath, the IMF's first deputy managing director, made strong recommendations in a recent speech in Berlin . There is indeed a wide scope for greater integration within the EU and, and I quote, "better harmonisation of taxes and subsidies between countries would strengthen investment in cross-border infrastructure and discourage 'state aid' trade-offs". On the contrary, the recent increase in national measures, especially in the face of the energy price shock, risks undermining the single market by giving countries that provide significant fiscal support to their sectors a competitive advantage over other EU countries." I would like to echo this call: the control of state aid in the EU is not a bureaucratic burden; This is an essential condition for achieving a fair and optimal allocation of resources within our single market. It should now be fully reinstated. "The field of decarbonization is the best example of this. In view of the externalities linked to carbon emissions, decarbonisation targets should be set at EU level, rather than at the level of individual Member States, to ensure that efforts are concentrated where marginal abatement costs are lowest in the EU. This will ensure the largest possible emission reductions for a given amount of green investment.
